title: PIA Working: Groups hail NNPCL Boss Ojulari over N7.2tr Profit, N66 fuel discount
body: By John Alechenu, Abuja Civil society groups have scored the Group Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited, NNPCL, Engr. Bashir Bayo Ojulari, high on implementation of the Petroleum Industry Act, PIA. The Parliamentary Support Network and allied groups said Ojulari’s leadership has translated PIA into tangible benefits for Nigerians. Speaking at a press conference in Abuja on Friday, Amb. Muhammad Abdulrazaq and Comr. Adams Umoren, who spoke on behalf of the Parliamentary Support Network and Reformers Network, said the company’s 2025 Audited Financial Statements and the nationwide N66-per-litre petrol discount are concrete proof that the PIA is working. They said, “It is with a deep sense of national pride that we stand before you today. We gather not merely to mark another public engagement, but to reflect on a decisive chapter in Nigeria’s petroleum history -one defined by the bold vision of PIA and determined leadership translating that vision into measurable results.” According to them, the 2025 audited accounts presented to President Bola Tinubu showed Profit After Tax of N7.2 trillion, a 33 percent increase over 2024 despite volatile global prices. Dividends of N5.8 trillion were declared, remittances to the Federation Account rose significantly, and crude and condensate production hit a five-year high of 1.77 million barrels per day. “These numbers represent more money available for roads, schools, hospitals, security, and social programmes that touch the lives of ordinary citizens. They represent a national oil company that is beginning to function as a reliable contributor to the Federation rather than a perpetual source of fiscal anxiety,” they said. The groups said the performance was achieved despite market volatility, downstream deregulation and legacy infrastructure challenges. They singled out the N66-per-litre discount on Premium Motor Spirit introduced at NNPCL retail stations to mark Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary and extended to end of October. The groups stressed the discount is funded from the company’s retail margin, not from the Federation Account. They added, “It is not a return to the old subsidy regime. It is a deliberate act of corporate responsibility that prioritises relief for motorists, transporters and households struggling with cost of living.” The groups also noted progress on gas infrastructure including the AKK pipeline as foundation for industrial growth and power stability. “We recognise that no reform is without challenges. Legacy issues, global market volatility, and the sheer scale of transforming a decades-old institution will continue to test resolve. Yet the direction of travel under Engr. Ojulari is the right one,” they stated in the text of the press conference. They urged sustained focus on production growth, cost discipline, gas commercialisation and transparent governance, while calling on legislators, regulators and industry players to consolidate gains. End Sent from my iPhone The post PIA Working: Groups hail NNPCL Boss Ojulari over N7.2tr Profit, N66 fuel discount appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: AI Is Coming For Every Company, Says Nvidia Boss
body: Artificial intelligence will ultimately become a key aspect of all companies, the head of AI chip giant Nvidia said during a visit to Stockholm, where he urged Europe to ramp up its AI industry. “Every single company will be an AI company eventually. Every single industry will be impacted by AI,” Jensen Huang told an event late Thursday, part of a European tour that includes a Nvidia-hosted conference in Berlin next week. “The important thing for us is to recognise that Europe needs to build out the entire stack,” he said, referring to the AI technology chain from data centres to chatbots and other apps. Speaking later to AFP, Huang said his company had invested $8 billion in Europe over the past year. “We’ve strategically invested in different parts of that ecosystem, really high quality companies that we believe could help lift it, the whole ecosystem in Europe,” he said, citing the British data centre and AI cloud provider Nscale and the Dutch cloud provider Nebius as examples. “In the last one year, we’ve invested $8 billion already. We have another couple of billion dollars in the pipeline,” he added. “We’re helping Europe create the AI ecosystem.” Huang was in Stockholm for the launch of Sferical One, a Swedish supercomputer using Nvidia chips that will keep sensitive Swedish data and expertise in the country. During his visit, Volvo Cars also announced it was expanding its partnership with Nvidia to improve safety technology in its planned self-driving vehicles. AFP The post AI Is Coming For Every Company, Says Nvidia Boss appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Ukraine needs at least EUR 70 bln more for defense next year – Zelenskyy
body:
Ukraine will need at least another EUR 70 billion next year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated, also calling on European leaders to help secure this support.

"The war will cost EUR 155 billion next year. And we need at least EUR 70 billion more from you – for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support," Zelenskyy said addressing the participants of the European Council meeting.

He said that Ukraine stops most Russian assaults on the front line thanks to drones and cuts Russian supply lines with these technologies.

"And our drones are helping to weaken Russia’s economy. Right now, we could produce two or three times more drones – depending on the type. But we simply don’t have enough money for that," the president said.

He urged leaders to invest in Ukrainian defense, as well as in the joint production of drones and other weapons systems in European countries.

title: FIFA sanctions Spain over Islamophobic chants during Egypt friendly
body: By Adegboyega Adeleye Spain have been fined $20,000 and ordered to close at least 15 per cent of their stadium for their next friendly after supporters directed Islamophobic chants at Muslims during a match against Egypt earlier this year. FIFA announced the sanctions on Friday over incidents during the teams’ 0-0 draw at Barcelona’s RCDE Stadium on March 31. Some Spain fans were heard chanting, “Who doesn’t jump is a Muslim,” twice during the World Cup warm-up match. After the second chant, a stadium announcer warned supporters and an anti-discrimination message was displayed on the scoreboard. Spain’s football federation, the RFEF, condemned the chants at the time; coach Luis de la Fuente called them “intolerable”, while Spain winger Lamine Yamal, who is a Muslim, described them as disrespectful and racist. The RFEF argued to FIFA that the word “Muslim” was neither insulting nor pejorative, and that the incident should be assessed under rules covering political, ideological or religious messages rather than those on discrimination. FIFA’s disciplinary committee rejected the argument. It said discriminatory language did not have to include an explicit slur, adding that a term could be discriminatory when used as an insult, taunt or marker of inferiority. Spain must close at least 15 per cent of the available seats for their next friendly, with the closure focused primarily on sections behind the goals. Subject to FIFA approval, the seats may instead be occupied by community or special-interest groups, including families, students and anti-discrimination organisations. The RFEF was also fined $20,000. Spain’s next possible friendly is scheduled for June, but the stadium sanction could be delayed until a free date during next autumn’s Euro 2028 qualifying if Spain reach the Nations League finals. Egypt’s football association condemned the chants as a “repugnant act of racism” but said the actions of a small group of supporters would not harm relations between the two federations. title: Bulgaria Asks NATO for Air Defense After Ship Attack
body:
Bulgaria has asked NATO for aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone equipment and air patrols, Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Oct. 16, as drone strikes on merchant ships creep toward the country’s Black Sea coast.
Stoyanov told reporters that Sofia requested “the entire spectrum of available assets” to show a strong allied presence in the region, according to Bulgarian outlet Novinite .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
He said it is still unclear what help Bulgaria will actually receive.
Stoyanov said Romania and the Baltic states have similar needs, and that defense ministers from Turkey and Romania, along with the chiefs of the general staff of all three countries, are expected to meet soon. He also cautioned that absolute security in the Black Sea cannot be guaranteed, even with allied forces deployed.
Earlier this week, Stoyanov said Bulgaria would deploy two additional drone systems and more missile systems to the Black Sea area, Newsweek reported, citing Bulgarian news agency BTA.
The request follows a turbulent fortnight off Bulgaria’s coast. On Oct. 6, drones hit two commercial ships , the Alfa Watan and the Able, in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew went missing, while the Able’s 18 crew members were rescued. It was the first such attack in the economic zone of a NATO member.
A week later, on Oct. 13, the Ukrainian-owned, Malta-flagged cargo ship Chelsea 3 was hit by three drones roughly 18 nautical miles off the coast near Byala. Its crew survived. Prime Minister Rumen Radev said a second vessel was struck and sunk about 17 nautical miles off the village of Krapets, and Reuters said 11 sailors were missing.
Radev said Bulgaria lacks solid evidence to accuse any specific party but suggested that Russia benefits from the attacks. He summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who said she had no information on Russian involvement and did not rule out a third-party provocation, according to ARY News. Ukraine claims that Russia is responsible.
The Oct. 6 attack came a day after a drone strike sank the Turkish-owned grain ship Royad Mammadov off Romania, killing two crew members. The Romanian Naval Authority said the incident occurred in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, outside its territorial waters.
President Volodymyr Zelensky blamed Russian drones, though Romanian authorities have not officially confirmed a drone strike.
Calls for NATO help are coming from a government that has distanced itself from Kyiv.
Radev, a former president and long-time critic of military aid to Ukraine, won the April 19 parliamentary election in a landslide. On June 9, Stoyanov said Bulgaria would send no more weapons to Ukraine, adding Bulgaria had approved 13 military aid packages since 2022.
On July 14, Radev said Bulgaria would no longer take part in the Coalition of the Willing that seeks to provide postwar security guarantees to Ukraine; he has halted government-supplied military aid since taking office but has not stopped commercial arms sales to Kyiv.
Speaking at the NATO summit in Ankara earlier that month, Radev said Bulgaria had exhausted what it could give from state stockpiles but could still repair Ukrainian military equipment.
Sofia also reportedly vetoed EU sanctions on Patriarch Kirill , the head of the Russian Orthodox Church and a confidant of Russian President Vladimir Putin, and sought the removal of oil billionaire Vagit Alekperov from the lists. Radev argued that religion should stay separate from sanctions policy.
Bulgaria is not a military heavyweight, but it matters to Ukraine for what it can produce.
Because of its communist-era industrial base, it is one of the few countries outside Russia that can produce Soviet-standard munitions, and output surged after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Emilian Gebrev, owner of arms maker Emco and a survivor of two nerve-agent poisonings, said that Russian military intelligence agents repeatedly sabotaged his facilities . Bulgarian prosecutors have charged six officers serving in Russia’s Main Directorate of the General Staff (GRU) in connection with the incidents.
Bulgaria borders neither Ukraine nor Russia, but it holds a strategic position on the Black Sea. With Russia bombing Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, Kyiv increasingly relies on Danube River ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.
Romania’s foreign ministry says, per Maritime Executive , that between 20% and 30% of globally traded wheat and grain transits the corridor. That makes the waters off Bulgaria both a lifeline for Ukraine’s exports and a growing test of whether NATO can protect shipping in its own backyard.
Anastasiia Bzova is journalist covering politics, culture and current affairs. She focuses on delivering accurate, accessible reporting that helps readers understand the issues shaping their opinions.

title: Greece and Germany Put Submarines at the Centre of Defence Talks
body: Germany wants a role in Greece’s next generation of submarines. Defence Minister Boris Pistorius raised the idea of joint work on the advanced Type 212 CD class when he met Greek Defence Minister Nikos Dendias on Wednesday at the Crete Firing Range. The Hellenic Navy’s submarine renewal isn’t expected to be funded until after 2030. Talks on which vessels to choose will only start once Greece’s 2027 national elections are over. Even so, Pistorius suggested the submarines could be built in Greece itself and called the country a “trusted partner.” Dendias said Athens wants closer defence ties with Berlin. He pointed to joint training, hosting German troops, better interoperability between the two militaries, and buying common equipment. He also invited Pistorius to visit Athens officially to keep the dialogue going. The two ministers also covered: Their forces’ shared role in the NATO-led KFOR mission in Kosovo Pilot training at Kalamata Greece’s interest in the IRIS-T SLS air defence missiles recently tested on Crete The post Greece and Germany Put Submarines at the Centre of Defence Talks appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: EU fast-tracks merger of three European firms into one SpaceX rival. It wants to end reliance on US satellites that failed Ukraine this week
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); The EU plans to fast-track antitrust approval for Project Bromo, a satellite venture aimed at reducing Europe's reliance on American space technology, Bloomberg reports . The news comes amid the latest reports that the US administration has switched off Elon Musk's Starlink service to Ukrainian forces amid US President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, according to Reuters. Project Bromo would merge the satellite arms of Italy’s Leonardo and France’s Airbus and Thales into a single European player capable of competing with SpaceX and American and Chinese rivals. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has backed the project, Eunews reports. “These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” she said at an international space summit in Paris last month, citing Bromo by name. A year of quiet groundwork before the filing The partners have been preparing the ground for months. Over the past year, they discussed potential competition concerns with EU officials to resolve them before filing a formal application, according to Bloomberg. The companies have not yet applied, but Brussels expects them to do so in the coming weeks. For large deals, regulators usually hold preliminary consultations to flag obstacles early. If the companies offer concessions, such as selling some assets, the deal could clear after a first-phase review of a little over a month. If competition concerns remain, the Commission could open an in-depth probe lasting several months. The caveat behind the Starlink-rival label The push is part of a wider European scramble for space autonomy. Ukraine is building a satellite system of its own beyond any single company’s control, and France recently poured 1.35 billion euros into the operator Eutelsat. For Ukraine, such systems are indispensable, as Kyiv's operation against Russia's war capabilities relies on them. title: Ghana’s fertility rate too high for development – Reproductive health specialist warns
body: Ghana’s fertility rate is above the level needed to move from low-income to high-income status and the strain is already visible in schools, hospitals and roads, a Reproductive Health Specialist, Dr Godfred Bonnah Nkansah, has warned. Citing the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey, he said Ghana’s current fertility rate, which was 3.9, meant that the average woman was giving birth to about four children. He said evidence showed countries moving from low to high income do best when fertility fell between 2.1 and 2.8 children per woman, which was a level at which families could invest enough in each child for them to become human capital to the nation. “At our current 3.9, we are about 1.1 more than where we are supposed to be. That calls for greater efforts to provide reproductive health education and services to both men and women,” he added. Dr Nkansah said this at a one-day training for journalists focused on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) and responsible reporting organised by the Alliance for Reproductive Health Rights (ARHR). The training formed part of the ARHR’s effort to strengthen informed public conversations on SRHR and support accurate, ethical and evidence-based media reporting. It provided journalists the opportunity to deepen their understanding of key SRHR issues and emerging misinformation and narratives around SRHR and gender. Dr Godfred Bonnah Nkansah, a reproductive health specialist, speaking at the one-day media training on sexual reproductive health organised by Alliance for Reproductive Health Rights Fertility Fertility rate is the number of children a woman will have in her lifetime. The global average is 2.4 children per woman. In sub-Saharan Africa, it is 4.6 children per woman, which implies that the African woman is giving birth to at least five children. Dr Nkansah said the consequences of Ghana’s current fertility rate were far-reaching and already visible, pointing out that educational infrastructure was under immense pressure, as the investments made were struggling to contain the numbers. That, he pointed out, compromises the quality of human capital development in the country. “If you go to health, our hospitals are always overcrowded. The no-bed syndrome is because we have far more people than our current number of hospitals can contain,” he said. He said the growing number of the country’s fertility rate also puts pressure on road infrastructure. Dr Nkansah said without action being taken, poverty would increase, because government would be unable to meet the socio-economic needs of ever-larger numbers of people. He said the message was not a call for a fixed family size but for people to give birth to a number of children they could comfortably take care of. A senior media practitioner, Linda Asante-Agyei, urged media practitioners to use their platforms to educate parents on the need to provide sex education to their adolescent children, stressing that sex education was very important. She also urged them to separate science from the opinions people have about adolescent health and sexual reproduction.

title: 5 things to know about Elon Musk’s new flying car Tesla Roadster
body: By Mmesoma Okafor Elon Musk’s Tesla has unveiled its redesigned Roadster, an electric sports car featuring rocket-inspired technology that allows it to perform brief aerial manoeuvres. The vehicle was unveiled on Thursday, October 15, 2026, at a SpaceX testing facility in McGregor, Texas, where a prototype was shown driving up an inverted ramp, flipping in mid-air and landing with the help of thrusters. Although the demonstration has been described as a flying-car breakthrough, the Roadster’s ability to sustain flight like a conventional aircraft has not been established. Here are five things to know about Elon Musk’s new Tesla Roadster. 1. It uses SpaceX-inspired thrusters to lift off The new Roadster combines Tesla’s electric-car technology with compressed-gas thrusters developed through collaboration with SpaceX, Musk’s aerospace company. During the unveiling, the prototype used the thrusters to flip in mid-air and land. The system uses highly pressurised air rather than conventional rocket fuel to produce thrust. However, the demonstration does not establish that the vehicle can fly over long distances like an aeroplane. 2. Tesla claims it can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in under a second The Roadster is designed to deliver exceptional acceleration alongside its experimental aerial capabilities. Tesla demonstrated a run in which the vehicle reportedly accelerated from zero to 60 miles per hour (approximately 97 km/h) in about 0.8 seconds using its thruster technology. The figure remains a company-reported performance claim rather than an independently verified result for a production vehicle. 3. It comes in three versions Tesla has outlined three configurations of the new Roadster, each designed for a different level of performance. Performance: The road-focused version, featuring active aerodynamics and a suction system designed to improve traction. Thrust: Adds rear-mounted compressed-gas thrusters to enhance acceleration. Rocket: The most experimental configuration, featuring additional thrusters intended to enable aerial manoeuvres. It is designed as a single-seater and is available by invitation. The Rocket version is the closest to what Musk describes as a flying car, but its flight capabilities and practical use remain to be established. 4. Production is targeted for 2028 Tesla first announced the next-generation Roadster in 2017, but the project has faced years of delays. At the October 15 unveiling, Musk said production would begin in 2028. This remains a target rather than a confirmed delivery date, meaning prospective buyers may have to wait longer before the vehicle becomes commercially available. 5. Reservations cost up to $250,000 Tesla’s reservation page listed a $50,000 reservation payment for the Performance version and $250,000 for the Thrust version following the unveiling. The Rocket configuration was listed as invitation-only. These amounts are reservation payments, not confirmed final purchase prices. Tesla has not announced definitive production pricing for all three versions. Questions also remain about the vehicle’s safety, regulatory approval and whether its most ambitious features will be available for ordinary road use. title: Voters more worried about Iran war than immigration or crime: polls
body:
As midterms approach, the conflict and its consequences loom large as campaign issues
As election day nears, two new polls show the Iran war has emerged as one of the most important issues shaping voters’ midterm decisions.
National polls from Fox News and The Associated Press-NORC place the war behind only economy-related issues, government corruption, and health care among voters’ top four concerns.
Significantly, the Iran war has surpassed immigration and crime, two issues on which President Donald Trump performed particularly well in 2024, among voters’ top concerns. In the 2024 campaign, pre - and post -election polling showed those issues as ranking higher as a priority for voters than foreign policy.
The Fox News survey showed 75% of respondents were either “extremely” (42%) or “very” (33%) concerned about the war in Iran. According to the AP-NORC poll , 62% of registered voters named the war as one of the most important issues, and a further 31% said it was “an important issue, but not one of the most important.”
The Fox poll further found that six in 10 voters oppose U.S. military action against Iran, and those voters favor Democratic congressional candidates by 56 points.
Some of the specific economic concerns voters mentioned, including gas prices and the cost of living, have been driven by an energy crisis fueled by disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz , blurring the line between economic and foreign-policy concerns.
Both polls were conducted in roughly the same window. AP-NORC surveyed 1,119 adults, including 925 registered voters, between Oct. 8–12 , with a 3.9-point margin of error, while Fox surveyed 1,202 registered voters Oct. 9–12, with a 2.5-point margin of error.
Many election analysts have compared this midterm election to that of 2006 , when the combination of an unpopular war in the Middle East and economic frustration at home helped deliver that year’s Democratic wave, in which the party gained six Senate seats and 31 seats in the House.
As Jim Antle of the Washington Examiner wrote in RS this week, “today, the public has even less patience for the current war than in 2006.”
In addition to the war’s importance to respondents, the polling also indicates that voters are souring on Trump, and his foreign policy.
The AP-NORC poll shows a mere 33% approval rating for the president’s foreign policy, the lowest that percentage has been across eight polls by the same firm during Trump’s second term. The 35% approval rating for Trump’s foreign policy in the Fox News poll is similarly the lowest recorded by Fox since his return to office.
Republican candidates across the country have certainly noticed. In tight races in Michigan , Maine, Iowa , and elsewhere, Republican nominees have called for a swift end to the war, though some maintain that this can still be accomplished militarily.
In leaked private audio reported by Axios earlier this month, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate, admitted that his campaign’s primary problems were driven largely by the war in Iran and its effect on gas prices.
On Tuesday, Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.), who is running for governor of his state, said it was time to “wrap up” the war.
“The president is doing what he believes is best for the United States of America,” Tiffany said . “What I’m focused on is being the best governor possible in Wisconsin.”

title: Rosatom to deliver electricity to Indonesia from floating power units
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom signed an agreement with Indonesia on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum to supply electricity to the country from floating nuclear power units, a TASS correspondent reports.
Rosatom and Indonesian company PT Pembangkit Listrik Nuklir concluded an agreement to supply electricity to consumers in the North Maluku region (eastern Indonesia) using floating nuclear power units. As part of the project, Rosatom will deliver two PEB-100 floating nuclear power units with a total capacity of 200 MW to provide electricity to the north of Halmahera Island in the North Maluku region.
"I would like to note that this is the world's first export agreement for the supply of electricity from a floating nuclear power unit. I am confident that for the global business community, it will be a striking example of how, with systemic government support, private business can initiate large-scale infrastructure projects in nuclear energy sphere, which are capable of transforming the national economy," Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev said in a comment on agreement signing.

title: NLA/KGL Licence Contract: Why Ghana must reform the law to maximise the state’s benefit
body: The growing debate surrounding the relationship between the National Lottery Authority (NLA) and KGL Technology Limited should not be reduced to a question of whether KGL should or should not operate within Ghana’s lottery ecosystem. This question has become particularly important following President John Dramani Mahama’s directive for a comprehensive review and possible renegotiation of the NLA–KGL agreement. The directive requires examination of the contract’s legal basis, financial terms, revenue-sharing arrangements, fees, commissions, exclusivity provisions, liabilities, transparency, audit rights and other matters affecting the public interest. Where renegotiation is necessary, the stated objective is to secure improved fiscal returns to the State, strengthen governance and accountability, and protect the public interest. The review process has since progressed. In April 2026, NLA Director-General Mohammed Abdul-Salam said the review committee had completed its work and that negotiations were continuing, particularly around improving the State’s share of the revenue. This is an important opportunity. But the review should not end with a better contract. It should also lead to a better legal and financial structure. The more important question is this: Is the current legal and financial structure of the NLA–KGL arrangement the best structure for ensuring that the Ghanaian state receives the maximum possible economic benefit from the country’s lottery industry? If the answer is no, then the conversation should move beyond personalities, political accusations and media controversy and focus on reforming the system. One possible reform deserves serious consideration: amending the law to allow KGL, or any similarly structured private lottery partner, to make its statutory or contractual payments directly into the Consolidated Fund or into a dedicated National Lottery Fund administered under the authority of the Minister for Finance. This would give government greater visibility over the revenue generated, strengthen fiscal accountability and ensure that the state’s share is determined through the appropriate public-finance framework. THE CURRENT ARRANGEMENT DESERVES A SECOND LOOK It is important to acknowledge the current management of the National Lottery Authority for reportedly transferring GHS10 million into the Consolidated Fund out of approximately GHS173 million paid by KGL to the Authority. That development raises an important question. If KGL paid substantial sums to the NLA, but only a comparatively small portion subsequently reached the Consolidated Fund, then the debate should not simply be about how much KGL paid. The bigger question is: How much of the money ultimately reaches the Ghanaian taxpayer? This distinction is critical. Money paid by KGL to the NLA is not necessarily the same as money received by the Government of Ghana. Between the two points, the NLA has operational, regulatory, administrative and other expenditure obligations. The result is that a substantial payment made by a private-sector partner to a public institution may translate into a much smaller amount ultimately transferred to the Consolidated Fund. This is precisely why the current structure deserves examination. WHY SHOULD KGL PAY THE NLA FIRST? The National Lottery Authority was established to regulate, supervise and manage national lottery activities. Under the National Lotto Act, 2006 (Act 722), the NLA has significant operational, regulatory, supervisory and management responsibilities. Section 2(2) establishes the Authority as the institution responsible for conducting National Lotto, while Section 35(1) provides for the Authority’s regulatory, supervisory and management functions. Section 4(1) also provides that a person other than the Authority shall not operate any form of lottery. These provisions establish the NLA as a central institution within the lottery ecosystem. However, regulating an industry and managing public revenue are not necessarily the same function. This is where Ghana may need to rethink the architecture. If KGL’s contractual obligations generate substantial revenue for the state, why should the money first pass through an institution that must subsequently meet its own operational and administrative expenditure before transferring a portion to the Consolidated Fund? A more straightforward structure could be considered: THE PRESIDENTIAL REVIEW SHOULD PRODUCE BOTH A BETTER DEAL AND A BETTER SYSTEM This is where the current review becomes particularly important. The government, NLA and KGL now have an opportunity to reach a sustainable arrangement that recognises the legitimate interests of all three sides. Once the commercial outcome is agreed, the law should be amended where necessary to give that outcome proper legal effect. If the renegotiated agreement establishes a new revenue-sharing structure, the legislation should support it. If the State’s share is to flow directly to the Consolidated Fund, the law should provide a clear legal basis for it. If the NLA’s role changes, the legislation should reflect that. Otherwise, Ghana could end up with a new contract operating under an old legal structure. That would be reform in form, but not necessarily reform in substance. A PROPOSAL THAT DESERVES SERIOUS CONSIDERATION Interestingly, the proposal for a new revenue structure is not simply an argument being made from outside the review process. I am reliably informed that the concept of restructuring the payment mechanism so that the State receives its agreed share more directly was among the proposals put forward by KGL during the review discussions involving the Ministry of Finance and the Attorney-General. If this is ultimately confirmed and incorporated into the outcome of the negotiations, it would be significant. It would mean that the discussion is not simply about increasing the amount KGL pays. It is also about changing the mechanism through which the State receives and accounts for its share. That distinction matters. The objective should not be to create a structure that simply moves more money into the NLA while leaving the same institutional revenue-flow challenges in place. The opportunity is to design a system in which the State’s share is clearly identified, transparently accounted for and paid into the appropriate public-finance system, while the NLA receives the resources it requires to perform its statutory functions. This would also provide an important basis for a possible consensus among the three principal interests involved: Government gets a clearer and potentially stronger fiscal return. The NLA receives predictable funding to perform its mandate. KGL retains a commercially sustainable role and receives a fair return on its investment. That is precisely why the proposal deserves serious consideration as part of the final outcome of the review. But for such an arrangement to be sustainable, the law must be amended to reflect the agreed structure. If the parties agree during the review that the State’s share should flow directly into the Consolidated Fund or another legally established public fund, the relevant provisions of the National Lotto Act and associated regulations should be amended accordingly. Otherwise, the parties could agree to a fundamentally different commercial arrangement while remaining constrained by an old statutory revenue mechanism. The review therefore presents an opportunity not merely to renegotiate the NLA–KGL contract, but to align the contract, the law and Ghana’s public-finance system. This would separate revenue collection from expenditure management . It would also give government a clearer picture of the actual economic contribution generated by the lottery partnership. THE PROBLEM WITH THE CURRENT MODEL The current arrangement potentially creates three different figures: What KGL pays; What the NLA retains and spends; and What ultimately reaches the Consolidated Fund. For the ordinary Ghanaian, however, the third figure is arguably the most important. The public is interested in how much revenue the state ultimately receives and what that revenue is used for. If a company pays hundreds of millions of cedis to a public institution but only a fraction eventually reaches the central government account, there is a legitimate public-finance question that deserves an answer. This does not necessarily mean that every cedi retained by the NLA is wasted. The NLA has legitimate expenses. It has employees to pay, systems to operate, winnings to facilitate, regulatory functions to perform, technology infrastructure to maintain and other institutional obligations. But that is precisely why government should determine, through the normal public-budget process , how much the NLA needs to perform those functions. The fundamental question is whether the NLA should effectively serve as both a major revenue collection point and the institution determining how much of that revenue eventually reaches the central government. WHAT HAPPENS TO THE MONEY BEFORE IT REACHES GOVERNMENT? This is where greater transparency is required. There have been public discussions about NLA expenditure in areas such as operational costs, the Good Causes Foundation, salaries, commissions, payment of winnings through Point-of-Sale terminals and debt servicing. Rather than making unverified accusations, the appropriate response is simple: Let the accounts speak. Government, Parliament, civil society and the media should be able to establish clearly: How much KGL pays the NLA; How much the NLA retains; How much the NLA spends on administration; How much is paid in commissions; How much is spent on technology and technical services; How much is allocated to good causes; How much is paid into the Consolidated Fund; and What economic and social value is ultimately generated for Ghana. If these figures are transparently published, much of the controversy surrounding the arrangement can be resolved through evidence rather than speculation. THE BIGGER PROBLEM MAY ACTUALLY BE THE INFORMAL LOTTERY MARKET There is another issue that deserves significantly greater public attention. If claims that a substantial portion of Ghana’s lottery market is controlled by illegal or unregulated operators are accurate, then the country may be losing significant tax and regulatory revenue outside the formal system. That should concern both the NLA and the Ghana Revenue Authority. An operator that conducts lottery business outside the formal regulatory and tax framework potentially deprives the state of revenue while competing with businesses that operate within the law. The question therefore should not only be: “How much is KGL paying?” It should also be: “How much revenue is Ghana losing from the part of the lottery industry that is outside the formal regulatory and tax system?” That is a much bigger public-interest question. Government should undertake a comprehensive review of the entire lottery ecosystem, including illegal operators, taxation, licensing, commissions, technical-service contracts and the distribution of lottery revenues. COMMISSIONS AND TECHNICAL-SERVICE COSTS ALSO DESERVE REVIEW There have also been concerns about the level of commissions paid to Lotto Marketing Companies and technical-service providers. If substantial percentages of gross revenue are paid as commissions or technical-service fees, government should determine whether those arrangements represent value for money. This should not be treated as an attack on private companies. Private-sector participation is necessary. Technology companies, payment providers, marketing companies and lottery operators can bring investment, innovation, infrastructure and expertise that government may not possess. But every public-private arrangement must ultimately answer one question: Is the state receiving fair value for the economic rights and opportunities being granted? If the answer is yes, the figures should demonstrate it. If the answer is no, the contracts and regulations should be reviewed. KGL’S CONTRIBUTION SHOULD BE RECOGNISED – BUT SO SHOULD THE STATE’S INTEREST The debate about KGL should also recognise the broader economic contribution associated with its operations. KGL has demonstrated the capacity of an indigenous Ghanaian company to develop and operate technology platforms supporting large-scale commercial transactions. Its involvement in the digital lottery ecosystem has created investment, employment, technology and other economic opportunities. That matters because Ghana needs more locally owned companies capable of moving beyond traditional businesses into technology-driven sectors and competing at scale. However, recognising KGL’s contribution does not mean that the company should receive preferential treatment or that government should accept an inefficient financial arrangement. The interests of the private sector and the public purse are not mutually exclusive. The objective should be to create a framework in which: KGL can operate profitably, the NLA can effectively perform its regulatory mandate, and the state receives a transparent and fair return. If KGL has invested capital, developed technology and built operational capacity that the state currently benefits from, those investments should be recognised. At the same time, government must ensure that the economic value generated from the arrangement is distributed in a manner that serves the broader public interest. This is why the debate should focus less on whether KGL should exist within the lottery ecosystem and more on whether the contractual and legal framework governing its relationship with the state delivers the best possible outcome for Ghana. KGL pays the state’s agreed share directly into the Consolidated Fund or a dedicated National Lottery Fund. The Ministry of Finance would then determine, through the appropriate budgetary process, the resources required by the NLA to perform its regulatory and operational responsibilities. This would create a cleaner financial chain: Lottery revenue – State account – Budget allocation – NLA operations rather than: Lottery partner – NLA – NLA expenditure – Balance transferred to state The first model could provide greater fiscal discipline, transparency and parliamentary oversight. WHY THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE SHOULD HAVE A CENTRAL ROLE The Ministry of Finance has responsibility for the management and coordination of the country’s public finances. Revenue belonging to the state should, as much as possible, be captured within the government’s central public-finance architecture. This allows the government to make decisions based on national priorities. If additional revenue becomes available, government can determine whether it should support healthcare, education, infrastructure, youth employment, social protection, debt management or other national priorities. The NLA would then receive an appropriation sufficient to perform its statutory functions. This is not about weakening the NLA. It is about strengthening financial accountability. THE NLA SHOULD FOCUS ON ITS CORE MANDATE The National Lottery Authority has an important statutory mandate. Its priority should be to: regulate the lottery industry; supervise licensed operators; protect consumers; prevent illegal lottery operations; ensure compliance; improve industry standards; ensure transparency in lottery operations; and maximise legitimate revenue available to the state. The Authority should not necessarily be expected to operate as a quasi-treasury for large amounts of public revenue. If the Ministry of Finance receives the state’s share directly, the NLA can focus on the functions for which it was established while receiving the resources necessary to execute them. That creates a clearer institutional division between revenue collection, regulation and expenditure. CONCLUSION: KGL should be allowed, where appropriate and subject to proper contractual and fiscal safeguards, to pay the state’s agreed share directly into the Consolidated Fund or an appropriately established National Lottery Fund. The Ministry of Finance should then determine, through the proper budgetary process, the resources required by the NLA. At the same time, the entire lottery ecosystem should be audited and reviewed — including illegal operators, commissions, technical-service arrangements, taxation, licensing and NLA expenditure. This approach would neither be a favour to KGL nor an attack on the NLA. It would be a reform designed to protect the public interest. Ghana does not necessarily need less private-sector participation. Ghana needs better-structured private-sector participation. The objective should be straightforward: A commercially viable private-sector partner. A properly funded and accountable regulator. And a Ghanaian state that captures the maximum possible value for its citizens. That is the conversation worth having. Nii Amarh Amarteifio Political & Branding Strategist Accra Email: mantsebiniiamarh@gmail.com

title: Nigeria’s metering rate jumps to 63% as unmetered electricity customers drop to 4.7 million
body:
Nigeria’s electricity metering rate rose marginally to 63.1 per cent in August 2026 from 62.4 per cent in the preceding month, helping reduce customers without meters to 4.7 million, according to metering factsheet data published by the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC) on Wednesday.
Metered customers in Nigeria rose from 7,903,819 in July to 8,045,565 in August, a 1.8 per cent increase, the data showed.
However, newly metered customers declined during the period, falling from 159,980 in July to 141,746 in August.
The figures indicate that although metered customers continued to grow, the pace of new installations slowed in August.
The data implies the total number of active electricity customers in the country increased from 12,671,795 in July to 12,749,789 in August.
This represents an increase of 0.6 per cent, or 77,994 customers, in the month.
Arbitrary estimated billing due to metering gaps has been a major challenge in electricity billing in Nigeria over the years.
A significant portion of registered electricity customers in Nigeria lack access to prepaid meters, forcing distribution companies to rely on estimates rather than actual consumption when calculating their bills.
Similarly, poor power supply, driven by infrastructure constraints and frequent grid collapse, continues to undermine reliable electricity supply in the country.
Joseph Tegbe, the Minister of Power, vowed, following his appointment in June, to identify power distribution, metering, transparency, and sub-national participation as key areas of intervention in the industry.
A breakdown of the 11 electricity distribution companies’ (DisCos) performance showed considerable differences in their metering rates.
Eko Electricity Distribution Company recorded the highest metering rate at 89.6 per cent in August, up from 89.3 per cent in July.
Ikeja Electric followed with a metering rate of 87.7 per cent, slightly below the 87.9 per cent reported in July.
Abuja Electricity Distribution Company recorded a metering rate of 82.6 per cent, up from 82 per cent the previous month.
Port Harcourt Electricity Distribution Company also improved its metering rate to 71 per cent in August from 69.6 per cent in July.
Benin DisCo’s metering rate rose from 63.2 per cent to 64.4 per cent, while Ibadan DisCo improved from 58.6 per cent to 59.2 per cent.
Enugu DisCo recorded a metering rate of 52.4 per cent, slightly up from 52.1 per cent in July.
The factsheet showed that Jos DisCo had the lowest metering rate in August at 37.6 per cent, up from 36.5 per cent in July.
Yola DisCo followed at 39.2 per cent, up from 37.8 per cent.
Kaduna DisCo recorded 42.3 per cent, relative to 41.3 per cent in July, while Kano DisCo’s metering rate increased from 41.6 per cent to 42.8 per cent.
The relatively low rates mean many customers served by these companies remain without meters.
The August figures indicate that Nigeria’s electricity metering coverage continues to improve, but progress varies across distribution companies.
While Eko, Ikeja and Abuja have metered more than 80 per cent of their active customers, Jos, Yola, Kaduna and Kano remain below 43 per cent.
The overall increase in metered customers also came alongside a rise in the number of active customers, highlighting the need for distribution companies to sustain and accelerate installations to reduce the metering gap.

title: Don’t Scare Away Electorate Through Violence, Oyo Guber Candidate Warns Politicians
body: Kemi Olaitan in Ibadan The governorship candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Oyo State, Adegboyega Taofeek Adegoke, has admonished politicians and their supporters not to scare away the electorate through thuggery and violence ahead of the 2027 general election. He stated this while speaking with journalists in Ibadan, and calling on the political parties and their candidates to talk to their supporters and followers to allow peace to reign, saying thuggery and violence will scare away voters. He warned that no member of any political party can singlehandedly bring the candidates to government, adding that they will need the people, the electorate to win elections. On Wednesday, members of Accord Party in the state had clashed with some hoodlums at Molete area leading to the death of one person, while many sustained various degree of injuries, a situation which also caused panic among the residents of the area in Ibadan, the state capital. Also, the All Progressives Congress (APC) alleged that their convoy was attacked by thugs in Ibadan a few weeks ago. The Oyo ADC governorship candidate said part of the problem is the high rate of youth unemployment, noting that majority of the state population is made up of youths that are not gainfully employed, promising that if elected governor, he will provide jobs for the youth in the state. He called on all candidates in the 2027 elections in Oyo State to ensure that they maintain and allow peace to reign. He also called on political leaders to measure what they say at the campaigns, saying they should avoid hate speeches but tell people what they want to do and how they want to achieve them. He said: “Anytime I go out for campaign, I don’t go out with thugs. I don’t like violence, I don’t support violence. I preach peace always. “We should talk to our supporters, our followers to allow peace to reign. We should not scare away the electorate because without them we cannot win elections. We cannot win election with our party members alone, we need the people. “If our youth are fully engaged, they will not be available for thuggery and violence. I want to appeal to my colleagues, that we should not allow people to turn Oyo State to an avenue for attacks, an avenue for thuggery, where hoodlums will reign supreme. We don’t want that in Oyo State. “Our campaign should be issue based. We should not incite the people. We should measure what we say. Don’t attack one another. Tell the electorate what you want to do and let them judge you. “That is why I said my agenda is summarised in Nine Points – ‘SOLUTIONS’. So tell people what you want to do and avoid hate speech.”

title: 2027: Tinubu afraid to face Nigerians, has no business seeking re-election — ADC campaign
body: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has accused President Bola Tinubu of being afraid to face Nigerians, saying his reported decision not to campaign across all 36 states ahead of the 2027 election amounts to contempt for the electorate. The council said the move could give its presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, an advantage, arguing that Nigerians deserve a leader willing to defend his record, answer questions and explain his plans for the country. The ADC-PCC Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, stated this while receiving a delegation of youths under the aegis of Young Voters for Atiku (YVA). Ologbondiyan said a president seeking re-election should be prepared to meet voters and account for his performance, rather than rely on official engagements as a reason to avoid nationwide campaigning. “What President Tinubu has done is a clear act of contempt against the Nigerian people. The APC is known for its contempt for Nigerians. How can a man who wants to be re-elected as president, after failing woefully, say he does not want to visit the people he seeks to govern? It is an aberration of norm,” he said. He rejected the argument that official duties could prevent Tinubu from campaigning nationwide, citing former Nigerian presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari, as well as American presidential candidates Donald Trump and Kamala Harris. “Saying that he (Tinubu) will be attending to official assignments is untrue, fake, deceitful and insincere. Didn’t former Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo, Goodluck Jonathan and Muhammadu Buhari attend to official duties while campaigning for their return tickets? Didn’t Donald Trump campaign? Didn’t Kamala Harris campaign? Why is Tinubu’s case different?” Ologbondiyan queried. He further alleged that public anger over hunger, poverty, insecurity and economic hardship explained the president’s reported reluctance to engage voters across the country. “He knows Nigerians are hungry and angry. He knows that the average Nigerian finds it difficult to eat and to be secure. He has failed on all fronts, so he is afraid to face Nigerians. He is running away from the reality he created,” he said. Ologbondiyan urged young Nigerians to reject the APC in 2027, warning that another term for the ruling party would prolong the hardship citizens were experiencing. “I appeal to every young Nigerian to reject them. Let us collectively reject hunger, reject poverty, reject hardship and reject insecurity. The APC has brought only pain to Nigerians. It is time to say enough is enough,” he said. He described Atiku as physically fit and mentally alert, saying the former vice-president was prepared to campaign across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. He also pledged that an ADC government would pursue economic recovery, wealth creation, improved security and better living standards. “Atiku Abubakar will bring back subsidy to reduce cost of petroleum products, create wealth, end hunger in our land, secure our nation and restore our battered economy. He has the experience, the capacity and the compassion to rescue Nigeria. He is fit, ready and prepared to lead Nigeria out of this present predicament,” Ologbondiyan added. The ADC-PCC also claimed that the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council had strengthened its own political standing, alleging that the event attracted no endorsements from ADC members or sympathisers. title: Global crude oil market is not efficient anymore — Russian presidential advisor
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The international oil market has ceased to be efficient but the real war, both economic and political, is waged for it, Advisor to the Russian President Anton Kobyakov said at a press conference during the Russian Energy Week forum.
"The modern oil market is a strange phenomenon. It is far from being the largest segment of the global economy but informationally it is extremely important. It is quite small compared to the debt market, about 100 times smaller, but it is very, very loud and politicized. It has ceased to be efficient - today you need to expend a barrel of oil to extract the same quantity. Yet, a real war is being fought over this market, over oil and its refining. A real war, both economic and political," Kobyakov said.
The Russian Energy Week international forum is being held in Moscow on October 14-16 with the support of the Russian government, the Russian Ministry of Energy, and the Moscow government. Roscongress Foundation is the event organizer. TASS is the information partner of the forum.

title: 'Gas deals will follow' — Zelensky warns Trump could ease more sanctions on Russia
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia risks paving the way for further sanctions relief for Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 16.
Zelensky warned that easing sanctions could eventually lead to the normalization of relations with Moscow, despite Russia showing no readiness to agree to even a ceasefire in Ukraine .
"There's intuition, there's intelligence, and there are various details," Zelensky told reporters in Brussels.
"In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well."
"It will all come down to the banking system, individual people, and the chemical industry."
Zelensky said his main concern was the fate of frozen Russian assets. European diplomats previously told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow was seeking their release from the United States in exchange for agreeing to an energy ceasefire with Ukraine.
"What I consider to be risks are frozen assets," he said. "If I don't defend them, who will do it?"
The deal has strained Ukraine-U.S. relations after Washington unexpectedly announced an arrangement allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelensky criticized the decision on Oct. 9, warning that allowing Russia to export diesel would provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its war.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the moment when we are talking about peace, the U.S. is allowing Russia to export diesel."
Tensions had already escalated after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising global fuel prices, a claim disputed by experts . His administration also threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halted the attacks.
The latest rift follows months of failed attempts to negotiate an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. As diplomatic efforts have stalled, Russia has continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of the coming winter.
Russia offered the United States nothing in return for sanctions relief on diesel.

title: Datacenter industry critical for economy — Russian presidential advisor
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The datacenter industry is vitally important for the economy and the society, Advisor to the Russian President Anton Kobyakov said at a press conference during the Russian Energy Week forum.
"The datacenter industry, as we all see now, is vital for the economy and society. And our partners and competitors, China and the US, are building very, very many of them. The situation where artificial intelligence, although a 'classic bubble' that I note will burst soon due to rising interest rates and the need to convert assets into cash, does not change the fact that by 2030, the AI industry will still consume up to 5-7% of global electricity," he said.
New power generating capacities are also needed for industry, both civilian and military, and for the development of electric transport, Kobyakov added.

title: Global trade not free anymore — Russian presidential advisor
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. It can be stated that global trade is not free anymore, Advisor to the Russian President Anton Kobyakov said at a press conference during the Russian Energy Week forum.
"It is the right time now to develop deep conversion. Taking geopolitical constraints into account also, the real pirate war begin. It can be stated that global trade has ceased to be free," he said.
The Russian Energy Week international forum is being held in Moscow on October 14-16 with the support of the Russian government, the Russian Ministry of Energy, and the Moscow government. Roscongress Foundation is the event organizer. TASS is the information partner of the forum.

title: No prospects for resuming EU-Russia energy cooperation — Russian MFA
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The EU’s anti-Russian stance leaves no prospects for resuming energy cooperation, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told a briefing.
"As for a full-scale resumption of energy cooperation between the European Union and our country, such prospects are currently nowhere to be seen, judging by their statements and actions. Brussels continues to send the exact opposite signals," the diplomat said.
"There are also voices calling on their governments within the European Union to come to their senses and follow the US administration's current steps. However, these voices are facing pressure," she added.

title: Association of Small-Scale Industries empowers trade executives in Bono East with a mentorship programme
body: The Association of Small-Scale Industries (ASSI), in collaboration with the Ghana Enterprises Agency (GEA), has held a mentorship and coaching programme aimed at strengthening the capacity of trade association members in the Bono East Region. Held in Techiman, the event aimed to equip these leaders with the skills needed to foster sustainable business growth and improve workplace performance, bringing together executives from various trade associations across the region, including chairpersons, vice chairpersons, secretaries, and organisers. Speaking at the event, National President of ASSI, Christian Balagi, emphasised the critical need for such interventions. He noted that the programme was tailored to promote personal development, strengthen leadership capacity, and enhance overall workplace efficiency among small-scale industry players. “Small-scale enterprises face a lot of challenges, including access to funding,” Mr. Balagi stated. He therefore appealed to the government to provide increased support to address these financial barriers, which often hinder the growth potential of local businesses. Osman Ibrahim, the Bono East Regional Chairman of ASSI, described the engagement as a critical link in the industrial sector. He highlighted the unique role that ASSI members play in training apprentices who would eventually become master craftsmen. “There should be a healthy link between master craftsmen and their apprentices,” Mr. Ibrahim noted. He further added that the growth and expansion of ASSI and its members would contribute significantly to the growth of the economy and create more jobs for the teeming youth in the region. The collaboration with the Ghana Enterprises Agency (GEA) underscores the government’s commitment to supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). By providing mentorship and coaching, the programme aims to create a ripple effect—empowering executives who will, in turn, mentor their members and apprentices. Participants left the programme with renewed vigour and practical strategies to implement in their respective associations. The initiative is expected to not only enhance the operational efficiency of these trade associations but also contribute to the overall economic development of the Bono East Region and Ghana at large. As the executives return to their various trades, the hope is that the knowledge gained will translate into tangible growth, job creation, and a more robust small-scale industrial sector.

title: Russian diesel fuel production capacity enough for exports — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Russia's diesel fuel production capacity is more than sufficient to supply the domestic market and export deliveries, even taking into account refinery turnarounds, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum.
"Diesel fuel production capacity is twice the demand of the domestic market. It is enough even taking into account maintenance work on individual units; it is enough both to secure the domestic market and to support export supplies in line with the figures we discussed earlier," Novak said.
The figures are slightly lower this year, taking into account the facilities undergoing turnarounds, but overall there is enough fuel for the domestic market and exports, Novak noted. "Any attacks, if they lead to the shutdown of primary equipment for repairs, adversely impact product output," he added.

Delivery estimates for the iPhone Duo slipped into next year in less than an hour after Apple opened preorders for it at 8AM ET on Friday.
At the time of writing we are seeing late January delivery dates for every configuration on Apple’s website . The foldable is slated to launch in stores on October 23rd, and Apple typically reserves some units for in-store availability. So while online orders are delayed, you might be able to get one sooner in-person at an Apple Store.
The long delay could be due to high demand for Apple’s first foldable iPhone , low supply on Apple’s side, or a mix of both. Apple announced the iPhone Duo in September, featuring the shorter passport-style design Samsung introduced earlier this year. The Duo starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model and comes in “star white” and “night sky.” You can still preorder it on Apple’s website, but you might be in for a long wait before you get to unfold it.

title: US military’s shortage of missile defense munitions to persist until at least 2030 — TV
body:
NEW YORK, October 16. /TASS/. The US military is facing a critical shortage of missile defense munitions, and the shortfall is expected to continue for another five years, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter, CBS News reported.
According to the report, inventories of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles are expected to remain at critically low levels until 2030 due to shipments to Ukraine and the depletion of arsenals in the Middle East. It noted that during the Iran hostilities, the US military had expended up to 61% of its pre-war stockpile of PAC-3 missiles and approximately 82% of its THAAD interceptors, while new contracts take between 3.5 and 4.5 years to fulfill.
According to CBS News, defense contractor Lockheed Martin unveiled a plan to quadruple annual THAAD interceptor production from 96 to 400 units. US officials and industry experts estimate that even if no additional munitions are used, it will take at least five years to replenish stockpiles to December 2025 levels due to limited production capacity.

title: “Be’sat Equality, Sincere Assistance Maneuver” in Tehran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – The “Equality, Sincere Assistance Maneuver”, featuring acts of faithful assistance, the distribution of livelihood foodstuff packages, and provision of dowry items was held in Tehran on Friday.
