title: Around one fifth of Western firms left Russia, those remaining operate responsibly
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. About 80% of Western companies that were present on the Russian market before the onset of the special military operation continue their operations in the country, behaving as conscientious and socially responsible business entities, Russian presidential commissioner for the protection of entrepreneurs' rights, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP) Alexander Shokhin said in an interview with TASS.
"We see a lot of pressure both from parent companies and official structures, urging them not to draw too much public attention to their presence in Russia. Indeed, many companies have stayed. Some 15-20% of companies have left, while the rest have remained and are behaving as conscientious employers and socially responsible businesses. <…> Moreover, they realize that they must abide by certain rules of the game, such as demonstrating social responsibility, paying taxes, and complying with other legal requirements, so that they wouldn’t be relegated to the category of entities temporarily managed by Russian executives," Shokhin said.
However, Western businesses understand the threat of retaliation from Russian authorities, he added. "The more sanctions packages the European Union or other countries impose, the more vulnerable they become, because they realize that many of those decisions are based not on economic or other criteria, but rather on geopolitical ones and the principle of reciprocal action. We understand that a complete mirror-like response is hardly possible. They impose sanctions, but it is difficult for us to impose sanctions on those who do not do business with us. Therefore, so to say, those who work conscientiously end up on the front line, forced to answer ‘for the other guy’ sitting in the State Department or the European Commission," the RSPP chief explained.
The Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs is also subject to Western sanctions, he noted. In particular, Shokhin cited the US State Department’s wording that the RSPP is subject to sanctions because it brings together executives and major companies that make a significant contribution to strengthening the country’s budget, its technological development and defense capabilities.
"We don’t dispute this. Moreover, we consider it positive that the US State Department recognizes us as the country’s leading business association. After all, we aren’t being accused of, say, any kind of unscrupulous conduct, but we are being accused precisely of doing what we were created to do. This means we are performing our functions well. Nevertheless, for our partners, caution certainly wouldn’t hurt," he stressed.
Shokhin expressed confidence that Western businesses would be represented at the Russian Industrialist forum in St. Petersburg scheduled for October 22-24. "However, we see that companies sometimes feel uncomfortable joining our platform, partly because the RSPP, as an association of employers, is under sanctions," he concluded.

title: PTDF Reaffirms Continuous Funding For Research Projects in Varsities
body: Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City The Executive Secretary, Petroleum Technology Development Fund (PTDF), Prof. Shua’ibu Shehu Aliyu, has reiterated the Fund’s commitment to strengthening research, innovation and human capital development in Nigerian universities. The secretary said the PTDF seeks not only to support academic excellence but also to promote researches that address real national and industry challenges. Prof Aliyu, who made this assertion at the University of Benin, Benin City, during PDTF Professional Chair in Renewable Energy: Close Out ceremony on Thursday, noted that as Nigeria’s energy landscape continues to evolve, there is a growing need for research institutions to develop practical and commercially viable solutions in renewable energy and other emerging technologies. Aliyu, who was represented at the occasion by Ereh Iyalla, Head Gas Division, PTDF, asserted that the seminar theme – Agrowaste to Fuel: Biodiesel Development, Opportunities and Challenges for Youth Employment to the 21st Century – was timely and highly relevant to Nigeria’s quest for sustainable energy, environmental protection, economic diversification and youth employment. The paper was delivered by Chairholder, Prof. Kensington Obahiagbaon. Aliyu noted that: “The focus on converting agricultural waste into biodiesel demonstrates the potential of research and innovation to transform challenges into opportunities. Beyond providing an alternative energy source, such innovations can support waste management, entrepreneurship, local technology development and employment opportunities for young Nigerians. He stated further that: “As Nigeria’s energy landscape ontinues to evolve, there is a growing need for research institutions to develop practical and commercially viable solutions in renewable energy and other emerging technologies. “We therefore encourage researchers to ensure that reseach outcome move beyond academic publications to technology development, demonstration, industry adoption and commercialization.” Prof Obahiagbaon, a professor of chemical engineering, in his presentation, noted that the global dependence on fossil diesel has created twin problems of gas emissions and energy insecurity. According to him, global energy crisis, climate change, and waste management burden have made agro-waste to fuel a critical pathway for the 21st century, adding that using agro-waste as biodiesel feedstock is a core principle of the circular economy. “It converts a liability into an asset: waste becomes fuel, and waste management becomes a revenue stream.” Speaking on the challenges and future direction of biodiesel development in Nigeria, Obahiagbaon said feedstock availability and cost, ensuring a stable and affordable supply remain crucial. He advocated the development of sustainable standard for biodiesel production. The Vice Chancellor, University of Benin, Prof. Edoba Omoregie (SAN), in his opening remarks, noted that in the past six years of your existence of the chair, it has proven to be a start-up for the institution. “We will continue to partner with graduates in every field of study.” According to him, everyone knows the importance of renewable energy. “We are involved in this effort to try to draw attention to renewable energy as a major finding source of energy. Because of the problem of climate change, we know that it is worth looking at renewable energy sources to be able to mitigate the impact of climate change.”

title: Cross River Secures $20m Investment for 4,000-Hectare Oil Palm Plantation
body: Funmi Ogundare The Cross River State Government has signed a concession agreement with ValueFronteira Limited for the development of a 4,000-hectare oil palm plantation in Ijiegu Yache and adjoining clans in Yala Local Government Area of the state, with the investor committing more than $20 million to the project over five years. The project, which is expected to create thousands of jobs and boost agricultural production in six clans including Ijiegu, Wonye, Uchu, Ichui, Ukani and Ewor, is part of the state government’s agricultural transformation agenda aimed at strengthening food security, promoting rural development and improving livelihoods. Speaking at a stakeholders’ meeting and site handover ceremony held in Ijiegu Yache, Cross River State, the Managing Director of ValueFronteira Limited, Maurice Ekpong, explained that the organisation would invest over $20 million within five years to establish the plantation. He stated that the project would generate thousands of employment opportunities and significantly transform the economies of the host communities and Cross River State. Ekpong’s announcement was welcomed by traditional rulers, community representatives, youths and women leaders, who expressed optimism that the investment would create jobs, particularly for young people, while improving economic activities and livelihoods across the communities. The Clan Head of Wonye, HRH Mohie Damian Ododo, described the project as a dream come true, pledging the collective support of the clan heads for its successful implementation. He also affirmed ValueFronteira as a corporate member of Yache land. Other traditional rulers and representatives at the event included HRH Mohie Isaac Omaji, Clan Head of Ijiegu; HRH Mohie Innocent Okaiiba Aji, Clan Head of Ichui; HRH Mohie Ogar Idazor, Clan Head of Ukani; Augustine Obozor, representing Ewor Clan; and Pius Idagu, representing Uchu Clan. In his remarks, the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor and Director-General of the Bureau of Public Private Partnerships, Dr. Francis Ntamu, assured stakeholders that the concession process was transparent and competitive, leading to ValueFronteira’s emergence as the preferred investor. He disclosed that the project had received the full approval of the State Executive Council (SEC), adding that: “It aligns with the government’s drive to attract investment and strengthen critical sectors of the economy.” He expressed the state government’s hope that the investment will contribute to positioning Cross River as a major agribusiness destination in Nigeria, while supporting its broader objectives of food security, rural development and economic empowerment. “The development is expected to expand commercial agricultural activities in Yala, create employment opportunities and stimulate economic growth in the host communities,” Ntamu stressed. The government delegation also included the Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Environment and Solicitor-General of the state, Rosemary Onah, and Brian Ugbe, a Director in the Ministry of Agriculture, who represented the Commissioner for Agriculture.

title: AMA evacuates refuse along Graphic Road, warns against indiscriminate dumping
body: The Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) has evacuated heaps of refuse illegally dumped along Graphic Road to improve sanitation and maintain a clean and healthy environment across the metropolis. The refuse, which had been collected into sacks and abandoned along the roadside by unidentified persons, had accumulated at the location, creating an unsightly environment and posing potential public health risks to residents, pedestrians, and motorists. The evacuation exercise, supervised by the Metropolitan Coordinating Director, Mr Douglas N.K. Annoful, also saw the removal of a structure put up by a mentally challenged woman on a portion of the pavement in the area and formed part of the Assembly’s ongoing sanitation interventions aimed at preventing the accumulation of waste along major roads, streets, and other public spaces within its jurisdiction. Mr Annoful, who was accompanied by the Director of Waste Management, Engineer Prosper Kotoka, and the Director of Finance, Mr Abeeku Amissah, inspected the affected area and supervised the removal of the refuse to restore cleanliness and improve environmental conditions. Head of Public Affairs, Mr Gilbert Nii Ankrah addressing the media expressed concern about the indiscriminate dumping of refuse, stressing that such practices undermined the Assembly’s waste management operations, while placing an additional burden on public resources that could otherwise be directed towards other essential services. He appealed to members of the public to support its sanitation efforts by reporting individuals caught dumping refuse indiscriminately along streets, roadsides, drains and other public places through the Assembly’s See Something, Say Something WhatsApp reporting channel. (0544 914 628). He noted that timely reports from residents with the location of illegal dumping activities and other available evidence would facilitate investigations. He said that public participation remained critical to the success of its 24-hour waste collection operations and broader efforts to address sanitation challenges across the metropolis. He reiterated the Assembly’s commitment to strengthening waste collection services, particularly through its ongoing 24-hour waste collection exercise, which was intended to ensure timely evacuation of refuse and prevent waste accumulation at unauthorised dumping sites. He assured that the Assembly would continue to intensify public education, monitoring and enforcement activities to discourage indiscriminate waste disposal and promote compliance with sanitation by-laws. He reaffirmed the AMA’s commitment to ensuring that Accra remained clean, safe and healthy, while urging residents, traders, businesses, and other stakeholders to cooperate and adopt responsible waste disposal practices.

title: Zelensky explains how Ukraine uses Starlink to intercept Shahed drones
body:
According to him, after Starlink’s performance was reduced, the Ukrainian military lost the ability to intercept some of these targets.
He made this announcement during a press conference in Brussels, according to Ukrinform.
“We sometimes imagine that Starlink is used by the Armed Forces of Ukraine to carry out precision strikes. No. We do not use Starlink to attack or respond within the territory of the Russian Federation. That is precisely why we appealed to SpaceX and the White House to grant us this capability. If we had it, we wouldn’t have had to ask,” Zelensky said.
He explained that Ukraine uses Starlink to operate interceptor drones that destroy “Shahed” rockets attacking the civilian population, and called the speed restrictions on the system an unpleasant and dangerous surprise.
“That’s why they didn’t shut down Starlink, but reduced its speed, and when they reduced the speed, we were unable to shoot down a certain number of ‘Jet-Shaheds.’ This is very unpleasant. We were unable to use it [the tool] to protect the population. This is very painful and unpleasant. The ‘Jet Shahids’ were traveling at speeds of over 400 km, but they reduced our speed to 70…,” the President said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov, a special advisor to the President on technological issues, stated that SpaceX imposed speed limits on Starlink terminals while in motion overnight, and the Ukrainian Defense Forces did not receive any warning.
A source in the Ministry of Defense also reported that the Starlink operational restrictions detected overnight complicated the work of unmanned systems , logistics, and the Defense Forces’ “middle strike” operations.
In addition, the President’s special advisor on technology, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, emphasized that by limiting the operating speed of Starlink terminals, SpaceX is effectively depriving Ukraine of the ability to defend itself against “Shahed” drones.

title: NGX Group, Partners Advance Cross-Border Investment Collaboration Through Dangote Refinery Offer in Egypt, Ethiopia
body: Nigerian Exchange Group Plc (NGX Group) and its partners are advancing cross-border investment collaboration among African capital markets, with engagements in Cairo, Egypt and Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, exploring how market infrastructure and institutional partnerships can improve investment access across the continent. Using the Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE offer as a practical context, the discussions focused on connecting investors across jurisdictions and mobilising African capital for industrial development. Held on Thursday, the engagements were hosted in Cairo by the Egyptian Exchange (EGX), in collaboration with the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), and in Addis Ababa by the Ethiopian Securities Exchange (ESX). They brought together exchange leaders, financial institutions and other capital market stakeholders to explore practical approaches to improving market connectivity, broadening investor participation and mobilising African capital for productive investment. Speaking during the discussions, Group Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of NGX Group, Temi Popoola, emphasized the importance of addressing longstanding structural barriers that limit investment flows across African markets. He noted that the continent possesses substantial pools of institutional capital, but stronger market infrastructure and cooperation are needed to connect these resources with investment opportunities across national borders. “Africa has substantial capital within its own markets, particularly across pension funds and insurance companies. The challenge is how to connect that capital to investment opportunities across the continent. The Dangote Refinery offer provides a practical opportunity to address some of the infrastructure barriers to cross-border investment. Beyond a single transaction, it is about creating connections that enable African capital to finance African growth,” Popoola said. President and Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, highlighted the refinery as an example of the scale of industrial investment required to strengthen Africa’s productive capacity, reduce dependence on imports and support long-term economic growth. He emphasised the importance of developing stronger channels through which African capital can support major industrial projects across the continent. He also commended NGX Group for its role in bringing African exchanges together around the initiative and acknowledged the participating exchanges for their collaboration. Group Chairman of NGX Group, Alhaji Umaru Kwairanga, stressed that lasting progress would depend on sustained institutional cooperation and the development of market infrastructure that makes cross-border investment more accessible and efficient. “Our task is not simply to collaborate around one offer, but to develop lasting partnerships that support cross-border investment and capital formation across Africa. This requires cooperation among exchanges, regulators, financial institutions and businesses, alongside investment in the infrastructure and technology that make participation more accessible,” Kwairanga said. At the Cairo engagement, Executive Chairman of the Egyptian Exchange, Omar Radwan, highlighted the potential for instruments such as Egyptian Depositary Receipts (EDRs) to provide a channel through which Egyptian investors could access selected African businesses. He expressed EGX’s readiness to work with Dangote Industries to explore a possible framework for such an arrangement. President and Chairman of Afreximbank, Dr. George Elombi, reaffirmed the bank’s longstanding financing relationship with Dangote Industries and its commitment to supporting African industrial development. He highlighted the importance of mobilising African investment towards enterprises capable of contributing to the continent’s economic transformation. In Addis Ababa, discussions focused on expanding investment opportunities for Ethiopian investors and strengthening Ethiopia’s participation in Africa’s evolving capital market landscape. Chief Executive Officer of ESX, Yodit Kassa, welcomed the engagement, noting its significance for Ethiopian investors and the country’s growing capital market. “The Dangote Petroleum Refinery offer represents an important opportunity for Ethiopian investors to participate in the growth of one of Africa’s leading industrial enterprises. It also reflects the growing confidence in Ethiopia’s capital market and our readiness to work with leading institutions across the continent,” Kassa said. The Cairo and Addis Ababa engagements followed earlier stops at the Nairobi Securities Exchange and the Botswana Stock Exchange, extending discussions on cross-border investment across multiple African markets. The discussions also highlighted the practical requirements for cross-border participation, including regulatory recognition, distribution, investor verification, settlement, custody and access to reliable information. The offer provides a real-world opportunity for exchanges, regulators, intermediaries and financial technology platforms to address these considerations and explore workable solutions within their respective regulatory frameworks. For participating markets, it also raises the question of how local savings can be channelled more efficiently into productive enterprises across the continent. NGX Group remains committed to working with partner exchanges and financial institutions to strengthen market infrastructure, expand cross-border investment access and advance collaboration among African capital markets, contributing to the continent’s long-term economic and industrial development.

title: Beyond the NYSC Camp: Cross River’s rot, the locust years, and the demands of recovery
body: Joseph Odok The outrage over the dilapidated National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) Orientation Camp in Obubra is justified and overdue. Corps members have endured crumbling hostels, inadequate water, failing sanitation and facilities so degraded that the NYSC leadership has threatened or moved to suspend further postings. Capacity has collapsed from roughly 2,500 per stream to little more than 1,000, with hundreds seeking relocation. The state government’s swift decision to shut the camp for comprehensive overhaul and temporarily relocate orientation exercises to the University of Education and Entrepreneurship in Akamkpa is the correct, responsible response. Yet the camp is merely the most visible tip of a much larger iceberg of institutional and infrastructural decay that accumulated over years of announcements without delivery.​ That decay did not begin in 2023. It was deepened, accelerated and normalised during the eight years of Benedict Ayade’s administration. Those were the locust years: budgets of kinetic crystallisation, quabalistic densification, olimpotic meristemasis and quantum infinitum that promised first-world transformation while delivering near-zero performance. Signature projects (the Bakassi Deep Seaport, an international airport, Super High way, dozens of factories) were commissioned on billboards, in television studios and newspaper pages far more often than they appeared as functioning realities on the ground. Of the much-trumpeted 38 factories, the overwhelming majority remained empty shells or stalled constructions years later. Tinapa, once a bold statement of ambition, was left to weeds and debt. The civil service grew demoralised; promotions stagnated for years; morale sank. Critical maintenance (desilting of drainage channels, upkeep of fire service assets) was neglected. Fire vehicles fell into disrepair or were effectively lost to the system without adequate replacement; today’s limited operational capacity is the product of remedial effort.of Governor Bassey Otu not inheritance.​ Floods and erosion that now regularly embarrass the state are not acts of God alone. They are the predictable consequence of years in which systematic desilting and drainage maintenance received deaf ears. The same pattern held for roads, erosion-control sites and public institutions. Projects were announced with fanfare and then left to rot or to the mercy of contractors who delivered substandard work. Most road were rather painted with tar and not asphalt and they decayed within time frame of their construction. Yala became a home of dust, Obudu and Bekwara roads are still a consequence of Ayade’s mess. Major parts of CRS were disconnected from the national grid with many communities no longer having access to electricity on a phantom promise of power plant that were nothing but avenue to loot the state. The cost of destruction is always lower than the cost of rebuilding. Cross River is still paying that price. Those who raised these issues during the Ayade years were not always celebrated as patriots. Some were treated as enemies of the state. Critics faced arrest and prolonged detention on inflated charges. I spent 117 days in custody for the offence of speaking uncomfortable truths. Many residents, conditioned by the politics of “food on the table” and praise-singing, dismissed such criticism as personal hatred. Today some of the same voices who once defended or ignored the rot have discovered sudden rage against Governor Bassey Otu. The injustice lies less in the existence of legitimate impatience than in the selective amnesia that denies the scale of what was inherited and the direction of the current recovery effort. A government reflects the mood of its people. Years of applause for grandiose budgets and digital inauguration ceremonies helped produce the decayed Cross River we now inhabit. The emerging public consciousness that refuses to allow leaders to sleep is healthier for democracy. It is already yielding concrete results. The rapid government intervention on the NYSC camp is one. The handling of the Denis Odama matter (where the governor directed the withdrawal of a complaint initiated by aides and secured the critic’s release) is another signal that this administration can still distinguish between accountability and vengeance. Ongoing desilting exercises, efforts to restore fire service capacity after long neglect, recovery of Tinapa from years of limbo, road works across several corridors, and attempts to stabilise a demoralised civil service form part of a policy direction of recovery, consolidation and gradual development. These efforts sit on the foundation left by earlier administrations, including those of Duke and Imoke, and seek to reverse the damage of the intervening locust years. None of this excuses slow delivery or substandard remedial work. Cross Riverians are right to demand higher standards. More federal transfers and improved revenue create an opportunity, yet the accumulated rot far exceeds what any single budget cycle can erase. Governor Otu must recognise the impatience of a people who have waited too long. He must cut waste deliberately, communicate more transparently about the use of public funds, and ensure that rehabilitation meets acceptable quality thresholds. Accountability and openness are not optional extras; they are the only durable foundation for the recovery agenda. It is easier to destroy than to rebuild. The present outrage, if channelled constructively rather than as selective bitterness, can accelerate the rebuilding. Cross River deserves leaders who treat criticism as feedback rather than treason, and citizens who remember how the rot was allowed to deepen. The NYSC camp is a symptom. The cure requires sustained vigilance, honest reckoning with the past eight years of non-performance, and a government that matches the people’s rising expectations with visible, measurable, transparent action. That is the standard against which recovery must be judged. . Dr Joseph Abang Odok, a Senior Lecturer, a Social Change Agent, a Lawyer and a Philosopher, writes from Lokoja

title: 2027: DLA governorship candidates back Tinubu, rule out defection
body: By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Governorship candidates of the Democratic Leadership Alliance DLA have endorsed President Bola Tinubu for re-election in 2027, saying their party has no presidential candidate. This was as they however ruled out defecting to the ruling All Progressives Congress APC. The Independent National Electoral Commission INEC had just days ago published Mr Adebisi Moses Olusoji as the presidential candidate of the party, but the governorship candidates on Friday declared that the DLA has no standard bearer. The candidates, who spoke under the Forum of Governorship Candidates of DLA, said they would use their grassroots structures to secure the President’s victory. The forum, led by its Chairman and the party’s Taraba State governorship candidate, Hon. Aboki Bayonga, announced the decision at a press conference in Abuja on Friday. He said the candidates would work with Arewa for Asiwaju (A4A) to mobilise support for the President. “As the Forum of Governorship candidates of DLA, we are here today declaring our support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu as our Presidential candidate in 2027,” Bayonga said. “Not that we have dropped our aspirations under our own platform. But as for the presidential, we are for Asiwaju 100%. We will work for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to come back. We will do everything possible to make sure that Asiwaju is back 2027.” The candidates said their support for Tinubu was strictly for the presidential election and would not affect their ambitions to contest governorship, senatorial, House of Representatives and state House of Assembly seats on the DLA platform. Bayonga said the endorsement followed consultations among party members, who agreed to back Tinubu because the DLA had no presidential candidate of its own for the 2027 election. He stressed that the decision was not an abandonment of the party. Other governorship candidates present included the Secretary of the Forum, Alhaji Adamu Idrisu Chado (Kaduna); Hon. Bekky Folorunso James (Osun); Prof Valdya Tame (Adamawa); Hon. Ibrahim Musa (FCT); Hon. Sam Umar (Plateau); Alhaji Sani Mohammed (Gombe); Hon. Nnamdi Ugwu (Enugu); and Hon. Brent Micheal (Bauchi). Explaining the decision, Bayonga said: “There are so many reasons for our decision, but time will not permit us to sit down and mention them, but if I can mention a few, like the NELFUND [Nigerian Education Loan Fund] that place our children, whether you pay them school fees, you don’t pay their school fees, they depend on themselves. “In terms of agriculture, recently trailers of fertilizers were moving around the country, and they would give you a fertilizer and add you 50,000. It helped the farmer, especially those at the rural area. “Again, in terms of road construction, you can see what the president is doing concerning road network. He is making a solid road that in years to come, those roads will still be permanent.” He said the forum also compared the presidential candidates before reaching its decision. “And for us, because we don’t have a presidential candidate, but apart from that, we look at all the presidential candidates, we say, look, you cannot leave opposition and go and join opposition. You will not succeed. Therefore, looking at all of them, we compare them, we find out that, the present government have a lot of things that if given another four years, he will achieve them, and Nigeria will be better.” Bayonga said a single term might not be enough to complete programmes that require long-term planning and funding. “We want continuity. Four years is not enough to complete every programme, especially projects that require long-term planning and funding,” he said. Asked whether the endorsement had the approval of the DLA national chairman and other governorship candidates of the party, Bayonga said: “Yeah. I am the chairman of the forum of governorship candidates of DLA. And you can see all of us are here. And we agree, and we had a meeting, general meeting yesterday. We agreed upon what we are doing here.” He said the candidates assessed the political situation and the options available before concluding that Tinubu deserved another four years to consolidate his administration’s programmes. Bayonga expressed confidence that their political networks and relationships with voters in their states would help mobilise support for the President, arguing that grassroots influence was not determined solely by party affiliation. According to him, many of the candidates were politically active before joining the DLA and had built relationships with their communities, which they intended to deploy for Tinubu’s re-election bid. On concerns that a second term could lead to a life presidency, Bayonga dismissed the possibility, insisting that the office remained subject to constitutional provisions and the will of Nigerians. “The presidency belongs to the Nigerian people. Nobody owns it, and nobody can remain there beyond what the Constitution allows,” he said. The post 2027: DLA governorship candidates back Tinubu, rule out defection appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Abu Dhabi launches TAMM Global to export AI-powered government services worldwide
body: Abu Dhabi has established TAMM Global, a new company that will export the emirate's AI-powered unified government services platform to international markets. The Department of Government Enablement – Abu Dhabi (DGE) announced the creation of the company under the directive of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council. TAMM Global will develop, manage and deliver an integrated system of digital government services, owning and operating specialised digital platforms while holding the associated intellectual property rights. Ahmed Al Kuttab, chairman of DGE, said TAMM had become an integral part of how people and businesses interact with government since it was launched in 2005. “Through the announcement of TAMM Global's establishment, we are building on that success by making capabilities developed and proven effective and efficient in Abu Dhabi available to governments seeking to deliver better outcomes for their people,” Mr Al Kuttab said. The platform currently brings together more than 1,200 public and private-sector services through a single digital gateway, saving each user about nine visits to government service centres per year – equivalent to an estimated 12 hours annually. Customer satisfaction has risen to 94.5 per cent, up from 78 per cent in 2022, before artificial intelligence was integrated into the platform, while the cost of providing services has fallen by 30 per cent. As an independent private-sector company, TAMM Global will team up directly with governments, organisations and institutions worldwide, licensing the platform's architecture and implementation methodologies. Governments will be able to adapt prebuilt services and digital capabilities to their own legal and regulatory frameworks, enabling faster deployment without replicating every stage of development. TAMM's international standing has grown considerably in recent years. In 2025, it was named the world's best e-government initiative at the UN-backed World Summit on the Information Society Prizes, and this year won the Government category across Europe, the Middle East and Asia in the Gartner Eye on Innovation Awards.

title: STC interdicts driver over Pokuase overtaking incident
body: Intercity State Transport Coaches Limited (STC) has interdicted a driver captured in a viral social media video allegedly making contact with a Sprinter bus during an overtaking manoeuvre at Pokuase before driving away from the scene. In a public notice issued on Friday, October 16, the company said the driver had been identified and interdicted pending the outcome of an investigation and the disciplinary process. Management said it had commenced an immediate investigation into the incident and was awaiting an official report from the Pokuasi Police Command to help establish the facts. The video shows an STC bus attempting to overtake a Sprinter bus before making contact with it and leaving the scene. STC described the driver’s conduct as unacceptable, stressing that it did not reflect the safety standards and professionalism upheld by the company. The management said it was treating the incident seriously and would take appropriate action after the necessary investigations and disciplinary processes. It also reaffirmed its commitment to passenger safety and responsible road use, thanking members of the public for bringing the incident to its attention.

title: Ekumfi: How $6m EXIM participation built a $53m industrial asset — now poised for a 24-Hour Economy breakthrough
body: Ghana’s industrialisation journey may be entering a defining chapter. Ekumfi Fruits & Juices Limited is emerging as a potential model for turning development-finance investment into agricultural prosperity, youth employment, industrial expansion and export growth. With Ghana EXIM Bank participation — its existing credit now restructured to approximately US$6 million — Ekumfi has built an industrial enterprise with an estimated asset value of US$53 million — a modern fruit-processing facility, Ghanaian juice brands, and a foundation for international market expansion. Yet this substantial investment has lived with a contradiction. Despite significant processing capacity, the company has been constrained by inadequate supplies of pineapple and other fruits, and by the 20% excise duty imposed on locally manufactured fruit juices in 2023. At times, production has been limited to roughly two days a week, leaving equipment and infrastructure underused. The cost reaches well beyond the company. Farmers lose an established industrial buyer. Young people miss employment and enterprise opportunities. Ghana loses manufacturing output and export earnings. Ekumfi’s challenge has never simply been the existence of a factory. It has been building the agricultural and financial ecosystem needed to keep that factory running at its potential. Today, the government’s excise reforms, the Feed the Industries Programme and the 24-Hour Economy agenda create an opening to address those structural constraints. The Excise Duty Removal Creates a New Opening Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson announced the abolition of the 20% excise duty on locally manufactured fruit juices in the 2026 Mid-Year Budget Review on 23 July. The exemption, enacted under the Excise Duty Act, 2026, took effect on 1 October 2026. For Ekumfi, the change can improve price competitiveness, strengthen operating margins, stimulate consumer demand and free up room for reinvestment in agricultural production. But removing the tax solves only one side of the industrial equation. The more fundamental challenge is raw material. A processing plant cannot run three shifts a day when its agricultural supply chain supports only a fraction of installed capacity. This is where Feed the Industries becomes decisive. Feed the Industries: Linking Ghana’s Farms to Its Factories The Feed the Industries Programme, under the 24-Hour Economy framework, is designed to connect agricultural production directly to industrial demand. For Ekumfi, that means a coordinated fruit-supply system drawing on commercial estates, smallholder farmers, youth agricultural enterprises, out-grower cooperatives and agricultural service providers. Management estimates that sustained 24-hour operations would require more than 9,000 acres of pineapple and other fruits. Crucially, the land is already in place. Ekumfi has secured 9,500 acres for juice, tea and tepache feedstock — more than the full 24-hour requirement — with full capacity achievable within 36 months. The constraint is no longer land, but the planting finance, inputs and grower mobilization needed to bring it into production. That is not merely an agricultural challenge. It is a major economic opportunity. Rather than relying solely on company-owned plantations, Ekumfi can establish structured partnerships with thousands of farmers and young entrepreneurs growing fruit under agreed quality, delivery and pricing terms. The factory gains dependable supply; growers gain a defined industrial market. Feed the Industries can turn Ekumfi’s raw-material shortage into rural wealth creation. GH₵52,000 Per Acre: A New Opportunity for Youth and Pineapple Growers The most compelling dimension of the proposed expansion is the opening it creates for youth, smallholders, landowners and agricultural entrepreneurs to participate directly in the pineapple value chain. Under the proposed cultivation model, one acre of pineapple could generate an estimated GH₵52,000 in gross revenue per successful harvest cycle . Young people could start commercial farming on modest plots; existing growers could scale up. If the full 9,000-acre requirement were planted with pineapple at this revenue level, gross farm-gate value could reach GH₵468 million per harvest cycle. Because Ekumfi also needs other fruits, the real mix will depend on acreage allocated to each crop. The programme could be structured around one-acre, five-acre and ten-acre production units for young growers, backed by land access, improved planting material, technical assistance, mechanization and structured off take agreements. The opportunity extends well beyond the farm gate: seedling multiplication, land preparation, irrigation, harvesting, transport, aggregation, farm management and agricultural technology could each support thousands of livelihoods. Management estimates that the full Ekumfi value chain — nurseries, land preparation, cultivation, harvesting, haulage, aggregation, processing, packaging and distribution — could support around 18,000 jobs in the Central Region alone . One distinction matters. GH₵52,000 is potential gross revenue , not guaranteed profit. Growers must cover cultivation, labour, inputs, financing and transport, and a pineapple cycle can run longer than a year. Even so, the model shows how industrial demand can anchor commercial agriculture. Instead of simply urging young Ghanaians into farming, the country can offer them a defined industrial market, structured production support and a real pathway to commercial income. From Two Days a Week to US$4 Million a Month Management estimates that with adequate raw material, working capital and market access, sustained 24-hour production could deliver monthly turnover of about US$4 million — US$48 million a year . Moving from two days a week toward continuous operation would sharply improve utilization of existing equipment, utilities, labour and infrastructure, while expanding market presence and multiplying demand for local produce. The lesson for Ghana’s industrial agenda is clear: the country can unlock substantial value not only by building new factories, but by helping existing ones run at full capacity. Could Ekumfi Repay Its EXIM Credit Within Two Years? One of the most consequential implications concerns Ekumfi’s obligations to Ghana EXIM Bank. At US$48 million in annual turnover, the company would generate materially stronger cash flow to support restructuring and repayment. Illustratively, a 15% free-cash-flow margin would yield about US$7.2 million before further financing needs or restrictions on distributions. At that level, the restructured US$6 million EXIM credit could be cleared within 24 months. That means about US$3 million a year, or US$250,000 a month, which is less than half of the illustrative annual free cash flow. Even at half that margin (7.5%), annual cash generation of about US$3.6 million would still cover the principal schedule. A two-year plan repays EXIM in full while leaving headroom for working capital, cropping and interest, rather than sweeping every cedi to a single lender. Restructuring the existing EXIM exposure into a US$6 million credit does two things. It gives Ekumfi a defined, serviceable obligation, and it leaves room for other financial institutions to participate, providing the working-capital, raw-material and expansion finance that no single lender should carry alone. The actual timeline will still depend on interest, operating margins, working-capital needs and agreed repayment terms. The broader point stands: restoring industrial productivity offers development financiers a more credible recovery pathway than leaving major manufacturing assets idle. A structured recovery programme can align EXIM’s repayment interests with agricultural expansion, higher factory output and growing export revenue. From Ghanaian Pineapples to a Global Juice Brand Ekumfi’s processing platform can produce value-added beverages from pineapple, citrus, ginger, passion fruit and other local crops. With adequate volumes, competitive pricing, consistent quality and established distribution partners, the company can extend its reach across African, European, North American and Middle Eastern markets. The gains ripple through the economy: more fruit production creates farm income; more manufacturing creates industrial jobs; packaging and distribution support other businesses; exports earn foreign exchange. This is the central promise of agricultural industrialization — converting locally grown crops into internationally marketed finished products, and capturing value through processing, branding and distribution rather than exporting raw produce. Why Ekumfi Survived Where State-Led Factories Stalled Ekumfi’s story becomes sharper when set beside the record of state-led agro-industrial investment in the same region and beyond. The record is sobering. The state-owned Ayensu Starch Company has shut down repeatedly since 2002 over raw-material shortages and equipment failures. The Komenda Sugar Factory , rebuilt in 2016 for about US$35 million, has barely operated since. NABCO placed some 100,000 graduates in temporary public roles that ended without a pipeline into lasting enterprise. And under One District, One Factory (1D1F) , more than 300 factories stand idle or unfinished today. The common thread is not a shortage of public money. Over three decades and more, the state has committed capital to factories and programmes without the sustained private ownership, management discipline and equity at risk needed to keep them running when conditions turned difficult. Ekumfi took a different route. Backed by private sponsors with their own capital committed, it has kept its factory, brands and markets alive through the excise burden, raw-material shortfalls and financing delays — and today sells Ghanaian juice at home and abroad. That is a lesson the state should note. Rather than building and running factories on its own, or simply recovering legacy debt from the private ventures that survived, government and its development finance institutions should consider taking equity positions alongside committed private sponsors . Equity aligns the state with the upside as utilization rises, strengthens the balance sheet lenders look to, and leaves day-to-day management with operators who have proven they can keep a factory running. Ekumfi offers a ready test case. A Practical Model for the 24-Hour Economy Ekumfi can serve as a demonstration project for how Feed the Industries and the 24-Hour Economy work together. The model connects six elements: Agricultural expansion — develop 9,000+ acres of pineapple and other fruits through company estates, commercial growers and outgrower arrangements. Youth and farmer empowerment — enable growers to target gross crop revenue of up to GH₵52,000 per acre per successful harvest cycle. Industrial production — progressively raise factory utilization toward sustained 24-hour operation. Market development — expand domestic distribution and exports to support projected turnover of US$48 million a year. Financial recovery — service the restructured US$6 million EXIM credit from operating cash flow, while other institutions participate in funding growth. State equity partnership — convert public support into equity alongside private sponsors, sharing in the upside of a working factory rather than funding stalled ones. Delivery requires collaboration among Ekumfi, Ghana EXIM Bank, the Ministry of Food and Agriculture, the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, the 24-Hour Economy Authority, agricultural investors and commercial financiers — and a phased implementation plan with independently validated yields, acreage, processing capacity, customer demand and working-capital needs. The Bigger Picture: Turning Industrial Investment Into National Wealth Ekumfi’s story poses a question for Ghana’s development-finance strategy: what happens when the country invests in a major industrial asset but not in the supply chain needed to sustain it? The answer is an underused factory, mounting financial pressure, lost farm income and missed exports. The reverse is just as true. When agriculture, manufacturing, finance and markets are coordinated, the same investment becomes an engine of growth. For young people, the opportunity can begin with a single acre of pineapple. For established farmers, it means scaling up with a dependable industrial buyer. For Ghana EXIM Bank, it offers a pathway to improved recovery through higher production. For Ghana, it demonstrates how Feed the Industries can turn agricultural potential into manufacturing output, export earnings and rural prosperity. The Ekumfi Opportunity Is Bigger Than One Factory Ghana does not need to abandon valuable industrial investments because they have faced difficulty. It needs to identify and remove the constraints holding them back. For Ekumfi Fruits & Juices, that means connecting a modern processing factory to thousands of acres of productive farmland, empowering young growers and expanding markets for Ghanaian-made beverages — moving from limited weekly runs to 24-hour operation, from raw-material shortage to a structured supply chain, and from financial pressure to a firm foundation for repayment and export growth. The factory has been built. The asset exists. The land has been acquired. The task now is to feed the factory, empower the farmers, create wealth for the youth and build a globally competitive Ghanaian juice brand. That is the promise of Ekumfi under Ghana’s Feed the Industries and 24-Hour Economy agenda.

title: World Gymnastics official calls visa denials for Russian athletes 'sad'
body:
ROTTERDAM, October 16. /TASS/. The Dutch authorities’ refusal to issue visas to several Russian athletes has created a "sad" situation, World Gymnastics Secretary General Nicolas Buompane told reporters.
The Dutch city of Rotterdam will host the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships on October 17-25. Earlier, the Netherlands denied entry visas to Olympic champions Angelina Melnikova and Viktoria Listunova, as well as Anna Kalmykova.
"It’s very sad because the aim is really not to mix sports and politics. We hear this all the time, but at the end of the day, it’s politically driven somehow," Buompane said. "All efforts have been made to try to convince the Dutch government to provide visas to all athletes," Buompane added.
The World Championships will serve as the first team qualification event for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games. Based on the results, the top three men’s and top three women’s teams will earn Olympic quotas. Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev said on Tuesday that the Russian Olympic Committee would appeal to the International Olympic Committee and World Gymnastics, demanding that the tournament in Rotterdam be stripped of its Olympic qualifying status.

title: ‘Not true’: Public warned against viral fundraiser for Toluwanisings’ family
body: By Wasiu Rokibat Lanre Alewilese, a friend and colleague of Nigerian gospel singer Toluwanisings has disowned a viral fundraising appeal purportedly seeking financial assistance for his wife and children, warning members of the public against donating through unauthorised channels. A fundraising flyer bearing the late singer’s photograph circulated on social media, calling on well-wishers to contribute towards the welfare of his immediate family. Reacting to the development, Alewilese, who is also a gospel singer, issued a disclaimer, describing the fundraising appeal as false and urging the public to report the account responsible for circulating it. “Disclaimer!!! This is not true please. Please let’s report this page massively. If at all something like this will come up it will be from this page. Thank you,” the statement read. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Akanni Lanre kayode (@lanrealewilese) Fans, sympathisers and members of the public were urged to verify any fundraising initiative through the singer’s official platform before making financial contributions. The development follows the announcement of Toluwanisings’ death on October 14, 2026, which prompted an outpouring of condolences from fans and members of the gospel music community. Vanguard News The post ‘Not true’: Public warned against viral fundraiser for Toluwanisings’ family appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: 4 arrested, 142 parcels of suspected Indian hemp seized as officers reject GH¢50k bribe
body: Police in the Northern Region have arrested four persons and seized 142 compressed parcels of suspected Indian hemp following an intelligence-led operation on the Bimbilla-Tamale highway. The operation was carried out on Thursday, 15 October, at about 6:30 p.m. by the Northern Regional Special Operations Team, codenamed Red Maria, led by Chief Inspector Abu Isahaku and comprising 13 personnel. According to the police, the team intercepted a mini commercial bus with registration number GW 7800-14 travelling from Bimbilla towards Tamale, driven by 46-year-old Alhassan Zeblim, and a search conducted on the vehicle revealed 142 compressed parcels of suspected Indian hemp concealed in four jute sacks. A statement issued by the police said the driver told the police officers he was transporting the consignment to an unidentified tricycle rider in Tamale and subsequently contacted the intended recipient, leading police to an agreed meeting point. “At the location, police arrested Ibrahim Yussif, 34, the tricycle rider, and his brother, Bawa Yussif, 56, who had accompanied him to receive the consignment,” the statement said. It said during interrogation, Ibrahim Yussif identified Mohammed Haruna as the owner of the consignment and led the team to a drinking spot known as Sarafina in Tamale, where Haruna was arrested. Police said the suspects offered officers a bribe of GH¢50,000 in an attempt to secure their release. “The suspects offered the arresting team a bribe of GH¢50,000, which the officers rejected,” the police said. The exhibits recovered include 142 parcels of suspected Indian hemp and one tricycle. All four suspects and the exhibits have been handed over to the Regional Drugs Law Enforcement Unit for further investigation.

title: ‘Operate Within The Law’, SSG Counsels Kaduna Governing Boards
body: The Secretary to Kaduna State Government, Dr AbdulKadir Mu’azu Meyere has advised members of Governing Boards and Councils, to acquaint themselves thoroughly with the laws establishing their institutions and operate strictly within them. Dr Meyere pointed out that a Board or Council provides policy direction and oversight, while day-to-day administration remains the responsibility of the management. The Secretary to the Government who gave this advice at the inauguration of Governing Boards and Councils of Kaduna State Agencies and institutions, told them that ‘’respect for that distinction is the surest guarantee of a harmonious tenure. ‘’ ‘’Hold your statutory meetings regularly, keep proper records, declare any interest that may conflict with that of your institution, and be guided at all times by due process,’’ he further advised. The SSG observed that their appointments is an expression of the confidence that Governor Uba Sani reposes on them, adding that ‘’public office is a call to service and we should therefore receive it in that spirit.’’ ‘’You were carefully selected for your integrity, competence and experience, and drawn from across the three Senatorial Districts of our State, so that the institutions you now oversee may benefit from the widest pool of knowledge and the fairest representation of our people,’’ he said. Dr Meyere advised the Chairmen and Board members to deliver measurable results, by establishing ‘’amicable working relationship with your management.’’ ‘’Set for yourselves clear targets and deliverables that build directly on the achievements of His Excellency in your sector, monitor them closely, and report on them regularly,’’ he added. The Secretary to Kaduna State Government further charged them to put the citizens first and work together as a team that is serving one Government. ‘’Let fairness, equity and the needs of our communities guide your decisions. Those of you who oversee enforcement agencies must ensure that they act firmly, but with courtesy and full respect for the rights of citizens. ‘’No agency succeeds alone; our health institutions must plan together, our security and enforcement agencies must share information and act in synergy and collaboration, and our training institutions must align what they teach with the needs of our health system, our farms and our growing economy,’’ he said. The SSG promised to support them to discharge their responsibilities, advising them ‘’to channel your reports, recommendations and requests through your supervising Ministries and the appropriate structures of Government so that they receive prompt attention.’’ The SSG Iinaugurated Governing Boards and Councils of 12 agencies and institutions on behalf of Governor Uba Sani and they include, the Kaduna State Primary Health Care Board. The rest are the Kaduna State College of Education, Gidan Waya; Nuhu Bamalli Polytechnic, Zaria, the Kaduna State Residents Identity Management Agency and the Kaduna State Drugs and Medical Supplies Management Agency. In addition, the Boards of Kaduna State Vigilance Service; the Kaduna State Traffic Law Enforcement Agency; the Kaduna State Facilities Management Agency and the Kaduna State Agricultural Development Agency were inaugurated. Also, the Shehu Idris College of Health Sciences and Technology, Makarfi; the Kaduna State Water Corporation; and the Institute of Vocational Training and Skills Development duly inaugurated. In his address, Dr Meyere also reminded that Governor Uba Sani has been pursuing a transformative urban and rural development agenda anchored on security, human capital development, rural transformation and inclusive governance. ‘’In health, the administration is renovating and upgrading our Primary Health Care Centres across the State, to provide basic emergency obstetric and newborn care and other essential services. ‘’The Governor Uba Sani administration has distributed free essential medicines and modern equipment to health facilities in all twenty-three Local Government Areas. ‘’Government has also approved the recruitment of 1,800 health personnel, and the process of recruiting more health workers is ongoing to ensure adequate manpower for our health facilities,’’ he reminded. Dr Meyere also said that the administration of Governor Uba Sani is focused on skills-based learning, adding that ‘’the Institutes of Vocational Training and Skills Development at Soba, Rigachukun and Samarun-Kataf are equipping our youth with practical and employable skills.’’ ‘’Our farmers have, for three consecutive years, received free fertiliser and other farm inputs, while road projects across the State especially in rural areas are linking farming communities to markets and reducing post-harvest losses,’’ he added.

title: Astana Media Week: AI’s Opportunities and Risks for Journalism
body: The tenth edition of Astana Media Week is taking place in Kazakhstan’s capital from October 14 to 16, with media professionals from Central Asia and other regions discussing how artificial intelligence (AI) is changing journalism. Dzhanibek Suleyev, a veteran Kazakh web publisher, and Alexander Smolin, former editor of Orda.kz , once one of the country’s most popular online news outlets, spoke to The Times of Central Asia about how to take advantage of this technological leap while minimizing its risks. A New Revolution in Information Production AI can generate large volumes of content in seconds, but Suleyev argues that the technology cannot replicate a journalist’s judgment: finding an original angle, choosing the right person to interview, or persuading them to speak candidly. “I can’t say definitively whether the invention of AI is a blessing or a threat. That’s a question for philosophers,” he said. Suleyev sees parallels with the advent of online journalism. The media, he noted, have repeatedly adapted to new technology. What once seemed radical – reading news on a computer or phone rather than in a newspaper – quickly became routine. In the process, new professions emerged, including search engine optimization editors, audience analytics specialists, multimedia journalists, and social media editors, while demand for printing and newspaper distribution declined. Online publishing also dramatically lowered the cost of launching a news outlet. “Just as the media’s move online in the 2000s did, AI is now reducing the cost of producing information. But there is a fundamental difference between these two revolutions,” Suleyev said. “The first changed how information was produced, distributed, and consumed. The second is also affecting the very process of creating journalistic content.” The Right to Fair Compensation That transformation raises an immediate financial problem: search engines can deliver AI-generated answers without users visiting the websites that originally reported the information. Suleyev says this is costing publishers traffic and advertising revenue. Evidence of declining traffic is already mounting. Google search referrals to more than 2,500 news websites worldwide fell by 33% between November 2024 and November 2025, according to a report by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism. Researchers cautioned, however, that it remains unclear how much of this decline can be attributed directly to AI-generated summaries. On October 12, major publishers, including The New York Times and The Economist , joined a coalition seeking greater control over how AI companies use their content and fair compensation for that use. Suleyev believes such issues must be discussed by the media community and addressed through legislation. Relying on AI Alone Is a Losing Strategy Smolin is more optimistic about AI’s practical benefits. Tasks that once took a journalist two hours of searching can now, he said, be completed in minutes. Generating illustrations has also become easier, reducing the need for some in-house design work. “There’s a saying I really like: to use artificial intelligence, you need to develop your own intelligence,” Smolin said. “I’m fully in favor of developing AI in the industry, but only in combination with our own skills and abilities. AI is simply an assistant that you cannot rely on completely.” But speed creates risks. Smolin says newsrooms are already accumulating examples of journalists who blindly trusted AI-generated information and subsequently had to apologize for publishing errors. He also acknowledged that AI is beginning to replace some newsroom jobs. In smaller outlets, he said, journalists may find themselves operating AI systems rather than producing original reporting, with only a handful of colleagues gathering comments and attending press conferences. Yet he doubts such operations can compete with outlets offering original journalism. “A machine always produces a template. What makes something interesting to read is a human perspective,” Smolin said. He does not expect widespread layoffs in newsrooms in the near future. There is currently a surge in content produced by generative models, including text, photographs, and video, but he believes enthusiasm for the technological novelty will eventually fade. “Without a doubt, producing information has become much cheaper and easier, but trust in it has also declined,” he said. AI systems can produce false information through hallucinations, while misleading content can also be generated deliberately. These risks, Smolin argued, make editorial oversight more important than ever. “Fact-checking has always been the number one responsibility of journalists and editors. AI doesn’t change that,” he concluded. Legislation Will Continue to Evolve During Astana Media Week, Kazakhstan’s First Vice Minister of Culture and Information, Kanat Iskakov, called on the media community to develop common principles for using AI . He argued that public trust in the media should rest on three pillars: strong newsrooms, journalistic accountability, and technologies that help ensure information is reliable. An algorithm can produce an article, he said, but it cannot be held accountable for its words. That responsibility remains with journalists and their newsrooms. Kazakhstan’s Law on Artificial Intelligence , which came into force on January 18, 2026, already requires synthetic AI-generated content to carry machine-readable labels , allowing software to identify it automatically, as well as warnings that are understandable to users. However, questions remain over how AI-generated material should be used in newsrooms and how publishers should be compensated when their work is used by AI companies. As the technology continues to develop, the rules governing its use are likely to evolve with it.
