He has an hour of oxygen left when he is swallowed, and the lessons his father taught him may be his best chance of getting out. Josh Brolin plays his father Mitt, appearing in flashbacks that gradually explain the relationship. The two actors had already worked together in Weapons , but Whalefall puts their scenes at the centre of how we understand Jay. And to achieve them, both actors thrived on the tension between them, even if it took a toll. “With him, it was fun because he got super into it, and it was super uncomfortable, even for me,” Brolin tells The National . “The discomfort that you see on the screen, I think that was a result of that discomfort on set.” Abrams has kept a similar distance from co-stars before. During Wolfs , he resisted George Clooney and Brad Pitt’s attempts to befriend him, preserving the awe his character felt towards theirs. A September GQ profile described him wincing at the word “method”, though he was more comfortable explaining the thinking behind it. “If everyone’s game for it, we might as well let these real dynamics hang,” he said. It was Abrams who kept the tension going even when cameras stopped rolling on the Whalefall set. He explained that breaking it would have risked losing something he and Brolin had created and were both feeling. He acknowledged that this would not be the right approach to every film, but it suited this one. Their scenes give Abrams a different challenge from the physical demands of the survival story. With Mitt, Jay has years of disappointment and resentment behind him, alongside a desire to connect that neither quite knows how to express. The film needs us to understand why the relationship continues to occupy him, even while he is trying to stay alive. “Josh is always going to new places, and he’s always challenging himself. You don’t always find that,” Abrams says. “You hope you would find that in a partner – that they’ll go full throttle. “If someone’s been doing it for a while, they find their tricks and the things that work for them. But Josh is willing to go there and keep exploring. I’m grateful that he’s still excavating and still going there.” Brolin remembers being fascinated by experimental theatre, particularly the idea of actors rehearsing for six months to see what effect their work might have. “I think young actors are looking back at certain actors and saying, ‘What was that? Instead of just entertainment, what is getting into a role? What is full conviction? What is experimenting?’,” he says. “You try to do movies that slap you awake. You want to have a full experience.” In the film, Jay can shut his father out but still want his approval. Abrams makes both impulses feel true, drawing us close to someone who struggles to let anyone in. How much of his real life goes into that is harder to separate. “It’s everything,” Abrams says. “It’s the things that you don’t want to look at or are painful to look at. Then it’s going to hopefully go in to new territory and new lands you’ve never been to before. That’s definitely the hope.” Whalefall is in cinemas now across the Middle East

title: Snowbirds to perform final air show demonstration
body:
The Royal Canadian Air Force’s Snowbirds will perform their final air show with the Tutor jets in Moose Jaw, Sask., Friday, before the iconic aircraft are retired for good.
The annual season home closing show is set to be livestreamed online — although there will be one more chance to see the CT-114 Tutors in action before they are sent to Trenton, Ont., for disposal.
The Snowbirds are scheduled to perform a flyover at the Grey Cup game in Calgary on Nov. 15.
The aging Tutor jets are being retired and the Snowbirds will go on hiatus until the team can be trained on the replacement Pilatus aircraft, the CT-157 Siskin.
Captain Philip Rochon, the public affairs officer for the team, says it’s a bittersweet time as the pilots say goodbye to the planes the Snowbirds have flown for nearly six decades.
Rochon says over the summer months, the Snowbirds received an outpouring of support from Canadians across the country, including former pilots.

title: Yle's Puppy Live goes international as Dutch public broadcaster buys rights
body:
The broadcaster plans to adapt Yle's popular puppy livestream. The six puppies, now almost a week old, have posed for their first portraits.
Yle’s Pentulive (Puppy Live) programme has been sold to the Netherlands, according to Ville Alijoki , Yle's Culture and Factual Content managing editor.
The rights buyer is Het Klokhuis, an educational and current affairs programme for children that is part of the Dutch public broadcasting network.
Pentulive follows a mother dog and her litter for around eight weeks, from the puppies' birth until they leave for their new homes.
Alijoki and producer Jyri Loikkanen had already begun planning how to format the show to be sold internationally when the Dutch broadcaster made contact.
A programme format sets out how a production works so that it can be adapted by different teams, in different countries or across multiple production seasons.
This year, Pentulive has also been shown by Sweden's public broadcaster SVT as part of a programme exchange, attracting 250,000 views.
Alijoki said he could see the programme reaching an even wider international audience. He described it as an example of slow television that offers people an escape from the worries of the world.
"There's a certain magic to it, something people miss when the world is sometimes quite dark," he said.
The six puppies will soon be one week old. New portrait photos will be published every week, with the first images now available.
Their mother, Hilkka, gave birth to six puppies — two females and four males on 10 October.
The puppies have not yet been given official names, so the breeder has assigned each one a nickname. Viewers can join the online chat on Saturday, 17 October, at 18:00 to vote on a theme for their names. The suggested themes have been submitted by viewers.

title: Aurus opens pre-orders for restyled Senat model
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Aurus has opened pre-orders for the restyled Aurus Senat executive sedan, the company said.
The vehicle's price starts at 48.5 million rubles ($580,000).
"Today, we are opening pre-orders for the updated Aurus Senat," Aurus Commercial Director Artyom Yusupov said.
The brand's flagship sedan has undergone a comprehensive modernization: changes were made in both interior and exterior of the model.
As previously reported, the updated Aurus Senat features completely redesigned front and rear optics, a refreshed radiator grille, an expanded color palette, and updated wheel rim designs.
The hybrid powertrain, based on a 4.4-liter V8 gasoline engine producing 598 h.p., works in tandem with a 62 h.p. electric motor and a domestic 9-speed automatic transmission. The car's maximum speed is 250 km/h, and acceleration from 0 to 100 km/h takes 6 seconds, Aurus said.

title: President Mahama urges investors to employ trained local residents as 1,238-acre industrial park takes off
body: President John Dramani Mahama has urged investors at the Afienya Industrial Park to prioritise the employment of trained residents from the host communities as construction of the 1,238-acre facility begins. He said a training programme should be introduced to equip residents of Afienya and surrounding communities with the skills required to secure jobs in the industries expected to operate at the park. Speaking at the sod-cutting ceremony on Thursday, October 15, President Mahama said the project’s success should be measured partly by the employment opportunities it created for people in the host communities. “I believe that if enterprises are located here, there should be a programme that trains the local people so that they can get some of the jobs that are created in this industrial park,” he said. He said residents should remain central to the park’s development and benefit from the economic activities it would generate. President Mahama added that the benefits should extend beyond factory employment to farmers, transport operators, local suppliers and small businesses that could provide goods and services to companies operating at the park. The Afienya Industrial Park is expected to accommodate more than 120 enterprises, with serviced plots and ready-to-use factory shells. The priority sectors include cocoa, cashew and oil palm processing, textiles and garments, pharmaceuticals, medical consumables, automotive components and light engineering. The facility will also provide opportunities in logistics, data services and business process outsourcing, alongside dedicated space for renewable energy and green manufacturing. President Mahama said the Ghana Free Zones Authority had informed him that the Tema Export Processing Zone had no space left to allocate to prospective investors. He said the situation made the provision of new industrial infrastructure urgent, adding that part of the financing for the project would come from the proposed New Economy Programme. The Chief Executive of the Ghana Free Zones Authority, Dr Mary Awusi, said 14 companies had already been allocated land at the Afienya Industrial Park. She said the Authority wanted young people to benefit from employment, skills development and technology transfer arising from the investments. Dr Awusi added that free zone enterprises already supported their host communities through initiatives in education, healthcare and skills development. The Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, expressed appreciation to the chiefs of Ningo-Prampram and Shai-Osudoku for their cooperation in making the land available for the project. She said their goodwill had enabled the government to acquire the land without disputes. In a vote of thanks, the Authority’s Director of Corporate Affairs, Dr Patience Acorlor, thanked the chiefs and people of Afienya and surrounding communities for making their land available for the project. She said their support was important to the success of the industrial park. President Mahama urged investors to establish their businesses at the park, develop their products in Ghana and use the country as a base to reach markets across Africa and beyond. “Establish your businesses here, develop your products here,” he said.

title: Media doing its job, but politicians fuelling insults on social media – NMAG president
body: The President of the New Media Association of Ghana (NMAG), Eugene Osafo-Nkansah, has accused politicians of fuelling insults in Ghana’s political discourse, arguing that social media is amplifying the problem rather than creating it. He said political insults had existed long before the emergence of social media, but the growing reach and influence of digital platforms had made the practice more visible and increasingly concerning. Speaking at a Joy Prime round-table discussion on the topic “The Politics of Insults: Where Do We Draw the Line?” on October 16, Mr Osafo-Nkansah said politicians must take greater responsibility for the conduct of their supporters and the language used in political debates. “What’s happening is just a reflection of our society. And it’s just reflecting how powerful social media is. Politics of insults is not something new,” he said. According to him, the problem lies primarily in politics, with social media serving as a powerful tool through which inflammatory statements can spread rapidly to a wider audience. He explained that social media had transformed the scale of political communication, allowing people from different parts of the world to access discussions and content almost instantaneously, provided they had internet access. He said this increased reach had made political insults appear more widespread and alarming, even though he believed the number of people engaging in such behaviour was relatively small. Mr Osafo-Nkansah argued that politicians were at the centre of the problem because of their influence over political supporters and the platforms they use to communicate their messages. He expressed concern that political insults had become closely associated with partisan affiliations, arguing that political leaders must examine their role in encouraging or enabling abusive exchanges. “I think the core, the source, is still the politicians. They are the ones enabling them,” he said. He acknowledged that social media users also had a responsibility to use their platforms carefully, but maintained that efforts to address the problem would have limited impact unless politicians took the lead in changing the tone of political discourse. The NMAG president further expressed concern about what he perceived as political influence in cases involving arrests over political insults. He said, in his observation, almost everyone arrested over such comments had links to one political party or another, raising questions about the role of political affiliations in how these cases were pursued. “I don’t think that the police will just wake up and go and arrest people because of something they have said, but it will be done because of some political affiliation,” he said. Despite his concerns about the state of political discourse, the NMAG president maintained that social media remained an important platform for criticism, accountability and public engagement. He urged users to express their views objectively and challenge political leaders where necessary without resorting to insults, defamation or personal attacks. “You can actually be on social media, do whatever you are doing, criticise, be critical, but still be objective and put your case across without insulting,” he said. Mr Osafo-Nkansah said his participation in the discussion was intended partly to encourage digital media practitioners and other social media users to adopt more responsible communication practices. He said he was using his position as a digital media leader to encourage members to communicate their views without responding to provocation with abusive language. “Whatever you want to do, whatever you want to say, you can still use your platform and say it without necessarily insulting, defaming, or going personal,” he said. He maintained that while individuals must use their platforms responsibly, politicians have a crucial role to play in curbing the politics of insults by setting a better example in their own public communication and discouraging abusive exchanges among their supporters.

title: Tinubu has political will to develop N-Niger – Eradiri replies Duke
body: By Davies Iheamnachor PORT HARCOURT: The Media Director of the Tinubu Support Group, TSG, in Bayelsa State, Engr Udengs Eradiri, has stated that President Bola Tinubu has enough political will to develop Niger Delta inspite of the region’s terrain. Eradiri spoke while reponding to a remark by a former Governor of Cross River State, Donald Duke, on the challenges posed by the Niger Delta’s terrain to development, stating that he (Duke) lacked the knowledge and only playing politics with the region’s future. He described Duke’s position as reckless and misleading, stating the former governor lacked an adequate understanding of the Niger Delta’s geographical realities and had failed to appreciate how engineering, political will and sustained investment could overcome the region’s geographical challenges. Eradiri, an erstwhile President of the Ijaw Youths Council (IYC) Worldwide, pointed out the coastal road project being undertaken by the Tinubu administration as evidence of the President’s determination to confront challenges of infrastructure development in the region. He said: “All over the world, engineering backed with serious governance has conquered terrains worse than the ones in the Niger Delta to build critical infrastructure. We cannot see why the Niger Delta case should be different.” He faulted Duke’s position with what he described as Tinubu’s willingness to undertake ambitious infrastructure projects, noting that political will is required to put the best in the region. Eradiri said the Bodo-Bonny road and the coastal road project were examples of Tinubu’s determination to pursue infrastructure development despite geographical challenges. He said: “How did Tinubu complete a road to Bonny? He did it because of political will. How is Tinubu building the coastal road? He is doing it because he has the political will; the will that the likes of Donald Duke do not have, yet they want people to vote for them. “Tinubu has demonstrated the political will to do the most difficult things that others shy away from. These are the things required to lay a solid foundation for the development and prosperity of this country.” Eradiri insisted that the President’s approach to infrastructure development distinguished him from other political leaders who, according to him, noting that the region needed leaders capable of mobilising resources, deploying modern engineering and sustaining infrastructure investment. He noted that Duke’s position has exposed that he failed to relate with his colleagues in the region while serving as governor, adding that Bayelsa State and Niger Delta terrains are developable. “It is obvious that while sitting as the governor of one of the Niger Delta states, Donald Duke failed to relate properly with his colleagues to this point where he went on national television to embarrass himself about how his colleagues were tackling the terrain to develop their states. “Bayelsa State can be developed. Right now, if you see what is happening in the state as a result of the increase in allocations to states under President Bola Tinubu’s government because of his courage to remove fuel subsidy, you will understand that the terrain is not an excuse for underdevelopment,” he said. The post Tinubu has political will to develop N-Niger – Eradiri replies Duke appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Zelensky complains US still restricts Starlink operations for Ukrainian military
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The US has still not lifted restrictions on the operation of the Starlink satellite communication system for the Ukrainian armed forces, Vladimir Zelensky said at a press conference in Brussels.
"The restrictions on Starlink's operations for the Ukrainian military have not been fully lifted," the UNIAN news agency quoted him as saying. "Internet speeds from SpaceX are gradually being restored, but not yet to their full capacity," the head of the Kiev regime noted.
Earlier, Sergey Beskrestnov, an advisor to Zelensky and an expert in communications and unmanned systems, reported that SpaceX had limited the operating speed of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian military. According to him, this "disrupted a number of operations." On October 14, Zelensky said that shutting down Starlink was a mistake and asked SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to restore the service. On October 15, the RBC-Ukraine news agency reported, citing sources in the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, that Starshield, SpaceX’s military and intelligence satellite program that uses Starlink infrastructure, had resumed full operation.
Earlier on October 16, Reuters reported that the White House had restricted the provision of communication services to the Ukrainian military. The Pentagon leadership received a message stating that the Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed down. The report did not specify who made this decision. A Washington administration official told the news agency that President Donald Trump did not issue such an order.

title: UK expands sanction powers, enabling action against companies supporting West Bank settlements
body: Britain brought new regulations into force on Thursday, significantly expanding its sanctions powers in a move that could enable action against construction companies, developers, and financial institutions supporting settlement expansion in the West Bank.The measures took effect four days before the deadline for submitting bids for construction in the E1 area between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim, amid a diplomatic dispute between Israel and Britain over the closure of the British consulate in east Jerusalem.The new regulations expand Britain's sanctions framework concerning human rights and international humanitarian law. They allow sanctions against individuals and entities directly involved in activities classified as serious violations of international law, as well as those financing, facilitating, or promoting such activities, subject to specified legal conditions.Possible measures include asset freezes, financial restrictions, travel bans, and disqualification from serving as company directors. The regulations could also allow sanctions against entities involved in settlement-related activities if they meet the established criteria, but do not impose blanket restrictions on all companies operating in the area.UK sanctions expansion comes ahead of E1 settlement construction deadlineThe timing is particularly significant as Israel advances construction plans in the E1 area. The deadline for submitting bids for 1,234 housing units, part of a broader plan involving approximately 3,400 units, is scheduled for October 19, while consideration of the bids by the tender committee has been postponed until after November 19.Britain opposes the project, arguing that construction in the area would undermine the territorial continuity required for a future Palestinian state. Israeli officials view the development as part of settlement expansion and efforts to strengthen continuity between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim, rejecting the argument that international opposition should prevent the project from proceeding.The tender is expected to close in the coming days despite the postponement of the committee's review. Companies seeking to participate must therefore submit their bids before it becomes clear whether Britain intends to exercise its new sanctions powers against entities connected to the project.British advocates of expanded sanctions are seeking to deter companies and financial institutions from participating at the bidding stage, before contractors are selected and construction begins.British lawmakers warn banks over financing E1 constructionPolitical figures and organizations in Britain opposed to settlement construction have also been working to increase pressure on businesses that could participate in the project.Last month, members of Parliament contacted banks and financial institutions, warning of the risks associated with financing construction in E1. This week, the Britain Palestine Project, an organization supporting measures against settlements, warned that companies and contractors participating in the development could jeopardize their international business relationships.In letters sent to financial institutions, lawmakers called on banks to assess their potential exposure to the E1 project and raise the issue at board level, including the legal, economic, and reputational risks involved.Although the letters represent requests from lawmakers rather than binding government directives, they are intended to increase pressure on banks and other institutions providing financing and guarantees, encouraging them to avoid involvement in the project.Concerns over possible future sanctions could influence commercial decisions even before Britain announces restrictions against specific companies.Peace Now warns British sanctions could affect broader Israeli economyThe Israeli settlement watchdog Peace Now responded sharply to the regulations taking effect on Thursday, warning that their consequences could extend beyond companies directly involved in settlement construction."This is a real alarm. Today, it is already clear that settlements are not only an obstacle to peace and a danger to security, but also an economic threat to the country's future," the organization said.Peace Now accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich of advancing construction in E1 and warned that the consequences of sanctions could eventually affect the broader Israeli public."The price of this messianic adventure could be paid not only by settlers, but by millions of law-abiding Israeli citizens," the organization said. "Today, these are sanctions on settlements. Tomorrow, they will reach every household in Israel."Concerns about broader economic consequences were also raised last month. According to concerns expressed within the Israeli government, foreign importers and financial institutions could struggle to distinguish between companies operating in settlements and other Israeli businesses, potentially imposing stricter commercial conditions on companies that are not themselves subject to sanctions.For now, these remain assessments of possible consequences, and the scale of any economic damage, if it occurs, remains unknown.New sanctions rules could increase scrutiny of Israeli companies and banksThe regulations could also have further implications for the financial sector.If sanctions are imposed on a particular company or entity, financial institutions subject to British law would be required to comply with the applicable restrictions, including asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available.Companies not included on sanctions lists could also face additional information requests and more stringent reviews by banks and business partners, as part of compliance and risk-management procedures intended to ensure that transactions do not violate the restrictions.However, business ties with the West Bank do not, in themselves, automatically constitute grounds for sanctions against a company or bank.UK expands global human rights sanctions and introduces fast-track mechanismThe new regulations also cover matters unrelated to settlements. Britain will be able to impose sanctions for obstructing humanitarian assistance and for serious violations of the right to liberty and personal security, including unlawful detention.The regulations also introduce a mechanism allowing London to temporarily adopt sanctions already imposed by partner countries for up to 112 days while considering whether to introduce independent British sanctions.The mechanism will allow the British government to apply restrictions through an accelerated procedure based on decisions already taken by other countries.Britain advances separate restrictions on settlement trade and importsThe British move forms part of a broader plan presented by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on September 8, which also includes a proposed ban on imports from settlements and restrictions on related commercial activities.Separate legislation introducing the import ban has not yet been completed. In recent months, Britain has also coordinated with other countries in taking action against individuals and entities accused of involvement in settler violence and its financing.According to London's plan, the separate trade legislation also includes restrictions on advertising and marketing settlement real estate in Britain.In September, 12 European and Western countries, including Britain, France, and Canada, announced support for advancing trade restrictions concerning settlements, each in accordance with its domestic procedures. In some countries, the measures remain in the drafting and legislative stages.British opposition raises concerns over Palestinian workersThe sanctions have also generated debate within Britain.The opposition Conservative Party has previously warned that economic restrictions could harm Palestinian workers and businesses not involved in the activities targeted by the government.Conversely, Emily Thornberry, chair of Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, has supported measures against settlements while criticizing the time required to complete the legislation.British Prime Minister Andy Burnham clarified in Parliament this week that security and intelligence cooperation with Israel continues despite the political disagreements.The potential impact on Palestinian workers was also raised in a parliamentary question submitted to the British government.In a response issued earlier this month, the government emphasized that its measures target settlement activity it considers illegal, as well as violence and extremism, while Palestinian businesses will continue to benefit from existing preferential trade arrangements.However, the response did not include an estimate of the number of Palestinian workers who could be affected by restrictions on economic activity in settlements.The British government has not yet presented data that would allow an assessment of the potential impact on those workers.UK-Israel diplomatic tensions continue over east Jerusalem consulateThe regulations took effect one week after understandings were reached between Israel and Britain concerning the British consulate in east Jerusalem.Israel reduced Britain's diplomatic presence and halted additional activities in response to London's measures, but Britain has not reversed its sanctions policy.Although the new regulations are now in force, no new sanctions have been announced under them against companies, developers, or financial institutions involved in E1 construction.British Foreign Office clarifies sanctions are global, not Israel-specificA spokesperson for the British Foreign Office clarified that the updated regulations represent a change in global sanctions policy rather than a measure specifically targeting Israel or settlements.According to the spokesperson, the existing framework had allowed Britain to impose sanctions on individuals and entities involved in serious human rights violations or breaches of international humanitarian law worldwide.The updated policy expands the range of serious violations that could trigger sanctions, regardless of where they occur.The spokesperson stressed that the regulations are separate from the legislative process and sanctions measures concerning settlements considered illegal under international law, and do not introduce any trade-related restrictions.The Foreign Office also emphasized that the updated policy does not target any specific country.Rather, it is intended to allow Britain to respond more quickly to individuals and organizations involved in serious human rights violations or breaches of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

title: Dortmund bus attack: Seat change may have saved me – Merino
body: By Adegboyega Adeleye Arsenal midfielder Mikel Merino says a last-minute change of seat on Borussia Dortmund’s team bus may have saved his life when it was attacked with explosives in 2017. Merino was 20 years old when three bombs, packed with metal pins and concealed in a hedge, exploded as Dortmund travelled to face Monaco in the first leg of their Champions League quarter-final. A large piece of shrapnel struck the headrest of the seat he usually occupied. But Merino had moved to the front of the bus because his “legs were feeling a bit tight”. “The seats in the front reclined, so I sat up there instead, and it may have saved my life,” the Spaniard said in an interview with The Players’ Tribune. “I think I have an angel on my shoulder. I’m actually fortunate to be alive at all.” Merino recalled a deafening blast, the bus nearly tipping over, and seeing blood on the floor as smoke and screams filled the vehicle. He later went to hospital to wait for teammate Marc Bartra, who underwent surgery for a broken wrist. The match was postponed until the following day. German national Thomas Wenergold was jailed in 2018 after admitting to carrying out the attack. Merino also spoke about his recovery from a stress fracture in his right foot, suffered in February, and his determination to make Spain’s World Cup squad. Doctors initially told him he could be out for six months, with the tournament only four months away. “I was too shocked to even feel sad. I just did the math in my head,” he said. “When I told my wife, Lola, that’s when I broke down. My brain already understood, but my heart needed me to say it out loud.” Merino said his escape from the Dortmund attack helped motivate him during rehabilitation. He underwent surgery, returned to action late in the season and played for Arsenal against Crystal Palace before Spain announced its squad the next day. “I have to play. I will be at the World Cup, no matter what,” he said. Merino was eventually named in Spain’s squad and went on to lift the 2026 World Cup, completing a remarkable comeback from injury. The post Dortmund bus attack: Seat change may have saved me – Merino appeared first on Vanguard News .

When the midrange Sony Xperia 10 VI was announced over two years ago with a Qualcomm Snapdragon 6 Gen 1 chipset and Android 14, Sony promised three major OS updates which would have included this year’s Android 17 release . However, according to a notice posted to the company’s UK support site , the Xperia 10 VI won’t be getting Android 17 after all.
In the notice Sony explains that a “detailed technical assessment” revealed that “limitations related to the device’s storage configuration” mean the Xperia 10 VI “does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate.” As a result, the company has “decided not to make this upgrade available” and apologized that the decision “falls short of our original announcement.”
Sony clarifies that while OS updates for the Xperia 10 VI are ending, the company will continue to provide four years of security updates which should extend until June 2028. Sony also points out that this specific issue only applies to the “Xperia 10 VI’s technical specifications” and does not impact promised OS updates for other Xperia models. But since the technical requirements of future versions of Android aren’t yet known, it’s hard to take Sony at its word given today’s announcement.
