title: Recap: Autonomy dominates the US Army’s 2026 conference in Washington
body: WASHINGTON — The Association of the United States Army showcased its annual conference from Oct. 12-14 in Washington, assembling defense industry officials, lawmakers and military personnel from around the globe to assess the future force and evolving threats. Dominating displays at this year’s show was an unmistakable surge in automation and unmanned systems, as well as weaponry and vehicle capabilities that continue to adapt to a frenzied pace of innovation at the heart of today’s conflicts. Army officials attending the conference emphasized the service’s need for rapid transformation as the technologies at the core of these conflicts seemingly evolve by the day. Defense News and Army Times covered these discussions — and more — from this year’s show. Catch up on all of our top stories from this year’s AUSA conference and be sure to read our latest coverage at defensenews.com/digital-show-dailies/ausa . .button{background-color:#0b6399;border:none;color:white;padding:10px 25px;text-align:center;text-decoration:none;display:inline-block;font-family:Arial;font-weight:600;font-size:14px;margin:2px 1px;cursor:pointer; var(--site-color, var(--atype-theme-primary, #004074))} .button hover {background-color:#0b6399;border:none;color:white;padding:10px 25px;text-align:center;text-decoration:none;display:inline-block;font-family:Arial;font-weight:600;font-size:14px;margin:2px 1px;cursor:pointer} Jump to a section: Drone Dominance A forward-looking philosophy Weapons and equipment Getting defensive Personnel Sponsored By: American Rheinmetall Back to Top Drone dominance Pentagon, Army go all in on autonomy The Pentagon wants to take its stockpile of autonomous weapons from thousands of units into the millions. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed AUSA attendees at the Project Agincourt panel on Wednesday, sharing that the Pentagon is requesting roughly $50 billion in reconciliation funding to support the push to scale autonomous and robotic systems. Read more here . Autonomous weapons are changing the way brigades fight At Fort Bragg, soldiers recently tested how unmanned systems could help troops breach obstacles while reducing exposure to battlefield hazards. During Project Sandhills 2.0 , soldiers planned flight routes and operated Bumblebee V2 small unmanned aircraft systems at Range 63. The project tested how unmanned systems could support contested obstacle breaching, while soldiers and industry partners collected feedback to inform future Army capabilities. Read more here . US Army to stand up command for unmanned and autonomous warfare The U.S. Army ordered the creation of its own command for autonomous systems a day after Hegseth announced a new four-star military command for unmanned and autonomous warfare. An Oct. 1 memo signed by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directs the Army vice chief of staff to establish the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM. It also tells the assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, who oversees how the Army buys weapons, to put one office in charge of purchasing its priority autonomous systems. Read more here . US Army expands drone marketplace to 33 nations The U.S. Army’s online marketplace for rapid drone acquisition is expanding internationally. Representatives of Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama signed a statement of intent to join the Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace during a ceremony Tuesday. Since the marketplace was stood up, it has processed $800 million in transactions. Read more here . Drone carrying M250 machine gun completes firing test A heavy-duty quadcopter carrying Sig Sauer’s new M250 light machine gun has completed a test requiring it to identify and engage targets from the air, the company announced Tuesday. Sig Sauer completed the test in concert with Israel Aerospace Industries, maker of the Fire Storm 250, a reusable drone that can stay airborne for two hours and is designed with a stabilized machine-gun mount. Read more here . US Army targets 2028 for first high-energy laser counter-drone weapons The first directed energy weapon selected by the U.S. Army for the Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program could be out of testing and ready for counter-drone operations by early 2028, Army officials told Military Times. In September, the Army awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract for LOCUST X3, its modular, palletized high-energy laser system. Earlier generations of the LOCUST system are actively fielded in operational environments, including at the U.S. southern border, according to AeroVironment. The first LOCUST X3 is slated for delivery by Q4 of FY 2027 and will be mounted on the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle. Read more here . .button{background-color:#0b6399;border:none;color:white;padding:10px 25px;text-align:center;text-decoration:none;display:inline-block;font-family:Arial;font-weight:600;font-size:14px;margin:2px 1px;cursor:pointer; var(--site-color, var(--atype-theme-primary, #004074))} .button hover {background-color:#0b6399;border:none;color:white;padding:10px 25px;text-align:center;text-decoration:none;display:inline-block;font-family:Arial;font-weight:600;font-size:14px;margin:2px 1px;cursor:pointer} Jump to a section: Drone Dominance A forward-looking philosophy Weapons and equipment Getting defensive Personnel Sponsored By: American Rheinmetall Back to Top A forward-looking philosophy ‘Noticeable shift in warfare’: Army under secretary on the lessons of modern combat The Army’s evolving priorities were reflected all over the AUSA show floor, according to Army Under Secretary Mike Obadal. In a sit-down with Military Times , Obadal highlighted areas that look nothing like the armor-heavy shows of years past. Obadal also discussed the high-low mix of exquisite and affordable munitions, faster acquisition cycles and why keeping a human in the loop remains the default for AI on the battlefield. Read more here . ‘We’ve drowned ourselves in buzzwords’: Acting secretary gives sermon-like first speech Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle’s AUSA speech differed significantly from his predecessor’s in 2025, but he quickly made it clear that the Army was holding the course set by former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who resigned Aug. 31 over growing disagreements and friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Telle hailed the Army’s work to streamline acquisition and reduce roadblocks to getting soldiers the gear they need, citing the Army’s work to reduce service “fiefdoms” from thousands to a few newly named portfolio acquisition executives. Read more here . The Army’s new warfare guidance Disrupt enemy command and control. Hit enemy forces with firepower , then assault with ground troops to finish the job. And be resilient enough to function despite what the enemy dishes out in return. That’s the essence of “How The Army Fights,” a new 46-page guide on how the U.S. Army can leverage the tactical to improve the operational . Read more here . 9 companies selected to build next-gen command and control software The U.S. Army announced that it is awarding initial contracts to several defense technology companies to build applications for its new battlefield software. The service will pay a one-year total of $93.6 million, spread out across nine companies, to create applications for its Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, software. The NGC2 will provide a shared network for technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications to operate within that will increase decision-making speed on the battlefield. Read more here . A second expeditionary cyber battalion on the horizon The Army will soon double the number of battalions it uses to train and deploy expeditionary cyberspace and electromagnetic warfare teams, according to the Army. At AUSA on Monday, head of Army Cyber Command Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank gave an approximate timeline for when the service would be delivering the new unit devoted to the exact same mission as the 11th Cyber Battalion, dubbed the Leviathans. Read more here . An Indo-Pacific manufacturing hub in Korea? As the Eighth Army in Korea builds out its logistics capability, it’s investing in advanced manufacturing with an eye to supplying spares, not only to local Army forces, but also to troops across the Pacific region . Eighth Army officials spoke earlier this year about how establishing a Korea-based regional sustainment hub, or center for logistics, maintenance and supply, could cut down the burden and cost of long-distance sustainment. At a roundtable event Monday, Eighth Army Commander Lt. Gen. Joseph Hilber indicated the force was moving out to build that sustainment hub. title: Pashinyan says he aims to sign peace agreement with Azerbaijan by end of his term in 2031
body: During Thursday’s government session, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that he intends to sign a peace agreement with Azerbaijan by 2031, which also marks the end of his current term and when the next parliamentary elections are set to take place in Armenia. The Armenia–Azerbaijan peace process entered a new stage after the 2025 US-mediated Washington summit, which brought together Pashinyan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, and US President Donald Trump, and resulted in the initialling — but not the signing — of a peace treaty. Pashinyan has been talking about the importance of signing the peace agreement every day this week and noted during the government session that signing and ratification of a peace agreement was his ‘most important task’. ‘But I have also set myself the goal of achieving a resolution of this issue by 2031. Naturally, this is also a task for the government and the political team, but as Armenia’s prime minister, I consider it very important in terms of my personal agenda as well that we resolve this issue by 2031. I see that this possibility exists; otherwise, I would not have spoken about it, and in the near future we must be focused on this agenda’, said Pashinyan. During the press briefing, Pashinyan was asked whether the 2031 deadline had been chosen so that he could complete it before the next elections and demonstrate results. ‘I have just been elected prime minister and have to plan my future actions. My term ends in 2031. What other dates can I give you? The term of this government and parliament is five years, isn't it? 2026 plus five equals 2031. What other number do you expect from me?’, he said . Although Armenian-Azerbaijani talks continue at various levels and in different formats, there are still unresolved issues between the two countries that prevent a peace agreement from being signed. One of the most important of these is border delimitation, and the issue of enclaves and exclaves. Armenia and Azerbaijan have four enclave and exclave clusters that have become the subject of political controversy in the process of demarcation and delimitation between the two countries. Karki, Barkhudarlyu, and Yukhari Askipara — Yukhari and Askipara are two separate villages that form a single cluster — are located in Armenia but are part of Azerbaijan according to the Almaty Declaration of 1991. Artsvashen, which is currently under Azerbaijani control, is considered to be part of Armenia. On Wednesday, explaining how he imagines the peace agreement with Azerbaijan, Pashinyan said that he believes there should be ‘no enclaves or exclaves on either side of the border’ as part of the peace agreement and that the two countries should exchange territories of corresponding sizes. Although Azerbaijan did not yet respond to Pashinyan’s recent announcements, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has previously demanded the return of Armenian exclaves that were Azerbaijani territory during the Soviet Union. In answer to a question about the importance of the enclave and exclave issue in the signing of the peace agreement, Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said on Thursday that, in contrast to the Armenian Constitution , the issue of enclaves and exclaves does not pose an obstacle to the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani officials, including Aliyev, have repeatedly stated that Armenia’s constitution contains territorial claims against Azerbaijan and demanded that it be changed, making it one of the biggest roadblocks to the signing of the peace treaty initialled in Washington in August 2025. The UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who is in Yerevan for the UN Leaders' Summit, urged Armenia and Azerbaijan to implement the provisions of the peace agreement during the press conference in Yerevan. He added that this naturally included the issue of detained persons. He was asked by reporters why the UN is not putting more pressure on Azerbaijan to release Armenian prisoners of war. ‘I am a strong supporter of the peace agreement. I hope all the provisions set out in it will be implemented. I regret the problems concerning the captives and the other issues. I hope all these matters will be resolved quickly’, said Guterres. Meanwhile, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has said he believes that the next meeting of foreign ministers within the ‘3+3’ regional format — Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Russia, Turkey, and Iran — could be held in Azerbaijan, followed by a meeting in Yerevan.

title: Republican Fitzpatrick Warns of Funding Consequences Over Ukraine’s Starlink Restrictions
body:
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick warned that Congress could withhold funding from US agencies responsible for restricting Ukraine’s military satellite service, The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday, Oct. 15.
“If we start going dark on Ukraine, there will be consequences, mark my words,” the Pennsylvania lawmaker said.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Asked what those consequences could be, he said: “Agencies won’t get funding if they’re not doing their jobs.”
His warning follows restrictions that disrupted Ukrainian drone operations during Russian attacks and prompted a bipartisan demand for an investigation.
Nine senators, led by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen and Republican Thom Tillis, asked the Pentagon’s inspector general on Oct. 15 to investigate disruptions to Starshield, communications and intelligence-sharing in Ukraine.
Their letter cited reports that American diplomatic, military and security personnel had been unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids amid disruptions to intelligence-sharing and early-warning capabilities.
The senators asked whether Pentagon officials or contractors contributed to the incidents, whether US officials approved or knew about the disruptions, and what measures were being taken to protect American personnel.
Separately, Reuters reported on Oct. 15, citing two US officials and a Western official, that the order to restrict Starshield in Ukraine originated inside the White House . The sources did not identify the decision-maker.
The restrictions affected satellite connections used by Ukrainian attack and interceptor drones. Connectivity was being restored for terminals moving at up to 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), Ukrainian officials said, but the speed ceiling continued to hamper some operations .
One Ukrainian source told RFE/RL that connections needed to work at speeds of at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour) to counter faster Russian drones effectively , as Kyiv Post previously reported.
Elon Musk distinguished commercial Starlink from the military-grade Starshield service, saying Starshield systems were owned and controlled by the US government and operational limits rested with the military and president.
The senators said Ukraine’s previous service arrangement allowed unlimited speeds and noted that at least some services were provided through contracts administered by the US Space Force.
British Defense Minister Wes Streeting said on Oct. 15 that he and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of Starlink service in Ukraine, Reuters reported.
Earlier Ukrainian accounts described partial restoration, including the 160-kilometer-per-hour ceiling. Streeting’s statement did not specify whether all speed restrictions had been removed.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Waymo to launch robotaxis in Toronto under pilot program for self-driving vehicles
body:
Self-driving taxi operator Waymo says it will launch a test phase in Toronto in the coming days, with the goal of carrying its first passengers in 2028.
The California-based company says the Ontario government has given it the green light to take part in a provincial pilot program that regulates testing of autonomous cars.
Waymo, a subsidiary of Google parent company Alphabet Inc., says the first phase includes high-definition street mapping and test runs of the robotaxis with a driver behind the wheel, starting this fall.
Skeptics of the technology say autonomous vehicles struggle to handle more complicated environments, including heavy traffic and bad weather, but Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana says the company is committed to safer streets and more accessible mobility.
For its launch in Canada, Waymo is partnering with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management, which will provide maintenance, customer service and other support functions.
Waymo’s distinctive white crossover SUVs will not be the first vehicles to traverse Toronto streets under the provincial pilot program, after California-based Gatik began a rollout of 50 autonomous box trucks for Loblaw in the city last year.

title: Strait of Hormuz to reopen if US forces withdraw from region — Iranian army
body:
RABAT, October 16. /TASS/. The Strait of Hormuz will be open to shipping once US forces withdraw from the Persian Gulf region, Iranian army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akrami-Nia said.
"If the US leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will open," the Fars news agency quoted him as saying. According to the defense official, in that case, "collective security will be established with the participation of regional states, and the global economy will improve."
"If they [the US] do not leave, then we [Iran] will expel them," the army spokesman added.

title: Wike questions Obi’s IDPs’ camps visits; Kwankwaso replies Shettima over ‘Bogus statistics’
body: By Ayobami Okerinde & Sekinat Osundiji Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Nyesom Wike, has questioned the sincerity of Peter Obi’s visits to internally displaced persons, IDPs, camps, suggesting that politicians may use displays of compassion to win public support ahead of the 2027 elections. Wike made the remarks on Thursday at the first Idoma Hall of Fame induction ceremony in Abuja, organised in collaboration with Ochetoha K’Idoma as part of the Idoma Centenary Plus celebration. Obi is the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC. In a related development, the vice-presidential candidate of NDC, Rabiu Kwankwaso, defended Peter Obi against Vice-President Kashim Shettima’s description of him as “the master of bogus statistics and incoherent economic prescriptions” . Shettima had criticised Obi on Wednesday at the inauguration of the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council at the State House Banquet Hall, Presidential Villa, Abuja. Describing Obi as “my very good friend”, the vice-president mocked his comparisons between Nigeria and other countries, particularly Bangladesh. “He seems convinced that a size 36 shirt tailored for Bangladesh will somehow fit Nigeria’s size 52 frame,” Shettima said. Wike Speaking on IDPs camps visits, Wike challenged the perception of Obi as a humble politician, citing the former Anambra governor’s visits to IDP camps, including one he made to mark his 62nd birthday in Plateau State in 2023. “Politicians can tell lies,” Wike said. “A man who did not celebrate his birthday when he was a governor now wants to be president and wants to celebrate his birthday in IDP camps? And you say, ‘Oh, he is very humble’. Which humility is that?” Obi, the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), recently said he had visited 12 IDP camps across the country in recent weeks. During a visit to the Ramin Kura IDP camp in Sokoto State, he shared pictures of himself interacting with children and described it as his 12th visit. The former governor also called on the government to improve conditions in the camps and urged political office holders to spend their holidays in Nigeria to experience the hardships faced by vulnerable citizens. Wike, however, warned Nigerians against being swayed by politicians who adopt public displays of modesty while seeking political office. He cited politicians who suddenly buy roasted corn and groundnuts in public or visit filling stations to comment on fuel prices, describing such gestures as attempts to appeal to voters. “You see a man who has never bought corn on the road suddenly buying corn and groundnuts in public. Who are you deceiving?” he asked. The FCT minister also urged Nigerians to assess the current administration’s performanceagainst the conditions that prevailed before it took office. Acknowledging the country’s economic and security challenges, Wike said the government’s efforts to address them should be considered before voters make political choices. “Nobody is happy that we are where we are. But if we are to trace our steps back to where we are coming from, are there attempts to improve the situation?” he said. He urged Nigerians to ignore politicians he described as “gamblers” as the country approaches the 2027 general election. Kwankwaso replies Vice President Shettima Reacting to Shettima’s comments during an interview on Channels TV on Thursday, Kwankwaso said he was not surprised by the vice-president’s remarks. “What else would you expect him to say?” Kwankwaso asked. “You see, I always listen to him (Obi). Like all others, I take time to check the statistics. As far as I’m concerned, most of the figures he was reeling out were correct. “And the only thing is, because as human beings, we are bound to make mistakes or slip of tongue, as they call it. But for him to come and make that statement, I don’t think he was correct.” Kwankwaso also praised Obi’s knowledge of development statistics, describing it as an advantage for a presidential candidate. “So I am happy that our presidential candidate is somebody who is conversant with the statistics not only in this country but all over the world, in Europe, in Asia, everywhere. And I think that is a good thing,” he added. Vanguard News The post Wike questions Obi’s IDPs’ camps visits; Kwankwaso replies Shettima over ‘Bogus statistics’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Money Transfers to Georgia Down 10.1% in September Amid Drop in Russia Transactions
body: Money transfers to Georgia from abroad fell by 10.1% year-on-year to USD 285.7 million in September 2026, marking the biggest annual decline recorded so far this year, according to the latest data published by the National Bank of Georgia (NBG). Transfers from Russia saw the sharpest annual drop, while the European Union and the United States remained the largest sources of transfers, together accounting for 72.3% of total inflows, or USD 206.7 million. Transfers from EU member countries alone amounted to USD 143.37 million, down 0.63% year-on-year and accounting for 50.1% of total inflows. The United States was the largest individual source of transfers, sending USD 63.39 million, or 22.1% of the total. Italy followed with USD 53.97 million (18.8%), Germany with USD 30.64 million (10.7%), Greece with USD 27.57 million (9.6%), and Israel with USD 26.3 million (9.2%). Transfers from Turkey totaled USD 11.34 million, accounting for 3.9% of the total, while those from Russia fell to USD 7.86 million, or 2.7% of all inflows. Although Russian transfers increased from USD 5.07 million in August , they fell 80.1% year-on-year, marking the steepest annual decline among the countries listed in the NBG data. Russian transfers amounted to USD 42.02 million in July and USD 51.42 million in June. The sharp decline follows the suspension of transfers to Georgia through Russia’s Zolotaya Korona money transfer system in July , which followed the EU’s latest sanctions package against Moscow. Among the reporting countries, the largest year-on-year increase was recorded in transfers from Lebanon at USD 1.22 million, an 80.5% increase. Transfers from Saudi Arabia increased 31.7% to USD 1.93 million, while those from Jordan rose 21.5% to USD 1.13 million. Transfers from Kyrgyzstan recorded the second-largest decline after Russia, falling by 72% year-on-year to USD 2.41 million. Inflows from Kazakhstan dropped by 33.9% to USD 5.01 million, while those from Poland fell by 33.2% to USD 2.01 million. Transfers from Azerbaijan and Ireland also declined by 15.7% to USD 2.86 million and 14.3% to USD 5.28 million, respectively. Meanwhile, transfers from Georgia to other countries totaled USD 36.9 million in September, down 3.5% from USD 38.2 million in the same month last year. Personal remittances to Georgia accounted for 11.2% of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), according to the World Bank’s 2025 data. title: Fuel crisis in Bali caused by tanker delay in particular — authorities
body:
TOKYO, October 16. /TASS/. The delay with arrival of a ship carrying 18 mln liters of fuel for the island became one of the causes of the fuel crisis in Bali, Governor of the Indonesian province Wayan Koster said.
"The ship was scheduled to dock on Sunday morning (October 11), but did not arrive until around 10 p.m. local time. This delay disrupted the scheduled fuel distribution to the depot," Koster said, cited by Antara news agency. "Distribution could not be restored immediately due to limited tanker trucks and available personnel. Consequently, fuel deliveries to gas stations were being carried out in stages," the news agency noted.
Fuel disruptions affected the public life but the tourism is safe thus far, the governor noted. ""We have not yet calculated the impact, but it is certainly affecting activities," Koster added.

title: Six Georgians convicted over 4 October ‘peaceful revolution’ released from prison
body: Six people convicted in connection with the 4 October events have been released from prison after reaching plea agreements with the prosecution. Publika reported from the scene as Kakhaber Kvachantiradze, Giorgi Talakhadze, Davit Giunashvili, Yuri Lomidze, Mikheil Tolaraia, and Gia Tolaraia left Gldani Prison after one year. The Prosecutor’s Office had accused all of participating in organised group violence. On 14 June they all reached plea agreements and were sentenced to one year of imprisonment and three years of probation. Speaking to TV Pirveli after leaving prison, Kvachantiradze said he wished freedom for all political prisoners and other people he described as ‘patriotic and decent’. He also expressed hope that an amnesty would be granted to people who considered their detention unjust. ‘I won’t say anything new — the whole country knows what kind of government we have. Sometimes a tactical retreat is necessary to achieve a strategic goal, Kvachantiradze said . Meanwhile, professional boxer Giorgi Kirvalidze, a defendant in the 4 October case, was detained again after completing a seven-day administrative arrest and leaving the Gurjaani detention facility. In a video published by activists, he can be heard being accused of violating article 366(2) of Georgia’s criminal code, which concerns insulting a judge. The offence is punishable by a fine, corrective labour for one to two years, or imprisonment for up to two years. Kirvalidze was sentenced to seven days of administrative arrest for insulting Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party. In response to the ruling, he addressed the judge, Tornike Kochkiani, saying: ‘You are an ordinary slave, Bidzina’s slave’. TV Pirveli reported that Kirvalidze also insulted Ivanishvili again during the same hearing. Kirvalidze, along with more than 30 other defendants in the 4 October case, had requested plea agreements with the prosecution. Under the terms of his agreement, he was sentenced to one year in prison and three years of probation. However, in late August, the Tbilisi Court of Appeals annulled the plea agreement at the request of the Prosecutor’s Office. During the appeal hearing, Kirvalidze said his remarks during the plea agreement proceedings had been made in a moment of agitation. Kirvalidze had been charged with participating in group violence and attempting to seize and blockade a facility of strategic or special importance. ‘A peaceful revolution’ The 4 October protest was timed to take place with the widely boycotted municipal elections . Months prior to the elections, some opposition figures promised to end Georgian Dream’s 13-year rule in a single day, but did not announce any concrete plans. The protest was billed as a ‘peaceful revolution’ meant to achieve what months of leaderless protests could not. Initially, the campaigners’ efforts seemed to pay off. On the day, tens of thousands gathered in central Tbilisi, briefly reviving the dwindling daily protests. Chaos soon followed: opera singer and opposition figure Paata Burchuladze declared that power belonged to the people, and opposition politician Murtaz Zodelava called for a march on the nearby Presidential Palace. A small group then breached a section of the palace fence, but was quickly pushed back by riot police, sparking sporadic clashes. The crowd split, frustration spread, and the rally fizzled out. Between frustration and persistence, the Georgian protest movement reflects on 4 October After the unfulfilled ‘peaceful revolution’ of 4 October, Georgia’s anti-government movement continues amidst debate, repression, and uncertainty. OC Media Mikheil Gvadzabia The ruling party quickly seized on the Presidential Palace episode to once again attack the anti-government movement, branding it, as many times before, a violent, foreign-orchestrated coup attempt.

title: New operational plans are currently underway: Iran Army spox
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Spokesman for the Iranian Army Brigadier General Akraminia has said that new operational plans are currently underway that will force hostile American vessels to flee to even greater distances.
Speaking in an interview on Friday, General Mohammad Akraminia emphasized, “Despite Trump’s repeated allegations, Iran’s current air defense capabilities far surpass pre-war and wartime levels.”
Iranian air defense units have successfully downed multiple US drones in the country's airspace in recent weeks, he said, adding, “US military vessels have been forced to retreat to distances exceeding 500 kilometers from the Persian Gulf coasts.”
"If America leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the region's countries, and the global economy will improve. If it doesn't leave, we'll expel it."
He, who is also the deputy coordinator of the Army's Ideological-Political Organization, reiterated that new operational plans are currently underway that will force hostile American vessels to flee to even greater distances.
Advanced combined and innovative military operations have been successfully rehearsed, he underlined.
National air defense coverage across the country has been significantly strengthened compared to pre-war levels, he stated, stressing, “The insecurity witnessed today in east of the Strait of Hormuz is a direct consequence of the destructive US presence.”
Regional states and the international community must acknowledge that the US is the primary root cause of this instability in the region, General Akraminia added.

title: Russia and Kyrgyzstan Sign Military Cooperation Plan for 2027
body: Russia and Kyrgyzstan signed a military cooperation plan for 2027 on October 15, a day after Russian lawmakers approved measures to simplify arms deliveries to Bishkek. Defense ministers Andrei Belousov and Ruslan Mukambetov signed the agreement in Cholpon-Ata, on the shores of Lake Issyk-Kul, ahead of a meeting of defense ministers from the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The plan’s contents have not been made public. Russia’s Defense Ministry said the two sides discussed military personnel training, military-technical cooperation, and the operation of the joint Russian military base in Kyrgyzstan. Russia’s military presence in Kyrgyzstan consists of four facilities, including Kant Air Base, around 20 kilometers from Bishkek, which Russian forces have used since 2003. It is part of the forces of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO). The other facilities are a Russian Navy communications station in Chaldovar, a seismic monitoring station in Mailuu-Suu, and a naval weapons testing base near Karakol on Lake Issyk-Kul. Belousov inspected the Issyk-Kul facility on October 14. The base tests anti-submarine weapons and systems designed to protect ships and submarines from torpedo attacks. The joint military base operates under bilateral agreements. Its current structure took shape after Russia’s military facilities in Kyrgyzstan were brought together under an agreement signed in 2012, which entered into force in 2017. On October 14, Russia’s State Duma ratified a protocol simplifying military-technical cooperation with Kyrgyzstan. Signed in November 2025, the protocol allows military equipment to be supplied under contracts between authorized organizations without additional import and export licenses. It also simplifies procedures for spare parts, repairs, and maintenance. The changes could speed up deliveries to the Kyrgyz military, although no new contracts have been announced. In 2025, Russia and Kyrgyzstan signed a strategic military partnership program covering 2026–2030. The two defense ministries have now agreed on their work for the coming year. Kyrgyzstan also maintains military ties with other countries. In February 2026, representatives of U.S. Central Command, the U.S. Air Force, and the Montana National Guard discussed joint training plans for fiscal year 2027 with Kyrgyz military officials.

title: Ghana Association of University Administrators suspends nationwide strike
body: The Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) has suspended its nationwide strike, effective Friday, October 16. Members are therefore to report to work from Monday, October 19. The association says the decision was taken after a final engagement with the Ministry of Education, with a firm assurance to address all their concerns. National President of GAUA, Rev. Kwaku Karikari Amoah, announced the suspension after a meeting of the association’s National Executive Committee (NEC), saying members had agreed to return to work while negotiations continued on the outstanding issues. “After we had done a thorough evaluation, we came to the consensus that about 80% of our grievances have been met,” Rev. Amoah said. He added that the remaining concerns would continue to be discussed with relevant government stakeholders. “On that basis, we agreed unanimously that we suspend the strike action so that our members will go back to the offices on Monday to work,” he said. Rev. Amoah said the association had raised several concerns before embarking on the strike, including market premium, what it described as wrongful placement on the Single Spine Salary Structure, a negotiated 40 per cent allowance for professionals in technical and public universities, the extension of the retirement rule beyond the fifth year, and a one-off allowance payment. He said the NEC reviewed each of these issues before deciding to suspend the industrial action. The GAUA President acknowledged the role played by the Education Minister in facilitating discussions aimed at resolving the concerns. “As the Minister just said, we brought our grievances to him for redress, and he has so far helped us and facilitated the process for some of these grievances to be addressed,” he said. Although the association considers most of its concerns to have been addressed, Rev. Amoah said engagements with government officials would continue until the outstanding matters were resolved. The suspension therefore allows members to resume their duties while discussions on the remaining grievances continue. Rev. Amoah said the NEC’s decision was unanimous and reflected the association’s assessment of the progress made through negotiations. He explained that the NEC was GAUA’s second-highest decision-making body after Congress and had the authority to take the decision on behalf of the association. He said the return to work would help restore normal administrative operations and support efforts to maintain calm across public university campuses. “GAUA has suspended its strike action, and we are going back to the offices to complement the efforts of our colleagues on campus to ensure that there is peace and tranquillity on our university campuses,” he said.

title: The Download: failed social media bans, and extending pets’ lives
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve. —Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. Here’s what we ought to do instead to keep kids safe . Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered. —Jessica Hamzelou I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? Read the full story on the promises and pitfalls of pet life extension . This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday. 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Form Energy and its iron batteries Form Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods. Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours. The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges. See how Form Energy hopes to make renewable power more reliable . —Jonathan W. Rosen Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from electric buses to portable rubber dams . The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Insurance is the next big obstacle for AI AI companies are racking up billions of dollars of legal liabilities from the damage their products cause. ( WSJ $) + The FTC has sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic over consumer harms. ( Axios ) + AI hacks leave a mess, and AI companies still aren’t cleaning them up. ( Wired $) + Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 A Russian drone entered NATO waters for the first time Attacks like those near Bulgaria and Romania are spurring requests for better defenses. ( Ars Technica ) 3 An AI sell-off has rattled global markets Many are questioning the sustainability of demand for data centers. ( Reuters $) + Anthropic reported slowing growth in its latest quarterly results. ( FT $) + Accenture has told employees they can only spend $29 on Claude each month. ( 404 Media ) + What’s at stake in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Governments are hacking people with ‘zero click’ spyware Delivered through millions of innocuous-looking online adverts. ( TechCrunch ) + Criminals stole $90 million from crypto wallets last week in a highly sophisticated hack. ( FT $) 5 Big Tech gave Trump $92 million for his ballroom Meanwhile the president himself won’t be spending a dime. ( WP $) 6 Celebrity deepfakes are everywhere now And they’re selling you stuff the actual celebrity has probably never even heard of. ( The Verge $) + Weaponized deepfakes have been on the rise for a while. ( MIT Technology Review ) 7 Can AI lighten parents’ mental load? It seems apps and agents can help—if you agree to share masses of your data. ( NYT $) + AI agents are a privacy nightmare. ( The Verge $) 8 The memory shortage’s latest victim is schools It’s becoming prohibitively expensive to equip students with laptops and tablets. ( The Atlantic $) 9 The world’s official timekeepers have agreed to ditch the leap second It’s a move that ought to cut the risk of time-based computer glitches. ( The Guardian ) 10 Tesla has finally unveiled its flying car It’s taken a decade to get here—and still won’t even be shipping next year. ( CNBC ) Quote of the day “Tech companies used to make an effort to support women…Now we’ve swung completely in the opposite direction. Supporting women in tech has become controversial. It’s become political. It’s become risky.” —Startup founder Sara Mauskopt explains why the cancellation of the Grace Hopper Celebration, one of the biggest gatherings of women in tech, hits so hard, Bloomberg reports. One More Thing SIMON MITCHELL Inside the experimental world of animal infrastructure In the mid-2000s, toads were meeting a gruesome end near Ede, a leafy old town in the Netherlands. Residents responded by building wildlife tunnels beneath the road to help them reach their breeding ponds safely. The crossings became popular. But a few years later, researchers found the local toad population had crashed from more than 10,000 to fewer than 1,000. The case reflects a wider global push to build wildlife crossings and other forms of “animal infrastructure.” But do they actually help animal populations recover? Read the full story to find out . —Matthew Ponsford We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Check out this podcast about the incredible, mysterious powers of fungi. + A four-year-old boy’s simple habit of waving to his neighbors is transforming his community. + From treehouses to geodesic domes, these homes show what happens when people build outside the rules . + Remember when the internet was made by people? The Museum of the Human Web is a playful archive of that era.

title: Europe's far right has a Putin problem
body:
Rassemblement National (RN) candidate Marine Le Pen in Paris, France, on Sept. 28, 2026. (Anne-Christine Poujoulat / AFP via Getty Images)
Europe's far-right parties grow increasingly divided on something that once united them — sympathies for Vladimir Putin's Russia.
As nationalists and right-wing populists across Western Europe move closer to power, many are seeking to distance themselves from their past admiration for a country waging Europe's largest war since 1945 while conducting hybrid attacks against much of the continent.
Despite finding common ground on dislike of liberalism, NATO, and the EU, Europe's far right is being forced to rethink its relationship with Moscow — much like it had to do with U.S. President Donald Trump.
France 's National Rally (RN) and the U.K.'s Nigel Farage now harden rhetoric on Russia while signaling a more conditional, rather than simply hostile, approach to Ukraine, as part of a strategy to cast a wider net of voters.
But the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has emerged as Europe's largest and most extreme nationalist party, is moving in the opposite direction.
The split comes at a critical moment. The National Rally's Marine Le Pen is a frontrunner for the French presidential election next April, the AfD is leading the German polls, and Farage's Reform party was, until very recently, a favorite to win the next elections in Britain.
Experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent explain the reasons behind this divide and what the coming string of European elections could mean for Ukraine.
For years, far-right leaders have been ranked among the most Moscow-friendly voices in European politics.
In 2014, Farage, the man who later led a campaign to push the U.K. out of the EU and whose Reform party now polls second at 22%, expressed his admiration for Putin as an "operator."
As recently as 2024, while Russia’s full-scale invasion had already been raging for two years, he suggested that the eastward expansion of the EU and NATO provoked the war.
Comments like these have made it easy for his opponents to blast him as a Putin fan.
Now, Farage seems intent on proving he is no such thing.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?"
Last year, the Reform leader called the Russian dictator a "very bad dude" and said NATO should shoot down Russian jets intruding into its airspace.
On Ukraine, he has cautiously affirmed support for Ukraine — even backing the idea of using frozen Russian assets for Kyiv's benefit.
And while he criticized plans for a post-war " reassurance " force in Ukraine as outlined by the Labor government, Farage backed sending British troops to the country, if on a temporary basis and as part of a U.N. peacekeeping mission.
Reports have emerged that Farage is even considering a trip to Ukraine as part of his quest to brush off his Russia-friendly image.
A similar shift is taking place across the English Channel.
Prior to 2022, Le Pen said that the Russian occupation of Crimea was not illegal, and her party took out a loan from a Russian bank.
But after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, she backpedaled.
Now, the three-time failed presidential candidate sees she has a real chance to win, with a court clearing a path to her candidacy despite last year's embezzlement conviction.
As the vote nears, she is treading cautiously on foreign policy.
Le Pen has condemned Russian aggression and has backed continued military assistance to Ukraine, even as she wants Paris to cut financial aid — citing France's own budget constraints — opposes Kyiv's EU membership , and is skeptical about future EU aid if it burdens France.
She also said she would be happy to visit Ukraine for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The RN's younger co-leader, Jordan Bardella, has taken a tougher stance on Russia, naming the country a threat — something that Le Pen avoided in a recent interview with the Financial Times .
Both party chiefs also blasted Moscow in September over its seizure of European business assets in the country and denounced Russian interference and destabilization efforts.
Elsewhere in Europe, far-right parties have proved they can tone down their views on Russia and Ukraine in exchange for government seats.
Matteo Salvini, head of Italy's League party, remembered for once sporting a T-shirt with Putin's likeness, has largely fallen in line behind Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's firmly pro-Western, pro-Ukraine course, save for some symbolic resistance.
And the former Dutch government also maintained its support for Kyiv, even though Geert Wilders's far-right Party for Freedom (PVV) was the strongest party in a short-lived coalition.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a right-wing populist, while expressing his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine, echoed Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S.
"Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin, and we have to do something," Babis said on Oct. 16.
This shift is far from uniform, however.
As Meloni, Italy's right-wing, anti-immigration prime minister, prepares for the 2027 elections, she faces a new pro-Kremlin challenger.
Roberto Vannacci, a retired army general, left the League in February to found his own nationalist party, National Future.
Vannacci, a former military attaché in Moscow, has famously said he prefers Putin over Zelensky.
With support reaching as high as 8% in recent polls, National Future has already surpassed Meloni's junior coalition partners.
But the most striking example is the AfD, currently the strongest opposition party in Germany, nearing 30% in polls.
The AfD was seen as so extreme that the far-right European Parliament group expelled it at the RN's urging in 2024, prompting the AfD to form a new ultranationalist coalition, Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN).
The party campaigns on a halt to military and financial aid to Ukraine, the lifting of sanctions against Russia, and the resumption of Russian energy purchases.
Given the AfD's particular brand of extremism and Berlin's role as the leading military donor to Ukraine, this is an especially worrying signal for Kyiv and Europe.
Like in the U.K., the next German parliamentary elections are expected no later than 2029.
With Russia's full-scale war nearing its fifth anniversary, many countries have seen the public's support for Ukraine cool — but not collapse.
Politicians vying for victory in upcoming elections have to take this into account, with the U.K. being a prime example.
Farage's party certainly has a reputation to fix, after its former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, was sentenced to prison for taking bribes from pro-Russian Ukrainian politicians.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?" Tim Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, comments on Reform's strategy.
A poll from last fall shows that 59% of Brits support continued assistance to Ukraine, and slightly over half back sanctions even at the cost of paying more for energy and food.
The support is somewhat cooler in France, where 47% favor continued arms deliveries to Ukraine, down from 65% in 2022.
Yet this is not an insignificant number, and the majority of French people — including a little over half of RN voters — see Russia as an enemy , according to polls.
Anton Shekhovtsov, a visiting senior fellow at Central European University in Vienna, notes that Le Pen likely remembers well the "reputational nightmare" her Russian loan has caused.
"Everybody just pointed to that loan and said, 'you're all Russian Trojan horses in France,'" Shekhovtsov said in comments for the Kyiv Independent.
Now, Le Pen likely sees an example in Meloni — a politician who emerged from a similar far-right background but maintained a pro-Western course, the expert notes. Meloni's government has been Italy's longest-serving since World War II.
But the AfD has doubled down on its pro-Russian course, despite the majority of Germans continuing to support Ukraine. It does not seem to be hindering its rise.
Jakub Wondreys, a researcher at the Hannah Arendt Institute for the Research on Totalitarianism in Dresden, offers an explanation.
"The key factor is the party's internal division, which we don't see elsewhere. It is specific to German politics, and to the AfD itself," Wondreys tells the Kyiv Independent.
While all parties have different wings, the AfD is notably decentralized, with the former border between West and East Germany surviving as a key divide.
The AfD's extremist, more Moscow-friendly wing is rooted in East Germany, a former Soviet satellite state. The "moderates" are stronger in the west, the researcher explains.
The AfD is growing nationwide, but the east remains its main stronghold — as evidenced by its recent victories in regional elections there. This means that the more extreme wing of the party is also its loudest and most influential one.
This split was laid bare when the AfD's two leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, disagreed over a trip by a group of their colleagues to Sochi last November.
Weidel, who hails from what was West Germany, criticized the visit, while Chrupalla, himself born in socialist East Germany, downplayed it, adding that he does not consider Russia a threat.
Recent polls show that 54% of Germans from what was East Germany think aid to Ukraine has gone too far, compared to 39% in the west. Eastern Germans are also less likely to see Russia as a threat.
Yet even an RN or Reform victory would not bode well for Ukraine, regardless of their change of rhetoric, experts warn.
As Bale points out, no matter its public posturing, a Reform government "might try to spend less money on defense aid behind everyone's back."
Just on Oct. 12, Farage pledged to take a "keen look" at whether British aid to Ukraine is being swallowed up by corruption there and signaled that London's support cannot be limitless.
The RN's victory might not end military support for Ukraine, but it will likely curtail the financial assistance and weaken the European sanctions push against Moscow.
And Shekhovtsov warns that even if Le Pen does not adopt overtly pro-Russian positions after the elections, her victory could be such an upset for France and Europe that it might shift political attention away from supporting Ukraine.
The coming election season has the potential to shake the European pro-Ukraine coalition to its core.
I hope you enjoyed this article. In our team, we believe fact-based reporting should be available to all – that's why we don't use any paywall.
If you'd like to help us provide you with more in-depth coverage of Ukraine's struggle against Russian aggression, European politics, and other topics, please consider joining the Kyiv Independent community .
Martin Fornusek is an assistant editor at the Kyiv Independent. Until recently, Martin held the role of foreign affairs reporter specializing in international and regional politics, history, and disinformation. Based in Lviv, Martin often reports on international politics, focusing on developments related to Ukraine and Russia. His career in journalism began in 2021 after graduating from Masaryk University in Brno, Czechia, earning a Master's degree in Conflict and Democracy Studies. Martin has been invited to speak on Times Radio, France 24, Czech Television, and Radio Free Europe. He speaks English, Czech, and Ukrainian.

title: Situation in Middle East harms security in Eurasia — Russian Security Council
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The situation in the Middle East is adversely affecting security across the Eurasian region and disrupting existing global logistics chains, Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexey Shevtsov said at a conference of the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the Commonwealth of Independent States and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization on security issues in Central Asia and Afghanistan.
"The situation in the Middle East not only has a negative impact on the security environment across the entire Eurasian region, but also disrupts established global logistics chains and undermines food and energy security," he said.
"It is precisely thanks to close cooperation ties that Russia and the countries of Central Asia are withstanding the current resource crisis without significant economic losses," the Russian Security Council deputy secretary stressed.

title: Gov Diri didn’t speak on Coastal Highway as local champion — Murray-Bruce replies Duke
body: By Bayo Wahab Former senator Ben Murray-Bruce has faulted Donald Duke over his description of Bayelsa State Governor Douye Diri as a “local champion” in the debate over the feasibility of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway. Murray-Bruce said Diri was speaking as a statesman who recognised the value of infrastructure built to international standards, insisting that the governor’s support for the project was not based on a narrow state-level perspective. He stated this in a series of posts on X on Friday while reacting to the exchange between Duke, the presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party, PRP, and Diri over the coastal highway project. Duke had questioned the feasibility and affordability of constructing the highway through Bayelsa’s swampy terrain, prompting the governor to defend the project and highlight his administration’s experience in building roads and bridges across swamps and mangroves. Responding to Duke’s criticism, Diri, through his Chief Press Secretary, Daniel Alabrah, said the former Cross River State governor was not abreast of developments in road construction and infrastructure in Bayelsa. “Clearly, he is not abreast of current developments in road construction and infrastructure development in our state,” Diri said. However, Duke, speaking during an interview on Arise Television on Thursday, dismissed the governor’s defence, arguing that Diri was considering the project from a state-level perspective rather than its broader implications for Nigeria. “The governor of Bayelsa, if he did say so, I don’t know the fellow, but if he did say so, I think he’s just being a local champion,” Duke said. Reacting, Murray-Bruce said he was surprised by Duke’s recent comments, recalling that they had travelled together along the coastline where the highway is being constructed and that Duke had previously praised the vision behind the project. “My dear brother Donald Duke, some years ago, you and I travelled along the stretch of the coastline where this road now runs, and I clearly remember your praise for the vision behind it. That is why your recent comments surprised me,” he said. While acknowledging the high cost of the project, Murray-Bruce argued that major infrastructure investments required substantial funding and should be assessed in terms of their long-term benefits. “Yes, the Coastal Highway is expensive. We agree on that. But nothing of lasting value in this world is cheap or free. Great nations are built by leaders willing to make bold, costly investments that will serve generations yet unborn,” he said. He added that President Bola Tinubu had committed to funding the project and was fulfilling that commitment. Murray-Bruce also rejected suggestions that the project was facing funding challenges, saying construction was progressing and describing the quality of the work as “second to none”. “There is no funding shortfall. The work is progressing, and the quality of construction is second to none,” he said. Defending Diri against Duke’s remarks, Murray-Bruce said the Bayelsa governor’s support for the highway reflected an appreciation of its significance beyond his state. “When Governor Douye Diri commended the road, he was not speaking as a local champion; he was speaking as a statesman who recognises infrastructure of international standard when he sees it. I agree with him completely,” he said. Murray-Bruce acknowledged Duke’s right to criticise the project as a presidential candidate but warned against allowing political interests to undermine infrastructure he described as nationally important. “Donald, I understand that you are running for president, and that your statement is political. That is the nature of the season, and I respect your right to make your case to Nigerians. But we must be careful never to undermine a project of national importance, or the President delivering it, simply for political advantage,” he said. Comparing the highway to the United States’ space programme, he argued that costly projects could still be necessary for national development. “When mankind went to the moon, it was neither cheap nor free. But it was necessary. So is this road,” Murray-Bruce said. The post Gov Diri didn’t speak on Coastal Highway as local champion — Murray-Bruce replies Duke appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Uzbekistan Confirms Cancellation of Saneg Oil Licenses
body: Uzbekistan has revoked some oil-field licenses held by Sanoat Energetika Guruhi (Saneg), a major Uzbek private oil and gas producer, after the company failed to develop deposits and meet licensing conditions. The move is another setback for the company, formerly known as Jizzakh Petroleum, following the collapse of its $100 million agreement to purchase the Fergana Oil Refinery. When the refinery sale was announced in 2022, Saneg was reported to account for approximately 80% of Uzbekistan’s oil production and hold development rights to 103 oil and gas fields. Officials have not said how many licenses have been canceled, which fields are affected, or what impact the decision will have on the company’s operations. Speaking at an October 8 press conference, Sohibjon Murodov, director of the State Assets Management Agency, said the affected deposits had not been developed and licensing conditions had not been met. He did not disclose when the licenses were canceled. The Ministry of Mining Industry and Geology is now preparing measures for the affected fields. Asked why Saneg had originally received development rights without competitive auctions, Murodov explained that under the previous system, the first applicant could obtain a license after paying the prescribed fees. Auctions for hydrocarbon licenses were introduced in 2023–2024. He stressed that the deposits themselves had remained state property. A Privatization Reversed The government transferred management of the Fergana refinery to Saneg, then operating as Jizzakh Petroleum, in 2020. In May 2022, it announced the $100 million sale, accompanied by a separate commitment to invest $380 million in modernization. The transaction was intended to address longstanding problems. Reporting at the time described shortages of raw materials and said the refinery had not undergone major modernization or reconstruction for two decades. Saneg’s investment commitments covered improvements to fuel production and processing facilities. Despite the announced sale, the state still held 58.5% of the refinery in May 2026, while Saneg owned 41.5%. By June, the State Assets Management Agency was its sole owner, according to registry information reported by Interfax. Explaining the termination in October, Murodov said financial difficulties in the investor’s other projects had prevented it from making purchase payments on time. The contract allowed termination if payments were three months overdue , he said. The agency consulted international legal advisers and notified Saneg before ending the agreement. Saneg had previously maintained that it had fulfilled its payment and investment obligations, according to Interfax’s June report. However, the amount of the overdue payments remains unclear, as does how earlier payments and investments will be treated and how much modernization work was completed. State-Directed Debt Recovery The state had already intervened in January to address financial problems at Saneg, oilfield services company Eriell, and engineering contractor Enter Engineering. Uzbek reporting has linked all three businesses to businessman Bakhtiyor Fozilov. A January 22 government resolution recorded combined unpaid wages of approximately $131 million owed to 38,700 employees across the three companies, according to reporting by Spot in March. The government ordered the sale of non-core assets to help repay the debts, with unpaid wages given priority. Assets were to be transferred to Saneg Aktiv for sale, with proceeds deposited in a special bank account and distributed under the direction of a government working group. The measures also covered tax liabilities and loans from unaffiliated banks. The assets listed for disposal included eight hotels at the Silk Road Samarkand tourism complex, company offices, and a medical center in Tashkent. The measures also restricted the companies’ ability to sell, transfer, or pledge assets independently. Officials were instructed to seek new investors for unfinished strategic projects, including modernization of the Fergana refinery. Recovery Under State Ownership On October 5, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reviewed efforts to improve the refinery’s finances and production . His administration reported that repairs had increased diesel output by 30%, bitumen by 60%, and aviation fuel output to five times its previous level, although it did not specify the comparison period or absolute volumes. Official accounts differ on how much of the refinery’s capacity is being used. The presidential statement set a target of increasing utilization from 40% to 65% by year-end. Yet Murodov said on October 8 that utilization was already approaching 100% . Neither account explains the discrepancy. Murodov also said an international audit was underway to establish the refinery’s liabilities and determine how its debts would be repaid or restructured. Another privatization is not currently planned. Four years after the original sale agreement, the government is once again overseeing efforts to secure the refinery’s raw-material supplies, increase production, and address its debts.

title: Fans threaten to boycott Davido’s December concerts over Adeleke’s support for Tinubu
body:
Some Nigerians on social media have threatened to boycott Davido’s three December concerts in Lagos after Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke endorsed President Bola Tinubu for a second term.
The backlash followed Mr Adeleke’s appointment as the Osun coordinator of Mr Tinubu’s 2027 presidential campaign, a development that surprised some supporters because the governor belongs to the Accord Party.
PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that Mr Adeleke pledged his support for the president during the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council inauguration at the State House in Abuja on Wednesday.
The governor said Mr Tinubu needed another four years to consolidate his administration’s economic reforms.
Davido announced on X on Thursday that he would perform for three consecutive nights at the National Theatre in Lagos from 17 to 19 December.
The concerts, tagged Oriadè: The Residency, will mark the singer’s return home and commemorate his 15 years in the music industry.
According to the singer, the performances will feature songs from his latest album, Oriadè, alongside selections from his earlier projects.
However, the announcement attracted criticism from some social-media users opposed to his uncle’s support for Mr Tinubu.
Some vowed not to buy tickets for the concerts, while others sarcastically urged the singer to rely on family members and the APC to fill the venue.
The controversy also revived discussions about Davido’s previous remarks against the APC during the Osun governorship election.
In an earlier post on X, the singer described APC supporters in the state as “enemies of progress”.
Some users cited the post while questioning the apparent difference between Davido’s earlier political stance and his uncle’s decision to support the APC president.
Others accused the singer of hypocrisy for remaining silent while Mr Adeleke openly rallied support for Mr Tinubu.
Several users also criticised the Adeleke family, arguing that the governor’s decision disregarded the sacrifices supporters made during the campaign that brought him to office.
They recalled the violence, hardship, and losses some residents allegedly experienced during the struggle for Mr Adeleke’s electoral victory, saying his support for Mr Tinubu undermined those sacrifices.
However, other users urged the public to separate Davido from his uncle’s political choices, arguing that the singer should not be punished for a decision he did not make.
As of press time, Davido had not publicly responded to the boycott calls.
Below are some of the comments posted in response to the concert announcement.

title: Maritime phase of Russian-Indian Indra 2026 exercise begins in Vladivostok
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The maritime phase of the joint Russian-Indian Indra 2026 exercise has started at the Russian Pacific Fleet’s main base in Vladivostok, the fleet’s press service said.
"The maritime phase of the joint Russian-Indian cross-branch exercise Indra 2026 has begun in Vladivostok at the Pacific Fleet’s main base. The Pacific Fleet corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and the Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri have sailed into the Sea of Japan to conduct maneuvers," the fleet said in a statement.
It said that during the maritime phase, the ships will conduct live-fire drills using their naval artillery systems against surface and air targets. "A separate exercise will involve repelling attacks by uncrewed boats and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) of a simulated adversary. Shipborne helicopters from the ships of the two friendly nations will fly in accordance with the exercise objectives and practice landing on each other’s vessels," the Pacific Fleet’s press service added.
It also said that the final stage will involve practicing the release of a vessel seized by pirates.
"The warships’ crews will conduct joint maneuvers and test communications between the vessels, as well as other elements of cooperation at sea," the press service said.
The joint Russian-Indian cross-branch exercise Indra 2026, comprising maritime, land, and air phases, began on October 14, 2026.

title: Millions of Ukrainians Could Flee Again This Winter: UN
body:
Millions of Ukrainians who fled Russia’s full-scale invasion and later returned home are at risk of being displaced again over the coming winter, the United Nations warned Friday.
The UN’s International Organization for Migration said repeated Russian attacks on civilian energy infrastructure were leaving families with few alternatives.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Winter is fast approaching in Ukraine and for many Ukrainians the months ahead could be the most difficult since the full-scale war began,” said Arthur Erken, the IOM’s regional director for Europe and central Asia.
“Millions of Ukrainians who fled and returned are now at risk of being displaced once again, as conditions deteriorate by the day and people face desperate choices in the struggle to survive.”
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in February 2022, triggering the biggest refugee crisis in Europe since World War II.
The agency estimates that nearly 3.6 million people remain internally displaced within Ukraine. Around 3.8 million people have returned to their homes, which are often damaged.
It said an estimated 1.45 million returnees lived in frontline districts, including 565,000 in the Kharkiv region alone.
Erken said Russian drone attacks “tend to attack civilian infrastructure”, and repeated strikes had damaged Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water systems.
He said reliable access to water was an urgent concern because water systems depend on electricity.
The IOM has developed 31 solar power stations across the country to support water systems, as these were “harder to attack and harder to destroy completely”.
Erken said that for 2.1 million older people living alone in apartment blocks, a prolonged loss of heat or electricity “can quickly become a humanitarian emergency”.
“Alternatives to electricity, including gas stoves and fuel, will be critical this winter,” he told a press briefing in Geneva, speaking from Vienna.
Erken said Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic were hosting the largest number of Ukrainian refugees.
“I’m sure that these countries are preparing for the eventuality that Ukrainians will try to leave the country, should the situation deteriorate,” he said.
The IOM said less than seven percent of its Ukraine crisis response plan for 2026 has been funded.
“The international community must act now,” said Erken.

title: India seeking to exchange experience in utilities services with Russia
body:
KAZAN, October 16. /TASS/. India is interested in an exchange of experience in the provision of utilities services in large cities with Russia, Jeysundhar Deviprasadh, the Consul General of India in Kazan, said, addressing the business forum "TIME: Russia - India. Mutual Efficiency" in Kazan.
"India offers its own approach to how to provide utilities services on a scale that is much or even ten times higher than in Kazan. Such cooperation would benefit both sides, for each of them makes its own contribution and can teach the other something useful and share its experience," he said at the session titled, "Russia - India: From Municipal Dialogue to Joint Tourism Projects."
Both sides have something to learn from each other, the consul general noted. "Kazan and other Russian cities [boast of] reliability, independence from harsh weather conditions, especially in winter, when temperatures fall to -30, uninterrupted hot water and gas supplies, and regular maintenance, including waste disposal and waste management," he explained.
According to him, the challenges facing cities are universal. "These primarily include vital infrastructure for people: water and fuel supplies. The other part [involving] solid and liquid waste removal is much more challenging. These problems are typical of not only India and Russia but also across the globe," he emphasized.
Kazan is hosting the second business forum "TIME: Russia - India. Mutual Efficiency" on October 14-17 on the premises of the Center of Unique Craftsmanship. The business program includes sessions across such key topics as investment and innovation, logistics, industrial production, international cooperation, the social environment, education, agriculture, medicine, business, media, culture, sports, and tourism. Among other participants, Indian federal government officials and representatives of Indian administrative divisions are attending. Also, the Indian ambassador to Russia is taking part. TASS is the event’s general media partner.

title: The AI Bill Is the Cheap Part
body:
Does it feel like your team is experimenting nonstop and working hard, yet you’re not really moving faster? Is the board scrutinizing your AI costs ballooning like my expenses when I enter an Italian menswear store?
Startups with 30+ engineers easily waste more than $1m a year on neglecting how their engineers operate. Isn’t it ridiculous to put all this focus on the AI agents? The real difference lies in helping your people. AI only multiplies whatever you already have in your hands. A poorly functioning team will just go about its way, producing poor results ever faster (and sometimes, ever poorer).
Turning your attention to tokens and compute cost is myopic and lazy. We’re reaching for the easiest thing right in front of us, neglecting the real issues. I remember one of the first rules I was taught in my first professional coding role: you don’t optimize without measuring first, or you’ll end up optimizing the wrong problems.
So let’s look at the measurements: what really afflicts tech orgs? And we don’t have to limit ourselves to the companies I happened to work with; there’s a lot more data available. Atlassian and other surveys routinely show more than 15-20% of engineers’ time getting wasted in bad processes and quality issues.
Even worse, I find the issue isn’t time clearly wasted, but the time we don’t realize is wasted. Beyond firefighting, there’s misalignment, misunderstandings, and busywork. Tackling those would result in a much bigger bang for your buck as a leader.
My recommendation is to collect real evidence of what’s happening across your organization for a period of two weeks and see where your time and costs are really going. To help you know what you’re looking for, here are the most common issues I tackle with clients, along with tips for handling them.
Quality issues, supporting the existing codebase, and responding to urgent requests often leave teams thrashing without making substantial progress on their declared priorities. How much time each week or iteration ends up going into unplanned work? That’s a good metric for time going to waste, which you can then trace back to the root causes and tackle them:
This is about work that’s just not important. For example, when the engineers tackle edge cases that don’t matter at the smaller scale. On the other end of the spectrum, we see Product and Engineering deciding to prioritize work that’s not really the most important and impactful due to various reasons. For example, you might already have a “Product X” team and thus keep feeding it work, even though Product X might not be the priority this quarter and the team might be better used helping out with other things.
Ensure that the team has enough context about everything it does to make better decisions, and make it clear that descoping features with Product before starting to work on them is important not just to save on tokens, but also to save our own precious time and focus.
When what was done isn’t what the other party meant. These happen more and more nowadays because product specs seem to be more and more haphazardly put together. Overwhelmed Product teams find themselves pressed for time and generating prompt-based specs that turn short ideas into detailed instructions without really understanding the issues and how all the different pieces should fit together in the end.
The context is important for tackling this issue as well. Engineers should have enough product mastery and understanding of the work they’re being asked to perform to be able to sniff out when things aren’t clear to them.
Work should be performed in smaller iterations to verification. That’s going away because people no longer have the healthy friction of needing to type the code themselves. Due to that, many PRs are too big and far ahead by the time someone else sees them. It’s still a bad idea.
We all like complaining about too many meetings and similar. Of course that could be the culprit, but there are also other internal issues, like having teams become too small, resulting in too much communication and management overhead. Often these sorts of issues are more easily spotted by someone external to the organization.
Taking the time to ensure that your organization and its operating system are streamlined will save countless hours and cognitive load that is worth much more than another Claude subscription or two.
Lastly, there’s the issue of doing things in a way that used to make sense in the past but no longer does. When time gets eaten up in all of these previous issues, teams ossify, missing opportunities to evolve and improve. They keep trying to work harder to solve something that requires a leap forward and finding a smarter solution.
