Injecting habitual innovation is the only sustainable path forward, and lucky for us it’s just gotten that much easier with AI. You can learn more about this by getting the free sample chapter of The Tech Executive Operating System that’s exactly about this topic.
Yes, the token talk is all the rage. You’ll get lots more clicks on LinkedIn talking about how you lowered your AI costs by 30% than working hard on reclaiming 5%, 10%, 20%, and sometimes even 50% of the team’s time. Nevertheless, it’s only the latter that would unleash your team.
Fix the root causes and work better. AI is usually the cheapest line item on your budget, but it happens to have the most eye-catching invoice.

title: Heavy cost for US to return to confrontation with Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – The US return to the military confrontation with Iran, at a condition when Washington continues to emphasize its own military superiority, could impose even heavier costs on the United States.
The experience of recent conflicts has demonstrated that possessing advanced weaponry and massive firepower does not necessarily equate to achieving strategic objectives. Factors such as depletion of military stockpiles, damage to military equipment, need to procure replacement ammunition, and Iran’s capacity to restore its defensive capabilities all serve to complicate the White House’s calculations regarding a potential re-engagement in military confrontation with powerful Iran.
In a report citing the financial and military costs of past US strikes against Iran, the British newspaper “The Times” highlights the significant strain this conflict has placed on Washington’s military resources. According to the report, US expenditures have exceeded $43 billion in this war, dozens of American aircraft have sustained damage, and the US stockpiles of interceptor missiles have come under pressure. Regardless of the final assessment of the conflict's military outcomes, these figures indicate that sustaining large-scale operations against Iran requires substantial financial and material resources, the resources that cannot be replaced or replenishment in the short term is impossible.
The significance of this issue becomes even greater when the direct costs of military operations are weighed alongside their strategic consequences. In military calculations, the number of attacks carried out or the volume of ammunition expended is not, in itself, the definitive measure of victory. What truly matters is the ratio between the costs incurred and the objectives intended to be achieved through those expenditures. If a military operation entails the extensive use of ammunition and damage to equipment, yet fails to eliminate the adversary’s capacity to continue their resistance, persisting with the same approach may simply lead to mounting costs with no guarantee that the desired outcome will ever be attained.
Erosion of Military Stockpiles: Washington’s Hidden Challenge
One of the most significant consequences of a military conflict is the strain placed on stockpiles of weapons and ammunition. The extensive use of interceptor missiles to counter threats from missiles and drones, particularly when attacks are sustained, can deplete ready-to-use stockpiles, thereby increasing the need for production and resupply. This issue is of particular importance to the United States. In addition to its military commitments in West Asia, Washington must also ensure its forces remain prepared to address potential crises in other parts of the world.
Replenishing arms stockpiles is not merely a matter of securing funding. The production of certain advanced systems and the ammunition they utilize requires complex supply chains, specialized raw materials, and specialized industrial capacity. However, even if new budget allocations are made, rapidly replacing expended stocks is not necessarily feasible. The higher the rate of ammunition consumption in a conflict, the greater pressure placed on production schedules, the prioritization of arms deliveries, and the allocation of resources toward other military missions.
Under such circumstances, Washington’s decision to launch a new round of strikes is not limited merely to an assessment of operational capability; rather, it must also account for the opportunity cost of expending munitions and the subsequent impact on US military readiness. In other words, every missile used in an operation must be evaluated within the context of the United States’ broader defense requirements.
Iran’s Capacity for Recovery and Difficulty of Achieving a Definitive Outcome
On the other side of this equation lies Iran’s capacity to maintain and restore its defensive capabilities. In a report, “The Times” notes that, despite military attacks and pressures, Iran has managed to recover a portion of its missile and drone capabilities. This is significant from the perspective of military calculations, as the effectiveness of an offensive operation depends, to a large extent, on the degree of its lasting impact on the adversary’s capabilities.
If military strikes fail to permanently dismantle a nation’s defensive capacity, inflicting damage at a specific point in time does not necessarily equate to eliminating that nation’s ability to continue its resistance. The potential to repair equipment, restore certain operational capabilities, and maintain the capacity to produce or deploy weaponry can alter the conflict’s equation over time. In such a scenario, the aggressor may be compelled to repeatedly expend further munitions and equipment to sustain military pressure—all while the ultimate outcome of this process remains uncertain. The strategic implication is clear: as long as the adversary retains the ability to continue resisting, one cannot conclude that their defensive capacity has been exhausted based solely on the volume of attacks carried out.
Why could a renewed attack be more costly?
The United States re-engaging in a confrontation with Iran could trigger a repeat of that same costly cycle. New operations would require ammunition, logistics equipment, fuel supplies, the movement of troops, and the protection of military bases and facilities. Should equipment sustain damage or the scope of the conflict expand, costs would rise accordingly. Furthermore, a prolonged crisis could impact energy markets and economic expectations, extending the repercussions well beyond the military battlefield.
On the other hand, the United States must also consider the possibility of a prolonged conflict and the need to remain prepared for unforeseen scenarios. Military operations might begin with limited objectives, but reciprocal responses and shifting conditions could expand their scope. Under such circumstances, the final cost will not necessarily align with initial estimates.
The fundamental question for the White House is whether the costs of a new confrontation would yield commensurate gains. If the objective is to durably weaken Iran’s defensive capabilities, the persistence of its missile and drone capacities could make achieving this goal more difficult. Furthermore, if the aim is to compel Tehran to accede to Washington’s demands, it remains to be seen whether military pressure would truly lead to such an outcome, or if it would merely generate additional costs.
The White House’s Strategic Calculus Test
A report by “The Times” once again draws attention to the gap between military superiority and the achievement of strategic outcomes. Possessing extensive military capabilities enables the infliction of damage, but it does not, in itself, guarantee that the adversary will cease resistance or that the aggressor’s political objectives will be realized. When assessing a conflict, one must simultaneously consider the costs incurred, the resilience of the parties involved, and the extent to which objectives have been achieved.
For Washington, returning to a confrontation with Iran—without regard for the lessons of past costs—means re-entering a path with a predetermined outcome. The strain on U.S. military stockpiles, combined with Iran’s ability to restore parts of its defensive capabilities, suggests that repeating such attacks will not necessarily shift the equation in favor of the aggressor.
Ultimately, the primary challenge for the United States is not merely the capacity to launch a new operation, but the ability to achieve a sustainable outcome at a manageable cost. If previous strikes failed to realize Washington’s intended objectives, any decision to follow the same path requires a clear answer to the question: what will be different this time? Absent such an answer, a renewed attack risks becoming less of a solution to the crisis and more the beginning of another phase of resource depletion and escalating strategic costs for the United States.

title: Blood supplies, autonomous systems shape US Army’s Indo-Pacific combat care plans
body: U.S. Army combat medical teams are experimenting with ways to prolong care in preparation for a possible fight in the Indo-Pacific theater , where vast distances and limited evacuation platforms affect a patient’s timely access to surgical care. A fight in the Indo-Pacific would look different from past wars, such as Iraq and Afghanistan, making maintaining the “Golden Hour” standard difficult. Instead of requiring medical care and evacuation to a surgical facility to occur within 60 minutes of a traumatic combat injury, the 18th Theater Medical Command, based at Fort Shafter, Hawaii, is rethinking the term to mean bringing advanced care to the point of injury. The “tyranny of distance” in the region makes implementing the Golden Hour challenging since it accounts for over 50% of the world’s surface, 18th TMC Maj. Gen. E. Darrin Cox told Military Times on Monday during AUSA 2026 . “In the past, what [the Golden Hour] has meant is getting someone from the battlefield to a [medical] facility in that 60 minutes, so here in the Pacific, that may not be possible,” Cox said. “So what we’re talking about when we say Golden Hour is the pathophysiology of injury and bringing care to that patient in that time before pathology becomes deranged.” As autonomous systems become increasingly relevant in militaries across the globe, the command is experimenting with ways it can assist patients with prolonged care at the point of injury, while keeping in mind the possibility of an attack. Blood Storage and Distribution Even though warfare and medical care are both “human endeavors,” Cox said, autonomous systems are a part of the future. The systems can help deliver care through managing a patient’s vital signs, triaging patients, delivering blood or monitoring a patient so a provider on the ground can take care of others. “We’re experimenting with autonomous delivery of blood and other Class A medical supplies,” Cox said. “They’re experimenting in Ukraine with autonomous evacuation of injured folks off the battlefield, so there’s a lot of work in that area.” “Not everything in Ukraine is directly applicable to the maritime environment you find yourself in the Pacific, but we take what we observe, we learn those lessons, and then we try to apply it to the operating environment that we’re in,” he continued. Alongside experimenting with autonomous systems, the 18th TMC is working with joint partners and allies to ensure access to blood distribution facilities, storing it west of the International Date Line. “We were able to successfully bring blood from Japan to Australia last year during the Talisman Saber exercise ,” Cox said. “That demonstrates developing those networks where we can move blood from potential storage locations to the points of need as different operations would surge.” In critically injured trauma patients, blood and its components are necessary at the point of injury, Cox said, whether it’s blood provided by other countries for American use or stored ahead of time in a facility. The best option is fresh whole blood, but that requires collection on scene, which has a limited supply, and refrigerated fresh blood has a limited lifespan. Another option is frozen products, both blood and plasma, but they need to be thawed with specialized equipment. Cox highlighted that many partners in the Pacific, like the Philippines, are developing their own armed forces blood program where they have a stockpile of blood in military hospitals and accept donations. America is looking to have blood-sharing agreements with some joint partners, like Australia and Japan, which have a similar testing protocol to America’s and allow for the U.S. to use blood procured locally on U.S. casualties. “We’re also with our partners in the Philippines,” 18th Command Sgt. Maj. Jennifer Francis told Military Times. “We ensure that we share what we’re doing in the field, so that we can enhance their own capability. So we’ve made huge strides there in the Philippines.” Training on New Concepts Ensuring that the combat medics are familiar with these concepts and innovations ahead of a conflict takes training on “anything and everything” related to the options, she said. The Army has multiple “echelons of care,” but it all begins with basic self-care training and the more advanced Combat Lifesaver training before some reach the combat medic level. “Once you get to tactical combat casualty care, that’s a little bit more robust,” Francis said. “They have the basic application of tourniquet[s], and then going through some of the head-to-toe trauma.” In the Indo-Pacific theater, the overall medical care is not significantly different, unlike the environment, prompting the 18th TMC to continue to innovate through technology and training to keep trust with soldiers. The 18th utilizes an 8th Forward Resuscitative and Surgical Detachment, or FRSD, which is a 20-person team that can execute surgery in the theater, Cox said, and the command is tinkering with different configurations of tents versus fixed mobile containers that can be taken on or off an Army watercraft, land or underground. At the May 2026 Land Forces of the Pacific Symposium and Exposition in Hawaii, the 8th FRSD demonstrated a care simulation on a cut suit which modeled a surgical unit aboard a vessel. Boats or ships should transport patients because evacuating by air en masse would be less likely, Army medics told Military Times at the event. The team began using autonomous small multipurpose equipment transports, or SMETs, uncrewed, eight-wheeled robotic combat vehicles guided with a remote control, to carry patients.

title: Guterres urges faster action and financing to stop biodiversity loss
body:
The United Nations Secretary-General appealed on Friday for governments, businesses and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations and all life on Earth.
Guterres was speaking in Yerevan, Armenia, ahead of the opening of the COP17 UN biodiversity conference next week.
“The food we eat, the water we drink, the very air we breathe – all are the gifts of biodiversity,” he told the Leaders’ Summit. “Yet every day, humankind saws another branch off the tree of life.”
The UN chief said factors such as climate disruption, overgrazing and excessive use of fertilisers and pesticides “are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos”.
As a result, more than a million species face the risk of extinction, “edging us ever closer towards an uninhabitable world,” he warned, adding that “it doesn’t have to be this way”.
Mr. Guterres said the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, agreed four years ago , had inspired action worldwide.
Nearly 90 per cent of parties have established national biodiversity targets, while more than half have developed national road maps. Since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection.
However, “progress is uneven, and far too slow”, he said. Even if countries fulfil their current commitments, only 26 per cent of terrestrial ecosystems and 12 per cent of marine ecosystems would be protected by 2030 – “well short” of the Framework’s goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by that date.
He also highlighted “major gaps” in national targets linked to economic systems, including commitments to reduce incentives that harm nature. Finance, technical capacity, cooperation and data collection remain inadequate, he said, noting that biodiversity financing is less than half of the $200 billion agreed under the Framework.
He stressed that biodiversity cannot be treated separately from conflict, food insecurity, disease threats or climate change. “Addressing any of these crises requires addressing them all,” he said. “And there is no time to waste.”
The Secretary-General first called for government leadership, urging countries to meet the “30 by 30” target and “shift from policies that destroy nature, to practices that sustain it”.
Priorities include zero-waste and circular economies, sustainable farming, regenerative agriculture, stronger monitoring and transparency and firmer enforcement of existing laws.
He welcomed the Yerevan Declaration and its commitment to integrate biodiversity into government policies, budgets and regulations.
His second appeal focused on finance as “the stark truth is, we are spending money on the wrong things”. He noted that for every dollar invested in protecting nature, $30 is spent on activities that damage it.
“In 2023, $7.3 trillion flowed into nature-negative industries,” he said, including polluting heavy industry, destructive agribusiness and fossil fuels.
“I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”
The Secretary-General said that meeting global biodiversity, climate and land-restoration goals would require annual investment in nature-based solutions to reach $571 billion by 2030 – equivalent to about 0.5 per cent of global gross domestic product.
“But governments cannot do this alone,” he said, calling for the private sector to step up. He pointed to the UN-backed Cali Fund as a mechanism through which companies benefiting from nature can help finance its protection.
Mr. Guterres also cited the rapid growth of renewable energy. The cost of solar power has fallen by almost 90 per cent since 2010 and investment in clean energy is now nearly double investment in fossil fuels. Moreover, renewable energy prevented emissions last year equivalent to the combined emissions of the United States, the European Union and Japan.
“But these benefits are not shared equally around the globe,” he said, noting that many developing countries have been unable to invest sufficiently in both nature and human development due to debt burdens, limited public budgets and an inequitable international financial system.
The Secretary-General’s final appeal was for broad participation, particularly from young people, civil society, women, Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
“Environmental decline often falls hardest on the most vulnerable, and those who did the least to cause the problem. But the solutions often arise from these same groups,” he said.
With 76 days remaining until he leaves office, Mr. Guterres said that confronting climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution had been among his highest priorities.
“Let us act with the urgency this moment demands,” he said. “For our children. For our future. And for all life on Earth.”
Fewer than half of the national targets set to protect the world’s plants, animals and ecosystems are on track, the UN warns in a new report, days before countries gather in Yerevan, Armenia, for the COP17 biodiversity conference.

title: Gaza: 340 children killed despite ceasefire agreement - UNICEF
body:
A little over one year since a ceasefire agreement was announced between Hamas fighters and Israel, more than 340 children have been reported killed and hundreds more injured, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Friday.
For families “mourning the loss of their children, those terrible statistics do not equate with a ceasefire”, stressed spokesperson Ricardo Pires.
He added that in the last two weeks in Gaza alone, five boys and two girls have been reported killed and at least 33 children seriously injured in airstrikes, drone strikes and gunfire across the Strip. Another two boys died of injuries sustained previously, Mr. Pires told journalists in Geneva.
The consequences of the Hamas-Israel war are everywhere for children: “where they sleep, what they eat, whether they can learn”, he continued, citing the case of
16-year-old Norhan whose mother was shot while eight months pregnant. “She delivered her baby and then died the following day,” Mr. Pires explained. “Norhan’s father is living with a disability, so she now cares for her one-year-old sister Narjis and takes full responsibility. Her days are spent tidying the home, cooking, and playing with Narjis. Her three other siblings attend a UNICEF -supported learning centre and Norhan helps them with their studies after class, which as she says means, ‘They might just have a future.’”
Asked about reports that private traders in Gaza had halted cooperation with the Israeli authorities on allowing commercial trucks carrying food to enter the occupied enclave, the UNICEF spokesperson stressed that the uninterrupted flow of “humanitarian and commercial goods” remained essential, “so children can continue their recovery”.
He recalled being in Gaza City last year before the ceasefire began, when supplies “were not getting in” and famine was declared by UN-backed food insecurity experts.
“We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods and services that they require,” he insisted, “where children are not receiving what they need to survive and to continue to have hope for their future”.
The UNICEF alert comes as temperatures drop and displaced families in Gaza fill empty flour bags with sand to keep rainwater out of their tents. Aid agencies continue to repeat warnings that the situation in Gaza remains dire, after three years of war, sparked by Hamas-led terror attacks in Israel.
The ongoing sanitation crisis is a particular concern in the war-torn enclave, where Israeli bombardment has severely damaged the drainage network.
“There are vast pools of wastewater, such as the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin that is half-full,” Mr. Pires warned. “With the winter rains fast approaching, we’re running out of time to pump this out. Just as we warned a year ago, contaminated water could overflow and inundate downstream residential areas with potentially life-threatening impacts for children and their families. Children have drowned in sewage-contaminated water before.”
According to UNICEF, 800,000 children remain displaced in Gaza “and most live in tents or dangerous bombed-out buildings”. An estimated 60,000 children have seen either one or both parents killed during the war, or since the ceasefire, while nearly every child needs some form of mental health support to recover.
As part of UN assistance to Palestinians in Gaza, UNICEF has helped more than 560,000 children return to learning since the ceasefire, including at over 200 UNICEF-supported learning centres.
The agency has also provided digital cash assistance – “a lifeline”, Mr. Pires stressed – to more than 380,000 people, along with safe water to 1.2 million people.

title: Surface Laptop Ultra review: a different kind of MacBook Pro
body:
After setting up Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, I spent five minutes just staring at it. I wasn’t surprised by its MacBook Pro-like design or blown away by its bright display. I was trying to work out what I’d actually do with a $5,900 laptop.
This isn’t just any regular Windows laptop. Microsoft has teamed up with Nvidia to build a high-end laptop to showcase Nvidia’s new Arm-based RTX Spark chips. It’s a big moment for Windows on Arm, as these chips can run demanding AI models locally, alongside the latest AAA games and creative apps. The promise is compelling, but the reality of local AI is much messier.
Getting the most out of the Surface Laptop Ultra, especially my top-of-the-line model, requires coding experience or the patience to experiment with models and AI agents until you find something that works. If that sounds like you, Microsoft might have built the Windows laptop you’ve been waiting for. If not, this might not be the MacBook Pro competitor Microsoft was hoping for.
[Product: Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra | https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fmicrosoft-surface-laptop-ultra-15-3k-touchscreen-nvidia-rtx-spark-n1x-18-core-2026-24gb-memory-512gb-storage-platinum%2FJJGXP3CQW2, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/surface/devices/surface-laptop-ultra]
It feels like Microsoft has finally built the hardware to rival Apple’s pro laptops, thanks to an all-aluminum design, large haptic trackpad, and high-end finish. Even the “nightfall” color is just like Apple’s space black.
There are plenty of meaningful differences, though. The 15-inch mini-LED display can run at up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR brightness, at 262 pixels per inch (3270 x 2180); the MacBook Pro peaks at 1,600 nits. That makes it the brightest display Microsoft has ever shipped on a Surface Laptop. Unlike the MacBook Pro, it’s also a 3:2 touchscreen, perfect for writing code, reading text, or editing photos.
The port selection is similar to the MacBook Pro, with one very big change. You get three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, a single HDMI 2.1b port, SD card reader, and headphone jack. Where it really differs is Microsoft’s new Magnetic Connect. It works just like the old Surface Connect, but through the USB-C port on the right-hand side. Just bring the connector close to the port, and it snaps into place. When you’re not charging, that port works just like the rest of the USB-C ports on the laptop.
Magnetic Connect is one of my favorite additions on the Surface Laptop Ultra. I love how you can reverse the magnetic USB-C charging end, attach it to the power brick, and use the regular USB-C connector at the opposite end of the cable to charge the rest of your devices.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0448.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0459.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The haptic feedback on the large trackpad is also a welcome addition. It works with things like clicks, drags, and window alignment throughout Windows 11, and the tactile feedback triggers in apps like PowerPoint as you drag and align objects or images in a deck, too. It’s subtle enough to make it feel like you’re really moving windows or interfaces around, but I do wish more apps supported it.
Microsoft has included a 1080p front-facing camera above the screen. The quality is fine for video calls, and it supports Windows Hello face authentication and Windows Studio Effects like automatic framing, eye contact, and background blur.
Not all of the Surface Laptop Ultra hardware is impressive, though. I’ve had issues where I’ve unplugged the charger at 100 percent only for Windows to then immediately report 97 percent battery life. Plugging in would put it back to 100 percent and then it would immediately drop back to 97 percent again each time I unplugged.
[Image: The magnetic USB-C charger is an impressive addition. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0475.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
It seemed weird so I asked Microsoft about the behavior, and it’s designed this way to make a battery last longer. “When it’s plugged in and the battery is full, the device pauses charging rather than constantly topping off, and resumes only once the level drops to 95 percent,” says Microsoft spokesperson Moses Nsereko. “This reduces wear over time. While plugged in, the indicator shows 100 percent to indicate a full charge. When you unplug, it shows the battery’s exact level right away, which may be a few percent lower.”
I’ve run into some issues with the display, too, where either things felt slightly laggy or there was noticeable ghosting. Moving a window around rapidly sometimes left a little trail. Changing power settings from the default “best power efficiency” mode to “best performance” seemed to fix most of the laggy feeling, and the backlight ghosting seems to be less noticeable the longer you run the laptop.
I also heard some loud pops and bangs from the built-in speakers on the Surface Laptop Ultra. They were loud enough to sound like firecrackers, and I thought the battery was about to die before I realized it was just speaker interference. Rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra solved this one, but it’s happened a couple of times now.
Speaking of rebooting, I’ve noticed that rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra is surprisingly slow. This seems like something Microsoft could easily fix with an update, though.
[Image: The Surface Laptop Ultra can run complex local AI models. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0184.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Local AI models and agents
The RTX Spark that powers the Surface Laptop Ultra is designed with local AI models and agents in mind. The variant I’ve been testing has a 20-core CPU that was codesigned by Nvidia and MediaTek paired with a 6,144-CUDA-core GPU — roughly comparable to a mobile RTX 5060 — plus 128GB of unified memory and a 1TB Gen 5 SSD. It’s the top-of-the-line model at $5,899, and I think if you’re considering this particular laptop spec then you have a very specific use case in mind. The base version is $2,599, and it comes with an 18-core CPU, 5,120-CUDA -core GPU, and 24GB of unified memory.
Out of the box, Microsoft prompts Laptop Ultra owners to pick an AI agent. You can choose between Hermes, OpenClaw, and Perplexity. I tried out Hermes and OpenClaw over the past week, but I ran into issues getting OpenClaw to work initially. A reinstall fixed a gateway issue, and then I could name my agent and start using it for local AI tasks.
I configured both Hermes and OpenClaw to use the Qwen3.8-27B model, one of the more powerful local AI models. Because it uses the full power of the Surface Laptop Ultra, it will spin up its fans at full throttle and 100 percent GPU for even the most basic of queries. I asked Hermes to resize and convert some photos from PNG to JPG, a task that would take seconds using a PowerToy utility. It took minutes to complete, all while the fans were buzzing away and the laptop was getting hot.
It’s probably my fault for using such a large model for a basic task, but without testing every single local AI model it’s hard to know which one to pick for each task you need. I asked OpenClaw to build me a smart home dashboard, but it spent 30 minutes spinning up the laptop’s fans and calling various tools to eventually produce nothing but an error.
I don’t have a base Surface Laptop Ultra to test, but it’s easy to see that 24GB of unified memory will mean fewer local AI models to choose from.
[Image: Local AI models are best for coding tasks right now. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0125.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I struggled to come up with many compelling use cases for the power of these chips for local AI work. A lot of tasks could simply be done far more quickly and without the laptop fans spinning up by using a free cloud model. The power here is really in leaving the agent running at full throttle to build something overnight, or run a task across large datasets that would normally cost a lot of money in cloud tokens.
I did like that I could do things locally, though, without worrying about the privacy aspects of cloud models. I fed Hermes some audio and video files and it went ahead and created a local llama.cpp server to enable audio transcription. It took some fiddling to get it working, but it could certainly save me having to install transcription apps or pay for a cloud service like Otter.
The thing I didn’t like is that these agents are far from user-friendly, and I’m surprised that Microsoft or Nvidia hasn’t developed its own local AI interface that simplifies a lot of this work. I need to spend more time with both Hermes and OpenClaw, but as someone who doesn’t code it’s clear this is all really targeted toward developers and power users.
Gaming and creative tasks
The Surface Laptop Ultra might not be an official gaming laptop, but it’s certainly capable of running far more of the latest games than Apple’s MacBook Pro. Normally I’d be nervous about Windows on Arm and gaming, given the weak GPU on the Qualcomm Snapdragon X series chips. But this is the first time we’ve seen an Arm CPU paired with a stronger Nvidia GPU, and most games run well for a laptop that’s not the size of a gaming one.
Instead of running a bunch of benchmarks at different settings, I decided to try and find the optimal settings that would allow me to play at around 60fps or more in each game. Because this is an RTX GPU, you also get full support for DLSS, Frame Generation, and ray tracing. So you can enable Frame Generation if you want to get to 120fps to match the 120Hz display.
I was able to run Black Myth: Wukong at 70fps on average at native resolution (3270 x 2180) with medium settings and DLSS performance mode enabled. I ran the same medium settings and DLSS performance in Cyberpunk 2077 and averaged 66fps, and Forza Horizon 6 managed an average of 57fps.
Most games will need to run at medium settings and DLSS performance or balanced to get around 60fps, but there are some exceptions where you’ll need to lower settings or resolution. Gears of War: E-Day averaged 40fps on medium settings and DLSS performance, and I only managed to bump this to 48fps on low settings. I also had to move Doom: The Dark Ages to low settings and DLSS performance to hit an average of 60fps.
[Image: Gears of War: E-Day running on the Surface Laptop Ultra. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0156.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I’m spoiled by using an RTX 5090 on a 32-inch 4K screen every day with maxed-out game settings, but I didn’t mind the look of medium settings on a 15-inch display. It felt more like dropping down to console settings, and in some games it’s hard to distinguish the texture differences on a smaller display. I’m one of those gamers who prefers to run at 60fps with lower settings rather than max out the settings and have to play at 30fps, though.
While game compatibility is good for most titles, there are some where you’re going to run into emulation issues. Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered was limited to 30fps at 1440p regardless of whether I used low or medium settings. I believe this is because the game is CPU-heavy, so a native Arm port would probably help for this type of game.
There aren’t many native Arm games, though. I tried out the new Arm version of Marvel Rivals, and it averaged 64fps with medium settings and DLSS performance and 75fps with low settings. I think we’ll only see Arm ports where there’s a lot of CPU activity involved that the Prism emulator — which translates CPU instructions from x86 to Arm — can’t handle well enough, because otherwise it’s very capable.
We may see more Arm ports for games that have anti-cheat engines. Anti-cheat engines are a lot more complicated to emulate, so developers have to create Arm-compatible versions. While games like Arc Raiders, Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, and Fortnite all work out of the box, Nvidia and Microsoft are working with EA, Activision, and Riot Games to get titles like Battlefield, Call of Duty, Valorant, and League of Legends fully supported.
The Surface Laptop Ultra is also a very capable machine for creative and everyday tasks. I managed to export our 4K video test in two minutes and 18 seconds on the Surface Laptop Ultra using Premiere Pro. That’s around a minute behind the top-of-the-line MacBook Pro, but beats the base M5 chip and is around 30 seconds behind the M5 Pro. I did have to create this using Premiere Pro’s own export tool, rather than sending it to Media Encoder like how we usually run this test. There seems to be a bug in the beta Arm version of Media Encoder that prevented it from running the export correctly.
Where the Surface Laptop Ultra really falls behind Apple’s M5 chips is in CPU performance. Single-core and multi-threaded CPU tests like Geekbench or Cinebench show how much weaker the MediaTek CPU is against a $6,999-plus MacBook Pro 16 with an M5 Max or even an M6 Mac Mini. Even some of the GPU tests for Geekbench show the RTX Spark falling behind Apple’s MacBook Pro, and the Puget Bench Photoshop, Premiere Pro, and DaVinci Resolve are all noticeably behind the M5 Max.
I’ve also been testing the battery life of the Surface Laptop Ultra, which seems to be around seven hours if you’re using local AI models and a mix of apps and gaming. If you’re doing less intensive work, it’s averaging out at 10 hours or more. I’ll know more the longer I use the Laptop Ultra, so check back for updated battery impressions.
[Image: Surface Laptop Ultra is designed for Blender and other creative apps. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/VERGE_10_04_2026_0044.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The Surface Laptop Ultra doesn’t really offer a clear performance advantage over the MacBook Pro outside of some AI workloads like image generation and the ability to run CUDA compute natively. It’s not transformative for the Windows world like the M1 chips were for macOS, largely because Qualcomm already supercharged Windows on Arm with its Snapdragon X series two years ago. That makes it difficult to recommend unless you’re specifically interested in running local AI models, coding, or experimenting with AI agents.
The Surface Laptop Ultra, and Nvidia’s RTX Spark in general, targets developers and power users who want a laptop that can handle those workloads alongside creative apps and the latest games. For that audience, there’s a lot to like. For everyone else, more affordable laptops can handle everyday productivity, creative work, and some light gaming without the hefty price premium.
Microsoft has come closer than ever to building a Windows alternative to the MacBook Pro. The hardware looks and feels great, and Nvidia’s GPU brings CUDA support and decent gaming capabilities to a high-end laptop design. But the Surface Laptop Ultra’s biggest selling point is also its biggest question mark: local AI. It all feels like a work in progress. If you’re ready to experiment with it, this could be a compelling glimpse of where Windows laptops could go next. If you’re not, it’s a lot of money to spend on an experiment.
---
Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra specs (as reviewed)
* Display: 15-inch (3270 x 2180) 120Hz mini-LED, up to 2,000 nits peak HDR
* Processor: Nvidia RTX Spark N1X 20-core CPU / 6144-CUDA-core GPU
* Unified memory: 128GB LPDDR5x
* Storage: 1TB SSD (Gen 5)
* Webcam: 1080p front-facing Surface Studio Camera
* Connectivity: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4
* Ports: 3x USB-C / USB4, USB-A 3.1, SD card reader, HDMI 2.1b, Magnect Connect charging, 3.5mm headphone jack
* Biometrics: Windows Hello facial recognition
* Weight: 4.41 pounds / 2kg
* Dimensions: 12.95 x 9.4 x 0.75 inches / 328.8 x 238.7 x 19.16mm
* Battery: 92Wh
* Price: $5,900

Few phones have been more anticipated than a foldable iPhone, but it’s finally here. The iPhone Duo was unveiled during Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 models.
Apple’s first foldable has a 5.4-inch outer screen, and it unfolds to show off its 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR screen. Apple Pencil support is coming later this year. While it lacks Face ID for facial unlocking, there’s a Touch ID sensor along its edge to identify your fingerprint. The device has an IP68 rating, with Ceramic Shield 2 on its back, with Ceramic Shield covering the front display. It has the same A20 Pro chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro. Notably, the Duo has the same 48-megapixel fusion camera as the 18 Pro, though it doesn’t have variable aperture.
The foldable will come in two colors, Star White and Night Sky, and starts at $1,999 for the 256GB version. You can preorder an unlocked version now ahead of its Friday, October 23rd release date from Apple and Best Buy .
The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first take on a foldable and comes with all the first-generation quirks you’d expect. Its outer screen can feel cramped, but the inner matte display is a real standout for content consumption.

title: 5 Best Resources to Learn About World Models in 2026
body:
World models could be the next big shift in AI. Learn more right now.
World models are becoming one of the most interesting areas of modern AI research. Instead of simply mapping an input to an output, a world model learns how an environment behaves . It can predict what might happen next, simulate possible outcomes, and help an AI system plan its actions. Although recent systems have brought world models into video generation, robotics, embodied AI, and physical reasoning, many of their fundamental ideas come from reinforcement learning and model-based planning. There is no single resource that takes you from the fundamentals all the way to systems such as Dreamer , Genie , and modern world foundation models, but we do have enough resources to understand how it all works. Here are the five best resources I found for learning about world models in 2026.
If you are completely new to world models, I would start here rather than jumping directly into recent world-model papers. UC Berkeley's CS 285: Deep Reinforcement Learning , taught by Sergey Levine, covers the foundations required to understand why world models are useful in the first place. The course covers reinforcement learning, control, and deep learning, and also includes dedicated material on model-based reinforcement learning. The most relevant parts are the lectures on planning, optimal control, learned dynamics, and model-based reinforcement learning. It has lecture recordings, notes, and assignments, so you can study both the mathematics and practical implementations.
Once you understand some reinforcement learning, Stanford's Introduction to World Models lecture provides a much more direct entry into the topic. The lecture is part of Stanford's Spring 2026 CS348K course and is available online with downloadable PDF slides. It covers visual and spatial computing workloads including generative AI-based world creation, latent world representations, non-pixel-based approaches, and embodied agentic AI. It's not a full course, but it is a good starting point for understanding what world models actually are.
This is probably the single most important resource for world models. The original World Models work by David Ha and Jürgen Schmidhuber popularized a simple but powerful idea: an agent can learn a compressed representation of its environment, learn how that representation evolves, and then train a controller using its internally simulated environment. The architecture consists of three main components.
The most interesting idea is that an agent can sometimes train inside its learned environment rather than interacting with the real environment for every training step. The project website is good for beginners — it includes explanations, diagrams, animations, experiments, and links to the implementation. Even though modern systems such as Dreamer and large video-based world models are more complex, the core intuition is very similar.
Once you understand the basic idea behind world models, the next step is figuring out what to read. There are now hundreds of papers related to learned dynamics, model-based reinforcement learning, latent environments, generative simulators, and embodied world models.
This Stanford reading list provides a much more manageable starting point. It currently highlights ten important papers tracing the progression from early neural world models to modern approaches. The list includes World Models , PlaNet , Dreamer , DreamerV2 , SimPLe , DayDreamer , Genie , and TD-MPC2 . This sequence is useful because you can see how the field evolved.
The original World Models showed that an agent could learn a compact internal simulator. PlaNet explored planning directly inside learned latent dynamics. Dreamer shifted toward learning policies using imagined trajectories. Later systems extended similar concepts into robotics and large-scale generative environments.
Instead of randomly searching for papers on world models, you can simply work through this reading list one paper at a time.
Researchers associated with Tsinghua University created the Awesome World Model repository alongside their survey, Understanding World or Predicting Future? A Comprehensive Survey of World Models . The survey was accepted by ACM Computing Surveys , while the repository continuously organizes papers and resources across different branches of world-model research. It covers areas such as:
The accompanying survey is especially useful once you have learned the basics, because it explains how all these apparently different research directions fit under the broader world-model umbrella. I would not recommend reading the entire repository from top to bottom. Instead, bookmark it and use it as a reference whenever you want to explore a particular branch of the field.
If you prefer learning from a book rather than jumping between lectures and research papers, Michael Brenndoerfer's World Models Handbook is one of the most relevant resources available. It can be read online for free, and a PDF version is also available for purchase. The book is still being completed: the site currently lists 72 planned chapters, with 39 published. It starts with a small end-to-end world model before introducing foundations such as dynamical systems, partial observability, Bayesian filtering, system identification, uncertainty, physics, and causality. Later sections move into modern architectures, including recurrent state-space models, transformers, autoregressive token models, diffusion and flow models, predictive embeddings such as JEPA, and multimodal foundation models . It also covers planning approaches and major research lines — Dreamer, MuZero, TD-MPC, Genie, Cosmos, and vision-language-action models.
World models are not one particular neural-network architecture. They lie at the intersection of reinforcement learning, representation learning, planning, video generation, robotics, control, and embodied AI , which makes them difficult to learn by simply opening the newest paper.
A better strategy is to work backward from the fundamentals. First understand how an agent can learn and plan with a model of its environment. Then study the original neural world models architecture. After that, explore how newer research extends the same idea to latent representations, large-scale simulators, video prediction, robotics, and physical AI.
Kanwal Mehreen is a machine learning engineer and a technical writer with a profound passion for data science and the intersection of AI with medicine. She co-authored the ebook "Maximizing Productivity with ChatGPT". As a Google Generation Scholar 2022 for APAC, she champions diversity and academic excellence. She's also recognized as a Teradata Diversity in Tech Scholar, Mitacs Globalink Research Scholar, and Harvard WeCode Scholar. Kanwal is an ardent advocate for change, having founded FEMCodes to empower women in STEM fields.

title: Quebec sovereigntists see fundamental rift with Alberta separatists
body:
With just days before Alberta’s vote on an independence referendum, longtime Quebec sovereigntists are distancing themselves from the western province’s separatists.
Question 10 of 10 on Monday’s referendum ballot asks whether Alberta should remain in Canada or if the government should start the legal process to hold a subsequent, binding referendum on separation.
Advance polls opened Tuesday and run until Saturday.
Quebecers may have a sense of déjà vu after voting on a similar question in 1980, when René Lévesque’s Parti Québécois asked whether the province should begin negotiations to leave Confederation. Nearly 60 per cent of Quebec voters were against Lévesque’s proposal.
A second referendum followed in 1995, narrowly won by the “No” side. But ardent sovereigntists see profound differences in the two movements.
Marie-Anne Alepin, president of the Société St-Jean-Baptiste de Montréal, a prominent Quebec nationalist group, believes Alberta is using the threat of separatism as leverage in negotiations with Ottawa. She sees the referendum as a means of pressure rather than a genuine desire to form a country.
“They want a bigger role within Canada and we want to leave,” she said. “They want more control over their oil and gas … we don’t want pipelines.”
But that hasn’t stopped some leaders in the Alberta separatist movement from claiming common cause.
Quebec elected the PQ — which has promised a third independence referendum — to a minority government on Oct. 5, leading figures in the Alberta separatist movement to rally behind premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and declare him a possible ally.
“Quebec rejected the status quo today,” wrote columnist Cory Morgan — a founding member of the Alberta Independence Party in 2001 — on social media after the PQ’s victory. “Alberta can do the same in two weeks by choosing to send a message with Option 2 on Question 10.”
Alberta separatist Jeffrey Rath also took to social media the day after the provincial election, saying that “for the first time in history, Alberta Independence will have the support of the elected government of Quebec.” He also congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and “the country of Quebec.”
The two, along with lawyer Keith Wilson, lamented that Quebec’s quest for independence is seen as legitimate while they say Alberta separatists are sneered at.
During a visit to Calgary last year, St-Pierre Plamondon said he would recognize an independent Alberta should the province vote to separate. Rath said he met with the PQ leader during that visit.
But while they believe in the democratic process of a referendum, many Quebec sovereigntists do not identify with the Alberta separatists.
Former PQ leader Jean-François Lisée did not mince words when asked about Monday’s referendum.
“It’s mostly a waste because defeat is certain,” he said. “There’s really nothing much to gain from watching the Alberta independence movement, except maybe negative lessons.”
It’s a feeling shared by other sovereigntists.
Louise Harel, who was a PQ minister during Quebec’s 1995 sovereignty referendum and later served as interim leader of the party, agrees with Lisée. Both say the Quebec and Alberta sovereigntist movements are fundamentally different.
In their view, Quebec sovereigntists are motivated to preserve their cultural and linguistic identity, while Alberta separatists are motivated by the economy and political libertarianism. They also see a desire for Alberta to get closer to the United States, while Quebecers are wary of talk of assimilation.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she is against secession, while PQ leaders have openly called for sovereignty.
“In Quebec, the idea is to give a unique historical nation in North America, which … has valiantly resisted assimilation, the powers it needs to survive in a globalized world,” said Harel. “But there is no such issue of identity or culture in Alberta.”
While sovereigntist Quebecers also feel economically disadvantaged within Canada, Lisée said, the sentiment isn’t at the core of the movement. He also stressed that Quebec’s sovereigntist parties have historically been social-democrat, while the movement in Alberta seems tied to conservatism.
Daniel Turp, a Université de Montréal law professor who represented both the Bloc Québécois and the PQ, sees differences in the referendum process itself. Quebec’s two independence referendums included a single question on sovereignty.
As a result, there were mass mobilizations from both federalist and sovereigntist factions for weeks.
Public support for independence also varies widely between the two provinces.
On the eve of the 1995 referendum, public opinion was split evenly in the polls. Three days before Quebecers cast their ballots, Canadians from across the country made their way to Montreal to urge them to vote against independence.
Poll aggregator 338Canada shows less than 25 per cent support for Alberta to leave Canada as of Oct. 11.
“There hasn’t been a love-in in Alberta yet,” Turp said. “Maybe we’re not as worried because the polls show the option to remain will win.”
More than 90 per cent of registered voters cast a ballot in the 1995 referendum, which federalists won with 50.58 per cent of the vote.
“That’s the kind of voter turnout you see in countries where voting is mandatory,” said Harel. “I would be extremely surprised if voter turnout in the Alberta referendum were the same.”
But the sovereigntists do not reject the Alberta separatist movement entirely. All four said they sympathize with the desire for autonomy and self-determination.
“If Alberta were to vote yes, and then Ottawa would say, ‘well, you can’t leave,’ we will be on the side of Alberta,” said Lisée.
Harel added that while she does not see ideological similarities between separatists in Quebec and Alberta, the democratic process must be respected. She said that the Alberta referendum can give legitimacy to the one promised by the PQ.
Asked if they worry that a no vote on Monday could affect the PQ’s promised referendum, all four said no.
Alepin believes the two movements are too different for Albertans to influence Quebecers’ appetite for sovereignty.
Meanwhile, Lisée predicts that “the defeat of the yes side in Alberta will be a negative but very insignificant factor in (Quebec’s) referendum debate.”
If Alberta stays within Canada, Turp believes the province may be inspired by Quebec’s approach to negotiating more autonomy with Ottawa.
“And then they can organize a second referendum, like we did,” he added.

title: Parashat Noah: How prayer becomes an ark that carries us through turbulent times - opinion
body: 'And God said to Noah, 'Come into the teiva, you and all your household'” (Gen. 7:1).The teiva – the ark – is one of the defining images of the parasha: a vessel of refuge carrying Noah, his family, and the living creatures through the waters of the Flood toward a renewed world.Yet the Hebrew word “teiva” has another meaning. It can also mean “a word.” The Baal Shem Tov, the 18th-century founder of the Hassidic movement, takes “Bo el hateiva” (“Come into the ark”) as an instruction to enter the words of prayer.Fittingly, this teaching opens “Amud Hatefila” – “The Pillar of Prayer” – an extensive compilation of his teachings on prayer found in Baal Shem Tov al HaTorah, parashat Noah.Here the ark becomes the starting point for an entire approach to prayer – one of deep concentration, attachment to the sacred letters, and awareness of the Divine within them.In prayer, he teaches, you should immerse yourself in each word “with your whole body and all your powers.” Rather than allowing the words simply to pass through our lips, we are invited to experience them fully.'Worlds, souls, and Divinity'The Baal Shem Tov takes the teaching further. Within every letter, he says, are “worlds, souls, and Divinity.” As letters join together to form words, prayer becomes more than a sequence of words to be recited. The teiva itself becomes a spiritual space that can hold and carry us.Yoram Raanan's painting gives striking visual expression to this understanding of “teiva.” He created the work spontaneously, allowing paint to drip and flow across the canvas. From this spontaneous process, a ship emerged. Its great curved form fills the lower half of the painting, while long vertical lines rise like masts above it.Within the form of the ship, a stringed instrument, perhaps a lute, came into being. The curved hull becomes the body of the instrument, while the vertical lines perform both functions visually – at once masts and strings. Ship and instrument inhabit the same form – one carrying us across, the other giving voice to sound.Above them, small forms move through the expansive blue-green field. Some appear as golden birds, others as drifting clouds, while still others remain more elusive. “They intermingle,” Raanan says, “like the words of prayer.”The transformation seems particularly fitting for the Baal Shem Tov's understanding of “teiva.” The ship carries us; the instrument gives voice to prayer. The word becomes both vessel and sound.Throughout the painting, forms seem to shift and flow into one another. Water becomes sky. Ship becomes lute. Birds and other forms seem to pass between different realms.The painting gives visual form to something difficult to describe: to enter the teiva is not merely to pronounce a word of prayer, but to enter its sound, its movement, and the world it contains. Just as the ark carries its passengers through the waters of the Flood, the words of prayer can become a vessel that carries us.But the ark does more than carry. It is also a place of protection. When the world outside becomes stormy, the teiva offers refuge.The Baal Shem Tov's teaching gives this ancient image an inner dimension. In difficult or turbulent times, we, too, can find a protective space within sacred words and prayer.And Raanan's lute adds another possibility: music, too, can become a place of refuge. Sound moves through us and changes how we feel, carrying us when words alone are not enough.This image has particular resonance just after the cycle of the Jewish holidays. We have emerged from weeks of prayer, reflection, celebration, and sacred time, and suddenly we are back in the ordinary rhythm of the year.The Baal Shem Tov's teaching offers us a way to take something of that experience with us: the words of prayer can carry and sustain us as we move into the year ahead.Noah could not remain in the ark forever. Eventually, the waters receded, the door opened, and he stepped onto dry land to begin again. The ark had carried him through the Flood; now he had to build life anew.Raanan's teiva, at once ark and lute, seems to hold both possibilities. The ark offers refuge; the lute gives us a song for the journey. We enter the teiva, and it carries us into the year ahead.The writer is the author of Art of Revelation: A Visual Encounter with the Jewish Bible, a commentary on the paintings of her husband, artist Yoram Raanan. She teaches Jewish meditation and is currently writing 'Art of Transformation,' a book exploring the relationship between art, Jewish spirituality, and inner transformation, from which this article is adapted.

title: Parashat Noah: The main thing is the intention
body: One of the most dramatic events to shape the world and humanity was the Flood, which swept across the earth and destroyed everything on it, leaving only Noah and his family, the animals he had brought into the Ark, and the fish in the waters.At the beginning of Creation, the world was created in perfection and goodness, destined to exist without death or disease.However, following Adam's sin and his expulsion from the Garden of Eden, evil entered the human experience.Humanity eventually reached a state in which, in the words of the Torah, “the earth was filled with violence.”Violence, corruption, and the absence of moral boundaries undermined the very foundations of human existence, until the world reached a breaking point.The Flood was therefore a turning point in the history of Creation, an attempt to halt the downward spiral and open a new chapter in the history of the world.When Noah and his family emerge from the Ark, they encounter a world entirely different from the one they had known: ruined, desolate, and silent, no longer filled with the human activity that had been inseparable from their lives.Try to imagine that moment. A small family stands before an immense, empty world, with no cities, no communities, no other human beings, and nothing of the familiar world they once knew.No one is there to welcome them. There is no one with whom to share their feelings, and no certainty about what life will look like from that point onward.What would be the first thing you would choose to do in such a moment? How does one respond to destruction on a scale that is almost impossible to comprehend?The Torah describes Noah's first act:“Noah went out, together with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives.“Noah built an altar to the Lord, and taking from every clean animal and every clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar” (Gen. 8:18-20).Noah does not begin his new life by trying to rebuild the world, constructing a home for himself, or first attending to his family's practical needs. The first act described in the Torah is building an altar and offering a sacrifice to God.This act acknowledges the Creator's sovereignty, gives thanks, and submits oneself before the One who governs the world. Noah recognizes that even when reality appears harsh and incomprehensible, the world does not operate by chance. In the very midst of devastation and destruction, he expresses his connection with the One who spoke the world into existence.Then an unexpected turn takes place. The Torah describes how Noah's act leads to a divine promise concerning the future of all humanity:“The Lord smelled the pleasing aroma, and the Lord said to Himself: I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth; nor will I ever again destroy every living thing as I have done” (Gen. 8:21).World continues to exist with evil in itGod promises that He will never again bring a Flood to destroy all life on earth, and that the world will continue to exist even though evil remains within it.Yet this very promise raises a question. For many years, Noah stood alone against an entire generation, admonishing its members, trying to influence them and change their ways. Nevertheless, the Flood was not averted. Yet now, after the destruction, a single act of his elicits such a profound response. What was it about this act that gave it such extraordinary power?The Mishna in Tractate Makkot states:“Rabbi Hananya ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring merit to Israel; therefore, He gave them an abundance of Torah and commandments, as it is stated: 'The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious'” (Makkot 3:16).The Rambam, Maimonides, explains this teaching of the Mishna, establishing an important principle for understanding the significance of the commandments:“One of the fundamental principles of faith in the Torah is that if a person fulfills one of the 613 commandments properly and correctly, without involving any worldly objective whatsoever, but performs it purely for its own sake, out of love, that person merits the World to Come through it.“Rabbi Hananya therefore said that because of the great number of commandments, it is impossible for a person not to perform at least one of them perfectly at some point during his lifetime, thereby meriting the eternal survival of the soul through that act” (Commentary on the Mishna, Tractate Makkot).These words express a central principle of serving the Creator. The commandments are not merely a list of actions a person must perform; they express the relationship between the individual and God.A person may perform a good deed to earn honor or gain status. He may also act out of habit or loyalty to the tradition in which he was raised. In the language of our Sages, all these may be considered commandments performed shelo lishma – not purely for their own sake.Maimonides points to the central goal of fulfilling the commandments: performing them lishma, for their own sake, out of love for the Creator and a desire to fulfill His will, without any personal interest mixed in.We can now understand that Noah's efforts before the Flood do not diminish his righteousness. However, when a person acts before an entire community, additional motives may accompany his actions.After the Flood, the situation is entirely different. Noah builds an altar and offers a sacrifice without seeking to prove his righteousness to anyone, compete with anyone, or gain status. After all, the world is empty of other people. He acts solely because he wishes to serve his Creator and acknowledge His goodness. This is a pure act performed lishma, for its own sake.Such a clean and genuine act, performed entirely for the sake of Heaven, has the power to ensure the world's continued existence forever. For this is the very purpose of Creation, and now that this purpose has been fulfilled, humanity can endure.This idea is relevant to our everyday lives as well. The deeper test often comes precisely when no one is watching.Imagine someone driving alone late at night who finishes drinking a cup of coffee. He could throw the empty cup out the window, thinking that no one will notice.Yet in that moment, he discovers whether keeping the environment clean and acting responsibly toward it are values he truly believes in, or whether he observes them only because he fears the reaction of others.In a generation in which sharing our experiences and actions has become central to social life, this aspect of serving God deserves our attention as well.People share acts of kindness, charitable donations, volunteer initiatives, and other good deeds on social media.This has a positive side: publicizing a good deed can inspire others, encourage them to act, and create additional circles of generosity.However, alongside the benefits of sharing, we must not lose the ability to do good without telling anyone about it.When every action becomes an opportunity to share, a person may grow accustomed to measuring a deed's value by the degree of exposure and recognition it receives. Instead of asking whether he has done the right thing, he may find himself wondering whether he will receive positive responses and whether others will think more highly of him as a result. It is therefore important to preserve an inner space where our good deeds remain between ourselves and our Creator, without needing applause or expecting recognition.The writer is rabbi of the Western Wall and holy sites.

title: Zelenskyy: We receive information regarding ballistic missile launches specifically from the U.S
body:
Ukraine works with many countries on intelligence data, but receives information regarding Russian ballistic missile launches specifically from the United States, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reported.

"And regarding intelligence data, we always say that we are grateful to our American partners. Many countries share intelligence with us. We are talking about dozens of countries. We have established this kind of work during the war. This is very substantial, serious assistance. We are grateful to them," Zelenskyy said at a press briefing in Brussels on Friday.

"Regarding ballistics, specifically ballistic launches, we receive this information from the United States of America. Here, as you see, there are many challenges precisely related to ballistics," he added.

title: Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan Launch Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Cable
body: Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have launched a fiber-optic communications link across the Caspian seabed. The approximately 380-kilometer cable connects Aktau and Sumgait, with Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Ilham Aliyev announcing the launch in Baku on October 15. Until now, a significant share of Kazakhstan’s international internet traffic has passed through Russian networks. The new route gives operators the option of directing data through Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey. This is particularly important during outages or congestion on existing connections. The cable, manufactured and tested in China, has a design capacity of at least 400 terabits per second and was laid by Kazakhstan’s Kazakhtelecom and Azerbaijan’s AzerTelecom. The project had been under discussion since 2019; in 2024, planned investment was estimated at more than $50.6 million. Marine surveys began in August 2025. The underwater cable was laid the following August, and the line was launched in October 2026, 14 months after the surveys began. Kazakhstan also hopes to use the new connection to attract technology companies. Bagdat Mussin, chairman of Kazakhtelecom’s management board, said the cable could support Kazakhstan’s Data Center Valley, a complex under development in Ekibastuz for cloud computing and artificial intelligence. However, better international connectivity addresses only part of that challenge. As The Times of Central Asia previously reported , Kazakhstan must also secure affordable electricity and attract international customers if its data center ambitions are to succeed. For now, the practical impact of the new connection remains uncertain. Operators have yet to disclose how much traffic it will carry or what share of traffic currently routed through Russian networks could be redirected.

title: FM Sybiha: Black Sea could become second Strait of Hormuz for global food security
body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this in an interview with Ukrinform .
“Russia is using food as a weapon. We see this, just as we see it exploiting migration policy. Russia is well aware of how vulnerable certain countries are to such actions, particularly efforts to undermine global food security,” the Foreign Minister said.
According to Sybiha, Russia’s blockade of the Black Sea is aimed not only at disrupting shipping but also at creating food shortages in certain African countries, which could trigger new waves of migration to Europe.
“This is a deliberate and clear strategy on Russia’s part. We must have our own strategy for restoring freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, unblocking it, and securing ceasefires in both the energy sector and at sea. We have concrete proposals and new participants who have joined this process for the first time. These include India and Egypt,” the Minister stressed.
Sybiha recalled that in 2022, when navigation in the Black Sea was blocked, global food prices rose by 25%.
“We are once again on the brink of such an increase. The food security of many countries around the world depends on Ukrainian grain, and this is about more than grain alone. Because of Russia’s blockade of the Black Sea, those countries are not receiving products on time,” the Ukrainian Foreign Minister emphasized.
He added that some agricultural land could remain unsown because of the risks created by Russia, which would also affect prices next year.
“Therefore, the consequences are already being felt, and they will only intensify. The Black Sea could become a second Strait of Hormuz, this time in terms of food security,” Sybiha stressed.
He noted that all mediators actively involved in the process were now awaiting a response from Russia, while Ukraine was working with all its European partners to maximize the transit of Ukrainian grain through their countries to designated destinations.
“This will be difficult because Ukraine is one of the world’s largest agricultural producers and can feed up to 400 million people. Collective pressure is therefore needed to force Russia to unblock the Black Sea,” the head of Ukrainian diplomacy concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that European partners are becoming increasingly aware of the threat posed by Russian escalation and the need to counter the “shadow war” Moscow is waging against the West. They also recognize Ukraine’s important role in strengthening European security.

title: Truancy: Akwa Ibom warns parents, plans to ‘intercept’ loitering students
body:
The Akwa Ibom State Government says it will deploy a special monitoring task force to tackle truancy, street hawking by school-age children during school hours, and children not enrolled in school.
The state’s Commissioner for Education, Ubong Umoh, announced the measure in a statement dated 14 October, saying the ministry had observed children of basic and pre-tertiary school ages roaming the streets and hawking during school hours despite the state’s free and compulsory education policy.
Under the proposed enforcement measure, the task force will intercept pupils who arrive late to school or leave class during school hours. It will also confront parents and guardians who fail to enrol their children or wards in school, according to the statement.
The ministry identified school hours as 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. on weekdays.
Mr Umoh said the measure was intended to keep children in classrooms, improve their safety, curb truancy and classroom distractions, and prevent child abuse.
He said the initiative would also support the implementation of the state’s free and compulsory education policy.
The commissioner, however, did not specify when the task force would begin operations, how it would be constituted, or the penalties that would apply to parents and guardians who fail to comply with the directive.
The directive follows the state’s poor performance in the 2026 National Examinations Council Senior School Certificate Examination.
PREMIUM TIMES reported in September that Akwa Ibom ranked 36th among the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, with only 37.42 per cent of candidates obtaining at least five credits, including in English Language and Mathematics. The performance represented a major decline from the state’s 12th-place ranking in 2025.
The state government later disputed the newspaper’s report, claiming results from 83 of 214 public-school examination centres had not been released. However, it had not yet provided the official data it said supported its position.
On 7 October, Governor Umo Eno declared a state of emergency in the education sector and approved recruiting an additional 2,000 teachers.
The new directive on school attendance adds enforcement against truancy and non-enrolment to the challenges facing the state’s education authorities.

title: Dr. Mohammed Amin Adam writes: Ghana’s 2026 domestic debt financing
body: Ghana’s recent public debt situation appears to have improved, but the central policy question is whether the debt position and financing system have become durable, transparent, and market based. The recovery has benefited from debt-service relief under the DDEP, external restructuring, IMF programme discipline, expenditure compression, favourable gold prices, and domestic policy measures. These supports have eased immediate pressure, but they do not by themselves remove refinancing risks. The decisive test is whether Government can meet obligations, finance budget deficits, and extend maturities without accumulating arrears, suppressing investor returns, relying on opaque placements, or weakening the domestic yield curve. Since the DDEP, debt has also been managed through a widening set of tools outside regular competitive auctions: reopenings and possible placements of DDEP bonds, non-cash issuance, payment-in-kind coupons, Sinking Fund prefunding, and a planned liability-management programme.
