title: Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support
body:
Sally Rooney's books are displayed for sale at a bookshop in London, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Kin Cheung/AP hide caption
Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics.
Now the 35-year-old writer's books will no longer be sold in the UK because of her own closely-held political beliefs. She had promised to donate the revenues to Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group that the UK has designated a terrorist organization.
In a statement this week, her publisher explained: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."
"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said.
The move comes after Rooney — who has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — announced last year she would be donating funds from the proceeds of her books to Palestine Action, which was controversially banned in the U.K. under terrorism legislation.
Israel vehemently denies allegations of genocide.
UK-based Palestine Action says on its website it uses "disruptive tactics" to target "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex and seeks to make it impossible for these companies to profit from the oppression of Palestinians."
It has targeted facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and, in a major security breach, last year managed to break into Britain's largest air force base. The activists spray-painted two aircraft at the base blood red, in what the group said was a protest against Britain's military support for Israel.
Palestine Action was also responsible for vandalizing one of President Trump's golf courses in Scotland in March last year, when activists painted the course with the words "Gaza is not 4 sale." Reacting on social media , Trump called those responsible "terrorists."
FILE - From left, Paul Mescal, Sally Rooney and Ed Guiney participate in Hulu's "Normal People" panel during the Winter 2020 Television Critics Association Press Tour on Jan. 17, 2020, in Pasadena, Calif. Richard Shotwell/Invision/ AP hide caption
When the British government banned the group in July last year, it said it was on the grounds that Palestine Action is responsible for "serious damage to property." It was the first time a terrorist designation had been given to an organization that does not call for violence against people.
"Its activity has increased in frequency and severity since the start of 2024 and its methods have become more aggressive, with its members demonstrating a willingness to use violence," the British government said at the time.
The government also said that the group's "activities meet the threshold of being concerned in terrorism as set out in the Terrorism Act 2000," adding that it assessed "that Palestine Action commits and participates in acts of terrorism."
But critics questioned this assessment, saying it raised concerns about freedom of speech.
U.N. Human Rights Chief Volker Türk urged the U.K. government to rescind the decision, saying it "appears disproportionate and unnecessary."
"It limits the rights of many people involved with and supportive of Palestine Action who have not themselves engaged in any underlying criminal activity but rather exercised their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association," Türk said.
Amnesty International UK also raised concerns, saying "the UK has a deeply flawed and overly broad definition of terrorism."
Under the U.K. law, anyone who provides financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison.
For fear of arrest, Rooney says she has stopped traveling from her home in Ireland to the U.K. to attend award ceremonies and other events since the law came into force.
But the novelist has defended her support of Palestine Action, saying in an opinion piece in The Irish Times last year: "if this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."
It was in that op-ed that she announced she would use the British proceeds of her work "as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."
Now however, her books won't be sold in Britain at all, so there will be no further proceeds.
The Normal People author was undeterred, saying in a statement shared with NPR: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."
Since the ban on Palestine Action, several thousand people in the UK have been arrested for supporting them, mainly for carrying placards and wearing T-shirts.
The ban has been challenged in the courts, with the UK's high court ruling against it in February. A court of appeal later overturned that decision. Next month, the case heads to Britain's highest court.
In August, the U.S. Department of the Treasury followed the UK's lead in sanctioning Palestine Action, calling them "far-left terrorists."
A previous version of this story incorrectly referred to the group Palestine Action as Palestinian Action.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: Astana Plays Host to the Swimming World Cup
body: More than 300 swimmers from 39 countries are competing in Astana for the final leg of the 2026 World Aquatics Swimming World Cup. This is Kazakhstan’s first time hosting an event in the series, which will determine the overall men’s and women’s World Cup winners. The competition is taking place from October 15 to 17 at Barys Arena, concluding the three-stage Silk Road series, which began in Baku and continued in Tashkent. The World Cup is organized by World Aquatics, the international governing body for aquatic sports. Unlike the Olympic Games, swimmers compete in a 25- rather than a 50-meter pool, meaning races involve more turns. Competitors, whose ranks include Olympic and world champions, are vying for medals in freestyle, breaststroke, butterfly, and backstroke events over distances ranging from 50 to 1,500 meters. There are also individual medley and relay events. Athletes are also competing for overall standings points accumulated across the series’ three legs. The series carries a $1.2 million prize fund . On the opening day, October 15, two Kazakh swimmers set national records . Aibat Myrzamuratov completed the men’s 50-meter breaststroke in 26.50 seconds, while Sofia Spodarenko broke her own record in the women’s 50-meter butterfly. Kazakhstan’s Minister of Tourism and Sports, Yerbol Myrzabossynov, stressed the tournament’s significance for local swimmers, who have an opportunity to compete against some of the world’s leading athletes on home soil. Kazakhstan has entered 22 swimmers in the competition. Kazakhstan is expanding its calendar of international sporting events. According to the Ministry of Tourism and Sports, the country expects to host seven world championships across various disciplines in 2026 and 2027. These include the World Wrestling Championships , which will take place at Barys Arena from October 24 to November 1.

title: Keyamo blames Atiku over Nigeria Airways liquidation, Fani-Kayode disagrees
body:
Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development Festus Keyamo and his predecessor, Femi Fani-Kayode, have disagreed over the circumstances surrounding the collapse of Nigeria Airways and the role the administration in which former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar served played in liquidating the national carrier.
In a video posted on his official X account, Mr Abubakar said Nigerian families are going through hard times and struggling to afford food, healthcare, transport, and rent. At the same time, many live in fear of kidnapping and attacks.
“Bola made life expensive. I will work to make life affordable again and restore the security every Nigerian deserves,” he said.
In response, Mr Keyamo accused the former vice-president of hypocrisy, citing the liquidation of Nigeria Airways in 2004 and the long delay in settling its former workers’ entitlements.
He noted that the administration of former President Olusegun Obasanjo, in which Mr Abubakar served as the vice-president, left thousands of workers without pensions and gratuities.
According to Mr Keyamo, President Bola Tinubu approved and released ₦36 billion to settle the former employees’ outstanding entitlements, adding that beneficiaries have begun receiving payment.
“Twenty-two years later, after many of them have died out of frustration, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is now clearing the mess you left behind,” he said.
He also criticised Mr Abubakar for taking credit for the Obasanjo administration’s achievements when convenient, while distancing himself from its decisions when criticised.
Mr Fani-Kayode, Nigeria’s aviation minister from November 2006 to May 2007, challenged Mr Keyamo’s account of the airline’s collapse in a post on X on Thursday.
He asserted that the airline was already in severe decline before Mr Obasanjo returned to power in 1999, and went further to say Nigeria Airways had 32 functional aircraft when the former president left office as a military head of state in 1979. Still, by 1999, he had only one aircraft left.
“The company was liquidated primarily due to chronic insolvency, operational collapse and mismanagement in its operations which took place between 1979 and 1999,” he said.
Mr Fani-Kayode argued that the Obasanjo administration had little or no choice but to liquidate the airline after years of decline and failed attempts to revive it.
He also disputed the claim that the administration was solely responsible for the unpaid entitlements of former employees, saying the issue of their pensions remained unresolved even after the airline was wound up.
Mr Fani-Kayode said that, as aviation minister in 2006, he presented a memorandum to the Federal Executive Council seeking approval to pay outstanding pensions to former Nigeria Airways workers.
According to him, the memorandum was rejected after some cabinet members opposed the payment, arguing that former board members and management officials contributed to the airline’s collapse.
Mr Fani-Kayode said he disagreed with that position but could not secure approval for the proposal.
He added that the matter was taken up by the administration of former President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua, which paid most of the pensioners. At the same time, the administration of Muhammadu Buhari also made payments.
Mr Fani-Kayode commended the current administration for settling the outstanding entitlements but said the payments should have been made earlier.
Nigeria Airways began in 1958 as WAAC (Nigeria) Ltd, following the restructuring of the West African Airways Corporation. The Federal Government originally held a 51 per cent stake in it, while other shares were held by Elder Dempster Lines and British Overseas Airways Corporation. The government became the airline’s sole shareholder in 1961.
The airline operated domestic and international routes, connecting Nigerian cities with destinations across Africa, Europe and North America. At its peak, it was a prominent part of the country’s aviation industry.
However, its fortunes deteriorated over several decades amid mounting debt, poor management, political interference, overstaffing, and corruption allegations.
The airline had a fleet of 32 aircraft in 1984 , which fell to three by October 2000. By May 2003, its fleet had reportedly shrunk to one aircraft amid financial distress and operational difficulties.
The airline’s financial trouble also affected its international operations. In early 1987, the International Air Transport Association suspended it from its clearing house over accumulated debts exceeding $1.1 million. The suspension constrained its ability to issue tickets involving other member airlines through the clearing system.
The airline’s decline also prompted an investigation into allegations of corruption and financial mismanagement.
In 2001, the Obasanjo administration appointed a judicial commission to investigate the airline’s affairs during military rule from 1983 to 1999.
A November 2003 report by South Africa’s Business Report said a government white paper on the investigation detailed an alleged $400 million graft case involving former aviation ministers, former managing directors, and other officials associated with the airline.
The report also said the investigation identified alleged over-invoicing, questionable payments, and other financial irregularities. It also reported that the commission recommended recovering more than $400 million from companies and former officials implicated in its findings, with some individuals recommended for prosecution.
Efforts to rescue the carrier through restructuring and privatisation failed to restore its operations. The International Finance Corporation, the World Bank Group’s private-sector arm, was engaged to advise on the privatisation process but later withdrew.
The dispute over Nigeria Airways has continued long after the airline stopped operating, particularly over the pensions and severance benefits owed to its former employees.
In January 2025, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the National Assembly’s Joint Committee on Aviation said the Federal Government owed former Nigeria Airways workers N36 billion. The lawmakers threatened to withhold approval of the aviation budget unless provisions were made for the payment.
In May 2026, former workers again appealed to the Federal Government to release the outstanding entitlements. In July, a ministerial committee was preparing to oversee the disbursement .
On 12 September, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the Federal Government had paid severance benefits to 2,100 former workers, while another 600 beneficiaries had been cleared for payment. The benefits across the nine batches amounted to N18 billion.
The Ministry of Finance said President Tinubu had earlier approved the settlement and directed that the matter be concluded. The ministry said the process involved identifying eligible beneficiaries, validating records, and establishing financial obligations before payments began.

title: Uzbekistan Seeks Recognition of Its Driver’s Licenses in Germany
body: Uzbekistan is seeking recognition of its driver’s licenses in Germany to make it easier for its citizens to work in the country’s transport sector. The talks are linked to efforts to place Uzbek citizens in jobs with German transport and logistics companies. No agreement on license recognition has been reached so far. The issue was discussed at a meeting between Elyor Toshtemirov, deputy head of Uzbekistan’s Migration Agency, and representatives of the German companies Global Talent Alliance and TSK Logistik. The participants discussed driver training and the requirements of German employers. The Uzbek agency intends to raise the possibility of license recognition with the relevant German authorities. Another proposal involves establishing a joint German-Uzbek driving school to train bus and truck drivers. Training would follow German standards so that graduates could qualify for jobs with transport companies in Germany. Under current German rules, drivers with licenses issued outside the European Union and European Economic Area can generally use them for six months after establishing residence in Germany. After that, they must obtain a German license. Professional truck and bus drivers must also meet separate qualification requirements . The meeting also addressed difficulties Uzbek citizens face in obtaining German work visas. Following the talks, the Migration Agency and Global Talent Alliance signed a cooperation agreement. Its terms have not been disclosed in detail. Uzbekistan has already reached an agreement with the United Arab Emirates on mutual recognition of driver’s licenses. The relevant memorandum entered into force on January 27, 2024, allowing citizens of both countries to use their national licenses during short-term visits. It also allows Uzbek residents in the UAE to exchange their licenses without taking theoretical or practical driving tests.

title: Boeing prepares to close F/A-18 Super Hornet production after four decades
body:
Boeing is preparing for the end of F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler production under a US Navy contract that establishes how manufacturing equipment and tooling will be handled after the final aircraft leave the assembly line.
The US Navy awarded Boeing a US$16.7 million contract on September 29 to support the systematic shutdown of the production lines. The work is scheduled to continue through November 2030, several years after manufacturing of new aircraft ends.
The 2030 date does not represent an extension of aircraft production. Instead, the contract covers the inventory and evaluation of government-owned equipment, including decisions on which specialized tools must be retained to support the existing fleet.
Boeing had already announced plans in 2023 to end Super Hornet production after completing its remaining orders. Congress subsequently funded another 17 F/A-18E/F Block III aircraft under a US$1.3 billion contract awarded in 2024, extending manufacturing beyond the previously planned shutdown.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
Deliveries of those final aircraft are expected to begin in late 2026 and conclude in the spring of 2027.
The end of manufacturing will come more than three decades after the first F/A-18E/F flew in November 1995. The Super Hornet entered US Navy service in 1999 and gradually replaced earlier F/A-18 variants as the service's principal carrier-based fighter.
Production also gave rise to the EA-18G Growler electronic warfare aircraft, which entered service in 2009 as a replacement for the EA-6B Prowler.
Ending the assembly line will not end Boeing's work on the Super Hornet. The US Navy plans to operate the type into the 2040s and has been extending the service life of existing aircraft through the Service Life Modification (SLM) program.
The work can increase the life of selected Super Hornets from 6,000 to as many as 10,000 flight hours and incorporates upgrades associated with the Block III configuration.
The production shutdown comes as the US Navy begins developing the aircraft intended eventually to succeed the Super Hornet.
Boeing was selected in September for the F/A-XX program , a sixth-generation carrier-based combat aircraft planned for introduction during the 2030s. The program is intended to provide greater range and survivability than the F/A-18E/F and operate alongside unmanned aircraft.
The timelines mean the transition will extend for years. New Super Hornet deliveries will end in 2027, well before the F/A-XX is expected to enter operational service, while upgraded F/A-18E/Fs are planned to remain in the fleet into the following decade.
Boeing will also continue military aircraft production in St. Louis after the Super Hornet line closes. The company is increasing F-15EX production and developing the F-47 for the US Air Force, in addition to its work on the F/A-XX.

title: Magyar on meeting with Zelenskyy: Hungary ready to provide diplomatic assistance for ceasefire, lasting peace
body:
Hungary is ready to provide diplomatic assistance for the earliest possible ceasefire and the establishment of a lasting peace in Ukraine, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar stated following a meeting with President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels.
"I assured the President of Ukraine of my full solidarity in view of the inhuman Russian aggression against his country, which has been ongoing for almost five years. I told him that Hungary is ready to provide assistance by all possible diplomatic means to establish the earliest possible ceasefire and a lasting peace," Magyar wrote on Facebook on Friday.
He also reported that following the meeting, the parties agreed to continue consultations at the ministerial level, paying special attention to the situation of national minorities in both countries.
Magyar welcomed the political agreement between Hungary and Ukraine regarding the strengthening of the rights of the Hungarian minority in Zakarpattia, and called the Verkhovna Rada's adoption of the law on national minority education and the beginning of its implementation a first step toward restoring mutual trust.
Magyar also thanked the Ukrainian parliament for its September resolution regarding crimes against the Hungarians of Zakarpattia in 1944–1946, specifically forced labor and mass deportation.
"We agreed that it is in the interest of both countries to put political and economic relations on a new foundation," he noted.

title: Man Arraigned for Allegedly Diverting N34.8m Meant for Spaghetti Purchase
body: The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) has arraigned a man identified as Abdulmajid Halifa Nazifi before a Kano State High Court over the alleged misappropriation of N34.875 million meant for the purchase of spaghetti from BUA. Nazifi was arraigned on wednesday before Justice Musa Karaye on a one-count charge of criminal misappropriation. According to the charge, the defendant allegedly misappropriated the money belonging to Fahad Balarabe Adaji between September and October 2024 in Kano. The prosecution alleged that the money was transferred, on the defendant’s instruction, into the First Bank account of one Muazu Abdullahi for the purchase of IRS spaghetti from BUA but was diverted for his personal use. Gunmen abduct Catholic priest in Benue Tinubu to Miss Campaign Rallies in Over 20 States The alleged offence contravenes Section 308 of the Kano State Penal Code Law and is punishable under Section 309 of the same law. The defendant, however, pleaded not guilty when the charge was read to him. Following his plea, prosecution counsel, Mustapha Maiwada, asked the court to fix a date for trial and remand the defendant in a correctional facility. Justice Karaye ordered that Nazifi be remanded in a correctional centre and adjourned the case until November 2, 2026, for further hearing.

title: Government secures financing to fix water shortages in Tamale, Yendi and Damongo
body: Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson has announced a €323 million financing package for the Northern Ghana Water and Sanitation Project, aimed at addressing persistent water shortages in Tamale, Yendi and Damongo. The package comprises €98 million in grants and a €225 million highly concessional facility from the European Investment Bank (EIB). Dr. Forson outlined the financing following a meeting with EIB Vice-President Ambroise Fayolle, describing the discussions as productive. “I have just concluded a productive meeting with European Investment Bank Vice-President Ambroise Fayolle on the financing package for the Northern Ghana Water and Sanitation Project,” he said. The European Commission will provide a €68 million grant, while Invest International, the Dutch government initiative, will contribute a further €30 million grant. The EIB’s highly concessional facility accounts for the remaining €225 million. According to the Finance Minister, the project will address recurring water shortages and improve sanitation across the three communities.

title: Oil-rich nations must turn fossil fuel wealth into sustainable energy — Expert
body:
A professor of Energy and Environmental Economics at Pan-Atlantic University, Ekundayo Mesagan , has urged Nigeria and other oil-producing countries to transform their fossil fuel wealth into sustainable energy systems amid growing global pressure to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Mr Mesagan said such countries could channel fossil fuel revenues into financing renewable energy, developing green infrastructure, and adopting cleaner technologies instead of relying heavily on oil and gas for economic growth.
He made the recommendation during his inaugural lecture titled “Making Lemonade from Lemons: The Fossil Energy and Sustainability Puzzle” on 9 October, noting that oil-producing countries face the challenge of balancing the economic benefits of fossil fuels with the environmental consequences of their extraction and consumption.
“The topic of my lecture today is how we can make lemonade from lemons by navigating the dilemma between fossil energy and environmental sustainability,” Mr Mesagan said at the event.
His recommendations come as countries grapple with the pressure to minimise emissions under the 2015 Paris Agreement, which seeks to keep global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius.
Nigeria is a signatory to the agreement and has committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2060, even as it continues to invest in its oil and gas industry to bolster economic growth and development.
Decades of oil exploration and production, particularly in the Niger Delta, have also raised concerns over environmental degradation and its impact on local communities, livelihoods and ecosystems.
Mr Mesagan said fossil fuels remain a key driver of greenhouse gas emissions, highlighting the difficulty of reconciling continued dependence on oil, gas and coal with global climate targets.
Global carbon dioxide emissions surged from about 22 billion tonnes in 1990 to approximately 39 billion tonnes in 2024, the professor observed, mirroring the continued challenge of moderating emissions despite international climate commitments.
According to him, the global shift to lower-carbon energy requires countries to cut back their reliance on fossil fuels while expanding renewable energy and investing in cleaner technologies.
His view of fossil fuels as “lemons” indicates that although fossil fuels offer considerable economic value and energy potential, their non-renewable nature and environmental consequences create long-term challenges.
He said the “lemonade” represents benefits like environmental sustainability through investment, innovation, and effective policymaking that fossil fuel wealth can provide.
The professor said capital investment in environmentally friendly technologies is a major way to reduce the pollution associated with fossil fuel production and consumption.
He urged Nigeria and other oil-rich developing countries to commit a portion of their oil revenues to building domestic capacity for renewable energy and green infrastructure rather than depending heavily on foreign countries.
He also called for greater investment in carbon capture, utilisation and storage, which involves capturing carbon dioxide emissions for storage or subsequent use in industrial processes.
According to him, the technology could help oil-producing countries cut emissions, strengthen their participation in carbon markets, and remain competitive as global climate policies tighten.
Mr Mesagan urged existing and proposed refineries in Nigeria to consider investing in carbon-capture technologies to reduce their environmental footprint.
He also expressed hope that the African Energy Bank, established by the African Petroleum Producers’ Organisation, will collaborate with the Africa Carbon Markets Initiative to advance carbon trading across the continent.
The don further advocated a diversified energy mix, urging oil-producing countries to invest oil revenues in solar, hydro and wind power while strengthening policies to support cleaner energy adoption.
He said effective governance, stronger pollution-control laws and carbon pricing are also necessary to ensure that investments in technology and innovation deliver meaningful environmental benefits.
Looking ahead, Mr Mesagan identified climate finance, access to green energy, and climate vulnerability as areas that require further research.
He highlighted the role of carbon-capture technologies and carbon markets in Africa’s pursuit of net-zero emissions, alongside the integration of renewable energy into artificial intelligence infrastructure and the socioeconomic implications of energy storage and the energy transition.
He called for collaboration among policymakers, engineers, economists and environmental scientists to develop solutions that would enable oil-producing countries to maximise the economic benefits of their natural resources while reducing environmental damage.

title: Issues related to freight, insurance of diesel supplies to US effectively resolved — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. All issues related to freight, insurance, and the supply of diesel to the US have effectively been resolved, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said.
"All issues related to freight, insurance, and supplies will be resolved. The suppliers and buyers need to sign documents between themselves now," he told reporters on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week.
There are no obstacles to supplies neither regarding freight nor insurance, considering how the US Department of the Treasury interprets the lifting of sanctions on diesel shipments, Novak added.

title: The Country Cramming for the AI Revolution
body:
Find this story in your account’s ‘Saved for Later’ section.
This article was featured in New York ’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here .
In May, I sat in a living room on the fringes of Hangzhou, one of the most technologically advanced cities in China and home to Alibaba, Unitree, and DeepSeek. In many ways, the party that was about to start resembled one that you’d find in any coastal metropolis: ten professionals in their 20s padding barefoot across the carpet, snacks on the dining table. Only the laptops scattered across the floor and couch suggested this was a different type of social gathering, one that has grown common in the past three years in China’s towns and cities. Our host, KC, has gathered a small circle of friends to learn AI.
KC’s face is still marked with acne; he is tall and thin, barely past 20, and already a vibe coder of some local fame. Today he’ll teach others how to use Codex and Figma to quickly build websites, Electron desktop apps, install packages — but the first step is teaching everyone to “put up the ladder,” the euphemism for deploying VPNs and relays that bypass OpenAI’s geo-block. Like any self-organized class, it doesn’t really begin until nearly two hours in. Only as the sky darkens do people settle down, grow patient, and start the class.
The demographic of the room is young, hungry, yet refusing to join or be excluded from the rat race of big tech — they self-identify as engineers, designers, influencers, or, to use a more fashionable term, one-person companies (OPCs). They are members of a social species typical of a generation facing 18.9 percent unemployment, astronomical real-estate prices in big cities, and a battered post-COVID economy, which a friend describes as petit bourgeois, overeducated, downwardly mobile young people who can just barely make the rent. A few years ago, low-cost towns like Liangzhu (where KC lives), Dali, and Anji started actively courting digital nomads and vibe coders like them. Amid government campaigns and a stream of social-media posts, young people started washing up there, hoping that learning AI while keeping their expenses low might change something.
During the self-introduction session, one woman mentions, a little shyly, her old life at Tencent — which she had disliked so much that she quit to explore “the many ways of not going to work.” Another, with long black hair, introduces herself as a novelist serializing a long book on Jinjiang Literature City, China’s biggest women-focused web-fiction platform. A third says she used to work in fashion and now runs an “aesthetics and shopping-companion” business with a friend and does self-media and AI projects on the side. They are all convinced that AI could empower their work.
Since ChatGPT, a new consensus has hardened across China’s tech industry: AI is the next mobile internet. On the surface, the country seems to have arrived at a near-universal embrace of new technology. Xi Jinping has described AI as an essential engine for China’s “new quality productive forces.” From a Marxist-Hegelian perspective, AI is on the right side of history, and history must march forward. As Evan Osnos, a staff writer with The New Yorker , recently wrote, the future could be made in China. But beneath the AI frenzy lies a real dread: people’s fear of being thrown overboard by China’s next Darwinian round of industrial upgrading, with little choice but to go along.
At once an old Chinese reflex returned: When history accelerates and people lose their bearings, find a teacher. In a society where meritocracy and education still carry near-religious authority, the proper response to a disruptive technology is to embrace it and to enroll. Decades ago, it was “ English fever ,” when English-learning-as-self-transformation swept factory floors and university lecture halls alike, everyone convinced that fluency was their ticket out. Now the conviction has simply changed languages. Resisting this technology is futile, unwise — so better to seize the window before it closes. The state claimed AI will empower thousands of industries, with social-media timelines filled with proof that someone, somewhere, has already changed their lives with it. In response, for many people I met across China since the arrival of ChatGPT, one thing that kept surfacing was their hunger for learning about AI, a compulsion to keep upskilling. Lessons, lessons, lessons — I noticed how often the word surfaced during casual conversations.
In the U.S., backlash against data centers has united people across the political spectrum and generations. This “AI populism,” a term coined by the writer Jasmine Sun, reflects a belief that AI is not a neutral technology but an elite project driven by tech billionaires to concentrate power and displace workers. In China, on the other hand, a meme that’s now circulating goes: Westerners get restless when they can’t protest; Chinese people get restless when they haven’t found a teacher. People like KC self-organize classes; for others, the dread of getting left behind by AI has presented a business opportunity.
Hangzhou’s Future Sci-Tech City (未来科技城) is one of those municipal declarations of intent to materialize the future. It is home to Alibaba’s headquarters and to the towers, campuses, incubators, talent apartments, and financial-service complexes through which a local government announces that it, too, belongs to the next technological epoch. For the sheer density of engineers packed into its office parks, people jokingly call the area “the center of the programmer universe.”
The industry of paid knowledge, and its priesthood of “knowledge influencers,” is nothing new — in the mobile internet age, people built an entire economy around it. Now this industry has a new direction: evangelize AI. The company I’d come to see was the operator of one of the largest “make money with AI” communities, a membership business that monetizes the promise of AI. The company is called Shengcai Youshu (生财有术), roughly “The Art of Getting Rich.” It offers online classes, offline intensive training, and co-working space. Its Hangzhou office, where the founders sit, is one of the larger nodes in a network that spans the country. I was greeted by Mr. Tree, a middle-aged AI influencer on the company’s payroll, whose bio announces him to the world as being on a mission to “look for 100 business answers in the age of AI.” He is habitually nervous, easily and overly excited. His accent is not the polished, elite-educated kind, and he mispronounces his English words.
In one of the short videos of him teaching a class to a few dozen, he stands onstage before an audience old and young, their faces solemn, pens moving. “What is AI?” Mr. Tree asks loudly. “AI is your Silicon-based labor force! Most companies run nine-to-five, eight hours a day. AI runs 7-by-24 — round the clock, every day of the week!” Mr. Tree’s relentless high spirits are contagious, and they remind me of a Mormon elder in Orange County who once tried to bring me into his church when I was a college student freshly arrived from China. He walked me through the office, recording the whole tour on his DJI Osmo Pocket, as though everything he did needed to become material for his vlog.
The office’s theme color is green, the color of money (in fact, the company offers a class called “Making Dollars Together”). Meeting rooms have names like “Apostle of the Method” (传术师) and “Evangelist” (布道师). Along the corridors, the walls are covered, like those of any company proud of its own legend, with founder lore, milestones, and mottos. I read that the founder, Yiren, after leaving Alibaba in 2017, vowed to “help young people who, like him, had once been poor but hardworking, change their fate by making money,” the kind of declaration you might hear from a gilded-age robber baron or a self-made oracle like Benjamin Franklin or Jack Ma — mission fused seamlessly with the libertarian lore of self-salvation. Another line on the wall managed the same mix of sincerity and self-regarding heroism: Whatever saved you, use it to save the world.
That afternoon, when I visited the office, Yiren happened to be in. We shook hands politely. He was thin and shy, soft-spoken, his hair combed with a precision bordering on severity. It was hard to square this quiet figure with his career: a man with a cult following who had recently turned himself into an AI chatbot (on WeChat) and issued a standing invitation: Ask me anything about growth, entrepreneurship, your projects, or making money.
Yiren first found influence online writing paywalled dispatches with titles like “365 Ways to Make Money in a Year.” As paid followers grew, his company, The Art of Getting Rich, funneled that traffic into something far more elaborate. Today, paid members are encouraged to collect something called Dragon Balls — a goofy, gamified name for the points awarded to those who help the community grow: posting useful content, recruiting newcomers, and then climbing the leaderboard. On one wall, a diagram lays out the order of ascent. You begin as an ordinary member by paying the yearly fee, then become a Dragon Ball holder, then a Navigator, then you enter the Deep-Sea Circle — the executive tier — until, at last, you gain access to the co-working floor among the senior members and stand, in effect, at partner level.The higher you climb, the more people and resources become available to you. Am I in a cult? I wondered. The headquarters of some pyramid scheme?
Membership is not cheap. Entry to the online community costs ¥3,365 today, against an average Hangzhou private-sector salary of ¥7,671 a month, roughly half a month’s wages for an ordinary worker. What keeps people coming, I think, is a residual faith in upward mobility — the hope that behind a changed economy there remains a way in. The company is now nine years old, with more than 80,000 paying members to date and over 2,000 offline events hosted per year across Chinese cities. The more I read the company website — which promises to help people “break into new circles, trade notes with bosses and operators, find a community that fits, and never walk the road to wealth alone” — the more it resembled a kind of church, a place where career, marriage, and a child’s education might all be worked out.
Mr. Tree took me into a room with 20-odd people in their 20s to 40s. Some were solo entrepreneurs and senior members using the office as a co-working space, heads down at work. Mr. Tree asked everyone to stop so he could introduce me as a visitor from San Francisco, prompting someone to shout, “Take us to Silicon Valley!” The whole office laughed.
Beyond The Art of Getting Rich, which hosts AI courses of every kind, the cheaper, messier imitators — “DeepSeek 101,” “Get Wealthy With AI,” “Learn to Distill,” “Super AI Agent” classes — have now multiplied to fill every corner of the internet. AI is the only path forward. The last chance for ordinary people to defy fate and remake their lot. AI won’t replace people, but people who can’t use AI will be replaced by people who can. Before the pitch, the sellers usually offer a few tidy success stories: a stay-at-home mother, for example, who used DeepSeek to turn out video scripts at 30 yuan a job. Since last year, state-sponsored media has taken to calling this paid-knowledge economy a mess, warning that ordinary people are being “cut like leeks” — fleeced — by a course-selling economy that “takes advantage of people’s ‘skill anxiety’ about new technologies.” Online, I found one member’s verdict on The Art of Getting Rich’s own classes:
“Tried The Art of Getting Rich for a few days. Pricey! Over a thousand yuan. Got inside and found nothing of substance: they have the students themselves post their money-making stories to fill the place up, and if you post enough you can offset the tuition.”
And yet. After the office visit, I read some of the articles shared on the company’s news feed, and to my surprise, they were not bad. One walked through pairing Claude with Obsidian to create a kind of product-copy engine, for the struggling e-commerce seller managing a sprawl of listings that each needs its own picture-and-text blurb. This article explained “the attention that AI tends to dilute,” and how to manage “context window,” and the way to prevent models from suffering “pattern collapse” and turning lazy. Most of it didn’t strike me as novice knowledge; Claude and Obsidian are no strangers to Silicon Valley’s hyperproductive tech set. But picture the reader who might actually pay ¥3,365 to learn it further. Maybe he’s a man in his 40s with a middle-school education, somewhere in China’s export-dependent manufacturing belt, running his business on instinct and hard work but not a word of English. He sells water bottles, desk lamps, and plastic toys across the border to the richer half of the world and is in a perpetual battle with the blank spot where the Amazon product copy should go. Picture him handed Claude and Obsidian. The distance the article is trying to close is enormous, and it is closing it in earnest.
These are the people Mr. Tree and The Art of Getting Rich mean to reach: the ones from traditional manufacturing, from trades with no exposure to AI at all. In June, he posted, to his own feed, a thank-you note from one of his students, another typical profile:
“I’m working as a security guard right now. I came across The Art of Getting Rich late last year … for more than half a year I’ve been using all kinds of AI without stop … every day at work I’m interacting with Claude Code, on my phone and on my computer at home. My stint as a guard is almost over now — I’m about to start a job at a semiconductor-packaging company! Once the new work settles, I’ll keep building my AI skills.”
Mr. Tree’s caption reads: “Dude says he’s a security guard. Hell of a thing .”
This spring, a Chinese sociologist named Lian Si published A Journey Without a Map , an ethnography of ten groups of young people. Si is no dissident. He is executive vice-president of the China Youth University of Political Studies. Yet even from inside the system, his verdict lands hard. Many young people in their 20s are living in a reality unlike that of previous generations who could take economic miracles for granted. Uncertainty has become an ordinary fact of daily life, with risk seeping into every part of life — school, work, home, and marriage. I thought, Even a Party-approved scholar is allowed to say that now. His counsel to the young: Stop climbing. “Make peace with the ordinary,” he has said. “Shake hands with failure.”
In my search for a story about China’s AI optimism, I instead found stories about choicelessness and coping — about a crippled sense of agency, narrowed down to the few things still within reach, in a world that offers only one correct way to make sense of your own struggle: It would be your own fault if you got left out. Here is a state with vanishingly little upward mobility, promising “common prosperity” anyway by doubling down on high technology. When the Party holds fast to a Hegelian History — History with a capital H — in which technological ascent is not a choice but a necessity, what options remain?
If Mr. Tree’s story is true, then this silver lining is real — the upward mobility AI promises isn’t something people simply conjured out of desperation. Xiaokai, a 25-year-old film director I met near Hangzhou, is an example.
If you didn’t already know that he employed seven people and ran an AI video studio turning over several million yuan a year, his manner and thick Dongbei accent might place him as a street-corner hustler. Every 30 minutes he gets up to smoke. He wears slippers and a pair of beige shorts, his long hair tied back at the nape. Xiaokai’s humor is the Dongbei kind: bleak and wearily cynical, interspersed with random self-deprecating commentary, no tolerance of pretense or bullshit.
Xiaokai left his home in Dongbei, China’s rust belt, at 18 to chase a dream of acting. Like many children of the Dongbei, he grew up while his parents were away as migrant workers. His was a lonely childhood, and he was raised by a grandfather and a television playing Jackie Chan and old Shaw Brothers films. Before he discovered Way to AGI (one of the largest AI-learning communities online) in 2023 and taught himself AI filmmaking, Xiaokai thought he was a man with no prospects: a third-tier diploma from art school and behind him a string of failed ventures, livestreaming among them. Dongbei people make the best livestreamers, he told me. When he opens his mouth, the street smarts pour out, and you understand at once that this is a man who will never let himself go hungry.
Beside Xiaokai sat Big Wang, 42, Xiaokai’s COO. He’d been up all night working on a video for a district government in Shanghai, a celebratory piece, all gleaming towers and grand accomplishments, in the house style you can call the old cadres love . The peculiar challenge of this government commission is that the AI video needs to convincingly resemble a real production, complete with drone footage and a big-budget feel. Every building, every detail has to be faithful to the real thing — which is why Big Wang had spent the night hunting down each hallucinated tower and street, until nothing in the frame was something the machine had dreamed up. The trick, Xiaokai explained, is to conduct a whole orchestra of AIGC models into setting still images in motion — the right prompts, endless small adjustments — until a three-minute city documentary leaps onto the screen, sweeping and grand, the camera gliding as though it had really been there. Shot conventionally, he said, the thing would cost well over a million yuan. This one went for around a hundred thousand. At lunch, he insisted on paying and ordered far more than we could eat.
Neither of them could have pictured the life they have now — so much work coming in that they are up through the night without rest. The company does so well that they can’t say aloud what a single commission costs, for fear of the envy it would stir among their peers. They showed me a screenshot of one rival’s message, sent in pure spite. “He saw how much we’re pulling in, saw we’d landed a big one,” Xiaokai said, “and he just lost it.” Xiaokai’s social media is a model template of Chinese Gen-Z success, a timeline crowded with highlights: red carpets at the Beijing and Shanghai film festivals; his work aired on CCTV, the state broadcaster; the press anointing him “the first Gen-Z in China to turn AIGC into money”; and, flaunted for all to see, the 2024 Award of Excellence in the AIGC Short-Film section of the Beijing International Film Festival.
With today’s AI capabilities, Xiaokai explained, the best kind of plot is “a story that keeps losing people”: As it advances, it sheds characters, so you have to worry less about consistency. (Too many faces is a real problem in the current state of the models — the longer the clip, the more the features begin to warp and slide.) A perfect project, then, would be an Agatha Christie–type story — characters are trapped in isolated settings, then disappear one by one. Then he showed me a clip: a knife pressing slowly into human skin. The sound raised goosebumps over my whole body. “Look — the blood coming out, how real it looks. Killer.” He pointed it out to me, delighted with himself.
Even as a success story, Xiaokai is emblematic of a market so grim it demands endless grind. (I visited Xiaokai’s studio on a Saturday; three people were still working and all looked sleep deprived. They only take one day off each week.) Next year he plans to put a down payment on an apartment and get married — at a moment when the overwhelming majority of 20-somethings like him are adrift in China’s simmering deflation and cruel job market. He joked that once he had checked off the to-do list of his life, he’d finally make art about his hometown.
Dongbei is in deep demographic decay. Its young people leave for school and rarely return. A genre has emerged under the name “Dongbei Renaissance,” composed of films, fiction, music, all circling the region’s postindustrial ruin and its bleak iconography: abandoned factory compounds, laid-off workers, family shame, murder, violence. The people who make them are the children of the 1990s state-enterprise collapse looking back on their parents’ wrecked world, a point of view that has carried a constellation of writers and filmmakers into the mainstream.
Xiaokai wants to turn his core memory of Dongbei into an AI film. The memory, as he described it: a wide frozen river beside a vast, emptied factory town. Every winter the river froze thick enough to walk on. To keep from slipping, people scattered coal cinders across the ice; the coarse grains bit under a boot or a tire and held.
Xiaokai described every detail as though the film already existed. It’s a story about a father and a son. Across the frozen river runs a thin black path — coal ash the father has laid down, stroke by careful stroke, so that the son, away in some distant southern city, can find his way home safely. But the father dies before the son returns. The son learns of the death, comes home, and finds the ice long since melted.
In Silicon Valley, the running argument between the accelerationists and the doomers is premised on the idea that AI is the only variable that matters. It could go extraordinarily well or extraordinarily badly; utopia or dystopia will arrive in a matter of years, even months. The great AI researchers assured me, all the same, that one day we will stand to superintelligence as apes stand to us. But when I think of the film Xiaokai wants to make, or read the latest gospel Mr. Tree posts, or catch up on KC’s new projects, what stays with me is not Silicon Valley’s arithmetic about AI or Beijing’s grand plan, but people’s stubborn insistence on their own dignity, defiant of a future the big men are summoning.

title: No end in sight to war in Strait of Hormuz — Russian presidential adviser
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Military operations in the Strait of Hormuz are unlikely to end anytime soon, Russian Presidential Adviser Anton Kobyakov said.
"The fight for Hormuz continues. Estimates of commodity volumes passing through the waterway have changed dramatically, with current figures 1.5-2 times below the pre-war level of 20 million barrels per day. Some put the figure at 10-13 million barrels. In general, there is no end in sight to the war there," he pointed out at a press conference on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week.
TASS is the event’s information partner.

title: Kremlin ‘Fully Agrees’ With Trump’s Zelensky Criticism
body:
The Kremlin expressed “full” agreement Friday with U.S. President Donald Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over stalled peace efforts.
“The fact that Zelensky doesn’t want to take responsibility and enter a peaceful settlement process is unambiguous,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
“Here, we fully agree with President Trump’s point of view,” Peskov said.
Trump sharply criticized Zelensky in an interview with the Newsmax outlet, saying he believes Russia and Ukraine will end up reaching a ceasefire after the Ukrainian leader steps down.
“He doesn’t want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn’t,” Trump said of Zelensky and the conflict running for more than four and a half years.
Trump noted that both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelensky would like to see the war end, “but I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
Putin continues to demand that Ukraine cede full control of the Donetsk region as a prerequisite for any ceasefire agreement — a condition Kyiv has repeatedly rejected.
Sources close to the Kremlin told Bloomberg last month that Putin expects Russian forces to take full control of the Donetsk region by late February 2027.
At a summit in Brussels on Friday, European leaders pushed back against the growing rift between Washington and Kyiv, offering unconditional backing to Zelensky as winter approaches.
Despite their public backing, European officials reportedly plan to privately urge Zelensky to tone down his public criticism of Trump.

title: Zelensky, Hungary's Magyar hold first 'one-on-one' talks at EU summit
body:
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar met for their first bilateral talks in Brussels on Oct. 16, as their countries seek to open a "new chapter" in relations.
Both leaders are in Brussels for a two-day EU summit, where Kyiv seeks to drum up European support amid deteriorating ties with the U.S.
The meeting comes the same week Zelensky signed a law on the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step Hungary had demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU accession talks to proceed.
"We see the Ukrainian parliament's adoption of the minority education law and the immediate start of its implementation as a first step towards rebuilding mutual trust," Magyar said on X after the meeting.
The Hungarian prime minister also said that both countries would continue talks at the ministerial level, focusing on the situation of national minorities.
Magyar underscored that both countries agreed on the need "to build a new foundation for our political and economic relations" and expressed solidarity with Ukraine in the face of "Russia's brutal aggression."
After Ukraine passed the minorities bill, Hungary lifted its veto on the opening of two more negotiation clusters for Ukraine, allowing their official launch on Oct. 13.
The law gives Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority and other EU-language minorities more room to use their native language in education.
Ukrainian officials have said it would formalize existing education rights for national minorities rather than bring major practical changes.
Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.
Zelensky said the meeting focused on Ukraine's EU accession efforts, as well as opportunities for bilateral cooperation, trade, and agricultural issues.
"We also discussed diplomacy and efforts to end Russia's war," the president said, adding that the leaders agreed to exchange visits.
"We're moving on our relationship with Hungary; we had a very good meeting," Zelensky said later at a press conference in Brussels. He did not rule out traveling to Budapest.
"I hope that we will get to the point where a new chapter opens (in Hungarian-Ukrainian relations)," Magyar said about his meeting with Zelensky a day prior, saying the two could then meet again in Berehove, a Zakarpattia Oblast town considered the heart of the Hungarian-speaking community in Ukraine.
Magyar has floated a meeting in Berehove since the spring, but no firm date has been set so far. The two held brief conversations in June in Brussels, and then again in July at the NATO summit in Ankara.

title: Women, girls pioneers of resistance behind frontlines of war
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei has said that women and girls of the country are the pioneers of the resistance behind the frontlines of war imposed against the country.
In a message issued on Friday on the occasion of the National Day of Nurses, which marks the birth anniversary of Hazrat Zainab (SA), the daughter of Imam Ali (AS) and the granddaughter of the Prophet [PBUH], the Leader instructed health officials of the country to pay due attention to the health community in order to promote healthcare issues in the country.
The Leader of the Islamic Revolution described the role of women and girls of the Islamic Iran during this unparalleled era of the Iranian nation’s resurgence as truly remarkable, highlighting the revitalizing and hope-inspiring role of nurses as well as their significant impact on the physical and mental health and security of society.
“Today, the Zainab-like women of Islamic Iran, through their strong presence in various arenas, particularly in city and village squares, are at the forefront of practical advocacy and resistance behind the front lines of hard warfare,” Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei stated.
The Leader added that the powers of the time, which seek to inflict suffering, pain and repression on the Iranian nation, do not consider themselves capable of confronting this vast force.
Turning to National Nurses Day, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said the anniversary of Hazrat Zainab’s birth has rightly been designated to honor nurses because of her compassion for those in pain and her self-sacrifice in serving them.
These qualities are evident among nurses, whose work, like that of doctors, teachers, religious scholars and relief workers, is life-giving and a source of hope, he underscored.
The Leader described nurses as “angels of mercy” when they bring calm, hope and healing to patients despite their distress and impatience. Unlike doctors, he noted, nurses must maintain a continuous, persistent and patient presence at patients’ bedsides. Their work goes beyond physical treatment, soothing psychological and emotional suffering and often preventing despair, the Leader noted.
The role of a nurse, much like that of certain other groups, such as physicians, teachers and educators, clergy, and relief workers, is the one that brings revitalization and hope, he said, adding, “Unlike physicians, the role of nurses in the treatment of patients requires a sustained, diligent and constant care.”
At a time when the malevolent network of the Global Arrogance spares no effort to inflict various forms of oppression and atrocities upon freedom-seeking and resilient nations, most notably the Iranian people, and seeks to impose suffering upon the great nation of Iran by creating restrictions on access to medical treatment and medicine, paying attention to nurses and strengthening the nursing profession is of vital importance that must be taken into serious consideration, the Leader emphasized.
The Leader further pointed out that nurses are angels of hope in the society and their endeavors should be paid due attention.
Preserving and enhancing the knowledge, skills, capabilities, vitality, motivation, and dignity of nurses, especially those who have dedicated themselves to render quality services within public or non-private institutions, has a significant impact on the physical and mental health and security of society, he continued.
Hence, health sector officials are expected to pay due attention to this important issue and must do their utmost efforts in realizing the objectives of the nursing community in the country in the best form possible, the Leader reiterated.
Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei also praised the outstanding role played by the nurses and medical staffers in the country during the 12-, and 40-day wars imposed by the US and Israeli regime against the country and commemorated the name and memory of the nurses who were martyred during the two wars and wished rapid recovery for the injured.

title: Ukrainian military strikes million-dollar Russian radar in Krasnodar Krai, General Staff claim
body:
The Ukrainian military struck a Russian Nebo-U radar near the settlement of Magri, in Krasnodar Krai, on the night of Oct. 16, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.
"The Nebo-U is a long-range, three-coordinate radar designed to detect and track aerial assets, including aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles," the General Staff said in a statement .
"Striking such systems reduces the enemy's ability to monitor airspace and detect aerial assets in time. The estimated cost of the radar station is about US $100 million," they said.
The General Staff did not give details about what Ukrainian munition was used to carry out the strike.
A day prior, an overnight attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh region carried out with the Neptune coastal missile system hit six Su-34M bomber jets, destroying four and damaging two, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 15.
On Aug. 23, Ukrainian drones struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said then.
Krasnodar Krai, a strategic region along Russia's Black Sea coast, has increasingly come under Ukrainian drone attacks as Kyiv extends the range of its strikes deep into Russian territory.

title: Media Trust Group Launches Converged Digital Newsroom
body: Media Trust Group, publishers of Daily Trust newspapers and owners of Trust TV, Trust Radio and other media platforms, will on Thursday, October 22, launch its Converged Digital Newsroom, a technology-driven initiative designed to transform how the Group gathers, produces and distributes news across its platforms. The initiative brings together editorial operations across Daily Trust, Trust TV, Trust Radio, Aminiya, Digital Trust and other platforms in a more integrated newsroom, enabling journalists to collaborate, share resources and deliver timely, relevant and engaging content to audiences across multiple channels. The newsroom will leverage digital technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI) tools, to support editorial workflows, content production, news distribution and audience insights. These capabilities will enhance efficiency and collaboration while keeping editorial judgement, verification and accountability firmly in the hands of journalists. Speaking ahead of the launch, the Group Chief Executive Officer, Ahmed I. Shekarau, said the converged newsroom represents a strategic step towards building a more connected, responsive and sustainable media organisation. “The future of the media lies in our ability to understand and serve our audiences better. By bringing our platforms together, we are strengthening our capacity to deliver credible journalism, respond to changing audience needs and make our content more accessible across different channels. “This is an investment in the future of the Media Trust Group, positioning us to take advantage of technological innovation, deepen our relationship with audiences and create greater value for our commercial partners,” he said. The Group Editorial Director and Editor-in-Chief, Ibrahim Shehu Adamu, said the initiative would encourage closer collaboration among journalists and editors while enabling the Group to tell stories more effectively across print, broadcast and digital platforms. “Our audiences do not consume news in the same way or on the same platform. Our responsibility is to meet them where they are, with credible, relevant and engaging journalism. The converged newsroom allows us to bring the strengths of our different platforms together, improve editorial coordination and deliver a richer news experience. “Technology, including AI-powered tools, will support this transformation by helping us work more efficiently, streamline newsroom processes and respond faster to developing stories. However, our commitment to accuracy, editorial independence and public-interest journalism remains unchanged,” he said. Better for audiences, greater value for advertisers For readers, viewers and listeners, the converged newsroom will support more coordinated news coverage, richer multimedia storytelling and easier access to news, analysis, interviews, video and audio content across the Group’s platforms. It will also strengthen the Group’s ability to respond to audience interests and feedback, particularly as more Nigerians consume news through mobile devices and digital channels. For advertisers and commercial partners, the integration creates opportunities for coordinated, cross-platform campaigns spanning newspapers, television, radio and digital media. By combining the strengths of its brands with a deeper understanding of audience behaviour, Media Trust Group aims to deliver more effective brand storytelling, wider audience engagement and improved campaign measurement. The initiative forms part of the Group’s broader strategy to build a digitally driven, audience-focused and commercially sustainable media organisation, leveraging technology and innovation to strengthen journalism and respond to the changing demands of the media industry.

title: EU Delegation Pledges Assistance for ‘People of Georgia’, Says No EU Funding Goes to Authorities
body: Reiterating the pledge to spend EUR 38 million on new projects in Georgia, the EU Delegation in Georgia said the bloc no longer provides funding to Georgian authorities but continues to aid the “people of Georgia.” The funding was first announced by the EU Ambassador to Georgia Pawel Herczynski during the Europe Day celebration in Georgia’s eastern Kakheti region on October 10. He said the funding would support projects focused on rural development, businesses, women’s empowerment, and environmental protection, hoping to sign the projects by the end of this year. Later, in an October 16 Facebook post , the delegation said that the projects would “continue to make a real difference in the lives of families and communities across Georgia.” The projects will focus on developing “economic opportunities in small cities and towns” and “skills for a changing labour market”; promoting “socio-economic development in rural areas, especially driven by women”; improving “access to markets and better food quality”; combating “violence towards women and girls”; supporting “safe and orderly migration”; strengthening “climate adaptation and disaster preparedness”; and continuing “support for communities in Abkhazia.” “Due to Georgia’s democratic backsliding, the EU no longer provides funding to Georgian authorities. But we continue to deliver assistance to the people of Georgia. We reaffirm that commitment,” the statement said The Embassy also highlighted the bloc’s long-standing support for Georgia, saying the EU had invested more than USD 2 billion in the country since 1992, including “transforming agriculture, supporting people in remote areas start their own businesses, improving air quality, and coordinating the upgrade of the East-West highway, among many other areas.” The announcement comes amid continued strain in EU-Georgian relations, with the EU “de facto” halting Georgia’s integration in 2024 amid democratic concerns and reducing contacts with the Georgian Dream government. The EU officials have repeatedly stated that Georgia remains a candidate country “in name only,” while recent EU reports also noted that the bloc “continued to halt financial assistance directly benefiting Georgian authorities.” The plans for new projects come as Georgian Dream has continued to restrict foreign funding directed towards civil society and media support, including through a series of laws and amendments. It also follows the recent announcements by two German political foundations, the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom and the Konrad Adenauer Foundation, that they were exiting Georgia after Georgian authorities rejected their funding applications under stricter grant laws. title: Russia’s Battlegroup North takes control of Volchansk-Budarki highway in Kharkov Region
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Russia’s battlegroup North has established full control over the Volchansk-Budarki highway, which Ukrainian troops had been trying to use as a logistics supply route, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The Battlegroup North has also fully taken under control the Volchansk-Budarki highway. The Ukrainian armed forces’ units had been constantly attempting to use this route for logistics, specifically, to deliver ammunition and food to their firing positions," the ministry said in a statement.
It added that during active combat operations, assault troops adjusted artillery fire, while operators of strike unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) identified the movement routes of Ukrainian forces’ vehicles from the air, striking supply convoys in advance and depriving the enemy of ammunition and food deliveries to their positions. Having secured their positions in populated localities, servicemen of the Battlegroup North began clearing buildings, basements, and the surrounding area of enemy troops.
Units of the Battlegroup North, advancing simultaneously on several fronts, continue to expand the security zone along the Russian-Ukrainian border in Ukraine’s Sumy and Kharkov Regions. The troops are advancing around the clock, pushing the enemy back from the state border to ensure the safety of the civilian population, the ministry reported.

title: UN: civilian casualty toll in Ukraine remains at record high
body:
Intensified attacks by Russia across Ukraine in September continued the trend of 2026, where the number of civilian casualties significantly exceeds figures recorded in previous years, having devastating consequences for the civilian population, the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) reported, releasing its monthly update on civilian harm in Ukraine.
As noted by the HRMMU, repeated attacks on energy infrastructure threaten to further exacerbate these sufferings.
The HRMMU verified that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September, bringing the total number of killed and injured 85 percent higher than in September 2025 (249 killed and 1,068 injured).
Civilians were killed or injured in 22 regions of Ukraine and Kyiv, with particularly high casualty numbers recorded in the capital, Kherson, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhia. In Kyiv alone, civilian casualties were recorded on 22 out of 30 days – more frequently than in any previous month since the start of the full-scale invasion.
In October, the number of civilian casualties also remained high, the HRMMU reported. For example, on the night of October 6–7, the Russian armed forces carried out an attack using cruise missiles and drones across several Ukrainian regions, including Chernihiv region, where 22 civilians were killed and 45 injured in Pryluky. The HRMMU documented other mass-casualty attacks on civilians, including in Kramatorsk on October 8, Zaporizhia on October 10, and Lutsk on October 14.
"The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in recent years. In just a few days, attacks by the Russian armed forces resulted in mass casualty incidents in Kharkiv, Zaporizhia, Kramatorsk, and Kyiv," said Head of the HRMMU Danielle Bell.
Verified data for September includes 18 killed and 44 injured civilians in Russian-occupied territory of Ukraine. The actual figure is likely significantly higher, as a lack of access and independent sources of information complicates the verification of many incidents.
The high number of civilian casualties in September and October occurred against the backdrop of the Russian armed forces resuming systematic attacks on energy infrastructure across Ukraine. On August 30, the Ministry of Defense of Russia announced that it had begun preparations for delivering "massive strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities." On September 30, an attack damaged generation, distribution, and transmission facilities in three regions and Kyiv, causing emergency power outages.
Attacks on Ukraine's electrical and thermal infrastructure continued in October. During a recent attack on October 13–14, the Russian armed forces struck a number of energy facilities across Ukraine, including three main power plants in Kyiv. According to Ukrainian authorities, the attack temporarily left 600,000 people in Kyiv without electricity.
In a report on attacks on energy infrastructure during the 2025–2026 winter, the OHCHR documented the consequences of such attacks for civilians and concluded that these attacks likely violated foundational principles of international humanitarian law.
