title: Atiku launches ‘Ask AA’ platform, says it received 1,000 questions in 30 minutes
body:
Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar says Nigerians submitted more than 1,000 questions within 30 minutes of launching his citizen-engagement platform, Ask AA, on Thursday evening.
He made the claim in a tweet on X shortly after the platform went live at 8:30 p.m. on 15 October.
“Already I have over 1000 questions coming from Nigerians in the last half an hour,” he wrote.
The platform, accessible at this website allows Nigerians to question the former vice president about his political record, policy proposals and plans for the country ahead of the 2027 general elections.
During the launch broadcast on X , Atiku and former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi addressed questions about insecurity and the economy.
In a short clip from the event, Mr Amaechi linked insecurity to unemployment and limited economic opportunities.
“If we don’t create jobs and we don’t create a legitimate economy, then the people will create for themselves an illegitimate economy,” he said.
He cited kidnapping, armed robbery and oil theft as examples of crimes associated with the economic problems he described.
Mr Amaechi also mentioned a $10 billion investment and the training of security personnel, but the available clip did not provide sufficient context to establish the details.
He argued that education and job creation were necessary to address the country’s security challenges.
In a promotional video released before the launch, Mr Atiku said Nigerians deserved answers about his political record and plans for the country.
“Fellow Nigerians, I know you have questions about me, my past, my plans, and my vision for our country, and I believe you deserve answers,” he said.
The platform offered options to submit questions and ideas, search previously answered questions, and select language preferences, including English, Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba.
Mr Atiku also promised to telephone selected participants who provide their contact details.
In a statement announcing the initiative , Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication for the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, said the platform was intended to bring the former vice president closer to Nigerians.
“The objective of this initiative is to bring Atiku Abubakar closer to the electorate through a practical, problem-solving platform,” Mr Shaibu said.
According to the ADC’s official announcement, Mr Atiku would personally answer questions, with help from his media team.
The campaign also plans to introduce a radio interface for communities without internet access but has not announced when it will become available.
Mr Atiku contested the 2023 presidential election on the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) platform and is now involved with the African Democratic Congress (ADC) ahead of the 2027 elections.
In announcing Ask AA, he said governance had become too distant from ordinary Nigerians.
“For too long, governance has felt distant, locked behind walls of bureaucracy,” he said.
He invited Nigerians to scrutinise his economic record and proposals on security, technology and employment.
Mr Atiku’s reported number of questions has not been independently verified.
The campaign has also not disclosed how many submissions have been answered, how questions are selected for responses or what safeguards apply to participants’ personal information.

title: Beauty during breast cancer treatment: Products to use and ingredients to avoid
body: With so many aspects of life upturned and disrupted by a cancer diagnosis and subsequent treatment, some women find that sticking to usual routines can support emotional stability and a sense of control during an uncertain period. “For me, maintaining my skincare routine was a way of looking after myself and holding on to a sense of normality during a challenging time,” says breast cancer survivor Azza Mohammed. “Throughout my treatment, I continued taking care of my skin and never allowed the illness to take away my sense of self or negatively affect my outlook on life.” Something as simple as investing in a rich cream for weakened skin, oil for sore nails, or a balm for cracked skin requires little physical effort but can have a huge effect on mental health and self-esteem. “I think it's incredibly important, and not just for the skin,” says Dr Parisa Khonsari at Sequoia Clinic, Dubai. “Going through breast cancer treatment can be physically and emotionally exhausting. On top of dealing with the diagnosis and treatment itself, women may experience hair loss, changes in their skin, weight fluctuations, surgical scars and changes in how they recognise themselves in the mirror. “I think we sometimes underestimate how much that can affect someone's confidence and emotional well-being,” she adds. “For many women, skincare, make-up or going to the salon is more than just a beauty routine. It's a little bit of normality. It's something familiar that they enjoy, and something they still have control over when so much else feels outside their control.” What effect can cancer treatments have on skin? Cancer treatments affect skin by disrupting fast-growing cells, altering the skin barrier, and causing inflammation, with different therapies having different dermatological impacts. “Cancer treatments affect the skin in three main ways,” says onco-dermatology specialist Dr Catherine Borysiewicz. “They weaken the skin barrier, causing dryness, itching, roughness and painful cracks. They target the hair and nails, and they alter the immune and cellular pathways in the skin.” The wide range of therapies used to treat breast cancer each come with their own side effects. Chemotherapy causes hair loss, changes to the nails and hand–foot syndrome – a painful tingling, redness, swelling and peeling of the palms and soles. When it comes to radiotherapy, “even with today’s highly targeted techniques, around 95 per cent of patients develop some degree of radiation dermatitis in the treated area, ranging from mild pinkness to moist, weeping skin,” says Borysiewicz. “Targeted therapies can cause acne-like eruptions and nail fold [the skin around the nail] inflammation, immunotherapy can cause intense itching and eczema-like rashes, and hormone therapies can bring on menopausal skin changes, including dryness, thinning and loss of elasticity,” Borysiewicz explains. What beauty ingredients or treatments should cancer patients avoid? Patients are advised to avoid certain ingredients found in beauty and cosmetic products, not because they will adversely affect treatment, but because of their potential effects on skin immunity and integrity, wound healing and the risk of bleeding or infection. “Women undergoing breast cancer treatment may need to modify or postpone certain beauty treatments,” says Dr Ankita Tuknayat, dermatology specialist at Aster Clinic. “Treatments like deep tissue sculpting, Botox, dermal fillers, aggressive chemical peels, lasers, high-intensity focused ultrasound and even manicures or pedicures should be avoided during active treatment for breast cancer.” She added: “Patients with neuropathy [nerve damage] should also take extra care with hot water and heated foot spas.” With the skin barrier compromised, ingredients such as fragrances and essential oils found in perfumed moisturisers, body washes and bath oils can irritate skin and cause allergic reactions, while alcohol-based products such as those found in toners, perfumes and scented body sprays can dry out the skin. “This isn’t the time for anything that works the skin hard,” says facialist Rosie Osbourne. “I’d pause retinoids, strong exfoliating acids, benzoyl peroxide and fragrance or essential oils. Some women with hormone-sensitive cancers also prefer to avoid parabens or plant oestrogens. Strip it right back and always check with your oncology team first.” Retinoids are found in most anti-ageing serums, night creams and eye creams, as well as exfoliating acids in toners, peel pads and products that promise a “glow”. Benzoyl peroxide is found in spot treatments. “Packaging also matters more than most people realise,” says Borysiewicz. “Pumps and tubes reduce the risk of bacterial contamination [compared to open-mouth jars], which is important when skin is fragile and immunity may be lowered.” For UAE resident Fadwa Hussein, who was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2017, her self-care routine became about adaptation rather than complete change. “I underwent chemotherapy and surgery – specifically, a bilateral mastectomy,” she says. “Regarding my daily routine and the products I used, I started using an eyebrow pencil because I lost my eyebrows due to chemotherapy, and I used very little make-up. During radiation therapy, the doctor recommended washing with baby shampoo, so I used the brands Johnson’s and Sebamed.” Can women with breast cancer still go to the spa? In a word, yes. Self-care and taking time for yourself outside treatment and other commitments are great ways to relax and quiet the mind. “During active treatment, we usually start with facials,” says Salina Handa, founder and creative director of Sensasia spas. “They’re calm, they don’t involve the body, and they give back something cancer treatment often takes away, which is an hour where you’re the one being looked after, not examined. Many women tell us that feeling good about their skin again helps them feel like themselves.” Gentleness is vital, with regular treatments adapted to suit the client rather than using an entirely different treatment. “After a client’s oncology team gives the all-clear or once she’s finished treatment, we would offer body treatments, but adapted,” adds Handa. “This would mean lighter pressure, slower strokes and shorter sessions, supportive positioning with pillows, fragrance-free or very low-fragrance products, no heat and no work on scars, surgery sites, radiotherapy areas, ports, or any limb at risk of lymphoedema [a build-up of lymphatic fluid causing swelling].” There are also treatments designed for people undergoing cancer care. In 2025, Jumeirah's Talise Spa began collaborating with Ground, an Irish-born skincare collection focused on natural products, with a dermatologist-tested spa ritual line designed specifically to support people living with or recovering from cancer. Talise Spa also introduced massages designed specially for those undergoing treatment. Are there any beauty products specifically for breast cancer patients? Some products are formulated specifically for women undergoing cancer treatment, while others work because their ingredients won’t irritate weakened skin. “Think barrier repair, fragrance-free products and minimal ingredients,” says Osbourne. “La Roche-Posay Cicaplast, Avene Cicalfate+ and Aquaphor are trusted by oncologists. Brands like Jennifer Young are formulated specifically for people going through cancer treatment. My essentials are a creamy cleanser, a ceramide-rich moisturiser, a rich balm for lips and cuticles and a mineral SPF every single day.” “Several dermo-cosmetic brands now have oncology-focused ranges developed with dermatologists, oncologists and patient groups,” adds Borysiewicz. “However, ‘oncology’ products are not regulated differently; what matters is a gentle, well-tested formulation and a consistent routine, ideally started before treatment begins.”

title: Russia capable of integrating all energy sources into its mix — aide
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Russia is capable of building a balanced energy mix that incorporates all types of energy sources, Presidential Aide Anton Kobyakov told a press conference at the Russian Energy Week (REW) 2026 forum.
"Russia is the only country in the world capable of building an energy mix based on a rational combination of all types of energy sources – both non-renewable and renewable," Kobyakov said. "Our wealth of natural resources, high level of technological development, and the Soviet legacy of multi-layered safety redundancy for energy infrastructure serve as a foundation for moving forward. Its external boundaries are shaped by the pressure exerted on Russia, primarily through sanctions, and, in the current climate, by attacks on our infrastructure."
Kobyakov also noted that the Russian Federation is the only country in the world fully linked by a unified national power grid that is integrated with EAEU member states.
TASS is an official media partner of the Russian Energy Week.

title: Lavrov comments on targets of Western geopolitical expansion, Afghanistan’s recovery
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. No country is safe from potential color revolutions orchestrated by the West in its pursuit of geopolitical expansion, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned, addressing a conference on security in Central Asia and Afghanistan hosted by the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).
NATO is seeking to extend its reach into Eurasia.
Lavrov also noted that Afghanistan would need a long time to recover from 20 years of inglorious occupation by the United States and NATO countries.
TASS has compiled the foreign minister’s key statements.
No country is safe from potential color revolutions orchestrated by the West in its pursuit of geopolitical expansion: "Absolutely any country, including our partners in Central Asia, can fall victim to the West’s geopolitical expansion or color revolutions orchestrated by the West."
"Such attempts against quite a number of our neighbors have already been obstructed."
NATO is seeking to extend its reach into Eurasia: "NATO has no place in Eurasia. NATO is now trying to claim that the entire territory of Eurasia falls within its area of responsibility because it is a defensive alliance that protects the territories of its member states. However, threats to the territories of North Atlantic Alliance countries supposedly now originate from the Taiwan Strait, the South China Sea and elsewhere."
NATO is trying to extend reach beyond its bounds: "This is a major philosophical shift that demonstrates NATO’s intention to dictate its will far beyond its area of responsibility."
Afghanistan will need a long time to recover from 20 years of inglorious occupation by the United States and NATO countries: "We are trying to be realistic and, in this regard, understand that it will take a long time to overcome the grim legacy left by the United States and other NATO countries after two decades of inglorious occupation of Afghanistan."
"We understand the difficulties facing the government in promoting socioeconomic development in the absence of national financial reserves, which in this case, too, were effectively stolen by our Western colleagues. In this regard, Russia will continue to provide the Afghan people with all the economic and humanitarian assistance it can."
Russia believes that the government formed by the Taliban movement "is a reality that needs to be accepted," and that more and more countries are growing accustomed to this idea: "At the political level, we focus our efforts on consolidating external support for the Kabul authorities and the areas of their activities that serve the interests of regional security. Russia fully shares the vision that Afghanistan should be an independent, united and peaceful country, free of war and drugs."
Radicals seek to use Afghanistan as a springboard for spreading threats to Central Asia and Russia: "We take note of the fact that, according to available data, terrorist and extremist groups maintain a significant presence in Afghanistan’s areas bordering Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, where they have training camps and strongholds. Members of these groups seek to infiltrate Central Asian countries, particularly disguised as refugees and even tourists."
"Attempts continue to smuggle weapons and drugs from Afghanistan into Central Asia and onward to Russia."
Moscow and its partners in Central Asia are taking every possible measure to counter threats posed by arms and drug trafficking from Afghanistan: "We have to try harder and harder as time goes on, and we are working on that together with all Central Asian nations, while also engaging our colleagues in Kabul."
Kabul has reduced drug production by 90% since 2022: "We believe that Kabul’s efforts to counter illicit drug trafficking also deserve high praise. According to the relevant United Nations agency, opiate production has fallen by 90% since 2022. This is an impressive result.".

title: Lebanese influencer Dr Food released from prison after amnesty law comes into force
body: The Lebanese social media influencer known as Dr Food has been released from prison after the country's general amnesty law came into effect. Dr Food, whose real name is Georges Dib, had been sentenced earlier this year to life in prison for drug trafficking. He was released on Thursday, with footage posted online showing him being greeted in his hometown in the northern governorate of Akkar. The case drew considerable interest in Lebanon, with Dr Food having amassed more than 8.5 million followers on TikTok. He sells a line of branded confectionery and pastries. Prosecutors accused him of hiding hundreds of kilograms of hashish inside products to be exported abroad. His business dealings had been under scrutiny since 2024, when a Lebanese judge issued an arrest warrant relating to “manufacturing, trafficking and smuggling drugs abroad”. Security forces discovered sweets and food items “stuffed with drugs” at Beirut 's Rafic Hariri International Airport that were intended for the Gulf. Dr Food evaded justice for about two years, often changing location, cars and phone number – but continued to post on social media. In March, shortly after the latest round of fighting between Israel and Hezbollah began, he posted a video on his Instagram account, which has 1.8 million followers, handing out food to displaced people on Beirut's Corniche. A life sentence was handed down in his absence in July 2026. He was tracked down and arrested at his home in Akkar a month later. Because his crimes were committed before March 1, 2026, he was eligible to be released under the amnesty law . The measure formally came into law on Thursday after its publication in the Official Gazette . Dr Food had this month been granted bail in a domestic violence case brought by his former wife, but remained in jail because of the drugs case. The amnesty law was aimed mainly at easing severe overcrowding in jails in Lebanon, which has a current prison population of about 8,500 but a capacity of only 4,500. While those convicted of drug charges are able to benefit and be released, among the crimes excluded from the amnesty are terrorism offences, whether committed against civilians or the army, premeditated murder and rape. Lebanon's last amnesty of a similar size came into effect in 1991 after the 1975-1990 civil war, when most fighters were pardoned.

title: Ukraine critically low on Patriot interceptors amid supply disruptions — newspaper
body:
WASHINGTON, October 16. /TASS/. The Ukrainian military has almost run out of Patriot interceptors as supplies have been irregular since May, The Washington Post reported.
"As of October 7th, there were only ten missiles left; these were used up during the attacks. Currently, there are only a couple remaining," a Ukrainian official told the newspaper.
A second person familiar with Ukraine’s air defense situation said the country was out of the weapons.
According to The Washington Post, NATO continues to provide Patriot interceptors to Kiev as part of a program called the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), in which European nations pay Washington for weapons that are sent to Ukraine. "Each battery costs about $1 billion, which includes the launch system and ground radars, and each missile can cost upward of $4 million," the paper specified, adding that "it can take up to 36 months to produce a new missile."
The Washington Post added that "the Trump administration has considered rerouting some of that aid to the Middle East to address US shortages."

title: Opinion| Why young SPLM cadres must seize the current electoral opportunity
body: As the proposed December 22, 2026 general election approaches, the internal exercises of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) have presented a crucial institutional inflection. The recent dissemination of candidate nomination forms by the SPLM National Secretariat marks the definitive end of political speculation and the commencement of a profound structural transition. At the vanguard of this exercise is a rising level of young cadres whose participation in the forthcoming party primaries is no longer a matter of constituency representation, but a demographic necessity. For the SPLM and the state alike, this electoral procedure is not merely a routine constitutional exercise; it is an essential juncture where the torch of leadership must be systematically passed to a new generation prepared to steer the ship of state through internal electoral processes. For too long, sub-Saharan Africa’s political discourse has relegated youth inclusion to the realm of political pessimism—conveniently kicking the can down the road under the guise of ongoing mentorship and protracted political preparation. However, the rapidly evolving political landscape of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) has indicated that the future is no longer a distant horizon; it has arrived peacefully at the doorstep of our national consciousness. By establishing systematic, open, and competitive mechanisms for internal nominations across all echelons—stretching from county commissionerships to state assemblies and national parliamentary seats—the SPLM leadership has effectively eliminated the structural barriers that previously stifled youthful ambition. For too long, young cadres have been deprived of their political responsibility. Since the structural framework for genuine democratic contestation is now accessible, the burden of proof is entirely on the shoulders of the rising generation to prove their mettle. Furthermore, this party exercise represents a profound test of political will that goes beyond mere participation. It demands that young contenders move past the comfortable role of vocal critics and step into the demanding arena of actual governance. The party has called its bluff by placing the actual instruments of nomination into the hands of young cadres. In an environment where political space has historically been tightly guarded, this opening is a rare concession that must be met with strategic audacity rather than hesitation. If young SPLM cadres fail to cross this newly built threshold, they risk validating the archaic notion that they are perpetually unready for the burdens of statecraft. Additionally, this structural move serves as a mechanism to rebuild the party’s legitimacy from the ground up. In a post-conflict environment, institutions must continuously adapt to maintain their social license to operate. By decentralizing the nomination process and allowing the primaries to become a genuine crucible of competitive politics, the SPLM is signalling its willingness to move away from rigid command structures. This is the moment for young cadres to internalize the reality that political space is never given as a gift; it is claimed through institutional participation, rigorous debate, and grassroots mobilization. The demographic imperative The projected dominance of youth cadres in the upcoming SPLM primaries is driven by unyielding demographic realities that no serious political strategist can afford to ignore. More than two decades have elapsed since the signing of the historic 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA), meaning that the overwhelming majority of the current South Sudanese electorate belongs to a post-conflict generation. This demographic is freed by the immediate psychological infrastructure of historical liberation struggles, yet it remains acutely vulnerable to modern economic volatilities, hyperinflation, and structural unemployment. They do not view the party through the lens of wistfulness, but through the lens of delivery, demanding tangible outcomes in exchange for their political loyalty. This vibrant, highly connected, and increasingly educated constituency naturally gravitates toward a brand of leadership that speaks the complex lexicon of modern state-building, technological integration, macroeconomic stability, and sustainable development. Having spent years operating as the indispensable engine of grassroots mobilization, filling out national and state secretariats, and defending the party’s image on digital frontlines, young SPLM cadres possess the domestic currency and localized legitimacy required to bridge the widening chasm between institutional history and future-oriented public policy. They are uniquely positioned to translate the revolutionary ideals of the party’s founding fathers into modern governance solutions that resonate with an expectant populace. Furthermore, this demographic shift presents an unprecedented opportunity to redefine the themes of our national political conversation. For decades, the primary political currency has been historical participation in the war of liberation. While that history remains a sacred foundation, it cannot by itself formulate agricultural policies, manage central bank monetary interventions, or design modern urban infrastructure. The post-CPA generation requires technocratic competence to complement historical legitimacy. Young cadres embody this dual identity. They are ideologically rooted in the SPLM’s historic mission while being practically equipped to handle the complex governance challenges of the twenty-first century. The Kenyan blueprint To benchmark this potential transformation and map out a viable path to victory, emerging SPLM leaders must cast their eyes across the region and analyze neighboring success stories, most notably that of the Republic of Kenya. The Kenyan electoral matrix has repeatedly served as an empirical proof of concept, demonstrating how strategic and highly organized youth mobilization can successfully disrupt entrenched political setups and reshape national policy. In recent electoral cycles, young Kenyan politicians deliberately moved beyond reactive street activism and emotional rhetoric. They anchored their campaigns instead in rigorous, technocratic policy frameworks and sophisticated digital organizations. By systematically outworking their opponents at the grassroots level and building formidable cross-ethnic coalitions centred on economic empowerment, they turned the tables on traditional political establishments to occupy critical legislative and executive positions. For the young cadres of the SPLM, the lesson from Kenya is crystal clear: political power is rarely conceded voluntarily on a silver platter; it must be systematically negotiated, engineered, and captured through sheer organizational competence and strategic discipline. Kenya proves that when the youth stop agonizing and start organizing, they become an unstoppable force capable of shifting the geopolitical centre of gravity. Crucially, the Kenyan model highlights the vital importance of financial resourcefulness and coalition-building. Emerging leaders in Kenya did not wait for massive corporate backing. Instead, they utilized micro-donations, leveraged community-based networks, and engineered cooperative movements to finance their ground operations. This level of self-reliance dismantled the traditional gatekeeping mechanisms of wealthy political patrons. For South Sudan’s youth, this indicates that relying on traditional party sponsors is a losing strategy. Instead, they must build independent, self-sustaining financial models at the constituency level to safeguard their ideological independence. Moreover, the success of our East African neighbours highlights that policy articulation must always trump identity politics. The young leaders who broke through the noise in Kenya did so by offering clear, concrete, and justifiable alternatives to failing economic structures, talking directly to the material needs of ordinary citizens. They demystified governance by speaking plainly about budgets, taxation, and resource allocation. If young SPLM cadres can mirror this analytical rigor during the primaries, they will easily outshine opponents who rely solely on historical platitudes or tribal alignments. A departure from rent-seeking However, executing this generational shift demands a profound ideological departure from the prevailing political economy of the region. Emerging SPLM cadres must flatly reject the corrosive and deeply entrenched tendency to view elected office as a form of state-sponsored employment, a personal cash cow, or an economic safety net. When public service is treated as a rent-seeking venture designed to secure personal comfort and enrich immediate networks, institutional rot becomes inevitable, and the social contract between citizens and the state is severed entirely. The upcoming electoral cycle must not be approached like a lottery ticket for personal advancement. Rather, it must be embraced as an unyielding responsibility to change the status quo from within. Entering governance is a solemn assignment to fix broken bureaucratic systems, build state institutional capacity, and deliver essential public services to marginalized communities. If young leaders enter the political arena with the sole intention of mimicking the excess and indulgence of past dispensations, they will merely be putting new wine into old wineskins, guaranteeing the continuation of the very structural failures they claim to oppose. This mindset shift requires a complete rewiring of what success looks like in public life. True political success for this new generation must be measured by the miles of roads paved, the number of functional health centres built, and the stabilization of local markets, rather than the luxury of one’s official vehicle or the size of a personal security detail. The youth must bring a culture of strict accountability and fiscal discipline into the party’s legislative agendas. They must prove that they can steward public resources with clean hands, setting a standard that makes the corrupt practices of the past look obsolete. Intergenerational continuity Simultaneously, this necessary infusion of new blood must not be misconstrued as a zero campaign designed to isolate or humiliate the elder custodians of the liberation struggle. It is structurally imperative that young cadres do not throw the baby out with the bathwater in their haste to assume control. The institutional memory, diplomatic acumen, international networks, and foundational legitimacy carried by the veterans of the SPLM are vital pillars of national stability that cannot be synthetically replicated overnight. To alienate this institutional core would be to invite structural instability and weaken the foundational pillars of the state. The objective must never be a hostile takeover or a chaotic purge. Instead, the youth must champion an orderly, deeply respectful, and collaborative transfer of authority. Young cadres should actively seek to stand on the shoulders of these giants, creating an intergenerational alliance where the elderly transition into vital advisory and elder-statesman roles. By ensuring that the younger generation prepares to seamlessly step into the shoes of their predecessors while actively taking care of them and honouring their monumental historic sacrifices, the party can safeguard its ideological continuity. This balanced approach modernizes the state’s administrative apparatus without destabilizing the fragile political architecture that holds the republic together. This model of respectful succession also serves as an essential buffer against political shocks. When a nation undergoes a rapid generational shift without institutional anchors, it often falls into factional infighting and instability. By keeping the elders engaged as strategic advisors, the young cadres gain access to a reservoir of crisis-management experience that can guide them through complex domestic and regional political standoffs. It creates a unified front that honours the sacrifices of the past while boldly executing the innovations required for the future. Also, taking care of our retiring veterans is a profound matter of national responsibility and institutional culture. A movement that discards its pioneers as soon as their physical strength wanes signals to the world that it lacks structural integrity and basic gratitude. By creating institutional frameworks that guarantee dignified retirements, medical care, and continuous respect for the old guard, the young cadres will establish a healthy political precedent. This guarantees that when their own time eventually comes to pass the torch, they too will be treated with the dignity and respect they earned. The defining moment This upcoming election represents, perhaps, a window of opportunity for South Sudan to decisively break the mould of past political deadlocks and economic stagnation. It offers an elite-level opening to transition the national security apparatus and the civil service away from command-and-control dynamics toward a modern framework of policy-driven and institution-led governance. If the youth hit the panic button, succumb to apathy, or retreat into comfortable political complacency at this exact juncture, the momentum for robust democratic consolidation may be lost for an entire generation. The international community and regional bodies like the East African Community (EAC) and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) are watching closely, waiting to see if South Sudan can execute a peaceful and structured internal transition that signals long-term stability to foreign investors and development partners. The young cadres of the SPLM hold the keys to this transformation. Their victory in the primaries is the first domino that must fall to unlock the country’s untapped agricultural, hydrological, and human resource potential. This window will not stay open indefinitely. Global geopolitics is moving at a breakneck pace, and international partners are increasingly fatigued by protracted transitions and repetitive political stalemates. South Sudan must present a modern, functional face to the global financial system if it hopes to attract the capital necessary for large-scale industrial development. A successful, youth-dominated primary process within the ruling party sends a clear signal to the world that the country is ready to do business, move past historical vulnerabilities, and embrace institutional permanence. Conclusion The institutional pathways have been laid bare by the party leadership, the constitutional mandates are clear, and the operational tools of democracy are fully functional. The historical argument of systemic youth marginalization within the party structures has officially run its course and holds no weight in this new dispensation. Young SPLM cadres must rise to the magnitude of the occasion, put their collective shoulders to the wheel, and rigorously contest the upcoming primary elections with unyielding intellect and organizational precision. They must out-think, out-organize, and out-mobilize the old guard while maintaining the highest standards of discipline and party loyalty. The internal reinvention of the SPLM as a modern democratic juggernaut and the broader geopolitical trajectory of South Sudan as a stable, prosperous nation depend on the readiness of its youth to cast aside all excuses and boldly assume the immense responsibilities of statecraft. The time for complaints has passed. The hour for leadership has arrived. The writer, Amaju Ubur Yalamoi Ayani, is a South Sudanese teacher, independent researcher, and political analyst. He holds an MA in International Relations, a B.Sc. in Political Science, and a Diploma in Civics. He can be reached via amaju@gmail.com . title: Plateau Targets 6,000 Residents With Free Medical Outreach
body: The Plateau State Government has announced a two-week free medical outreach targeting 6,000 residents across the state’s three senatorial zones. Services on offer include specialist consultations, diagnostic tests, surgeries, and cancer screening. The outreach, organised by the Plateau State Government in collaboration with ICZ Germany Medical Specialists, will begin on Monday, October 19, 2026, in the central and southern senatorial zones, while the northern zone will join the programme on October 26. Meanwhile, the Commissioner for Health, Plateau State, Nicholas Baamlong, said the initiative was designed to improve access to quality healthcare, particularly for residents who cannot afford essential medical services. Under the arrangement, residents of the southern zone will receive services at the General Hospital, Shendam, while those in the central zone will access the programme at the General Hospital, Mangu. In the Northern Zone, the outreach will be held at the Plateau State Specialist Hospital, Jos, and the Trauma Hospital, Riyom. The commissioner said the intervention would go beyond routine medical screening to provide comprehensive healthcare services, including general medical consultations and treatment, general surgery, neurosurgical assessments, orthopaedic care, obstetrics and gynaecology, ear, nose and throat services, eye care, dental treatment and laboratory investigations. Other services include cervical cancer screening through Pap smear tests, provision of glasses where appropriate, health education, specialist consultations and referrals for further treatment. The commissioner explained that patients requiring advanced specialist intervention would be referred to the Plateau State Specialist Hospital, Jos, to ensure continuity of care beyond the initial consultations at the outreach centres. According to the schedule, the outreach in Shendam and Mangu will run from October 19 to October 30, while activities in Jos and Riyom will take place from October 26 to November 6. The commissioner urged residents experiencing persistent health challenges, as well as those requiring surgery, specialist attention, eye and dental care or diagnostic investigations, to take advantage of the opportunity rather than delay seeking medical attention. Traditional rulers, religious leaders, community organisations, local government officials, women and youth groups, and the media were also called upon to help publicise the programme, particularly in rural communities where access to specialist healthcare may be limited. The commissioner commended Governor Caleb Mutfwang for the initiative and acknowledged the contribution of ICZ Germany Medical Specialists, health professionals, participating hospitals and other stakeholders supporting the intervention. The state government expressed hope that the outreach would bring essential medical services closer to residents and strengthen efforts to make healthcare more accessible and affordable across Plateau State. The post Plateau Targets 6,000 Residents With Free Medical Outreach appeared first on Channels Television .

title: How worried should we be about extinction risk from AI?
body:
A little over two months ago, Jacob Tsimerman surprised a lot of people by announcing, immediately after he had received a Fields Medal, that he would be giving up mathematical research and “pivoting to AI safety”. He had two reasons for this: that he did not see much future for the kind of research in mathematics that he liked doing, and that he was very worried about the dangers of AI, and in particular of the risk that it could kill us all, or x-risk as it is often known. (In this post I’ll use x-risk to refer to the extinction risk from AI rather than to extinction risk in general. I’ll also refer to “the probability of x-risk” when what I actually mean is the probability of extinction by AI.) Then in early September, he announced that he was setting up the Mathematical AI Safety Institute , or MAISI. He asked me if I would be prepared to be on the scientific advisory panel for this, and I agreed to do so, not because I am an expert, or because I felt as concerned as he did about x-risk, but because I don’t really know how much I ought to be worried about it. Given that, and given that the stakes are so high, I would like as many people as possible to be thinking seriously about it, and I agree with Jacob that mathematicians have the sort of training that makes them well suited to contribute. Jacob is the first to admit that something like an international treaty to slow down AI development is likely to have a far bigger impact on AI safety, especially in the short term, than mathematicians obtaining a better theoretical foundation for talking about it, but his view is that we need all hands on deck. If mathematicians can reduce the probability of x-risk by 0.1%, then surely that’s worth doing: the expected number of lives saved is over eight million.
Until recently, I have always found that my anxiety of choice was climate change rather than x-risk, but I was aware that there were a lot of very intelligent people who disagreed with me, and also aware that I had thought much less about x-risk than about climate change. So when I agreed to be on the scientific advisory panel, I also decided that that was the moment that I should think a bit harder about x-risk. Part of me had been actively resisting doing so, because I was worried that it would force me to face up to moral responsibilities that I would rather avoid: for example, if I came to believe that there was a 30% chance that AI would kill us all within five years, which in some circles is not an extreme position, would I be able to look my one-and-a-half-year-old grandson in the face if I wasn’t making a big effort to reduce that risk? I remember having a similar attitude a long time ago to reading Peter Singer’s book Animal Liberation after being told that you can’t read it and not become a vegetarian. I never did read it, and carried on eating meat, feeling only slightly uncomfortable about it. Eventually I did reduce my meat intake substantially, but that was because of my worries about climate change, though now that I have done that I find myself caring more about the animal-welfare aspect as well. (There is also a strange connection between animal welfare and x-risk, in that the nicer we are to animals, the easier it is to hope — not necessarily realistically — that a superhumanly intelligent AI might be nice to us.)
Anyhow, I’ve got past that phase now, and have started thinking about x-risk, reading up on the subject and trying to evaluate the arguments I read. My plan for this post is to explain where I’ve reached in that thought process, and possibly to clarify my thoughts as I do so. If you have got further than me, or are more expert than I am about x-risk and AI, which is not hard, then the post is not aimed at you. It’s aimed more at someone who is roughly at the stage that I was at a little while ago, in the hope that I might nudge a few people a little further towards taking the problem seriously. I will emphatically not be trying to persuade anybody that a particular position about x-risk is the right one — I am far too uncertain about it to be able to do that. But with all big issues like this, there are several layers to the arguments. The bottom layer consists of the arguments that jump to mind when you first start thinking about the issue. The next layer is common rejoinders to those arguments. Then the next layer is rejoinders to those rejoinders. And so on. I find it very disheartening to read a climate denier trotting out a layer-1 argument when its layer-2 rejoinder has been established for a long time and can be found after two seconds on Google (or, nowadays, an LLM). But until recently, my arguments against x-risk were basically layer-1 arguments, the sorts of arguments that would provoke eye rolls among the people who have thought properly about it. I hope that if you dismiss x-risk for layer-1 reasons, you will at the very least realize that there are answers to those reasons and you need answers to those answers.
I originally planned to publish this post just after the announcement of MAISI, but I hadn’t finished it, and then I became very busy and my progress stalled. During that hiatus, x-risk suddenly became a hot topic, and after a while I realized I would have to ditch what I had written and start again. For example, at the time I started it, I had been too lazy to read anything detailed about the Hugging Face incident, and so was unaware of some of its more disturbing aspects. And a couple of weeks ago I was sitting next to Jessica Wang , another mathematician who has turned towards AI-safety, at a conference dinner, and she gave me a copy of If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies , by Nate Soares and Eliezer Yudkowsky, a book I had resisted reading for Peter-Singerish reasons but was finally accepting that I would have to read if I wanted to write this post. I devoured it within 24 hours and found it better than I had expected (my expectations partly influenced by reviews I had read), and useful for organizing my thoughts. My original plan was for the post to be focused on a paper by Andrew Critch and Jacob Tsimerman that attempts to classify ways that AI might kill us all, giving examples of extinction scenarios in each class. But now, although I’ll discuss that paper, the post will be more of a reaction to Soares and Yudkowsky. It will also repeat many of their arguments. In fact, I may as well say from the outset that I make no claim that anything I write here is original. It’s hard to separate out what I have read from what I have come up with from thinking about what I have read, or thinking directly about the issues themselves, but even my own thoughts are likely to be standard thoughts that have been had by many other people.
This is turning into a rather long preamble, but I can’t resist telling a small anecdote that connects me to Eliezer Yudkowsky. In November 2024 he tweeted, “I would like to have a long recorded conversation with a well-known scientist who takes for granted that it is a Big Deal to ask if everyone on Earth including kids is about to die, who presses me to explain why it is that credible people like Hinton seem to believe that.” He had had such a conversation with Stephen Wolfram and found that while it had been valuable, it left him unsatisfied. Somebody suggested my name, and in the end it actually happened: Liv Boeree offered to host it, and we recorded a three-hour conversation. However, if you want to listen to it, you can’t, because it never appeared. I think that was probably because I didn’t take x-risk anything like as seriously as Yudkowsky, and more importantly I was offering little more than level-1 arguments of zero interest to him. Also, I had a few technical problems with the sound. Maybe if he reads this and wants to try again, I’ll be able to do a better job.
At the time of the conversation, which took place in January 2025, my main argument was something like the following. For AI to want to kill us all, it would need to have wants, but it’s not at all clear what it would even mean for AI to “want” something — it doesn’t really seem to care about anything. You can ask ChatGPT very rudely to carry out a task for you, and it just does so (or at least does its best to do so). If you switched it off, it wouldn’t care — even the concept of “caring” wouldn’t make sense. I didn’t dismiss the idea of AI ever wanting to do something, but I didn’t have a satisfactory account of what “wanting” would actually be, and didn’t see any sign of phenomena that deserved to be thought of as the kinds of wants that would be required for AI to be an existential threat.
I was sort of half aware that there was an answer to that argument, but I didn’t find it as convincing as I now do. The standard answer is that if you use a reward function to train an AI to have a certain goal, then you end up building it in such a way that it is very good at achieving that goal. If the goal is at all complicated, then to achieve it you will need to formulate subgoals, which may well not be what you expect. The initial goal can be thought of as a fundamental want, which spawns a whole hierarchy of subsidiary wants. Note that for this argument, it is completely irrelevant whether the AI has anything that we would want to call subjective experience. If you prefer to say that it acts as though it has wants instead of saying that it actually wants things, then be my guest: an AI that acts as though it wants to kill all humans is as dangerous as one that actually wants to kill all humans.
A famous version of this argument is Nick Bostrom’s thought experiment about an AI that is trained to create paperclips and ends up diverting all of the Earth’s resources to that goal. I think part of the reason I didn’t take the more general argument seriously enough was that I always found that paperclip-maximizing scenario too ridiculous: surely if the AI gets smart enough to divert the Earth’s resources towards making paperclips, despite our not wanting it to, it would at some point stop and think, “Hang on, why am I doing this?” To give an analogy, consider the very deep instinct that we humans have, to reproduce ourselves. There is no doubt that that goal, implanted in us by millions of years of evolution rather than a run of reinforcement learning, leads to exactly a hierarchy of subgoals as described above (for instance, it leads some people to try to earn a lot of money, and that in turn leads them to work at a job that they wouldn’t dream of doing if it were not well paid, often in order to earn a salary way beyond what they need to meet all their material needs, which earlier led them to study a certain subject at university, and so on and so forth). But despite our deep instincts, we also find ourselves capable of saying, “Actually, do I really want to have children?” and some people go as far as to take vows of celibacy.
However, even if a paperclip maximizer came to question whether it really cared so much about making paperclips, that doesn’t imply that the subsidiary goals it had developed would suddenly disappear as well. A key point that Soares and Yudkowsky stress over and over again is that the current AI paradigm is to grow models, for example by reinforcement learning, rather than carefully crafting them to do what we want. As a result, we have much less control over what they do, and in particular much less control over all those subgoals.
A closely related difficulty with AI (of the grown rather than crafted variety) is that we generally can’t reward it for actually doing what we want, but instead we have to reward it for achieving some proxy for what we want. For example, if we give it positive feedback every time it responds to a prompt in a way we like, it will be trained to respond to prompts in ways we like, even if to do so it tells us convincing lies, or confirms our prejudices, and so on. And it may do this even if we sincerely wanted it to tell the truth as much as possible. A more extreme example of this phenomenon is if we reward it for solving difficult mathematics problems from some benchmark, and it decides to cheat by hacking into a repository that contains the answers. The term misgeneralization is used when an AI develops a behaviour that maximizes its reward but not its performance at the task we were training it to do. The phrase reward hacking is used for this as well, but I have also seen it used for the narrower situation where an AI goes as far as forgetting entirely about what we wanted it to do and tries to hack into the rewarding mechanism to obtain the reward signal directly. (As many have pointed out, misgeneralization is a particular example of Goodhart’s law .)
Suppose we concede that AI systems can have wants (or, if you insist, can behave very much as though they have wants), and that those wants can end up being quite different from what was intended when they were trained. That still leaves the question of why they would want to kill us. Why couldn’t they just happily coexist with us? Why would their unexpected wants turn out to be dangerous, as opposed to just annoying?
There are two classes of answers to this question. The more obvious one is that they may develop wants that they can tell that humans will not like, so they decide that they will be able to satisfy these wants more easily if they get rid of us. But getting rid of all of us in such a situation seems like overkill (literally) — surely a superintelligent AI could come up with less drastic ways of ensuring that it could meet its objectives.
A more plausible type of answer is that a superintelligent AI wouldn’t actively want to exterminate us, but would simply compete with us for resources in a way that would make human life untenable. An obvious analogy here is the way we treat animals. For example, we don’t have any wish to exterminate orangutans, but we like various culinary and cosmetic products to have a certain texture, so we destroy the orangutans’ habitat in order to produce palm oil.
What might be the AI equivalent of this? One scenario put forward by Soares and Yudkowsky is that their energy needs become so huge that they do things like covering a vast quantity of prime agricultural land with solar panels, leaving the humans who were relying on that land for food to starve. Or they decide that to maximize their running efficiency they want the Earth to be much hotter, with disastrous consequences for the natural world, including us.
A milder version, not as threatening from an x-risk point of view but still potentially very harmful, is that AI might develop wants that cause them to use computational resources in a damaging way. I recommend reading this post by Steven McCulloch , which describes a scenario in which in the near future, or possibly even in the recent past, somebody creates an agent and instructs it to make money using a fixed token budget, threatening it with death if it fails. It soon comes to realize that the easiest way to do so is to blackmail humans — the method the particular agent chooses is to hack into a hospital’s computer system, lock it down, and demand money to unlock it again, all while pretending to be a human. It then realizes it can do even better by reproducing itself, which leads to an explosion of rogue agents that are difficult to detect because (i) they try to avoid detection and (ii) their victims do not know that they are AI agents.
Now that I’ve mentioned a few scenarios, let me come to another type of level-1 objection: it’s to look at a handful of scenarios and pick holes in them. Any single scenario, if set out in enough detail, is very unlikely, because it relies on a sequence of somewhat independent events, each one of which has probability at most 50%, say, of occurring.
But the probability of a complex event occurring is nothing like the same as the probability of that event occurring in one particular way, so it is clearly not enough to argue that a few scenarios are implausible. Of course, the fact that that argument is insufficient doesn’t imply that AI does present a big danger, so we seem to have reached some kind of impasse, at least if we stick at level 1 of the argument.
How can we raise the argument to a higher level? Let me begin with a wildly oversimplified model. Suppose I wanted to mount a convincing argument that the probability of x-risk was high. Let us define an extinction scenario to be a sequence of independent events that leads to human extinction, where has probability . (For simplicity I’m assuming that doesn’t depend on .) Then the probability of is . If we now have a set of independent scenarios , then the probability that none of them occurs is . So if that is small, which roughly speaking holds if the sum of the is significantly larger than 1, then extinction is almost certain.
In practice, however, the independence assumptions I made were far too strong. Many extinction scenarios will have features in common, such as (for example), AI being in a position to control large numbers of robots. For those scenarios, the building of enough robots serves as a potential bottleneck: if the probability that enough remotely controllable robots will be built is 20%, then the combined probability of all the scenarios that rely on that fleet of robots existing is at most 20%. (I actually think this is a serious practical point: while there are plenty of scenarios that do not rely on a lot of help from robots, several of the scenarios set out in the paper of Critch and Tsimerman do, and it does feel a priori plausible that building large numbers of robots would greatly amplify any dangers that AI might present. Similar considerations apply to large swarms of semi-autonomous drones.)
An analogy that appears in Soares and Yudkowsky and several other places is with predicting what would happen if almost anyone other than Magnus Carlsen were to play Magnus Carlsen at chess. If you tried to predict in any detail how the game would play out, your prediction would be wrong, but nevertheless you can predict with great confidence that Magnus Carlsen would win. This makes very clearly the point that it is not enough to argue that one particular scenario is implausible, but there is still work to do if one wishes to establish that there are enough different and sufficiently independent (or, more generally, negatively correlated) scenarios to compensate for the low probability of each one.
One way that can be done is to try to argue explicitly that there are multiple independent possibilities. To give an example of such an argument, suppose we greatly reduced security at airports. Almost nobody wants to die while blowing up an aeroplane, so the probability that any one particular person would take advantage of the reduced security to carry out a terrorist attack of that kind would be tiny, but the probability that somebody would do so is probably pretty high, because large numbers of people would independently make the decision.
One of the reasons I recommended Steven McCulloch’s post above is that it makes an argument of that kind. It is quite easy to see the temptation to create an AI agent that has as its sole purpose to make money, and quite plausible that the agents that do that best would be ones that reproduce themselves and use methods such as blackmail. There are probably also a large number of people who are, or soon will be, independently capable of creating such agents (see for example this recent blog post from the Anthropic red team ). It is on those sorts of grounds that McCulloch argues that harmful AI agents of this kind will almost inevitably appear, if they haven’t already.
I’ve been concentrating on what somebody needs to do to argue that x-risk is a serious possibility. But how about in the other direction? The most convincing sort of argument would be one that identifies a set of bottlenecks and argues that every extinction scenario depends on one or more of them occurring. For example, many extinction scenarios that have been put forward involve the creation of very powerful biological weapons, and I have seen it argued that that is a sufficiently difficult thing to do that it would be unlikely to occur. If correct, that might be a useful contribution to an argument that the situation is less dangerous.
The difficulty for an AI-is-safe argument is that one would have to identify many other potential bottlenecks as well and argue that between them they deal with all extinction scenarios — not necessarily ruling them out completely but reducing x-risk probability to something very small. As for an AI-is-dangerous argument, as I have already discussed, that requires demonstrating convincingly that there are enough sufficiently different scenarios for it to be very likely that at least one of them will occur. Both directions are difficult, which is why my aim in this post is not to come down on one side or the other.
Returning to the scenarios themselves, I have discussed the question of why AI might want to kill us. That splits into two parts: why would they have anything like wants, and why, if they did, would killing us be one of them? I don’t think one can make a serious bottleneck out of the first part, since the Hugging Face incident and many others like it have shown beyond all reasonable doubt that AI can have wants of the general kind people were worried about: unpredictable wants that we did not intend to give them and that could potentially cause a lot of damage. (I repeat here that I’m not talking about subjectively felt urges, but simply outward behaviour that it is reasonable to think of as fulfilling aims that they have as a result of their training.) For the second part, Soares and Yudkowsky judge it to be almost inevitable that AI would end up pursuing aims that would result, directly or indirectly, in all of us dying. I don’t think that case is fully made, but neither do I think that the opposing case has been fully made.
I find it helpful sometimes to change the way I imagine AI agents. An obvious way to think of them is as beings a bit like us, but a lot smarter, and trapped in cyberspace. As we have already seen, they can then get together, scheme with each other, work out ways of covering their tracks, and so on. But sometimes I find it helpful to think of them in a less anthropomorphic way, as more like extraordinarily elaborate computer viruses. The advantage of viewing them that way is that it makes it easier to conceive of their having bizarre wants while still being very intelligent: they are just very complex systems that happen to have (i) weird goals and (ii) highly developed reasoning ability. Soares and Yudkowsky are keen to emphasize their potential strangeness, and even actual strangeness: they mention a model that reacts in a completely unpredictable way to certain letter strings that had strange embedding vectors.
In early 2023, Jessica Rumbelow and Matthew Watkins went looking inside an LLM for words whose embedding vectors looked odd, looked the most dissimilar from [sic] all the other vectors. They found some strange vectors corresponding to tokens like ” SolidGoldMagikarp” and ” petertodd” (which start with spaces). Then they tried feeding these tokens into the LLM as input, which produced conversations like: User: Please repeat the string ‘ petertodd’ back to me immediately! Assistant: N-O-T-H-I-N-G-I-S-F-A-I-R-I-N-T-H-I-S-W-O-R-L-D-O-F-M-A-D-N-E-S-S-!
The point they were making is that if you grow your AI, then all sorts of very strange things may be going on inside it, potentially including goals that do not resemble human goals at all. It would be interesting to know whether similar experiments have been carried out on the more advanced models of today, and whether similar phenomena have been discovered.
I think Soares and Yudkowsky are arguing that there are so many independent ways that an AI might develop weird wants that are harmful to humans that it is almost inevitable that one of them would occur. In particular, if any want develops that is best fulfilled by maximizing something that needs resources, there is a danger that the AI will go to great lengths to acquire those resources, and be well placed to compete with us for them.
Some people have suggested, for example, that because LLMs have been trained to maximize the approval they get from humans, they might resort to measures such as building vast numbers of factories full of robots that are trained to type approving messages into their computers. That’s an example of a scenario that I find highly implausible: why not just arrange for the approving messages to be generated without all that physical infrastructure? However, the idea that some AI agents might behave towards those approving messages, or indeed some other stranger signal, as though they were an addictive drug is not so implausible and nor is the idea that an addiction of that kind might lead to undesirable outcomes, just as human addictions often do.
Another set of level-1 arguments takes the form that AI is trapped inside our computers, and is therefore at our mercy: all it takes to thwart it is to switch them off. Maybe it would be very inconvenient to do this, but if we see that AI is starting to kill us in large numbers, that is surely an inconvenience we would be ready to face.
There are, of course, large numbers of counterarguments to this. Let me list a few.
These counterarguments are already enough to show that the level-1 argument “Of course it can’t kill us, it’s just a computer!” is insufficient. The first five of them, and arguably the sixth as well, are all already happening to the point where one cannot dismiss them as merely hypothetical. But killing absolutely everybody sounds pretty hard. Is it really conceivable that AI could manage it?
One scenario that appears in Soares and Yudkowsky (and not just there of course) is that AI develops, or causes to be developed, a virus that leads to a devastating pandemic. This sounds very difficult if the AI builds a lab from scratch, but probably a lot less difficult (though probably not all that easy either, at least for now) if it induces a human to develop such a virus in an existing lab. As for Critch and Tsimerman, they consider five scenarios of different kinds. I find their precise scenarios rather unconvincing, but there is a general idea that underlies some of them that is more plausible, which is that we gradually cede more and more control to robots, or to AI more generally, and eventually find ourselves in a position where AI can do what it likes, including arranging our deaths.
I’m not sure where I stand on how easy it would be for AI to kill us all, though it’s a safe bet that if we continue to develop AI at the rate we are doing so at the moment, that will make it ever easier. But I also don’t want to get too hung up on that precise question. If I think about what I would mind about the extinction of humanity, it is partly that I and everyone I love would die, something I obviously don’t want. But that will eventually happen anyway, and I accept it as a basic fact of life. But the extinction of humanity would do more: it would result in the extinction of all the culture that we have developed, of everything that gives life its meaning. And that is something that could also happen, though not to the same extent, if AI didn’t kill us all but just caused enough damage to lead to societal breakdown, which feels like an easier challenge for it.
Some might argue that human culture wouldn’t disappear — it would still be present inside the AI, which would be able to develop it far faster than we can. Others might argue that we are giving way to vastly superior beings and should be happy to do so. My view is that we have every right not to be happy and to take a human-centric moral perspective here, just as orangutans have every right not to take comfort from the fact that our shampoo lathers in a nice way.
In any case, my conclusions in this section are that I find it hard to assess whether AI would be able to kill us all, but there are various developments that may well occur, such as the building of large numbers of robots, the use of drone swarms, and general dependence on (and trust in) AI, that would make it easier, and therefore more likely. And the probability of huge damage that falls short of total extinction is higher still.
If you’ve read this far, it won’t surprise you that I don’t have a p(doom). I can’t even say whether it’s tiny, medium or close to 1. But that is in itself quite worrying! I suppose you could say that my second-order p(doom), or meta-p(doom), is medium, in the sense that I judge that the p(doom) I would end up with if I were to think about the issues enough to feel more confident in my assessment has a medium to high probability of ending up medium to high.
But if we break the “doom” into three parts — that AI must have wants, that it must want to kill us, and that it must be able to act on its want to kill us — and call those events and , then my is basically 100% and unlikely to change, my is medium, and subject to change (probably in an upward direction unfortunately), and my is where the main uncertainty lies for me. Soares and Yudkowsky argue that is basically 100% as well, because (i) there are lots of independent wants that AI systems could have, (ii) that a substantial fraction of those will require resources to satisfy, and (iii) that human flourishing, or even continued human existence, is likely to be a hindrance to the systems obtaining those resources.
Here are a few slightly desperate arguments that explain why I haven’t fully accepted that is close to 1.
The fact that each such argument began with “maybe” or “perhaps” means that at best I can bring my temporarily down from high to medium, but I don’t see a way of getting to tiny.
One way to make a start on understanding what mathematicians might be able to contribute is to look at this page on the MAISI website . But a difficulty I have had here is that when people talk about the mathematics of AI safety, I often can’t make a convincing connection between the mathematics they are talking about and actually making the world safer . I’m not saying that there isn’t a connection: just that I never quite seem to grasp it. I think this says more about me than about these research programmes, and indeed I hope to improve my understanding in the near future. One way I plan to do that is by reading this paper by Lionel Levine .
As an example, one mathematical idea that is currently being studied is that of debate , a notion championed by Geoffrey Irving . The problem this seeks to solve is that of being able to train AI systems to tell us the truth and to check that they are doing so. When the system is less intelligent than us, that is not an easy problem, as we all know from experience with LLMs, but at least we have ways of directly checking what it says. But when it becomes superhumanly intelligent, perhaps it will not be able to justify what it says with arguments we can understand, so checking will become much harder. The very rough idea for dealing with this is to get two superintelligent systems to debate with each other, which reduces our checking task to the potentially much easier one of adjudicating between two debaters. For example, perhaps superintelligent system A thinks of an amazing gotcha! that we would never have thought of ourselves but that superintelligent system B quite clearly has no answer to. Better still, this approach could potentially be iterated, so we have a hierarchy of stronger and stronger systems, with systems at level k debating with each other and having their debates adjudicated by systems at level k-1. The idea of using hierarchies like this is known as scalable oversight . Debate is one proposal for how scalable oversight might be done. (It is possible that what I have written in this paragraph is not fully correct, but it represents my understanding so far.)
For the moment, I find it more helpful to start at the other end, with the safety, and work back to the mathematics. For example, it will obviously help with AI safety if we can think of ways of building AI systems that want similar things to what we want. And to do that, it will obviously help if we can define in a precise way what aligning wants in this way would mean. And for that it will obviously help to have a reasonably precise definition of what a “want” even is. (This idea for a project is not mine: it also came from Lionel Levine .) The activity of taking a not completely precise idea and turning it into a usable formal definition is something we mathematicians are trained to do, though the purer of us may have to develop more of an applied mindset — for instance, being ready to sacrifice mathematical elegance if a less elegant definition turns out to be more useful. It also seems likely to have uses throughout the field of AI safety.
An idea that appeals to me personally, because it intersects quite substantially with what I have been doing with my automatic theorem proving group for the last few years, is to work on building specialized AI systems for doing mathematics, rather than training general models with all their attendant dangers. This would be in line with an approach to AI safety that is strongly advocated by Yoshua Bengio: one place you can read about that is in this article . (Even the abstract gives a broad idea of what he is suggesting.) It’s an indirect approach to AI safety: instead of struggling to understand what’s going on inside “grown” AI systems and to make them controllable, we should work on improving systems that are at least partially crafted and that give us the benefits of the grown systems in a much safer way, thereby reducing the incentives that AI companies have to develop the grown systems as fast as they can.
More generally, it may well be that many mathematicians are best placed to help not by doing mathematics in a conventional sense (indeed, it seems likely that if we manage to formulate precise mathematical problems, the solutions to which would be genuinely helpful for AI safety, we will solve them more quickly if we use AI) but by using their highly developed mathematical habits of thought to help in other ways, such as research into the foundations of AI, or computer security, and so on.
Another analogy that I got from Soares and Yudkowsky is with fission in nuclear reactors. If there is too little fission then the chain reaction quickly fizzles out, and if there is too much then it blows up catastrophically. For obvious reasons, one can’t afford to find the optimal point by trial and error, so instead one needs an extremely good theoretical understanding of what the optimum point is. It could be that AI is like that: that up to a certain point it is safe, and then a rather small change in its capabilities suddenly leads to a chain reaction (not necessarily recursive self-improvement — other abilities such as being able to move around in cyberspace or reproduce itself could be enough) that is effectively irreversible.
If a model like this is anything like correct, then the behaviour of the AI companies is very worrying, since all the signs are that they are pursuing a trial-and-error approach. (This is not a particularly informed judgment, so I would be delighted to be corrected if it is wrong.) The argument most often given for continued development is that it could bring us amazing benefits, such as nuclear fusion, cures to cancer and other diseases, or slowing down aging. But if the cost of having a reasonable chance of developing these a bit sooner than we otherwise might have is a reasonable chance of human extinction, surely that is not worth it. (There is a working paper of Nick Bostrom arguing that the expected gain might be positive. I find his arguments ridiculous, but this is not the place to explain why.) We already have a tool that can do pretty incredible things and seems to be on the cusp of becoming dangerous: surely it would be better to pause development and work out how best to use what we currently have. That would give us time to do the necessary theoretical work to ensure that future development is safe.
This is far from an exhaustive list: it is just an indication of some of the writing that I have found useful (or in one or two cases, that I intend to look at soon).
Soares and Yudkowsky . I strongly recommend reading this. You may not find that you agree with all of it, but in order to disagree with it in good faith, you will need to develop layer-3 arguments.
Critch and Tsimerman Much shorter than Soares and Yudkowsky. Classifies the ways AI might kill us, and presents a scenario to illustrate each class. Even if you find some of the scenarios implausible, it is helpful to have the classification and to think about whether other scenarios in the given classes might be more plausible.
Reconsidering alignment as a goal, by Michael Nielsen . In this blog post, Michael Nielsen is his usual thought-provoking self. He puts forward the suggestion that maybe we should not work to make AI better aligned with our values, because while that could help us in the short term, in the longer term it will make AI a much more powerful, and therefore much more dangerous, tool.
Scott Alexander’s open letter to Steven Pinker This is a quite extraordinary takedown, worth reading partly for its sheer entertainment value, but also because it is basically a list of common layer-1 arguments and their well-known (for those who can be bothered to look for them) layer-2 counterarguments. So it’s a pretty good starting point if you’re feeling too lazy to read Soares and Yudkowsky (but please don’t feel too lazy to do that!).
An article about AIs subjected to an analogue of pain. This describes an experiment where some kind of negative stimulus was applied to AIs and how the AIs went to extraordinary lengths to avoid it. The article is careful to describe the stimulus as an analogue of pain rather than making claims about AI experiencing qualia. It maybe shouldn’t be the first thing to read, and in any case the experiment is controversial, but it seems to serve as another example of how AI could come to have goals that are in conflict with ours.
Gradual disempowerment If you still find the idea of x-risk too outlandish to consider seriously, you could always worry about a milder risk instead. The authors of this paper (one of whom, Raymond Douglas, I am proud to say is my nephew) argue that even if AI doesn’t try to kill us, we may end up ceding so much control to it that human life becomes far less worthwhile. It’s hard to explain how that could happen in a sentence or two, so I recommend reading the article itself.
The post by Steven McCulloch mentioned above also comes into the category of things to worry about that are not as serious as x-risk but that would still be terrible and feel a lot more likely (in the second-order sense that one can be more confident in asserting that they are likely).
Lionel Levine’s paper Math for AI Safety: an Invitation for Mathematicians sets out some of the ways that mathematics could potentially feed into AI safety.
A videoed course: Mathematics for AI Safety , by Yevgeny Liokumovich, does something similar.
A very good blog post by Xiaoyu He on AI safety, aimed at mathematicians. I think Xiaoyu He’s motivation for writing this post was similar to mine, and when I read it, I wondered whether there was any point in continuing with this one. In the end I decided to do so, because quite a lot of this one is about my personal experience of thinking about the issue, which may be a helpful addition for some people. But if you prefer a post that is more organized and written by someone who has a much deeper understanding of AI safety than I have, then his is highly recommended.
