title: SBU dismantles 5 more draft evasion schemes, suspects include doctors, taxi driver
body:
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI), and the National Police have blocked five new draft evasion and military service evasion schemes, detaining 12 organizers of the illegal operations across various regions of Ukraine, the SBU reports.
In a Telegram post on Friday, the agency reported that three fixers who arranged fictitious disabilities for liable citizens for money were detained in Kyiv.
To achieve this, the SBU noted, the suspects involved acquaintances who are doctors, who falsified medical histories, examination results, and documents regarding inpatient treatment for their clients.
"Law enforcement officers detained the organizers of the crime 'red-handed' while receiving money for a fake medical discharge from a skin and venereal diseases department," the message states.
Additionally, in Zaporizhia, a traumatologist, the head of a rehabilitation department, and the head of an X-ray room were exposed for giving evaders fake diagnoses of severe illnesses.
According to the investigation, the organizer of the scheme is currently abroad, from where they searched for "clients" and coordinated the doctors who entered false data into medical documents.
According to the Ukrainian security service, three fixers who organized a channel for the illegal departure of draft-age men to a neighboring country were detained in Vinnytsia region.
"The perpetrators transported draft evaders to the border area in their own vehicles and instructed them on how to cross the river outside official checkpoints," the report specifies.
Furthermore, in Kherson, SBU employees together with the SBI exposed a taxi driver who transported mobilized individuals who had voluntarily abandoned their military units, bypassing checkpoints.
According to the report, the organizer of the scheme was detained in Odesa region while transporting deserters to whom he promised to show an "alternative" escape route to the European Union.
Also, in Sumy region, two residents of Shostka were exposed for administering a Telegram channel that leaked the movement routes of Territorial Recruitment Center (TRC) and police representatives in the border area.
Currently, all detainees have been served notices of suspicion in accordance with the crimes committed under several articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.

title: ATR delivers new ATR 72-600 to Cape Verde’s CVsky
body:
ATR has delivered a new ATR 72-600 to Linhas Aéreas de Cabo Verde (LACV), the state-owned airline operating domestic flights across Cape Verde under the CVsky brand.
The aircraft, registered D4-CCP, was formally delivered at ATR's facilities in Toulouse on October 7 and is the first of two new ATR 72-600s scheduled to join the carrier under lease agreements.
D4-CCP is being painted in CVsky colors in France and is expected to arrive in Cape Verde by the end of October.
The aircraft is leased from Singapore-based Avation, which confirmed that the operating lease is backed by a sovereign guarantee from the Cape Verde government. The transaction also makes CVsky a new customer for the lessor.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
CVsky currently operates two ATR 72-600s, D4-CCM and D4-CCN, both configured with 74 seats. The aircraft were manufactured in 2018 and joined the airline in 2025.
The airline uses the turboprops on domestic services linking the islands of the Cape Verde archipelago, where short sectors dominate the network. According to ATR, the average domestic flight lasts about 36 minutes.
The type also allows CVsky to serve airports with relatively short runways, including Maio, São Nicolau and Fogo, whose runways measure approximately 1,200, 1,400 and 1,500 meters, respectively.
ATR aircraft have operated in Cape Verde for more than three decades. The manufacturer said the first ATR 42-320 arrived in the country in November 1994.
CVsky was established in 2024 to provide domestic passenger and cargo services and is wholly owned by the Cape Verde government. The airline received its Air Operator Certificate in December 2025 and now handles inter-island services previously dependent on other operators.

title: Pressure Mounts On Michael Carrick As Man Utd Face Historic Clash Against Leeds
body: Manchester United travel to historic rivals Leeds on Sunday with pressure mounting on manager Michael Carrick, while Manchester City aim to extend their perfect Premier League start despite uncertainty over their future. Brighton could be one of the big winners should City suffer severe sanctions for breaking financial rules. The Seagulls are riding high, just two points behind second-placed Arsenal, ahead of their grudge match against Crystal Palace. AFP Sport looks at the pick of the action from the English top flight this weekend. Man Utd’s worst start in 40 years United are off to their worst league start in 40 years and were plunged further into chaos by defender Lisandro Martinez’s attack on the club’s hierarchy over a lack of investment in the squad after Tuesday’s 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid. The Argentine took aim at technical director Jason Wilcox after the Red Devils’ main transfer business during the summer window focused on bringing in three midfielders. But Martinez himself has been one of those most culpable for a miserable start to the campaign for his part in goals conceded to Fulham and Tottenham in recent weeks. United have won just one of their opening six league games and were also dumped out of the League Cup by Brighton. Leeds last beat the Red Devils at Elland Road back in 2002, but did inflict the only home defeat of Carrick’s interim spell in charge last season when the sides met in April. Carrick is under increasing pressure as the latest manager struggling to reverse a sharp decline at Old Trafford since Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013. But he said the hostile atmosphere his side will face in Leeds gives United the perfect chance to bounce back. “What a great game (on) Sunday to prepare for. It’s a fantastic game for us, for the club, for the history, for the supporters,” said Carrick. “Everything to do with the game is a great game so we’ll be ready for that.” City case leaves league in limbo Manchester City sit pretty at the top of the table with six wins from six league games, but that could all count for nothing if they do not successfully overturn a guilty verdict on more than 100 charges of breaking Premier League rules. Enzo Maresca’s men shut out that distraction to win 3-0 at Liverpool last weekend and rallied impressively in the second half despite losing 4-2 to Paris Saint-Germain in a thrilling Champions League tie on Tuesday. But the uncertainty over their future has left the entire league in limbo. City deny any wrongdoing and the long-running case still has at least a few months left to run before the appeal process concludes and potential sanctions are announced. “My underlying thought is none of this is good for football and there are no winners,” said former England manager Gareth Southgate. City can stretch their lead at the top to six points when Ipswich visit the Etihad on Saturday, with Arsenal not in action until 24 hours later at Nottingham Forest. ‘Ruthless’ Brighton eye Champions League Arsenal’s only defeat this season came in a 3-0 trouncing by Brighton, who could reach new heights this season with a clutch of the established giants struggling. Brighton have soared through the divisions and into Europe on the back of owner Tony Bloom’s expertise in data analytics. But they are yet to play Champions League football. Despite routinely selling their prized assets to wealthier clubs, Brighton’s smart recruitment of both players and coaches has ensured they have continued to thrive. That has also made them popular among neutrals, but manager Fabian Hurzeler wants his side to show their nasty side against rivals Palace on Sunday. “We want to be ruthless. We want to create this energetic atmosphere where it makes it so hard to come to this place,” said Hurzeler. “We have to keep building this together with our fans and not be the nice football club anymore.” Fixtures (all times GMT) Saturday Everton v Chelsea (1130), Fulham v Hull, Brentford v Liverpool, Manchester City v Ipswich (all 1400), Newcastle v Aston Villa (1630) Sunday Brighton v Crystal Palace, Leeds v Manchester United, Bournemouth v Sunderland (all 1300), Nottingham Forest v Arsenal (1530) Monday Tottenham v Coventry (1900) The post Pressure Mounts On Michael Carrick As Man Utd Face Historic Clash Against Leeds appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Russian strike on Kharkiv market leaves two killed, 17 injured
body:
Oleh Syniehubov, Head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, reported this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
“As of this moment, two people have been confirmed killed – a 71-year-old woman and a 58-year-old man. My sincere condolences to their families and loved ones. A total of 17 people have been affected: 12 sustained injuries, while five suffered acute stress reactions. Ten people have been hospitalized, two of them in serious condition,” Syniehubov wrote.
Enemy drones were reported to have struck the Osnovianskyi, Shevchenkivskyi and Industrialnyi districts of the city.
“In particular, the energy system was targeted. We are doing everything necessary to deal with the aftermath and restore the supply of essential services to the public,” Syniehubov said.
As reported, Russian forces attacked three districts of Kharkiv in the morning of October 16. According to Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov, strikes were recorded on a market, as well as energy and transport infrastructure. At that time, two people had been reported killed and 16 injured.

title: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back
body: MANILA, Philippines – In a wide-ranging discussion with WNYC’s Brian Lehrer for the second edition of Democracy Dialogues on October 16, Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa warned again of the growing, still unaddressed threats to democracy posed by authoritarian governments, powerful technology companies, and now, artificial intelligence. Play Video The conversation, held at The Greene Space in New York, centered on Ressa’s new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators , which lays out practical strategies for citizens to resist authoritarianism, and reclaim control over the technologies shaping their lives. Drawing from Rappler’s experience under former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte, Ressa argued that the Philippines offers important lessons for the United States and other democracies now confronting similar threats, emphasizing how the fight can start at the individual level, and that it will take a global effort to reverse the current course of the world. The two dictators: Political leaders and Big Tech Ressa identifies two forms of authoritarian power threatening democracy: traditional political dictators and technology companies that have long wielded enormous influence over information, public opinion, and society. She argued that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg represents an even greater concentration of power than Duterte because, unlike political leaders who can face prosecution, technology executives operate with limited mechanisms for accountability. “The bigger dictator, and you’ll see this in both How to Stand Up to a Dictator and The Fight Back , is actually Mark Zuckerberg,” Ressa said. “While Duterte is now detained at The Hague … We have systems of accountability for that, but for the technology that rules our lives, we have none.” She added: “My dictators: One is on trial and the other one has gained more power.” Ressa also warned of an emerging alliance between political leaders and technology billionaires, which she describes as an “authoritarian stack.” Through political funding, government contracts, and control over critical technology infrastructure, powerful companies can gain influence over government functions and democratic institutions. “This is power and money. Look at the power and money,” she said, arguing that the concentration of political and technological power amounts to a “tech coup” unfolding in plain sight. Ressa also described the Philippines as an early example of how social media could be weaponized to undermine democracy. She recalled how during the Duterte administration, Rappler faced coordinated online attacks followed by legal cases and government investigations , and how the hashtag #ArrestMariaRessa began circulating in 2017, two years before her actual arrest. She realized later that that had been “fertilizer” for a narrative that allowed the government to shape public opinion in order to make the arrest. “When you repeat a lie a million times, it becomes a fact,” Ressa reiterated. AI as the next frontier of authoritarian power Beyond social media, Ressa warned that artificial intelligence presents a new and potentially more dangerous challenge to democratic accountability. She described three stages in the evolution of technology’s influence over individuals: social media capturing attention, chatbots creating a sense of intimacy, and autonomous AI agents acquiring the capacity to perform actions independently. Speaking about her work as co-chair of the United Nations’ Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, Ressa argued that increasingly powerful AI systems are being deployed without sufficient safeguards or accountability. “As early as July, we had actually already said, and these are from the scientists, that the frontier models cannot be controlled by the people who are making it,” she said. “And if you really feel that, then you should not be releasing these. You should not be treating the public around the world as Pavlov’s dogs.” Ressa criticized the argument that rapid AI deployment is necessary to compete with China, saying geopolitical competition should not become an excuse for exposing the public to potentially harmful technologies. “The question here is, if we go back to impunity, right? Who is accountable for this?” she asked, saying the problem is the lack of legislation. She emphasized that AI governance cannot be left to the United States and China alone. Developing countries and other governments must have a meaningful role in shaping global rules, particularly because they may bear significant consequences of decisions made by the world’s largest technology companies. “The world needs to have a place at the table,” Ressa said. She also discussed how AI has undermined journalism, noting that Google Search’s use of AI summaries has caused a drop that is “catastrophic for news organizations. This is part of the tech-fueled crisis that journalism faces now, along with how 85% of digital advertising in the Philippines now goes to these tech companies owning the platforms. Must Read Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity That fuels the “market failure” for journalism right now she said. Without journalism, authoritarian power wins. “Why do you need journalists? Because the journalists are the ones that do the investigative report that hold power to account,” she said. Ressa urged audiences to support independent news organizations through subscriptions and donations. She also argued that societies must consider building alternative, public-interest technology infrastructure rather than remaining dependent on platforms controlled by a handful of corporations. Aside from supporting independent journalism, she also outlined other strategies for fighting authoritarianism, which includes identifying authoritarian forces in one’s country, protecting elections from manipulation, and organizing communities to resist abuses of power. Must Read Limit AI now or humanity will lose its agency, says Nobel laureate Maria Ressa Being mindful of one’s own tech use, prepare for threats She also urged people to become more conscious of how technology influences their behavior. “Track your screen time. Track how much time you spend on screens,” she advised. “And then the second step in chapter one is delete the social media app that makes you angriest.” Ressa cautioned against becoming overly dependent on AI chatbots, warning that outsourcing thinking and writing to these systems could weaken people’s ability to reason independently. “Don’t stop thinking, especially if you’re young. Like, write. Don’t stop writing because using a chatbot is like trying to run a marathon and outsourcing going to the gym,” she said. Avoid “cognitive surrender,” she said. Prepare for authoritarian threats before they happen Again drawing from Rappler’s experience under Duterte, Ressa emphasized that organizations and individuals must prepare for authoritarian threats before they become crises. “What we learned in Rappler, and this is like practical advice, whatever it is you’re most afraid of, imagine it. Take it, own it, embrace it, and then workflow a response to it,” she said. She recalled how Rappler developed contingency plans for a possible government shutdown, dividing responsibilities among teams and regularly conducting drills to ensure the newsroom could continue operating. Ressa also urged journalists to avoid amplifying authoritarian propaganda merely to criticize it. Rather than becoming distracted by inflammatory statements, she said journalists should identify lies, provide context, investigate underlying systems of power, and help audiences understand why events matter. “If it’s a distraction, don’t amplify. If it’s a lie, just call it a lie and then find the deeper meaning,” she said. Ressa closed the discussion by emphasizing that defending democracy is ultimately a matter of individual and collective action. Her central message was that hope is not something citizens should passively wait for. It must emerge from their willingness to defend democratic institutions, support one another, and confront abuses of power. “Hope comes from action,” Ressa said. “Act! That’s what I’m saying. Act, right? That’s what the moment demands. If we act, we can do something about it.” – Rappler.com [ANALYSIS] A day at the UN: What does AI mean for humanity? When Big Tech rewards the worst of who we are, what can you do?

title: 2027: Dickson urges INEC to restore omitted NDC candidates in final list
body:
The National Leader of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Seriake Dickson, has urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to “promptly” restore omitted names of NDC candidates in the final list of candidates for the 2027 general elections.
Mr Dickson, a former governor of Bayelsa State, appealed in a post on his Facebook page on Thursday night.
“We urge INEC to remedy this apparent omission promptly,” he appealed.
PREMIUM TIMES reports that the NDC governorship candidates in Kano, Kaduna and Cross River States were omitted from the final list of candidates for the 2027 election recently published by INEC on Saturday.
The NDC leadership had attributed the omission to an error.
In the Facebook post, Mr Dickson, the Bayelsa West senator, said the NDC was working “diligently” to correct the omission.
“Our candidates and supporters are assured that the party has been working diligently and has taken adequate steps to address the cases of those whose names were not published by INEC a few days ago,” he said.
“All affected candidates registered with the party before the statutory 21-day period required by law.”
The national leader said the NDC fielded qualified candidates, from the presidential candidate to those in state houses of assembly, who, he argued, “emerged through a rigorous and painstaking screening process.”
“We are confident that INEC will correct this omission without delay,” he stated.
Mr Dickson said consultations and campaigns would continue in all states while the NDC sustains ongoing engagements with INEC on the missing names of its candidates.
“We will continue lto fight without giving up until we are victorious,” he maintained.

title: Emergency blackouts in Kyiv, as Klitschko announces start of heating season
body:
Emergency blackouts were implemented across Kyiv due to Russian attacks on the city's energy infrastructure, Ukraine's biggest private energy firm DTEK said on Oct. 16, as Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced the start of the city's heating season.
"We remind you that during emergency shutdowns, schedules are not valid," DTEK said . Kyiv already operates under scheduled power outages , allowing residents to plan their days around them, but Russian attacks on the city's energy infrastructure led to additional emergency power outages over the past weeks.
On the same day, Klitschko announced that Kyiv's centralised heating system will be turned on, starting with social institutions such as schools, hospitals, and kindergartens. The decision was sparked by "extreme conditions" created by constant bombardment, Klitschko said.
Two areas of the city, the Dniprovskyi and Darnytskyi districts, would not have their centralised heating switched on due to "significant damage" to a power facility in the area, Klitschko said, while repair efforts were ongoing.
Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin, is home to over 3 million people, with average temperatures of -4.6 degrees Celsius to -1 degrees Celsius (23.7 degrees Fahrenheit to 30 degrees Fahrenheit) in the winter months.
In Kyiv Oblast, Buchanan, Obukhiv, and Fastiv districts were also experiencing emergency blackouts, DTEK said .
In Western Ukraine, the city of Lutsk was left without power, Andriy Razumovsky, secretary of Lutsk City Council, announced on social media.
"Due to an attack by enemy drones, the city was left without electricity. Utilities are operating on backup power sources," Razumovsky said .
Overnight on Oct. 13 to 14, Russia launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, wreaking destruction in a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities in Kyiv.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that all three of the city's combined heat and power stations were attacked, as well as critical infrastructure in the Kyiv Oblast that provide power to Kyiv and central regions.
"The targets of Russian ballistic missiles were power system facilities in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and the region," he said.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media on Oct.14, adding that 600,000 people were left without power.

title: Austria slams Ukraine's opaque finances, with 'so many numbers swirling around'
body:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker criticized the lack of transparency in Ukraine's finances, as President Volodmyr Zelensky attends the Oct. 16 EU leaders' summit to lobby for more financial support.
"So many numbers are swirling around that you have to put them in order... you have to make it transparent, where this (budget) hole comes from," Stocker told journalists.
Zelensky is asking EU allies for increased budgetary support, with Kyiv foreseeing a sizeable budget gap for 2027, though the exact size remains difficult to determine.
However, Stocker was not against providing financial support for Ukraine, as his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babis, seems to be .
"We have to classify so that we know how we can shape the support and solidarity with Ukraine in the future," Stocker said.
The Kyiv Independent reviewed the draft budget in Ukraine's parliament, which, as of Oct. 7 , contained a Hr 1.66 trillion ($40 billion) budget shortfall for 2027.
But then Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi wrote on social media on Oct. 14 that Ukraine's needs for 2027 "top $52 billion." He also said the "military's off-budget requirement is estimated at $45 billion."
Adding to the confusion is that officials either refer to a single budget hole or spin out the country's defense needs as a separate financial gap.
A senior EU official familiar with Ukraine's 2027 financial planning strategy told the Kyiv Independent that the numbers Koretskyi posted are "again new numbers."
The estimates the EU had received amounted to approximately 70 billion euros ($78.8 billion), the official said.
Stocker said he is ready to believe Ukraine about rising costs "due to these intensified and massive attacks by Russia... but the fact that this is immediately reflected in a budget gap is something you will have to talk about."

title: Memory Under Noise: Why AI-Assistant Memory Engines Lose the Evidence
body:
We benchmarked five open-source memory systems to answer a practical question: which one should power an assistant that needs to remember a growing conversation history? Our recommendation is hybrid RAG over the original transcripts. It was the most accurate option at every noise level, and its total run cost was a fraction of every dedicated memory engine we tested. A more elaborate memory architecture needs to earn its place by beating that baseline.
The results below use an 8K-token context budget with 90% unrelated history. Costs cover the full 1,000-question run, including memory building and answering. Graphiti’s result is at 50% noise because we did not run it at 90%.
96.8% accuracy for $1.70. Chunking the raw history and combining keyword and vector search beat all five memory engines. Accuracy fell only 1.7 percentage points as noise grew from 0% to 90%. It preserves the original wording and attribution, then gives the answer model enough relevant text to work with. For conversational recall, this is where we would start.
89.9% accuracy for $20.39. Its combination of semantic, keyword, graph and temporal retrieval kept relevant evidence available as history grew. At a 2K context budget, it was statistically tied with RAG. That makes it the most compelling dedicated engine in this comparison when context is tight. The trade-off is operational cost: roughly 12 times RAG’s total run cost, and median retrieval latency rising from 2.8 to 15.6 seconds as the store grew.
82.7% accuracy for $20.73. It stayed close to its 84.3% clean-history score while returning under 1,000 context tokens on average. Its fixed quotas per memory category keep context compact, but leave useful evidence out even before much noise is added. Choose this trade-off deliberately if compact context matters; we would not choose it to maximise recall.
81.5% accuracy for $7.03, down from 90.9% without noise. It was the least expensive dedicated engine at 90% noise, but its top-20 memory limit became a bottleneck as unrelated history accumulated. In persona conversations, extraction also dropped speaker names, weakening answers about who said what. It deserves consideration when a small set of extracted facts is enough; we would not trust the default retrieval for detailed recall over a long history.
69.7% accuracy for $18.28 after memory building finished. The earlier unfinished build scored 66.3%. Tuning retrieval to fill each person’s share of the context budget with similar observations raised accuracy to 77.5%. Its default mix of similar and recent observations gives too much space to recency as history grows. Our recommendation: finish the background build and tune retrieval before relying on it. Even after tuning, it remained behind RAG and Hindsight here.
53.6% accuracy at 50% noise for $19.84. Returning only ten graph facts often failed to supply enough evidence for multi-part answers. We would not pick this default configuration for question answering over conversation history. Use a graph because your application needs explicit relationships and temporal structure, then verify that its retrieval can answer your actual questions.
The important distinction was what retrieval returned. RAG and Hindsight filled the available budget with relevance-ranked text. Fixed item counts and slots reserved for recent memories let irrelevant history crowd out the evidence. Simply pasting in the latest history also failed: the full-context baseline fell from 98.0% to 52.4% once older evidence no longer fit.
Extraction creates another weak point. The extraction engines scored 6–18 percentage points worse on facts mentioned once than on repeated facts; RAG stayed around 98–99% in that comparison. Missing context is not the whole story either: answer terms appeared in many wrong Mem0 and Hindsight answers, pointing to incomplete, misattributed or mis-dated memories. A fact being stored somewhere does not mean an assistant can use it correctly.
We tested Hindsight, Mem0, Honcho, OpenViking and Graphiti against hybrid RAG, full-context and no-memory baselines on 1,000 questions drawn from four conversation and email corpora. Unrelated history grew from 0% to 50% to 90%, with the model, embedder, answer prompt and judge held constant. These recommendations concern conversational question answering; the study does not measure every engine’s editing, inspection or other product features. Small differences such as Mem0 versus OpenViking are not a reliable basis for a ranking.
Tadas Subonis, AAI Labs. The full 14-page paper is in English.

title: Joyce Bawah Mogtari urges women leaders to build strong support networks
body: Senior Presidential Advisor and Aide to President John Dramani Mahama, Joyce Bawah Mogtari, has urged women in leadership to surround themselves with people who will support their growth, defend them against unfair treatment and offer honest advice. In a Facebook post on Friday, October 16, she reflected on a discussion with former Electoral Commission Chairperson Charlotte Osei at the Obaasima Conference, where the challenges women encounter in leadership featured prominently. Ms Bawah Mogtari said the conversation reinforced the importance of having a dependable support system in workplaces where women’s abilities and achievements are often questioned. She said a genuine support network should go beyond public expressions of solidarity to include people willing to speak up against injustice, offer constructive criticism and celebrate the progress of others without feeling threatened. Such relationships, she noted, can make a significant difference in how women navigate the pressures of leadership. Ms Bawah Mogtari said the Obaasima Conference should provide a platform for women to share their experiences, learn from one another and develop meaningful connections. She stressed that while leadership can be difficult for women, having trusted people to rely on can make the journey more manageable and rewarding.

title: Bawumia engages GUTA over import duties, VAT and rising business costs
body: Former Vice President and New Patriotic Party (NPP) flagbearer for the 2028 elections, Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, has held talks with the Ghana Union of Traders’ Associations (GUTA) on challenges affecting traders, including high import duties, rising demurrage charges and the cost of doing business. In a Facebook post on Friday, October 16, Dr Bawumia said executives and representatives of GUTA outlined concerns over high import duties, the reported increase in VAT for informal sector operators to 20%, limited access to EXIM loans, high shop rents and goodwill payments, as well as foreign nationals taking over aspects of the retail trade. He described the engagement as productive and said the association also presented proposals to address some of the challenges. The discussions also focused on how Ghana could move from dependence on imported goods towards local production. Dr Bawumia said he and the traders explored incentives that could encourage businesses to manufacture more goods locally, potentially creating jobs and expanding opportunities for Ghanaian businesses. He thanked GUTA for the engagement and the ideas it presented, saying the discussions had provided useful insights into the difficulties facing traders. The meeting forms part of conversations on possible policy measures to improve the business environment, ease operational pressures and support domestic production and private-sector growth.

title: Fuel prices begin to fall as Star Oil cuts petrol to GH¢16.45
body: Some oil marketing companies (OMCs) have begun reducing fuel prices at the pumps as the second pricing window for October takes effect. Star Oil reduced its petrol price from GH¢16.64 to GH¢16.45 per litre, effective 8am on Friday, October 16, 2026. Other OMCs have told JoyBusiness they intend to review their prices, although some say they will monitor competitors before making adjustments. While motorists could benefit from lower petrol and diesel prices, users of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) face a projected increase of more than 18%. The Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies expects LPG to sell at about GH¢20.60 per kilogramme. Reasons for the adjustments The Chamber attributed the projected price movements to developments in the international petroleum market, exchange-rate pressures, and recent government interventions. According to its report, average crude oil prices rose by 2.03% to US$126.73 per barrel for the October 16 pricing window. The Chamber linked the increase to renewed supply concerns, citing uncertainty over a proposed US-backed energy ceasefire involving Ukraine and fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia amid the conflict with Iran. Despite the rise in crude prices, refined petroleum products recorded mixed movements. International LPG prices increased by 7.77%, while diesel and petrol prices fell by 6.68% and 3.93%, respectively. Meanwhile, the cedi depreciated by 1.61% against the US dollar, reaching an average bank rate of GH¢11.8222 between September 26 and October 11, 2026. The Chamber said the local currency had lost more than 11% against the dollar since the beginning of the year, with seasonal import demand and higher energy costs continuing to exert pressure. The weaker cedi is expected to limit how much of the decline in international petrol and diesel prices is passed on to consumers. Competition and the NPA’s price floor Some OMCs say competition will influence the timing and extent of their price adjustments. However, their pricing decisions must also comply with the National Petroleum Authority’s minimum price requirements. Market information available to JoyBusiness puts the petrol price floor at GH¢16.09 per litre and the LPG floor at GH¢13.87 per kilogramme. These floors represent minimum selling prices, not the pump prices that every company must charge. Actual prices may therefore vary among OMCs.

title: Can memories be trusted? Abu Dhabi exhibition explores how the past changes with every recollection
body: Every time we recall a memory, we risk changing it. Details shift, emotions take on new meaning and experiences we consider precious may bear increasingly little resemblance to what actually happened. This phenomenon, known as memory reconsolidation, is the starting point for Consolidation is Reconsolidation, an exhibition that brings together five UAE-based artists at Region, in Abu Dhabi's MiZa district. Running until Monday, the exhibition marks the launch of Hyphen Contemporary, a curatorial platform founded by Cecelia Jihu-Sara to champion emerging artists and introduce new collectors to contemporary art. Through photography, painting, sculpture and scent, the artists question how memories are preserved, distorted and reconstructed, whether through family archives, digital records or personal experiences. “The memories we recall most often are often actually the least reliable,” Jihu-Sara tells The National . The exhibition arrives at a time when almost every experience can be documented, yet the resulting records may be no more permanent or trustworthy than our own recollections. Jihu-Sara says the relationship between experiencing moments and recording them has changed. Concerts, gatherings and everyday encounters increasingly take place through smartphone screens, raising questions about what is preserved and what is lost. “Are you truly experiencing it?” she asks. “If you're behind your phone, who are you then experiencing it for?” Digital recordings may capture sights and sounds, but they cannot necessarily reproduce the emotions attached to an event. The vulnerability of online archives, from disappearing files to AI manipulation , further complicates the distinction between documentation and truth. These concerns are reflected in the work of Sara Kamar, born in Abu Dhabi in 2003, whose paintings and sculptures examine memory, identity and digital infrastructure. Her practice considers what happens when technology becomes an extension of human recollection, with smartphones and cloud storage increasingly replacing journals and physical photographs. Jihu-Sara thinks the immediacy of digital photography has also changed how people value their records, pointing to camera rolls filled with screenshots and images that are rarely revisited. A more sensory approach emerges in the work of Layla Doueidi, whose practice draws on her Syrian-Lebanese heritage, family archives and a recent return to Syria. Born in Beirut in 2001, Doueidi uses photography and scent to explore inherited and lived memories. Her wax works incorporate fragrances influenced by her father's career as a perfumer. Jihu-Sara says the appeal lies in how smell can trigger recollections that are difficult to access through images or words. A visit to Doueidi's studio, where the artist introduced her to various fragrances, demonstrated how differently people respond to the same scent. “I really love the kind of activation of the work that happens with the scent works, like the leaning in,” she says. “You really have to engage with the work and everyone has a different reaction to it.” Unlike photographs or paintings, scent demands physical participation. The same fragrance may evoke different memories depending on someone's experiences, while the blurred appearance of the wax reflects the haziness of recollection, particularly from childhood. Photography takes on a more fragmented character in the work of Martin Ong Yambao, a Filipino artist who incorporates found photographic material and the traditional healing ritual of pagtatawas, usually performed by a folk healer using prayers and molten candle wax. His unusual treatment of photographic images first caught Jihu-Sara's attention during Art Dubai earlier this year. Intrigued by the process, she arranged a studio visit and watched him manipulate the images using a candle. “I hadn't seen anything like it,” she says. “I just really fell in love with the works.” The process produces distorted imagery that reflects the way memories can change through repeated recollection. Yambao's connection to the exhibition's location emerged when he revealed that he already had a roll of film from Mina Zayed, which became particularly relevant to a show taking place in the district. Place and nostalgia are central to the work of Emirati artist Rayan Aljneibi, whose background in archival science informs her examination of how locations are documented, remembered and transformed. Her new works, including the Fragmented Recall series and steel pieces, examine the changing character of familiar surroundings. Jihu-Sara says she was struck by the distinctly local character of Aljneibi's photography. She had initially encountered the work through an Instagram post shared by fellow exhibiting artist Husna Samer, without knowing Aljneibi was Emirati. “There's such a feeling of nostalgia around her photos and these everyday kind of imagery and places and feelings that everyone here can relate to and recognise,” she says. Including an Emirati artist was not initially a curatorial requirement, but Jihu-Sara believes Aljneibi's work offers a meaningful examination of a country undergoing rapid transformation. Samer, the exhibition's youngest participant, uses symbolism and surrealism to explore identity, remembrance and the shifting meaning of home. Beyond its subject matter, Consolidation is Reconsolidation also establishes the ambitions of Hyphen Contemporary. Jihu-Sara's route into curating was unconventional. Raised in the UK, she studied mechanical engineering and worked as a project manager specialising in highways and railways before moving to the UAE two years ago. After working at a gallery in Alserkal Avenue, she enrolled in a master's programme in History of Art and Museum Studies at Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi. An assignment to imagine a museum for the capital led to the concept of Hyphen Museum, which eventually inspired her independent curatorial platform. Jihu-Sara says the hyphen represents connections between cultures, identities and experiences in the UAE, where people from different backgrounds constantly interact. It also reflects her ambition to connect emerging artists with people considering buying art for the first time. Drawing on her own experience purchasing her first artwork at an emerging gallery in East London, Jihu-Sara wants to make collecting more accessible while giving younger artists the space to present their practices seriously. “You can walk into a gallery, and no matter how much money you have, you're not going to spend $20,000 on your first artwork,” she says. “It kind of has to start somewhere.” That thinking informs the exhibition's deliberately restrained presentation. Jihu-Sara initially considered displaying twice as many works but reduced the selection to give each piece a distinct purpose within the wider narrative. She thinks smaller tightly curated exhibitions can be more welcoming to audiences unfamiliar with contemporary art, allowing visitors to engage with individual works without becoming overwhelmed. “I didn't want it to be like a bazaar,” she says. “It's not a shop. It's an exhibition.” Consolidation is Reconsolidation runs until October 19 at Region, MiZa, Abu Dhabi. It's open daily from 9am to 9pm

title: The defunding of the SANDF – the end of one debate, the beginning of another
body:
Over the past 13 articles, I have attempted to examine the defunding of the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) from a range of economic, financial, organisational and operational perspectives. The objective was not simply to argue for increased defence expenditure, but to better understand the extent of the defunding, its consequences and the alternatives available to South Africa.
The articles drew on official budget statistics, international comparisons, academic research, personnel and operational data, public opinion surveys and alternative approaches to defence management.
As this series concludes, it is appropriate to reflect on the main findings before turning our attention to what may be an even more important question: how should South Africa organise its national defence in an environment of sustained fiscal constraints?
Article 1: The Defunding of the SANDF – What Next?
South Africa has experienced one of the most substantial long-term reductions in defence expenditure internationally. Since 2000, defence expenditure has remained below 1% of GDP, declining towards approximately 0.5%. The magnitude of the reduction suggests a systematic process of defunding rather than a temporary budgetary adjustment.
Article 2: A Fundamental Mind Shift Is Needed?
The prospects of substantially increasing defence expenditure appear limited. Competing socio-economic priorities, fiscal constraints and political realities suggest that the SANDF cannot simply rely on future budget increases to restore its capabilities. A fundamental change in thinking is therefore necessary.
The traditional SANDF structure is not the only possible approach to providing national defence. Alternative configurations, ranging from a defence force without a standing military to a fully funded conventional military, warrant serious consideration. The purpose is not to advocate a particular option, but to broaden the defence debate.
International empirical research provides mixed evidence regarding the relationship between defence expenditure and economic growth. Higher military spending does not necessarily stimulate economic development, and the economic consequences depend on institutional quality, expenditure efficiency and wider economic circumstances.
The financial analysis revealed growing imbalances in the allocation of defence expenditure. Personnel-related costs, constrained capital investment, maintenance pressures and limited operational resources increasingly undermine the sustainability of the existing defence organisation.
The SANDF has experienced substantial personnel reductions without a corresponding fundamental restructuring of its responsibilities and organisational architecture. The challenge extends beyond total personnel numbers to the composition, allocation and effective utilisation of available human resources.
Article 7: Revisiting Public Views on the SANDF
Public opinion data revealed a complex relationship between South Africans and their military. Although considerable public pride and support remain, direct exposure to the SANDF is limited. Public legitimacy, visibility and perceptions of value are therefore important considerations in the defence funding debate.
Article 8: What the SANDF’s Facebook Page Reveals
The analysis of the SANDF’s Facebook communication highlighted the prominence of ceremonial and symbolic activities, alongside operational and community-related content. Public engagement also revealed recurring concerns about equipment, funding, leadership and organisational performance. Effective communication and public confidence remain important challenges.
Article 9: An Empirical Analysis of South Africa’s Arms Trade
The analysis of international arms transfers demonstrated the changing structure and geographical orientation of South Africa’s defence industry. Arms exports have expanded considerably since the 1990s, particularly in armoured vehicles, while the industry’s relationship with international markets has become increasingly important.
Article 10: A Guns versus Butter Perspective
Defence expenditure is fundamentally a resource-allocation decision. Governments must balance military requirements against competing demands for education, healthcare, infrastructure and social protection. Consequently, the allocation of resources to defence reflects economic realities, political priorities and public preferences.
Article 11: Managing Scarcity Differently
The SANDF’s challenges cannot be attributed to funding alone. Organisational management, procurement, financial controls, infrastructure and administrative continuity are equally important. Greater professionalisation of non-operational management functions could improve organisational performance without compromising military command.
Article 12: A Defence Estate Optimisation Strategy
The Department of Defence controls an extensive portfolio of land, buildings, infrastructure and specialised facilities. Better utilisation of underused assets could generate supplementary revenue, improve infrastructure maintenance and reduce pressure on the national budget, provided military requirements remain paramount.
The assumption that the SANDF must own all the equipment required to perform its functions deserves reconsideration. Leasing, availability-based contracts and alternative procurement arrangements may offer financial and operational advantages, particularly for non-combat and mission-enabling equipment. However, such arrangements must be evaluated against their full life-cycle costs, risks and operational implications.
Although the 13 articles approached the issue from different perspectives, several common findings emerge.
It is this final observation that provides the starting point for the next series.
The next series will move beyond documenting the defunding of the SANDF towards examining alternative approaches to providing national defence.
Drawing on my research paper, Exploring Alternative National Defence Approaches – A South African Case Study , the series will examine eleven conceptual defence configurations. These range from the complete absence of a standing military to a fully funded conventional Defence Force.
Each article will focus on one configuration, examining its organisational structure, theoretical foundations, international examples, potential advantages, disadvantages and possible application to South Africa.
These configurations should not be interpreted as eleven recommendations or mutually exclusive alternatives. Rather, they represent a conceptual continuum of possible approaches to national defence.
Importantly, each involves trade-offs between fiscal affordability, military capability, operational readiness, strategic autonomy, organisational complexity and long-term sustainability.
The objective of the new series will be to explore these trade-offs in greater detail, drawing on international experiences and examining their relevance to South Africa.
The first 13 articles have demonstrated that the SANDF faces a profound structural challenge. Decades of declining expenditure, constrained capital investment, personnel pressures and operational difficulties have created a growing disconnect between the country’s defence expectations and the resources available to meet them.
The conventional response has been to call for increased funding. While additional resources may be necessary, there is little evidence that South Africa’s broader fiscal and political circumstances will accommodate the substantial increases required to restore the existing defence model fully.
Perhaps the time has therefore come to ask a different question.
Instead of continually debating how much money the SANDF should receive, should we not also be debating how South Africa’s national defence should be organised and delivered?
The next series will attempt to contribute to precisely that discussion.
The challenge is no longer simply how to fund the SANDF we have, but whether the SANDF we have is the defence organisation South Africa needs, can afford and can sustain.
Dr Clive Coetzee is Senior Lecturer, Faculty of Military Science, Stellenbosch University.

title: Mammoth push past previous struggles vs. Oilers
body:
EDMONTON – The Utah Mammoth have not had much success against Edmonton in their brief existence.
But they changed that around on Thursday while further signifying they are a team to keep an eye on this season.
Clayton Keller scored a pair of goals as the Mammoth emerged with a 4-2 victory over the Edmonton Oilers. Barrett Hayton and Logan Cooley also scored for the Mammoth (6-2-0) who have won three straight.
“Obviously, they’re an unbelievable team over there,” Cooley said. “Some of the best players in the world, and when we have a showing like that, playing committed hockey, we can beat anyone in this league.
“I think that’s the confidence we need and the confidence we’re going to have going into the rest of the season.”
Edmonton came into the contest with a 5-0-1 record against the Mammoth and outscoring them 31-16. Edmonton was also 3-0-0 all-time at home against Utah, outscoring them 17-5.
“I’m really proud of the way we defended, the way we played away from the puck,” said Utah head coach Andre Tourigny. “We were really structured, were physical and I think we made it hard, every inch on the ice, for the team on the other side. They played really well, as well. It was a hard-fought game.
“We liked how hard we were to play against and how hard we defend. I think we were competing with emotion, but we were under control. I’m extremely proud of the boys.”
Utah should be pleased that they matched the offer sheet tendered by the New Jersey Devils for Hayton in the off-season. Hayton scored his first of the season and extended his points streak to five games.
“It took a lot. I think we had a ton of focus,” Hayton said. “They’re a great team over there, they’ve had a great start to the season, so it was a big challenge for us and I thought we embraced it.”
Oilers captain Connor McDavid, who extended his points streak to seven games and now has 18 on the season, said there is a lot to like about the young Mammoth squad.
“I thought they play very well,” he said. “They were solid and have as balanced as a lineup as you’re going to see throughout the league. They play four lines, are big, fast. There is a lot to like over there.”
Leon Draisaitl and Shakir Mukhamadullin replied for the Oilers (5-1-1) who saw a five-game winning streak halted. Edmonton was missing five starting forwards and a defenceman.
The two teams have a rematch on Saturday night in Utah.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

title: GoldBod supplies banks with US$282m in weekly forex sales
body: The Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod) says it sold US$282 million to commercial banks through its foreign exchange (FX) sales programme on Tuesday, October 13, and Thursday, October 15, 2026, as part of efforts to increase dollar supply to Ghana’s domestic market. In a statement, the Board said US$197 million was sold on Tuesday, followed by an additional US$85 million on Thursday. GoldBod explained that the transactions were conducted through its digital GoldBod GoFX platform to make foreign exchange earned from Ghana’s gold resources available to participating commercial banks. GoldBod said the programme is backed by Section 2(b) of the Ghana Gold Board Act, 2025 (Act 1140), which provides for the Board to supply foreign exchange to the country. According to the Board, participating banks submit requests for US dollars through the platform, with allocations made under the real-time monitoring of the Bank of Ghana. The Board reiterated that the arrangement constitutes spot FX sales rather than forex trading. It explained that it sells dollars earned from its gold operations to commercial banks in exchange for cedis, which are then used to finance its gold purchases. GoldBod said the supply of dollars to commercial banks helps businesses access foreign currency for imports, international payments and other legitimate obligations. The Board added that improved FX availability could help ease pressure on the cedi and imported costs, while supporting market stability and the financing of its gold purchasing operations.

title: ‘Call them out’: AI data centres becoming an Ontario municipal election issue
body:
AI data centres have become an issue in Ontario’s municipal elections, with grassroots groups pressing candidates to support stricter regulations.
Several Greater Toronto Area mayoral and city council candidates have signed a pledge promising to oppose building any data centres that fail to adhere to strict oversight and regulations.
Early signatories include incumbent Mississauga mayoral candidate Carolyn Parrish and incumbent Hamilton council candidates Cameron Kroetsch and Nrinder Nann.
Stop the Datacentre, a grassroots advocacy group, is looking for more signatories before municipal elections are held later this month.
The pledge asks candidates to sign on if they agree with the following conditions:
So far, the pledge has gone out to candidates in Hamilton and Mississauga, two cities that have had heated debates over data centres already.
In September, Mississauga city council approved a one-year moratorium on new data centre approvals after residents raised concerns about a data centre project proposed in northwest Mississauga, outlining fears around energy consumption, strain on the water supply and possible noise pollution.
Hamilton residents similarly pushed back against data centres in their city. But in July, city council voted down a moratorium on construction. Mayor Andrea Horwath and some councillors cited concerns around scaring away tech companies from investing in the city.
Martin Reid, who is running for re-election as Mississauga Ward 9 councillor, has signed the pledge. He was one of the councillors who set in motion the city’s moratorium.
Nick Tsergas, a Hamilton resident, created the pledge. He said he was motivated to hold politicians accountable after seeing the data centre issue take hold across the country.
Tsergas said the pledge is intended to hold signatories accountable to their commitments. If anyone ends up reneging on it, “we can call them out,” he added.
Tsergas was also motivated to start his record-keeping effort because of a lack of clarity from the province about whether data centres will be subject to specific regulatory standards. No legislation on the issue has been passed.
The Ford government released its AI data centre playbook in August, which includes proposed policies on how to govern data centres. But it is an evaluation tool, not binding legislation.
“We don’t know what those rules will look like, or when they arrive,” Tsergas said. “Will they be geared to protecting communities and addressing concerns, or will they be geared towards attracting data centre investment from large U.S. tech companies?”
The government’s playbook proposes prioritizing Canadian companies, community benefits and self-sustaining power systems.
However, Reid argues the proposed data centre that prompted his push for a moratorium does not satisfy several priorities outlined in the province’s playbook.
The project is proposed for a plot of land in the Tenth Line and Argentia Road area. The property was formerly farmland and was acquired by U.S.-based logistics company Prologis for the proposed development.
When the Prologis plans came across his desk, Reid did some digging and realized there was no land use designation for a data centre.
“It’s a warehouse, but it has 14 generators,” he said, alluding to the grey area that data centres fall into.
Tsergas also raised concern with classification, especially for data centres that propose to generate their own power.
“Is it a power plant or a data centre? What’s the noise going to be like? What’s the pollution going to be like?” he asked.
Reid identified safety concerns beyond environmental issues.
“Fire did not have a fire study for a data centre,” Reid said. “We have a building with lithium-ion batteries in it. It could be a ticking time bomb.”
Reid also said that Prologis did not plan on offering any community benefits.
“I went to them at one point and asked them to consider that, but they don’t have to do that from a development perspective. It’s not legislated, and they didn’t offer.”
Global News reached out to Prologis, which said it remains committed to the project at Tenth Line and Argentia, even with the city’s moratorium in place.
Prologis said construction would support 1,600 jobs. Once operational, the company estimates the project would sustain 63 direct, indirect and induced full-time-equivalent jobs.
Prologis also said that it is working with the provincial government to develop the data centre playbook, and that the Mississauga site will generate $1.6 million in annual property tax revenue for the city and region.
Tsergas stressed the purpose of his pledge is to seek clarity on how prospective candidates view the issue.
“We’re not asking people if they like or don’t like AI. We are just asking people if they think rules should exist before a major development goes in, and what at minimum those rules should be.”

title: Kipiani, ‘Katsro’: Figures Associated With Criminal Underworld Arrested on Group Violence Charges
body: Vakthang (Vato) Kipiani and Avtandil Bilanishvili, known as “Katsro,” two figures long associated with Georgia’s criminal underworld in media reports, have been arrested alongside another person, Shota Kipiani, on charges of group violence. Bilanishvili has also been repeatedly associated in the media with Bera, Bidzina Ivanishvili’s son, with the two rumored to have enjoyed a friendship. Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office said they physically assaulted a person, whose identity has not been disclosed, in a restaurant in Tbilisi on October 14. The three have been charged under Article 126, Paragraph 1, Subparagraph “b” of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which covers violence committed by a group and carries a prison sentence of up to two years. “An investigation conducted by the Ministry of Internal Affairs established that on October 14, 2026, at a restaurant in Tbilisi, Vakhtang Zhvania (a.k.a. Vato Kipiani), Avtandil Bilanishvili and Shota Kipiani physically assaulted the victim, who suffered physical pain,” the Prosecutor’s Office of Georgia’s October 15 statement said. All three detainees are exercising their right to remain silent, their lawyer, Marika Pkhaladze, told Interpressnews on October 16. Pkhaladze said she would not comment on the case at this stage, given her clients’ position. Kipiani, 47, has been linked to Georgia’s criminal underworld in media reports for years. According to RFE/RL’s Georgian service, he reportedly has multiple prior criminal convictions and was last detained in Georgia in 2021 at Tbilisi International Airport after being expelled from Ukraine. In 2020, prosecutors also reportedly accused Kipiani of failed attempts at organizing the murder of the Peikrishvili brothers, described in media reports as criminal authority figures, from Ukraine. Bilanishvili is the son of Kako Bilanishvili, 75, who media reports also describe as a criminal authority. Bilanishvili first drew wider public attention in 2019, when the Interior Ministry questioned him in connection with the death of 19-year-old footballer Giorgi Shakarashvili . The ministry later said Bilanishvili did not appear in the video footage examined in the case, according to the RFE/RL. Bilanishvili has been previously reported in Georgian media as a friend of Bera Ivanishvili. Georgian opposition-leaning channels have previously circulated photos of them together on social media. Their relationship has not been independently established. An important change will soon be made to global timekeeping that aims to prevent potential infrastructure failures akin to the Y2K bug scare. On Thursday, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) voted to scrap the leap second, an ad hoc time adjustment that’s occasionally added so tracked time standards mirror the Earth’s real (and inconsistent) rotation.
BIPM members previously agreed in 2022 to cease using leap seconds on or before 2035, but this is now being expedited to take effect on May 20th next year, aligning with World Metrology Day. There’s an unprecedented reason for its retirement being brought forward: changes to the Earth’s rotation may soon require timekeepers to subtract time instead of adding it in order to keep astronomical time in line with atomic time. This has never been attempted before, and there are concerns that doing so could wreak havoc on critical infrastructure that relies on time synchronization.
Those fears aren’t unfounded given Foursquare, Reddit, LinkedIn, Yelp , and many other tech platforms have suffered outages in the past when leap seconds have been added. Companies including Meta, Google, Microsoft, and Amazon have all supported efforts to scrap the system. Following the BIPM vote, timekeepers will instead switch to using “leap hours,” allowing atomic and astronomical time to gradually drift apart until an entire hour needs to be added — which isn’t expected to happen for around 3,000 years.
