title: Leonardo DRS wins place on US counter drone contract
body: Leonardo DRS has been awarded an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract with a ceiling of 500 million dollars and a three-year period of performance by Joint Interagency Task Force 401, giving it the right to compete for orders to field counter drone sensing equipment to American forces, according to the company. The arrangement covers the rapid delivery of integrated counter uncrewed aircraft system sensing capabilities supporting force protection and low altitude air defence, with task orders competed over the life of the contract. John Baylouny, president and chief executive officer of Leonardo DRS, said: “Today’s threat environment is evolving faster than ever, and our customers need proven capabilities delivered at operational speed. This JIATF IDIQ positions DRS to accelerate the delivery of integrated C-UAS sensing technologies through rapid fielding of operationally relevant capabilities that help protect forces and strengthen low-altitude air defense as new threats emerge.” Max Cohen, senior vice president and general manager at the Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies business unit, said: “Our counter UAS and air defense radars have demonstrated proven detection, tracking, and force protection performance in operational environments. We design, manufacture, and deliver combat-proven sensing systems at speed, and we’re ready now to support JIATF with mission-ready expeditionary radar capability that can be fielded rapidly as operational needs for C-UAS evolve.” The award is one of ten made under an effort the American side calls Domestic Shield, aimed at protecting prioritised military facilities and assets inside the United States from drones. Combined ceilings across the ten run to roughly 4.15 billion dollars. Seven firms, including RADA Technologies, hold awards at the 500 million dollar level, alongside Allen Control Systems, Digital Force Technologies, DroneShield, Napatree Technology, SRC and L3Harris WESCAM. Echodyne and PVP Advanced EO Systems hold 250 million dollar awards and SmartShooter 150 million. The task force is directed by Brigadier General Matt Ross. Brent Ingraham, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology, said the multi-vendor marketplace enforces strict open architecture standards, which is the mechanism intended to let new sensors and effectors be swapped in as the threat changes. Orders under the arrangement have already started moving. SRC received a first delivery order worth 10.24 million dollars for one Gryphon R1440 and two R1540 radars with integration, installation, support and training. RADA came to Leonardo DRS through the merger with the Israeli radar maker RADA Electronic Industries in 2021, and its compact active electronically scanned array radars are widely used for short range air defence and counter rocket, artillery and mortar work, including on American vehicle-mounted systems. Leonardo DRS is the American arm of the Italian group Leonardo and trades on Nasdaq. The post Leonardo DRS wins place on US counter drone contract first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: A Surfacing Strategy: Chinese Unconventional Oceanic Warfare
body:
The evolution of maritime warfare has largely moved in expanding the form of conflict and the direction of it. Originating from largely surface conflict and eventually amphibious assaults, maritime conflict shifted to expanded domains, attacks from below by submarines and above by aircraft carriers. However, in the continued evolution of maritime conflict since World War II, various new technologies and strategies have shifted the way war is conducted, as well as preparations for war. This is reflected most clearly in the case of China and Chinese maritime expansion. Although it began and evolved by replicating traditional naval strategy, adopted from Soviet Union systems and adapted for Chinese needs and limitations, it has since evolved dramatically to employ a vast array of unconventional methods.
This article will analyze these unconventional methods, focusing centrally on China’s evolving systems and strategies, while also drawing parallels to other unconventional strategies of other nations. That said, this article is centrally focused on Chinese maritime strategy evolution and its ramifications. These tools, by examining an undercurrent of strategy applied to different facets of the undersea domain, establish an argument on Beijing’s military-civil infrastructure, through research vessels, cargo fleets, fishing boats, and autonomous drones. In such a way, this infrastructure operates without acting as a clear and present threat or exigency for war; rather, it functions simply as an inconvenience or mild concern, one which becomes increasingly threatening, despite not acting as an obviously military entity. The article is in turn divided into key sections, focused on military-civil fusion, submarine strategies, the role of unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs), and anchor dragging.
The underwater domain has seen a disproportionate advancement in large part due to its modern nature. Submarines are highly technical weapons of war, and as a result, see the most significant growth and unconventional adaptations. China’s newest submarine, the Type 095 , is also referred to as a sail-less submarine because of its unique proportions, designed to be swifter and stealthier. These are, in fact, two separate hulls under parallel development rather than a single design: satellite imagery placed the Type 095 fitting out at the Bohai shipyard in Huludao in February 2026, sporting a conventional sail and a distinctive X-form rudder, while a separate, still-unnamed vessel of roughly 120 meters surfaced independently at Jiangnan Shipyard near Shanghai that June, evidence Beijing is now running simultaneous next-generation attack-submarine programs across at least two yards. By reducing noise, it is able to better avoid acoustic detection systems, such as those employed by the U.S. and Japan’s ‘Fish Hook’ detection system , specifically surrounding the First Island Chain.
This development has followed a striking increase in Chinese submarine production, including a 2+1 production of nuclear attack submarines per year . The undersea domain is not limited to submarines specifically; however, for example, the mapping and data collection of the ocean floor work to enable submarine piloting. His data has been gathered throughout the Indo-Pacific region as well as the Arctic, through military-civil fusion doctrine , established by Xi Jinping as a national strategy, and has seen systematic incorporation. UUVs in particular have been deployed by Chinese vessels to map the seafloor, under the International Seabed Authority’s designation; however, these UUVs were found to spend only about 6% of their time in these designated zones . Additionally, a majority of these vessels were found to be tied to state companies and were reported to have conducted suspicious activity. Such activity includes mapping undersea cable networks, potentially for sabotage purposes, as well as UUV data collection near the U.S. Pacific Submarine Fleet’s homeport in Guam .
This data collected under a scientific and civil guise has been reported to have been communicated with Chinese state systems such as the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN). Such data gathering under a civilian guise has been reflected in other reports, such as Chinese shipping systems, as recently as September 2026, wherein COSCO was accused of surveillance while transporting cargo. While the COSCO case has been denied publicly, the expansion of Chinese trade in the Arctic draws attention to such possibilities of espionage undertaken through trade, the very same trade which is expanding uniquely and without competition into the Arctic. These Arctic expeditions were preceded by years of icebreaker data recording . Such icebreakers are utilized with the technology required to map the saefloor and collect data to enable submarine piloting in the region. Buoys have been deployed with recording infrastructure to collect data in the Arctic, which has raised concern among Canadian officials .
Anchor dragging serves as a form of deep-sea sabotage unique to Russia and China, corresponding with seabed mapping. The maps of the seafloor enable a surgical strike specifically on undersea communications cables, such as those conducted in the Baltic and Taiwan . Anchor dragging and GUGI operations are unique because they specifically create kinetic conflict between nations with plausible deniability, and thereby not sparking any wars, while still acting in offensive operations.
There is also the case of shadow fleets to skirt sanctions, trade route chokepoints, Chinese sponsorship of pirates, fisherman harassment, the Batanes issues, so forth. The tools utilized by China rest not within traditional means of war but instead flow into a system of gray-zone maritime strategy adopted by Russia and China alike, to avoid open war. Through habituation, the subtle encroachment of Chinese vessels in waters around Taiwan, the Batans, and Alaska has slowly become accepted; Chinese actions, while never outright tolerated, have become increasingly accepted.
Russia’s shadow fleet illustrates such a case: after sanctions barred Russia’s traditional shipping fleets, the nation utilized other commercial ships for strategic ends. The assembled fleet is roughly 400 to 600 aging tankers, a range CSIS has independently tracked , which continue to transport the majority of Russia’s seaborne crude outside the reach of Western price caps, insurance regimes, and, of course, sanctions. These vessels sail under the guise of different nations, through shell-company ownership, and often without identification transponders- something paralleled in China’s expansion in the Arctic. China has also employed vessels without “functioning” transponders to deliver goods to the Arctic LNG 2, and reiterates the notion of commercial shipping as strategy.
The Shadow Fleet, as it’s come to be known, serves as an economic lifeline for the Kremlin as well as a weapon of war with no clear national association. The Eagle S. is a tanker flagged under the Cook Islands and linked to the shadow fleet; however, it was seized by Finnish authorities after dragging its anchor for 66 miles across the Gulf of Finland in December of 2024. This anchor dragging severed the Estlink 2 power cable as well as a number of telecommunications cables; another merchant vessel under the Hong Kong flag served the Baltic connector gas pipeline in October 2023. The Chinese-owned Yi Peng 3 also severed cables between Sweden and Lithuania in November 2024, dragging an anchor for nearly 300 kilometers. CBS News’s 60 Minutes has documented this Eagle S-Balticconnector-Yi Peng 3 sequence in detail, tracing each vessel’s anchor-drag track via satellite data. Russia retains a Main Directorate of Underwater Research, an operational force tied to a variety of undersea sabotage operations and missions, such as anchor dragging. Known by the Russian acronym GUGI, the directorate answers directly to the Russian Ministry of Defense, as opposed to participating in the Navy chain of command, as well as operating a vessel, the Yantar, equipped with submersibles capable of reaching the depths of undersea cables.
Western defense officials have tracked the Yantar loitering over transatlantic cable junctions from Ireland to the Baltic, per UK Ministry of Defence and Royal Navy monitoring reports , noting that the submersible remote-controlled vehicles are explicitly capable of tapping cables for intelligence, as well as laying explosives upon them for future sabotage. GUGI’s vessels deliberately survey and manipulate the seabed without an incident of any deliberate attack, under the guise of research and science, thus insulating any actions from sparking conflict. In other words, Russia’s strategy of a shadow fleet and research vessels conducting operations is an adoption of an existing Chinese strategy of military-civil fusion.
China’s undersea cable incidents work in tandem with the Russian operations- in 2025, a Togo-flagged vessel, the Hong Tai 58, crewed by Chinese personnel, loitered near the Taiwan-Penghu No. 3 cable, before releasing its anchor and serving the aforementioned cable. Taiwanese authorities detained the vessel and its captain in the aftermath of the incident. January of the same year saw a Cameroon-marked vessel, the Shunxin39, cut a cable near Keelung after loitering nearby, which Taiwan’s coast guard confirmed to be Chinese-owned despite its flag of convenience. Operations that rest just below the threshold to spark conflict, but work to erode and sabotage Western systems, degrading Western influence, power and regional capability.
China has employed commercial ships for espionage operations as well, with a Reuters 2026 report claiming that COSCO, the state-owned Chinese shipping conglomerate, has operated signals-intelligence equipment aboard its vessels, and thus collected military communications around the U.S., Europe, and throughout Asia, which U.S. officials confirmed to Reuters on the condition of anonymity. Correspondingly, the Pentagon had previously added COSCO to a list of companies linked to the Chinese military in January of 2025, per the Department of Defense’s Section 1260H designation ,- the same year a U.S. Naval War College report concluded the PLA was utilizing China’s commercial fleets for intelligence. The Naval War College’s China Maritime Studies Institute detailed the fishing fleet’s intelligence role specifically , identifying trained specialists embedded within militia crews. China’s 2017 National Intelligence Law (Article 7, per China Law Translate’s official English translation ) obliges Chinese state firms to assist state intelligence work when asked, in part fueling military-civil fusion doctrine, and providing Beijing with endless strategic assets for use across the world.
China’s maritime militia operates in the South China Sea to project state power through civilian forces; it is power projection through influence that is present, if in a non-evidently violently. The People’s Armed Forces Maritime Militia act as civilian operators under governmental action, and utilize civilian boats, based primarily out of Hainan, which harass rival claimants and foreign naval vessels. As such, Beijing is not acting as a provocative, aggressive nation, but rather a nation that utilizes proxy forces, without sparking conflict.
Philippine officials have documented repeated incidents in which Chinese Coast Guard vessels, side by side with maritime militia boats, weaponized water cannons against Filipino fishing boats near Scarborough Shoal in December of 2025. The Philippines’ Batanes Islands have also seen increased Chinese aggression through diplomatic actions, as well as the Armed Forces of the Philippines has tracked a persistent presence of Chinese research vessels working around the Bashi Channel, akin to the Chinese UUV operations near Guam. UUVs, are alone, outside of their data collection, act as novel weapons of war- seen through AUVs and remote-controlled UUVs, or gliders. These systems include the AJX002, an extra-large UUV or XLUUV, which was synthesized for the strategic purposes of minelaying, particularly in and around the First Island Chain. The undersea drones that were functioning primarily for surveillance have been designed for military and destructive purposes. The AJX002 has been paired with the HSU100, a reconnaissance variant of an XLUUV fitted with retractable masts, to turn the vessel into a glider design from an AUV, for long-range intelligence-gathering expeditions. Beijing has also experimented with at least five XLUUV designs; several are capable of ferrying torpedoes and mines across the ocean. These play a kinetic role in the prior wall of intelligence that detected submarines and underwater actions through the Underwater Great Wall, a network of seabed sensors, now utilizing long-range gliders, autonomous UUVs, and newly defended by military UUVs. The civilian seabed-mapping campaign using UUVs aforementioned only strengthens this notion of military-civil fusion, particularly utilized by UUVs and enabled by AI technology.
Additionally, this minelaying strategy, if deployed by a “research” expedition around Taiwan, would lead to a critical blockade crucial to overtaking the island nation. Should these mines be planted weeks or months in advance around chokepoints or ports, or planted subtly by UUVs, China would hold a keen advantage in the waters around the strait and island. While the captains of vessels can be detained and prosecuted, uncrewed drones, if unflagged or operating under a guise, such legal action cannot be successfully prosecuted.
Overall, the strategies of submarines, anchor-dragging, sanctions-evading, maritime militias, and autonomous underwater drones create an overarching image of Chinese unconventional means of warfare. While each act and method is uniquely deniable and non-escalatory by design, the culmination of each method of power projection creates a strong Chinese presence in the Indo-Pacific and Arctic regions, without a single warship present. Tankers with drag anchors across critical cables fly under false flags, while research vessels operate with designated permits, and a system of undersea infrastructure designed for submarine enabling and detection alike. Each development in this system of maritime power projection builds upon a structure that has already, evidently, been established. In such a way, the slow and subtle habituation to Chinese operations in the world’s oceans, through a civilian cover with military means, establishes a status quo wherein Chinese operations are capable from the Baltic to the Bashi Channel.
Western and allied responses have been primarily reactive, at the time of writing. NATO’s Baltic Sentry was launched in January 2025 to better patrol the undersea infrastructure in the Baltic, in large part a response to the Russian cable-cutting. However, there is no standing international posture to counter gray-zone maritime activity as a unified strategy, as it appears to be. Such an asymmetry of action- the limited responses of the West compared to wide options for Chinese engagement- is a critical design of the unconventional strategy. As Beijing’s own investment shifts from crewed research vessels toward uncrewed platforms like the AJX002, the political cost of coercion will only continue to fall, and the window for building deterrence around attribution, rather than around the presence of a detainable crew, is closing.
Jack Lindstrom is a graduate researcher from the University of California, San Diego, pursuing a Master’s in International Affairs. He is also a junior researcher for the Mackinder Forum, where he conducts research on great power strategy and historical shifts of international competition.

title: Joyce Bawah Mogtari says Obaasima Conference should help women connect and learn
body: Senior Presidential Advisor and Aide to President John Dramani Mahama, Joyce Bawah Mogtari, has called for the Obaasima Conference to serve as a space where women can openly discuss their leadership experiences, learn from one another and build relationships that strengthen their professional and personal development. In a Facebook post on Friday, October 16, she reflected on a conversation with former Electoral Commission Chairperson Charlotte Osei, whose account of the challenges of being a woman in leadership prompted her to consider the value of shared experiences and mutual support. Ms Bawah Mogtari said the discussion highlighted the pressures women may face, from rumours and workplace prejudice to colleagues who question their ability to handle responsibilities. She said creating opportunities for women to discuss such experiences openly could help them find practical ways to navigate difficult working environments and encourage one another. She identified the importance of finding a supportive circle of people who will offer honest counsel, stand against unfair treatment and celebrate each other’s achievements. According to Ms Bawah Mogtari, that spirit of connection and solidarity should be central to the Obaasima Conference, enabling women not only to exchange ideas but also to build lasting networks of support.

title: Why the SANDF should consider drones for battlefield resupply
body:
The fighting around Sake and Goma in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in January 2025 brought a basic logistics problem into sharp focus. Troops can only remain effective for as long as ammunition, medical supplies and other essential stores continue to reach them. Once those links are disrupted, the value of weapons, vehicles and even well-trained personnel begins to diminish.
This became evident as M23 forces moved towards Sake. The Southern African Development Community Mission in the DRC’s (SAMIDRC’s) main operating base came under increasing pressure, while Defence Minister Angie Motshekga later told Parliament that the position had effectively been surrounded by the advancing forces. South African troops remained in contact for several days under artillery and ground attack. Fourteen South African National Defence Force (SANDF) members were killed during the fighting around Sake and Goma.
Resupply soon became part of the problem. Reports at the time pointed to growing pressure on ammunition stocks and increasing difficulty in moving reinforcements and supplies by air. A resupply flight reportedly reached Goma on 26 January, but the worsening security situation and the loss of normal access to the airport made further support increasingly difficult.
The problem did not end when the most intense fighting subsided. By March 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa described the SANDF position in Sake and Goma as “precarious”. Negotiations with the forces controlling the surrounding area included the movement of food and the provision of water and electricity. Sustaining the force had become part of the operational problem.
It would be an exaggeration to suggest that drones could have resolved what happened around Sake. The circumstances were far more complex than a simple failure of resupply. The experience nevertheless raises a legitimate question: what alternatives does the SANDF have when roads are cut, airfields are unavailable, and the normal means of moving supplies become too dangerous or cannot be used?
One option worth examining is a dedicated unmanned resupply capability for the final leg of the logistics chain.
The requirement need not begin with a large or particularly sophisticated aircraft. A more useful starting point may be a platform capable of carrying between 25 and 50 kg over a radius of approximately 50 to 100 km, while operating without a prepared runway.
Those figures are modest when compared with the capacity of a truck or transport helicopter. That is precisely the point. A cargo UAV should not be expected to replace either.
Bulk logistics will continue to depend on trucks, transport aircraft and helicopters. Fuel, water, large ammunition loads and the daily requirements of a deployed formation cannot realistically be sustained by small, unmanned aircraft. The potential value of a drone lies in moving items that weigh comparatively little but are urgently needed.
Ammunition is an obvious example, but the requirement extends beyond it. Medical stores, blood products, radio batteries, communication equipment and specialised components may all become critical if a unit is isolated. A broken component weighing a few kilograms may disable an important piece of equipment. The replacement part does not require a truck. It requires a reliable way of getting from the logistics base to the unit that needs it.
This is where the idea of the “last tactical mile” becomes useful.
Imagine a forward position 60 km from a secure base. Under normal circumstances, the distance presents little difficulty. Once the road has been mined, observed or occupied by hostile forces, the same 60 km becomes a serious logistics problem. A helicopter might still reach the position, but using a crewed aircraft to deliver a relatively small load could expose people and an expensive platform to unnecessary risk. There may also be nowhere suitable to land.
A vertical take-off and landing UAV changes the options available to the commander. A fixed-wing VTOL design could depart from a small logistics area, fly efficiently over the required distance and deliver directly to a forward position without the need for a runway. A modular cargo arrangement would allow the load to change according to circumstances.
The case for such a system becomes stronger when viewed as a fleet rather than a single aircraft. Several smaller UAVs could be dispersed between logistics nodes. Mechanical failure or the loss of one aircraft would reduce capacity, but it would not necessarily stop the operation. The personnel implications are also different. Losing an unmanned cargo aircraft is not comparable with losing a helicopter and its crew.
The concept is not beyond South Africa’s existing technological base.
Local companies already work across a wide spectrum of unmanned aviation. ALTI produces compact VTOL aircraft. Denel has accumulated considerable experience through the Seeker programme. Milkor has developed the considerably larger Milkor 380, while Paramount introduced the V-Raven VTOL platform at AAD 2026. The CSIR-supported Aerospace Industry Support Initiative has also assisted Kusasa Aerospace in developing a drone payload delivery system.
None of these systems is the answer to the SANDF logistics problem. They were designed for different roles and occupy different parts of the UAV market. Their significance lies in what they reveal about the domestic industrial base. South Africa already has experience in unmanned flight, composites, avionics, VTOL technology and systems integration.
The missing capability appears to sit somewhere between the smaller surveillance aircraft and the larger military UAVs.
That gap deserves investigation before any decision is made about procurement.
The SANDF could begin with a field trial built around a simple logistics problem. Establish a supply point, position forward elements at different distances and require participating systems to move representative loads between them. Range and payload would matter, but so would the time needed to prepare the aircraft for another flight. A system that carries an impressive load but spends hours on the ground between sorties may prove less useful than a smaller aircraft that can fly repeatedly.
Maintenance would also have to be considered from the outset. So would manpower.
A cargo drone intended for field deployment should not require a large technical team every time it moves. If operating the aircraft creates another complex supply and maintenance burden, part of its advantage is lost. The same applies to specialised launch equipment or fixed infrastructure. The attraction of the concept lies partly in its ability to operate from austere locations.
Trials would also need to move beyond ideal conditions.
Electronic warfare is now an ordinary feature of military operations. GPS interference disrupted communications and hostile counter-UAS systems cannot be treated as unusual circumstances. A logistics aircraft that depends entirely on uninterrupted satellite navigation and a permanent data link may be of limited value once it enters a contested environment.
Its behaviour after losing contact would therefore matter. So would its ability to follow a pre-programmed route and navigate when external systems become unreliable.
South African conditions introduce further practical questions. Heat and altitude affect aircraft performance. Wind and rain may reduce the load that can be carried or the distance that can be flown. Night operations introduce another set of requirements. These factors should be tested in the field rather than assumed from manufacturers’ specifications.
There is also no reason to ignore the aircraft’s vulnerabilities. Cargo UAVs can be shot down. They can be jammed, detected or forced off course. Operating drones alongside artillery, helicopters, and other aircraft creates an airspace management problem that would have to be addressed. A logistics UAV is not a means of avoiding all the difficulties associated with battlefield resupply.
Its usefulness lies in providing an alternative when the usual options are limited.
For that reason, the SANDF should first define the problem it wants the industry to solve. The initial requirement could remain relatively simple: move a militarily useful load over a tactically useful distance, operate without a runway, keep the ground-support requirement small and retain enough autonomy to function when communications are unreliable.
Industry could then demonstrate what is achievable.
This approach would also avoid designing a procurement programme around a particular aircraft before the operational requirement has been properly tested. Payload, range and configuration should emerge from experimentation rather than from assumptions about what the final system ought to look like.
The fighting around Sake deserves to be studied from this perspective. It was not only a combat action. It also provides a recent example of what happens when a deployed force finds its normal lines of supply increasingly constrained.
The SANDF may face similar circumstances again. Peace-support operations can place relatively small contingents far from established bases. Border deployments involve long distances and difficult terrain. Disaster relief may require supplies to reach communities after roads and bridges have failed.
In none of these situations would a cargo drone replace the existing logistics system. Its contribution would be narrower, but potentially significant.
Sometimes the decisive requirement is not another truckload of supplies. It is 25 or 50 kg of the right supplies reaching the right position before the existing logistics system can get there.
Sake provides a strong enough case for the SANDF to determine whether it should have that option.
Prof Dewald Venter from the Vaal University of Technology is Associate Professor in Tourism Management and Military Heritage Researcher.

title: Press review: Russian asset grab back on EU agenda and Starlink or no, Ukraine to fight on
body:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. This week's EU summit returns to the idea of seizing Russian assets; facing threats of being cut off from Starlink, Ukraine makes other plans; and what is the future of the US Green Card Lottery. These stories topped Friday's newspaper headlines in Russia.
The EU opened a two-day summit in Brussels on October 15. For the first time since the special military operation began, the Europeans postponed discussions on Ukraine to the second day of the event as they decided to discuss the European Union’s new budget for 2028-2034 first. Earlier, the European Commission (EC) proposed a bloated budget of €1.76 trillion.
Meanwhile, European auditors are ringing alarm bells about the growing debt, which could climb to €1 trillion by 2027 and cause a "hole" in the current budget. Moreover, all EU economies are struggling amid the energy crisis around the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
The problem is also aggravated by Kiev's growing demands. According to the draft budget, the EC proposed allocations of up to €88.8 billion for 2028-2034.
However, there is no extra money, and the EU is now coming back to the idea of using frozen Russian assets by transferring them to a special European structure to finance Ukraine further down the road. "This idea is being considered and revisited," French member of the European Parliament Thierry Mariani told Izvestia. "Belgium, which holds the bulk of these funds, dissuaded its partners from putting that idea into practice in December, and the EU eventually agreed a €90 billion loan. Today, Kiev insists that this issue be reconsidered," he noted. "As regards Belgium, it considers this idea crazy as Moscow could immobilize European assets in response," Mariani warned.
Today, the likelihood of using these assets for a loan to Ukraine is extremely low. Such a step would require absolute unanimity within the European Union, Mikhail Vedernikov, a senior researcher at the Institute of Europe of the Russian Academy of Sciences, explained to Izvestia. However, some leaders, including Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, have openly opposed this initiative and promised to block it. Nevertheless, Slovakia will hold an early election in 2027, with Fico’s positions assessed as quite weak. If left-liberal politicians who support the policy course pursued by Brussels come to power in Bratislava, a decision on assets may well be made in a year, the expert concluded.
Apart from Russia’s assets, European bureaucrats will discuss additional restrictions on Moscow. According to Politico, the EU is planning to call for more restrictions on Russian oil exports in the summit communique. Earlier, Brussels approved a 22nd sanctions package, blacklisting hundreds of new Russian individuals, lenders and oil tankers. However, the EU’s sanctions policy cannot affect Russia’s policy on Ukraine, Mariani argued. "This shows that this sanctions policy does not work and only leads to impoverishing the population," the politician maintained.
Tensions between Kiev and Washington will seemingly escalate after Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky said that the Ukrainian armed forces will continue to target Russian oil refineries. Earlier, according to media reports, the Americans warned Kiev that the United States would in that case "immediately" cancel intelligence sharing, cut off the Starlink satellite internet system, and halt military aid.
Even as this has not happened yet, the possibility remains, observers say. Therefore, the Zelensky regime is apparently preparing to wage combat against Russia without support from the United States, relying on NATO’s European allies and the EU instead. This slightly increases Russia’s chances of achieving the objectives of its special military operation and defeating the enemy faster. Whether things progress that way - only time will tell.
A recent remark from SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has been making the rounds in the media and with pundits, after the billionaire called on Zelensky to resign, otherwise "the slaughter" would continue. The call came after almost identical statements from US President Donald Trump.
"It is Musk who owns the rights to Starlink, therefore he can de facto influence Ukraine’s defensive capabilities," retired Lieutenant-General Yury Netkachev, a military expert, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. According to him, with the diesel deal and ambitions to ease sanctions on Russia, Trump has provided Moscow with an opportunity not only to improve its economic situation but also buttress its position in negotiations to end the conflict.
However, Netkachev warned, one should not be lulled into a false sense of security by this "friendly" position of the current US administration, for Trump’s foreign policy options could be significantly curtailed following the Congressional election, and the US political elite may return to supporting Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Kiev's intelligence situation isn't all lost without the US. "Two-thirds of the intelligence received by Ukraine come from European countries, primarily France," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told France Inter. According to him, among other things, European countries share satellite images that Kiev uses to detect targets. His remark came amid reports that the US has threatened to limit information sharing because of strikes on Russian oil refineries. Barrot also said the Europeans provide the bulk of support for Ukraine. The EU has recently transferred €6 billion to Kiev, he added.
The US State Department was ordered to reopen the Green Card Lottery by October 18 and publicly announce the registration dates on its official platforms. The order came from a US federal judge in California, according to the court’s database updated on Wednesday night. Registration will remain open for 30 days, in line with the court order. In other words, anyone who wants to can enter the 2027 drawing.
The issue reverberated after the Trump administration formally refused to open registration citing delays, even as back in November 2025 the US Department of State shared plans to reopen registration for the 2027 fiscal year running from October 1, 2026 on its website.
It is worth noting that the Green Card Lottery is a mandatory process, as Congress authorizes the allocation of up to 55,000 such documents annually to foreign citizens. However, only a portion of all available Green Cards are distributed through the lottery, not all of them. According to the US Department of State’s website, 20.8 million people applied for the 2026 program, from which 129,516 individuals were selected. Among Africans registered for the DV-2026 Diversity Visa Program, the bulk was from Algeria (5,457 applicants), Afghanistan led all Asian countries with 4,200, the Bahamas - North America with 23, 599 Australians led the way for Oceania, and 1,596 Peruvians from South America. Russia led all European countries with 5,510 registered and selected applicants, followed by Ukraine with 5,283.
Even as the DV-2026 program was mandated by federal law enacted by Congress, the Trump administration effectively delayed the start of the registration process, Marina Chernykh, a research fellow at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, explained to Vedomosti. According to her, the California court ruled that the US State Department provide an opportunity for applications to be submitted, whereas the federal government insisted that it is no longer possible to carry out the program as originally intended now that the established deadlines have passed. The Trump administration has the right to appeal the ruling at the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Filing an appeal would not automatically nullify the court ruling as a separate court decision will be required for that. The case could eventually be taken to the US Supreme Court, the expert noted.
"And the US Supreme Court is highly likely to rule in Trump’s favor as the majority of judges there are conservative. At the same time, it cannot be assumed that the administration can simply ignore the ruling as it was handed down by a court of first instance," the expert concluded.
The agreement on partnership and cooperation concluded between Russia and the European Union signed more than three decades ago makes little practical sense after Brussels openly declared Russia its opponent and adversary, said participants in a round table discussion at the Federation Council on Thursday.
The EU has essentially transformed into an anti-Russian military bloc, Rossiyskaya Gazeta quoted Grigory Karasin, chairman of the upper chamber’s Committee on International Affairs, as saying. There have been statements from European politicians, including Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski or European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, about preparations for war with Russia in 2029-2030.
The matter is not limited to rhetoric only as Sweden and Finland have joined NATO, EU countries are sharply increasing their defense expenditure, military construction has been expedited, and exercises to simulate scenarios of a blockade of the Kaliningrad Region and Russia’s Baltic seaports are held near national borders.
Karasin also pointed to the EU’s expansion plans at the expense of Moldova, Ukraine and Armenia. At that, the senator emphasized, Russia is not threatening European countries nor is it planning to do so, while the European people seem to agree, as evidenced by the rising popularity of opposition parties in Germany and France.
The EU has undergone a major evolution, Federation Council Deputy Speaker Konstantin Kosachev argued. Originally a purely economic association, the EU is increasingly mulling militarization, including its own army. "Never before has there been a single international organization built on regional economic integration that set establishing an army as its goal. This is a first," Kosachev noted. "The idea of militarization has completely consumed the minds of European politicians, who have also embraced extreme Russophobic rhetoric," he added.
Kosachev commented on the Partnership and Cooperation Agreement, which was signed in 1994 and entered into force in 1997. He singled out Article 55 as the most objectionable part of the document which envisaged the unilateral harmonization of Russian laws with European ones. "Thank God, this article--along with all the other provisions of the agreement--has been frozen," he said. The agreement’s initial ten-year term expired in 2007 and it has been automatically renewed on an annual basis ever since until one of the parties provides written notice to the contrary. "It has lost any practical meaning. The EU has openly declared us its adversary and enemy, while the agreement envisages partnership and cooperation," Kosachev maintained.
African countries are facing electricity shortages even as they have enough oil and gas and capabilities to generate power from renewables. Key obstacles include a lack of capital and grid weaknesses. Russian technology could be in demand in the fields of nuclear-and natural gas-based power generation, hydropower and energy-related engineering, but prospects here depend on project economics and the specific needs of certain countries. Russian and African experts told Vedomosti which areas of partnership can yield a long-term effect and what has prevented a transformation from individual supplies to complex projects.
Today, African countries need to supply electricity to a growing population, their industries, transport, and digital economy, Alexey Maslov, a professor and director of the Institute of Asian and African Studies at Lomonosov Moscow State University, noted. While many of these countries possess gas, oil, and coal reserves, along with potential for hydropower, solar, and wind energy generation, the mere availability of such resources does not guarantee a stable supply, he argued.
According to Nikita Panin, an expert at the analytical department at the HSE Centre for African Studies, countries with a developed industrial base need large-scale power generation. Meanwhile, the need for localized power generation is already reflected in projects currently under discussion between Russian companies and their African partners. There is no universal solution for the continent as the specifics of each country require an individual approach, he explained.
As African partners view it, technology transfer should be accompanied with the development of local competences, Anna Abaho, a senior lecturer in international relations and security research at Nkumba University in Uganda, told Vedomosti. She linked Russian-Ugandan cooperation to industrial electrification, food production, irrigation and refrigeration of agricultural products. The country needs engineers and technical specialists capable of maintaining the equipment for that, she said.
A transition to purer energy does not mean Africa will abandon traditional sources in the next few years. The continent is expanding access to electricity amid the rising demand from industries, transport, and cities. For this reason, a variety of technologies, ranging from gas and hydropower to solar generation, energy storage, and nuclear projects, will be needed in the energy mix, Maslov argued.

title: What is the US Army doing in Panama? A bit of everything.
body: Muted American flag patches on the right shoulders of camouflage-clad men and women in the jungle are one sign of an expanding partnership between the U.S. and Panama. American optometrists in the country’s Darién Province are another. U.S. military salvage and dive teams training near the Panama Canal offer a third. As Washington shifts its attention toward the Western Hemisphere, a reinvigorated jungle school is just one part of the evolving U.S. military presence in Panama . More than 20 years after the U.S. turned over its bases to the Central American country, the partnership offers a glimpse of what the Pentagon’s renewed focus on its own hemisphere could mean on the ground. “The Western Hemisphere is now the priority hemisphere,” Col. Jacob White, deputy commander of Joint Security Cooperation Group-Panama (JSCG-P), said in an interview from the unit’s Panamanian headquarters . “We want to move faster and be more present down in this hemisphere.” Decades after the U.S. launched a deeply polarizing invasion to topple Panamanian dictator Manuel Noriega, the disparate missions are part of the U.S.’s increasingly prioritized relationship with the country that hosts the only land bridge connecting the two American continents and the only waterway connecting the Atlantic and Pacific. The Trump administration, and thus the Pentagon, has elevated “defense of the U.S. Homeland” to the highest national security priority, downgrading China — which previously took the top spot — as a threat. In April 2025, the U.S. and Panama announced an agreement to counter Chinese influence in the region and secure the Panama Canal, laying the foundation for other joint activities. According to Henry Ziemer, a fellow with the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Panama never stopped being important to the U.S. military. It has the strategically important Panama Canal and Darién Gap, and the country sits at the intersection of some of the Trump administration’s major priorities: canal security, migration and drug trafficking. Over the last year, Ziemer said, Panama’s importance has increased “as we’ve seen supply chain disruptions at other critical waterways like the Strait of Hormuz.” Roughly 5% to 6% of global trade passes through the waterway, with approximately 70% of that traffic passing to or from the United States. “For many subsequent administrations and decades, I think the United States took [its] eye off this neighborhood, off the Western Hemisphere,” said Kevin Marino Cabrera, the U.S. Ambassador to Panama, emphasizing that developments in the region have direct impacts for the U.S. “You can’t talk about migration without talking about Panama,” he said, referring to the Darién Gap, which at its peak saw more than half a million migrant crossings per year. Panamanian service members also report drug smuggling through the narrow strip of land. From the U.S.’s perspective, the “border begins in Panama,” Ziemer said, adding “it’s a lot easier to secure the Isthmus of Panama than it is to secure the whole Southwest land border, right?” Cabrera said the partnership was mutually beneficial, though, as Panama also deals with cartels, drug trafficking and migration issues — though differently than the U.S. “Our plan is to defeat the cartels, to maintain the Darién closed, so that we can secure the U.S. Southern border and keep our communities safe,” he said, adding, “we’re working together with Panama because they have many of the same goals.” Though the gritty terrain of jungle school makes it a highlight of the partnership, the U.S. military’s inroads in Panama extend well beyond the boundaries of Aeronaval Base Cristóbal Colón, where course is housed. Typically a country may host a U.S. Army Civil Affairs team or two — the Army’s special operations forces contingent that connects military forces with civilian populations — but Panama is home to an entire U.S. Civil Affairs company, White said, that works in virtually every district. Those teams, he said, identify gaps in civilian infrastructure, such as dilapidated schools or unsafe bridges. The U.S. has military salvage dive teams operating around the canal and cross-training with Panamanian forces. Engineer soldiers rotate through the country, building out structures for jungle students. Military doctors work alongside Panamanian medical professionals to assist local populations, performing colonoscopies and cataract surgeries. Dentists and optometrists — even veterinarians — rotate through rural parts of the country. White said one of the lessons the U.S. learned during its decades-long wars in Iraq and Afghanistan was that the military cannot quickly create trust. “In a crisis, you simply can’t surge trust,” he said. “And so, being here — present — doing things on the regular with SENAFRONT and SENAN, with the government of Panama — and with their permission to do it — it helps build that trust.” Though Panama does not have a standing Army, SENAFRONT and SENAN are two branches of the Panamanian Public Forces. On a tactical level, Panamanian instructors at the jungle school say the course, which includes Panamanian and U.S. soldiers, makes them feel that, in an emergency, U.S. soldiers would at least grasp how challenging it is to operate in a jungle environment. With terrain different from the U.S.’s Hawaii jungle course, Panama’s environment replicates other jungle biomes where the U.S. may find itself in conflict. The Western Hemisphere, White said, abounds with jungle landscape. But as the U.S. hones its focus on Central and South America, expanded U.S. activity inevitably raises questions about sovereignty. Decrepit military quarters line roads in and out of Aeronaval Base Cristóbal Colón, which the U.S. called Fort Sherman when it occupied it. Most sit abandoned, used only as shady hideaways for jungle instructors between missions. Officials have been adamant that the future does not hold permanent military basing for U.S. troops. White said the U.S. contingent works to uphold the Neutrality Treaty of 1977 — which guarantees the Panama Canal remains neutral and open for ships of all nations to transit peacefully. To do that, he said, the U.S. military is operating “by, with and through the Panamanians.”

title: Agricultural enterprise with Polish capital attacked in Volyn region, killing 1 – official
body:

title: Fincantieri Cuts Steel for Italian Navy’s Final PPA
body: Fincantieri has cut steel for the ninth Multipurpose Patrol Ship (PPA 9) at its Riva Trigoso shipyard, marking the start of construction on the Italian Navy’s final PPA vessel. OCCAR press release On October 15, 2026, the First Steel Cutting Ceremony for the ninth Multipurpose Patrol Ship (PPA 9) was held at Fincantieri’s integrated shipyard in Riva Trigoso, officially marking the commencement of construction of the vessel and a significant milestone for the Programme. The ceremony represents the formal launch of production activities for the ninth unit of the PPA Class, which will become the seventh and final ship delivered to the Italian Navy under the Programme. In accordance with established shipbuilding tradition, the laser cutting machine was ceremonially activated by representatives of the Italian Navy, acting as Customer, OCCAR as Contracting Authority, and FINCANTIERI as Prime Contractor. The event marked the first physical stage in the construction process and underscored the continued cooperation between all Programme stakeholders. Following Contract Amendment No. 10, PPA 9 will be constructed in the Full Combat Configuration, the most advanced and capable variant of the class. Designed to conduct operations across the full spectrum of maritime missions and principal warfare domains, the vessel will incorporate enhanced combat system capabilities to ensure the highest standards of operational readiness, survivability and mission effectiveness. The commencement of construction of PPA 9 demonstrates the continued progress and maturity of the Programme, which remains a cornerstone of the Italian Navy’s fleet renewal effort. To date, five of the seven vessels contracted for delivery to the Marina Militare Italiana, the Italian Navy have entered service, while the sixth unit, PPA 8, is currently under construction. As the seventh and final unit to be delivered under the Programme, PPA 9 represents the culmination of a significant naval procurement initiative, providing the Italian Navy with a highly capable, flexible and technologically advanced platform designed to meet current and future operational requirements. – End – The post Fincantieri Cuts Steel for Italian Navy’s Final PPA appeared first on Naval News .

title: Large uncrewed underwater vehicle launched in Sweden
body:
The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Armed Forces have successfully developed, built, and launched a demonstrator for a large uncrewed underwater vehicle (LUUV).
The demonstrator has progressed from concept to a functional vehicle and completed sea trials, concluding the first phase of the project. The next phase is expected to focus on further developing its capabilities. The results will inform ongoing work on software, sensors and autonomous functions, as well as future product development.
The demonstrator is intended to support the development and evaluation of future underwater capabilities and operate alongside existing naval platforms, including submarines.
Its development has used Saab’s software-centric approach and Autonomous Ocean Core, the company’s autonomous control system for surface and underwater vehicles. The project also draws on Swedish expertise in submarine design and sensor integration.
The LUUV project builds on Saab’s previous work and investments in autonomous underwater systems. It is now led by the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV), in cooperation with the Swedish Armed Forces and Saab. The results will help Swedish authorities assess options for the future acquisition and operational use of autonomous underwater systems.
“This project demonstrates how new technologies can be rapidly translated into practical operational value. The uncrewed underwater vehicle can contribute to increased endurance, enhanced situational awareness and strengthened underwater capabilities. The fact that we have also been able to develop and test the system in such a short timeframe demonstrates the strength of the collaboration between the Swedish Armed Forces, FMV and Saab,” said Mats Wicksell , head of Saab’s business area Naval.

title: One Ukraine out-produced third of EU’s steel. Russian strikes have now cut its output to zero
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine produced no steel at all last month, Oleksandr Kalenkov, president of the Ukrmetalurgprom association, says , according to Ukrainian Radio. Russian missiles have destroyed the blast furnaces at its plants, stopping an industry that ran for more than 150 years. Over its independence, Ukraine smelted more than 42 million tons of steel a year, more than a third of what the entire 27-nation EU produces now. That industry is now in catastrophe: before the war, it accounted for over a third of Ukraine’s exports and up to 12% of GDP, and a month of zero output tears a hole in the entire economy. “What is happening now is not just a hard or critical situation. It is a tragic situation when an industry more than 150 years old produced zero steel last month,” Kalenkov says. The collapse is the end of a long descent, and 15 years ago the sector earned half the country’s foreign currency, Kalenkov notes. Steel remains Ukraine’s second-largest foreign-currency earner, employing more than 70,000 people directly and paying close to $1 billion a year in taxes. A pillar knocked out piece by piece since 2014 The war has chipped at the industry for more than a decade. Ukraine lost about a third of its capacity in 2014, including almost all its coking-coal mines and finally the Pokrovske mine, and in 2022 it lost the Mariupol production site, another 40% of what it then made, he recalls. Even the plants left on government-controlled land have worked in survival mode since. In 2021, the last year before the invasion, the mining and metals complex still accounted for more than a third of all exports and accounted for up to 12% of GDP, rising above 40% of regional output in Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. The strikes that finished the furnaces The decisive blow came from the air. Since August, a huge number of missiles, both ballistic and cruise, have targeted the plants, and practically all the blast furnaces still working were destroyed, he adds.
