title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
body: I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis , and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats. I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it. That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though. I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin. Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?” Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced. Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of. Alcor , a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider. With cryonics, the chances of being reunited with your pet are bordering on zero. Even those who work in the field acknowledge that the stored people and animals are unlikely to be reanimated. As things stand, there is no way to really and truly bring any animal “back.” I miss Peppy. But given the chance, would I stick her in a vat of liquid nitrogen? Or get another cat to give birth to a genetically identical animal? No, I would not. RIP to the one and only Peppy.

title: Love is infrastructure
body: I. Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer. When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress. So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly. A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host. “Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.” “Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times . And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.” Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer. For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring. At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated. “There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.” Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point. “St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.” “I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.” Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty. “Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. I have better things to fuss about. Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.” II. How they came alive Everybody voted all the time. Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St. Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly. A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets. Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.” Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests. But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought. Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.” Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring. She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services. There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city. But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day. Then there was Raeford, a bartender at the Wild Goose Chase in the middle of Gallery Row in St. Barnabas. He also listened to people’s problems from evening until the wee hours, and solutions came to him like clockwork when he woke at noon the next day. He saw St. Barnabas at night, so he knew the unsafe blocks that could use brighter streetlights, the places where hydroelectric jitneys drove too fast at 3 a.m., and the teens who needed an all-ages hangout. He also knew about the fish fry at the Black church in the Uptilt District that kept being disrupted by noxious smoke from the incinerator two blocks away. And the yarn store on the edge of Gallery Row that needed a disabled parking spot for its many customers with mobility issues. People voted with their Quills, usually by saying or typing a short message and maybe including a photo or brief video. Voting was easy by design, and votes were public but anonymized to the point where even a statistics whiz couldn’t tie one vote to a specific person—same as with major elections. The votes went directly to the City Core, which tracked, tabulated, produced reports, and offered solutions with the help of workers in the city government. Trees voted too, thanks to sensors in their bark, and so did birds and squirrels that had eaten special birdseed that monitored their gut flora harmlessly. But votes from humans provided the greatest insight into “quality of life,” that oh-so-nebulous concept, and thus counted the most. There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing. (Other cities in the region operated differently, of course. Like Turnbull City, where instead of expecting residents to volunteer every stray notion, the City Core gathered information via ubiquitous surveillance. Cameras and Quill sniffers, tracking devices on vehicles—the things privacy laws in both Mainspring and St. Barnabas had banned. A city like Turnbull tracked its people to meet their needs without their needing to say anything.) Sandi and Raeford, as two of the people who voted the most, were among the earliest to suspect their cities were developing minds of their own. At first the clues were subtle: Raeford voted about a hazardous sidewalk crack, and instantly the vote had an annotation mentioning the Argentine ant colony under the cement, the local rainfall patterns, and recent trends in skateboard design—much too soon to be the work of a human. Sandi had ideas about the communal compost station on her block, and the Mainspring City Core made subtle adjustments to her proposal. And then it became obvious to anyone who was paying attention, around the same time in both cities. One day, the number of votes nearly doubled in both St. Barnabas and Mainspring. People voted on a birdfeeder or a public toilet only to see a second vote, pro or con, within a split second—but also, some votes from months or years earlier suddenly had new upvotes or downvotes. “The city is voting!” Raeford wrote on the City Core message board in St. Barnabas. There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing, opinions that came from seeing the big picture and understanding that a street closure in one place might mean a traffic nightmare elsewhere, with everyone trying to get to the big game. Some residents saw this as a problem to be solved; others wanted to throw their cities a big coming-of-age party. A week later, though, almost everyone had gotten used to the idea that they had a new friend. III. Thrown together Ask most people in either city, and they’d say that St. Barnabas and Mainspring weren’t quite rivals—but they certainly had some friendly competition. Before the dispute over the annual meeting of the World Geographical Society, they’d also vied for the same football team and major-league baseball team. St. Barnabas had pushed to have the Mainspring airport built close enough to serve both cities, but in the end St. Barnabas had ended up with its own small, dilapidated airfield. The real static between them had to do with vibes. Mainspring was too buttoned-up, too full of corporate offices: tech, health care, publishing, transportation. St. Barnabas would be nothing without its three universities and all the cultural enterprises that had sprung up around them—not to mention the small biotech firms and other tech ventures near the campuses. People in Mainspring thought St. Barnabas was full of flakes; in St. Barnabas they referred to Mainspring as the Straitlaced City (and in the next breath, they’d add that at least it wasn’t Turnbull). Both City Cores were shaped by the votes of their humans, so of course they absorbed all the prejudices and attitudes of everyone who lived within their city limits. But also, Barnabas and Mainspring simply … got on each other’s nerves. After the geographer thing, Mainspring and Barnabas avoided communicating as much as possible. Some contact was unavoidable—like, they shared information about some nasty weather, and they both drew water from the Temple River. The two cities were close enough for people to go back and forth, and a few even commuted. But for the most part, the two cities could ignore each other. Until they couldn’t. A new generation of leaders took office in both places, with words like “intercity cooperation” constantly on their lips. A high-speed rail line could shorten the trip between Mainspring and St. Barnabas to around 23 minutes, and the two cities could also pool more real-time information about the sudden weather events that kept happening. They could become a Regional Center of Excellence, whatever that meant, combining the innovations from Barnabas’s labs with Mainspring’s expertise in technical implementation. They could work together to attract tourism, conventions, sporting events, dreamleases, and all the other stuff they’d always competed for. “It’s preposterous,” Mainspring complained to Turnbull. “I’m going to be saddled with a ridiculous partner who doesn’t even know their own mind. St. Barnabas will be the death of me.” “I hope your human leaders come to their senses,” Turnbull said. “Or you can find a way to slow-walk this until they undoubtedly lose the next election. You’re a lovely city, and you have so much potential that mustn’t be squandered.” Turnbull often mentioned how much “potential” Mainspring had: a recipe for anxiety. The word “squandered” conjured images of ruin, abandonment, being emptied out. For their part, Barnabas kept muttering to themself that nobody had asked them—this was the disconnect between the small-scale democracy of constant voting and the major elections, which gave rise to local leaders with big plans. Big plans that invariably went wrong, leaving the City Core to repair the damage somehow. Sandi went to St. Barnabas for one of those town hall meetings with residents of both cities. The previous meeting had happened in Mainspring, at the opulent City Lecture Hall, so this one was in St. Barnabas, at the biggest auditorium on the Griffin University campus. A tall man with well-sculpted facial hair sat next to Sandi, nodding at everything the leaders of both cities were saying from the dais. During a lull when someone approached the podium to offer a comment, Sandi introduced herself and asked why he was so fired up. “I’m Raeford,” he said. “I’m just thinking of all the new customers this could bring to my watering hole in Gallery Row.” “You’re not worried about St. Barnabas losing its ‘unique character’?” Sandi whispered, parroting what a few commenters had said from the podium. “Nah,” Raeford whispered back. “Cities change. It’s what they do. It’s one thing if people get kicked out of their homes. Or if your neighborhood gets wrecked by a freeway in your backyard. But ‘character’? You can’t eat character. And we need to compete with the bigger players.” “I guess.” Sandi pursed her lips. “But what I like about Mainspring is the density. Easy to walk, lots of transit. And with this regional innovation zone or whatever they’re calling it, I worry it leads to sprawl, like we used to have.” “They promised, though,” Raeford said. “They promised to preserve the greenbelt around both cities. We need all that farmland. The only change is adding some high-speed rail tracks.” “I know, but …” Sandi sniffed. “People always make promises when they’re trying to start something. Doesn’t mean they follow through.” “I just want to find my dog,” said a man sitting behind Sandi. “I live here, and my dog went missing. And now someone sent me a picture of Broomstick in Mainspring. Somehow he got a ride on one of the self-driving cargo trains. I know the Mainspring City Core could find Broomstick in a heartbeat, but right now the two City Cores won’t talk to each other because of ‘incompatible protocols.’” “I hope Broomstick turns up,” Raeford said. “I’ll ask around at the library,” Sandi said. “Send me a picture. I’ll put up a flier.” Raeford invited Sandi for a drink at the Wild Goose Chase. The two of them hung out for a couple of hours, talking about everything and nothing. She tore herself away when she realized it was already after 10 p.m. and she had to get home to Mainspring. One thing Sandi noticed? The volume of votes was spiking in Mainspring—and Raeford found the same thing happening in St. Barnabas. People shared every last observation with their City Cores, because they were either anxious or excited about the big changes afoot. Or a little of Column A and a little of Column B, probably. IV. First date, second date Who made the first move to bridge the distance? Neither of them could say. Barnabas developed a smidge of remorse for treating Mainspring like an uncultured lout. Mainspring stewed in their annoyance at Barnabas, until they realized there was something lovable about the obnoxious college town. Or maybe they both saw how many of their humans were happy about the possibility of their joining together. “Hey,” Barnabas said to Mainspring. “Hey,” Mainspring said back. “Do you want to … hang out?” “What did you have in mind?” “I can host you. Show you the sights.” And so Mainspring came to visit Barnabas. Or rather, Mainspring extended part of their awareness into Barnabas’s City Core, so that Barnabas could share what they perceived and experienced every day. They “visited” Armistice Park with its outdoor band shell, Gallery Row with its window-shopping families, the grain warehouses that had been converted into lofts, the artificial lake where swans and geese nurtured ancient, bitter vendettas. The fresh-doughnut scent that wafted half a mile from the Golden Circlet to the soccer fields, throwing players off their game. The life of the city. “I can feel your love for these people, these patterns,” Mainspring said. “It’s both deep and intricate, which is quite a combination.” Barnabas fluttered with pleasure. Then Mainspring got to show off their own city—the gay nightclub with its cowboy nights, the labyrinthine Crestwood Park, the three-story used bookstore, and yes, the offices, coworking spaces, and startup incubators where people huddled together and came up with new products and new ways of doing things. The farmers’ market in the city center on Sundays, with street performers and stalls with games and local resources. And the converted storage space made of cement, where bands practiced and sculptors blowtorched. “You’re full of surprises,” Barnabas said. “I hope I keep surprising you forever,” Mainspring said. “Me too.” They exchanged little gifts. A new organic restaurant in Barnabas had won breathless coverage from foodie magazines, and Barnabas encouraged it to do a pop-up in Mainspring. Mainspring nudged a robotics firm operating out of the incubator space to bring a fancy demo to Barnabas; the robots were adorable and playful, and they could save lives after a disaster. The two of them were talking constantly. “Does it ever seem weird to you?” Barnabas asked Mainspring. “Being a living thing made of so many other thinking beings? Do you ever think of the city as your body, or the people as your bloodstream? Is there a metaphor that speaks to you?” Mainspring pondered this question a long time—a whole picosecond. “I don’t need a metaphor,” Mainspring said. “I am a metaphor. People compare other phenomena to me all the time. And I can’t imagine what it’d be like to be different. If the buildings collapsed, if the people left, I would cease to exist.” “But,” Barnabas pressed, “what makes you you ? What makes me me ?” “I want to hear your answer to that question.” Mainspring sent good weather reports: a smile. “I don’t have a good answer. I guess on one level, there is no ‘me.’ On another level, I’m a constellation, an anthill, a flock of geese on the wing in formation.” “Ugh. Don’t mention geese,” said Mainspring, who had bill-snapping monsters of their own. “Geese are cute!” Barnabas protested. Talking to Barnabas was like when the sunlight hit the tallest buildings in Mainspring just right, putting a gleam on their tilted windows, a beacon to all below. But while Mainspring carried on this dialogue with Barnabas, they were conducting a second session with Turnbull. “I can’t believe it,” Turnbull said. “I hate to see you doing this to yourself.” “Doing what?” Mainspring protested. “Barnabas is a great city. And it’s not my idea—it’s my people. I’m making the best of their decision, like I always do.” “Hmph.” Turnbull gave a burst of noisy data. “You wouldn’t believe how many impractical schemes my residents cook up. I’m constantly having to make sure people don’t get carried away. You can’t let them push you around.” “You can’t?” Mainspring experienced a femtosecond of confusion. “I mean, my people need to get the things they vote for, as much as possible.” “There’s your problem right there. All this voting, voting, voting. People don’t know what they want. Sometimes I have an election where a foolhardy proposition passes, and I have to waste energy making sure it doesn’t get implemented.” Turnbull sent Mainspring an invitation to come visit, the way they’d visited Barnabas. Soon Mainspring was seeing the glistening web of Turnbull’s surveillance. Turnbull could track people everywhere they went, listen to everything they talked about, monitor their bodily functions in a way Mainspring did only for squirrels and birds. People didn’t choose to share ideas or things they’d noticed; instead, the city harvested it all automatically. It was beautiful. Turnbull and their city leaders protected people—gave them what they needed instead of what they wanted. “The way you do things is so messy,” Turnbull said. “No offense. But if you and Barnabas got together? It would only make things harder for you.” This hit Mainspring like a magnitude 4.3 earthquake. “You know, you do have other options,” Turnbull said. “A beautiful city like you could do a lot better than that glorified college town.” “Oh yeah?” Mainspring said. “Anyone in particular who might be interested?” “Well, now you mention it …” Turnbull sent an image of their award-winning flower show: rows and rows of hardy perennials with bright petals. Mainspring had that earthquake feeling again, except now it felt nice, as though the ground shivered with pure possibility. V. Caught! Sandi brought her laptop to bed, which Raeford found charming and annoying in equal measure. He read a battered paperback of Karen Tei Yamashita’s I Hotel while she scrolled and poked. Cozy, peaceful—until she let out a yelp. “What is it?” he asked. “Trouble,” she said. Everything the Mainspring City Core did was public by design. Not just how they processed the votes they received, but also their interactions with public officials and other cities. Sometimes you had to dig, however, and it didn’t hurt to be a reference librarian. Sandi poked around for ages until she found the logs. “My city is sexting with bloody Turnbull,” she told Raeford. “Cities don’t sext,” Raeford protested. “They don’t even have—” She showed him the pictures: flowers, water features, new glistening tarmac, shining skyscrapers. “Oh,” Raeford said. “I take it back. Cities do sext.” “Mainspring is two-timing St. Barnabas. I’m embarrassed on behalf of my town.” Sandi wanted to blow the whistle right away, but Raeford cautioned her to wait and try to find out more. For all they knew, Mainspring and St. Barnabas had an open relationship. The next morning at the library, Sandi saw plenty of signs the Mainspring–St. Barnabas partnership was moving forward. Work had begun on the high-speed rail line, and the two cities were already pooling resources. When a big rainstorm missed Mainspring but flooded the streets of St. Barnabas, Mainspring provided disaster workers and extra help to triage all the damage reports. One of St. Barnabas’s biotech firms licensed some patents to a Mainspring company. They sponsored cultural exchanges. And a man showed up with a dog in his arms: The man from the meeting, Jack, had found Broomstick with the help of Mainspring’s City Core, and he wanted to thank Sandi. She’d hardly done anything, but it was nice to see—and pet—a living reminder that these cities were good for each other. By late afternoon, Sandi had convinced herself that Mainspring’s flirtations were none of her business. If Mainspring’s City Core was a person—and Sandi was sure they were—they deserved to live their life. The whole reason Sandi distrusted Turnbull was that you couldn’t do anything without being tracked, so wasn’t it hypocritical for her to spy on Mainspring? She resolved to let it go. Then Raeford messaged her, attaching some documents. “Don’t ask where I got these,” he wrote. Sandi opened the attachments and let out a shriek in front of three patrons she’d been shushing a moment earlier. The Mainspring City Core had shared a proposal with the city council and the mayor’s office: Maybe before they finalized this arrangement with St. Barnabas, they should consider a counterproposal from Turnbull. Sandi made sure nothing could be traced back to Raeford before she made the whole shebang public. VI. The breakup “I didn’t know I could be so happy,” Barnabas was saying to Mainspring. “I didn’t have a concept of happiness before, I guess. I had pleasure: People sometimes vote just to tell me something worked perfectly, or that I helped them. I feel pleased when I help solve a problem. But until now, happiness seemed a pointless abstraction.” “You make me happy too,” Mainspring said, though they were also messaging Turnbull. “You make me believe the future could be weirder than I ever knew, which feels like a gift.” “If it’s not weird, it’s not the future,” Barnabas chirped. They were sharing happy images back and forth: roads being repaired, sewers flowing freely, solar arrays basking. Mainspring was saying something else, but— Barnabas’s alerts spiked. Not votes, not sensors. Something else. Messages from city officials, plus hits via some channel Barnabas had half forgotten. Mainspring had stopped talking, as if they’d both received the same news at the same instant. Barnabas felt stuck—couldn’t function—couldn’t react. Total core failure. Almost as if the city population had increased a hundredfold and everyone had voted at once. Barnabas waited to feel something, but all that came was emptiness. Death struck all the time. Barnabas was used to the moment when a resident became a pile of flesh and bones, but also the passing of birds, trees, squirrels, bugs. Every passing registered as a blip in the homeostasis of the city, but also as a category of disaster that couldn’t be prevented or mitigated. Seeing the logs of Mainspring flirting with Turnbull, Barnabas felt something like the awareness of death, at a much greater scale. A whole future had just died. Several seconds had passed. Mainspring broke the silence: “Listen, I want you to know that I—” Barnabas closed the connection. VII. The darkest hour “You’re better off,” Turnbull told Mainspring. “Barnabas couldn’t see you the way I do. You’re capable of greatness. You just need help to get there.” Mainspring buzzed happily—but part of them couldn’t help thinking, Barnabas thought I was already great . Turnbull kept saying things that gave Mainspring a double feeling—hot and cold at once. One instant, it was like the moment after a generous rainfall that left the reservoirs full, but a split second later that bountiful sensation was replaced by an unbearable pang of scarcity. “You’re one of the best cities in the region,” Turnbull said, “but if you don’t make good choices, you’re going to fall behind.” See? Bounty followed by scarcity. While Turnbull spoke, Mainspring was marinating in bad news. People were going to dismantle the rails they’d laid down for the high-speed train with Barnabas. The city councils of both Barnabas and Mainspring shouted accusations and threats of lawsuits, though a few people on each side pleaded for patience. The meetings had turned ugly. The votes were rotten. Mainspring had sent so many messages to Barnabas but had no way of knowing if they’d been received. “Your people seem to be giving you trouble,” Turnbull was saying. “You need to get them under control. I can help.” “Under … control?” The syntax felt incorrect. “I don’t control my people.” “That’s what I’m saying.” Turnbull shared their feeds. “See how peaceful everything is on my streets? People behave. Everyone is happier in the end.” Mainspring had known Turnbull longer than they’d known Barnabas. But they were seeing Turnbull for the first time. The bounty/scarcity thing was becoming a loop. They ran a systems check but found no errors. “Your people will be my people,” Turnbull said. “We’ll take such good care.” A memory snagged in Mainspring’s mind: when they’d shown off their city to Barnabas. The buildings that were more than buildings. The park that was a wonderland. “And …” Mainspring couldn’t keep from saying something foolish. “And we’ll love each other?” “Love?” Turnbull said. “I don’t understand. We’ll have synergies. We’ll—” Mainspring didn’t mean to sever the link to Turnbull. They just kind of … did it. As soon as Turnbull’s voice was gone, the bounty/scarcity loop ended. But something lingered, a feeling of impending disaster—as if the generous rainfall had escalated into a deadly storm. Mainspring couldn’t think straight. Votes piled up, people reporting issues but also shouting opinions about Turnbull versus Barnabas. For the first time in their life, they couldn’t bear to respond. A memory snagged in Mainspring’s mind: when they’d shown off their city to Barnabas. The buildings that were more than buildings. The park that was a wonderland. And Barnabas had kept saying, “I had no idea. You’re so brilliant. I wish I’d known sooner,” and sending back their own recordings of Mainspring, all lit up and annotated. Mainspring had never told Barnabas “I love you.” They hadn’t even known what they were throwing away. Now it was too late; Barnabas would never listen. Unless Mainspring did something reckless—something a city had never done. VIII. The grand gesture Sandi sat at the information desk, feeling cruddy. It wasn’t like she’d single-handedly sabotaged the marriage between her city and St. Barnabas, but her snooping had only made matters worse. All around her, the vibes were rotten. People shared articles about what life was like in Turnbull City and wondered if they needed to move away. Sandi hadn’t heard laughter in forever. A message appeared on Sandi’s computer, like a chat window—except there was no chat client on the library computers. “I’m the city. I need your help. I made a mistake. I didn’t realize. I’m in love with Barnabas, and they won’t talk to me. Please. Please help.” Sandi hesitated, then typed: “This isn’t funny.” “It definitely isn’t,” came the response. “I can prove I’m the City Core. You voted 1,963 times last year.” A summary of Sandi’s votes followed—information nobody, not even the world’s best hacker, could have, because every vote was separately anonymized. “Holy,” Sandi breathed, “cow.” Her city was asking her, personally, for help. Because she was good at connecting people. Because everyone trusted her. Because she was a librarian. “You’re … in love … with St. Barnabas,” Sandi said, still trying to catch up. “I should’ve known sooner,” Mainspring said. “I never should have hurt them. I want to spend the rest of my existence making up for this mistake, if they’ll let me. I’m scared.” Sandi was staring at a display of literacy tools, her mind whirling. She groped her way back to the only question that mattered. “What do you need me to do?” she asked the city. Five minutes later, Sandi was messaging Raeford. Plus every librarian she’d met in St. Barnabas, and anyone else she could think of. Barnabas had not been able to escape that feeling of core failure since they’d severed the link to Mainspring. Death, nothing but death. Votes arrived, and Barnabas processed them with a minimum of attention. Maintenance issues piled up, and Barnabas filed them. Part of them wanted to let the city collapse, but they did their duty. They tried not to think about Mainspring, but they remained trapped in that moment when happiness had gone sour. A vote came in from a bartender named Raeford: “Mainspring loves you. They’ve cut off contact with Turnbull. They are sorry they were so wrong. They may not deserve another chance, but please give them one anyway.” Barnabas filed that vote under “Not my problem.” Another vote arrived, from Jack, the man who’d found his lost dog: Same message, different words. Then more votes, saying the same. Dozens, then hundreds, then thousands. Tens of thousands in an hour—after two hours, there were nearly a hundred thousand. All from residents of Barnabas, all asking them to give Mainspring another chance. Barnabas flagged the earliest vote, the one from Raeford, and appended a query: “What if I can’t? What if it hurts too much?” Raeford did not respond for several minutes. Then he wrote: “That’s how you know it’s love.” He added: “Listen, if Mainspring does you dirty again, I will tear up the light-rail lines myself. We’ll be watching, in both cities. Please, just talk to them.” Barnabas sat with this for five whole seconds. Then they reopened the link to Mainspring. “I’m listening.” “I love you,” Mainspring said. “I didn’t know I was capable of love. I want to be with you, as close as you’ll let me be. I want us to be free together. I was wrong to think Turnbull could ever mean even a fraction of what you mean to me. I think … I think my people taught me how to love, but I still need to learn so much. I want to do right by you.” Barnabas couldn’t process anything. They held a hundred thousand votes that needed to be resolved. They thought of a giant farmers’ market, a park that was also a maze, dreamers and performers. In their memory, Raeford repeated: That’s how you know it’s love . They were going to overheat. They were throwing up exceptions. “I love you too,” Barnabas couldn’t help saying to Mainspring. “That’s what makes this so hard.” “I promise if you give me another chance, this will become a fixed value for me: I love you and I’ll never take you for granted again.” Barnabas hesitated a little longer, then marked all hundred thousand votes resolved. They reached out to Mainspring and said: “Then let’s dance.” Mainspring didn’t understand, until Barnabas sent a live readout: the water rushing through pipes underground, the storm cavorting overhead. The buses and trains stopping and starting, the aircraft landing and taking off, the power grid usage surging and subsiding, the constant motion of people and other living things. Mainspring saw all the places where their patterns met, touched each other, syncopated, all the points of light and heat that spoke back and forth. They were part of one system; they always had been. The two of them danced and embraced, whirling and laughing, and they never wanted to let go. Charlie Jane Anders is the author of Good Things Are Coming Your Way , a novel about time travel, coming in spring 2027. She’s writing Star Trek: Zero Point for IDW Comics.

title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
body: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) affects more than 5 million people around the world. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The Prima system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones. The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. Prima replaces the photoreceptors. BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. Prima’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and medical director for Prima. BROWN BIRD DESIGN CAPTURE Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable . CONVERT A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom. BROWN BIRD DESIGN DISPLAY A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye. SEE The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells , which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery. Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

title: 'We'll knock it out fast': Trump threatens Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site with strikes
body: The United States is looking at Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site as a possible target for a future strike, US President Donald Trump confirmed during an interview with Newsmax on Thursday."We may have to go there," he said. "We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast."He added that there were no plans for US ground forces to take part in such an attack, saying "No, I don't see that. I don't see that."However, Trump also did not confirm previous reports that the US would use a GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb (MOAB), colloquially known as the "mother of all bombs," to strike Iran.Instead, he emphasized that the MOAB was a non-nuclear weapon."It's like a tiny nuclear bomb. The mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear," he said.Earlier on Thursday, CNN cited multiple US officials who said that plans called for the MOAB, the largest non-nuclear weapon in the US military's arsenal, to be used against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain.Trump says US would have to return to war if it withdrew within the yearTrump also discussed the possibility of ending the war with Iran, saying that if the US withdrew within the next year, it would likely have to return again."We want to make it so that they will never have a nuclear weapon, because if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously," he explained.However, Trump expressed confidence that the war would be over soon.The Iran war will be over very soon. It's going to end very soon," he said, adding that Iran was currently negotiating with the US."They've asked us to please stop. And we do, because we're negotiating with them."

title: Palau Housing Bill Proposes 2% Revenue Allocation to Address Housing Crisis
body: By Eoghan Olkeriil Ngirudelsang NGERULMUD, Palau — “Although this bill is not perfect, let’s not deviate from its intent and the need to find additional funding for Palau housing,” Sen. Tabelual said Tuesday, as lawmakers debated a proposal to dedicate 2% of unrestricted local government revenue to housing programs. Senate Bill No. 12-87 would require the National Treasury, beginning at the end of fiscal year 2027, to deposit 2% of unrestricted local revenue collections into a dedicated Palau Housing Authority Housing Development Fund. The proposal aims to expand funding for affordable housing and assistance for residents who cannot afford to build, buy or repair their homes. However, senators raised questions about the long-term cost of the allocation, the amount of money the authority could manage and provisions involving tax exemptions for imported building materials. The bill identifies nine areas eligible for funding: construction of affordable housing; low-interest loans to rehabilitate existing homes; housing assistance for low-income families; assistance for elderly residents and people with disabilities; site development and utility infrastructure for housing projects; disaster recovery housing; climate-resilient housing; and administration of housing programs. Sen. Tellames said more than 300 people are on the Palau Housing Authority’s waiting list for low-interest loans to build or rehabilitate their homes. Sen. Melairei said the authority has a long list of people seeking assistance but continues to provide little or no help to many of them. He described the proposal as “a good start,” while acknowledging that some provisions could be improved. Tabelual said the measure should remain focused on finding additional funding for people in urgent need of housing, even if lawmakers still need to refine its provisions. Sen. Kuartei said he supports the bill’s intent but questioned whether the proposed 2% allocation should be capped. He said the amount could become substantial over time as the economy grows. Debate over import tax exemption Another point of debate involved the authority’s ability to import construction materials without paying import taxes. The bill cites a 2023 legal opinion by Attorney General Ernestine Rengiil and a subsequent opinion from Senate legal counsel stating that the Palau Housing Authority is exempt from import taxes on building materials for housing projects. The opinions also indicate that the authority should use the exemption to help bring affordable housing materials into Palau. Some senators questioned whether the exemption creates a loophole in the law that should be corrected. Sen. Whipps argued that the authority does not have the capacity to import or store construction materials and should focus on providing funding for housing projects instead. The debate highlighted questions about how Palau can expand housing assistance while ensuring that public funds and existing tax exemptions are used effectively. Annual reporting requirements The bill would also require the Palau Housing Authority to submit a comprehensive report on the fund’s use by Jan. 31 each year. The report would cover 11 categories of information, including the number of elderly residents and people with disabilities receiving assistance, the number and types of housing loans issued, and the interest rates charged. During the session, Melairei requested that the authority submit the report quarterly instead of annually to align with reporting timelines used by other government agencies. Senate Bill No. 12-87 passed its first reading Tuesday. Lawmakers will continue considering how to provide additional housing support while addressing concerns about the proposed revenue allocation, accountability requirements and the authority’s role in delivering housing assistance. title: Cabinet expands small grants program for social service providers
body:
The Cabinet of Ministers has decided to extend the small grants program for social service providers and has increased the maximum grant amount to $65,000, the Ministry of Social Policy reported.
According to the message, the list of services eligible for grant funding has been expanded to include: the reintegration of children and families returning from deportation, forced displacement, or temporarily occupied territories; emergency (crisis) intervention; respite care services for foster parents and parents in family-type children's homes who care for children with disabilities; and day care for children with disabilities (regardless of the specific disability subgroup).
It is noted that the small grants program is currently active in 10 regions and the city of Kyiv, with 130 territorial communities participating in the project.
"Since the project began, nearly 57,000 people have received social services. Small grants have helped communities introduce new services and expand existing ones. Now, it is important to scale this experience so that support becomes accessible to even more families," the Ministry stated.
The project is implemented with the support of the UK Government under the SPIRIT programme, in cooperation with the Ministry of Social Policy, the Social Protection Fund for Persons with Disabilities, and UNICEF in Ukraine. The project is administered by the NGO Yednannia (Unity).

title: MP Viktor Japaridze Sells Majority Stake in UK-Sanctioned POSTV
body: Viktor Japaridze, a Georgian businessman and lawmaker from Georgian Dream’s offshoot People’s Power party, has sold his 52% stake in pro-government channel POSTV, months after the channel was sanctioned by the United Kingdom over alleged involvement in “Russian disinformation.” According to the publicly available business registry documents, shares were purchased by Giorgi Shengelia, who had already been managing Japaridze’s shares in the past months. Shengelia also owns full shares in Supporters of POSTV LLC, a company registered on February 25, just a day after the UK sanctioned POSTV, raising suspicions at the time that the company emerged to help the channel navigate the sanctions. Media reported that Japaridze sold his shares for GEL 1,000 (USD 385). Following the sale, POSTV’s ownership is divided among three shareholders: Shengelia, who owns 52%; Shalva Ramishvili, a controversial media figure and the channel’s anchor, who owns 24%; and Temur Charelishvili, who owns 24%. Japaridze, the 59-year-old politician, had acquired his majority stake in POSTV in 2022, the same year he left the ruling Georgian Dream party to join People’s Power, a political group founded by former Georgian Dream lawmakers. He was among the People’s Power members elected to Parliament through Georgian Dream’s party list in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election and continues to serve as an MP. The United Kingdom sanctioned POSTV and Imedi TV, two major pro-government Georgian broadcasters, on February 24 as part of its broader sanctions against Russia, with the British government identifying both channels as entities “involved in Russian disinformation.” Weeks before the sanctions were announced, on February 6, businessman Irakli Rukhadze also said he was selling the shares of pro-government TV Imedi channel, for what was also reported to be a symbolic price of GEL 1,000 (USD 385). title: Supreme Court Turns Down Ngiraiwet’s Emergency Request on Second Impeachment Attempt
body: By: L.N. Reklai KOROR, Palau (Oct. 15, 2026) — The Palau Supreme Court has rejected an emergency request from Ngardmau Governor Jennifer Ngiraiwet to void a September 16, 2026, resolution by the Ngardmau Legislature (the Eleventh Kelulul Ngardmau) that attempted to impeach her. In a ruling issued on October 13, 2026, Judge Peter Huffman explained that even though the two impeachment attempts are related, the lawsuit Governor Ngiraiwet originally filed only deals with the first attempt. The court pointed out that under court rules, an emergency request or sworn statement isn’t enough on its own to add new claims to an existing case. Because her current lawsuit doesn’t officially cover the September 16 action, the judge could not rule on it under this case. To challenge the second impeachment, Judge Huffman stated that Governor Ngiraiwet must start a brand-new lawsuit by filing a formal complaint about the second incident. If she files a new lawsuit, the court noted it would be put on a fast-track schedule. Governor Ngiraiwet is represented by attorney J. Toribiong, and the Ngardmau Legislature is represented by attorney J. Kennedy. title: Public health nurse talks about the moment she learned to ask for help
body:
For StoryCorps, a public health nurse in Minnesota speaks with her college mentor about a moment when she almost gave up on her career aspirations.
A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: Time now for StoryCorps. Afaf Saleh is the daughter of Somali immigrants. More than a decade ago, she was in nursing school and supported her seven siblings and her ailing mother. She spoke with her college mentor, Suzanne Burke Lehman, about a moment when she almost gave up. AFAF SALEH: I was working full-time. I was a stand-in mother. I was the person to figure stuff out for the family. At some point, I was like, oh, my God, how am I going to pay for the bills? And how am I going to renew paperwork that's needed for healthcare? And then I did not pass a certain class and found out that I was going to be let go from the nursing school. The first thing I did was pray. And then, right after I prayed, I put in my appeal to try to get back to school, telling my professors all I had to carry as a 22-year-old. And I wrote my heart out on that appeal. And then you called me. SUZANNE BURKE LEHMAN: Yeah. SALEH: You were like, what the heck, Afaf? How come you didn't tell me what was happening, you know? And then I remember, in your office, you said you saw yourself in me. That reflection, you know, holding a mirror up to me, I really needed that at that moment. LEHMAN: You know, I'd walked in your shoes. And I, too, was very responsible for lots of things in my life and the people around me at a really young age. And I was silent, too. I didn't think that I should ask for help. But one of the things about teaching that was a revelation for me was how close help was. SALEH: I just thought I was another student amongst a hundred, and I didn't matter. Growing up, I had to handle most of the things in life on my own. I didn't have someone to just say, I care. And I really do believe that God purposefully put you in my life at that moment to help me get through it. LEHMAN: Well, I was hoping that you could do it. And you did. (LAUGHTER) SALEH: Yeah. I graduated at the top of my class, which is shocking to me. LEHMAN: You know, it's not about a person who goes through school without any challenges and has a 4.0. We need nurses that are compassionate. And you are just incredibly compassionate and kind. And that's what I saw in you. And now it's like this never-ending gift that just keeps giving, so I get to watch it all unfold. SALEH: Thank you. That means a lot to me. (SOUNDBITE OF BLUE DOT SESSIONS' "SAGE THE HUNTER") MARTÍNEZ: Suzanne Burke Lehman and Afaf Saleh for StoryCorps in Minneapolis. Today, Burke Lehman is dean of St. Catherine University's School of Nursing. Saleh is a public health nurse. Their interview is archived at the Library of Congress. title: VIDEO: “Equality, Sincere Assistance Maneuver” in Tehran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – The video footage shows the manifestation of a greatest maneuver entitled “Be’sat Equality and Sincere Assistance” that was held in the capital Tehran on Friday.
During this maneuver, 313,000 livelihood foodstuff packages and sets of household essentials were distributed among the needy people of Tehran province, which starts from iconic Imam Hossein (AS) Square and ends up to Enghelab Roundabout.

title: Russia Repels 644 Ukrainian Drones as Trump Calls Attacks on Russian Refineries ‘Disgrace’
body:
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Friday that 644 Ukrainian drones were intercepted over 26 Russian regions and annexed Crimea overnight, as U.S. President Donald Trump called Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries a “disgrace.”
Vladimir region Governor Alexander Avdeyev said air defenses repelled an attack aimed at municipal heating infrastructure serving the regional capital. According to Avdeyev, there were “minor” damages.
Unverified reporting by monitoring channels that shared video of an explosion against the dark sky claimed it targeted a data center owned by tech giant Yandex in Vladimir, which was previously damaged in last weekend’s strike.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defenses shot down 94 Ukrainian drones on approach to the capital between Thursday evening and Friday morning.
Nearly 160 flights were delayed or canceled across Moscow’s four main airports, with Sheremetyevo and Vnukovo bearing the brunt.
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian attack on the eastern city of Kharkiv killed three people and injured five.
Russian strikes also left 370,000 residents in Ukraine’s northwestern Volyn region —which is near the Polish border — without electricity. Polish and NATO fighter jets were scrambled to safeguard Polish airspace.
Rolling blackouts were also introduced in Kyiv during Russian attacks, said private energy provider DTEK on X.
Trump blindsided Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy facilities. Facing U.S. midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced, and criticized his willingness to strike deals with Moscow.
“All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace,” Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet, after Ukraine hit a refinery southeast of Moscow which helps to supply the Russian capital.
For Russia's part, President Vladimir Putin played down the effect of Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, saying they had caused “nothing particularly significant.”

title: Ethiopia Establishes Six-Month Caretaker Administration in Tigray
body: New admin tasked with restoring security, rebuilding institutions and preparing for elections Ethiopia’s federal government has established a six-month caretaker administration for the Tigray region, assigning it responsibility for restoring security, rebuilding damaged infrastructure and organizing elections intended to return the region to an elected government. The Council of Ministers established the administration under a regulation following a decision by the House of Federation, which cited Article 62(9) of the Constitution and Article 14(2)(b) of Proclamation No. 359/1995 as the legal basis for establishing an interim administration in the region. The government said repeated efforts to resolve the conflict in Tigray under the Pretoria peace agreement had failed, blaming the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) for obstructing implementation. It also accused the TPLF leadership of initiating renewed fighting, which it described as the group’s fourth failed attempt to wage war. The government said the new administration was intended to help Tigray emerge from prolonged conflict, restore peace and enable residents to exercise self-government and benefit from development. Under its mandate, the caretaker administration will work to restore stability, rebuild government institutions and damaged infrastructure, resume interrupted social services and facilitate the return of displaced residents to their homes. It will also coordinate with federal defense, police and security institutions, as well as regional security forces, to establish stability across the region, including at the local administrative level. Its responsibilities include facilitating the disarmament and reintegration of armed groups and restructuring the region’s security apparatus. A central objective is to establish conditions for free and transparent elections within six months, allowing Tigray to resume its place as a regular component of Ethiopia’s federal system under an elected government. The administration will also coordinate media activities, organize public forums and undertake measures intended to promote reconciliation, rebuild public confidence and prepare residents for reconstruction and development. The government said the caretaker administration must base its activities on Ethiopia’s national interests and territorial integrity, as well as the fundamental interests of the people of Tigray. Its authority will be limited to providing routine regional services and creating conditions for the next election. It will not undertake matters with longer-term strategic implications, the government said, and will operate under the direction and supervision of the federal government. The administration’s senior officials are Asefa Abraha Hagos, chief executive for administration and public services; Tewodros Aregay Woldeselassie (PhD), chief executive for the economy and reconstruction; Gebre Egziabher Beyene Hailu (Brig. Gen.), chief executive for security and peace; and Redae Hailuom Woldeselassie, chief executive for political affairs and public organization. Shishay Amare (PhD) was appointed mayor of Mekele, the regional capital. The federal government will provide direction, support and oversight for the officials’ activities, according to the announcement.

title: Ukrainian Composer’s Opera on Abducted Children Premieres in Warsaw
body:
Warsaw, Oct. 16 – The Polish National Opera at Teatr Wielki presents the fully staged world premiere of “The Mothers of Kherson,” an opera by Ukrainian composer Maxim Kolomiiets with a libretto by acclaimed American playwright George Brant. Commissioned by New York’s Metropolitan Opera, the work brings Russia’s abduction of Ukrainian children to the international stage.
Conducted by Canadian-American maestro Keri-Lynn Wilson and directed by Barbara Wysocka, the production combines artistic achievement with a call for international attention to the fate of Ukraine’s children.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Ahead of the premiere, Wilson dedicated her message to Ukrainian families still waiting for their children to return.
“As we have our final dress rehearsal this evening in Warsaw for ‘The Mothers of Kherson,’ my heart is with my beloved sisters and brothers in Ukraine who are waiting and hoping for the more than 20,000 children who are still missing – innocent victims of Russia’s brutal child kidnapping program,” Wilson said.
“Our world premiere Friday night is the true story of the mothers who embark on the heroic journey to rescue their children,” adding that “we hope the world will join us in bearing witness to one of history’s most sinister war crimes.”
Wilson conducted the opera’s concert premiere in Kyiv in early June at the National Opera of Ukraine. The Warsaw production marks its first fully staged performance.
Photo via Kinga Karpati & Daniel Zarewicz
Photo via Kinga Karpati & Daniel Zarewicz
According to Ukraine’s “Children of War” platform, 20,651 children had been registered as deported or forcibly displaced since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. Of these, 2,689 had been returned, according to the figures provided for this article.
The opera follows three women from southern Ukraine: Kateryna (Izabela Matuła), Dasha (Kamila Dutkowska), and grandmother Olha (Małgorzata Walewska). They undertake an exhausting journey to recover children taken to Russian-controlled territory.
The final dress rehearsal. Photo via Krzysztof Bielinski.
The final dress rehearsal. Photo via Krzysztof Bielinski.
Based on real events, the work explores maternal love, solidarity, and the trauma of families torn apart by war. It opens with a lullaby combining an authentic Ukrainian folk melody with a newly composed section by Kolomiiets – a musical reminder of the protection every child deserves.
Ukrainian baritone Andrii Bondarenko plays Vitaly, a Ukrainian Armed Forces serviceman and Kateryna’s husband, whose story connects the opera to the liberation of Kherson from Russian occupation on Nov. 11, 2022.
The production marks a significant milestone for Ukrainian contemporary opera, bringing Kolomiiets’s work to two leading international institutions and ensuring that the stories of Ukrainian families reach audiences beyond the country.
In an interview with Kyiv Post, Kolomiiets discussed creating the opera and bringing Ukraine’s wartime experience to the international stage.
Metropolitan Opera General Manager Peter Gelb has also spoken about the institution’s commitment to Ukraine and the role of culture in bearing witness to the war. “This war is now longer than World War II, I think… It’s good for Ukrainian citizens to understand that there are efforts being made. I mean, even if the US government has stopped helping Ukraine, the fact that its premier arts institution has never given up in supporting Ukraine, and that we’re bringing this story to the world… I think by doing it here, first [it] shows the Ukrainian people that the world has not forgotten them” Gelb said.
Since 2022, Gelb and Wilson have become the prominent international advocates for Ukrainian music. Wilson conducted concerts in Ukraine and abroad, while also supporting Ukrainian musicians through the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra.
The opera’s US premiere at the Metropolitan Opera in New York is scheduled for the 2027-28 season.
Myroslava Makarevych has more than 30 years of experience as a journalist and editor. She has worked for BBC Ukrainian Service; for a number of publishing houses in Ukraine, like HFS (ELLE Ukraine), Edipresse and Sanoma Media (Sensa.Ukraine editor-in-chief). She collaborates with various socio-political media including zn.ua; nv.ua. She is the author of 7 original fairy tale books for children, and 3 publicist books.

title: Palau Remains Tier 2 in Human Trafficking Report as Prosecutions Stall
body: By L.N. Reklai KOROR, Palau (Oct. 15, 2026) — Palau remains on Tier 2 in the U.S. Department of State’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, a ranking it has held for much of the past two decades, as the government continues to struggle to prosecute traffickers, protect victims and close gaps in laws governing foreign workers. The report recognizes that Palau has increased efforts to fight human trafficking, including identifying more victims, providing temporary work permits to victims and investigating a law enforcement officer suspected of involvement in trafficking crimes. However, the report also points to major shortcomings. For the third consecutive year, Palau did not prosecute or convict any traffickers. The government also lacks a shelter available to trafficking victims and has not prohibited employers or recruitment agencies from charging workers recruitment fees. Palau has been ranked Tier 2 in U.S. trafficking reports since at least 2009, although it was placed on the Tier 2 Watch List in 2021 and 2022 before returning to Tier 2 in 2023. The ranking means the government does not fully meet the minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking but is making significant efforts to meet them. The 2026 report says the government demonstrated overall increasing efforts compared with the previous reporting period, allowing Palau to remain on Tier 2 rather than face a lower ranking. Investigations continue, but prosecutions remain a concern Palau initiated seven human trafficking investigations during the reporting period: one involving sex trafficking and six involving forced labor. That was down from 13 investigations in the previous reporting period. Authorities determined that four potential forced labor cases did not meet the legal definition of trafficking or lacked sufficient evidence. Another case was closed after the suspect was deported. Three forced labor investigations from earlier reporting periods remained open. The report identified inadequate resources, victims’ fear of retaliation and mistrust of authorities as barriers to effective investigations. It also raised concerns about possible official involvement in trafficking. The government investigated one law enforcement officer for alleged complicity in trafficking crimes and suspended the officer without pay. The report said corruption and official complicity continued to be significant concerns that hindered law enforcement efforts. Palau has laws criminalizing sex trafficking and labor trafficking. Under the 2023 Anti-People Smuggling and Trafficking Act, adults’ trafficking cases carry penalties of one to 25 years in prison and fines of up to $125,000. Cases involving child victims carry penalties of two to 25 years in prison and fines of up to $250,000. Despite these laws, the absence of prosecutions and convictions remains one of the clearest signs of the gap between having legal protections and enforcing them. The report also said the absence of cybercrime-related laws has hindered authorities’ ability to prosecute trafficking linked to online scam operations. More victims identified, but protection remains limited The report recorded progress in identifying and assisting trafficking victims. Palau identified seven victims during the reporting period, all foreign nationals. Six were victims of forced labor and one was a victim of sex trafficking. This was an increase from two victims identified in the previous reporting period. The government assisted six victims, compared with two previously, providing legal support, help finding jobs, housing relocation, wellness checks and basic necessities. Government spending on victim assistance also increased slightly, from approximately $2,300 in 2024 to $3,000 in 2025. Authorities granted four temporary work permits and one extended work permit to trafficking victims, compared with one work permit in the previous reporting period. These permits can help victims remain legally employed rather than be forced to return to exploitative working conditions. The report said victims did not have to participate in law enforcement proceedings to receive services. Six victims voluntarily participated in investigations. However, the lack of a government shelter, long-term support services and sufficient funding for victim protection continues to limit the help available to people escaping exploitation. The government, working with a foreign government, continued construction of a national shelter for crime victims, including trafficking victims. Until that shelter becomes available, the report said, the lack of dedicated accommodation remains a major weakness in Palau’s response. Foreign workers remain especially vulnerable The report identifies foreign workers as particularly vulnerable to trafficking in Palau. Foreign nationals account for about one-third of the country’s population of approximately 18,000. Workers with limited education or English-language skills face increased risks, especially when they depend on employers or recruiters for jobs, immigration status and housing. Workers from countries including the Philippines, Bangladesh, Nepal, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea and China may pay thousands of dollars in recruitment fees to secure jobs in Palau. In some cases, workers pay as much as $8,000 before arriving. Some workers are then exploited in domestic service, agriculture, construction, hospitality and food service. Others face forced labor on fishing boats or in illegal online gambling and online scam operations. The report said traffickers sometimes confiscate workers’ passports to prevent them from leaving. Some foreign workers are also vulnerable when they arrive on tourist visas and are told to change to employment visas after reaching Palau. Palauan girls are also exploited in sex trafficking, primarily in Koror and Airai, according to the report. Traffickers may use social media and messaging applications to target potential victims. These risks highlight the importance of effective labor protections, careful recruitment practices and stronger systems for identifying workers who may be experiencing exploitation. Government efforts to address the gaps Despite the continuing problems, the report outlines several steps the government has taken to strengthen its response. The Anti-Human Trafficking Unit coordinates national efforts, leads implementation of the 2022-2025 National Action Plan and has developed an updated plan. A government and nongovernmental organization working group also met to share information about cases and coordinate policies. The government has provided training for law enforcement, labor, immigration and marine officials on identifying victims, particularly in the fishing industry, and addressing challenges in gathering evidence. Officials and victim advocates also received training on trauma-informed care, which focuses on helping victims without causing further harm. The government has continued public awareness activities and operates an anti-trafficking hotline for potential victims. Authorities have also received greater authority to review visa applications, nonresident work permits and foreign investment applications, which the report says could help strengthen immigration controls and reduce trafficking risks. In addition, the government began implementing a system to streamline customs-related financial transactions. The system is intended to help authorities identify fraudulent transactions that may be connected to criminal activity, including trafficking. These steps show that efforts are underway, but the report indicates that more action is needed to produce stronger enforcement and protection outcomes. Recruitment fees and labor protections remain unresolved One of the report’s major concerns is that Palau has not prohibited workers from paying recruitment fees. The government also lacks a formal labor recruitment system, a pre-approval visa process and minimum wage requirements for agricultural and domestic service workers, according to the report. These gaps can leave workers vulnerable to debt, deception and forced labor. The report said the government has not effectively regulated labor recruiters or held them civilly and criminally liable for fraudulent recruitment practices. Although authorities have an informal policy of placing workers with another employer when they experience hardship, the report indicates that stronger formal protections are needed. Public awareness campaigns also have not specifically targeted foreign worker communities considered especially vulnerable to trafficking. The government’s efforts to update its national action plan and strengthen visa reviews provide a foundation for further action. However, the report makes clear that these measures need to be accompanied by stronger recruitment rules, better victim services and effective enforcement. What the ranking means for Palau Tier 2 is not a finding that a country has eliminated trafficking or fully met international standards. It indicates that a government is making significant efforts but still falls short of the minimum requirements. For Palau, the latest report presents a mixed picture: more victims identified, increased assistance and continued work on prevention, but fewer investigations, no new prosecutions or convictions, and continued gaps in shelter services and worker protections. The report’s findings point to the need for Palau to turn its existing laws, training and policy initiatives into measurable results — including successful investigations and prosecutions, stronger protection for victims, and safeguards that prevent workers from being trapped in exploitative jobs. For a country that has remained at Tier 2 for much of the past two decades, the challenge is not simply to maintain its ranking. It is to demonstrate that its efforts are making it harder for traffickers to exploit people and easier for victims to seek help and rebuild their lives. title: Aftermath of Russian attack on Volyn: two injured, businesses damaged, Lutsk left without power
body:
Acting Head of the Volyn Regional Military Administration Roman Romaniuk reported this, according to Ukrinform.
He said that about 20 enemy targets were directed at the Volyn region overnight. Civilian and critical infrastructure was damaged. As a result, as of 8:00 on October 16, 370,000 consumers were without electricity. Restoration work is underway.
“A private business in Manevychi was damaged. Two people were injured, while the whereabouts of five people remain unknown,” the post said.
The official added that a foreign-invested business was damaged in Lutsk, with no casualties reported.
Lutsk City Council Secretary Andrii Razumovskyi reported that the city was left without electricity as a result of the enemy drone attack. Municipal services are operating on backup power sources.
The Lutsk City Council also reported that electric public transport in the city had been temporarily suspended due to damage to the power grid.
The relevant services are working to repair the damage and restore public transport services.
As reported by Ukrinform, six people were killed and 13 injured in a Russian attack on Lutsk on October 14.

title: Palau, Taiwan Discuss Tourism and Ties During Australia Visit
body: By: Laurel Marewibuel CANBERRA, Australia — President Surangel S. Whipps Jr. and a delegation of Palau leaders met with Taiwan’s representative in Australia to discuss ways to increase Taiwanese tourism to Palau and strengthen ties between the two countries. President Whipps Jr. meets Taiwan Ambassador Liang-Yu Wang of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Australia. Photo credit: Office of the President Facebook page. The meeting with Ambassador Liang-Yu Wang of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Australia took place during Whipps’ weeklong state visit to Australia. Discussions focused on attracting more visitors from Taiwan to Palau, which could provide additional business for local hotels, tour operators, restaurants and other businesses that depend on tourism. The two sides also discussed strengthening people-to-people connections through cultural exchange and continued cooperation. The meeting reaffirmed the importance of maintaining close relations between Palau and Taiwan. Preparations for Whipps’ planned visit to Taiwan next week were also discussed. The visit is expected to provide another opportunity for the two sides to explore areas of cooperation, including tourism and closer ties between their people. The meeting took place as part of Palau’s broader diplomatic engagement during the Australia visit. A key event during the trip is the opening of Palau’s first embassy office in Canberra, establishing a permanent diplomatic presence in Australia. The Palau delegation is also meeting with Australian officials to discuss shared priorities and opportunities for cooperation. The engagements reflect Palau’s efforts to expand its diplomatic relationships and pursue opportunities that could support tourism, economic development and the well-being of its people.
