title: How the UAE kept trade flowing and struck new deals during the Iran conflict
body: In this episode of Business Extra , recorded as part of Davos on Air at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai , The National’s Rory Reynolds speaks to Fahad Al Gergawi, Undersecretary at the UAE Ministry of Foreign Trade. As global trade faces growing uncertainty from geopolitical tension and supply chain disruption, the UAE continues to pursue new avenues to strengthen its position as an international trading hub. Mr Al Gergawi discusses how the country has responded to disruption caused by the Iran war, including plans to expand alternative trade corridors and reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz . The conversation also examines the UAE’s expanding network of Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements, and how these trade deals are helping businesses access new markets, attract investment and strengthen economic resilience. Mr Al Gergawi explains how the UAE is navigating an increasingly fragmented global trading environment, including its continuing negotiations with the European Union and efforts to forge new international partnerships. He also shares his outlook for the UAE’s economic recovery, and why long-term planning and adaptability remain central to the country’s trade strategy.

title: 2027: Tompolo Explains Why Oyo Should Stand with Tinubu
body: The Grand Patron of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, High Chief Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, has called on the people of Oyo State to vote massively for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s reelection as one of their own. He made the call as he donated 32 vehicles to the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement in Oyo State for grassroots mobilisation. Speaking through his representative, the Managing Director of Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, Chief Kestin Pondi, at the inauguration of the movement’s Oyo State structure held at the Liberty Stadium in Ibadan yesterday, Tompolo said the vehicles were donated to support the Movement’s campaign, which is aimed at mobilising votes for Tinubu’s re-election and the election of other candidates under the All Progressives Congress (APC). The PBAT Door-to-Door Grand Patron reminded Oyo people that President Tinubu is their son and they should ensure that he returns to office to complete the two-term turn of the south. Tompolo commended the president for the far-reaching reforms in critical sectors, saying that among other positives, the reforms have increased resources available to state governments to pay salaries, pensions and execute major projects. He called on members of the Movement to take the message of the president’s reelection to all parts of the state, stressing that the people of Oyo State should be among those who give Tinubu another four years to consolidate his reforms. “We are here today to tell you that we are coming to join you to canvass for votes across the country for your son, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. What Tompolo is preaching is that Tinubu is doing very well. Tinubu’s reform policies are fantastic. We want you to support President Tinubu’s reelection for him to continue with the good work he is doing,” he said. Also speaking at the rally, the APC governorship candidate for Oyo State, Senator Sharafadeen Abiodun Alli, stated that the Oyo APC put in all efforts to deliver the state. According to him, Oyo State has stayed disconnected from the centre for too long. Alli thanked Tompolo for his donation and for his support for President Tinubu. This is as he called on party members and his supporters to ensure that the vehicles donated by the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement are deployed across the state during the campaigns. He said: “We are very grateful. I want to assure you that we are going to make judicious use of all these vehicles and all other items that you may want to give us or from any other support group. “As far as we are concerned in Oyo State, we have stayed out of the government for too long, and we are sincerely working assiduously to ensure that we take over the mantle of leadership in Oyo State,” he stated. Earlier, the National Coordinator of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, Mr. Sunday Asuku, called on the people of Oyo State, especially the youths, to firmly support Tinubu’s re-election. Asuku described the president’s reforms as necessary for the country’s economic growth and sustained development. He further described the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) as one of the people-oriented policies that has made a positive impact. Asuku urged members of the Movement to take the campaign for President Tinubu’s second term to every nook and cranny of the state.

title: Canadian Coast Guard welcomes final Bay-class vessel into its fleet
body:
The Canadian Coast Guard (CCG) has welcomed the Bay-class search and rescue lifeboat, the CCGS Baie de Gaspé, into its fleet.
This event marks the final dedication of the Bay-class search and rescue lifeboats, all of which were constructed in Canada. The vessel is the 20th lifeboat in the Bay-class series constructed under the Government of Canada's National Shipbuilding Strategy (NSS). It was built by Chantier Naval Forillon, in Gaspé, Québec.
The CCG accepted the high-endurance lifeboat in October 2025. Its homeport is Rivière-au-Renard, Quebec, where it supports search and rescue operations along the Gaspé Peninsula.
The CCG’s new search and rescue lifeboats are specifically designed, equipped, and crewed to respond to incidents at sea. These vessels are self-righting and can operate up to 120 nautical miles from shore, maintaining a maximum 30-minute state of readiness at all times with a typical ability to respond the moment an alert is received, according to the officials.
Through the NSS, the Government of Canada is investing in the renewal of the CCG’s fleet and creating skilled jobs in Canada’s shipbuilding industry and marine sector.
“When lives are at risk on the water, Canadians count on the Canadian Coast Guard to answer the call. Built by the skilled workers at Chantier Naval Forillon in Gaspé, the CCGS Baie de Gaspé is a testament to Québec’s shipbuilding excellence and Canada's ability to build world-class vessels here at home. This twentieth and final Bay Class lifeboat represents an important milestone in protecting Canadians, strengthening our maritime capabilities, and supporting the Canadian workers and industries that help keep our country safe," David J. McGuinty , Minister of National Defense, said.
“Dedicating the Canadian Coast Guard Ship Baie de Gaspé is a proud moment for the Canadian Coast Guard. As the final Bay Class Search and Rescue Lifeboat, it completes a fleet that has transformed our capabilities across the country, and will proudly serve Canadians with reliability, speed, and resilience for decades to come," Kevin Brosseau , Commissioner, Canadian Coast Guard, commented.
In 2018, Chantier Naval Forillon and Hike Metal Products were awarded the construction of four new Bay-class vessels each, in addition to the existing contract awarded in 2015 to build six boats each. The total value of the contracts for these 20 vessels was approximately $180 million.

title: PNCC Warns Palau Residents of Fake Adobe Signature Emails That Could Steal Passwords
body: Scammers impersonate people you know to trick victims into clicking links KOROR, Palau (Oct. 15, 2026) — Residents are being warned about an ongoing phishing scam targeting email users in Palau, where fake document-signing requests designed to look like Adobe Acrobat messages could expose passwords and compromise personal accounts. The Palau National Communications Corporation (PNCC) issued an alert Thursday warning that scammers are sending emails that appear to come from people the recipient knows. The messages may look like legitimate requests to review or sign documents, but clicking the links could allow scammers to steal login information and gain access to accounts. The scam takes advantage of people’s trust in familiar names and their willingness to respond to what appears to be an ordinary work or personal request. PNCC is urging residents to verify unexpected document requests before taking any action, even when an email appears to come from a friend, family member or coworker. Do not click first and ask questions later PNCC advises recipients to call or text the supposed sender using a trusted phone number to confirm whether the document request is genuine. People should not use contact information provided in a suspicious email to verify the message. Residents should also avoid clicking links, opening attachments, scanning codes or replying to suspicious emails. Checking the actual sender’s email address, rather than relying on the displayed name, can help identify messages that may be fraudulent. Another warning sign is a message that pressures the recipient to act immediately. Scammers may use urgent language to make people panic and click before checking whether the request is legitimate. PNCC recommends enabling two-step verification on important accounts. This adds another layer of security and can help prevent unauthorized access even if a password has been stolen. What if you already clicked the link? People who have already clicked a suspicious link, signed a document or entered their personal details should act quickly. PNCC advises them to change their passwords immediately, starting with their email account. Anyone who used a work device or account should notify their company’s information technology team. If financial information was shared, they should contact their bank. A compromised email account can put more than one account at risk, particularly when the same password is used for multiple services or when email is used to reset other account passwords. PNCC also reminded the public that the corporation will never ask customers to provide their passwords, personal identification numbers (PINs) or payment details through links. The alert serves as a reminder that an email bearing a familiar name or the appearance of a trusted service does not automatically mean the request is genuine. Before signing an unexpected document, residents should verify who sent it. A quick phone call could help prevent the loss of account access or the exposure of personal and financial information. Source: Palau National Communications Corporation, public service alert issued Oct. 15, 2026. title: Mozambique’s army is losing a crucial counter-insurgency battle
body:
When terrorists attacked Cabo Delgado nine years ago on 5 October 2017, the Mozambique Defence Armed Forces (FADM) was taken by surprise, despite its three decades of experience fighting armed conflicts inside the country.
Until then, Mozambique had been largely spared the terrorist threats experienced by other African countries and beyond. The FADM had scant control over Cabo Delgado province and was unprepared for a rural guerrilla war imposed by local jihadists with external support. It lacked combat capability, logistics, modern military equipment, air combat assets and military intelligence.
The FADM has since benefitted from substantial external training and efforts to improve logistics and equipment. But this has yet to translate into results on the ground, where communities still suffer inadequate security and human rights violations at the hands of state forces. And it is in these communities that the FADM should be gaining the upper hand against insurgents.
Insurgents’ seizure of district capitals and TotalEnergies subsequent suspension of its US$20 billion gas extraction project in 2021 forced the government to request external support, some of which benefitted the FADM.
The Southern African Development Community Mission in Mozambique (SAMIM) helped the FADM dismantle terrorist bases and neutralise leaders, restore state authority, strengthen maritime security and protect access routes within the province. The Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) helped recover territories key to the gas industry’s logistics and trained the FADM in counter-terrorism, as did the European Union (EU), Algeria, United States (US) and other allies.
Of all these programmes, the EU’s has had the greatest impact, channelling roughly €89 million into training and the acquisition of non-lethal equipment. The EU Training Mission in Mozambique trained over 1 600 military personnel, divided into 11 FADM Quick Reaction Force companies. The courses covered command and control, communication, civil-military cooperation, human rights and international humanitarian law.
Mozambique reactivated its military cooperation with Algeria, focusing on operational training, counter-terrorism and technical capacity building for army personnel. Specialised training of an FADM battalion currently underway in Algeria is expected to include tactical instruction, among other elements.
Through the US’ Joint Combined Exchange Training programme, the FADM receives instruction in small-unit tactics, operational planning, combat medical care and civil protection.
These initiatives are gradually transforming the FADM’s capabilities and increasing the survival rates of military personnel. However, inadequate logistics and equipment remain a major operational weakness, with much of FADM’s gear originating from Russia and China. Military personnel report obsolete and non-functional weaponry, which has led to deaths on the battlefield, and insufficient transport for troops and for evacuating the injured.
In response, the Ministry of National Defence has built partnerships to secure logistics, supplies and equipment for the FADM. In March, an agreement was signed with India to supply defence equipment and transfer technology for the assembly and repair of aircraft, land vehicles and patrol vessels.
In 2024, a defence cooperation agreement with Turkey was ratified by Mozambique’s Council of Ministers to develop an industry focused on military aviation and weapons, combat vehicles and the manufacture of naval assets.
The US is providing $1.5 million for a new programme to strengthen Mozambique’s capacity to manage and secure weapons and ammunition, and to reduce the risk of conventional weapons being diverted to criminal and terrorist groups.
However, the impact of these partnerships has yet to be felt on the ground. Since SAMIM’s withdrawal in mid-2024, the FADM has independently led offensives, patrols along major roads, and established defensive positions to contain terrorists’ advance. But weaknesses are showing.
Terrorist groups that had been confined to remote bases regained momentum and began attacks on major roads to steal food, abduct drivers and passengers, and demand ransoms. Joint police and FADM escorts were introduced, but the insurgents staged deadly ambushes, killing police officers, soldiers and civilians.
Human rights violations are another problem. Mozambican troops have repeatedly been accused of sexually exploiting displaced women, killing civilians suspected of collaborating with terrorist groups and committing war crimes against captured terror suspects. While the EU’s training emphasises human rights, reports of civilians being killed by the FADM continue.
With training provided to the FADM by various countries, the problem of multiple military doctrines hinders a coherent approach to human rights. And Mozambique’s political leadership has not clarified the matter. In his September speech marking the FADM’s 62nd anniversary, none of President Daniel Chapo’s recommendations addressed the need to respect human rights in counter-terrorism operations.
This is where Mozambique is losing the war against terrorism. As long as the FADM fails to gain the support of local communities in Cabo Delgado, the insurgents will keep thriving. They do not need to be militarily superior to government troops, as they are characterised by small, lightly armed bands practising guerrilla warfare.
To survive, they need to hide from government forces, which is made possible by the rough terrain, poor road access and distance from the centres of state power. And they benefit from local communities who agree not to report insurgents to government agents.
Effective counter-insurgency requires government forces to distinguish between active rebels and non-combatant community members. Rather than being targeted or killed by security forces, these community members should be encouraged to cooperate by reporting the insurgents’ presence.
The recent establishment of a counter-terrorism centre offers hope that Mozambique can benefit from interagency coordination to better plan and conduct its counter-insurgency operations. But for this to happen, the FADM must reverse its culture of human rights abuses against communities affected by the insurgency and foster effective civil-military cooperation.
Written by Borges Nhamirre, Researcher, Transnational Threats and Organised Crime, ISS.
Republished with permission from ISS Africa . The original article can be found here .

title: IsDB Group, Nigeria, Cameroon, Others Partner on Devt
body: Sunday Okobi The Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) has moved to strengthen the longstanding partnership between Nigeriaand the IsDB Group to advance cooperation under the IsDB Group Country Engagement Framework (CEF) 2026–2028. The bank disclosed that the move was also to support Nigeria’s development priorities, such as infrastructure, private sector development, Islamic finance, and economic diversification. The action, according to a statement issued and made available to THISDAY by the IsDB Communication Director, Ahmed Abu Ghazeleh, was taken yesterday when Chairman of the IsDB Group, Dr. Muhammad Al Jasser, held a productive bilateral meeting with the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy of the Federal. Republic of Nigeria and IsDB Governor, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, on the margins of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. Dr. Al Jasser expressed appreciation for Nigeria’s continued support for the IsDB Group, and commended the country’s efforts to diversify its economy and enhance competitiveness. He reaffirmed the group’s commitment to supporting Nigeria’s development agenda through the IsDB and its affiliated institutions: the Islamic Corporation for the Development of the Private Sector (ICD), the International Islamic Trade Finance Corporation (ITFC), the Islamic Corporation for the Insurance of Investment and Export Credit (ICIEC), and the IsDB Institute (IsDBi). The two parties reviewed the IsDB Group’s expanding portfolio in Nigeria, and also discussed progress in implementing the CEF, which aims to accelerate economic transformation through infrastructure development, inclusive human capital development, private sector growth, and the expansion of Islamic finance and the halal economy. The meeting also highlighted the approval of six projects across priority sectors, including agriculture, renewable energy, health, infrastructure, and climate resilience. “These projects are expected to make a significant contribution to sustainable growth, economic resilience, and improved livelihoods across the country. “Building on the momentum from the IsDB Group Day held in Lagos earlier this year, the discussions reaffirmed Nigeria and the IsDB Group’s joint commitment to delivering impactful, large-scale development programmes aligned with the country’s long-term development objectives and Agenda 2050,” the statement added. Meanwhile, Al Jasser also met with the Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Ms. Kristalina Georgieva, on the sidelines of the 2026 World Bank–IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok to discuss expanding cooperation in Islamic finance, financial stability, capacity development, and knowledge exchange. The statement disclosed that the discussions reviewed progress under the IsDB–IMF cooperation framework, including joint initiatives in Islamic finance and the forthcoming joint report on Islamic banking and financial stability. “The two leaders also explored opportunities to strengthen collaboration on regional economic analysis, macroeconomic developments, and financial stability, with particular attention to issues affecting IsDB Member Countries,” it added According to the statement, Dr. Al Jasser emphasised the importance of scaling up joint capacity-development programmes through the IsDB Institute and the IMF Middle East Centre for Economics and Finance, building on the institutions’ recent cooperation in Islamic banking, financial regulation, and related policy areas. The meeting reaffirmed IsDB and the IMF’s shared commitment to promoting practical cooperation through joint research, capacity development, policy dialogue, and knowledge-sharing initiatives that support resilient, inclusive, and sustainable economic growth. IsDB and Cameroon Sign EUR 212.35 Million Financing Agreement for Major Transport Project. Also, the statement noted that in Bangkok, Thailand, IsDB and the Republic of Cameroon signed a EUR 212.35 million financing agreement to support the Douala–Bafoussam Road Rehabilitation Project, a major transport initiative covering a critical corridor that connects the country’s Littoral and West regions. The agreement, the statement said, was signed by the Chairman of the IsDB Group, Al Jasser, and Cameroon’s Minister of Economy, Planning and Regional Development and IsDB Governor, Mr. Alamine Ousmane Mey, on the sidelines of the annual meetings in Bangkok. The project aims to enhance regional connectivity, lower transportation costs, facilitate the movement of goods to domestic and international markets through the Port of Douala, and expand access to economic opportunities for communities along the corridor. It includes rehabilitating 218 kilometres of national roads and 108 kilometres of feeder roads, and improving social infrastructure, including classrooms, health centres, water facilities, markets, and agricultural facilities. After the signing ceremony, the two sides held bilateral discussions to explore ways to further strengthen cooperation to support the country’s development priorities. Dr. Al Jasser commended the strong partnership between the IsDB Group and Cameroon, noting that cumulative IsDB Group approvals for the country have surpassed the established target and that the active portfolio spans several sectors, including energy, transport, and agriculture. He reaffirmed the IsDB Group’s commitment to supporting Cameroon’s sustainable and inclusive development agenda. The bank chief emphasised the need to accelerate project implementation to maximise development impact and ensure timely delivery of approved investments. The discussions also reviewed progress in preparing Cameroon’s upcoming Country Engagement. Framework (2027–2030), which is expected to guide future cooperation in priority sectors, including agriculture, energy, water, transport, education, and health. Since Cameroon joined the IsDB in 1977, the IsDB Group has approved US$4.22 billion in financing for the country, reflecting nearly five decades of development cooperation. Also, the IsDB and Benin Republic strengthened the development partnership by signing €326 million in financing agreements. Al Jasser and the Benin Republic Delegate Minister to the Minister of Economy and Finance, in charge of External Resource Mobilisation and Debt Management, Mr. Hugues Oscar Lokossou, disclosed this at a bilateral meeting in Bangkok, which provided the opportunity to discuss Benin’s development priorities and explore avenues for further cooperation, particularly in infrastructure, agriculture, and other sectors. Following the meeting, IsDB and the Republic of Benin signed co-financing agreements for two key development projects, which included the Godomey–Ouidah–Hillacondji Road Capacity Expansion and Upgrading Project, with a total cost of €576.06 million, and will receive €306.89 million in IsDB financing to improve road safety and efficiency, reduce travel times and transport costs, and strengthen regional connectivity and trade along the Abidjan–Lagos corridor. “The Sustainable Intensification of Legume-Based Systems for Soil Fertility, Agricultural Resilience, and Food Security Project, with a total cost of €20.70 million, will receive €19.17 million in IsDB financing to promote sustainable legume-based agriculture, improve soil fertility, strengthen food security, and enhance climate resilience across five development poles,” the statement added. Al Jasser, according to the statement, reaffirmed the IsDB Group’s commitment to its longstanding partnership with the Republic of Benin, emphasizing the importance of continued collaboration to advance sustainable development and deliver tangible benefits to communities.

title: Czech Prime Minister Babis rails against EU budget support for Ukraine
body:
Editor's note: The story has been expanded with additional comments made by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis expressed his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine in its next seven-year budget, in comments made to journalists at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels.
The EU operates on a seven-year budget cycle that needs to be unanimously agreed upon, and leaders hope to reach consensus on the 2028-2034 budget before the end of the year, as 2027 will be a bumper year for elections across the bloc.
While consensus on the budget as a whole remains out of reach, support for Ukraine seemed like a consensus issue until Babis' latest comments.
"I don't like that there are 100 billion euros ($112 billion) from the European budget for Ukraine, that this money should be borrowed," Babis said.
"It should not be in the multi-year financial framework, where member states don't have enough money," he added.
The 100 billion euros figure is already outdated, reflecting the amount initially proposed for the budget by the European Commission earlier in the year.
That figure was reduced to 89 billion euros ($100 billion) in June as part of a first compromise proposal, and it remained unchanged in the second and latest compromise , published Oct. 10.
"In any case, Czechia will not guarantee for it," Babis added.
Surprising in the other direction was Babis' criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump, after portraying himself as aligned with Trump for several years. "Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin , and we have to do something," Babis said, echoing President Volodymyr Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S. against Ukraine. Babis said the day before that Europe needs to agree on how to proceed with issues such as peace talks, given that at the moment, "we are completely out." His turn on Trump brings Babis closer to the European mainstream, with many EU leaders not holding back in condemning the U.S. president for his latest overtures towards Moscow.

title: Abu Dhabi's IMI rejects UK Ofcom report into Telegraph bid
body: International Media Investments (IMI) has rejected Ofcom’s report into RedBird IMI’s bid for The Telegraph , criticising its “methodology, reasoning and conclusions which were reached before the evidence was examined”. The British media regulator’s report, which has been released by the UK's Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, followed a protracted takeover saga involving the British newspaper group which ended when it was acquired by German media conglomerate Axel Springer in April. The report was part of an initial review by Ofcom but that was halted after Redbird IMI sold the newspaper group at a profit. While the purpose of the report was the actual acquisition, the UK government chose to publish the report without the completion of the full process. IMI, the Abu Dhabi-based media company which was part of a joint venture with RedBird bidding for The Telegraph , responded to the report with a statement criticising the regulator’s investigation and defending the editorial independence of its titles. IMI’s media assets include The National and Sky News Arabia. In a statement released on Friday, IMI said: “Ofcom was tasked with assessing a commercial media company. It failed to do so. In an astonishing admission written into the report itself, Ofcom states that it was ‘not necessary to rely on information about the reported past behaviour of IMI associated businesses’. In plain English: a public regulator tasked with evaluating IMI admitted on the record that it ignored IMI’s actual track record to reach its verdict.” The Culture Secretary Lisa ​Nandy later ⁠said ⁠she would ​not refer Axel Springer's ⁠purchase of the Telegraph to a ⁠more detailed competition investigation and the government's interest in the takeover would lapse ‌as a result ⁠of her ​decision. 'Undermining investor confidence' A respected British business leader and politician added his voice to IMI's criticism of the publication of the Ofcom report. "Britain cannot spend half its time courting investment from the Gulf and the other half putting up barriers when that investment arrives," billionaire property developer Nick Candy and treasurer of the Reform Party told The National . "The Government's handling of the RedBird IMI deal was a total disaster and a missed opportunity for British business, and revisiting a two-year-old report now only serves to undermine international investor confidence further. If we want Britain to be taken seriously as a destination for global capital, we need to start acting like it." For its part, IMI accused Ofcom of using “an arbitrary and biased set of assumptions, conflating the commercial interests of a private company with the conduct of a sovereign state”. “It is not the role of a British media regulator to adjudicate the laws and governance of foreign nations,” IMI added in its statement. IMI pointed out that Ofcom “gave no weight” to the company’s legally binding undertakings – notably never to influence The Telegraph’s editorial decisions. An Independent Editorial Trust would have had veto power over the appointment and removal of the Telegraph’s Editor-in-Chief. Indeed, IMI noted, Ofcom’s report made no findings of editorial interference against the company. Ofcom accepted The National’s strong compliance record with the Editors’ Code of Practice, that there have been no IPSO rulings against it, and that every historical allegation regarding its newsroom predates IMI’s ownership. Furthermore, Ofcom “admits that there appears to be a viable commercial incentive and rationale for RedBird IMI’s acquisition of the Telegraph ”. IMI also criticised the way the Ofcom report was presented. “Regulatory decisions in British media have historically been decided on conduct, binding commitments, and commercial incentives. The RedBird IMI bid was not judged on the facts or on IMI’s track record. It was judged on its origin and not its conduct. IMI encourages investors to read the report thoroughly. “Allegations are not findings. Association is not control. Speculation is not evidence. IMI rejects any suggestion that it has ever interfered, or would ever interfere, in the editorial independence of its media outlets.”

title: Op-Ed| An election without a visible contest? South Sudan’s December test
body: An election should gradually make political choice visible. Citizens should begin to recognize those seeking office, understand their proposals, and question their ability to govern. With South Sudan’s general elections scheduled for 22 December 2026, concern about limited candidate visibility deserves serious attention. However, limited visibility does not prove that elections will be cancelled, and it would be inaccurate to claim that every prospective candidate is silent. The available evidence presents a more complicated picture: some political activity is taking place, but the breadth, accessibility and competitiveness of the emerging contest remain uncertain. The central question is whether preparations will give citizens a meaningful choice across the country, rather than merely produce a ballot on the appointed date. On 3 October, Radio Tamazuj reported that the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement planned to open internal nominations from 5 to 9 October. The report described the SPLM as the most visible party in electoral preparations and noted that other parties had not announced comparable nationwide candidate-selection activities. This supports concern about uneven political visibility, rather than a conclusion that no preparation exists. The distinction between party selection and formal candidacy is essential. Collecting a party’s nomination form does not mean an aspirant has been formally accepted by the National Elections Commission. Internal selection, electoral nomination and public campaigning are separate stages. Conflating them can exaggerate readiness and leave citizens uncertain about who will actually appear on the ballot. The SPLM itself distinguished its internal exercise from the national electoral process. There is also evidence of opposition political activity. On 8 October, Kornelio Kon publicly denied withdrawing his presidential bid after a separate statement circulated claiming that he had abandoned the race. That episode demonstrates that prospective competitors are speaking, while exposing how contradictory information can confuse voters. Announcements of political intention must be verified, particularly when they concern withdrawal, disqualification or endorsement. Public discussion should therefore distinguish an aspirant from an officially nominated candidate. Until the relevant electoral procedures establish eligibility and nomination status, declaring an intention to contest should not be presented as confirmation of a place on the ballot. Clear terminology protects the public from misunderstanding the stage the election has reached. The absence of large rallies is also an imperfect measure of readiness. Parties may organize internally before a formal campaign period, while public engagement can occur through radio, meetings and community networks. Nevertheless, citizens need authoritative information about the timetable. Without clear dates for nominations, campaigning and polling, they cannot judge whether apparent quietness reflects a lawful sequence, delayed preparation or restricted political space. The National Elections Commission’s own mandate includes candidate nomination, campaign regulation, civic education and electoral dispute resolution. Its public information recognizes citizens’ rights to nominate, seek nomination and express their choice through a secret ballot. These responsibilities place a substantial obligation on the commission to explain how political participation will work in practice. For voters, the practical questions are straightforward. Who is eligible to contest? When will nominations be completed? Where can verified candidate information be obtained? How can an exclusion be challenged? When may candidates campaign, and what protections apply? An election becomes more credible when institutions answer these questions consistently and in languages communities understand. Candidate visibility also depends on freedom of movement. On 13 October, Radio Tamazuj reported Kon’s allegation that security officials prevented him from boarding a flight from Juba to Wau without providing a written explanation. His spokesperson said the trip included meeting alliance members and supporters. The outlet reported that the National Security Service spokesperson could not immediately be reached for comment. The allegation therefore requires an official response and clarification; it should not be presented as a judicially established finding. [5] The broader issue is significant. If political actors cannot travel predictably and lawfully, citizens outside the capital may hear little from potential competitors. An apparently quiet electoral environment can reflect barriers to participation rather than a lack of ambition. Authorities should explain restrictions transparently, apply lawful rules consistently and provide accessible remedies where decisions are challenged. Political parties themselves also bear responsibility. They should explain their selection procedures, communicate their positions and maintain contact with communities. Parties cannot demand public confidence while leaving voters uncertain about their leadership, policies and intentions. Where internal disputes or limited resources affect preparation, honest communication is more useful than silence. Visibility, however, should be judged by substance. Posters, convoys and crowded meetings do not establish that citizens have received a credible programme for government. Candidates should explain how they would address insecurity, public finances, food production, education, health services and corruption. They should also identify what their office can realistically deliver and how the public could assess their performance. Media access is therefore central to electoral competition. A candidate with limited resources may reach communities through local radio more effectively than through expensive travel. Broadcasters should provide fair opportunities for political debate, distinguish reporting from paid promotion and correct false information promptly. Citizens need opportunities to compare proposals, including from women, young people and independent aspirants. Security and civic freedoms remain major concerns. In July, the South Sudan Human Rights Defenders Network warned that shrinking civic and political space could undermine the credibility of the December elections. This was the organization’s assessment, but its relevance is clear: competition requires people to speak, associate and assemble without intimidation. Candidate visibility cannot be separated from the conditions under which candidates and supporters operate. Institutional preparation is also underway. The NEC reported training state election officials in voter registration on 2 September. That is a useful step, although training alone does not establish that registration, nominations and the remaining electoral stages can be completed successfully. Each phase requires resources, realistic scheduling and public verification. Regional diplomacy similarly combines support with demands for safeguards. The African Union’s declaration of 29 September called for a feasible, consensual and time-bound electoral roadmap, adequate financing and wider political inclusion. These requirements underline the difference between endorsing the goal of elections and confirming operational readiness. Will elections take place on 22 December? The public record reviewed for this article does not justify a definitive prediction. Preparations and political declarations demonstrate an intention to proceed. They do not remove uncertainty about implementation, participation, or credibility. Equally, limited public campaigning is insufficient evidence that the vote will inevitably be postponed. The coming weeks should provide measurable answers. Citizens should see clear nomination procedures, verified information about contestants, accessible registration arrangements and lawful opportunities for political engagement. Electoral authorities should publish progress against deadlines, while political parties explain their readiness and security institutions protect participation impartially. South Sudan’s long wait for elections should end with an informed electorate exercising a meaningful choice. The country needs more than candidates becoming visible; it needs a fair opportunity for different candidates to be seen, heard and questioned. December’s credibility will depend on whether institutions turn that opportunity into a reality for citizens beyond the political centre. The writer is a researcher and writer specializing in humanitarian and development issues in South Sudan, holding a degree in Sociology and Political Science from the Catholic University of Eastern Africa and a Master’s in Peace and Development Studies from the University of Juba. He can be reached via mogtomloyo@yahoo.co.uk . The views expressed in ‘opinion’ articles published by Radio Tamazuj are solely those of the writer. The veracity of any claims made is the responsibility of the author, not Radio Tamazuj. The post Op-Ed| An election without a visible contest? South Sudan’s December test appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Government agrees 60 million euro fuel-price relief package, rejects Finns Party proposal
body:
The package includes lower vehicle tax, a higher cap on commuting expense deductions as well as subsidies for businesses in transport, agriculture and forestry.
The government has reached an agreement on a 60 million euro package aimed at easing the impact of rising fuel prices.
Environment and Climate Minister Sari Multala (NCP) confirmed to reporters in Parliament on Thursday that a deal had been agreed, noting that all governing parties support the package as a whole.
The measures include a reduction in vehicle tax, an increase in the maximum commuting expense deduction, and fuel subsidies for the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors.
The government has also agreed to introduce flexibilities in the fuel distribution obligation, which sets requirements for the share of renewable fuels blended into transport fuels. The limits on cross-fulfilment and over-compliance will both rise from 30 percent to 100 percent, allowing companies to meet their obligations more cost-effectively, the government said.
However, the government has not adopted the broader reduction in the distribution obligation advocated by the Finns Party.
The package consists of: 30 million euros for fuel subsidies for businesses in the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors, 20 million euros to reduce vehicle tax, up from the previously agreed 10 million euros, and 10 million euros to raise the maximum commuting expense deduction from 7,000 euros to 7,800 euros in 2027.
Multala acknowledged that the measures would have only a limited impact on consumers’ fuel costs.
"We cannot afford to make tax cuts worth hundreds of millions, for example," she said.
According to a press release , published by the ministry on Friday, the 60 million euro package will be funded from within the government's spending limits.
Of the total, 40 million euros will be redirected from funding for biogenic carbon capture capacity that will go unused this year, with the remaining 20 million euros coming from the cutting of funding for basic transport infrastructure management.
The Finns Party has criticised the agreement, arguing that the package should have gone further in easing the fuel distribution obligation to bring down prices at the pump.
Jani Mäkelä , chair of the Finns Party parliamentary group, said his party had accepted the agreement because "some solution had to be found".
"The government seemed to be quite incapable of acting in this matter, and the prime minister also had to save face," Mäkelä said.
Mäkelä further argued that easing the distribution obligation, as proposed by his party, could have reduced fuel prices at the pump by a significant amount.
He said the fact that the government had agreed on the package was not sufficient reason to rule out that option.
"If the distribution obligation cannot be compromised in a situation where the price of fuel is so high, it reflects a certain mindset," Mäkelä said.
Multala was asked whether the Finns Party could have been persuaded to accept the agreement if the funding had come from money allocated to climate action. She replied that the question should be put to the party itself.
Speaking in Brussels on the sidelines of an EU meeting, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) said that easing the distribution obligation would not have brought down fuel prices quickly.
"Being in the government means that when we are making decisions together, sometimes it is difficult to defend them, even if we have made the decision ourselves," Orpo said.
He stressed that the government had little room for manoeuvre during the negotiations, but noted he was pleased that the money had been directed towards commuters and professional transport.
Fuel prices are also on the agenda at the EU summit. Orpo said high prices at the pump were linked to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine.
Hanna Kalenoja , a leading transport expert at the Central Chamber of Commerce, said the measures would not directly affect petrol and diesel prices.
Instead, they would ease costs for some motorists and businesses, but not all, she noted.
The vehicle tax reduction will be reflected in the tax bills of eligible car and van owners, rather than at the petrol station.
For example, a household whose vehicle tax period began in July would not see the reduction until its next tax period in July next year, Kalenoja said.
She estimated that the vehicle tax cut would save eligible motorists around 12 euros per year. The reduction applies to older cars and vans.
The increase in the maximum commuting expense deduction, meanwhile, could benefit people with high travel costs.
The government also plans to raise the maximum deduction, with Kalenoja estimating that the change would benefit people who commute more than 60 kilometres.
The deduction can be adjusted through a revised tax card, although eligibility depends on the circumstances of the commute. In some cases, expenses can be deducted based on the use of a private car if public transport is not reasonably accessible.
The fuel subsidies are aimed at businesses in the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors. A similar subsidy was made available retrospectively through the State Treasury in 2022.
Kalenoja said she was largely relieved by the government's decision, particularly because it did not ease the distribution obligation.
The requirement sets the minimum share of renewable fuels that must be included in transport fuels. Reducing it would lower the share of low-emission biofuels.
According to experts, easing the obligation would not necessarily have an immediate impact on pump prices. Kalenoja also warned that it could undermine planned investments in the biogas sector.
"It is a big relief that the decision not to lower the distribution obligation was made now," she said.
The Confederation of Finnish Industries (EK) also welcomed the decision in a statement on Thursday.
However, Kalenoja said it was disappointing that the government had not included a reduction in diesel excise duty in the package.

title: Former NPA Boss Dabo, Resigns as APC Chairman, Dumps Party
body: Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano The Caucus Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Dambatta Local Government Area of Kano State, Aminu Dabo, has resigned from the ruling party. Dabo, a former Managing Director of the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), resigned as both caucus chairman and as a member of the party with immediate effect. According to a press statement signed by his media and publicity aide, Audu Usman, Dabo is yet to announce his next political move. In his resignation letter dated October 7, 2026, and addressed to the APC Chairman of Dambatta Gabas Ward, Dambatta Local Government, Dabo said the decision followed “careful consideration of my personal reasons and future endeavours.” “I remain grateful for the cordial relationship I enjoyed and appreciative of the experience gained during my time of service,” he said, thanking the party leadership for the opportunity and confidence reposed in him. “I sincerely appreciate the support and opportunity I have received from the party leadership,” the letter added.

title: Palau Deploys Its First Two Spotter Buoys to Improve Ocean Monitoring
body: Palau has deployed its first two Spotter buoys, expanding access to real-time ocean observations and strengthening the country’s capacity for marine research, ocean monitoring, and public awareness of ocean conditions. The two buoys are deployed in Ngarchelong Northern Lagoon and Koror Western Lagoon. Their deployment provides new opportunities to collect and access valuable data about Palau’s surrounding waters. The Spotter buoys were provided by the Pacific Islands Ocean Observing System (PacIOOS) through a collaboration with the Coral Reef Research Foundation (CRRF), Ngarchelong State Government, and Koror State Government. The buoys collect ocean data, including significant wave height, wave period and direction, barometric pressure, and sea surface temperature. These observations can help researchers better understand ocean conditions and support efforts to improve public awareness of changing sea and weather conditions. The data from both buoys are publicly accessible online, allowing researchers, local communities, educators, and other interested users to explore ocean observations. The public can access the data through the following links: Ngarchelong Northern Lagoon: http://spotter.sofarocean.com/public/SPOT-32531C Koror Western Lagoon: http://spotter.sofarocean.com/public/SPOT-32528C The deployment of these two buoys marks an important step toward strengthening Palau’s ocean monitoring capabilities and making marine data more accessible. The observations can support scientific research, education, and informed decision-making related to Palau’s marine environment. The post Palau Deploys Its First Two Spotter Buoys to Improve Ocean Monitoring appeared first on Island Times News .

title: Russian strikes on Kharkiv kill three, injure seven
body:
Ukrinform reports this, citing local authorities.
“Two enemy strikes have been recorded in the city – one in the Shevchenkivskyi district, where reports of casualties are coming in. The second was in the Industrialnyi district. The consequences are being clarified,” Mayor Ihor Terekhov said.
Meanwhile, Kharkiv Regional Military Administration Head Oleh Syniehubov reported that three people had been killed. Five people were injured and are receiving all necessary medical assistance.
Later, Syniehubov reported that two more people had been injured in the Shevchenkivskyi district, bringing the total number of casualties to seven.
All emergency services are working at the site of the attack.
According to Syniehubov, the strike in the Industrialnyi district caused a fire.
As reported, in the evening of October 12, Russian forces launched missile strikes on two districts of Kharkiv. Four people were killed and 41 injured in the Kholodnohirskyi district.

title: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
body: The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed. The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service. Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of ‌Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. A person in Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday, October 15, that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). US pressures Ukraine over refinery attacks The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections. But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz. In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior US official said: “No such request was ever made by the president.” The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request. Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the US Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone. Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones. Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, said on X on Wednesday that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment. Decline in relations Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on October 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv’s continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop. The US delegation also explained Washington’s decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow’s stance on peace talks. That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to ​US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict. In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Trump criticized each other, with Zelenskiy calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal “weak.” Trump called for elections in Ukraine and Zelenskiy’s ouster. Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. Trump said on Tuesday Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Following the move to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Tuesday and Wednesday to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision. The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft ​for missile-warning missions and a spy ​constellation for the National Reconnaissance ⁠Office, Reuters reported in 2024. – Rappler.com

title: MPB Calls for Unity Among Veterans as Pensioners Protest in Abuja
body: Linus Aleke in Abuja The Chairman of the Military Pensions Board (MPB), Air Vice Marshal Mikail Abdulraheem, has urged military veterans to unite under a common platform to strengthen their advocacy for improved pensions and welfare. Abdulraheem made the call at a press conference following a meeting with protesting military pensioners in Abuja. He explained that the board was bound by the legal framework governing military pension administration and could not act outside its provisions. He advised pensioners seeking changes to existing legislation to approach the National Assembly. The chairman also urged veterans to overcome divisions within their ranks, noting that a united association would be better positioned to influence government policies on pensions and other welfare matters. “Veterans should form a very strong, cohesive body that can speak with one voice,” he said, adding that political leaders and presidential aspirants should give due consideration to their concerns, particularly during election periods. Abdulraheem further appealed to journalists to verify allegations concerning the board before publication, warning that unsubstantiated reports could undermine public confidence in the institution and jeopardise the interests of military retirees. “Whenever you hear something negative about the board, please do not be in a hurry to publish. Verify it with the board, and we are ready to speak to you,” he said. He stressed that responsible reporting was essential to protecting the board’s credibility and the pension interests of serving personnel who would eventually retire. “I want you to understand that I am a son of a veteran. I will become a veteran myself in the future. If I cheat veterans today, I will also be affecting myself because I will eventually belong to the same community. It is therefore not in my interest to deny anyone what is legitimately due to them. However, we must be guided by the law. “There are situations where people may have strong feelings about an issue, but the law provides the procedure that must be followed. I appeal to everyone to approach this matter with an open mind. Let us discuss the specific issues raised in the letter before moving on to other matters. “The National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission was also invited to provide clarification so that the relevant calculations and applicable provisions could be examined transparently. The board is guided by the relevant pension legislation, including the applicable provisions of the Pension Reform Act. We want the issues to be discussed openly and resolved based on the facts and the law,” he said. A military veteran, Master Warrant Officer Sadura Augustine, said the pensioners had visited the board’s headquarters to discuss issues affecting military retirees and seek clarification on their pensions. “The issue before us concerns the consequential adjustment and the amounts received by pensioners. We believe in transparency and access to information. The National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission has a salary structure relevant to pension computation, and we want to understand how it was applied in our case. “Our concern is that the announced percentages do not appear to correspond with the increases received by some pensioners. We want to understand our gross pension entitlements and how the adjustments were calculated to arrive at the amounts we are now receiving,” he said.

title: Palau Swimmers Win Five Matches in Taiwan-Palau Exchange
body: By: Laurel Marewibuel KOROR, Palau – Thirteen members of the Palau National Swim Team competed with students from Taiwan’s Central Police University Department of Maritime Police in a friendly swimming exchange Oct. 8, winning five of six matches, according to Elaine of the Taiwan Embassy. The program included two spirited 500-meter relay races. Palau won the first, a matchup between the Palau National Swim Team and the Taiwan students. For the second race, swimmers from both sides were divided into two combined teams. Elaine said the contest remained close from start to finish. “We had six matches in total, and Palau won five of them!” she said. “But every match was really competitive and exciting. It definitely shows how well pickleball has developed in Palau!” The exchange also included a practical demonstration of rescue skills. The maritime police students showed participants how to perform unassisted rescue towing, then divided them into groups to practice the technique. Deputy Director-General Hsu Ching-chih of Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration presented certificates of participation and gifts to members of the Palau National Swim Team at the close of the event. Elaine said the competition highlighted the swimmers’ involvement and the excitement of the matches. She also praised government officials for supporting sports and encouraging people to remain active. “It’s also great to see government officials actively promoting sports and encouraging people to stay active!” she said. Organizers prepared new pickleballs as prizes, with the aim of encouraging participants to continue playing after the tournament. “We also prepared brand-new pickleballs as prizes, hoping to encourage everyone to keep playing and stay active even after the tournament!” Elaine said. The event combined athletic competition with hands-on instruction, bringing the Palauan swimmers and Taiwanese maritime police students together in the pool and in rescue-skills practice. Elaine’s remarks described an exchange marked by close races, participation from both groups and an effort to encourage continued activity. The post Palau Swimmers Win Five Matches in Taiwan-Palau Exchange appeared first on Island Times News .

title: Midterms 2026: What Comes Next for the US and Europe?
body:
The US will elect a new House of Representatives and a third of the members of the Senate in its midterm elections on 3 November. For President Donald Trump a lot is at stake: if the Republicans lose their majority in Congress it will be far more difficult for him to pursue his policies. Europe’s press discusses the ramifications of the midterms for the US, Ukraine and Europe.
More stringent domestic controls on the way
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
El País (Spain) predicts there will be a change of course after 3 November:
“History shows that voters often punish the president’s party in mid-term elections. … This year, the Democrats are considered clear favourites to win the House of Representatives while the race for the Senate is too close to call. ... Government oversight and accountability will then be far more frequent and stringent, and foreign policy decisions will become more complex. ... Congress established the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency by law and it is the only body that can attach conditions to its budget or hold officials to account in the event of abuse. ... On 3 November, Americans will decide a large part of Washington’s political agenda.”
Trump could attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the election result, US expert Lauric Henneton (France) writes in Le Monde:
“While Trump may fail to overturn the election result, he could succeed in reviving the narrative of a stolen election. A narrative fuelled by images, social media, investigations, legal challenges, refused election certifications and judges – who are inevitably perceived as politically biased. ... Trump is unlikely to be able to ‘steal’ the midterm elections. He could, however, attempt to convince millions of Americans that they were stolen from him, delegitimise the Democratic majority for two years, further erode electoral legitimacy, and turn 2028 into an election of revenge.”
Radio Kommersant FM (Russia) suspects Europe is pursuing the following strategy:
“One gets the impression that both Kyiv and the leaders of the key EU countries have, in effect, interfered in the US election campaign and, with their stance on Trump, are highlighting the failure of his policies towards Europe with the goal of bringing about a victory for the Democrats. It seems they are simply hoping to weather out the storm with this unpredictable politician who is inclined to make compromises with Moscow and wait until November 2028 in the hope that a Democratic candidate will win the next presidential election and the halcyon days of Joe Biden will return, when the US, Europe and Ukraine stood united against the Kremlin.”
Making voters believe Zelensky is the obstacle
Trump is targeting his own voter base with this announcement of a partial ceasefire, opposition news website Vot Tak believes (Russia) :
“This ‘energy truce’ conveys the impression that the situation is under control, while the allegations against Zelensky will serve as an excuse should the measures fail to produce the desired result. Trump does not need to convince everyone that Ukraine is the cause of the crisis, his aim is more modest and easier to achieve – he wants to give a sufficient number of disgruntled Republican voters a reason to believe that he is trying to resolve the situation but that someone is standing in his way.”
A Republican defeat could lead to major upheavals in foreign policy, former World Bank economist István Dobozi explains in Népszabadság (Hungary):
“If he suffers a crushing defeat, Trump might conclude that in the remaining time of his presidency he should no longer focus on minimising the short-term domestic costs, but rather on maximising his legacy in global politics. After 3 November, the US and the world could well wake up to a Trump who is politically weakened in the US and more unpredictable than ever, and whose foreign policy is focused on boosting his historical self-image. This could be particularly dangerous in the case of Iran.”

title: Russian FM Lavrov to visit Iran next week for mutual talks
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Russian Foreign Ministry on Friday announced that Sergey Lavrov will pay a working visit to Tehran on October 19 to meet and hold talks with his Iranian counterpart Seyyed Abbas Araghchi.
Earlier, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met with his Russian counterpart in Turkmenistan on the sidelines of Commonwealth Independent States (CIS) meeting on October 09.

title: Saab, FMV and the Swedish Armed Forces launch LUUV
body: Less than one year after contract award, Saab, the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Armed Forces have successfully developed, built and launched a demonstrator for a Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (LUUV). Saab press release Developed at pace and according to plan, the demonstrator has progressed from concept to a fully functional vehicle. Following successful sea trials, the first phase of the project has been completed. The next phase is expected to focus on developing more advanced capabilities. The results will support the continued development of software, sensors and autonomous functions, while also contributing to future product development. The vehicle illustrates how close collaboration between industry and government authorities can significantly reduce the time from identifying an operational need to testing a new capability. “This project demonstrates how new technologies can be rapidly translated into practical operational value. The uncrewed underwater vehicle can contribute to increased endurance, enhanced situational awareness and strengthened underwater capabilities. The fact that we have also been able to develop and test the system in such a short timeframe demonstrates the strength of the collaboration between the Swedish Armed Forces, FMV and Saab,” says Mats Wicksell, head of Saab’s business area Naval. The demonstrator has been developed to support the development and evaluation of future underwater capabilities and to enable operations alongside existing naval platforms, such as submarines. The rapid development has been enabled by Saab’s software-centric approach and the integration of Autonomous Ocean Core, Saab’s autonomous control system that provides surface and subsurface vehicles with autonomous capabilities. Combined with Swedish expertise in submarine design and sensor integration, this has made it possible to take the project swiftly from concept to sea trials. The LUUV project builds on Saab’s earlier investments and work in autonomous underwater systems and is now led by FMV in cooperation with the Swedish Armed Forces and Saab. The project provides a basis for Swedish authorities’ decisions regarding the future acquisition and operational use of autonomous underwater systems. -End- The post Saab, FMV and the Swedish Armed Forces launch LUUV appeared first on Naval News .

title: No kids, no apologies: Why Filipino women are opting out of motherhood
body:
An expert says the 'era of high fertility' that drove the country to overpopulation is over
R ubie Montejo was 24 years old and financially struggling as a call center agent when she first considered not having children.
âI was questioning a lot of my decisions and what direction to take with my career,â she said in a mix of English and Filipino. âAnd then, I thought to myself, I don't think I wanna involve another human being in this life when I have so many questions and confusion myself.â
She eventually told her mother about her decision and was met with unexpected support. However, things were different outside her home in the province.
Her neighbors voiced familiar warnings â cautioning Montejo that she would face regret, solitude, and lack of support from her would-have-been children in her old age.
â[Not having children] wasn't that normal before, especially if you grew up in the province as I did. Women were expected to, you know, marry at a certain age and then bear children after or before their 30s,â Montejo recalled.
But with her mother backing her choice, she gradually gained confidence. Now a 33-year-old, single, social media strategist, Montejo has fully embraced a child-free lifestyle.
âI could imagine [then] that it would be so much more difficult if a child were involved [in my life],â she said.
32-year-old Bea (not her real name) decided to have one child with her husband of three years and plans to stop there, despite relatives urging them to have one more so the child feels less lonely.
She explained that restructuring their existing savings would be a hassle if they had a second child. âIt brings more happiness to be able to provide the comfortable life you can give your child,â Bea said in a mix of English and Filipino.
The number of children born per woman has steadily declined over three decades, dropping to a historic low in 2025.
In the past few years, more and more women like Montejo and Bea have openly decided to limit childbearing.
Back in 1993, the total fertility rate â the average number of children born to a woman during her lifetime â showed that women favored having around four children.
The figure gradually decreased to three in 2013, then sharply declined in 2017. By 2023, the Philippinesâ fertility rate fell to 1.9, for the first time falling below the 2.1 replacement threshold needed to maintain a stable population.
The 2.1 replacement rate ensures two children replace their parents , with a 0.1 buffer for childlessness or early mortality. When a country slips below this threshold, the population declines in the next generation.
In 2025, the country had a record-low fertility rate of 1.7, showing that Filipino women now give birth to approximately one child. For many others, they even choose to have none at all.
Although the Philippines remains within the working-age demographic range, its population has begun to resemble those of Asian neighbors such as Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, which are already aging.
Compared to these countries, the Philippines remains in transition. The Commission on Population and Development (CPD) expects the country to become an aging society by 2028, when Filipinos aged 65 and above reach 7% of the population.
The World Health Organization classifies a country as an âaging societyâ when the proportion of older people reaches this threshold.
Jose Ramon Albert, senior research fellow at the Philippine Institute of Development Studies (PIDS), said this new pattern is gradually displacing the longstanding concern of overpopulation.
âPhilippine population policy was built around one fear: that population growth would outrun the economy's capacity to feed, educate, and employ people. The [data] tells us that the era of high fertility is over,â he told Rappler.
Mylin Quiray, Information Management and Communications Division chief of CPD, enumerated changing marriage patterns, increasing contraceptive use, declining number of desired children, and child health and survival as some of the top reasons for the trend.
However, she pointed to womenâs socioeconomic status as the main driver.
âThey're employed, they're educated â so the delay in fertility is happening,â she said.
Albert noted that as women have begun to outperform men in schools and stepped into diverse workforce roles, marriage and parenthood may become lower priorities for them.
Jireh Ramos, a 29-year-old law student who has been married for five years, opted for a child-free lifestyle to focus on higher education.
âI'm very intentional with the life I'm building right now. I have a career, I have law school, I have relationships, and I have a lot of things I want to experience in my life,â she said.
Ramos also feels content with their current routine at home: she studies for hours in a separate work room from her husbandâs, shoots videos as a content creator on TikTok with 61,000 followers, takes breaks, and catches up with her husband at the end of the day.
Besides the need to focus on their own economic well-being, women also face pressure from rising household living costs, said Albert.
âCan you really blame people for deciding against having children or maybe deciding just to have one child instead of, like, three â when everything is getting more expensive while [salaries] in the Philippines do not keep up with inflation?â said Montejo.
Ramos also echoed the sentiment about costs and said, âKids, in this economy, right? Itâs perfectly valid. It really is expensive [to raise a child].â
Providing for a child's essential needs, wants, education, and development requires a substantial portion of a household's financial resources.
Bea revealed they spend P30,000 to P40,000 per month for their one-year-oldâs needs. âMilk, diapers, vaccines, regular check-ups, and baby essentialsâ¦if you include his play school, thatâs probably around P40,000 per month,â she said.
Beyond monthly expenses, some couples already plan to set aside P3â5 million for one childâs education â from preschool through college â while accounting for rising tuition over the years.
The Philippines also saw a shifting pattern in marriage â or rather, a decreasing need for it.
In the Philippine Statistics Authorityâs (PSA) 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey, 42.7% of women aged 15-49 and in childbearing age have never married.
In the PSAâs separate 2023 data , the number of registered marriages in the country has continued to fall since 2022.
Albert noted that family formation itself has changed â couples now delay marriage, do not marry at all, or cohabit instead. âFor many women, marriage is no longer an economic necessity, and childbearing is a choice weighed against other goals,â he said.
In 2020, common-law or live-in marital arrangements among households rose to 14.7% in 2020 from 9.2% in 2015.
As more opportunities open for women, Albert added that entering into marriage could also become less appealing without a âlegal exitâ such as divorce, so women would rather explore other forms of relationships.
Social media has also broadened exposure to alternative life paths centered on education, career, travel, or other forms of family formation through influencers.
Like Ramos, Montejo also does content on TikTok and openly discusses her childfree lifestyle. In one reel, she talked about the risk of passing down health conditions to children as a valid reason not to have kids.
On the other side of it, she pointed out that online platforms also harbor negative perspectives. She pointed to parents who "openly talk about how they wish they didn't have children."
âYou see people talk about it openly like, âoh, this is the worst decision I've ever made in my life,â and that's gonna influence you for sureâ¦ we didn't have that before,â she added.
While the national fertility rate dropped to an all-time low, regional data still paint a different picture.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and Zamboanga Peninsula have fertility rates of 2.4 and 2.3, respectively, still above the replacement fertility rate. Women in rural areas still choose to have more than one child.
Women in the poorest financial bracket have an average of 2.8 children, compared to 1.1 in the richest.
CPDâs Quiray admitted gaps in expanding education, family planning, and contraceptive use in the countryâs poorer households and far-flung areas as possible explanations for the disconnect.
Minimum wage still varies per region , with Metro Manila having a nominal minimum wage of P695 while BARMM, Caraga, Bicol Region, and others are still at the P400 mark as of March 2026.
Experts noted that wage disparities make it more difficult for families in lower-income regions to afford raising children compared to reduction in highly-urbanized areas.
Albert stressed that empowering women in these areas to make informed family planning decisions requires expanding their access to healthcare, education, and jobs. âInvest early and where the children are,â Albert said.
A falling fertility rate is not necessarily a bad thing, said the PIDS fellow, as it proves that the Philippines has successfully curbed overpopulation and is taking bold steps for women in society.
Instead of mitigating the decline, Quiray said the CPD is focusing on further increasing womenâs capabilities.
âMore than the human numbers, it's really the quality of life that mattersâ¦ We cannot dictate or mandate Filipinos to have children or not to have children,â she said.
The CPD, under the current Philippine Population and Development Plan of Action , listed eight multisectoral objectives, including empowering women in the workforce, promoting healthy aging, responsible parenthood, and others.
When presented with more paths in life, Montejo and Ramos said women are freer to choose a lifestyle that suits them, whether or not with a child.
For Bea, motherhood does not dictate the limits of her potential. âWomen today have so many choices regarding what they want to do, aside from being a mother.â (To be concluded) â with reports from Jake Gomez / Rappler.com
