title: Palau Tax Records Can Strengthen Business Credit
body: By: Gustavo Pessoa A business that keeps records to pay tax is also building evidence that may help a lender understand it. The connection is imperfect, but it offers Palau a practical way to improve business finance: make reliable local records easier to use in a credit assessment, with the borrower in control of their disclosure. The IMF’s financial system study published in January describes gaps in business documentation and lending requirements shaped by US bank headquarters. It identifies US credit scores and audited accounts as obstacles for local applicants. It also notes that the 2023 tax reforms encouraged better business records. A record created for one public purpose could consequently help resolve an information problem in another. This possibility matters because a lender assessing a small business must answer a straightforward question: what cash will remain available to repay the loan? A property title does not answer it. Neither does a promising business description. A history of sales, expenses and existing obligations provides a starting point, particularly where a firm lacks a record in a credit system designed around another jurisdiction. Tax information alone is insufficient. Reported turnover is not profit, and accounting profit is not necessarily cash available for repayment. An applicant may have unpaid customer invoices, seasonal expenses or a large existing debt. A lender needs to reconcile those features with bank statements and other records. The objective is to make a local business intelligible, while retaining a proper assessment of repayment risk. Palau could begin with a voluntary, standard business credit file. A participating firm would assemble its tax returns, a simple account of expenses, relevant bank statements and a schedule of outstanding obligations. Clear definitions would help distinguish amounts reported over different periods. Assistance could focus on correcting inconsistencies before an application reaches a lender, instead of producing an impressive document that fails basic verification. The design should start with participating lenders. US bank branches cannot be presumed to accept a new local document because an authority endorses it. Their headquarters would need to confirm which information is usable, how it would be verified and what additional requirements remain. A pilot could identify where better local records change the assessment and where a separate credit policy still prevents approval. That distinction would make the exercise valuable even when loans are refused. Applicants should receive an intelligible explanation: insufficient repayment capacity, missing information, unacceptable security or a rule governing eligibility. Different reasons demand different remedies. Collecting anonymised results could help authorities distinguish a documentation problem from a broader constraint on the supply of credit. Privacy is essential to the arrangement. Tax compliance should not expose an entire business file to anyone claiming a financial interest. A borrower should choose which lender receives the information and understand the permitted use. Errors need a correction process. Access should have a legal basis and a limited scope, with safeguards appropriate to a small community where commercial details can identify a firm. The IMF’s January Board assessment , which concluded the 2025 consultation, encouraged addressing structural barriers to financial intermediation. Better records would tackle one barrier, while decisions about collateral, commercial incentives and lending terms would remain. A pilot with clear results could show where documentation improves access and where other reforms are required. A tax return should never become an automatic entitlement to borrow. It can become part of a credible account of how a business earns and uses money. If lenders can assess that account at reasonable cost, some viable Palauan firms may receive a fairer hearing. Testing that proposition with consenting borrowers and willing lenders would give policy a concrete basis for its next step. Gustavo Pessoa is a professor of Economics and Finance at Fundação Getulio Vargas in Brazil. The views expressed are his own. The post Palau Tax Records Can Strengthen Business Credit appeared first on Island Times News .

title: Opinion| South Sudan in wrong hands: A defense university for a state that has yet to defend its people
body: There is something profoundly tragic, almost comical, about a government racing to establish a defense university while the country it claims to defend is struggling to secure peace, feed its citizens, pay its soldiers, and make its existing public institutions function. In South Sudan, the government appears determined to build the roof before laying the foundation, then ask the international community to finance the construction. President Salva Kiir Mayardit’s directive to establish a specialised university for defence, security and strategic studies raises a fundamental question: what exactly is the government defending when the state itself remains institutionally fragile, the peace process is faltering, and millions of citizens are trapped in insecurity and humanitarian distress? I do not oppose a defence university in principle. Every sovereign country has a legitimate interest in professional military education, strategic research and national security. My objection is to the grotesque contradiction between the government’s grand announcements and its failure to fulfil more urgent national responsibilities. A university cannot substitute for a functioning defence force, and an impressive institutional name cannot conceal the absence of effective governance. Juba University, the University of Bahr el Ghazal and other public universities need resources to strengthen their operations. Public infrastructure projects remain unfinished, while questions persist about the condition of Akon International Airport and the prolonged construction of the State House. Soldiers and other organised forces, including civil servants at all levels, need reliable salaries and professional support. Electoral institutions require funding, hospitals need medicines, and citizens need food, security and peace. Yet the government is already directing financial resources towards a new institution whose projected establishment costs, operational requirements, and opening date have not been publicly specified. Is this nation governed through a coherent development plan, or through a succession of political announcements designed to manufacture the appearance of progress? In political science, this contradiction resembles what scholars describe as a capability trap: a government adopts the outward appearance of institutional development without building the practical capacity required to deliver public services. It can also resemble blame avoidance, policy diversion and bureaucratic foot-dragging when new initiatives distract attention from unresolved obligations. These concepts do not, by themselves, prove that the President or his government is deliberately misleading the public. Nevertheless, they provide a compelling framework for scrutinising a leadership that repeatedly announces new ambitions while fundamental state responsibilities remain unmet. The deeper concern is political. The SPLM-IG leadership appears increasingly preoccupied with retaining power within a fragmented governing coalition whose constituent interests do not necessarily converge on a common national vision. If political survival takes precedence over peace, institutional accountability and national reconstruction, South Sudan will remain trapped in a cycle of crisis management without genuine recovery. A government may preserve its grip on the presidency while losing the country it was elected to govern. The international community must therefore stop confusing presidential directives with national progress. International partners should demand transparent budgets, measurable institutional outcomes, independent audits, credible implementation of the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS), and clear evidence that public expenditure serves the national interest. Targeted accountability measures against individuals credibly implicated in corruption or serious abuses should be considered where legally justified, while humanitarian assistance must continue to reach vulnerable civilians without political obstruction. South Sudan does not need donors to finance another grand announcement while existing obligations remain neglected. It needs partners willing to distinguish genuine state-building from the performance of state-building. My position is simple: peace is South Sudan’s most urgent national project; security is meaningless without the protection of citizens; and education is an investment only when it strengthens, rather than distracts from, the institutions a country already needs. A defence university may eventually become a valuable national asset. But if the government can mobilise political attention for a new university while failing to resolve the crises confronting existing institutions, the public is entitled to question its priorities. The greatest danger is not that South Sudan lacks plans, committees, directives or ambitious projects. It is that the country may be governed by a political establishment that mistakes the survival of its leadership for the survival of the state. A nation cannot recover merely because its President continues to issue orders. Nor can its future be secured by educating officers in strategic studies while neglecting the political settlement, institutional discipline and public accountability that make national defence meaningful. If the international community is serious about South Sudan, it must invest in the survival of the state and the welfare of its people, not simply in the political survival of those who occupy its highest offices. South Sudan must not be allowed to become a country where the government keeps building new promises while the foundations of the nation continue to crumble. The writer is a South Sudanese constitutional lawyer, academic, and political figure. He studied law at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda. He is an independent legal researcher and constitutional expert and serves as a lecturer and Deputy Dean of the College of Law at Starford International University in Juba. He is also a member of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition (SPLM-IO). The views expressed in ‘opinion’ articles published by Radio Tamazuj are solely those of the writer. The veracity of any claims made is the responsibility of the author, not Radio Tamazuj. title: Tinubu/Shettima PCC: Nigeria Must Sustain Economic Reform
body: Aminat Hassan in Abuja One of the spoke persons of the Tinubu/Shettima Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) 2027, Segun Showunmi, has urged Nigerians to sustain President Bola Ahmed Tinubu-led administration’s economic reform programme and consolidate what he described as the foundations of national renewal. Showunmi, in an interactive session with journalists in Abuja yesterday argued that the country was at a defining moment in its development and needed continuity of policy direction, stronger institutions and accelerated implementation of reforms to achieve sustainable economic growth. He said the 2027 presidential election would provide Nigerians with an opportunity to decide whether to continue with the current administration’s development agenda, expressing the conviction that a second term for Tinubu would offer an opportunity to deepen ongoing reforms and translate their expected benefits into improved living standards. “My position is clear: I support President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a second term because I believe Nigeria must keep moving forward,” Showunmi stated. He maintained that the Nigerian project transcended individual politicians, political parties and electoral contests, describing the country’s long-term development as a collective responsibility requiring national unity, sustained investment and consistency of purpose. According to him, Nigeria must not abandon its pursuit of prosperity but should consolidate ongoing efforts to build a more productive, stable and competitive economy. Showunmi acknowledged that Nigeria had long faced structural economic challenges, including inadequate infrastructure, limited productivity and difficulties in converting its human and natural resources into broadly shared prosperity. However, he expressed optimism that the country could overcome these constraints through sustained economic reforms, increased investment and stronger productive capacity. He said the Tinubu administration had embarked on reforms intended to reposition the economy, address longstanding distortions, strengthen public finances and create conditions for sustainable growth. The political advocate argued that the value of the reforms should ultimately be measured by their capacity to stimulate investment, generate employment, improve infrastructure, strengthen businesses and enhance the government’s ability to provide essential services. “We are not simply trying to manage an economy. We are building the foundations of a nation that can compete, produce, innovate and prosper,” he said. Showunmi maintained that countries which achieved lasting prosperity did so by sustaining their development ambitions, strengthening institutions and providing the policy stability required for productive investment to flourish. He urged Nigerians to look beyond immediate political considerations and focus on the country’s development prospects over the next decade and beyond, including industrial expansion, infrastructure delivery, skills development and improved opportunities for businesses. Explaining his support for Tinubu’s re-election, Showunmi identified leadership, policy direction, institutional capacity and the ability to mobilise citizens around a common national objective as important considerations in determining the country’s future. He said the administration’s focus on economic restructuring, infrastructure, education, energy reform, investment mobilisation and public-sector institutions represented important areas of national development. According to him, continuity in government would provide an opportunity to build on existing initiatives, strengthen implementation and accelerate progress towards the country’s economic objectives. He nevertheless emphasised that the next phase of governance should place greater attention on delivering tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary Nigerians. “A second term should be a period of accelerated delivery, expanded opportunity and a more visible connection between national economic progress and household prosperity,” he stated. Showunmi said Nigerians should expect the next phase of the administration’s agenda to produce stronger investment, increased domestic production, improved infrastructure, expanded opportunities for young people and a wider distribution of economic benefits. Highlighting initiatives undertaken by the Tinubu administration since May 2023, Showunmi pointed to developments across education, electricity, transportation, agriculture, healthcare, taxation and public administration. He cited the Nigerian Education Loan Fund as an additional avenue for eligible students to finance tertiary education, describing access to education as an important component of the country’s long-term human-capital development. He said Nigeria’s young population represented a strategic national asset that required investment in knowledge, technical skills, digital capabilities and entrepreneurial development. On electricity, he referenced the Electricity Act 2023, which provides a framework for states to develop electricity markets within the applicable legal and regulatory arrangements. According to him, greater participation and investment in the electricity sector could create opportunities for locally responsive energy solutions and improved power supply. Showunmi also identified major road projects, including the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, Sokoto-Badagry Super Highway and Abuja-Kaduna-Zaria-Kano highway, as examples of the administration’s infrastructure ambitions. He said transportation infrastructure remained essential to integrating the national economy, connecting communities to markets and lowering the cost of moving goods and services. In agriculture, he called for a more commercially productive sector capable of feeding the population, supporting agro-industries and generating export earnings. He also advocated improved access to essential healthcare services and a coherent public-finance and taxation framework capable of supporting infrastructure development while maintaining a competitive environment for businesses. With the 2027 presidential election approaching, Showunmi urged Nigerians to support Tinubu for a second term, describing the choice as an opportunity to consolidate economic reforms and accelerate the country’s development agenda. He said his position was based on the belief that continued policy direction would allow the government to build on initiatives already underway and pursue more ambitious economic and social outcomes. He identified increased investment, industrial development, improved infrastructure, expanded youth opportunities, stronger communities and more widely shared prosperity as priorities for the next phase of governance. Showunmi also called for a closer connection between national economic performance and improvements in household welfare, arguing that the benefits of development should be felt more directly by citizens. He said the next phase of the administration should focus on translating national ambitions into practical outcomes that Nigerians could see and experience in their daily lives. “My support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is an expression of this conviction. I believe his administration’s reform programme offers Nigeria an important opportunity to consolidate its economic foundations and accelerate the pursuit of inclusive prosperity,” he stated. He urged citizens, entrepreneurs, workers, farmers and young people to contribute to the national development process through enterprise, investment, innovation and collective commitment to national progress.

title: AFRIFF 2026: Women Feature in 85% of Selected Films
body: -Festival will focus on AI in Cinema Mmachi Okafor The Africa International Film Festival (AFRIFF) has unveiled 135 films, new international co-production agreements and artificial intelligence initiatives as it marks its 15th edition, with 85 per cent of its selected feature films directed by, produced by or centred on women. The festival announced the programme at a press conference held at Mikano International headquarters in Victoria Island, Lagos, bringing together diplomats, government officials, corporate sponsors and film industry stakeholders ahead of the seven-day event scheduled for November 1 to 7, 2026. The milestone edition, themed “Frames of the Future” with programming built around the concept of “Africa’s Creative Intelligence,” will feature 23 feature films among its 135 selections and culminate in the AFRIFF Globe Awards on the final night. Festival founder Chioma Ude said the significant representation of women in the feature film selection emerged organically during the selection process, describing it as a reflection of the direction in which the industry is heading. She also addressed concerns about artificial intelligence and its implications for employment in filmmaking, arguing that the technology should be viewed as a tool for creative development rather than simply a threat to jobs. “AI is not going to take anyone’s job, but rather the person who knows how to use AI will replace those who don’t,” Ude said. The festival’s programme combines regional storytelling and directorial debuts with acclaimed international productions, with its opening and closing films highlighting different aspects of contemporary filmmaking. Opening the festival is ‘Lady,’ directed by Oliver Omoresu. The African neo-noir film is set in Lagos and follows a young taxi driver tasked with transporting a group of sex workers along their nightly routes. Gucci Franklin leads the cast alongside an ensemble of actors. The closing film, ‘It’s the Blackness,’ marks the feature directorial debut of veteran actor Hakeem Kae-Kazim. The black comedy-drama, which incorporates romantic elements, stars Kalu Ikeagwu and Marcy Dolapo Oni. It follows two close friends navigating personal ambition, family pressures and complex immigration challenges. Beyond its African selections, AFRIFF will present international films through partnerships with diplomatic missions. These include the American film ‘If I Go, Will They Miss Me,’ written and directed by Walter Thompson-Hernández and starring Oscar nominee Danielle Brooks, as well as Marco Bellocchio’s ‘The Traitor,’ presented in partnership with the Italian Embassy. An Oscar-winning Norwegian film will also be screened in collaboration with the Norwegian Embassy. Technology and creative independence will feature prominently in the anniversary programme, with initiatives designed to equip emerging filmmakers with new skills, expand distribution opportunities and strengthen the position of African creators in the digital economy. In collaboration with TikTok, AFRIFF will host a hands-on AI Creative Film and Content Creation Lab on November 6. The session will focus on helping emerging filmmakers integrate artificial intelligence tools into content creation, pre-production and micro-drama production. AFRIFF is also partnering with Pulse Nigeria to introduce the Pulse Rising Filmmaker Award, a new category intended to recognise and provide financial support for filmmakers at the early stages of their careers. Its international partnerships are expanding as well, with Oman sending a 10-person delegation carrying scripts in search of Nigerian co-production partners. South Africa and Brazil have also signed three-year, multi-project co-production and residency framework agreements with the festival. The agreements are expected to create opportunities for cross-border collaboration, allowing filmmakers to explore joint productions, exchange expertise and build stronger connections between African and international film markets. Diplomatic representatives at the press conference also highlighted the importance of international cooperation in strengthening the film industry. United States Consul General Brandon Hudspeth reflected on the role of storytelling in shaping national identity, noting that American storytellers had helped define how the world understands the United States throughout much of its 250-year history. He said Nollywood was playing a similar role for Africa, using film to communicate the continent’s experiences and identity to global audiences. Hudspeth also emphasised that the future of filmmaking would depend on combining human talent with technology to tell stories that resonate internationally. As part of its participation, the U.S. Mission will showcase 10 American feature films and host masterclasses featuring Oscar-nominated producer Alex Madigan in November and gaming executive Mike Fischer in December. France also expressed support for international collaboration. Laurent Favier, Consul General of France, said the challenges facing the film industry required cooperation among creative professionals and institutions. “No studio, platform, or artist can meet these new industry challenges alone,” Favier said, explaining that the partnership focused on developing new international co-productions in fiction, animation and documentaries. For Dr Shaibu Husseini, Director-General of the Nigerian Film and Video Censors Board, AFRIFF’s 15-year journey represents more than an annual cultural gathering. He described the festival as a platform that has contributed to the visibility of African storytelling and the growth of the creative economy. “AFRIFF has not merely been a date on the cultural calendar, but a monument to African storytelling and a catalyst for economic growth in the creative sector,” Husseini said. With its 15th edition bringing together filmmakers, technology innovators, investors and international partners, AFRIFF is positioning the festival as a meeting point for creative exchange and new business opportunities.

title: Poland provided aid to defend Kyiv, Zelensky says
body:
Polish aid helped Ukraine defend Kyiv during recent attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels where he met with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Oct. 15.
Zelensky said Poland had provided ammunition used by Ukraine's anti-aircraft guns. Zelensky also hinted at other, more sensitive Polish support which would have to remain confidential; "sometimes it should remain between the two of us," he said.
Tusk gave Ukraine message of solidarity - "you are not alone."
"I would like to assure you, as I have already stated publicly here: Ukraine, your people and you personally – you are not alone… you can count on me personally, on Poland, and also on the EU. After my talks here in Brussels with all the leaders, it is absolutely clear that anything that could help Putin and Russia in this war is unacceptable for Europe and Poland," the Polish Prime Minister said .
In response, Zelensky thanked Tusk for Poland's help for Ukraine as it faces an upsurge in Russian attacks.
"We are very grateful to the Prime Minister, his team, the government, and the entire Polish people for standing with us in this absolutely barbaric war waged by Russia against Ukraine. Thank you for your support and for maintaining close contact throughout these extremely difficult months. These are very hard times. It is no longer just about days and nights – they are attacking us 24/7,” Zelensky said .
The meeting comes as tensions between Kyiv and Washington D.C. show no sign of easing, amid an American push to strong-arm Ukraine into ceasing drone attacks on Russian oil refineries. President Donald Trump has recently falsely blamed Ukraine for record high diesel prices sparked by America's faltering war with Iran.
Polish and Ukrainian relations have also been strained in recent months. In May, a decision by Ukraine to name a military unit in honor of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army led to Polish President Karol Nawrotski stripping Zelensky of Poland's "Order of the White Eagle".
Yet, Poland remains an important strategic partner for Ukraine, as well as a critical source of military materiel.
The same day, in Warsaw, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced that Ukraine expects to purchase an additional 125 million euros (about $1.484 million) worth of Polish weaponry by the end of 2026, financed by a loan from the Polish government.
"We are currently discussing how to finalize this agreement. I hope this will happen in the near future—by the end of the year—since there is political will for it, and funds have been allocated in Poland’s budget,” Sybiha said.
Ukraine is Poland's biggest arms-export customer, taking two thirds of Polish armaments production in 2025, spending 1.68 billion euros (about $1.90 billion) on Polish arms. Besides supplying armaments on a commercial basisPoland has also donated significant amounts of military materiel to Ukraine, including tanks, fighter jets, and artillery systems.

title: A 4B LLM learns to write tools that other LLMs can use
body:
SMITH: S chema-grounded M ulti-task I terative T ool H oning
1 Appier AI Research 2 National Taiwan University
Tool-augmented language models are bounded by the APIs humans bothered to write; existing tool-creation systems patch this by prompting a frozen LLM at inference time, leaving the model that writes a tool decoupled from the one that uses it, with no signal that the schemas it produces are schemas it can actually invoke. We propose SMITH (Schema-grounded Multi-task Iterative Tool Honing), a reinforcement learning framework that jointly trains tool creation and tool use inside a single policy. Each rollout is either a build task (write a tool from a few examples) or a use task (invoke a pooled tool on a held-out question). Three separate reward axes catch schema, code, and outcome failures independently, so each failure mode contributes its own gradient. A 4B Qwen3 trained with SMITH on 13 procedural reasoning tasks with exact verifiers reaches 79.9 macro-average accuracy on held-out tasks, the best across all evaluated methods and ahead of an untrained 30B-A3B tool-writer. It also reaches 40.4 on TabMWP-Hard and 42.6 on out-of-domain GQA ( +7.6 over the best same-backbone inference-time baseline), without any visual or tabular training data. When invoked by a frozen 350M student, tools written by our 4B match those produced by a writer an order of magnitude larger. The same recipe also lifts Qwen3-8B and Granite-3.3-8B without modification.
Tool-augmented LLMs are only as capable as the tools someone already wrote for them: a calculator, a search API, a Python sandbox. When the right tool doesn't exist, the agent is stuck. Recent work (LATM, CRAFT, TroVE, KTCE) lets a model synthesize new tools on the fly, but almost always with a powerful model writing the tool and a separate, weaker model using it. The writer never finds out whether its interface was actually easy to call.
This creates two concrete training problems the paper has to solve. Reward decomposition: a tool can fail because its code is wrong, its schema is wrong, the two disagree with each other, or the tool is technically correct but poorly designed. Each needs a different corrective signal. Circular evaluation: scoring tool quality needs a judge, but a model judging its own live weights is unreliable, and a frozen external judge never improves alongside the policy.
SMITH is a multi-task RL framework, trained with DAPO (a clip-higher variant of GRPO), that mixes two rollout types into every batch: build and use . Both are optimized inside the same policy, so gradients from tool creation and tool consumption update the same weights every step.
The policy sees N = 4 question–answer pairs and must infer the general procedure behind them, then express it as an OpenAI-compatible (Python function, JSON schema) pair. The tool is then run against K = 16 held-out questions drawn from a harder difficulty band than the examples it was built from; the model never sees the ground-truth answers at generation time. A tool that only pattern-matches the easy induction examples scores near zero; only a genuinely reusable abstraction survives.
13 / 16 held-out (harder) questions correct → admitted to the tool pool
The policy receives a target question and a tool pool entry: one matching domain tool plus two distractor tools from unrelated categories, forcing it to identify the right schema. It has up to T = 5 turns to call the tool and answer; an efficiency penalty discourages burning through the turn budget. If no pool tool exists yet for the category, the model must build one first from the same in-context examples.
“How many 1-bits are in the binary form of 92,401?”
Pool entry — every schema is named solve(question) ; only the description tells them apart
Rather than collapsing everything into one score, SMITH keeps format , execution , and judge feedback as independent axes fed to DAPO, so each failure mode gets its own gradient instead of being averaged away.
Checks the response contains exactly one Python block and one JSON block whose function name and parameters actually match. A malformed pair terminates the rollout with zero reward on every axis.
The tool is handed to an evaluator model, which must call it to answer each held-out question. Only answers that came through a real tool call count. A model can't shortcut this by reasoning the answer out in text.
$$r^{\mathrm{eval}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{T}|} \mathbf{1}\!\left[\pi^{\mathrm{eval}}(q_j \mid \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{S}) \approx a_j\right]$$
An LLM judge scores code correctness, schema quality, and overall quality, kept as a separate axis from execution reward, not folded in. A syntax error is penalized directly; a schema/code mismatch halves the score.
$$r^{\mathrm{judge}} = \begin{cases}-0.5 & \text{syntax error}\\ 0.5\, s_{\mathrm{overall}} & \text{schema}\neq\text{code}\\ s_{\mathrm{overall}} & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
Breaking the circularity of self-judging. The evaluator \(\pi^{\mathrm{eval}}\) and judge \(\pi^{\mathrm{judge}}\) both start from the same base checkpoint as the policy, then are periodically re-synced to the latest policy weights. This lets the evaluator improve alongside the policy without the instability of scoring against live, still-updating weights.
Let \(c \in \{0,1\}\) mark whether the final answer matches ground truth. The reward is scaled by an efficiency multiplier \(\eta(\rho)\) that decays as the turn fraction \(\rho = \min(n/T, 1)\) grows, with a floor \(\eta_{\min}=0.3\) so the policy is never indifferent to correctness even at the turn limit (\(\eta_{\mathrm{mid}} = 0.7\)):
$$ r^{\mathrm{correct}} = 2c\,\eta(\rho), \qquad \eta(\rho) = \begin{cases} 1 - 2(1-\eta_{\mathrm{mid}})\rho & \rho \le 0.5 \\[2pt] \max\!\bigl(\eta_{\min},\ \eta_{\mathrm{mid}}\,(1-2(\rho-0.5))^2\bigr) & \rho > 0.5 \end{cases} $$
Every training batch is split evenly, \(\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{build}} \sqcup \mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{use}}\) with \(|\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{build}}| = |\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{use}}| = B/2\), and DAPO accumulates both losses in a single backward pass: \(\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DAPO}}(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{build}}) + \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DAPO}} (\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{use}})\). Build and use gradients therefore update the same parameters \(\theta\) every step. Any tool with \(r^{\mathrm{eval}} > 0\) is pushed into a shared Tool Pool for reuse by future use-task rollouts. This is the "iterative honing" in SMITH's name.
SMITH is trained on 13 procedural task categories from Reasoning-Gym , spanning arithmetic, algorithms, algebra, games, and logical reasoning, chosen because their answers are exact and automatically verifiable and each exposes a difficulty curriculum. Tools are induced on easy examples but graded on the hardest band of the same task family, deliberately separating tool-writing quality from instance difficulty.
The primary backbone is Qwen3-4B-Instruct , fine-tuned with LoRA (r = 64, α = 128) using DAPO for 60 gradient steps, build/use rollouts mixed 1:1. The recipe is also applied unmodified to Qwen3-8B and Granite-3.3-8B to test generality across model families. Baselines share the Qwen3-4B-Instruct backbone wherever possible: inference-time tool writers LATM , CRAFT , TroVE , and KTCE ; distillation baselines ReTool (from Qwen-32B traces) and LATM (distilled from GPT-4.1); and a deliberate scaling probe, LATM on Qwen3-30B-A3B . Transfer is measured on TabMWP-Hard (a strengthened tabular-reasoning benchmark) and GQA (visual question answering), neither seen during training, and on BFCL v4 , an externally specified function-calling benchmark.
SMITH is the only method that leads on genuinely held-out tasks while also using the fewest tokens. Against distillation, a 4B model trained with SMITH's RL objective generalizes more reliably than 4B models distilled from far larger oracles: ReTool leads on seen tasks (92.2) but drops nearly 30 points on unseen ones, a sign of overfitting to the demonstrator's distribution rather than learning a transferable build-and-use policy. Against more elaborate inference-time scaffolds (CRAFT, TroVE, KTCE) and a bigger tool-writer (Qwen3-30B-A3B), SMITH still wins on unseen tasks, using roughly 32× fewer output tokens than standard chain-of-thought.
Do SMITH's tools encode a genuinely reusable solution, or a private convention only the writer understands? We test both directions: pairing the RL-trained 4B writer with a much smaller consumer, and with a much larger one.
Pairing tools from the RL-trained 4B writer with a frozen LFM2.5-350M consumer lifts its held-out accuracy from 11.6 to 42.9 , matching a tool-writer eighty times larger (Qwen3-30B-A3B, untrained, at 41.5).
RG (Unseen) accuracy of LFM2.5-350M as the tool-writing source changes; the writer itself is never fine-tuned on LFM2.5's outputs.
The reverse direction also holds. Pairing SMITH's 4B-written tools with a much stronger Qwen3-30B-A3B consumer beats that same 30B model writing tools for itself (LATM*) on every task group, most sharply on TabMWP-Hard (0.7 → 38.8), lifting the task-weighted overall score from 70.2 to 76.6. A bigger tool user doesn't make its own self-written tool preferable. SMITH's 4B writer remains the better source of tools either way.
Neither TabMWP-Hard (tabular reasoning) nor GQA (visual question answering) appears anywhere in SMITH's training data. SMITH leads TabMWP-Hard outright and is the only 4B, non-distilled method to top either column. The GQA gap to GPT-4.1-distilled LATM is the acknowledged cost of not distilling visual primitives from a stronger oracle.
The same RL recipe, applied unmodified, improves every backbone tested, including Granite-3.3-8B , which starts from a much weaker base. A Self-Judge variant (Qwen3-8B judging its own rollouts instead of an external 30B-A3B judge) pushes held-out RG even higher (85.9) but trades off OOD GQA, suggesting a smaller self-judge is weaker but less biased on in-distribution data.
SMITH is never trained on BFCL v4 's schemas, multi-turn traces, or judges, so a gain here isolates a learned tool-use prior rather than benchmark-specific fitting. It lifts BFCL overall accuracy on both Qwen backbones, most sharply on Qwen3-8B.
We isolate whether joint training, rather than simply having a specialist builder and a specialist user, is the active ingredient. Pairing a separately-trained 30B-A3B builder with a separately-trained 4B tool-use specialist ( Decoupled Create/Use ) does not beat a single model trained on tool creation alone (58.9 vs. 68.8 RG Unseen). Only the full objective, which keeps execution reward and judge reward as disentangled axes and closes the loop in one policy, reaches the best aggregate score.
Tool creation alone yields a strong in-distribution bump but underperforms on OOD GQA; coupling build and use without disentangled rewards lifts in-distribution accuracy but hurts held-out transfer. Only keeping process quality (format, judge) and outcome correctness (execution, use) as separate reward axes gets both.
SMITH jointly trains a single language model to create and use reusable tools, closing the feedback loop between tool writer and tool user so the policy is optimized directly on its own execution outcomes. Trained on 13 Reasoning-Gym tasks, the 4B model attains the highest held-out accuracy among all evaluated methods, leads TabMWP-Hard, and writes tools that transfer to a 350M student never seen during training, matching tools from a writer an order of magnitude larger. The same recipe lifts Qwen3-8B and Granite-3.3-8B without modification: coupling creation and use inside one trained policy is a scalable path to generalization, without a larger frozen teacher, a more elaborate scaffold, or out-of-domain supervision.
