title: 48 hours in Tashkent: How best to explore the Uzbekistan capital
body: Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan and its largest city, has stood at the crossroads of the Silk Road for centuries. It has also been destroyed and rebuilt several times. Once a caravanserai, a roadside inn that offered lodging for merchants primarily along the Silk Road , much of the city was destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1219. Centuries later, in 1966, an earthquake left large parts of Tashkent in ruins. The 20th-century city that emerged from the reconstruction was very different, with wide avenues, vast public spaces and imposing Soviet-era buildings. Today, Tashkent is a mix of Soviet modernist buildings, Islamic monuments, green spaces and a new generation of creative designers, artists and hoteliers giving the city a contemporary identity. Here is a tried-and-tested itinerary to explore Tashkent in 48 hours. Day 1 9am: Explore old Tashkent After eating breakfast at Farovon Tashkent hotel, I start my day by walking 10 minutes to the old part of Tashkent past mud houses and mulberry trees. There, the Hazrati Imam Complex, with turquoise domes, sand-coloured brickwork, carved wooden doors and intricate tile work replaces the concrete architecture of the city centre. The complex was built around the grave of Abu Bakr Kaffal, also known as Hazrati Imam, one of the city’s early Islamic scholars and a preacher, who was also a master of making locks and keys. From there, I wander through the 16th-century Barak-Khan Madrasah. The spaces that once housed students have now become shops selling traditional crafts from carved wooden Quran stands and miniature paintings to ceramics and fabrics covered in colourful Suzani embroidery. Entry to the complex is free and it is open daily from 9am to 9pm. Visitors should dress modestly, with women required to cover their heads when entering the religious sites. 11am: Get a glimpse into its rich Islamic heritage Close by is the Centre for Islamic Civilisation, which opened in March 2026. Spread across a vast site, the centre explores the history of Islamic civilisation through faith, science, art, literature and craftsmanship. Inside, I journey through centuries of history from early Quranic manuscripts behind glass, some decorated with gold, to ceramics, metalwork, calligraphy and miniature paintings. The centre is open from 9am to 10pm. Entry is $25 for foreign visitors. 1pm: Get a taste of plov Plov is an one-pot rice dish that is omnipresent in the country, with each region proud of its own variation. Besh Qozon, near the Tashkent Television Tower on Guards Colonel Khodjaev Street, a 10-minute cab ride from the old city, is famous for the gargantuan quantities of plov cooked at the restaurant every day. I watch cooks prepare plov in enormous kazan cauldrons. Long paddles move through mountains of rice, carrots, onions and chickpeas, with large pieces of meat, tied in bundles, added to the mixture and cooked in sheep fat and vegetable oil. Steam rises from the pots as the cooks work with an ease that comes from years of repetition and waiters serve it on plates deftly, with the dishes topped with garlic bulbs or quail eggs. 3pm: Explore its Soviet legacy Tashkent's Soviet legacy is particularly striking in the city’s architecture, with a blend of brutalist forms, grand modernist structures and use of elaborate mosaics and sculptural elements alongside Uzbek Islamic motifs called Tashkent modernism. After lunch, I venture to Hotel Uzbekistan, a 15-minute drive away. The building is a notable example of brutalist and modernist architecture, built about 90 metres from Amir Timur Square. Established in the 1970s, the hotel's honeycomb-like facade is not only decorative but also helps filter the intense sunlight. A detour worth taking, if you're interested in architecture from the era, is to the Tashkent State Circus. It is closer to the old city and is another remarkable Soviet-era building. Its sweeping white dome and clean modernist lines give it the appearance of a futuristic space shuttle. 5pm: Browse the Teplo shop From there I make a stop at the Teplo shop on Nukus Street, a concept store and cultural space, a 10-minute drive from Amir Timur Square. I browse through the work of young Uzbek designers displayed alongside traditional crafts. Fashion, ceramics, textiles and graphic design come together, with familiar Uzbek motifs and Suzani embroidery reinterpreted in a more contemporary way on jackets and dresses. 8pm: Have an Uzbek feast at Lali Lali, which opened in 2024, is a 15-minute cab ride from my hotel and is part of a chain across Central Asian countries. The extensive menu takes you across the different regions of Uzbekistan, with old recipes combined with modern culinary traditions. Furnished in azure, blue tones and local ikat fabric-covered sofas, it has an open kitchen. Order iconic Samarkand plov, manty with beef and lamb shashlik. 10pm: Call it a day From there, I retire to Farovon Tashkent for the night. A new boutique property, it is decorated in traditional style with rugs, carpets and ceramics, in the historic part of the city. Day 2 9am: Ride the Metro The Art Deco-style Tashkent Metro is an unexpected architectural experience and is spotlessly clean. Each station has its own theme and design, with marble, granite, mosaics, chandeliers and reliefs celebrating everything from Uzbek history and literature, to science and space exploration. Chorsu Station is the closest to my hotel, but I love Kosmonavtlar Station, with shiny green glass columns and ceramic medallions, where the theme is the Soviet space dream, depicted in deep blues and cosmic motifs. Alisher Navoi Station is another marvel, with carved arches and intricate ceramic panels in cobalt and emerald hues. The Tashkent Metro is open daily from 5am until midnight. The price of one ticket is 2,000 Uzbekistani som ($0.14). 11am: Haggle at Chorsu Bazaar For a slice of everyday Tashkent, I take the Metro back to Chorsu Bazaar, getting off at Chorsu Station. The bazaar's building is noted for its an enormous blue dome, which dominates the market and is an interesting example of Soviet architecture influenced by traditional Central Asian market halls. Underneath the dome, the atmosphere is energetic and lively. Sellers stand next to huge pyramids of spices, dried apricots, walnuts, raisins and pomegranates. I browse through traditional clothes, pottery and ceramics. Hungry for lunch, I then walk through the food court, where the smell of coriander, cumin and roasting meat fills the air. It is open daily from 7am until 7pm. 2pm: Enjoy a visual feast at the State Museum of Applied Arts This compact museum, which can be reached from the Kosmonavtlar Metro station, is housed in a beautiful mansion of former Russian diplomat Alexander Polovtsov. It is decorated with ganch – painted plaster – and wood, with exquisitely painted and carved ceilings with cornices. It showcases the best of Uzbek art and crafts, including knives from Chust, ceramics from Rishtan, silk from Margilan, traditional clothes and gold embroidery from Bukhara, Suzani embroidery and ikat fabrics. I love the section on different kinds of skullcaps from across the country, with specific motifs and symbolism, and the traditional musical instruments. The museum is open from 9am to 6pm and the entrance fee is $2.50. 5pm: Meet the locals at Tashkent Central Park It is worth venturing across town to Tashkent Central Park, a favourite destination for families, with 100-year-old acacias and oak trees, as well as statues, sprawling lawns, amusement rides, a carousel and fountains. I see men playing accordions and walk past food stands and shallow ponds filled with fish. With babies in strollers, young people jogging, and others sitting on benches, this is truly a slice of local life. It is open from 10am to 11pm. 8pm: An Uzbek dinner Dinner at Afsona on Uqchi Street comes highly recommended. Decorated with carved wood and blue-and-white ceramics, with folk music playing in the background, this upmarket restaurant serves Uzbek cuisine with a contemporary touch, from crisp samsas to pumpkin manti and lagman noodles. If you are feeling adventurous, try their horse meat dish called norin. Finish with chak chak, a fried honey cake with almonds. How to get there There are several daily flights to Tashkent. From Dubai, travel with flydubai, Uzbekistan Airways or Centrum Air; from Sharjah fly with Air Arabia; and from Abu Dhabi book a trip with Etihad Airways, which launched the route in August.

title: Beijing residents dispose of drones ahead of ban on ownership
body: By Xiaoning Mo and Michael Li https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-12/beijing-residents-dispose-drones-ahead-of-ban-on-ownership/107229144 Share article (ABC-Australia) Kristine’s brother had only owned his drone for a year when Beijing authorities announced drones would be banned in the capital. Not just flying them, but also possessing and storing them. Before the new rules take effect on November 15, drone owners must move their aircraft out of the capital or dispose of them through government-approved buyback and recycling programs. Those who flout the rules will “face strong action”, including confiscation and fines up to 5,000 yuan ($1,050). Many people have been lining up at drone buyback sites, but some owners are getting back less than a quarter of the purchase price. Kristine’s brother decided to send his drone, which he bought for $2,000 last year, to her in Sydney rather than sell it at a loss. “He’s still quite reluctant to let it go but, because of this rule, he has no choice but to dispose of it,” said Kristine, who wanted to use only her first name to protect her brother’s safety in Beijing. “[He thought] it would be nice if it could stay in the family. “If he gave it to me, I could let my kids play with it, and it would still serve some purpose.” Meanwhile, Beijing resident Matthew Zhang sent his drone to his parents’ home in nearby Tianjin and planned to travel there to use it whenever he needed it. “It is definitely inconvenient, but at least I can still use it,” Mr Zhang, an aerial photographer, said. ‘Security is the first priority’ Most of China’s major cities have introduced civilian drone no-fly zones in sensitive areas, including airports, military zones, core commercial districts and government buildings. But Beijing will be the only city in China to ban the ownership of drones. The city had already banned unapproved outdoor drone flights in August 2025, but recently stepped up its security measures after a small plane crashed into Beijing’s tallest building in June . Announcing the possession ban in September, Beijing’s government said it was intended to “firmly strengthen the capital’s security defences”. Taobao has blocked sales of motorised flying products, including powered paper planes, to Beijing addresses. (Supplied: Taobao) The new regulation applied to all “unmanned aerial vehicles” and appeared to extend to radio-controlled model aircraft, toy drones and toy flapping-wing aircraft. Taobao is among several Chinese e-commerce platforms that have restricted drone purchases using a Beijing delivery address. Hsiao-Huang Shu, a researcher at Taiwan’s Institute for National Defence and Security Research, said it was “deeply ironic” that a city in the world’s biggest consumer drone-making country was banning drone ownership “For Beijing, security concerns are the first priority,” Dr Shu said. He said Beijing had already developed counter-drone systems, including electronic jamming, electronic fences and measures to destroy them, such as lasers. Dr Shu said that after the June incident, authorities might have decided to eliminate potential risks, including drone possession. “They are using this opportunity to close the barn door after the horse has bolted,” he said. The ABC has approached the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs for comment. Balancing innovation and control China dominates the global drone industry. According to data-gathering firm Statista, Chinese company DJI is the world’s leading manufacturer of civil drones for commercial use, and China’s drone industry generates the highest revenue when comparing global figures. China had nearly 3.3 million registered civilian drones by the end of 2025, up 51 per cent from 2024, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC). Drones are also the workhorses of China’s low-altitude economy, delivering parcels and used in farming, tourism and emergency rescues. CAAC forecasts the low-altitude economy to reach 3.5 trillion yuan (about $740 billion) by 2035. In March, China underscored the “healthy and orderly” development of the industry in its 15th Five-Year Plan, the government’s policy road map from 2026 to 2030. Lizzi C Lee, a fellow on the Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute based in Washington, DC, said the Beijing ban did not mean China was walking away from the low-altitude economy. She said just days before Beijing’s possession ban announcement, Shanghai had begun rolling out a new dedicated drone route, delivering food from a fast-food outlet to a popular waterfront park. “The interesting story here is really the tension between encouraging innovation and controlling the risks that come with it,” Dr Lee said, adding that the same tension was seen in the development of humanoid robots and autonomous driving. She said other cities might not follow Beijing’s lead. “I think we might see more compartmentalisation,” she said. “More scrutiny and controls in politically sensitive urban airspace, while manufacturing, R and D [research and development] and commercial deployment continue elsewhere,” she said. The post Beijing residents dispose of drones ahead of ban on ownership appeared first on Island Times News .

title: New ECOWAS Commission President General Birame Diop to address AFRIDEX 2026
body:
The organisers of Nigeria’s Africa International Defence Exhibition (Afridex) 2026 have confirmed that the new Commission President of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and a former Senegalese Minister of the Armed Forces, General Birame Diop, is set to speak at the first iteration of the landmark event.
With more than 30 years of experience in both military and international security leadership, Diop is set to bring invaluable insights and experience for delegates to engage with. A former Minister and Chief of General Staff of the Senegalese Armed Forces, Diop served as Military Adviser in the United Nations Department of Peace Operations from 2021 to 2024.
From 2002 to 2003, Diop also served as Deputy Chief and Chief of Air Operations during his time with the then United Nations peacekeeping mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUC, now MONUSCO), before later serving as Chief of Staff of the Senegalese Air Force.
According to a press release issued by the event’s organisers, the General’s participation coincides with an increasingly complex security environment, one which has forced African governments to confront new challenges while simultaneously attempting to strengthen sovereign defence capabilities, regional cooperation, and long-term security resilience.
As such, it is important that regional bodies such as ECOWAS, which play an important role in promoting regional integration, peace, security and stability across West Africa and the wider continent, actively engage with and participate in events such as Afridex.
According to the same press release, Abbie Butler, Content and Delegations Director at Afridex, said: “We are honoured to welcome General Birame Diop, his team and defence chiefs from across all ECOWAS Member States to AAfridex 2026. Their participation highlights the importance of regional leadership and cooperation in shaping Africa’s future defence and security priorities.
“Afridex provides an important opportunity for African leaders, armed forces and the global defence and security community to come together, understand evolving requirements across the continent and develop the partnerships required to strengthen capability, readiness and resilience.”
Key activities include the Strategic Conference, taking place on 27 and 28 October 2026 under the theme: “Advancing Africa’s Sovereign Security Capability Through Innovation and Industrial Growth.”
It is understood that the conference will examine a wide range of priority areas ranging from capability development and regional security cooperation to resilience, readiness, and long-term industrial growth.
Taking place in parallel with the Conference, Technical Theatres offer a unique opportunity for defence and security professionals across Land, Maritime, Air, Cyber, Space and Digital capability domains to engage in a practical learning environment.
The Ministers of Defence in Africa Summit, described as the senior-level strategic programme of Afridex, is set to provide ministers, service chiefs, capability planners and defence industry leadership with key opportunities for engagements through closed-door roundtables and bilateral engagement corridors.
Afridexwill take place from 26 to 29 October at Eko Atlantic, Lagos, Nigeria, bringing together government officials, armed forces leadership, procurement stakeholders, capability planners and global industry leaders across the Land, Maritime, Air, Cyber and Space domains. The event is set to include more than a simple tradeshow.
It will provide a platform for governments, militaries, and industry leaders to engage directly on the rapidly evolving defence and security priorities shaping Africa and the capabilities needed to address them today and moving into the future.
According to the event organisers, ECOWAS armed forces chiefs (or equivalents) attending Afridex 2026 include:
Lieutenant General Fructueux Gbaguidi (Benin); Rear Admiral Manuel António Pereira Semedo (Cabo Verde); General Lassina Doumbia (Côte d’Ivoire); Minister of Defence Baboucarr Ousmaila Joof (The Gambia); Lieutenant General William Agyapong (Ghana); Lieutenant General Ibrahima Sory Bangoura (Guinea); General of the Army Tomás Djassi (Guinea-Bissau); Major General Davidson F. Forleh (Liberia); General Olufemi O. Oluyede (Nigeria); Vice Admiral Oumar Wade (Senegal); Lieutenant General Amara Idara Bangura (Sierra Leone); and Brigadier General Tchakpélé Aklesso (Togo).
Visitor registration for Afridex 2026 is open. Defence and security professionals, industry stakeholders and organisations looking to engage with African markets are invited to register to attend.

title: UK and Germany strengthen defence ties in London talks
body:
UK and Germany strengthened defence-industrial cooperation at the latest talks at Lancaster House.
The talks build on the Trinity House Agreement and Kensington Treaty, reinforcing cooperation between the two nations across air, land, sea and space.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard and German counterpart State Secretary Jens Plötner joined industry leaders to discuss industrial priorities for collaboration.
UK-German work on key industrial collaboration and new technology was advanced yesterday as Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard hosted his German counterpart, State Secretary for Armament and Innovation Jens Plötner, at Lancaster House in London.
The latest UK-Germany Ministerial Group on Equipment and Capability Cooperation (MECC) meeting brought together senior officials and military leaders from both nations to review progress on joint defence capability programmes and to deepen the industrial partnership between the UK and Germany, two of NATO’s leading defence powers.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP said:
Germany is one of our closest and most valued defence partners, and today’s talks demonstrate our determination to turn that ambition into real capability for our armed forces and real opportunity for our defence industries.
As threats to our shared security evolve, the UK and Germany are standing together, strengthening our forces, our industrial bases and our resilience in lockstep.
Discussions built on the Trinity House Agreement, signed in October 2024, which set out an ambitious programme of bilateral cooperation across air, land, maritime, cyber and space domains. The agreement sits under the wider Kensington Treaty, signed in July 2025, which provides the strategic framework for the UK-Germany relationship.
Among the flagship programmes on the agenda was Deep Precision Strike, a joint UK-Germany initiative to develop long-range strike capability, reflecting the shared ambition of both nations to address critical capability gaps and strengthen NATO’s deterrence.
The talks follow the Prime Minister’s visit to Berlin on 8 October, during which the UK and Germany agreed to deepen cooperation on space and to establish a new UK-Germany Counter-Hybrid Partnership, strengthening joint resilience against grey-zone threats.
Following the MECC meeting, Minister Pollard joined State Secretary Plötner at the German Embassy in London for a panel discussion which saw senior policymakers and industry leaders take stock of defence-industrial progress and identify practical priorities for deepening cooperation.
Minister Pollard was joined on the panel by State Secretary Plötner, Dr Philipp Kerth, co-founder and chief executive of German defence technology company Hypersonica, and Alex Zino, Director Business Development & Future Programmes at Rolls-Royce.
The MECC forms part of a wider programme of UK-German engagement in the lead-up to the EU-UK summit. The UK-Germany defence relationship continues to grow as both nations work towards a more resilient Euro-Atlantic security architecture, underpinned by a modern, innovative and competitive defence industrial base at the heart of NATO’s deterrence and readiness.

title: Zelensky thanks EU's 'real leaders' for their continued support as bloc confirms new sanctions package on the way
body:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived for the second day of an EU leaders' summit on Oct. 16, ready to discuss support for Ukraine's energy grid, 2027 budget, and EU membership bid.
Zelensky's visit comes as the U.S. government pivots in a decidedly pro-Russian direction, leading Kyiv and Brussels to condemn Washington's betrayal of Ukraine and emphasize their close ties.
"Our message to President Zelensky is very simple. The support of the EU to Ukraine remains as strong as ever. This is no time to withdraw support... no time to relieve Russia sanctions. It is time to increase our support, increase our pressure," European Council President Antonio Costa said.
"I cannot count the many times you were here, and it shows the closeness that we have," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen added.
"I'm so thankful that we have such huge support from EU leaders, real leaders," Zelensky said ahead of the EU leaders meeting, accompanied by Costa and von der Leyen.
"I am thankful the EU stands with us," Zelensky said.
"We supported Trump's energy ceasefire, but we see Russia did not respect it, and so we have to increase the pressure," von der Leyen told journalists, before announcing that the EU is working on a new 22nd package of sanctions against Russia.
"Dear Volodymyr, you can count on us not only to support you in war but most importantly for your future as a member of the EU," Costa said.
Costa and von der Leyen both congratulated Zelensky and Ukraine's parliament for passing key reforms that allowed Kyiv's EU membership bid to proceed earlier in the week.
"The goal is toward the end of the year to open the final two clusters," von der Leyen said, in reference to the to-do lists of reforms Ukraine is partway through unlocking.
Zelensky then headed to a meeting with Costa and von der Leyen, after which they are expected to announce a new dedicated EU task force to help Ukraine advance the rule of law, which is essential for the country to unlock EU support funds and become a member of the bloc.

title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That's not a problem we need to solve
body: Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms. Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online. It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks. When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street . Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them. A less safe internet for all Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked. Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences. Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation. What could work instead? Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place. For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. Both teens and parents are also frustrated by features designed to keep us all online for longer than we want. Another approach would be to expand the availability of user-controlled tools so that families have easy, flexible, and user-friendly ways to limit access to what is undesirable. For example, keyword-based content filtering can enable a student who is targeted with a specific nickname or inside joke to block any post or comment containing it. Platforms are unlikely to know which word or term a child might want to block, nor can policy seek to address such dynamic types of harm. Policy can, however, offer tools that would put power back in users’ hands. Poor privacy practices, anxiety-producing content streams, and a near-inescapable need to use digital technologies for everyday tasks, communication, and information-seeking have rightfully led parents and teens to want real change in how companies conduct business. Circumvention shows where policy falls short. Stricter enforcement will mean yet more data collection, and it won’t meet kids and parents where they are. Michal Luria is a senior research fellow at the Center for Democracy & Technology, leading the organization’s work on evaluating and designing sociotechnical systems. Aliya Bhatia is a senior policy analyst at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Free Expression Project where she leads policy advocacy and research on issues related to children’s safety online, multilingual technologies, and human rights governance of online platforms. Danah Boyd is the Geri Gay Professor of Communication at Cornell University, where her research focuses on the intersection of technology and society. Her latest book is Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census .

title: China’s ByteDance sets up AI safety team, launches global hiring drive
body: Chinese tech giant ByteDance’s AI research unit Seed has created an Alignment & Preparedness team and launched a global drive to recruit 10 researchers, saying it will make a long-term investment in AI safety for its increasingly capable models. The hiring push comes as scrutiny of AI-agent safety grows in China and the US, especially as developers give them autonomy to access the Internet. AI alignment refers to efforts to ensure advanced AI systems act in line with human goals and safety requirements, particularly when carrying out complex, multi-step tasks. ByteDance’s announcement is a rare public disclosure by a major Chinese AI developer of a dedicated effort focused on frontier-model safety, alignment and preparedness for emerging risks. State-backed newspaper The Paper reported on Tuesday, October 13, that Seed was the first Chinese frontier AI lab to establish a standalone safety and alignment department. The move also comes amid broader US-China discussions on AI guardrails, safety risks and channels for communicating about major AI-related incidents, even as the two countries compete for leadership in advanced AI. As model capabilities improve, safety and alignment are no longer simply safeguards against risk but core capabilities that will determine whether models can be deployed at scale, Seed said in a recruitment post published on its official WeChat account on Wednesday. Seed said it would provide the new team with computing capacity and research resources comparable to those available to frontier-model teams. The positions are based in Beijing, Shanghai, and San Jose, California. Its research will include safety training across model-development stages, automated testing for vulnerabilities, tools to monitor and explain model behavior, AI-agent testing environments and preparations for emerging risks. Seed said it would also seek independent testing and work with universities and research institutions, applying safety research across model training, evaluation and deployment. – Rappler.com

title: Armed youth kill 4 passengers; Tonj East conflict escalates
body: The authorities in Warrap State’s Tonj East County have reported that four passengers, including a soldier and a girl, were shot dead by armed youth on Tuesday as communal conflict intensified in the area. Speaking to this publication on Thursday, Tonj East County Caretaker County Commissioner Machuei Bith said the incident happened in Ngap Anet Boma. “A businessman, bus conductor, soldier and a girl who were all passengers were shot dead by the armed youth in Ngap Anet Boma under Ngap Agok Payam in Tonj East County,” he said. “They were travelers in three commuter vehicles traveling from the Romich area in Tonj East County heading to Tonj South County when they fell in the deadly road ambush on Tuesday.” According to the commissioner, the assailants mistook the travelers for their wounded adversaries from the Thiik Majok community, whom they believed were being transported to Tonj Town for treatment. “As you know, there is conflict between the Thiik Majok and Akok Deng communities, and when the armed youth from Ngap Anet, part of the Akok Deng Achuil community, spotted commercial vehicles, they suspected that their wounded enemies were being escorted by the army for treatment to Tonj South County,” Bith added. Four wounded passengers were admitted to a hospital in Tonj Town, and the authorities have launched investigations in collaboration with traditional leaders. A resident of Tonj East, who preferred anonymity for security reasons, said all government soldiers on board were disarmed by the youth and that eight weapons were later returned to a military barracks in the Romich area. “It was reported that one commuter vehicle departed Ngap Agok to Tonj South County, but it was ambushed by the local armed youth identified as Gelweng (armed cattle protection forces),” he explained. “Eight guns taken from the soldiers escorting the convoy were later returned to a military barracks, but two guns are still missing.” Meanwhile, Bona Malual, chairperson of the civil society network in Warrap State, called for cessation of hostilities among the feuding communities and urged for freedom of movement and free trade in the region. “We call for calm and immediate cessation of road attacks because we have other communities who are not part of the ongoing conflict, and they have the right to travel from one point to another, and their right must be respected,” he said. The post Armed youth kill 4 passengers; Tonj East conflict escalates appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Zelenskyy says ‘we’re done’ with Trump’s energy truce
body: KYIV, Ukraine – Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday, October 15, after President V olodymyr Zelenskyy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump, and criticized Trump’s willingness to strike deals with Moscow. By effectively walking away from Trump’s demand that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and openly criticizing the US leader , Zelenskyy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine’s latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia’s refinery throughput, helping supply the capital. Regional governor Pavel Malkov said on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack had caused a fire at the refinery. Russian President Vladimir Putin played down the effect of Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russian refineries, saying they had caused “nothing particularly significant.” After Trump’s surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites, Kyiv suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel prices on global markets. But in the days that followed, Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people. Zelenskyy’s relations with Trump have been testy, particularly after a February 2025 Oval Office meeting descended into a shouting match. Zelenskyy has since praised Trump and US help for Ukraine, and in recent days said Ukraine fully backed the energy ceasefire despite waves of Russian attacks. Patience ran out In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s patience had run out. “The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done,” he told the newspaper. Zelenskyy also criticized what he saw as Trump’s willingness to strike deals with Russia, apparent admiration for Putin and an affinity for those wielding power or considerable wealth. “He (Trump) speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people,” the FT quoted him as saying. “Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong.” In his comments to the FT, Zelenskyy also said he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink receptors this week, which curbed Ukraine’s ability to pilot its drones, were a policy decision. “It was not a technical problem, it was the will,” he told the FT. British Defense Minister Wes Streeting said on Thursday that he and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of the Starlink service in Ukraine and called for both sides to “move forward in a collective spirit.” “We need President Trump engaged on Ukraine. He has been, and the diplomatic track is as important in ending the war as making sure Ukraine has the weapons it needs to see off Russian aggression,” he said on Fox News. EU summit Zelenskyy was due to attend a European Union summit on Friday and in a series of meetings ahead of the gathering stressed the need to strengthen air defenses. In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump as president of the United States. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote. Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend had “damn well better stop”. Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington. Ukrainian officials say that for several days they have not received the usual warnings, which rely on US satellite detectors, from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles. Trump has denied withholding intelligence. At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. A source in Ukraine’s defense ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). Ukrainian officials say that is too slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones. Defense experts said, and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, meanwhile, showed that Russia had in just six weeks nearly finished building a major base in southern Russia for launching jet-powered drones. Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia. Trump is under pressure to lower fuel prices, with his Republicans facing midterm elections in less than three weeks,. Prices for diesel have reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, though Trump says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices. In the Black Sea, rescuers searched for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze in the latest attack on shipping along a vital route used by Ukraine. The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine’s targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was ongoing to do so. – Rappler.com

title: Pacific head rebukes Australia’s focus on pre-COP costs
body: CANBERRA, 15 OCTOBER 2026 (AAP)—The head of an influential Pacific nations group has taken a swipe at Australia’s fixation on attendance and cost of this month’s pre-COP event, while urging greater climate investment for the region. Palau President Surangel Whipps, who became Pacific Islands Forum chair after hosting the region’s annual summit last month, has spent the week in Canberra on a bilateral visit. The trip lands between the two central events of annual climate talks: the Fiji and Tuvalu-hosted pre-COP last week and next month’s COP31 in Turkey. In the lead-up to pre-COP, Australia placed an emphasis on inviting leaders and ministers to the talks. Not normally attended by such senior politicians, the goal was for the world to witness the impact of climate change on the globe’s most impacted region. While most of the Pacific’s leaders partook in the summit, few outside the region did so. In pointed remarks at the Australian National University, Whipps said criticism of the endeavour was short-sighted. “Some have dismissed the gathering by counting the leaders who were absent … rather than recognising the significance of those who came,” he said. “I read recently that all the big names were missing so let’s talk about size for a moment. “Pacific states are custodians of nearly 20 percent of our Earth’s surface … an area larger than Russia, China, the United States, Canada, Brazil, and Australia, and India combined. “There is nothing small about that. “Humanity actually depends upon the blue Pacific for its food, climate stability and connectivity,” Whipps said. He said Pacific island nations, often dismissed as small, ought to be redefined as ‘big ocean states’. “It is true that some of the world’s largest industrialised nations and its largest emitters and polluters were not present at this pre-COP but the big ocean states were,” he said. Tuvalu’s climate minister Maina Talia, also in Australia this week, said his country – the lowest-lying in the world – was delighted to play host. “More than 30 ministers were there representing their countries … we’re very happy with the outcome of the pre-COP,” he told the ABC. However, Dr Talia said he was “alarmed” by Australia’s continued expansion of fossil fuels, given the need rein in emissions to limit global warming. “We want to see that they will put a stop to opening new coal mines and gasses because that will definitely impact the lives of those living in small low-lying atolls,” he said. “We want to keep 1.5 (degrees) alive for us to stay in our own countries.” Whipps, who met Anthony Albanese on Wednesday morning, said it was “a fair question” as to whether the pre-COP was worth the cost, estimated in the tens of millions. “Here is how I would ask you to answer it: not by who was in the room, but by the result we collectively achieve at COP next month,” he said. The Pacific has set four regional priorities for COP31: keeping 1.5 degrees within reach, accelerating the renewables transition, funding, and recognising ocean stewardship. Australia and Turkey, hosting the larger summit from 09 November, are working towards support for the “Antalya Ocean Declaration”, underpinning that fourth goal. Whipps is also eager to win funding towards the Pacific Resilience Facility (PRF) to fund the region’s renewables transition, climate adaptation and disaster mitigation. Pledges from pre-COP to the region’s climate finance body only reached half of the initial US$500 million goal. Speaking in Fiji, regional leaders including Albanese said this funding was central to the Pacific’s hopes from COP31. “This is the moment to invest,” Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown said. “Your investment buys us time,” he said….
