title: 11 Negros Occidental wind projects advance along bird migration route
body: NEGROS OCCIDENTAL Philippines – Eleven wind farm projects are moving forward in Negros Occidental, all facing the Guimaras Strait, a bird migration route. The province’s coastline facing the strait is conducive to wind energy development because of its strong winds. Eleven cities and municipalities in Negros Occidental are set to host the projects. The cities are Cadiz, Silay, Victorias, Talisay, Bacolod, Bago and Kabankalan, while the municipalities are Manapla, E.B. Magalona, Pulupandan and Cauayan. The projects, scheduled for commissioning and commercial operations between 2027 and 2030, have a combined capacity of 3,767 megawatts (MW). William Carido of the Department of Energy (DOE) Visayas identified the project proponents during the “Be REeady” Caravan organized by the Provincial Energy Development Council (PEDC) in Himamaylan City on Wednesday, October 14, as the following: Bago-Negros Energy Corporation Envision Energy Philippines Corporation Apolaki One Incorporated Energy Development Corporation Triconti Southwind Corporation Freya Renewables First Gen Visayas Energy Incorporated Haraya Wind Energy Corporation Carido said the 11 wind farms are currently classified as indicative projects but are expected to proceed, as their proponents could face penalties from the DOE if they fail to meet their commitments. According to the DOE’s schedule, the 200-MW Cauayan Wind Project, developed by Envision Energy Philippines, is expected to be the province’s first wind farm to enter operation. Commissioning is targeted for October 2027, with commercial operations scheduled for December 2027. The next project is Bago-Negros Energy Corporation’s 300-MW wind farm in Bago City, covering phases 1 and 2. It is scheduled for commissioning in October 2028 and commercial operations in December of that year. Bago City held a groundbreaking ceremony on June 10 for phase 1 of the project, which has a capacity of 150 MW. Both the Cauayan and Bago projects are onshore wind farms. The last project scheduled for development is Haraya Wind Energy’s 1,215-MW Haraya IV-Negros Wind Project, which is expected to begin commercial operations in May 2030. The DOE has yet to identify a specific site within the province for the project. Rafael Coscolluela, a former Negros Occidental governor who now serves as a provincial consultant on energy and environmental issues, said the 11 projects would comprise both onshore and offshore wind farms. Offshore development poses significant challenges, he said. The DOE has yet to determine which cities and municipalities will host the onshore and offshore projects. Coscolluela said proponents would face lengthy procedures to secure an environmental impact assessment (EIA) and an environmental compliance certificate (ECC) from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources. The DOE Visayas office said energy projects with capitalization of at least P3.5 billion may qualify for a Certificate of Energy Project of National Significance (CEPNS), which can help streamline and expedite permitting. On concerns about the projects’ proximity to the Guimaras Strait bird migration route, Coscolluela said an initial agreement with proponents called for painting turbine blades in bright colors to make them more visible to birds. Coscolluela welcomed the wind farm developments, noting that Negros Occidental was declared coal-free on March 6, 2019, when then-governor Alfredo Marañón Jr. signed Executive Order No. 19-08. The order has not been repealed and remains in effect, he said. “The only hurdle is, can Negros Occidental benefit from the power to be produced by wind farms?” Coscolluela said. He said the province’s three distribution utilities could be encouraged to prioritize contracts with solar and wind power producers as their existing power supply agreements (PSAs) expire. Wind farms would also contribute to the province’s goal of gradually shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy as part of its energy transition and decarbonization efforts, he said. The national target is for renewable energy to account for 35% of the country’s energy mix by 2030, Coscolluela said. “SecuRE Negros,” an energy program backed by PEDC, aims to contribute to that national goal, he added. – Rappler.com

title: Australia’s ruling on coal ‘a clear signal’ to the world, Pacific minister says
body: CANBERRA, 14 OCTOBER 2026 (SBS)—Tuvalu’s Climate Minister has hit back at claims that last week’s Pre-COP event hosted by his country was a flop, while saying a phase-out of fossil fuels must be part of the discussion around COP31 in Türkiye. Dr Maina Vakafua Talia also told SBS News his nation welcomed a landmark Australian High Court decision on coal and gas emissions, which provoked outcry from the mining sector, as a “clear signal” of moral responsibility. Tuvalu, whose population numbers around 10,000, hosted a leader’s gathering at last week’s Pre-COP event shared with Fiji, part of a compromise struck by Australia to divide hosting rights with Türkiye. The event came under heavy Australian media scrutiny, with shadow energy minister Dan Tehan labelling the event an “embarrassment” and a “flop” over the low number of leaders attending beyond a group from the Pacific. While Talia acknowledged the Tuvalu meeting was only able to attract two global leaders from outside the Pacific (Timor-Leste and Mauritius), down from five initially expected, he described the turnout as “a big achievement for Tuvalu and for the Pacific.” “We need to be very ambitious,” he told SBS News in Canberra, talking up the event’s shift from “a boring dialogue” to “a more moving, emotional engagement” focused on the challenges facing low-lying communities like his. “The leaders were able to see for themselves, engage with the young ones, engage with our elders. One of the high representatives that came to Tuvalu told me, ‘My heart bleeds when I saw the kids, when I saw our elders. Now I understand’.” The Taku Pakasoa Declaration agreed to at Pre-COP urged nations to act to keep the 1.5-degree climate target in reach, as well as increasing access to Climate Finance. But there appears to be a diminishing appetite among nations for November’s Antalya agreement to contain language focused on the phase-out of fossil fuels like Coal and Gas. Türkiye’s climate minister Murat Kurum, who will oversee the COP31 presidency, told the Guardian last week the world is “already in a transition” away from fossil fuels, reportedly suggesting the issue could be addressed indirectly through other means. “If we are to discuss the 1.5 degrees, we are literally discussing the phasing out of fossil fuels,” Talia said. “We are talking about the backbone of some economies, but this is the reality that we have to face, and we really need to change the whole narrative, to change our priorities … to ensure that the survival of other peoples is always there.” Talia, who is set to share a related panel with energy minister Chris Bowen in Canberra, said he had faith Australia “can do more with the power that they have” to make the case for strong action, standing up to nations like India, Russia and China who are likely to argue for a moderate approach. While leaders were gathering for Pre-COP, Australia’s High Court delivered a landmark climate decision, finding in the case of Mount Pleasant Coal Mine in New South Wales, planning authorities must consider the entire carbon footprint of the project, including the emissions produced by the burning of fossil fuels overseas. The decision referenced the 2025 International Court of Justice ruling brought on by Vanuatu, which found nations have international law obligations to protect the climate. Talia said the Australian High Court ruling showed the impact of that ICJ precedent, and was one long-awaited by the Pacific nation. “”This is a good signal, a very clear signal, not just for the Pacific countries. It’s really a moral responsibility for countries,” he said. The Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union signed in 2024 was the first bilateral agreement to contain a significant pathway around climate mobility, with more than half the nation’s population applying in the initial ballot. “There is no treaty in this world we can allude to say that this is 100percent,” Talia said, conceding “there are challenges, but they are manageable at the moment.” He said the risk of a brain drain was one his government would have to manage but rejected the claim the treaty was “creating an avenue for people to escape”….PACNEWS The post Australia’s ruling on coal ‘a clear signal’ to the world, Pacific minister says appeared first on Island Times News .

title: Ukrainian air defenses down 114 out of 149 Russian drones launched at Ukraine overnight
body:
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
As reported, starting at 18:00 on Thursday, October 15, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 149 strike drones, including Shahed-type drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones. Of these, 108 Shahed drones were jet-powered.
The launches were carried out from the area of the Russian town of Oryol, as well as from the temporarily occupied areas of Hvardiiske in Crimea and Donetsk.
The enemy attack was countered by Ukrainian combat aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:30 on Friday, October 16, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or jammed 114 Russian drones, including 77 jet-powered Shahed drones, as well as Gerbera and other types of drones.
Hits by 27 enemy aerial weapons were recorded at 24 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 14 locations.
The Air Force emphasized that Russian UAVs are still present in Ukrainian airspace and the attack is ongoing. Citizens are urged to follow safety precautions.
As reported by Ukrinform, in the Odesa region, enemy strikes damaged private homes, an energy facility, and a household goods manufacturing company. Casualties were reported.

title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1695: Ukraine’s war budget has $52 billion hole as West ties aid to reforms
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Exclusives Russia is back at Dobropillia a year after it failed there. Now it’s the southern jaw of a pincer on Donbas’s last big free cities . This time Russia brought another army, and Dobropillia’s defenders have until the leaves fall to stop it. Military Ukraine’s military now orders supplies based on real front-line data, not guesswork, lawmaker says. Shift comes under new commander-in-chief . Ukraine’s new commander-in-chief, Drapatyi, is centering the army on soldiers’ lives and real front-line needs, a lawmaker believes. “Operation to strike Russian targets deep in swamps continues”: Ukrainian Commander Madiar says his unit hits 7,306 Russian troops in first half of October, up 59% on August . The pace held through weather that usually grounds drones, says Robert “Madiar” Brovdi, who calls the trend the opposite of de-escalation. Ukraine’s Navy says it hit six Su-34 bombers at a Russian airbase with Neptune missiles—the jets that drop glide bombs on Ukrainian towns (updated) . Footage from Borisoglebsk showed a large fire at the base after Russian officials declared a missile alert, though the damage has not been independently confirmed. Ukraine is going back to hitting Russian oil after its Trump-pressured pause, during which Kyiv got no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles . The pause was meant to seal a US-announced energy truce, but Russia kept hitting power plants while Ukraine lost early warnings and drone connectivity. To scale up air defense without straining the front, Ukraine enlists business. In under year nearly 100 companies have joined, their crews downing 60-plus targets . The crews fight under Air Force commands, using interceptor drones and automated turrets. Intelligence and technology Posting strike videos online may help Russia tune its drones’ optical targeting. Moscow now pays people to film hits, Ukrainian adviser warns . Russia is collecting footage of its Geran attack drones hitting Ukraine, probably to test the optical target-recognition systems that guide them in their final seconds. Ukraine’s shell factories outpace state orders, arms company chief says: Kyiv spent five months buying from them this year, leaving six to produce . Private plants were built under Russian fire with no state investment, says the head of Ukrainian defense maker Ukrainian Armor Ukraine’s hobbit-named robot fired on targets up to 1.3 km away in a demo for border guards . First reported carrying a wounded soldier, Ukraine’s Frodo robot has now fired for a border guard brigade—built, its maker says, to hit and run. Musk pointed at the US military over Ukraine’s satellite limits. Now a US official says the administration had nothing to do with them . Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says it is in talks with partners and SpaceX to maintain stable service and prevent sudden restrictions on satellite services used by its military. International Ukraine and Japan plan prefabricated backup crossings for Kyiv’s bridges: 720 meters of structures already delivered . The fifth phase of the Emergency Recovery Program, recently signed by the two countries, allocates $15 million for Ukraine’s infrastructure needs. After Trump, Musk tells Ukraine’s president to go. Zelenskyy says he won’t resign and will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian . The Ukrainian leader told British broadcaster Piers Morgan that this refusal is why some “big guys” want him replaced. US weighs relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers, days after freeing Russian diesel . Officials say only unsanctioned oil would sail, but Reuters says Trump’s diesel push could pressure them to let Russian fuel aboard. Ukraine’s war budget has $52 billion hole, and army needs $45 billion more on top . The West won’t send Ukraine the billions it needs until Kyiv delivers the reforms it promised. Humanitarian and social impact Russian drone cuts down unique energy line tower over Dnipro River in Kyiv. It can’t be rebuilt, and world is queuing for more power equipment . Ukraine’s grid operator Ukrenergo is already starting work on workarounds, but calls drones that cut down towers a new challenge. Two tankers burn off Romania’s Sulina as Bulgaria says it lacks proof Russia is behind the Black Sea ship attacks . Seven crew members of a San Marino-flagged chemical tanker were still missing hours after it caught fire at anchor off the mouth of the Danube. Russia’s largest drone attack on Kirovohrad Oblast since the full-scale invasion kills three in Kropyvnytskyi . Drones struck critical infrastructure, transport companies, logistics sites, and homes across the central Ukrainian oblast, with its capital taking most of the damage. On Monday she sat in her cousin’s Kyiv apartment, and by Wednesday a Russian strike had left a hole where the window was . Her cousin, his girlfriend, and an aunt survived inside, and rescuers lifted them out 15 minutes after the blast. A Russian drone damaged Cosmogony, Ukraine’s largest painting, in the section depicting the future. Its artist spent nearly two years creating it . The museum is weighing whether to restore the burned section or keep the fire’s traces as a reminder of the war. Political and legal developments Hungary held $82 million in cash and gold from Ukraine for months. Now, it faces torture complaints in Europe’s top court . Hungarian forces stopped two Oschadbank vehicles in March, carrying cash and gold from Austria to Ukraine. Ukraine detains a gas station worker and a Telegram commenter suspected of scouting targets for Russian strikes . One was allegedly reached through a former classmate in Russia, and the other allegedly took orders from a female handler there. Ukraine’s anti-corruption bodies, whose independence EU made condition for membership, have clawed back $5.1 million for state budget . Detectives found that a regional branch’s inaction had put millions at risk. Read our earlier daily review here .

title: US-Israel aggression severely damaged regional ecosystems
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that aggression and warmongering by the US and the Israeli regime have severely damaged regional ecosystems, driving catastrophic environmental destruction.
Addressing the 17th Summit of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17), held in the Armenian capital of Yerevan on Friday, Pezeshkian emphasized that US and Israel waged an unprovoked war of aggression against the Iranian nation which produced adverse effects on the ecosystem of the regional countries.
Condemning the destructive impact of wars of aggression on nature, Iranian President Pezeshkian termed it "ecocide," or environmental genocide, stating that preserving biodiversity can be important arenas for peace diplomacy.
Iranian president called for stronger international mechanisms to assess and repair environmental damage caused by armed conflict, warning that war threatens biodiversity far beyond national borders.
Turning to the Israeli massacre of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, he stressed, “Gaza stands as a stark testament to ecocide, with devastation whose horrific impacts will endure for generations.”
President Pezeshkian warned that war caused lasting environmental devastation, citing that Gaza's contaminated soil as proof that ecological damage crosses borders and requires international intervention.
Nations subjected to illegal sanctions and foreign-imposed wars must not be forced to pay the heavy toll of these crises, Pezeshkian warned.
Protecting biodiversity can be an important arena for peace diplomacy, he said, stressing, “Not only war is merely a threat to humans and infrastructure, but also as a direct cause of the destruction of nature.”
War burns forests, destroys wetlands, pollutes soil and water, and displaces animal species, he underlined.
“We believe that biodiversity conservation can serve as a significant arena for "peace diplomacy." In a region grappling with security crises stemming from the illegal and expansionist presence of powers, as well as climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations, the bridges that pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future lived in harmony with the natural world.”
Pezeshkian described the environmental devastation caused by the wars in the region, including in Gaza, as “ecocide” that must be condemned, adding that pollution and ecological damage transcend national borders.
He then called on the international community to ensure that nature is not treated as a “silent and defenseless victim” of war. He said international agencies and relevant institutions should strengthen mechanisms for assessing environmental damage, mobilizing financial resources, restoring damaged ecosystems and supporting countries affected by the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.
Highlighting Iran’s biodiversity, which spans the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests, the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, Sea of Oman and Caspian Sea, Pezeshkian said nature conservation is part of the country’s cultural and civilizational heritage. He noted that Iran has adopted a national biodiversity strategy and action plan, designated its Department of Environment as the national coordinating body, and prioritized the protection of endangered species and the expansion of protected areas.
The president also stressed that developing countries need fair access to financial resources, modern technologies, scientific knowledge and capacity-building opportunities to meet their environmental commitments.
He said countries facing economic sanctions or military aggression should not be left to bear alone the environmental costs of sanctions or wars they did not initiate. Without adequate funding and equitable technology transfer, he warned, global biodiversity targets would remain little more than declarations and negotiations.
“What has happened in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ‘ecocide or environmental genocide,’ which must be condemned,” he said.
Pezeshkian also pointed to the combined effects of climate change, drought, water scarcity, desertification, economic sanctions and restricted access to technology and financial resources on Iran’s environmental protection efforts.
He said Iran has been targeted by criminal wars for two consecutive years, involving the extensive use of destructive and prohibited weapons, with attacks in many cases deliberately aimed at damaging the environment, including strikes on fuel storage facilities in the capital.
The president called for genuine international cooperation to help Iran implement environmental programs and compensate for the damage inflicted.
He said Iran’s diverse ecosystems, species and genetic resources formed a natural and cultural heritage shaped by millions of years of evolution over time. From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and Caspian Sea, these resources underpin the country’s resilience and sustainable development, he said.
President Pezeshkian said Iran had adopted a national biodiversity strategy and action plan and designated the Department of Environment as its national coordinator. Priorities include expanding protected areas to 28 percent, monitoring key species, developing wildlife rehabilitation centers and implementing action plans for 25 vertebrate species. National task forces have been established for species including the Asiatic cheetah and Persian fallow deer, he said.
Turning to armed conflict, President Pezeshkian said war burns forests, damages wetlands, contaminates soil and water, destroys habitats and introduces pollutants and heavy metals into natural systems. Such harm can persist for years after fighting ends and affect the security and well-being of future generations.
He said the United States and the Israeli regime are causing environmental damage through military operations in the region, citing damage to industrial and energy facilities, fires, pollution and harm to protective infrastructure. He said environmental impacts crossed political borders and required solutions.
Referring to Gaza, he warned that damage to soil and ecological systems could endure for generations and described the destruction as ecocide, which he emphasized should be condemned.
President Pezeshkian also highlighted the challenges facing countries dealing with climate change, drought, water scarcity and desertification while facing economic sanctions and limited access to finance and technology. Biodiversity commitments, he said, would remain on paper without adequate funding, fair access to technology and capacity-building.
He called on United Nations agencies, international financial institutions and environmental and sustainable-development bodies to strengthen funding mechanisms, assess environmental damage, restore affected ecosystems and support countries dealing with the consequences of armed conflict. Countries under sanctions or subjected to military aggression should not be left to bear these costs alone, he said.
Pezeshkian said Iran’s commitment to biodiversity protection is rooted not only in its international obligations but also in its longstanding cultural and civilizational heritage.
He noted that Iran is a country with an ancient tradition of living in harmony with nature and has a remarkable diversity of ecosystems, species and genetic resources.
From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman and the Caspian Sea, Iran’s natural wealth provides a foundation for water and food security, public health, resilience to natural hazards and sustainable development, he said.
Respect for nature, Pezeshkian added, has long been part of Iranian cultural, religious and ritual identity. Traditional agriculture, animal husbandry, the use of medicinal plants and indigenous knowledge have also developed through centuries of interaction with the natural environment.
Protecting biodiversity, he added, could become an important arena for peace diplomacy, with environmental cooperation serving as a bridge between nations and helping advance peace with nature and a safer future for coming generations.
Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to share its scientific expertise, academic capabilities and experience with other countries, describing biodiversity conservation as an important avenue for “peace diplomacy.”
Cooperation could help bridge divides between nations and contribute to peace and security, coexistence with nature, and the well-being of present and future generations, he concluded.

title: Q&A| NDM: We cannot participate in a dialogue whose resolutions are predetermined
body: Bol Joseph Agau, Secretary General of the National Democratic Movement (NDM), said the inter-party dialogue has stalled, failed to make its resolutions public, and that any resolutions remain known only to a few people. He contends that an inclusive dialogue should include all political parties in decisions on amendments to the agreement. Radio Tamazuj caught up with him and sounded him out in an exclusive interview during which he said that South Sudan is not ready for elections under the current circumstances. He added that political leaders should avoid actions that aggravate existing conflicts and instead work together to promote peace, reconciliation and political understanding. Agau speaks about his party’s absence from the ongoing inter-party dialogue on elections, its concerns about the December 2026 polls, a dispute over its registered leadership, and what is needed to ensure a credible electoral process. Below are edited excerpts: Q: Why is NDM not participating in the inter-party dialogue on elections? A: Thank you for giving me this opportunity to explain NDM’s position so that the public can get the correct information about what the party is doing and why it is not participating in the inter-party dialogue. NDM is a member of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA). The alliance issued a press statement rejecting the inter-party dialogue because it was not the inclusive dialogue we had agreed to pursue. Since the peace agreement was extended for another two years, NDM and SSOA have maintained that there should be an inclusive dialogue in which all political parties participate in decisions regarding amendments to the agreement. However, the current inter-party dialogue has stalled. Up to now, no resolutions have been made public, and if there are any, they remain known only to a few people. The dialogue has put the cart before the horse. It should have taken place before the dissolution of the transitional government and the changes to the legal framework. On September 21, 2026, the SPLM used its parliamentary majority to amend laws in a manner that, in our view, was neither procedural nor based on consensus. Other political parties were not given an opportunity to express their views meaningfully. NDM cannot participate in a dialogue whose resolutions we believe have already been predetermined. Furthermore, those participating appear to be discussing power-sharing rather than how elections will be conducted. If the discussion is based on the peace agreement, that agreement has already been amended in parliament by the SPLM. If it is about a new agreement, we have not seen any negotiations or a mediator. This is why NDM decided not to participate. Q: Were you invited? A: Yes, NDM was invited. However, the letter reached our chairman, Dr. Lam Akol Ajawin, late in the evening on September 23, just hours before the dialogue was scheduled to begin on September 24. On that same day, we discovered that the Political Parties Council (PPC) had changed NDM’s registered leadership details on its website, replacing our chairman with a person we did not recognize as the party’s leader and replacing me as the second contact person. This raised questions about the status of our chairman at the dialogue. He had been invited as the leader of a political party, yet the institution responsible for registering political parties had allegedly altered the party’s official records. We considered this a serious contradiction and one of the reasons we could not participate. Q: Do you believe the ongoing inter-party dialogue can produce meaningful agreements on elections if some political parties, including NDM, are not participating? A: No! We do not believe the current inter-party dialogue can produce meaningful resolutions that will lead the country towards peaceful elections. We believe the SPLM’s enthusiasm for elections is not genuine and that the government is using the electoral process to advance its own political agenda. The constitutional and legal changes made in parliament have raised serious concerns about the legitimacy of the process. For elections to take place peacefully, political party leaders must work together. They should be able to coordinate campaigns and visit communities together. Leaders from the SPLM, SPLM-IO, SSOA, the Other Political Parties group and the Former Detainees should be able to travel together, engage citizens and seek their votes. Such joint activities would demonstrate unity and help reassure communities that their leaders can work together despite their political differences. However, the SPLM appears to be acting unilaterally, without recognizing that South Sudan belongs to all its people and not to one political party. The current dialogue will not produce the desired results unless the SPLM changes its approach and allows other political parties the political space they need to campaign. We are also concerned about the limited time remaining before the December 22 elections. We have only a short period left, yet the country has unresolved problems that have accumulated over many years. Peace and reconciliation have not received sufficient attention. Communities continue to experience communal violence, cattle raiding, abductions, and other insecurity. There are also reports of soldiers selling guns to civilians because they are not being paid and need money to meet their families’ basic needs, including food, medical care, and education. These realities must be addressed if the country is to hold peaceful and credible elections. Q: With elections scheduled for December 22, 2026, does NDM believe South Sudan is ready to hold credible, free and fair elections? What are the main obstacles? A: We do not believe the country is ready for credible elections under the current circumstances. There are immediate steps that need to be taken. First, political and civic space must be widened. All political parties intending to participate in the elections should be given airtime on the South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation (SSBC), just as political parties were given opportunities to use the media during the 2010 elections in Sudan. Political parties should be able to present their programmes, hold rallies and conferences, and communicate with citizens through television and other media platforms. The public needs to see that the political space is not reserved for the SPLM alone. Civic education is also necessary so that citizens understand their rights and know how to participate in elections. Second, political parties should be allowed to conduct joint campaigns and visit states to engage communities, discuss elections, and promote reconciliation. Our communities have experienced years of communal fighting, cattle raiding, abductions, and other forms of violence. These problems are not confined to one region. They affect communities across the country. Political leaders should use electoral campaigns as an opportunity to bring communities together and encourage peaceful coexistence. Third, there must be an electoral code of conduct. As we speak, we have not seen a clear process for adopting such a document. An electoral code of conduct should be transparent and known to all political parties participating in the elections. We are also concerned about the removal of the chairperson of the electoral commission when fewer than 100 days remained before the scheduled elections. Such a development raises questions about the preparations and the possibility of holding elections as planned. Fourth, the institutions responsible for conducting elections must be adequately funded. The electoral commission has repeatedly raised concerns about funding, and we are worried that the country has not made sufficient preparations, including the provision of ballot papers. Civic education takes time, particularly in helping voters understand how to mark their ballot papers correctly. These preparations cannot be completed properly without adequate resources and time. Another concern is the National Security Service Bill, particularly Section 57, which we believe poses a threat to politicians because of its provisions concerning arrests without warrants. Political candidates must be able to campaign without fear of intimidation or arbitrary arrest. We also need an independent and credible judiciary capable of resolving electoral disputes. These are some of the immediate steps that must be taken if South Sudan is to conduct credible elections. The main obstacles remain inadequate funding, limited political space, insecurity, insufficient preparations, and the short time available before the scheduled election date. Q: What specific conditions must the government meet for NDM to participate in the December elections? Would your party take part if these concerns remain unresolved? A: NDM has consistently called for an inclusive political dialogue. If there is anyone in the government who is genuinely patriotic, the best course of action would be to set aside the current approach and use the available resources to convene an inclusive dialogue. The African Union’s declaration of September 29, 2026, should be implemented, with support from IGAD, to facilitate an inclusive process. The dialogue should bring together political parties and groups that are currently outside the process so that they can agree on a new political direction for the country. We need a political settlement that all parties can support and a renewed commitment to implementing agreements in both letter and spirit. No political party can solve all the country’s problems alone. The SPLM cannot continue making decisions unilaterally while the people of South Sudan face serious challenges in service delivery. If you visit government health centers in many counties, you will find shortages of basic medicines. Many essential services depend on humanitarian organisations, while the population remains vulnerable. South Sudan needs a political dispensation that prioritizes the welfare of its people and addresses the country’s challenges through collective leadership. If these concerns remain unresolved, NDM will not participate in what we consider sham elections. We will not allow our participation to be used to validate or legitimise a process that we believe lacks the necessary political and institutional foundations. Q: NDM has called for inclusive political dialogue to address outstanding issues in the peace agreement. What alternative does your party propose if the current electoral preparations remain contested? A: I have already explained that we want an inclusive dialogue to address the outstanding issues in the peace agreement and establish a new political understanding. If credible elections cannot be conducted by December 22, the country will face a serious political and constitutional challenge as the transitional period approaches its scheduled end. The peace agreement provides for the transitional period to end on February 22, 2027. If elections are not held and there is no legitimate arrangement to guide the country beyond the scheduled election date, the government will face further questions about its legitimacy. We want the government to proceed with the electoral preparations it has announced while the public observes whether the necessary conditions are being met. I have taken it upon myself to update the people of South Sudan through my Facebook page about the number of days remaining before the scheduled elections. We also want to clarify that the registration of political party members is not the same as official voter registration conducted by the National Elections Commission. The priority should be to resolve the outstanding political disagreements, establish an inclusive process, and create the conditions necessary for credible elections. Q: Your party has accused the Political Parties Council of changing its registered leadership details. What exactly happened, and how could this dispute affect NDM’s participation in the elections? A: NDM was registered on June 29, 2026, and its registration was publicly announced on June 30 by the chairman of the Political Parties Council, Engineer James Akol. The announcement identified Dr. Lam Akol Ajawin as the party’s chairman and me, Bol Joseph Agau, as the second contact person. On September 22, 2026, we discovered that changes had been made to the records of registered political parties on the PPC website. According to our information, the changes followed instructions allegedly given to the PPC chairman by Hussein Abdelbagi, who was then serving as vice-president representing SSOA. The PPC chairman subsequently issued Order No. 5 of September 22, directing the information technology department to change the records on the website. Three political parties were affected by these changes, according to our account: NDM, the South Sudan National Movement for Change (SSNMC) and the Federal Democratic Party (FDP). In NDM’s case, Dr Lam Akol Ajawin was removed as chairman and replaced by a person identified as Majook. My name was also removed as secretary general and second contact person and replaced by Peter Lomude. We believe these changes were made without following the procedures provided for under Section 21 of the Political Parties Council Act of 2012, as amended in 2022. Our understanding is that changes to a registered party’s leadership should be initiated by the party and processed through the relevant institutional procedures. The council should consider and approve the changes before the information technology department updates the official records. We maintain that this procedure was not followed. On September 24, representatives of the three affected parties visited the PPC to raise their concerns. During that meeting, the council’s deputy chairperson, Dr Lona, reportedly told us that the changes had not been sanctioned by the council as an institution because it had not met to approve them. We consider the matter serious and are pursuing legal avenues to resolve it. We believe public institutions must protect the integrity of their records and ensure that political parties are treated according to the law. The dispute could directly affect NDM’s participation in the elections because political parties provide the platforms through which candidates contest. I intend to represent the people of Urol West, but I need the support of my party and its membership. Political support does not come only from an individual’s personality or personal relationships; it also comes from the organisation to which that person belongs. If the party’s official leadership and status remain disputed, our candidates and members could face difficulties participating in the electoral process. We believe the matter must be resolved lawfully so that our party can operate and participate in the political process without interference. Q: How is NDM engaging with other opposition parties on the elections, and could the party’s absence from the current dialogue weaken the opposition’s ability to influence the electoral process? A: NDM is a member of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance, which has rejected the current inter-party dialogue because we believe it does not meet the requirements of an inclusive process. We believe the dialogue was introduced in a way that undermines efforts to establish a broader political dialogue. Our concern is that its outcomes could be presented to the international community, the African Union and IGAD as agreements reached by political parties, even though some stakeholders remain outside the process. We believe the current process has been designed to favour the SPLM rather than to create a genuinely inclusive political settlement. For this reason, we maintain that all political parties and relevant stakeholders should be involved in discussions on elections and the country’s political future. Our position is that political disagreements should be addressed through dialogue, and we continue to call on political actors and our supporters to remain peaceful and avoid violence. Q: What immediate steps should the government, opposition parties and international partners take to resolve the current political disagreements and ensure a peaceful and credible electoral process? A: The African Union has already issued a declaration containing 15 points that we believe could help South Sudan move towards credible, free and fair elections. The government should implement the declaration and work with the African Union, IGAD, opposition parties and other relevant stakeholders to establish an inclusive political dialogue. South Sudan is not ready for elections under the current circumstances. Political leaders should avoid actions that aggravate existing conflicts and instead work together to promote peace, reconciliation and political understanding. We are concerned that political decisions are sometimes being taken in ways that worsen tensions in communities where conflicts could otherwise be addressed through dialogue. The government and opposition parties should work together to resolve outstanding issues in the peace agreement and establish the political conditions necessary for credible elections. My message to the people of South Sudan is to remain hopeful. Whatever difficulties the country is experiencing today will not last forever. Political leaders and governments are temporary, but the country belongs to its people. I believe that one day South Sudan will have leadership that prioritizes the welfare of its citizens, promotes food production, addresses insecurity, and ensures that people can access basic services. To NDM members across the ten states and three administrative areas, I urge you not to lose hope because of the dispute over the party’s registration records. We are pursuing legal avenues to resolve the matter and restore the party’s official status. We believe the work our members have done to establish the party should not be wasted because of changes to its records. I call on all our supporters to remain peaceful, maintain discipline, and pursue their political objectives through lawful means. We remain hopeful that the matter will be resolved and that South Sudan will move towards a more inclusive and peaceful political future. The post Q&A| NDM: We cannot participate in a dialogue whose resolutions are predetermined appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Scores Feared Dead, over 10 Injured in Edo Tanker Explosion
body: Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City Scores of people were feared dead, while 10 others were reported to have sustained varying degrees of injuries at the scene of a fallen petrol tanker laden with fuel. The incident occurred at about 4 a.m. on Thursday at Oluku on the Benin-Lagos Road in Edo State. The petrol tanker was said to have attempted a u-turn near Oluku market but fell spilled its contents onto the road. Witnesses said that shortly after the tanker fell, residents and other passers-by rushed to the scene and began scooping fuel. One of the witnesses said people who arrived early at the scene joined in scooping before security operatives arrived and cordoned off the area. He said the truck’s owner later brought another tanker to evacuate the remaining fuel from the fallen vehicle before its explosion, leaving several victims burnt beyond recognition, while many others sustained varying degrees of injuries. He said 10 injured victims were rushed to the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH) for medical attention, while the corpses were deposited at the hospital’s mortuary. When THISDAY visited the UBTH, the management was seen mobilising emergency services to treat those brought to the hospital. The Chief Medical Director of UBTH, Prof. Idia Ize-Iyamu, was seen leading the emergency response team across the accident, emergency, and burns units to stabilise severe casualties and minimise fatalities. The Edo State Sector Commander of the Federal Road Safety Corps, Preye Ezekiel Bedford, said FRSC official, Police, Fire Service and Edo State Traffic Management Agency were on ground to control traffic. On the casualty, he said he was still at the scene of incident and would get back. Meanwhile, the Edo State All Progressives Congress (APC) Campaign Council expressed deep sorrow over the tragic explosion. In a statement issued by its Director of Media, John Mayaki, the council commiserated with families reportedly affected by the incident, particularly those who may have lost loved ones, while praying for the speedy recovery of injured victims receiving treatment. The council described the incident as heartbreaking and called for urgent support for affected families and survivors. “Our hearts go out to the families affected by this unfortunate tragedy. We share in their grief and pray that Almighty God grants them the strength to bear their losses. “No family deserves to lose a loved one in such painful circumstances. No parent should have to bury a child, and no child should have to lose a parent to a preventable tragedy and no struggling market woman deserves to lose her wares,” Mayaki said. The council particularly commended the Chief Medical Director of the UBTH, Professor Ize-Iyamu, for her personal coordination of the hospital’s emergency response following the explosion. Mayaki described the CMD’s intervention as an example of leadership during a public emergency. “We commend Professor Idia Ize-Iyamu, Chief Medical Director of UBTH, for rising to the occasion and personally coordinating the emergency medical response to this unfortunate incident. “Her intervention, alongside the doctors, nurses, emergency personnel and other hospital workers involved in treating the victims, deserves public recognition and appreciation. “At a time when lives are at risk, what matters most is the ability of our institutions and their leadership to respond promptly, professionally and compassionately. “We thank the management and staff of UBTH for their dedication to saving lives and caring for those affected.” The campaign council also expressed appreciation to firefighters and personnel of the fire services, the Federal Road Safety Corps, the Nigeria Police Force, emergency management agencies, ambulance operators, volunteers and other responders involved in rescue and emergency operations

title: Airbus wins order for 75 A320neo Family jets despite years-long delivery backlog
body:
Airbus has secured a firm order for 75 A320neo Family aircraft from Aviation Capital Group (ACG), adding another large commitment to a narrowbody program whose available delivery positions extend years into the future.
The agreement announced on October 16 is the largest aircraft order in the nearly 40-year history of the US-based lessor and increases its historical orders for A320neo Family aircraft to 190.
Airbus and ACG did not disclose the split between A320neo and A321neo aircraft or the financial value of the transaction.
The manufacturer said the new order will allow ACG to offer A320neo Family aircraft to airline customers "well into the next decade," highlighting the increasingly long planning horizon required to secure new narrowbody aircraft.
ACG follows a strategy centered on acquiring new-generation narrowbody aircraft and leasing them to airlines. As of June 30, the company had 504 owned, managed and committed aircraft.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The lessor already has substantial exposure to Airbus narrowbodies. At the end of 2025, its portfolio included 58 owned A320neos and 61 A321neos, in addition to aircraft scheduled for future delivery.
ACG also placed a major order with Boeing earlier this year . In January, it finalized an agreement for 50 737 MAX aircraft, comprising 25 737 MAX 8s and 25 737 MAX 10s, scheduled for delivery in 2032 and 2033.
The new Airbus agreement illustrates how aircraft lessors are securing production positions far ahead of expected deliveries as airlines compete for limited supplies of new-generation narrowbody jets.
As of the end of September, Airbus had recorded 12,329 firm orders for the A320neo Family and delivered around 4,800 aircraft, leaving approximately 7,529 jets still to be handed over to customers.
Airbus has accumulated more than 20,400 orders for the A320 Family since the program was launched. The manufacturer is increasing production of the A320neo Family but continues to face supply-chain constraints as it works through a large order backlog.

title: Russia Builds Massive Jet Drone Launch Base Near Ukraine in Just 6 Weeks
body:
Russia has nearly completed a massive new launch base for jet-powered attack drones in its southwestern Rostov region in just six weeks, satellite imagery analyzed by Reuters shows, as Moscow ramps up attacks that are increasingly difficult for Ukraine to intercept.
The facility near Millerovo, roughly 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles) from a Russian air base, has grown from an empty field into a complex covering about 0.9 square kilometers (0.3 square miles) – roughly the size of 126 soccer pitches – between Aug. 31 and Oct. 14.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Defense experts say the site is designed to launch Russia’s latest jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, which can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (373 miles per hour).
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, identified eight launch platforms along the facility’s western edge. Two already had launch rails installed, according to Reuters’ analysis of satellite imagery.
The base could be operational within weeks, if not sooner, Monnik said.
“The speed of construction ... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly,” he said.
The construction comes as Russia sharply increases its use of jet-powered drones against Ukraine, with Kyiv and the surrounding region among the hardest-hit areas.
Russian use of the faster drones increased roughly sixfold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data.
Unlike slower, piston-powered drones, jet-powered models are harder to stop with relatively inexpensive interceptor drones that Ukraine has increasingly relied on to counter Russian attacks.
With the full-scale war in its fifth year, Ukraine expects Russia to intensify drone and missile strikes this winter, putting additional pressure on its air defenses.
The new facility could potentially launch 100 or more jet-powered drones in 24 hours, depending on available supplies and operational requirements, Monnik said. Russia typically launches its drones in smaller waves throughout the day.
The new site is located close to Millerovo air base, home to Russia’s 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment.
DroneSec assessed that the launch facility likely falls within the air-defense coverage of the military air base, potentially making it more difficult for Ukraine to strike.
The rapid expansion of Russia’s drone-launch infrastructure also poses a potential challenge for NATO countries, which face growing concerns over Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions.

title: FACT CHECK: Plane with drugs not same aircraft used to fly Duterte to The Hague
body: Claim : The post claimed that the plane found to be carrying illegal drugs from Laos is the same one used in bringing former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague. Rating : FALSE Why we fact-checked this: Amid recent reports of an aircraft from Laos allegedly carrying illegal drugs bound for the Philippines, a Facebook post by Tinood Politiko, which has garnered nearly 1,000 shares, claimed that the aircraft was the same one used to transport former president Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague, the Netherlands. The post also used AI-generated photo showing an aircraft and Duterte with the overlay text: “ SAME AIRPLANE LEARJET 55B N73GP” and “KATAPATAN BA ITO O MALALIM NA KONEKSYON? ” (Same airplane Learjet 55B N73GP. Is this right or there is a deeper connection?) The facts: Upon verification, the jet plane flagged in Laos has a tail number showing “N73GP,”a 1986 model of Gates Learjet 55B, which is different from the plane that carried Duterte to The Hague, Netherlands on March 11, 2025. Reports show that the plane used to to fly Duterte was Gulfstream G550 with tail number “RP-C5219” contrary to the fake post. The jet plane with alleged illegal drugs was reported by a Malaysian media site, containing 521 kilograms of suspected shabu worth P3.1 million, and is allegedly bound for the Philippines. One of the plane’s passengers is a Filipino citizen, who reportedly booked the aircraft supposedly to move vape products. Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) spokesperson Joseph Frederick Calulut shared on October 11 that full details have not been received from the Malaysian authorities. Ongoing trial: Last October 13, Duterte attended a status conference at the International Criminal Court, prior to his full trial on November 30. The prosecution has presented further evidence against the former president and emphasized their relevance to the drug war campaign. Duterte will be tried in connection with his crimes against humanity case resulting from his bloody war on drugs. — Axel Cainglet/Rappler.com Axel John Cainglet is a political science student at the University of the Philippines Manila. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, he is also the editor-in-chief of The Manila Collegian . Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

title: Ombudsman probes Cagayan’s Jojo Lara for potential plunder over construction ties
body: MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman launched a preliminary investigation into Cagayan 3rd District Representative Jojo Lara for possible plunder. The probe comes a year after Rappler first reported about Lara’s ties to JLL Pulsar, which has bagged P3.7 billion in contracts from the DPWH since 2020, coinciding with Lara’s congressional career. “There was supposed to be a divestment, which we think did not really happen,” Ombudsman Boying Remulla told the media on Friday, October 16. Remulla said the preliminary investigation covers Lara’s connection with JLL Pulsar and JDL5 Construction Corporation, another company believed to be owned by the congressman. “The money paid to these construction companies still went to his private bank account, with the amount of P1.9 billion,” he added. Rappler’s original investigation showed that out of the P3.7 billion in public works contracts of JLL Pulsar, P2.1 billion in projects were in Lara’s home province. Around P1.37 billion in contracts were secured since 2023, coinciding with the time he became vice chairperson of the House appropriations committee, which reviews the executive’s proposed national budget annually. Lara’s office previously denied any wrongdoing, telling Rappler that the congressman removed his shares from JLL Pulsar before he entered public office in 2019. Lara is now in his third and final House term. “His position as vice chairman of appropriations has nothing to do with this,” Lara’s chief of staff Vic Casauay said in October 2025. “Their contracts have dropped dramatically (since he became a congressman).” Based on the General Information Sheet submitted by JLL Pulsar to the SEC, Lara’s children own 96.28% of the company as of March 2025. Joseph Jeremy Lara and Joseph Joshua Lara own 26.2% each; Joseph Kyle Lara owns 23.8%; and Joseph Lara II owns 20.08%. The congressman’s daughter-in-law, Jessa Lara, has a 3.72% stake. – Rappler.com

title: Fincantieri: Steel cut for Italian Navy's 9th PPA
body:
Italian shipbuilding company Fincantieri has held a steel-cutting ceremony for the ninth multipurpose combat ship (PPA) at the Riva Trigoso shipyard.
The ceremony, which took place on October 15, 2026, was attended by shipyard director Antonio Quintano and SVP of Operations, Naval Vessels Division, Attilio Dapelo .
The vessel is part of the renewal plan for the Italian Navy's operational lines. The program is approved by the Government and Parliament under the aegis of the Organization for Joint Armament Cooperation (OCCAR).
The PPAs measure 143 meters in length, can exceed speeds of 31 knots, and support crews of about 171 sailors. Propulsion is provided by a combined diesel and gas turbine (CODAG) system complemented by an electric drive, enabling a blend of high performance and fuel efficiency.
Modular “fitted for” construction allows these vessels to be adapted over time: they can be delivered in a “light plus” configuration suited for patrol and self-defence, or equipped up to a “full combat” configuration with advanced defensive systems. This approach enables the Italian Navy to evolve capabilities based on strategic needs and technological developments.
The ships are also capable of deploying high-speed rigid hull inflatable boats (RHIBs) up to 11 meters long, launched via side cranes or a stern ramp — an important feature for boarding operations, rescue missions, and maritime security tasks.
The ships are designed to operate effectively in all main defense domains, with the ability to carry out multiple missions to ensure the highest level of readiness and operational flexibility.
In February this year, Fincantieri cut steel for the eighth unit in Italy’s PPA program.

title: Boeing 737 MAX 8 faces early teardown despite record demand for new aircraft
body:
A Boeing 737 MAX 8 is set to be dismantled for spare parts despite strong demand for the narrowbody jet and a large backlog that keeps airlines waiting for new aircraft.
GA Telesis announced on October 15 its first 737 MAX 8 disassembly program, aimed at supplying used serviceable material (USM) to airlines and maintenance companies.
The company did not disclose the identity, age, previous operator or owner of the aircraft, nor where the teardown will take place.
Components to be recovered include avionics, flight controls, landing gear equipment, hydraulic and pneumatic systems and nacelle parts. GA Telesis will inspect, repair or overhaul eligible components before offering them through its distribution network.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The unusual fate of a relatively new-generation aircraft reflects growing demand for spare parts as the worldwide 737 MAX fleet expands. GA Telesis cited persistent supply-chain constraints, long delivery times for new components and rising maintenance costs as reasons for developing a secondary market for parts earlier in the aircraft's life cycle.
The company said the strategy differs from the traditional aftermarket model, in which significant supplies of used components generally become available only after aircraft begin reaching retirement age.
The aircraft will not be the first 737 MAX 8 to be dismantled. AerFin acquired two former GOL aircraft earlier this year for parts, including jets that had entered commercial service only months before being withdrawn.
Similar cases have emerged among other new-generation narrowbody aircraft. Airbus A320neo jets only a few years old have already been dismantled to supply components, and an Airbus A220-300 formerly operated by EgyptAir became the first aircraft of its type to be parted out in 2025.
GA Telesis itself announced earlier this week the acquisition of three LEAP-1A-powered A320neo airframes for disassembly and expects to add two more before the end of 2026.
The growing number of early teardowns contrasts with strong demand for new narrowbody aircraft. Boeing and Airbus continue to hold large backlogs for the 737 MAX and A320neo families, with available production slots extending years into the future.

title: EU Renews Operation IRINI to 2029, Targets Russian Shadow Fleet and CUI Protection
body: The EU Council has extended the mandate of EUNAVFOR MED IRINI through March 2029, adding new tasks to monitor Russian shadow fleets and safeguard critical undersea infrastructure (CUI). EUNAVFOR press release The Council of the European Union has renewed the mandate of EUNAVFOR MED IRINI until 31 March 2029. With its renewed mandate, Operation IRINI emerges stronger than ever, with the political objectives of safeguarding European Union interests in the Mediterranean and contributing to peace and stability in Libya. Under its renewed mandate, IRINI will fulfil three strategic roles: safeguarding EU interests in the Mediterranean through credible protection and deterrence; contributing to the implementation of United Nations Security Council resolutions in support of peace and stability in Libya; and fostering Mediterranean partnerships through capacity building and training, as well as naval diplomacy, within the EU’s integrated approach. In addition to its existing tasks, Operation IRINI will take on three new responsibilities in the Mediterranean: – contributing to efforts to constrain the Russian shadow fleet; – strengthening EU and Member States’ maritime domain awareness; and – supporting the protection of critical maritime infrastructure. These responsibilities reflect the vital importance of the maritime domain to European security. Shadow fleet activities pose significant challenges to maritime security, the enforcement of international measures and the protection of the marine environment. The strengthened focus on maritime domain awareness and critical maritime infrastructure will provide the EU a better understanding of threats and illicit activities at sea, while supporting efforts to protect infrastructure essential to Europe’s security, connectivity and economic resilience. At the same time, Operation IRINI will maintain its strong connection to Libya. Exposing violations of UN arms embargo on Libya, as well as illicit oil smuggling, remains at the heart of its mandate. The Operation will also continue to support maritime security cooperation in the Mediterranean through capacity building, training and naval diplomacy. Operation IRINI also remains ready to scale up and respond to contingencies as the maritime security environment evolves. Building on years of operational experience and expertise in the Mediterranean, the European Union is strengthening Operation IRINI’s contribution to security and stability in the region and responding to an evolving maritime security environment. – End – The post EU Renews Operation IRINI to 2029, Targets Russian Shadow Fleet and CUI Protection appeared first on Naval News .

title: Iran slams Colombia’s opening of embassy in Occupied Al-Quds
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – The Iranian Foreign Ministry has strongly condemned Colombia’s decision to open an embassy in occupied al-Quds, describing the move as contrary to the United Nations Charter and the fundamental principles of international law.
In a statement released on Thursday evening, the ministry stressed that al-Quds is an inseparable part of Palestinian territory and said Colombia must accept responsibility for the consequences of its decision.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran strongly condemns the Colombian government’s action in opening an embassy in occupied al-Quds and considers it contrary to the Charter of the United Nations and the fundamental principles of international law,” it said.
“Al-Quds is an inseparable part of Palestinian territory, and all states are obligated under international law to refrain from any action that amounts to recognition of the Israeli regime’s occupation,” the ministry stated.
“Undoubtedly, the alignment of Colombia’s current governing authorities with an occupying and genocidal regime, and the legitimization of the occupation of Palestinian territory, stand in clear contradiction to the aspirations for independence and justice that have shaped a significant part of the history of the struggles of the people of Colombia and Latin America,” the statement said.

title: How Impactful’ll Oyebanji’s Second Term Be for Ekiti People?
body: Ekiti is richer than it was five years ago and more promising, with government figures putting growth from ₦2.4 trillion to ₦4.6 trillion and a projection near ₦8.8 trillion. As Governor Biodun Oyebanji begins a second term, the question is no longer whether Ekiti can grow, but whether that growth can be felt in farms, factories, classrooms, and careers, Raheem Akingbolu writes. Ekiti begins its next political chapter carrying a paradox that deserves a harder look. The state government says its economy has grown from about N2.4 trillion in 2019 to N4.6 trillion in 2023 and is now heading towards a projected N8.8 trillion. Yet the state’s 2023 road statistics tell a more sobering story. Of 425.95 kilometres of state roads, 124.47 kilometres were classified as bad, and another 92.02 kilometres had never been tarred. More than half the network was either failing or unpaved. For a state whose prospects rest on agriculture, trade, education, and tourism, the gap between the headline figures and the road beneath the traveller’s wheels is hard to ignore. From any angle one chooses to look at it, Governor Abiodun Oyebanji has made an indelible mark in his first term, which, of course, paved the way for this second journey. But in an economy like Ekiti’s, roads carry far more than traffic. They determine how quickly food reaches the market and what a farmer pays to get it there. They influence how easily a patient reaches a hospital, how attractive a town appears to an investor, and how long a visitor is willing to stay. Poor connectivity works like a tax on almost every other sector and is paid daily. The state has invested heavily in road construction, and that matters. The larger task now is to ensure those roads form part of a deliberate economic network. Such a network must reach beyond individual projects. Ekiti has an opportunity to position itself as a strategic inland connector between the South-West, the North and Abuja while deepening commercial ties with neighbouring states. The Ado-Ijan-Ilumoba-Omuo corridor deserves particular attention because of its link to the Federal Capital Territory and to assets such as the cargo airport, higher institutions and the Knowledge Zone. Also, the state government should begin the new term with a deliberate action to end the challenge posed by Igede-Aramoko-Itaore road which has almost become a national embarrassment. Indeed, Geography has handed Ekiti an advantage. Infrastructure is what can convert that advantage into economic power. Once people and goods can move efficiently, another underused asset comes into view. Tourism could become one of Ekiti’s fastest sources of new external revenue. Ikogosi Warm Springs, Arinta Waterfalls, Olosunta and Orole Hills, Efon Hills, Agbonna Hills, Esa Cave and a rich cultural heritage provide the raw material for a distinctive visitor economy. Yet attractions are only the beginning. The real opportunity lies in connecting them to good roads, quality accommodation, security, entertainment, destination marketing and a professional visitor experience. That calls for a different understanding of how government and private capital should work together. Government does not need to own every hotel, resort or entertainment venue. Its responsibility is to create conditions in which serious investors can commit resources with confidence. The Ikogosi concession offers one model. The challenge now is whether similar opportunities can be identified, properly structured, and marketed while ensuring host communities benefit from the economic activity that develops around them. Tourism, however, can not carry Ekiti’s economic ambition on its own. The state must also become a proposition that investors can understand at a glance. Investment promotion should move from broad invitations to targeted offers built around land, human capital, agriculture, road connectivity, aviation, educational institutions, and access to regional markets. Ekiti should know the industries it wants, the companies that fit them, and the infrastructure that would make investment commercially viable. This is where industrialisation moves to the centre of the second-term conversation. The governor’s own framing of the next four years points in the same direction. In his State of the State address, Oyebanji argued that social amenities and infrastructure must be connected to economic activity if people are to move sustainably out of poverty. The goal is an industrial ecosystem in which anchor companies generate demand for local suppliers, logistics operators, financial institutions, technology firms, processors and skilled workers, with the opening of factories as only the first step. Serviced industrial land, predictable approvals, reliable utilities, and clear investment information would offer investors something worth more than publicity: a business case they can confidently quantify. The cargo airport adds another dimension. The number of flights it handles will matter less than whether production, storage, cold-chain facilities, logistics, processing and distribution begin clustering around it. High-value agricultural produce, time-sensitive goods and industries reliant on efficient movement all stand to benefit. Yet the airport will become a genuine growth engine only if it is tied physically and economically to the wider road and industrial ecosystem. That brings the discussion back to agriculture, because no industry thrives without a dependable supply base. According to Governor Oyebanji, agriculture and trade account for roughly 60 per cent of the state’s economy, with agriculture contributing about N1.05 trillion. National labour data also recorded more than 311,000 people employed in agriculture in Ekiti in 2023. Those figures illustrate that farming is far more than a rural livelihood. It is one of the foundations upon which the state’s industrial future can be built. The governor has cited that economic profile as one reason his administration intends to continue prioritising agriculture, trade, investment, aviation and tourism as areas of comparative advantage capable of driving further growth. The opportunity lies in moving decisively from crop production to value creation. As being currently demonstrated by Agbeyewa Farms, Cassava can support starch, flour and other processing industries. Rice can sustain milling, packaging and distribution. Yam, maize, soya beans, fruits and other crops can feed increasingly sophisticated value chains. The reported agreement between Agbeyewa and the state on large-scale cassava cultivation could prove significant if it evolves beyond planting into a wider network of farmers, processors, financiers, logistics providers and manufacturers. The prize is not merely a larger harvest but a greater share of value retained within Ekiti. The employment picture sharpens the urgency. Ekiti had about 1.31 million employed people in the 2023 labour force data, yet more than one million were self-employed and roughly 86 per cent of all employment was informal. That describes an active population but also an economy in which too many people remain concentrated in small-scale and vulnerable work. The challenge is therefore to create an environment where businesses can grow, formal jobs can multiply and young people can build sustainable careers without leaving the state. That question inevitably leads to education. Ekiti has long carried the proud identity of the Fountain of Knowledge, earned through generations of teachers, scholars, professionals and intellectuals. Yet reputation alone is never enough. It must be renewed continuously. The Fountain of Knowledge must be protected, strengthened and deliberately reinvented or risk becoming a monument to past achievements rather than a living source of talent, research, innovation and economic opportunity. The task is, therefore, to treat education as a complete economic pipeline rather than a collection of schools and examination results. Teacher quality and professional development matter. So do technical and vocational education, science and technology, artificial intelligence, digital skills, research, and entrepreneurship. Universities need stronger links with employers and industry, while school leavers should have credible options across academic, technical, and vocational pathways. For Ekiti, educational success should no longer end at graduation. It should be measured by what graduation makes possible. The career path of graduates offers a useful test. The published quota of the Council of Legal Education places the law programme at Ekiti State University at 60 students, compared with 150 at the University of Ilorin, 250 at Obafemi Awolowo University and 270 at the University of Lagos. These are university programme quotas, not Nigerian Law School admission figures. Even so, they raise legitimate questions about the state’s capacity to produce legal professionals at scale and, more importantly, about what happens after university. Ekiti should know how many of its law graduates successfully progress into professional legal training and where avoidable bottlenecks exist. Medicine presents a similar challenge. Newly qualified doctors must complete housemanship before full registration, yet available 2026 listings place the combined housemanship capacity of three major Ekiti institutions at about 93 places. There are 34 at the Federal Teaching Hospital, Ido-Ekiti, 12 at the Federal Medical Centre, Ikole-Ekiti, and 47 at Ekiti State University Teaching Hospital. Comparable figures at UCH Ibadan, LUTH and UBTH are 117, 144 and 122 respectively. For a state that legitimately prides itself on education and produces medical graduates, the question is straightforward: how many can move from graduation to housemanship and then to full professional practice without the education system becoming disconnected from opportunity? The same principle should guide healthcare more broadly. Ekiti can strengthen its hospitals as centres of teaching, specialist medicine and research, as well as places of treatment. A stronger health ecosystem would create opportunities for medical professionals, diagnostics, pharmaceuticals, medical technology and private investment while reducing the need for residents to seek specialist treatment elsewhere. Over time, the state could emerge as a regional hub for selected areas of medical education and specialist healthcare. Technology offers another route to expansion, and it does not require Ekiti to imitate Lagos or any other commercial hub. With stronger digital infrastructure, practical technology education, innovation spaces and closer collaboration between universities and industry, young Ekiti residents can participate in national and global markets without leaving home. For a state of Ekiti’s size, the digital economy offers something especially valuable: employment that does not depend on physical proximity to a major market. All of this points to a wider shift in how development should be measured. Economic growth remains important, but GDP alone cannot reveal whether households are becoming more secure, whether graduates are finding meaningful work, whether farmers are earning more from their output or whether roads are lowering the cost of doing business. The development thinking gaining ground internationally, including the United Nations’ emphasis on implementation, resilience, human capital, technology and better measures of progress, carries a useful reminder. Development must ultimately be visible in people’s lives. Here lies the real significance of Governor Oyebanji’s second term. His practical temperament, his frequently demonstrated belief that problems can be solved and his habit of working with stakeholders provide a useful foundation. Significantly, he has already stated that the next phase of his administration will focus on leveraging investments in infrastructure to drive industrial productivity and economic prosperity, with particular emphasis on agricultural industrialisation and the knowledge economy through the Special Agro-Processing Zone and the Ekiti Knowledge Zone. The agenda ahead, however, is larger than continuity. It requires the different parts of Ekiti’s economy to reinforce one another. Roads must open markets. Agriculture must feed industry. Tourism must create businesses. Education must supply talent. The airport must support commerce. Technology must widen opportunity. The outcome should be a clearer economic identity for Ekiti. Picture a state where farmers move produce efficiently, processors secure reliable raw materials, manufacturers reach markets with ease and tourists travel in comfort. In that same state, graduates move smoothly into professional practice and technology entrepreneurs build successful businesses without first relocating to Lagos or Abuja. That is what it means to transform assets into an economy. The agenda is demanding, but it is not beyond the state’s reach. Ekiti already possesses many of the essential ingredients: an educated population, substantial agricultural capacity, major educational institutions, important tourism assets, expanding road infrastructure, an emerging aviation gateway and a government entering a second term with considerable experience. What is needed now is sharper prioritisation, faster execution and an unrelenting focus on outcomes. The broad direction has largely been articulated. The challenge is turning ambition into measurable economic results. That should be the measure of the next four years. The question is not how many projects are commissioned, roads inaugurated or programmes announced. It is whether Ekiti becomes easier to move through, more attractive to investors, more productive in agriculture, stronger in tourism, better at retaining its graduates, more competitive in technology and more capable of creating decent work. If that happens, the second term will achieve something greater than continuity. It will help ensure that the Fountain of Knowledge remains a living source of Ekiti’s future rather than a memory of its past. The final poser for Governor Oyebanji is whether his second term will be as impactful as the first term, or he intends to slow down.

title: Much Ado About EFCC’s New Zonal Directorate in Anambra
