body: David-Chyddy Eleke writes that the recent inauguration of the Zonal Directorate of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission in Awka, the Anambra State capital, was misconstrued for witch-hunt, but such fears were allayed as the Commission came prepared with answers. Last Friday, Awka, the capital of Anambra State played host to dignitaries who graced the inauguration of the Zonal Directorate of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), which is to oversee Anambra and Imo States. The directorate was created by an act of parliament on 22 October 2025, with just 21 personnel deployed to the office through an internal memo on 2 January. The office formally opened, but didn’t begin full operation until February 28, 2026. The inauguration was graced by dignitaries including the host governor, Prof Chukwuma Soludo; his Imo State counterpart, Senator Hope Uzodinma; Speaker of House of Representatives, Hon Tajudeen Abbas, several members of House of Representatives, State Assembly members, Executive Chairman of EFCC, Mr Ola Olukoyede; businessman, Chief Innocent Chukwuma of Innoson Vehicle Manufacturing (IVM); Lady Ada Chidozie of Dozzy Oil and Chairman of Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) and many others. The creation of the directorate had set tongues wagging in the South East, especially in Anambra where some indigenes wondered what economic benefits the zonal directorate would bring to the state. Previously, the creation of Zone 13 Ukpo command of the Nigeria Police Force which was attracted by billionaire oil mogul, Prince Arthur Eze had been condemned by many who insisted that he neither had an industry, factory or any business to absorb the teeming youths, but deemed it necessary to influence a police facility that could turn out an instrument for hunting and hounding youths. The argument continued for a while, then the opening of the EFCC Directorate. A commentator, Mr Mathias Uzoagba (not real name because his permission was not sought) in a post on social media heavily criticized both Anambra State Governor, Prof Chukwuma Soludo and the Federal Government about the establishment of the directorate. He said: “When it was time to sign a $7 billion memorandum of understanding (MoU) with global port operator DP World in to develop the Gateway Deep Seaport and the Ogun Blue Marine Special Economic Zone, the federal government did not remember South East, but now it is time to establish EFCC Directorate, they are bringing it to Anambra. Soludo should be ashamed of his mantra of progressives working together. Can’t progressives work together when it is time to attract meaningful development to Anambra State,” he asked rhetorically. As the argument raged, the actual inauguration ceremony presented an opportunity for both the Chairman of EFCC and Prof Soludo to clarify this. Governor of Imo State, Senator Uzodinma also added his voice to enlighten the people about what bringing the establishment close meant. The Executive Chairman of EFCC, Mr Olukoyede stressed in his speech that the establishment of a regional office of the commission in Awka, the Anambra State capital was to serve Anambra and Imo States and not to hound its people, stating that it can help them in several ways to safeguard their funds. He urged the people to look beyond the arrest of people, but to focus on how the commission coming close to them can guarantee the safety of their finances. “The establishment of this directorate is integral to the Commission’s ongoing expansion, made possible by the generous appropriations of the National Assembly and the critical interventions of President Bola Tinubu. There is no doubt that Anambra and Imo States deserve effective and responsive institutional presence. These states are renowned for enterprise, innovation, commerce and an extraordinary culture of industry. Across both states, we see Nigerians creating businesses, building industries, trading, investing and generating employment. “These legitimate economic activities must be protected from fraud, cybercrime, money laundering, investment frauds, diversion of public resources and other forms of economic and financial crime. Therefore, our coming to Awka is beyond geographical expansion. It is about taking the mandate of the EFCC closer to the people and closer to the economic activities we are meant to protect. EFCC exists not merely to arrest and prosecute. Our official mission encompasses prevention, enforcement and coordination in the effort to eradicate economic and financial crimes. This balance is extremely important. We must prosecute cases on the strength of evidence. We must trace and recover proceeds of crime. However, a fundamental question is, how do we prevent financial crime from occurring in the first place? If we can identify vulnerabilities before billions of naira are lost, prevent fraudulent transactions before citizens lose their savings, strengthen procurement systems before public resources are diverted and interrupt criminal financial flows before they mature, then we would have saved the nation enormous economic and social costs.” Beyond those explanations, which seemed tailored to answer questions on the lips of Anambra people about bringing a law enforcement agency like EFCC to them for intimidation, the Governor of Anambra State, who has been on the receiving end since his political feud with one of his predecessors, Mr Peter Obi started, also offered explanations. Soludo has been bashed by supporters of Obi who see him as colluding with government at the centre to keep the Igbo nation down by bringing only agencies that subjugate them. But he offered his explanations as if he came ready to clarify issues about the establishment of the commission in Anambra. Soludo said: “We are enthusiastic about having EFCC in Awka not because our people are criminals and whatever, but we are begining to drill down the fight against economic and financial crimes to the grassroots. Fighting crime is the responsibility of everybody. Ideally, EFCC should be in the 774 LGAs, but with just 6,000 staff, there is a limit. Welcome to Anambra, we will cooperate with you in everyway possible to ensure that your work goes well. The work of the EFCC is pivotal to our national development and many people may not appreciate it because what they see is EFCC arresting people. But in a society where you have pervasive economic and financial crimes, that society will not move forward economically or in development.” Soludo went further to tell the story of how the commission can help enforce transparency and his personal encounter. Though he failed to mention the controversy surrounding the minting of polymer notes during his time as Governor of Central Bank of Nigeria, it was obvious he was referring to that. He said: “My personal testimonies about the professionalism of this commission is that when I left office as CBN Governor, about three years after, EFCC was investigating an agency within the bank; the mint. I was chairman of board of the mint and I was given one month notice of investigation and I showed up. After about a year, I didn’t hear from them, so I wrote them and they said investigation so far didn’t show anything about me. “When some journalists mentioned my name in connection with the investigation, the former chairman of EFCC told them that I was not the subject of the investigation. Subsequently, they wrote me a beautiful letter and said their investigation showed I didn’t have anything to do with the matter. So I deeply appreciate the professionalism of the commission. I want to urge that if you invite someone and later fail to find them complicit, you must write and say so, especially in this part of the world when if you invite people, it finds its way to the pages of the newspaper because they see invitation as indictment.” Speaking further, Soludo assured that the establishment of EFCC Zonal Directorate in Anambra was not for witch-hunt, but can serve several other purposes. He applauded the professionalism of the EFCC, adding that in Anambra, the State will not wait until it came looking in its books, but will come knocking because the state needs the commission’s help in the areas of revenue, tax and training. “We need training for our civil service, training for staff of Local government and others. Many of these crimes people don’t know about, like procurement processes and rules,” Soludo said. Also, Governor Uzodinma of Imo State described the establishment of EFCC Zonal Directorate as a major step towards bringing the commission closer to the people. Uzodimma said the decentralization of the commission’s operations would save residents of the South-East the stress of travelling to Lagos or Abuja to attend to EFCC-related matters. He also praised EFCC Chairman, Ola Olukoyede, for what he described as a more humane approach to the commission’s operations. “Under the administration of the current chairman, the modus operandi of EFCC has a human face. People are beginning to know that they are not enemies; rather, they can be your friends,” he said. To further buttress the achievements of the directorate, which has remained beneficial to both states, the commission revealed that with a space of nine months in operation, it has helped people of both state reclaim lost and swindled properties and cash. It said within the period the regional office has been in operation, since February 2026, it has received a total of 393 petitions, investigating 311 of such petitions, secured 58 convictions and recovered 111 plots of land worth N323million. He said a total of N835.9million, $1,135, €400 have been recovered too. Giving the people the hope that the directorate is not for witch-hunt, but to secure them and help them recover stolen funds too.

title: Alphington Grammar Dinner Dance Farewells Year 12 Class at Leonda in Hawthorn
body: MELBOURNE, October 2026 — More than 250 guests marked the end of school for Year 12 students at the Alphington Grammar dinner dance. The event was held at Leonda by The Yarra in Hawthorn on Thursday 15 October 2026. School captains James Fokianos and Isabella George addressed the room. Principal Dr Vivianne Nikou and Michael Karamitos, chair of the School Council, also spoke. The Alphington Grammar dinner dance celebrated personal growth with welcome drinks and canapés, a multi-course sit-down dinner, speeches and a video presentation, the school said. Principal Dr Vivianne Nikou at Leonda by The Yarra, Hawthorn, on Thursday 15 October 2026. Photo: Kostas Deves Addressing the students, Dr Nikou said “central to leading an authentic life is a deep-seated commitment to values such as humility, honesty, integrity and living a life of purpose – to live in a way that leaves something worth inheriting for those who come after you.” “What a wonderful message for our young people to leave us with,” Karamitos said. “They are masters of their own fate, their character and discipline will help shape the people they become.” Alphington Grammar dinner dance valedictorian Students chose Archer Claffey as valedictorian of the year, recognising his personal qualities, the school said. Claffey spoke about the Hellenic values and close family community at the school. That community welcomed him when he arrived three years ago. Chair of School Council Michael Karamitos at Leonda by The Yarra, Hawthorn, on Thursday 15 October 2026. Photo: Kostas Deves He also thanked his parents and grandparents for the chance to attend the school. He said teachers there care deeply for their students and give up much of their own time to help them succeed. At the same time, Claffey said, teachers balance that work by nurturing students’ wellbeing and mental health during challenging times. The dinner follows the school’s graduation ceremony for the Class of 2026 at the Capitol Theatre , which Greek City Times reported on 11 October. Music and exams ahead School Captain’s Address at Leonda by The Yarra, Hawthorn, on Thursday 15 October 2026. Photo: Kostas Deves After the formalities, speeches and video presentation, guests danced to both English and Greek music well into the night. Year 12 students now turn to their written exams. The school said it wished all of them the very best. Photo gallery of the evening All photos are copyrighted by Kostas Deves The post Alphington Grammar Dinner Dance Farewells Year 12 Class at Leonda in Hawthorn appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Tinubu to Miss Campaign Rallies in Over 20 States
body: Baring last-minute change in plans, leaders of the All Progressives Congress (APC) will represent President Bola Tinubu in more than 20 States during the reelection campaign which will kick off in Kaduna, on October 24, 2026. This is according to the party’s campaign schedule released late Thursday. In a copy of the schedule sighted by Daily Trust, Tinubu would take a break from the campaign on November 2 when the trail lands in Cross River, absent from Gombe on November 3, Nasarawa on November 4, Ekiti on November 5, but join the campaign in Rivers on November 7. The President will be absent from Ebonyi on November 9, Jigawa on November 10, Ondo on November 11, Edo on November 12, then return to Plateau on November 14, absent from Yobe on November 16, Kebbi on November 17, Akwa Ibom on November 18, Anambra on November 19. Senators back Akpabio, say no contest in 2027 Population data needs urgent attention – Shettima The schedule shows that Tinubu would join the campaign rally in Oyo on November 21; move to rallies in Borno, Enugu and Bauchi on November 25, 28 and 29, respectively, but absent from Benue on November 30. The president is expected to continue his campaign tour in December, with rallies scheduled for Sokoto on December 5, Delta on December 12 and Kano on December 17. His final two scheduled appearances are in Adamawa on January 4 and Lagos on January 9, while other party leaders are expected to represent him at rallies in the remaining 12 states scheduled for December. Overall, the timetable provides for Tinubu to personally attend campaign rallies in 12 states, with the party relying on its leaders and campaign council members to cover the other states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). Tinubu had earlier explained that he would not attend every APC campaign rally, citing the need to balance campaigning with governance. Speaking on Wednesday at the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council at the Presidential Villa in Abuja, the president said there was a country to run, indicating that his responsibilities as head of government would limit his participation in some campaign activities. He, however, pledged to make time to address Nigerians directly as party leaders move across states and local government areas to canvass support for his re-election. But the opposition attributed the planned absence to the President’s health, with the Allied Peoples Movement asking him to campaign in all states or withdraw from the Presidential race. On his part, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar who is one of the leading Presidential frontrunners for next year’s election, alleged that Tinubu was afraid to stand before the people because of his scorecard. In a statement issued by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku said: “Tinubu says he may miss campaign rallies because Nigeria needs his attention. Where was that urgency when Nigerians pleaded for relief? He has had three and a half years to govern. In that time, families have been forced to cut meals, postpone medical care and watch their earnings lose value before they get home. “Now he wants another mandate. Before asking Nigerians for one, he must face them and account for the first term.”

title: Fuel scooping, recurring deaths
body: Many people were feared dead yesterday, while 10 others sustained varying degrees of injury when a fallen fuel tanker exploded at Oluku on the Benin-Lagos Road in Edo State. Daily Trust could not independently confirm the number of fatalities. However, some security officials, who declined to speak officially, said five people were reportedly killed in the incident. Oluku is a busy area where drivers of articulated and heavy-duty trucks often park to rest before continuing their journeys. The incident occurred near Oluku Market, destroying several shops, houses and vehicles in the area. Importation, insecurity threaten Nigeria’s food sufficiency How Senator Mandiya died in Abuja home The explosion occurred in the early hours of Thursday when a petrol tanker attempting to make a U-turn near the market fell and spilled its contents onto the road. Witnesses said that shortly after the tanker fell, residents and passers-by rushed to the scene and began scooping fuel from the road and drainage channels. One of the witnesses, who identified himself simply as John, said he had joined some people who were scooping the fuel before security operatives arrived at the scene and cordoned off the area. He said the truck owner had brought another tanker to evacuate the remaining fuel from the fallen vehicle when it exploded, leaving several victims burnt beyond recognition and many others injured. According to him, 10 injured victims were rushed to the University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH) for medical attention, while some corpses were deposited at the hospital’s mortuary. He said, “I was also among those scooping the fuel. I escaped by the whiskers. A soldier called me and drew my attention to the fact that the weather was hot and that the way people were rushing to scoop the fuel could ignite a fire. “As I looked back after he spoke to me, the tanker burst into flames, and people around the area scampered for safety. I thank the soldier; if not, I would have been burnt by now. “Two men who were directly under the tanker were burnt, while shops built on the drainage were also razed. We are yet to ascertain the number of people who died.” Another witness, Juliet Philip, blamed the incident on the refusal of some residents to heed warnings against scooping fuel from the fallen tanker. She said the perpetrators ignored some people, who attempted to stop them from the act, as they reportedly argued that petrol was selling for N1,500 per litre and they intended to sell what they collected. Philip explained that many people were trapped when the tanker exploded, adding that several shops at Oluku Market and vehicles parked in the area were destroyed by the inferno. “The market was seriously affected because the fuel spilled into the drainage channels within the market. Some people also scooped fuel and stored it in their shops,” she said. The witness explained that some residents refused to leave the scene despite efforts by security personnel to drive them away, adding that some even attacked the operatives. “Even with the presence of soldiers and other security agents, some people refused to leave. When the security personnel chased them away, some would return and attack the military and other personnel, including road safety officers,” he said. When our reporter visited UBTH, the hospital management had mobilised emergency personnel to treat victims of the explosion brought to the facility. The Chief Medical Director of UBTH, Prof. Idia Ize-Iyamu, was seen leading the emergency response team across the accident and emergency and burns units to stabilise severely injured victims. A source at the hospital, who requested anonymity, said several victims with burns were brought to the facility by officials of the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) and the police. The source said he counted about 10 persons with varying degrees of burns brought to the emergency unit, while some corpses were taken to the mortuary. “The Chief Medical Director was leading the emergency response to ensure that the victims were stabilised,” he said. ‘Casualty figure not yet known’ The Executive Secretary of the Edo State Emergency Management Agency (EdoSEMA), Jerry Idahosa, said the agency could not immediately provide the actual casualty figure because emergency responders were still at the scene battling the fire. He said, “It is by tomorrow (today) that we can ascertain the number of casualties because the fire is still burning. However, we have three persons who sustained injuries, including a soldier and two other persons who were close to the truck when it exploded. They are receiving treatment at the hospital.” The Edo State Sector Commander of the FRSC, Preye Ezekiel Bedford, said FRSC officials, police officers, firefighters, the Edo State Traffic Management Agency and military personnel were at the scene to manage traffic and assist with the emergency response. Although he did not disclose the number of fatalities, Bedford confirmed that 10 people sustained injuries in the incident. Recent deadly tanker explosions At least two persons were killed and one other injured on Sunday, February 8, 2026, when a petrol-laden tanker exploded along the Ihiala axis of the Onitsha-Owerri Road, opposite the FRSC office of the Federal Road Safety Corps. The explosion occurred after the tanker collided with a car and rammed into a barricade, spilling its contents and triggering a massive fire. Witnesses reported that the tanker was travelling at high speed when it lost control and crashed into the barricade. Similarly, two persons lost their lives on Saturday, March 21, after a gas tanker collided with a tipper truck in the Ajah axis of Lagos. Several properties, including warehouses and roadside shops, were also destroyed. The Controller General of the Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service, Margaret Adeseye, said the oncoming speeding tipper truck from the Epe end rammed from behind into a stationary 30-tonne gas truck that failed to pull over from the highway. No fewer than 45 persons were killed and 62 others injured in a petrol tanker explosion on October 21, 2025, at Essa community along the Bida–Badegi–Agaie Road in Katcha Local Government Area of Niger State. Head of Operations, NEMA, Minna Office, Hussaini Isah, disclosed that all the victims were affected while scooping spilled fuel from the crashed tanker. “All the victims were affected as a result of scooping fuel. Some of the victims were initially evacuated to Essa Primary Health Care, Idris Private Hospital, but were later moved to Umaru Sanda General Hospital, Bida, and the Federal Medical Centre, Bida. Fourteen critically injured persons were referred to Gwagwalada Specialist Hospital for further treatment,” he had said. Earlier that month, at least two people reportedly died in a petrol tanker explosion in Agbor in Ika LGA of Delta state. At least 98 persons were confirmed dead and 69 injured from the petrol tanker explosion that occurred in Gurara LGA of Niger State on January 20, 2025. About 20 shops were also destroyed during the incident. It was learnt that the explosion occurred when a tanker conveying petrol crashed and another tanker was brought to transfer the contents. No fewer than 209 persons were confirmed dead in the October 14, 2024 tanker explosion in Majia, Jigawa State. The chairman of an investigation committee set up to probe the incident, DIG Hafizu Muhammad Inuwa (Retd), said findings revealed that several factors, including damaged speed bumps and potholes near the scene, night driving, and excessive speed, contributed to the fire. “It was noted that the fire likely ignited due to friction between metallic containers and hard surfaces as victims attempted to scoop spilled fuel,” he added. What is driving scooping? The Head of the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) Operations Office in Benin, Kenoma Ojuedeire, attributed the growing practice of fuel scooping to greed, lamenting that Nigerians had failed to learn from previous tragedies. “For me, I think this is a result of greed because I don’t see why a normal person would go and scoop fuel, knowing that death is knocking. If you watch some of the videos on social media, you hear people saying that a litre of fuel is N1,500. Because of N1,500, they go and face death,” he added. Ojuedeire called for increased and sustained public sensitisation to educate residents on the dangers of scooping fuel from fallen tankers. Similarly, a civil rights activist, Kola Edokpayi, attributed the development to greed. Kola, who is the President of the Talawaka Parliament, said poverty alone could not explain the dangerous practice, noting that some poor people deliberately avoided scooping fuel because they understood the risks involved. “I say it is greed because there are people who are poor but desist from scooping fuel. When one is greedy, the person tends to ignore the attendant consequences of scooping fuel from a fallen tanker, even though many people have died in similar incidents,” he said. Edokpayi called for sustained reorientation and public sensitisation by the government and individuals to reduce deaths associated with scooping spilled fuel. Sociologist Collins Gambo blamed the growing desperation among Nigerians, declining social values and economic hardship for the recurring practice of scooping fuel from fallen tankers, warning that people are risking their lives in a bid to survive. Gambo said the practice reflected deeper social and economic problems that could not be addressed through arrests alone, urging the government to improve citizens’ welfare and tackle the conditions that drive people to engage in the dangerous act. Describing the act from a sociological perspective, Gambo likened it to “anomic suicide,” a concept associated with the breakdown of social norms and established social order. According to him, economic hardship remains one of the major reasons people risk their lives to scoop fuel, as many struggle to meet their basic needs and see the activity as an opportunity to make quick money. “People do not have the means of survival. They want to get this fuel so that they can sell and make a living temporarily,” Gambo said. He argued that the desperation to survive had made some people disregard the dangers associated with collecting fuel from accident scenes, particularly when they believed the proceeds could provide temporary relief from their financial difficulties. The sociologist also identified the erosion of cultural values and the declining willingness of people to sympathise with others in distress as factors contributing to the practice. He said tanker accidents should ordinarily attract public sympathy because they often result in significant financial losses to the owners, but some people now see such incidents as opportunities for personal gains. “People should empathise, but the empathy is not there, because there is a breakdown in cultural norms. When somebody loses something, people empathise; they want to take advantage of that situation,” he said. Gambo further linked fuel scooping to the perceived divide between the wealthy and the poor, arguing that some Nigerians view the practice as an opportunity to benefit from resources they believe are concentrated in the hands of privileged individuals. He said the perception that wealthy business owners and influential members of society were indifferent to the struggles of ordinary Nigerians could encourage some people to justify taking fuel from accident scenes. However, Gambo stressed that addressing the practice required both individual responsibility and deliberate government intervention. He urged Nigerians to show compassion towards victims of tanker accidents and their owners rather than exploit their misfortune for personal gain. He also called on the government to complement law enforcement with practical measures to improve citizens’ living conditions, noting that efforts to address the underlying causes of desperation could help discourage people from risking their lives to collect fuel.

title: Importation, insecurity threaten Nigeria’s food sufficiency
body: Nigeria joins the rest of the world today to mark World Food Day, an annual event celebrated on October 16 to commemorate the establishment of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in 1945. The 2026 World Food Day’s theme, “Innovate Today. Nourish Tomorrow,” urges countries to improve their food systems to ensure food security for future generations. However, Nigeria’s efforts to achieve food sufficiency have faced major setbacks since 2024 due to food imports, insecurity that has displaced farmers from their communities, production challenges, irregularities in food marketing and frequent policy changes. In July 2024, the Federal Government announced a 150-day duty-free import window for selected food commodities in a bid to curb rising food inflation caused by changes in government policies on subsidies and foreign exchange. Fuel scooping, recurring deaths Again, inflation drops amidst rising prices Although the measure was intended to ease the rising cost of food, many local farmers said the imports undermined their investments and affected their ability to compete with foreign products. Under the policy, the 20 per cent duty on wheat and beans was removed, alongside the 30 per cent duty on husked brown rice and the five per cent duty on sorghum, millet and maize. Data from the Nigeria Customs Service showed that the Federal Government lost more than N188 billion in revenue following the suspension of import tariffs on food commodities. Farmers who had invested heavily in labour, transportation, agricultural inputs and other production costs were among those affected. The influx of imported food forced some farmers to abandon production because they could no longer sell their produce at prices that covered their costs. Food import bills Data from the United States Department of Agriculture and World Grains showed that Nigeria imported about 10.1 million tonnes of grain in the 2025/2026 marketing year. The breakdown showed that wheat imports reached 6.7 million tonnes, up from 6.25 million tonnes in the previous year. Rice imports stood at 3.2 million tonnes, while maize imports rose to 260,000 tonnes from between 125,000 and 135,000 tonnes in previous periods. The figures point to Nigeria’s continued dependence on imported grains despite its agricultural potential. The Central Bank of Nigeria estimated that the country spent $2.34 billion on food imports in 2025 alone. The National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) also reported a sharp increase in expenditure on food and beverages, which rose to about N7.65 trillion in 2025 from N6.58 trillion in the previous year, representing an increase of N1.07 trillion. The local rice industry, which had attracted significant domestic and international investments, has also come under pressure from rising imports, widespread smuggling and unstable prices. The Director-General of the Rice Processors Association of Nigeria, Dr Andy Ekwelem, recently said that about 90 of the more than 150 rice mills in the country had shut down. He said the remaining mills were operating at between 30 and 70 per cent of their installed capacity. At a recent meeting with the ministers of agriculture and food security, the Chairman of the Rice Processors Association of Nigeria, Mohammed Abubakar Maifata, raised concerns over what he described as the continued large-scale importation of rice. The government officials, however, reportedly said they were unaware of the scale of the imports. Economic risks of food imports An agricultural economist, Dr Nathaniel Gas, said Nigeria’s growing dependence on imported food presented both opportunities and challenges for food security, raising concerns about the future of local agricultural production and the affordability of food for millions of households. He said food imports could help bridge gaps in domestic supply, but excessive reliance on foreign products that Nigeria could produce locally exposed the country to economic risks, including exchange-rate fluctuations and increases in global prices. “When the naira depreciates against the dollar, importers spend more to purchase food from abroad, and the additional costs are often transferred to consumers, just as the country had experienced with wheat during the Russia/Ukraine war. “This clearly shows that imported food does not always translate into cheaper prices in local markets. Importation also killed our cotton and tomato sectors and posed a serious threat to the poultry industry,” he said. Gas explained that the situation also placed pressure on local farmers, who were already grappling with high production costs, insecurity, expensive fertilisers, inadequate irrigation and poor access to storage and transportation facilities. He said when imported commodities competed with locally produced alternatives, farmers often struggled to sell their harvests at prices that covered their production costs. He, however, noted that food imports were not entirely harmful, as they could help prevent shortages when domestic production fell below demand. Insecurity, other challenges Farmers in several states, including Niger, Kaduna, Plateau, Zamfara, Katsina, Borno, Taraba, Benue and Kogi, are grappling with serious security challenges that threaten agricultural production and food security. Many have been forced to flee their homes, abandon their farms and lose their sources of livelihood. Kidnappings and attacks have also prevented farmers from accessing their farms and harvesting their crops, worsening the threat to food availability and supply. These challenges have disrupted the production of various crops and livestock, making it increasingly difficult to ensure a stable food supply across the country. Beyond insecurity, the agricultural sector faces several challenges, including high production costs per hectare, expensive livestock farming, underdeveloped market systems, poor infrastructure for value addition and dependence on imported food. The collapse of government financial support schemes, such as the Anchor Borrowers’ Programme for smallholder farmers, has further compounded the problem. Food fraud, including the adulteration of products to increase their perceived economic value, and inadequate regulatory oversight also threaten the sector. High borrowing costs, with bank interest rates in double digits, have made it difficult for farmers and agribusinesses to access financing. Climate extremes, pest outbreaks and insecurity have also discouraged many financial institutions from lending to the agricultural sector, further limiting investment and production. Dr Michael Ononugbo, Deputy Director and Special Assistant in the Office of the Deputy Governor, Economic Policy Directorate, Central Bank of Nigeria, said a thriving agricultural sector was critical not only to food production but also to employment generation, poverty reduction, trade expansion and macroeconomic stability. He, however, noted that the sector continued to face structural constraints that limited investment and productivity. Ononugbo said agricultural interventions must translate into measurable improvements in productivity, incomes, food security, employment, resilience and broad-based economic development. Similarly, the Nigeria Country Director of AGRA, Dr Rufus Idris, said in Abuja recently that the average age of Nigerian farmers was between 50 and 60, while more than 70 per cent of the country’s population was below 30. He said Nigeria’s future food security depended largely on creating opportunities for young people to engage in agricultural enterprises. Idris warned that with Nigeria’s population projected to exceed 400 million in the coming years, the country needed concerted efforts to enable young people to participate in food production and processing. He said failure to engage more young people in the sector could make achieving food security a major challenge for the country. Experts warned that the challenges confronting the agricultural sector could deepen Nigeria’s dependence on food imports, as some crop and livestock farmers have abandoned production due to market distortions and rising costs. The poultry industry has also been affected, with many farmers reportedly forced out of business by high production costs and shortages of essential inputs. The rising costs of day-old chicks, energy, transportation, logistics, labour and other production inputs have increased the cost of producing poultry meat and eggs, making them less affordable for many households. Food processing Young agricultural entrepreneurs who spoke to Daily Trust identified several challenges holding back their businesses, particularly inadequate processing infrastructure, limited access to finance and weak market support. Baliqees Salaudeen, an agripreneur, said the lack of processing facilities was a major obstacle to the growth of young businesses in the sector. “Young people are told to move beyond production into processing, but you cannot process to certified standards from your parents’ backyard. We need shared post-harvest facilities and aggregation hubs, built to certified standards, so young processors do not each carry the cost of heavy equipment,” she said. Another young agricultural entrepreneur, Tobi Jeremiah Olanrewaju, identified some of the major bottlenecks in the food production chain. “Every emerging agripreneur faces the same three bottlenecks: volatile prices, a lack of finance designed for young people, and weak ecosystem support. When you produce at scale without the means to store or process, the aggregator sets your price,” he said. Farmers count losses Farmers interviewed by Daily Trust identified the high cost of fertilisers, chemicals, tractor hiring and diesel as major obstacles to sustainable agricultural production. They said that despite spending heavily on farm inputs, the prices they received for their produce remained low, making farming increasingly unprofitable. Alhaji Sale Binnare, a large-scale farmer in Karim-Lamido Local Government Area of Taraba State, said recent increases in the prices of diesel and petrol had forced tractor operators to raise hiring charges by more than 30 per cent. He said farm produce prices had remained low despite the rising cost of inputs. According to him, freshly harvested maize sells for between N22,000 and N23,000 per bag in many rural areas of Taraba State, while a bag of NPK fertiliser costs between N45,000 and N50,000. He added that in areas without filling stations, petrol and diesel sell for between N1,500 and N2,200 per litre. Binnare said many farmers had reduced the scale of their operations this year, particularly in the production of food crops such as maize, cassava, millet and sorghum. He also predicted a decline in irrigation farming during the current season, saying many irrigation farmers suffered losses last year. “It is not wise for any farmer to invest his capital and at the end of harvest he will not recover what he invested. Worse still, many farmers take loans, and because of the losses they encounter, some are forced to sell their houses and farmland to repay the loans,” he said. Tanko Bobbo Andami, a former chairman of the Rice Farmers Association and a large-scale farmer in Taraba State, also said farming had become unprofitable due to several challenges. “I know many people who invested huge amounts of money in both wet- and dry-season farming but could not recover half of what they invested. That has discouraged people from engaging in farming activities,” he said. He added that the situation was particularly difficult for food crop farmers because grain prices remained low compared with those of cash crops such as soybeans, sesame seeds and melon seeds. Andami said many farmers had shifted to cash crop production, particularly soybeans, which sold for N80,000 per 100kg bag. He added that melon seeds and sesame seeds sold for between N90,000 and N150,000 in Taraba markets. He warned that the shift towards cash crops could reduce the availability of food crops and worsen food insecurity. Nuhu Kabir, a dry-season farmer, said irrigation farming declined last year due to poor returns on investment. “Last irrigation season, I invested over N3 million to produce paddy rice, but after harvesting and selling the produce, what I realised was less than the amount I invested. This has taught me to be careful about making huge investments in irrigation farming,” he said. Mechanisation, insecurity worsen farmers’ plight The Chairman of the Rice Farmers Association of Nigeria in Edo State, Mr Tony Aliu, said farmers lacked adequate access to tractors and other mechanised farming equipment, forcing many to rely on manual labour to prepare their farmlands. He explained that the situation had limited the number of hectares farmers could cultivate, thereby reducing their productivity. Aliu urged the government to open up more land and make it available to farmers at affordable rates to enable them to expand production. He identified the high cost of hiring land from communities as another major challenge. He also described insecurity as a serious threat to farming, saying kidnappings had prevented many farmers from accessing their farms and harvesting their produce. Aliu said price fluctuations and inadequate market access had further worsened the situation, blaming the influx of imported rice for the decline in the prices of locally produced rice. He also identified inadequate irrigation facilities as a major constraint to rice production, particularly amid changing weather patterns. “Last year, many farmers lost their produce due to weather changes. Because we don’t have irrigation in this part of the country, we were seriously affected. I lost several hectares due to this development,” he said. An economist, Alhaji Ibraheem Maigari, urged the government to address the major factors driving up food prices, including the high cost of fertilisers, energy, transportation and other agricultural inputs. He said reducing these costs would enable farmers to operate profitably while making food more affordable for consumers. Maigari said increasing domestic food production was a viable way to address rising prices, urging the government to invest in irrigation systems, rural road networks, storage facilities, affordable credit and improved security for farmers. Food prices dropped by 50%- FG The Federal Government said prices of essential food commodities have dropped by as much as 50 per cent nationwide following its interventions to boost agricultural production and food security. The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Senator Abubakar Kyari, said the government had distributed more than 10 million bags of fertiliser under its agricultural support programmes, alongside a Guaranteed Price Model targeting two million smallholder farmers. He added that an additional 1.9 million bags of fertiliser had been distributed to more than one million farmers. Kyari said other interventions included the distribution of more than 500,000 bags of free fertiliser to over 120,000 farmers across 25 states and the Federal Capital Territory by the National Agricultural Development Fund. He said the fund had also disbursed more than N16 billion across agricultural value chains through its on-lending product while promoting blended finance initiatives to attract investment into the sector. The minister said the government had also established Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zones (SAPZs), which are designed to bring infrastructure closer to farming communities and enable farmers to process raw produce into packaged goods. Kyari said the interventions were already yielding results, with essential food commodities recording price reductions of up to 50 per cent nationwide. Meanwhile, the Minister of Livestock Development, Idi Mukhtar Maiha, said the government had introduced several initiatives to improve livestock production and make animal protein more affordable and accessible to Nigerians. He identified key areas of intervention as improving the genetic quality of local breeds, increasing feed and fodder supplies, developing vaccines to control animal diseases, supporting farmers and investing in meat processing facilities and abattoirs across the country. Maiha said the ministry was working with key partners to strengthen the animal feed sector, which he described as critical to the development of the livestock industry. He said the initiative was aimed at encouraging investment in feed production facilities, slaughterhouses, meat processing plants, packaging facilities, logistics and marketing.

title: Senators back Akpabio, say no contest in 2027
body: Lawmakers in the upper legislative chamber have declared that the position of the Senate President in the upcoming 11th National Assembly is not vacant, passing an early vote of confidence in the incumbent, Senator Godswill Akpabio. The stance was made public following a motion moved by Senator Tahir Monguno and seconded by Senator Cyril Fasuyi (Ekiti North), with lawmakers moving to forestall political maneuvering ahead of the next assembly’s inauguration. Extending their endorsement to Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin and other principal officers, senators voiced unified support to keep the current leadership structure intact. “I hereby support the motion ably moved by Senator Monguno that the seat of the Senate President in the 11th Assembly is not open to any contest. It is already occupied by Senator Godswill Obot Akpabio.” Acknowledging the intense interest usually surrounding leadership seats, Akpabio noted that with executive contests concluded, attention naturally shifts to the legislature. “I know the position of president is gone, the position of vice president is gone, the only one that is left now is the position of Senate President. So, everybody will want to contest that,” Akpabio remarked, expressing optimism that many current members would return in the 11th Assembly. Our correspondent reports that while the declaration demonstrates strong political backing, the official election of presiding officers remains subject to statutory legislative procedures when the 11th Assembly is formally constituted. Beyond the leadership debate, Akpabio cautioned political analysts, television commentators, and panel speakers against taking floor debates out of context to score political points or damage reputations. He said media commentators should evaluate final Senate resolutions rather than isolated, heated exchanges during debates. Vigorous debate is a hallmark of lawmaking where members are expected to oppose and support various viewpoints. Lawmakers warned against misinterpreting sensitive discussions—specifically recent floor debates on reviewing the decriminalisation of suicide—as religious or ideological attacks. Addressing controversies tied to the suicide debate, Akpabio firmly rejected attempts to link terrorism with any faith, emphasizing that acts of violence and self-destruction violate fundamental religious doctrines. “Terrorists are not Muslims. Terrorists are not Christians.Terrorists are human beings who believe in taking their lives and the lives of others,’’ Akpabio said. Akpabio clarified that the legislative intent behind re-examining suicide laws is to differentiate between acts of terror and mental health crises. He said individuals driven to suicide attempts by severe mental health conditions from violent offenders, reaffirming that major faiths, including Islam, strictly forbid suicide and the taking of innocent lives. Reinforcing this point, a fellow senator cited Suratul An-Nisa (Chapter 4, Verse 29) of the Quran, underscoring that Islam explicitly prohibits self-destruction and unlawful killing. The lawmakers stressed that robust debate inside the chamber reflects active democracy at work—and warned against allowing misinterpretations to stoke religious or political division across the nation.

title: ‘Why Tinubu deserves second term’
body: Otunba Segun Showunmi, a former spokesperson for the 2023 Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) presidential candidate, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, has declared his endorsement for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s 2027 re-election bid. He urged Nigerians to unite around the administration’s vision and prioritize long-term national stability and economic renewal. Showunmi, who serves as the Convener of The Alternative Movement and was recently appointed a member of the Tinubu/Shettima Campaign Organization, stated that his endorsement transcends partisan considerations. He maintained that Nigeria stands at a defining threshold requiring continuity of policy to consolidate emerging economic reforms. “My support for President Tinubu is rooted in my conviction that the Nigerian project is bigger than any individual, political party, or election,” Showunmi said. “It is about the future of our children, the dignity of our citizens, the strength of our institutions, the productivity of our economy, and our place among the leading nations of the world.” Reflecting on the government’s economic agenda since May 2023, Showunmi highlighted critical structural policies aimed at repositioning the country away from an over-reliance on crude oil toward a diversified economy. He cited landmark initiatives across key sectors, including the implementation of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), which provides financial support for tertiary students and the Electricity Act 2023, granting states the framework to establish localized energy markets and boost local industrial output. He also cited the strategic transport corridors, including the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, the Sokoto–Badagry Super Highway, and the Abuja–Kaduna–Zaria–Kano expressway. According to Showunmi, these policy shifts lay the foundational grid necessary for Nigeria to operate as a major manufacturing, processing, and logistics hub across West and Central Africa. Emphasising that national stability remains the bedrock of economic progress, Showunmi noted that effective governance must ensure safety for farmers, artisans, and business owners to operate with confidence. He called for continued institutional support for the armed forces and security agencies, alongside socio-economic interventions that expand opportunities for Nigeria’s youth. “When I say prosperity is around the corner, I am expressing my confidence in the possibilities before Nigeria and in what sustained reforms, investment, and productive enterprise can unlock,” Showunmi added. “The task is to turn that potential into measurable improvements in incomes, jobs, services, and living standards so that prosperity reaches every table.”

title: Soldiers feared killed repelling terrorists in Borno
body: At least 10 soldiers and four civilians are feared dead following a coordinated assault by suspected Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) terrorists on a military base in Mairari, Borno State. The attack, which took place last Tuesday, occurred in the Guzamala Local Government Area, roughly 120 to 130 kilometers north of the state capital, Maiduguri. According to credible security sources, the insurgents stormed the military formation in large numbers, engaging troops in a fierce, hours-long gun battle. While troops reportedly fought back valiantly and neutralised scores of attackers, the terrorists ultimately inflicted heavy casualties and caused significant destruction to military hardware, including gun trucks and operational vehicles belonging to both troops and the Civilian Joint Task Force (CJTF). “More than 10 soldiers and four civilians have reportedly been killed after suspected fighters of the Islamic State-backed faction attacked the military formation,” a security source said on the condition of anonymity. Ali Bukar Mairari, a resident who fled the scene, corroborated the accounts, stating that more than 11 people were killed and multiple operational vehicles were set ablaze during the raid. Lawan Sheriff, the chairman of Guzamala, confirmed the attack, though he did not provide casualty figures. Information about the incident reached the public late due to the complete absence of telecommunication networks in the area. The assault on Mairari follows another recent security breach in the wider Lake Chad region, where terrorists reportedly seized more than 40 locally made fishing boats from fishermen in Tumbun Barebari, an area known as Abujan Ruwa. Mairari holds strategic importance as one of the few towns in the area to survive multiple Boko Haram onslaughts, having temporarily served as the headquarters of the Guzamala local government council after terrorists captured the official headquarters in Gudumbali. The continued insurgent stronghold in Gudumbali remains a source of frustration for local leaders. The Speaker of the Borno State House of Assembly, Abdulkarim Lawan, who hails from Guzamala, has repeatedly decried the inability of security agencies to reclaim the council headquarters, though his appeals have yet to yield the desired military action. Efforts to obtain an official statement from the Borno State Police Public Relations Officer, ASP Kenneth Daso, were unsuccessful, as calls and messages went unanswered at the time of reporting. The military high command has not yet released an official casualty toll or a formal statement regarding the Mairari incident as security operations and reinforcement efforts continue in the troubled northern fringes of lake Chad. Troops kill Lakurawa terrorists in Sokoto Meanwhile, troops of the Joint Task Force, North West, under Operation Fansan Yamma, have overrun a Lakurawa terrorists’ enclave in Waria Forest, Tangaza Local Government Area of Sokoto State, killing several terrorists and recovering weapons and five motorcycles. The operation was conducted on October 15, 2026, as troops of Sector 2 advanced through identified terrorist hideouts around Alela, Bilange and Kandam villages towards Waria Forest. According to a statement by the Media Information Officer of the Joint Task Force, Lieutenant Colonel Aliyu Danja, the troops engaged the terrorists in a firefight and overwhelmed them with superior firepower, forcing them to flee deeper into the forest. He said the troops pursued the fleeing terrorists, neutralising some of them before destroying their camps and other structures used to support their activities. Danja added that weapons and five motorcycles were recovered during the operation. He said troops had maintained a strong presence in the area and continued clearance operations to deny the terrorists freedom of movement and improve security in surrounding communities. The theatre command commended the troops for their courage and sustained efforts, urging residents to support ongoing military operations by providing timely and credible information about suspicious movements and activities in their communities.

title: The fearless ambition of Mohamed Faisal Mostafa
body: On the set of Dune: Part Three , Mohamed Faisal Mostafa watched closely as Timothee Chalamet, Zendaya and Jason Momoa prepared for their scenes. Each day, he saw how they learnt their lines, how they worked, how they treated the people around them. The Emirati actor wanted to reach that level himself, and here he could see what it took. “I sat back and I saw it all and I said to myself: ‘This is not unattainable.’ I can be there and, inshallah, I will be there so long as I keep consistent,” he says. Mostafa joined the production as a stunt performer. Director Denis Villeneuve knew he also acted and began finding opportunities for him to do more on camera. As the shoot was coming to an end, Mostafa went up to thank him for his support. “He said: ‘Mohamed, there’s no need to thank me. You’re a natural. You’re a very talented actor.’” Even recounting it now gives Mostafa goosebumps. He holds out his arm to show them. It was a moment he’d been ready for nearly his whole life. Long before he worked with Villeneuve, a young Mostafa was jumping off a moving bicycle for his brother, director Ali Mostafa. Ali was making home movies, and Mostafa was already fearless, at the age of six or seven, in front of his brother’s camera. As Ali kept making films, Mostafa kept helping. That bond is still strong decades later – every year on Ali’s birthday, he calls him “my brother, my teacher and my friend”. But for years, film was one of several possible futures. Mostafa played professional football, worked in finance, ran a digital transformation agency and was involved in his family’s business. Acting fitted around those pursuits, even as the parts grew bigger and took him further from home. He could keep building a career in business, with success nearly certain. But something in him knew he had to choose the harder path. “I think you need to find an area of focus if you want to succeed,” he says. Dedicating himself to film full time makes the auditions his UK agent sends him feel more consequential. A major production could give him the credit that leads to another job, then another. Yet a few lines are sometimes enough for him to turn one down. Even now, terrorists and other stereotypical Arab characters keep coming his way from major studios and streaming platforms, offering a route into the industry he has chosen to depend on. “Trust me, it is not easy to say no to these because some of them are massive, life-changing projects,” he says. “I love acting, and it’s the only thing I do right now. It’s also what’s going to generate me income, put food on my table and support my future.” But he has to consider what accepting a part would mean beyond his own career. He is willing to play a villain; the concern is a story that leaves an audience with another reason to distrust Arabs. He wants the roles he earns to expand what people understand about Emiratis and Muslim Arabs. He carries the responsibility for his country’s reputation as personally as he does for his own family’s. “It’s part of who I am,” he says. “It’s every action I do in the morning, when I wake up. I want to prove something to my family, my country, our leaders, myself.” There is a chance to take that work further at home, too. Dune: Part Three reaches cinemas this December and Dubai International Film Festival will return on December 8 after a decade-long hiatus. Mostafa has established MFM Media in Abu Dhabi, working on production services, product placement and Emirati talent management. He wants to help to get films made and give other performers the connections he struggled to find. DIFF’s return gives that ambition a place to develop, bringing filmmakers, actors and investors together in Dubai. Mostafa wants the next Emirati actor pursuing an international career to have more help and more work available here before setting off. His own route into film took years to become clear. As a goalkeeper for Al Ain and Al Wasl, Mostafa turned his childhood love of football into a career before serious injuries ended it. His work with Ali continued as his brother moved into feature films, casting Mostafa in City of Life (2009) and From A to B (2014), then giving him a larger role in the post-apocalyptic thriller The Worthy (2016). Mostafa also appeared in the Emirati military action film Al Kameen (2021), one of the biggest box-office hits the country has produced. An open audition in London for Disney’s live-action Aladdin (2019), which eventually starred Mena Massoud and Will Smith, gave Mostafa a glimpse of how far acting might take him. He did not get the role. At the time, he carried on with other pursuits, but the possibility stayed with him: he had put himself forward for a production watched around the world, in which he could have represented the UAE. “I realised that this can actually happen, and that I love acting and I’m not bad at it. So I had to keep going,” he says. Finding an agent in Britain involved repeated approaches and rejections. When Hijack – the Apple TV thriller also starring Idris Elba – came, Mostafa finally had an international role to prepare for. He would play Abdullah, a Dubai air-traffic controller investigating suspicious events around a flight to London. A driver collected him from a friend’s house on his first day of filming. During the journey, Mostafa questioned whether he was good enough to be there. Once he arrived, the more experienced actors treated him as an equal, and director Jim Field Smith welcomed his contributions. Mostafa helped with details of Emirati behaviour, including the way people hold their hands when greeting one another. He realised the pressure was helping him perform – a feeling he recognised from his years on the football field. “There’s nerves, but they’re nice nerves – the nerves that lock you in,” he said when Hijack was released in 2023. The 2024 television drama Khattaf asked more of him. Ali gave him a lead role to carry through a whole series, playing an Emirati fighter making his way through Asia’s underground combat scene. The boy who had done stunts for his brother now had years of sport and Muay Thai training behind him when stunt co-ordinator Najmeddin Scorpion began teaching him fight choreography. One move, known as the Black Widow, required Mostafa to hook a leg around another performer’s neck, swing around him and land on his own feet as the other man flipped away. He learnt quickly. An injury left his elbow so swollen it had to be bandaged, but his character was supposed to be injured in the next fight scene. The bandage stayed on for the camera – the injury served the scene, and that’s all that mattered to him. Away from the fight choreography, Mostafa was working out the character’s childhood and family relationships, comparing them with his own. He wanted to understand the parents, how they had become the people they were, and how their behaviour had shaped their son. Early in the shoot, he drew on painful memories from his own life when a scene required him to cry. By the time he filmed a sequence in prison, he had spent enough time with the character to find the emotion in his story. “I wasn’t thinking for a second about Mohamed. I was thinking about Khattaf, and I had tears rolling down my face, and I felt and I became,” he says. “That’s what acting is. Acting is becoming.” Talking about that scene brings out the goosebumps again. Mostafa wants another role he can spend that kind of time on, and another production willing to put him at the centre of its story. The ambition to join the main cast of a Hollywood film now comes with a clearer understanding of what he would want to do once he got there. Between Hijack , Khattaf and Dune , he has accumulated experience that has prepared him for the next step. He is grateful for each opportunity, although he has started to question how often he describes himself as lucky. It can leave out the work that earned him a place on those sets. “At some point, you have to realise you’re there for a reason. You were chosen,” Mostafa says. Alongside that confidence, his faith shapes what he wants to do with the opportunities he earns. Mostafa has grown up seeing words he uses in his religious life associated with violence in western news and films. They belong to his everyday experience of gratitude and service, and he wants audiences to understand what they mean to him. “Allahu akbar is the most beautiful term,” he says. “The direct definition of it is God is the greatest. No matter what happens in our life, we constantly remind ourselves that this is God’s plan, and He is greatest.” Holding a door open for someone is among the examples Mostafa gives when explaining his understanding of jihad. “Any act of service, any sacrifice, whether it’s small or big, is jihad.” Those words are part of the steadfast identity he carries into each audition. A role that reinforces their association with violence has consequences for him beyond the time he would spend playing it. He has to trust that there will be another opportunity after the one he declines. “When you walk with your value system intact, you might be saying no to those things. But I have this faith in God that other things will come that are much bigger.” Waiting for the right part leaves much of that future in other people’s hands. With support from Abu Dhabi’s Creative Media Authority, Mostafa established MFM at Yas Creative Hub, putting his business experience to work in film. “I can’t just be an actor with an agent in London waiting for auditions,” he says. “I have to create my movies. I need to collaborate.” The work he had been dividing his time between could now support his ambitions in film. Mostafa had arranged sponsorships for fighters and concerts; he could bring brands into productions and draw on his finance background in discussions with investors. The difficulties he had faced in finding representation gave him a reason to help other Emirati performers approach the industry. Mostafa takes a sip of coffee, holds it up, and suggests it might be one of the best he has had. “Just a little product placement,” he jokes. Behind the brand partnerships, however, is a struggle familiar to the filmmakers who approach MFM. “The biggest problem I’m seeing is funding,” Mostafa says. He is working to explain the film business to investors who are more familiar with property and technology, taking them through production costs, distribution and incentives. He expects it to take years. When City of Life had its premiere at DIFF in 2009, Mostafa watched the industry gather around his brother’s debut feature. When the festival returns, he will have a company to bring into those conversations, as well as his own ambitions as an actor. Finding the money for a film could give several performers their next job, and the time on set they need to improve. He saw how quickly that possibility could take hold on Dune . Fellow Emirati Rashed Dawood, a mixed martial arts fighter, was working on his first film as a stunt performer. Dawood discovered how much he enjoyed being on set and wanted to do it again. For him to develop that interest into a career, there would have to be another production, and another after that. “We’re not going to have a Dune come every year. We need to work on and scale up independent filmmaking,” Mostafa says. Mostafa needs the next production, too. He wants another chance to get as deeply into a character as he did in Khattaf . He is working to help get those films made, while pursuing the roles he believes he can carry. “I’m confident enough to know I can be in a blockbuster film as one of the main cast,” he says. “I just need to keep pushing, but I know I can do it.” The fearlessness that put him in front of Ali’s camera has stayed with him. Now Mostafa wants to take it into a role where audiences around the world will see an Emirati actor leading the story. He is ready for the scrutiny that will come with it, and for the work it will demand of him. “I would never be given that opportunity and not know the responsibility I’ll carry being there,” he says. “And also the responsibility I’d need to have to make sure I perform at the highest level because of what I represent.” Fashion Director: Sarah Maisey Photographer: Chris Whiteoak Shot on location at Jumeirah Beach Hotel and Mohamed's family home in Dubai

title: Philippines lauds Alex Eala for 'single-handedly' putting country on the world tennis map
body: The Philippine tennis body has lauded young sensation Alex Eala for raising the profile of tennis in the country, highlighting her decision to represent her nation at the 2026 Asian Games despite the risk of penalty. Eala had risked a hefty fine for skipping WTA's mandatory China Open as she represented the Philippines at the Japan Asian Games. While she lost her semi-final in Nagoya to Wang Xiyu, her actions did not go unnoticed. Eala has since suffered early exits in Singapore and Wuhan. But for the Philippine Tennis Association (PHILTA), she has already done a lot. “Alex Eala has already achieved what many once thought impossible. She has single-handedly put the Philippines on the world tennis map,” PHILTA secretary general John Rey Tiangco said. “Her rise to world No 18, her WTA title, and her victories over some of the world's best players are milestones that have changed the landscape of Philippine tennis.” Tiangco said Eala's decision to play for her country, even as other athletes decided to feature in China, was praiseworthy. Winning big in Wuhan 🤩 Shi Han defeats Eala in a three-set battle! #dongfengvoyahwuhanopen pic.twitter.com/CJPuZ2zuzL — wta (@WTA) October 12, 2026 “We are equally grateful for her decision to represent our country at the Asian Games, putting the Philippine flag ahead of other opportunities. “At this level of competition, victories and defeats are part of the journey. What matters is Alex's determination to keep improving, her discipline, and her commitment to the sport. “Alex has already won something bigger than any single tournament. She has inspired a nation and opened doors for the next generation of Filipino tennis players.” Meanwhile, Indonesia's Janice Tjen saw her Wuhan Open campaign come to an end in China on Thursday. American Ann Li, who upset the top seed Aryna Sabalenka in the second round, moved into the quarter-finals with a 6-1, 7-6 (1) victory over Tjen. Li will take on seventh seed Iga Swiatek of Poland in the last eight. Swiatek had on Thursday completed the 150th WTA 1000 win of ⁠her career.

title: Former Greek Army Officer Imprisoned for €300,000 Fuel Theft
body: A Thessaloniki appeals court has sentenced a former Greek Army non-commissioned officer to five years in prison for stealing 300,000 litres of fuel from a military pipeline in a rural area of Thessaloniki, with authorities now searching for him after he left court before the verdict. Four other defendants, all civilians, also received prison sentences. The court sentenced two alleged instigators to six years each, while the remaining two received sentences of three and four years, respectively. The former NCO denied involvement during his defence but left the courtroom before the judges delivered their verdict. Authorities are now seeking him so he can serve his sentence. The Thessaloniki Court of Appeal for Felonies found all five defendants guilty of aggravated theft, committed jointly and either completed or attempted, against the Greek state, or of instigating the offence. Some defendants have links to the petroleum industry. The court had granted mitigating circumstances at the original trial. The defendants who faced additional charges of fuel smuggling were acquitted of those allegations. Under the ruling, those sentenced to prison terms must serve their sentences. Of the two defendants who received prison terms rather than longer custodial sentences, one received a three-year suspended sentence, while the court converted the other sentence into a fine. Investigation uncovered multiple theft attempts The indictment covered five completed fuel thefts worth more than €300,000 and seven attempted thefts between 2013 and the end of 2014. Investigators began piecing together the case in November 2014, when a car plunged into an irrigation canal. Authorities had already received a report of an earlier fuel theft. According to the indictment, the vehicle was towing a trailer loaded with pipes, components and machinery. The crash site lay near an inspection chamber where investigators had found signs of forced entry. Their investigation linked the former NCO to the case. At the time, he served in a Thessaloniki military unit connected to the security and operation of the Hellenic Army’s fuel pipeline. All the defendants denied involvement during their statements to the court. Some claimed they had visited the crash site to photograph the area ahead of a planned search for gold. At the original trial, the court imposed prison sentences ranging from six to eight years, depending on each defendant’s role. It suspended the sentences under conditions pending the appeal proceedings. The post Former Greek Army Officer Imprisoned for €300,000 Fuel Theft appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Ukraine reports over 300 frontline clashes in past 24 hours, with most Russian attacks in Pokrovsk sector
body:
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook , releasing operational information as of 8:00 a.m. on Friday, October 16, according to Ukrinform.
According to updated data, the Russians carried out 83 airstrikes yesterday, using 271 guided bombs. The invaders also deployed 7,059 kamikaze drones and fired on populated areas and Defense Forces positions 2,551 times, including 76 times using multiple-launch rocket systems.
Enemy shelling targeted, in particular, Korenok, Nova Sich, Bachivsk, Tovstodubove, Sopych, Rohizne, Ivolzhanske, Mala Korchakivka, Pysarivka, Yunakivka, Khrapivshchyna, Volfyne, Bezsalivka, Sukhodil, Ulanove, Zapsillia, Kindrativka, Hirky, Kozache, Seredyna-Buda, Mogrytsia, Brusky, Khotin, Rudenka, Neskuchne, Iskryskivshchyna, Yastrubshchyna, and Luzhky in Sumy region, as well as Yanzhulivka in Chernihiv region. The Russian Federation carried out an airstrike on Vilna Sloboda.
Over the past day, Ukrainian aviation struck an area where Russian troops were concentrated.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk directions, the invaders dropped three guided aerial bombs over the past day and fired on the positions of the Defense Forces and populated areas 64 times.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna direction, Ukrainian defenders repelled 22 enemy attacks. The Russians attempted to attack in the areas of Starytsia, Izbytske, and Chuhunivka, toward Buzove and Radkivka.
In the Kupiansk sector, the Russian army attempted three times to improve its positions, conducting assault operations toward Novoosynove and Shyikivka.
In the Lyman sector, Russian troops launched eight attacks toward Novoyehorivka, Olhivka, Druzhlyubivka, Lyman, and Stary Karavan. Their attempts to breach Ukrainian defenses were repelled.
In the Sloviansk sector, the invaders launched two attacks toward Orikhuvatka and Mykolaivka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Ukrainian defenders halted three enemy attempts to advance in the Chervonyi area and toward Yurkivka.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, the Russians carried out 27 attacks: they conducted offensive operations in the Kostiantynivka and Dovha Balka areas, toward Rozkishne, Mykolaipillia, and Raiske.
In the Pokrovsk sector, the invaders attacked 60 times: they attempted to advance in the areas of Dorozhne and Molodetske, toward Toretsk, Pavlivka, Novopavlivka, Vilne, Kucherevy Yar, Hannivka, Dobropillia, Svitle, Krasnopodillia, Serhiivka, and Muravka.
In the Oleksandrivka sector, Russian forces did not carry out any assault operations.
In the Huliaipole sector, the Russian army attacked Ukrainian defenders’ positions 20 times, attempting to advance toward Rizdvyanka, Dolynka, Hirkyi, and Yehorivka.
In the Orikhiv sector, the invaders attempted to attack toward Pavlivka twice.
In the Dnipro River sector, Russian forces did not carry out any assault operations.
In the Volyn and Polissia sectors, no signs of the enemy forming offensive groups were detected.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russia lost 1,790 of its soldiers in the war against Ukraine over the past 24 hours.
