title: Al Pacino to Receive Life Achievement Award
body: Al Pacino will receive the Life Achievement Award from the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA), becoming the 62nd actor to receive the American union’s highest honour, according to the Associated Press (AP). The 86-year-old star of the iconic Godfather trilogy said acting and the colleagues he had met throughout his career had brought him some of the greatest joys of his life. “For most of my life, I have wondered and wandered, but I have always felt at home when I had a script in my hands and was among fellow actors,” Pacino said in a statement. “I am honoured to be recognised by SAG-AFTRA as it celebrates my journey,” he added. Pacino will accept the award at the 33rd SAG Awards ceremony on 28 February 2027 at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles. Netflix will broadcast the ceremony live. The post Al Pacino to Receive Life Achievement Award appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Le Pen Looms Large as Macron Enters Final Months on EU Stage
body:
The spectre of far-right leader Marine Le Pen winning France’s presidency with a pledge to go head-to-head with the European Union is already giving Brussels the jitters -- and looming large over Emmanuel Macron’s final months in power.
France heads to the polls in April and May, after which Macron will exit as he can only serve two terms as president of the EU’s second-largest economy.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
But as Macron met his EU counterparts for a Brussels summit, a European diplomat said Le Pen was already “in the room” -- with the frontrunner’s potential victory hanging over their talks Thursday and Friday on future spending and Ukraine.
Seeking to tighten the screws on the EU, Le Pen travelled to the Belgian capital on the eve of the leaders’ meeting to address the media, vowing to slash France’s contribution to the European Union budget and to cut short financial support to Ukraine.
European officials do not hide their concerns that Le Pen is trying to exert influence over EU affairs months before the vote.
“It was very cunning of her to hold her press conference” the day before, said a second European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity.
The National Rally leader also spoke at length to the Financial Times newspaper, read by policymakers in Brussels, warning of a potential showdown over the EU budget and difficult times for EU chief Ursula von der Leyen if she wins.
The interview was “quite scary” especially on Ukraine, said Francesco Nicoli, politics professor at Italy’s Polytechnic University of Turin.
A senior European official admitted Brussels could barely imagine what the EU would look like with a French far-right government -- with no known formal contacts between Le Pen and the EU executive to date.
For Macron, fears of a disruptive Le Pen presidency have sharpened focus on what he may yet achieve at EU level in his final few months in power.
The fervent European who has spent nine years pushing deeper EU integration maintains influence over his counterparts in Brussels, diplomats say, despite a pileup of crises at home from student protests to French debt turmoil.
“What is certain is that in Brussels there is the will to make the most of the fact he is still there, and to lock in whatever can be before a possible storm,” said Sebastien Maillard, of the Jacques Delors Institute.
Observers note that no other current EU leader has managed to take on a leadership role in the bloc, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz weaker than ever after the strongest far-right win in Germany since 1945.
“Macron understands what is happening around the (leaders’) table. He’s a very skilled negotiator and much more agile than Merz,” the first EU diplomat said.
EU watchers say Macron will need all his savvy to prevail in the fraught negotiations over the budget between the so-called “frugals” led by Berlin and capitals like Paris seeking a more ambitious budget.
Maillard said the French president had “acquired an international reputation” which could “to a certain extent, protect him from France’s domestic difficulties”.
The expert pointed to Macron’s influence over talks on Christine Lagarde’s successor as head of the European Central Bank and the EU budget talks.
“On foreign and security policy, Macron is in a strong position right now. On economic issues he’s weak,” academic Nicoli said.
The French leader himself, perhaps wanting to avoid Le Pen further overshadowing his summit talks, did not take any questions from journalists in Brussels Thursday.
“I think that’s why Macron is keeping a low profile. He doesn’t want to respond,” a diplomatic source said.

title: Serbia: 2026 snap parliamentary elections. Political legitimacy, the student movement and prospects for the country’s future. A research of the International Institute for Middle East and Balkan Studies
body: LJUBLJIANA. The International Institute for Middle East and Balkan Studies (IFIMES) [ 1 ], based in Ljubljana, regularly monitors and analyses developments in the Middle East, the Balkans and across the world. Its latest analysis, entitled “ Serbia ahead of the 2026 snap parliamentary elections: political legitimacy, the student movement and prospects for the country’s future development” , examines the early parliamentary elections scheduled in Serbia for 25 October 2026. Aleksandar Vucic It focuses in particular on the range of political options and electoral competition, the positions of both ruling and opposition parties, the role of the student movement and the interplay between economic indicators, political legitimacy and institutional reform. The analysis also explores the primary challenges that will shape Serbia’s future trajectory, political stability and capacity to deliver sustainable economic growth. The finalisation of the consolidated electoral list for Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections on 25 October 2026 marks an important procedural milestone. Beyond its formal significance, however, it raises broader questions about political representation, social mobilisation and the future balance of power in the country. According to the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), 18 electoral lists are contesting the elections, fielding a total of 2,418 candidates for the 250-seat National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. All members of parliament are elected from a single nationwide constituency. Securing an absolute majority requires at least 126 seats, while parties must pass an electoral threshold of 3% of the total votes cast to qualify for the allocation of parliamentary seats. Special rules apply to national minority electoral lists in accordance with the law. The electoral roll contains 6,450,523 registered voters.[ 2 ] The broad spectrum of electoral lists ranges from the ruling bloc centred around the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) – led by the “ Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia ” list — to established governing and opposition parties, a student-led list, national minority representatives, right-wing political groups and smaller political organisations. The flag of Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) While this reflects the diversity of choices available to voters, it does not necessarily reveal the actual political strength of the competing actors or the extent of their electoral support. The central question in these elections is therefore not simply how many lists are competing, but whether the electoral process can ensure that public discontent, political alternatives and the varied interests of citizens are genuinely reflected in the composition of the next parliament. SNS and Aleksandar Vučić: continuity of power and the challenges of political legitimacy The “ Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia ” electoral list, built around the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), tops the consolidated electoral list and forms the core of the current ruling bloc. Campaigning under Aleksandar Vučić’s name underscores the continuity of political leadership and the established identity of the ruling structures. According to a Faktor Plus opinion poll reported by RTS on 11 October 2026, the “ United Serbia – Aleksandar Vučić ” list commanded 48.6% support among respondents, compared with 37.1% for the “ Student List – Students Win ” [ 3 ] In Serbia, parliamentary elections are about more than deciding who sits in the legislature. They also serve as a broader test of the relationship between the executive, the ruling party, the opposition and social actors advocating changes in how institutions function. The quality of a political system cannot be judged solely by whether electoral lists have been formally approved and comply with legal requirements. Equally vital are the fairness of electoral conditions, access to the media, transparency in campaign financing, the effectiveness of institutions and public confidence in the electoral process. Against this backdrop, the legitimacy of the next government will rest not only on the number of parliamentary seats it secures, but also on whether citizens believe that political competition and the conduct of the elections have met democratic standards. The legal validity of elections must therefore be distinguished from the broader question of political trust in institutions. Aleksandar Vučić, who heads the “ Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia” electoral list, has declared that schools and universities will no longer serve as local party branches or meeting places for political parties, but will instead remain institutions dedicated exclusively to education and learning. “ Keep politics out of schools, out of universities. Anyone who doesn’t like it can look for another job. End of story. And that is my firm promise, because I will not surrender Serbia to the worst among us. I will not let them destroy our children. I will not let them destroy our future ,” Vučić said [ 4 ]. The student list: institutionalising public discontent and presenting a political challenge Positioned third on the consolidated electoral list is the “ Student List – Students Win “, headed by Ilija Srdanović. Ilija Srdanović Media reports indicate that Srdanović has once again declined a televised debate with Aleksandar Vučić [ 5 ]. By entering the electoral contest, the list seeks to channel the social mobilisation generated by student activism into the institutional political arena. The student movement and its electoral list are distinct entities. While the movement encompasses a broad range of views and aspirations, the electoral list must offer a clear and achievable platform. Despite the presentation of an 11-point programme, questions remain about how its proposals will be developed, funded and implemented. Particular attention should be paid to the list’s relationship with existing opposition parties and its positions on NATO, the status of Kosovo, relations with Republika Srpska and the Srebrenica genocide. The student movement is neither ideologically nor politically homogeneous. While some of its members advocate Serbia’s future NATO membership, others favour strengthening ties with Russia. Views also diverge on Kosovo, with some regarding it as an independent state and supporting formal recognition. This diversity raises the question of whether the electoral list can reconcile these competing positions within a coherent political programme that is sustainable in the long term. A further concern is that the “ Student List – Students Win ” does not include a single student, casting doubt on its direct representation of students and young people more broadly. In contrast, the “ Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia ” list includes 20 students. The political significance of these lists will depend not only on their composition, but also on the clarity of their programmes, transparency in their activities and the ability of their representatives to meet voters’ expectations. For the “ Student List “, its political standing will hinge on its electoral performance, the clarity of its programme and its capacity to meet voter expectations, as well as its ability to dispel suspicions of foreign influence by operating transparently. Another striking detail emerges from an analysis of the candidates’ ages: the combined ages of candidates on the “ Student List – Students Win ” exceed those of candidates on the “ Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia ” list by approximately 1,700 years. This creates something of a paradox: a list presenting itself as the voice of students and younger generations fields considerably older candidates than the list bearing the name of Serbia’s president until recently. The opposition and a fragmented political landscape: the challenges of building political unity The consolidated electoral list reflects the ideological and organisational diversity of Serbia’s political landscape. The “European Serbia” list, featuring Marinika Tepić and Zdravko Ponoš, brings together several political organisations, while other lists represent national-conservative, liberal-green and other political orientations. The withdrawal of several opposition lists highlights the difficulties of forging a common strategy. Meanwhile, the emergence of the student movement – commonly known as “ blockaders ” – has intensified competition for opposition votes and raised doubts about the feasibility of forming a united political alternative to Aleksandar Vučić’s government. Of particular note is the Strength of Serbia Movement – Bogoljub Karić (PSS-BK), which is striving to carve out a distinct third political option, championing traditional values, family, entrepreneurship and development opportunities for young people. Bogoljub Karić Invoking the slogan of the 1968 student protests, “ Be realistic, demand the impossible “, Bogoljub Karić seeks to connect the social demands of young people with concrete economic and development proposals. While political diversity may contribute to pluralism, diverging platforms and differing strategies risk hindering opposition coordination. The sheer number of electoral slates alone is therefore no measure of their collective political clout. Assessing political competition requires clear political programmes, a level playing field, an informed electorate and a future parliament capable of exercising effective oversight of the executive. National minorities: political representation and the integrity of the electoral process The consolidated electoral list includes representatives of the Hungarian, Bosniak, Albanian, Russian, Slovak and other national communities, underscoring the importance of minority representation in Serbia’s political system. Of the 18 electoral lists contesting the elections, nine represent national minorities. Yet the formal participation of minority slates does not automatically translate into genuine decision-making influence. Sandžak and southern Serbia (Preševo, Medveđa and Bujanovac) merit particular attention, as minority rights, economic development, public trust in institutions and political representation remain key concerns for local communities. Figures from the Republic Electoral Commission show that the 2,418 candidates have an average age of 46.3, with just 262, or 10.8%, aged under 30. Meanwhile, the “Student List – Students Win” has one of the oldest candidate age profiles, highlighting the issue of youth representation in political decision-making. The candidate pool comprises 1,134 women (46.9%) and 1,284 men (53.1%), with every electoral list successfully meeting the mandatory 40% quota for the under-represented gender. Even so, formal representation does not automatically ensure equal participation in decision-making. Electoral integrity and public confidence ultimately depend on transparent election administration, equal electoral conditions, the protection of voting rights and effective procedures for handling complaints. Any assessment of whether the elections were conducted properly must rely on verifiable facts, documented irregularities and the findings of relevant election observation missions, including the OSCE/ODIHR. The OSCE/ODIHR interim report highlights that the Republic Electoral Commission met all statutory deadlines in preparing for the elections and maintained transparency through public sessions broadcast live and open to the media and observers. The report further notes that the Commission published its rulings on electoral complaints promptly, while the Administrative Court upheld all ten Commission decisions challenged on appeal [ 6 ]. Serbia’s economic outlook: inflation, public debt, foreign investment and living standards Economic indicators play an important role in assessing Serbia’s political legitimacy and prospects for development ahead of the 2026 snap parliamentary elections. Beyond political stability, institutional performance and electoral integrity, citizens are directly affected by purchasing power, price movements, wages and pensions, public debt and the state’s capacity to attract investment that supports long-term economic development. Inflation and purchasing power Data from the Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia show that annual inflation, measured by the change in consumer prices against the corresponding month of the previous year, stood at 12.2% in December 2012, compared with 2.7% in December 2025. By August 2026, the annual inflation rate was 2.2%. Measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), which enables international comparisons, inflation in the same month reached 3.2% in the euro area and 3.4% in Slovenia. These figures indicate that consumer prices in Serbia rose at a slower annual rate in August 2026 than in either the euro area or Slovenia [ 7 ]. However, a slowdown in inflation does not imply a return to previous price levels, nor does it guarantee an across-the-board improvement in living standards. A meaningful assessment of purchasing power must also consider increases in net earnings, pensions and other sources of income, taking into account the cost of food, housing, energy and other essential goods and services. Ultimately, the balance between nominal income growth and living expenses remains a key barometer of public satisfaction with economic conditions. Foreign direct investment and Serbia’s economic competitiveness in the region Foreign direct investment (FDI) data reveal considerable variation across Serbia and the wider region. Serbia attracted €1.009 billion in FDI in 2012, €5.231 billion in 2024 and €3.477 billion in 2025. Over the same years, Bulgaria recorded €1.383 billion, €2.819 billion and €4.264 billion respectively, compared with €1.000 billion, €4.182 billion and €2.630 billion in Croatia. The figures illustrate fluctuations in investment flows and competition for capital within the region.[ 8 ] The long-term value of investment lies not merely in the amount of capital attracted, but also in its contribution to job creation, productivity, technological advancement, knowledge transfer and export competitiveness. Consequently, Serbia’s economic policy must look beyond attracting capital alone, prioritising the quality and sustainability of investment, alongside transparent incentives and fair market conditions. Pensions, the minimum wage and sustainable living standards Data on the average pension in Serbia show an increase from €204 in 2012 to €394 in 2024 and €437 in 2025. The reported figure for July 2026 stands at €484, while projections put the average pension at €520 in December 2026, €650 in December 2027 and €750 in December 2030. These projected amounts should be clearly distinguished from figures for pensions already paid out. The net minimum wage increased from €153 in 2010 to €256 in 2020, €340 in 2023, €404 in 2024 and €468 in 2025. The figure reported for January–August 2026 is €550, with a projected increase to €600 in January 2027. Rising pensions and minimum wages can boost household incomes and help reduce the risk of poverty. Yet nominal figures in euros alone reveal little about what people can actually afford. Assessing real purchasing power requires comparing income growth with inflation and the cost of essential goods and services, while also accounting for differences in purchasing power across countries. For Serbia, it is especially important that minimum wage increases are matched by productivity gains without placing additional strain on small and medium-sized enterprises, employment or economic competitiveness. Meanwhile, a sustainable pension system requires a balance between social protection, demographic trends, employment and the long-term health of public finances. The 2026 elections: political representation, democratic legitimacy and prospects for sustainable development The participation of 18 electoral lists featuring a total of 2,418 candidates reflects the diversity of formal political options ahead of Serbia’s snap parliamentary elections. Yet the actual extent of political pluralism and democratic legitimacy will depend on fair electoral conditions, public trust in institutions and the next government’s ability to tackle the country’s main political, social and economic challenges. Aleksandar Vučić and the political bloc centred on the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) remain key players in Serbia’s political landscape. Any assessment of their political continuity must take into account both their economic track record and the country’s future development priorities. According to projections by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Serbia’s GDP is expected to grow by 3.3% in 2026 and 4% in 2027 [ 9 ]. Whether these projections materialise will depend on investment, the capacity to implement reforms and the international economic environment. For citizens, however, what matters most is whether economic growth translates into tangible improvements in living standards, social security, housing affordability and prospects for young people. Slowing inflation, a declining public debt ratio and rising wages and pensions are positive indicators, but do not in themselves guarantee sustainable improvements in living conditions. Their real impact depends on purchasing power, the quality of public services, economic productivity and a fairer distribution of the benefits of development. Economic performance must therefore be assessed alongside the rule of law, transparency in public finances and the quality of institutions. Pledges to streamline the next government, including downsizing the cabinet to 12 ministries, should be judged by tangible improvements in administrative efficiency, transparency and institutional accountability. The number of ministries alone is no benchmark for reform success; what counts is good governance, clearly defined responsibilities and effective oversight of public spending. The central issue in the upcoming elections is therefore not simply who secures a parliamentary majority, but how the next government will address the challenges of political legitimacy, institutional reform and sustainable economic development. Projections for total GDP growth suggest that Serbia will become the region’s leading economy in 2027. Serbia’s long-term stability will depend on whether Aleksandar Vučić and the next parliamentary majority can leverage political continuity to strengthen state institutions, uphold the rule of law and foster sustainable economic progress. The task is not merely to retain political support, but to translate macroeconomic stability into rising living standards, greater social security and better opportunities for young people. The political legitimacy of Vučić and the future government will be judged not just at the ballot box, but also by their ability to deliver on public promises, ensure institutional transparency and accountability and contribute to Serbia’s long-term development. For Vučić, the challenge will be to reinforce his political leadership by delivering new, tangible results while upholding democratic standards and maintaining public confidence in the electoral process. title: Shah Rukh Khan to launch Indian music festival UNIFYD in Abu Dhabi
body: Bollywood superstar Shah Rukh Khan is launching a new music festival, UNIFYD, to be held in Abu Dhabi next year. Top Indian singers Arijit Singh, Karan Aujla and Sonu Nigam are among the first names announced on the line-up. The inaugural event is to take place on March 20 at Etihad Live on Yas Island. It is to bring together more than 15 artists across several stages for a one-day programme focused on Indian music and culture. The festival will be produced by D'YAVOL Live and District, in collaboration with the Department of Culture and Tourism in Abu Dhabi and Miral . Khan will oversee its artistic direction and creative vision. “I’ve spent a lifetime telling stories on screen and watching them bring people together. Music has that same extraordinary power," he said. "The festival promises to be a true spectacle in terms of its scale, energy and grandeur." Khan is no stranger to major events in Abu Dhabi, having hosted the IIFA Awards on Yas Island in 2024. Who is to perform at UNIFYD? Singh and Aujla are among the first acts to be announced, while Nigam is to perform a special set. It marks his first performance at a music festival, organisers said. The line-up brings together artists spanning Hindi film music and Punjabi music, with further performers still to be announced. Organisers also plan to expand UNIFYD to other cities and international markets after its debut in Abu Dhabi . “Indian music is already global," said Bunty Singh, co-founder of D’YAVOL Live. "UNIFYD gives that cultural force a festival platform that matches its scale, ambition and influence. Bringing together artists of this stature on the same day, in a line-up that has never existed before, is what makes the first edition so special.” When do tickets go on sale? Tickets will be available exclusively through the District app. The general sale opens at 10.30am on October 20. Ticket prices have not yet been revealed.

title: A Modern Trace Italienne: Rethinking Rear-Area Defense Against Drones
body:
Throughout the sanguine annals of military history, very few truths have endured. However, one comes close: Advances in offensive technology eventually demand corresponding innovations in defense.
Today, drone-enabled attacks across Ukraine, Russia, and the Middle East offer a grisly warning that has redefined the meaning of the rear area, once thought to be secure. Inexpensive long-range drones have struck targets and caused casualties. The lecture halls of the battlefield have always been staffed by unforgiving professors, and once again they are teaching us in blood. While certainly the rear area has not completely disappeared, the sanctuary long associated with it has been degraded. These attacks are not indicative of failure, as no base is ever completely invulnerable. However, we must examine the time we find ourselves in, as militaries worldwide are racing to integrate drones into their land, sea, and air forces .
The age of the drone might be best compared to the age of gunpowder , when military forces struggled for years to wield chemical-fueled firepower not only in battle but also against fortresses. Gunpowder eventually forced armies to rewrite the grammar of violence on land, sea, and in sieges .
After the fall of the Roman Empire and the loss of large, well-trained legions , local rulers instead put their faith in castles to provide for regional defense. However, the advent of gunpowder artillery altered the stopwatch for attacking fortresses, making what once took months possible in weeks, days, and sometimes hours.
As stone fortresses were reduced to rubble from the cacophonic screams of ever more powerful cannons, many contemporary Renaissance thinkers realized that the answer was not simply a thicker version of the wall they already possessed. It became clear that the cannon had profoundly manipulated the existing rules of warfare, such that the architecture of defense demanded not only innovation but also imagination. It is from that bloody process of experimentation that the trace italienne, the Italian form most commonly known as a star fort, was born. The introduction of the trace italienne brought a defensive system designed to deny artillery the rapid decision it had briefly promised.
Today, we must respond to new drone-enabled threats against our own rear areas. It is time to make our own trace américaine , a distinctly American defensive architecture built around hardening, depth, and interlocking fields of fire. The evolution should not be just the ability to defend against the drone, but also to fight back.
It is important to note that in the age of gunpowder, the cannon did not make the fortress irrelevant. Rather, it made the old way of fortresses nearly obsolete. The age of drone-enabled combat may now be doing the same to us today with respect to our airbases and rear areas. Today’s danger is not merely that drones can strike our bases, but also that we may be building these bases according to assumptions that the drone is slowly grinding away . It is for us to imagine a new way of defending our vulnerable rear areas.
How Gunpowder Altered the Grammar of Violence in Defense
The introduction of gunpowder to battlefields in Europe did not transform battlefields or sieges overnight. European armies required decades and centuries to adapt to the shift from muscle-powered to chemically fueled firepower. As always, weapons arrive on the field of battle with instruction manuals, but not the institutions, formations, or even the fortifications to best employ or survive against them. In land combat, gunpowder spurred new tactics and formations, such as the Spanish tercio . On the high seas, naval warfare evolved from a contest dominated by closing, ramming, and boarding toward one increasingly decided by cannon fire. As the democratization of gunpowder altered the formations and practices of battle on land and at sea, the next phase of the gunpowder revolution also affected siege warfare.
Fortresses from antiquity to the late medieval era plagued commanders and proved quite difficult to take. From Caesar’s circumvallation of Alesia in 52 BCE to the castles of medieval Europe, hunger, disease, and time could accomplish what muscle-powered missiles often could not. However, firepower, delivered by bombards and later cannons, transformed the stopwatch of siege from months to weeks and, at times, even hours. Christopher Duffy, in his work Siege Warfare: The Fortress in the Early Modern World 1494–1660 , tells the story of how stone that had provided sanctuary could now be pulverized into rubble, and at an accelerating pace.
The employment of cannon was decisive at the sieges of Harfleur in 1415, Constantinople in 1453, and Krems in 1477 .Yet even after these dramatic events, there was still little evidence that Europeans fully understood that artillery had fundamentally altered the relationship between attack and defense . This failure to rapidly imagine a new grammar of violence serves as an important warning for contemporary military thinkers in the embryonic stages of drone-enabled combat. Sometimes it takes several catastrophes and defeats to make the implications impossible to ignore, as military institutions throughout history have stubbornly ignored threats to their established practices. However, smoldering rubble is considerably more difficult to ignore.
For Renaissance Europe, Charles VIII of France’s cannon-enabled invasion of Italy provided horrifying evidence that the timeframe and rules of siege warfare had evolved. Within his siege train, Charles VIII carried a new generation of mobile artillery that fired iron shot and could be emplaced and fired with horrific efficiency. Duffy recounts contemporary descriptions of cannon accomplishing in hours what previously required weeks to months. In February 1495, Charles VIII arrived before the border fortress of Monte San Giovanni Campano with roughly forty horse-drawn bronze guns.
Charles’s artillery breached the fortress in only eight hours , and the French army stormed through and massacred the garrison. Military thinkers throughout Europe, such as Machiavelli , and even artists like Michelangelo , soon wrestled with the challenge of designing fortifications capable of withstanding artillery fire.
It appeared that the advent of gunpowder forever changed the character of warfare. Fortresses that had defined military power for centuries became, almost overnight, expensive places to die. It appeared that the cannon had not merely introduced another weapon onto the battlefield. But rather, it murdered the assumptions upon which the old defensive system had been built.
Europe did not answer the cannon with a better cannon, nor did it do so quickly. Italian engineers spent decades groping toward a solution. At Pisa in 1500 the defenders threw up earthen retrenchments behind the breach, and the assault failed. At Padua in 1509 , Venetian defenders employed low earthen works against a powerful imperial siege force. Over the decades, the defense began learning how to survive. The cannon had taken only hours to demonstrate the problem. However, it would take generations of experimentation to build the answer.
The trace italienne , dreamed of and built by Italian engineers, was a weapons system infused with architecture. The Italians stopped building upward and instead started building outward, with angular bastions projecting from the walls, providing deadly interlocking fields of fire. Beyond them came ditches, glacis, and ravelins that not only delayed an attacker but also provided defenders with more opportunities to rain fire upon them. The trace italienne formed a mutually supporting defensive system designed to counter the besieger’s guns. By the end of the sixteenth century, decades of experimentation had matured into what Duffy describes as the “ New Italian School .” The Italians had invented a deadly geometry that forced the attacker to pay in time, treasure, and blood for every meter of ground.
The first Europeans confronted by the increasing threat of artillery did not immediately produce the star fort. Instead, their early adaptations were often designed simply to survive, as walls were reinforced with earth. In doing so, they were learning how to absorb the cannon before they understood how to fight back against it.
Duffy makes an especially important observation about this transitional period. As late as the 1480s, European military architects had not fully appreciated that artillery could transform the active defense of fortresses. The enduring challenge was not simply to construct something capable of absorbing enemy cannon fire. Eventually, the Italians realized that the fortress could no longer remain a passive shield but had to become a weapon in its own right.
The distinction matters today as our objective cannot simply be to survive the drone. Rather, we must build positions capable of fighting it. For the American military experience during the post-9/11 wars, decades of attacks by vehicle-borne explosives, rockets, mortars, and insurgents shaped the physical architecture of our installations. Today the drone demands a new lethal geometry. In the current age of precise mass afforded by cheap drones , accompanied by missile barrages, it appears that the fiscal cost of offense is also lower than that of defense. Shahed drones cost around $35,000, and defending them with $4 million Patriot missile interceptors exacts a painful toll on the defense. The rear-area base of the drone age cannot simply hide behind its walls. Instead, we must hunt from outside and within them. Today’s rear-area bases can no longer be merely defended ; they must become bristling weapons of firepower .
Recovering the logic of the star fort will take imagination and innovation, as we must remember that the Italians did not defeat the cannon with a single new wall or weapon. Instead, they built a system, and we must do the same. We can take inspiration from several defining features of the star fort to identify key ways to rethink rear-area defense.
First, think in terms of interlocking fields of fire. The genius of the trace italienne was that the fortress itself bristled with firepower, with bastions protecting one another, and an attacker escaping one field of fire entered another. Defending rear areas against drone threats must do the same. Rather than relying primarily on a handful of defensive systems to protect hundreds of soft targets, we should increase the number of bastions not just on base perimeters but within the heart of the base and on several buildings to deliver both kinetic and nonkinetic effects. The deeper a drone penetrates the base, the more of the base’s defensive systems should engage it. Any drone that is lucky enough to cross the perimeter should discover that it has flown into the bristling teeth of the trace américaine .
Second, develop a modern ravelin. The trace italienne did not begin at the fortress walls, but beyond them. Its ravelins, which were detached, triangular fortifications positioned beyond the main walls, extended the defense outward, forcing attackers to fight through another layer before they could reach the fortress itself. The trace américaine could push that principle into the sky with persistent defensive drones patrolling the approaches to a base, extending their sensors outward to detect and track approaching threats. Some might patrol and return, while others could become expendable interceptors. Additionally, we may consider developing our own modern counterdrone gun bastions outside the base perimeter to begin attacking hostile drones before they reach the base or airfield perimeters.
Third, dig. Throughout military history, digging into the earth itself has proven excellent cover from ever more lethal firepower. As belligerents such as the North Vietnamese or Hamas utilized tunnels to escape from overwhelming firepower, we must take a page from this playbook. Our important and vulnerable command-and-control, ammunition, fuel, maintenance, and communications nodes should, when practicable, increasingly disappear beneath the earth. We might have to ask what actually needs to remain above ground at all . Today the drone has given our adversaries extraordinary eyes; one of our first responses should be to give those eyes less to see and fewer targets to strike.
Fourth, build the fortress engineers. The trace américaine will require more than a new defensive weapons architecture; it may also require innovations to our military engineering capability . We may need to evolve beyond traditional backhoes and bulldozers by equipping engineers with boring machines, trenchers, autonomous excavators, and rapid concrete delivery systems to turn an exposed base into a hardened position. Five centuries ago, the great fortresses required generations of specialized engineers to build. The drone age needs its own fortress builders.
Fifth, take airpower underground. We should also be willing to reconsider one of the strangest assumptions of modern airpower: that the most expensive weapons in the American arsenal spend their most vulnerable hours sitting above ground. Where geography, geology, and mission permit, the trace américaine should look downward. Switzerland and Taiwan have demonstrated that combat aircraft can be sheltered within subterranean or mountainous complexes, alongside portions of the infrastructure required to maintain them and return them to the fight. If the drone has made the open sky increasingly dangerous, some of our airpower must learn to disappear beneath it.
Finally, make deception architecture. The trace américaine must also manipulate what the enemy believes he sees . Into this hornet’s nest of defensive architecture and firepower we should also design deception, for the inevitable drones that still make it through our wall of fire. In our construction, we should build false aircraft shelters beside real ones as well as decoy command posts and barracks.
Perhaps most importantly, we may need to stop thinking about the base as a collection of buildings surrounded by defensive systems. Rather, the base itself must become the defensive system. The genius of the trace américaine cannot be the drone, the jammer, the interceptor, or the bunker. It must be the system that makes them fight together.
None of this will make a military installation invulnerable, nor should that be the standard by which we measure success, as no fortress ever was free from vulnerabilities. As we look to the success of the trace italienne , we see it robbed the cannon of its easy victory. The new system of fortifications restored the offensive-defensive paradigm.
We may never stop every drone, and we do not have to. The measure of success cannot simply be whether a system is capable of a 100 percent intercept rate. It must be able to absorb the blow, continue its mission, and fight back. Five centuries ago, gunpowder did not end the fortress. It killed one kind of fortress and forced humanity to invent another. The drone may now be demanding the same of us.
The garrison at Monte San Giovanni Campano stood behind walls that had reportedly once survived a seven-year siege. They had every reason to believe those walls would protect them until the guns came up the road. Eight hours later, their world was gone. We have already seen the drones coming, and we do not need to wait for our own eight hours to change the walls.
Antonio Salinas is an active duty US Army officer, a professor of strategic intelligence at National Defense University, and a PhD student in the Department of History at Georgetown University. Salinas has twenty-eight years of military service in the US Marine Corps and Army as an infantry officer, an assistant professor in the Department of History at the US Military Academy, and a strategic intelligence officer, with operational experience in Afghanistan and Iraq. He is the author of Siren’s Song: The Allure of War , Boot Camp: The Making of a United States Marine , and Leaving War: From Afghanistan’s Pech Valley to Hadrian’s Wall .
The views expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the official position of the United States Military Academy, Department of the Army, or Department of Defense.

title: The Long Goodbye: Why Greeks Take Forever to Leave
body: The Irish have the Irish Goodbye. The French have the French Exit. And the Greeks have a departure process that can take longer than the gathering itself. While an Irish Goodbye involves disappearing from a party without telling anyone, the Greek approach is rather more elaborate. There are announcements to make, relatives to farewell, conversations to finish and, inevitably, food to take home. It usually begins with a familiar declaration. “Άντε, να φεύγουμε σιγά σιγά.” Roughly translated, “Come on, we’d better start getting going.” The key phrase is σιγά σιγά, meaning slowly, or little by little. In the context of a Greek goodbye, it is less an instruction than a remarkably accurate prediction. Nobody is going anywhere just yet. In fact, the first announcement is rarely taken seriously. It simply alerts everyone that the departure process has officially begun. Someone suggests another coffee. Someone else remembers a story they meant to tell you earlier. A relative you haven’t spoken to all evening suddenly wants a detailed update on your life. “Κάτσε λίγο ακόμα.” Stay a little longer. And just like that, another twenty minutes disappear. Eventually, you stand up. This is an important development, although hardly a guarantee of progress. Experienced guests understand that once you’ve stood up, you must remain standing. Sitting down again is effectively an admission that you have abandoned your original plan. There is also the question of how many people require an individual farewell. In a room full of relatives, you cannot simply wave towards the general population and announce your departure. There are kisses to exchange, hands to shake and people who will be deeply offended if you somehow overlook them. The first round takes place in the living room. The second in the hallway. The third at the front door, where an entirely new conversation often begins. By now, somebody has remembered something important they meant to tell you three hours earlier. And this is where some Greeks have developed a few unofficial escape strategies. The most common is the early warning system, where you announce your intention to leave a good 45 minutes before you actually need to go. Another involves gradually moving your belongings towards the front door, hoping that proximity to the exit might eventually translate into an actual departure. More experienced guests may send their partner to start the car while they complete the remaining social obligations. None of these strategies is particularly reliable. Especially when somebody enters the kitchen. “Να σου βάλω λίγο φαγητό;” Shall I pack you some food? What follows is a negotiation in which the guest insists they don’t need anything and the host proceeds to pack it anyway. There is rarely any point resisting. Refusing leftovers can require a longer explanation than accepting them. By the time you’ve collected your belongings, you’re carrying more than you arrived with. Which raises an interesting question. Why don’t Greeks simply adopt the Irish Goodbye? The term, sometimes called the Irish Exit, describes the practice of leaving a gathering without announcing your departure. The French Exit refers to much the same thing, although the French themselves have the expression filer à l’anglaise, meaning to slip away in the English manner. Apparently, nobody wants to take responsibility for leaving without saying goodbye. For anyone accustomed to the Greek version, the Irish approach sounds wonderfully efficient. You collect your coat, locate the door and disappear. No explanations. No repeated kisses. No standing on the doorstep discussing somebody’s recent trip to the village. In a Greek family gathering, however, such a manoeuvre would be considerably more complicated. You would first need to retrieve your belongings unnoticed, avoid attracting the attention of anyone in the kitchen and somehow leave without being intercepted by a relative demanding to know where you’re going. Even if you succeeded, your absence would soon become a topic of conversation. “Πού πήγαν;” Where did they go? “Έφυγαν;” They’ve left? “Ούτε ένα γεια;” Not even a goodbye? Before long, somebody would be on the telephone trying to establish what happened and whether anyone had been offended. The Irish Goodbye may save time, but in a Greek household it could create considerably more work than simply saying goodbye properly. Of course, there is one final stage in the Greek departure process that deserves recognition. The car goodbye. Having successfully navigated the living room, hallway and front door, you are now seated in your vehicle, convinced that the evening has finally concluded. Then somebody appears beside the window. A final question. Another reminder. Perhaps a discussion about when everyone is getting together again. “Πάρε τηλέφωνο όταν φτάσεις.” Call when you get home. You promise you will. The engine starts. There is one final wave, another “άντε, γεια” and, at long last, you are on your way. The whole process may seem unnecessarily complicated, but there is something rather revealing about it. The Irish Goodbye is designed to make leaving almost invisible. The Greek goodbye does precisely the opposite. It turns departure into one final opportunity for conversation, hospitality and connection. Perhaps that is why nobody seems particularly interested in making it more efficient. After all, θα τα πούμε, meaning “we’ll speak again”, is one of the most familiar expressions in Greek conversation. And if the goodbye takes another half an hour, there’s plenty of time to make good on that promise. Just don’t sit down again. Read also Paul Frazis, Australia’s Commercial Broker of the Year: ‘Lending Is About People’ The post The Long Goodbye: Why Greeks Take Forever to Leave appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: US Navy drone lands autonomously on moving ship without GPS
body:
The US Navy has demonstrated a new capability designed to enable unmanned aircraft to operate and recover aboard ships in GPS-denied environments, advancing efforts to expand autonomous operations at sea.
As disclosed, the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division (NAWCAD) demonstrated that an unmanned system can navigate its mission and land aboard a Navy ship without GPS or pilot control.
The live-flight demonstration proved that a tactical drone can fly mission tasks and execute recoveries on a pitching vessel at sea – even when satellite navigation is jammed or unavailable – by using its own commercial-standard cameras, motion sensors, and electronics, according to the navy.
“In contested areas where satellites and communications are jammed, autonomy gives significant advantage to our sailors,” said NAWCAD Commander Rear Adm. Todd Evans .
“Breakthroughs like this help us scale unmanned capability fast and affordably across a distributed fleet.”
“In a high-end maritime conflict, GPS is the first operational link an adversary attempts to sever,” said NAWCAD aerospace engineer Peter Arslanian .
“By developing a modular adaptable system and putting it directly onto a UAS, we expand where and how the fleet can deploy unmanned systems with a simple software upgrade rather than expensive modifications to space-constrained ships.”
Traditional unmanned aircraft system (UAS) landings rely on multimillion-dollar radar systems and specialized flight deck recovery equipment. Installing this hardware can require ship modifications that take months to complete.
NAWCAD’s software-based approach eliminates the need for this specialized hardware. It combines onboard sensors, such as cameras, with advanced guidance, navigation, and control software developed by the warfare center’s Maritime Autonomous Guidance-Navigation-Control Intelligent Coupled Systems Lab.
In flight, the UAS uses its camera to recognize a ship’s shape and visual cues to guide its flight path like a human pilot, while its guidance and control algorithms predict the ship's rising and falling deck in real time so the aircraft can touch down smoothly. The software works with nearly any UAS computer hardware and can scale across unmanned systems of all sizes, from small tactical quadcopters to large, combat-class aircraft, the navy highlighted.
With initial flight demonstrations complete, the software is ready for operational testing on fleet platforms. NAWCAD plans to scale the technology to larger unmanned systems, including tactical resupply drones.
It is working with program offices to transition the capability into acquisition pipelines at the Navy’s Small Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems program office, the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program, and DARPA’s EVADE project.
The project was funded through the Naval Innovative Science and Engineering Program and the Office of Naval Research.
Recently, the US Navy deployed an uncrewed surface vessel alongside a carrier strike group for the first time.

title: Chinese Firm Offers Russia $2.9 Million in Drone Tech to Help Strikes Deep Inside Ukraine – Investigation
body:
A Chinese technology company is willing to supply Russia with nearly $2.9 million worth of communications equipment for attack drones, potentially helping Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) operate deeper inside Ukraine.
Shenzhen Xingkai Technology offered to supply 500 mesh modems to a factory in Russia’s Alabuga special economic zone after an investigative journalist posed as a Russian military supplier, according to The Insider.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The company quoted 19.5 million yuan, or approximately $2.87 million, for the shipment. Despite being told that the equipment was intended for military use, the manufacturer continued discussing the deal and suggested payments through accounts at DBS Bank, Ping An Bank and China Merchants Bank.
The Insider’s correspondent in Ukraine examined an Xingkai Tech mesh modem recovered from a Russian Gerbera drone. The investigation identified the Chinese manufacturer as a major supplier of communications equipment used in Russia’s Geran and Gerbera drones.
Mesh modems allow drones to pass signals between one another, effectively creating a communications network in the air.
In simple terms, one drone can relay commands to another, helping it stay connected to its operator even when the direct signal is weak or unavailable. The technology can extend the range over which Russian forces control drones and allow them to operate farther into Ukrainian territory.
Unlike drones that rely solely on a direct connection with an operator, UAVs using mesh networks can transmit information through intermediate drones acting as signal relays.
According to The Insider, Shenzhen Xingkai Technology accounts for around half of the market for high-performance mesh modems used in Russian Geran and Gerbera drones. The equipment is therefore a significant component of Russia’s drone communications supply chain.
The technology also allows Russian forces to maintain control of drones during flight and potentially exploit gaps in Ukrainian air defenses, the investigation reported.
Ukrainian military personnel warned in April that mesh modems used to control Shahed-type and Gerbera drones were allowing Russian forces to conduct reconnaissance deeper into Ukraine and expand their area of control.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Three children and one teacher killed in Oregon school shooting
body: Four people, including three children, have been killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon. The attack in the city of Bend was carried out by a 16-year-old boy, police said. An armed bystander pursued the assailant into the school and shot him dead, officials added. The children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A teacher was also killed. Another teacher and a ​seven-year-old pupil were taken to hospital with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a media conference. The attacker entered the school by shooting through locked doors, police said, without ​offering ⁠any further details. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek hailed the armed bystander who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life" at Silver Rail Elementary School. "No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day," Ms Kotek said. "As we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to cry privately." Bend, in rural central Oregon, is home to about 100,000 people and is about 280km south-east of Portland. Silver Rail Elementary School offers classes from kindergarten through to fifth ⁠grade – about ages five to 11 – and has about 450 pupils and 40 ⁠staff members, officials said. Police said they received a call at about 1pm that indicated a man had shot into a car at Silver Rail Elementary School. Moments later, emergency dispatchers received calls "reporting that a person had entered the school ​and began shooting", police said in a statement. Officers arrived within three minutes and found that the suspect had been shot dead.

title: Liquid AI Releases d1-ultra: A Multimodal Decision Model That Scores 65 on the AA Decision Index
body: Liquid AI has released d1-ultra , its most capable decision model to date. The Liquid AI d1-ultra decision model reads text, images, or both. It answers typed questions with a probability for each possible answer. It does this in one forward pass and generates no output tokens. For developers, that means classification, routing and scoring calls without paying for generated text. It is available now on the Liquid API at $0.042 per million input tokens. TL;DR Size: Parameters and context length not disclosed. Built on a larger open-weight backbone than d1. Runs on: Hosted Liquid API only. No downloadable weights or quantized variants announced. Performance: Leads all 8 categories in Liquid’s 112-evaluation suite, per Liquid. Best: 65 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, ranked #1 (Liquid-reported). Worst: No public per-benchmark breakdown or parameter count yet; claims are vendor-reported. What is a decision model? A decision model answers bounded questions with probabilities instead of free text. Liquid’s decision model docs describe 3 question types: Noul: a yes/no question that returns a probability between 0 and 1. Choice: one label from a set, with a probability per label. Score: a probability-weighted position on an ordered rubric. The docs recommend decision models for routing, moderation, guardrails, triage and LLM-as-judge replacement. They recommend a language model for summarization, chat and code generation. How does d1-ultra work? Each request carries a state (the context), optional images , and 1 or more typed questions . The model evaluates every question against the same input in 1 call. The d1 API reference shows responses with output_tokens always at 0. Liquid AI team states that d1-ultra uses a larger open-weight backbone than d1 , along with heavy Liquid-specific customizations. Combined with Liquid’s decision training pipeline, the gains are largest on knowledge tasks. Liquid AI team built d1-ultra for messy cases. Its examples include spotting a circuit board defect against a spec. Another is checking a damage claim against the customer’s photo. window.addEventListener("message",function(e){var f=document.getElementById("mtp-d1u-frame");if(f&&e.source===f.contentWindow&&e.data&&e.data.mtpH){f.style.height=e.data.mtpH+"px";}}); How does d1-ultra perform on benchmarks? Liquid AI compared d1-ultra against its earlier d1 and TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14 across 112 evaluations. According to Liquid AI’s announcement , d1-ultra outperforms Jev 1.14 across all tasks at the same price. On the independent Artificial Analysis Decision Index , Liquid reports d1-ultra ranks #1 with a score of 65. The index averages 4 evaluations at 25% each: AA-Omniscience-Decision: knowledge and hallucination HLE-MultiChoice: reasoning When2Call: tool calling WildGuardTest: safety classification For context, Artificial Analysis’s Oct 13 launch article listed Jev 1.13 first at 58. GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 followed at 54 each. Comparison: d1-ultra vs other decision models Feature d1-ultra d1 Jev (TypeSafe) Microsoft-Decision-1 GLiDE (Fastino) Developer Liquid AI Liquid AI TypeSafe AI Microsoft Fastino Labs Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Input Text, images Text, images Text Not disclosed Not disclosed Weights API only API only Closed Not disclosed Not disclosed AA Decision Index 65 (Liquid-reported) Not disclosed 58 (v1.13, Oct 13) 54 (Oct 13) 54 (Oct 13) Price $0.042 / 1M input Not disclosed $0.042 / 1M input $31 / 1M tasks (AA) $119 / 1M tasks (AA) Output tokens billed No No No Not disclosed Not disclosed How do you deploy d1-ultra, and what does it cost? d1-ultra runs on the Liquid API through the /decisions/v1/systemone endpoint with "model": "d1-ultra" . Liquid says Vercel AI Gateway and OpenRouter support is coming soon. You can test it first in the d1 Playground . Billing covers input tokens only. Per Liquid’s pricing notes , images cost 1.5 tokens per 32×32-pixel patch. A 1024×1024 image therefore costs 1,536 tokens. Each question is billed as its own prompt, including its text and all images. So 3 questions on 1 image bill that image 3 times. The endpoint docs cap requests at 8 images and 10,000 image patches. The full JSON body must stay under 4.5 MB. Key Takeaways d1-ultra returns probabilities for text and image decisions with 0 output tokens. Liquid reports a #1 score of 65 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index. It costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens, the same rate as TypeSafe’s Jev. Liquid claims the lowest calibration error in its tests, useful for routing thresholds. Size, backbone and weights remain undisclosed; access is API-only. Check out the official blog post , the decision model docs , and try the d1 Playground . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,561,020 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
body:
Russia has lost 1,561,020 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 16.
The number includes 1,790 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,414 tanks, 25,552 armored combat vehicles, 163,554 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,242 artillery systems, 2,217 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,708 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,958 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Pezeshkian arrives in Armenia for Intl. Biodiversity Summit
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has arrived in Armenia’s capital of Yerevan to attend the 17th Summit of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17).
Pezeshkian arrived on Friday for the summit, which brings together participating heads of state and government.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei added that Pezeshkian was also scheduled to hold talks and exchange views with some of the participating leaders on the sidelines of the summit.
Explaining the convention’s significance, Baghaei said the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity was established in 1992 and currently has 196 parties. He noted that all countries except the United States are parties to the convention.
Baghaei said that Iran was among the convention’s original signatories and officially became a party to it in 1996. Over the past three decades, he said, Iran has played an important role in developing mechanisms and rules for protecting biodiversity and the environment.
The spokesman also highlighted the environmental damage inflicted on Iran and the wider region during the US and Israeli regime’s military aggression against Iran.

title: World Bank sets fivefold minerals goal as Fed chairman Warsh flags financial stability risks
body: The World Bank aims to increase its critical minerals business fivefold over the next five years, while US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh expressed surprise at the resilience of major economies amid geopolitical shocks and tighter monetary policy. "In critical minerals, we ⁠plan to quintuple our business in five years … this ​week, ⁠we launched our ‌first country compacts with MDB partners, to build local industries and keep ​more jobs and value at home," World Bank president Ajay Banga said at the 2026 IMF -World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, as the multilateral lender seeks to support mining, processing and local industries. He also outlined plans to expand partnerships with countries developing critical minerals industries. The World Bank's new metals and minerals implementation plan is aimed at securing $19 billion in critical minerals financing over the 2026-2030 fiscal period, up from $3.6 billion in the 2021-2025 fiscal period. The lender has identified 20 countries with which it could partner on critical minerals development projects. It also launched its first country compacts with its partners this week, aiming to build local industries and retain more jobs and economic value in producing countries. Mr Banga also laid out a vision on Friday for how the World Bank should operate, focusing primarily on creating jobs, expanding economic opportunity and connecting private capital to developing nations that need investment. Addressing the plenary session at the annual meetings, Mr Banga said the current economic climate of tightening fiscal space, rising debt and global conflicts had made the work challenging – but not impossible. “Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address: making scarce resources go further, while helping countries create jobs at scale. They must be addressed together,” he said in prepared remarks. “The future of development will depend on bringing public finance , private investment, philanthropy and technology together around what each country needs. The partnership – and mix – should evolve as countries do.” He also spoke of the World Bank’s new initiative to focus on “small AI” – bespoke artificial intelligence-enabled applications that do not rely on the most advanced and expensive version of the technology, but can provide solutions for people in the developing world. “Practical, or ‘small’, AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers,” Mr Banga added. Separately, Mr Warsh said the Fed needed to consider financial stability risks as it assesses the outlook for the US economy , while declining to offer indications about its next interest-rate decision. ⁠Speaking at the annual meetings, heh said he did not “prejudge” policy decisions before the Fed’s meetings from October 27 to 28, when markets expect interest rates to remain unchanged. The Fed raised rates in September and made it clear that it intended to deliver price stability and withdraw some monetary policy accommodation, he said. “I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” Mr Warsh said. He said ⁠the Fed must ​continually bolster its credibility to get ⁠monetary policy right, adding that that includes the supervision and operations side ⁠of the central bank. He also expressed optimism about AI and its potential to transform the real economy, although he said the technology’s near-term impact on employment remained uncertain. Mr Warsh also said he was surprised by the global resilience and how many G20 member ⁠states are “hanging in there” amid the geopolitical shocks of recent months, ​as ⁠most ‌central banks tightened monetary ​policy to deal with inflation. “We're seeing common things and we're taking action and I view that as a positive development,” Mr Warsh said. “I believe, optimistically, ​you ‌might think ⁠naively, at least ​in the US, we're ​going ‌to come out of ⁠this stronger with a ⁠more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.” With reporting from Reuters and AFP

title: Israeli company used online ads to run spy operation against 'hundreds of millions of people'
body: Israeli digital advertising ⁠agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a network of online advertisements that it used to track ⁠targets and hack their devices, research groups said. Reports from Canadian group Citizen Lab and US advertising security company Confiant found that Discover-Tech's services gave Candiru, ​an Israeli spyware company blacklisted by the US government, as well as other Israeli surveillance groups, access to advertising platforms run by companies including Google, Comcast and Russia's Yandex. Discover-Tech's online ads, often ⁠for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds , reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said. People who visited sites or used apps with ​the malicious ⁠ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes try to extract phone numbers from smartphone users, researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur. Some ads would be used ​to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, the research groups said. But Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume. Discover-Tech was issuing at least 10 million ads a day around the world, with data-sharing arrangements called cookie matching allowing it to track people beyond the reach of its ads, Confiant co-founder Jerome Dangu said. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," he added. Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at Qatar's Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025. That was confirmed because the media group shared its network logs with the group, it added. Al Jazeera said in a statement that it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said. Mr Dangu said the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive ​categories", including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, including the Palestinian ‌territories, were saturated by the Israeli company's ads. "You go to almost ⁠any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them ​a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he added. Citizen Lab said it had evidence that the malicious ads were ​shown to people in the ‌UN, Nato, the European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. The ads also appeared in networks including technology companies such as Nvidia and Sandisk, as well as media organisations ⁠in Mexico, Israel and Europe. Discover-Tech is now to be frozen out of parts of the online ad market. Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies". IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email ​that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved entities last week after an audit identified policy breaches.

title: No answer on school funding for Royal Fleet Auxiliary
body: Ministers have been asked to extend Service Pupil Premium funding and wraparound childcare to the children of Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel, and have replied that existing arrangements are kept under review, according to an answer given in Parliament. Rachel Gilmour, the Liberal Democrat member for Tiverton and Minehead, asked what assessment had been made of the adequacy of welfare and family support for Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel and their families, and whether eligibility for schemes open to armed forces families would be extended to them. Calvin Bailey, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for Veterans and People, said: “The Ministry of Defence recognises the importance of supporting Royal Fleet Auxiliary (RFA) personnel and their families. RFA personnel and their families have access to a range of welfare and family support services, and we continue to keep these arrangements under review to ensure they remain appropriate to the needs of the workforce. “Support available for RFA personnel and their families includes enhanced leave entitlements and tailored assistance through mechanisms such as Occupational Health, keep-in-touch days, and reasonable workplace adjustments. Further support is delivered through the Employee Assistance Programme, the Defence Health and Wellbeing Portfolio, and Family and People Services, with the RFA workforce also benefitting from an extended welfare network under the umbrella of expert services, including the Navy Families Federation, ensuring holistic support for employees and their families.” Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel are civilians employed by the Ministry of Defence who crew the ships that fuel, supply and support the Royal Navy at sea, and their conditions sit outside the arrangements that cover service families. The Royal Fleet Auxiliary employs around 1,800 people and crews the tankers and stores ships that keep the Royal Navy at sea, along with the Bay class landing ships and the aviation training ship Argus. Its sailors are civil servants and not service personnel, which is the distinction the question was aimed at. Pay and conditions have been a running problem, with members of the RMT and Nautilus International taking strike action in 2024 over a long period of below-inflation awards, and the service has struggled to hold on to qualified officers. The post No answer on school funding for Royal Fleet Auxiliary first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: IDF releases Sinwar letter encouraging Oct. 7 terrorists to plan broadcast of massacre footage
body: The IDF released previously unseen documents written by Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar on Friday, two years after his assassination.Additionally, the IDF published footage of the military carrying out the assassination, including firing tank shells on the structure Sinwar fled to, and drone footage carrying out searches within the structure the following morning.In one document, Sinwar, the architect of the October 7 massacre, demanded that Hamas's Nukhba Force terrorists broadcast their acts to as many media outlets as possible in order to terrorize the entirety of Israel.“Allah came upon them without them expecting it and cast fear into their hearts. Two or three operations should be organized with the aim of burning down entire neighborhoods, a kibbutz, and the like.“They [the terrorists] will spray gasoline or diesel fuel from a special tanker, then burn the place, and broadcast the pictures,” he wrote.The documents also show how Sinwar tricked Israel's political, defense, and intelligence establishments into believing he was leaning towards a political settlement with Israel.Sinwar also wrote what could happen in the event that other terrorist organizations from the West Bank and the Iran-led “Axis of Resistance” would join in the massacre.“There may be indications of the enemy's collapse from the very beginning, and it is possible that the movements of our people in the 'interior,' in Jerusalem and the West Bank, as well as Hezbollah's intervention, will encourage this,” he wrote.“Therefore, we must be prepared to expand the attack to its maximum. The core of the plan should include control of the centers of power and command and control of our central forces,” he added.“Forces of the Palestinian factions can be sent to population centers, but our forces must be concentrated on important defined objectives and key positions.”What happened during Sinwar's assassination?Combat teams from the Nahal and 828th Brigades, respectively, were conducting operations in the Tel Sultan neighborhood of Rafah based on intelligence indicating potential high-value Hamas targets in the area, when they spotted terrorists leaving a building.A video of an IDF Merkava tank firing on Yahwa Sinwar's position in Gaza, October 16, 2024.A firefight ensued; the terrorists scattered, and unbeknownst to the soldiers at the time, Sinwar remained alone, abandoned in a building.He was killed in a firefight shortly thereafter.Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar being spotted by IDF troops, before being struck by a tank shell, October 16, 2024.Detailing the combat encounterSeveral weeks before Sinwar was killed, the IDF's Gaza Division assumed responsibility for the Rafah sector of the Gaza Strip.On the day of the engagement in which Sinwar was killed, lookouts spotted three armed terrorists moving through a damaged, IDF-controlled area roughly 300 meters from an ongoing engineering operation, the military said on Friday.Two of the terror operatives carried a blanket, and the third wore a tactical vest, the military added.A battalion commander spotted them, opened fire, and wounded one in the arm. This wounded operative was later confirmed to be Sinwar.Soldiers encircled the area using tanks and drones. One soldier was severely wounded and evacuated during a firefight.Sinwar, wounded from the aforementioned shooting, fled, entering a separate building from the other two terror operatives.Recording of communications between fighters of Battalion 828 during the operation that resulted in Yahya Sinwar's death, October 16, 2025 (Credit: IDF Spokesperson's Unit)An IDF Paratrooper Brigade company entered to search the building that Sinwar had entered. A platoon commander noticed a pool of blood, indicating a wounded terrorist nearby.Moments afterward, two grenades were thrown at the soldiers, one of which detonated, the military said.Soldiers rained heavy fire on the structure, including tank shells, machine gun fire, and small arms fire. That evening, an IDF drone entered the structure and located the remains of a body.Soldiers waited until the next morning to complete searches due to operational risks, the military noted.When search teams entered the structure, they were able to positively identify Sinwar and confirm his death.

title: Below (Netflix)
body: Josh Hartnett plays fisherman Calvin Penney, who is haunted by the mysterious death of his father decades earlier. body: Stephen King’s classic horror story is reimagined for a new generation in this eight-part series from Mike Flanagan, the creator behind The Haunting of Hill House and Midnight Mass .
