title: Greek Orzo Salad: A Fresh 11-Ingredient Summer Pasta Bowl
body: SYDNEY, October 2026 — Greek orzo salad brings cucumber, feta, tomato, artichokes and olives together in Patrice’s Allrecipes recipe, which home cooks rate 4.6 out of 5 from 636 ratings. Greek orzo salad from Patrice’s Allrecipes recipe. Photo: Allrecipes Greek orzo salad starts with kritharaki pasta Orzo is a short, rice-shaped pasta. In Greek kitchens it is usually called kritharaki (κριθαράκι), according to Wikipedia’s entry on the pasta shape . Cooks simmer it in soups and stews, or chill it for a cold pasta bowl. This Greek orzo salad follows the chilled route. Patrice, the Allrecipes member who shared it in April 2000, packs the bowl with the same summer produce you find in a village salad: cucumber, tomato, onion, olives and crumbled feta. Greek City Times has already covered hot uses of the same grain. It has published a homemade tomato saltsa recipe , as well as a traditional giouvetsi recipe in which the rice-shaped pasta bakes under meat and sauce. Unlike those mains, this dish is a make-ahead side. Allrecipes lists 393 calories, 57 g of carbohydrate and 14 g of protein per serve. Each serve also has 13 g of fat and 968 mg of sodium. Ingredients for the chilled kritharaki bowl Because the recipe makes about six serves — and several cooks say the bowl goes further than that — Greek orzo salad suits a barbecue, a picnic or a weekday lunch box. In addition, every item for this kritharaki mix is easy to find at the supermarket. 1½ cups (about 300 g) uncooked orzo pasta 2 cans (6 oz / about 170 g each) marinated artichoke hearts 1 cucumber, seeded and chopped 1 tomato, seeded and chopped 1 red onion, chopped In addition, Greek orzo salad needs crumbled cheese, olives, herbs and a sharp finish of lemon. 1 cup (about 150 g) crumbled feta cheese 1 can (2 oz / about 55 g) black olives, drained ¼ cup chopped fresh parsley 1 tablespoon lemon juice ½ teaspoon dried oregano ½ teaspoon lemon pepper Feta gives Greek orzo salad its salty, creamy bite. According to Wikipedia’s entry on feta , the cheese is a PDO product made from sheep’s milk or a sheep-and-goat mix. Marinated artichoke hearts do double duty in this kritharaki mix. The drained pieces go into the bowl, while their marinade becomes the dressing at the end. Artichokes have long been eaten around the Mediterranean, as Wikipedia’s entry on the plant notes. As for the pasta, cook the orzo only until it is al dente. Soft grains turn mushy once the salad chills and the marinade goes on. How to cook, chill and dress it Allrecipes lists 15 minutes of preparation, 10 minutes of cooking and about an hour of chilling. The method for this Greek orzo salad is simple, since most of the work is chopping and tossing. Bring a large pot of lightly salted water to a boil. Add the orzo and cook until al dente, 8 to 10 minutes, then drain. Drain the artichoke hearts and keep the marinade aside. Next, tip the warm kritharaki and the chopped produce into one large bowl so Greek orzo salad can chill evenly. Combine the pasta, artichoke hearts, cucumber, tomato, onion, feta, olives, parsley, lemon juice, oregano and lemon pepper, then toss well. Chill the bowl in the refrigerator for 1 hour. Finally, drizzle the reserved artichoke marinade over the salad just before you serve it. According to Allrecipes, the reserved marinade is the built-in dressing for Greek orzo salad. Still, many home cooks swap it for a bottled Greek vinaigrette or a homemade oil-and-vinegar mix when they want more zest. Tips from home cooks Hundreds of home cooks have rated this Greek orzo salad on Allrecipes, with 636 ratings and 471 reviews. Allrecipes member Catherine Anna Volk wrote: “Everyone loved it!” after she took the bowl to a garden club meeting. However, the artichoke marinade divided opinion. Dining Diva preferred a fresh dressing of olive oil, red wine vinegar, lemon juice and dried oregano. By comparison, CARRIANNE22 stirred in Italian dressing and extra red wine vinegar and said everyone loved the result. Other cooks changed the vegetables in their kritharaki salad. In particular, Jilly swapped black olives for kalamata olives and used leftover orzo. VeganJo replaced missing tomatoes with roasted red peppers. Amy added chickpeas for extra protein, while ProudMeat5347 stirred in pepperoncini and chopped salami for heat. Barbara Adamczyk also noted that the bowl yields far more than six serves. Given that, it suits a potluck table as well as a family dinner. Not every review of this kritharaki bowl was glowing, though. One cook found the salad dry and bland when made exactly as written and asked for more seasoning and olive oil. Overall, reviewers treat Greek orzo salad as a make-ahead side for cookouts and weekday lunches, given that it keeps well once chilled. It pairs naturally with the cucumber, tomato and feta flavours in Greek City Times’ note on horiatiki’s health benefits . The original recipe on Allrecipes includes step-by-step photos. Source: Allrecipes The post Greek Orzo Salad: A Fresh 11-Ingredient Summer Pasta Bowl appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: FM Sybiha: Ukraine receives confirmation of new aid packages from at least five countries
body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced this in an interview with Ukrinform .
“I am confident that there will be additional energy, humanitarian, and defense aid packages… I have confirmation of new packages from at least five countries. We already know who they will come from; the amounts are currently being finalized. And we will receive additional aid ,” said the head of Ukrainian diplomacy.
As reported by Ukrinform, the British government will provide Ukraine with 17 million pounds sterling (USD 22.5 million) to fund critical repair work on the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant’s containment structure, which was damaged by a Russian drone attack last year.
During a meeting with German Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi discussed strengthening air defense to protect against Russian attacks, as well as cooperation in the energy, transportation, and healthcare sect ors.

title: Investigation: The romance scam tricking men into ‘rescuing’ Ukrainian women from Russian occupation
body:
The Kyiv Independent uncovers how scammers on dating sites pose as women trapped in Russian-occupied Ukraine, using fake identities to talk foreign men into sending them money. (Daria Filippova / The Kyiv Independent)
Stefan, a 48-year-old Austrian national whose name has been changed at his request, had been looking for a Ukrainian partner. Having previously dated a Ukrainian woman, he said he was drawn to what he viewed as the importance of family in Ukrainian culture.
He met "Alona Panchenko," who claimed to be from the Russian-occupied city of Enerhodar in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, on the international dating website Christian Cupid. Soon after they matched, she suggested moving their conversation to email.
As their relationship continued, however, he began noticing that something was off.
Over the next three months, they exchanged lengthy emails but never spoke by phone or video. "Alona" said she had no mobile phone and could only communicate via an old tablet connected to public Wi-Fi due to conditions in occupied Enerhodar.
Her story grew increasingly desperate. She said she was unemployed, had run out of money, and had even been hospitalized with "severe exhaustion" after going two days without food. Eventually, she told Stefan the only way they could meet was if he helped her escape the occupied territory.
To support her story, "Alona" regularly sent photos that supposedly showed herself and life in Enerhodar.
The evidence she provided was fabricated. The Kyiv Independent traced her portraits to another person, found that photos she claimed she had taken in Enerhodar came from a local media outlet, and identified signs of AI manipulation in some images and videos. The ID she shared also contained an invalid number and an AI-edited portrait.
The request for money revealed another inconsistency. "Alona" instructed Stefan to list Ukraine as the recipient's country of residence when making the transfer through Western Union. That contradicted her claim that she was living in Russia-occupied Enerhodar, where Western Union does not operate.
Stefan says he never sent the money. But other men interviewed by the Kyiv Independent did.
Since 2022, the non-profit Helping to Leave has received thousands of requests to rescue people from Russian-occupied territories. Some of those requests were to rescue women who may have never existed at all.
The charity has helped thousands of people flee occupied areas , and its team was used to urgent pleas for evacuation. But over time, a different kind of request began arriving.
Foreign men started writing to Helping to Leave asking to rescue Ukrainian women they had met online, women they believed were trapped in Russian-occupied territories .
Some asked the charity to arrange an evacuation. Others had already sent money, believing they were paying for the woman's escape and that they would finally meet once she reached safety. They never did.
Over the past four years, the non-profit says it has received around 200 such requests, which now arrive up to four times a week, according to Nataliia, the project's communications specialist, who asked to be identified only by her first name due to the sensitive nature of her work with people in Russian-occupied territories.
Ukrainian and international media have long documented romance scams in which foreign men send money or travel to Ukraine to meet women who turn out to be fake. But the war has given scammers a new way to exploit the sympathy of unsuspecting foreigners.
An investigation by the Kyiv Independent into 58 cases referred by Helping to Leave found evidence that many of the women were not under Russian occupation at all.
Instead, scammers appeared to be using stolen photos, fake identities, forged documents, and, in some cases, AI-manipulated images and videos to convince men to send money.
The Kyiv Independent spoke to two foreign men who had online relationships with women claiming to be trapped in Russian-occupied territories. Their stories followed a pattern: no video calls, escalating crises, and urgent requests for money.
Karsten R., a German citizen, described a similar experience to that of Stefan with a woman calling herself "Viktoriia Kremenchutska." She claimed to be trapped in Russian-occupied territory, avoided video calls, and asked for money to escape.
After Karsten agreed to send money, she said she had begun her journey. But as she supposedly made her way out, she repeatedly asked for more funds — first to cross the checkpoint between occupied and Ukrainian-controlled territories, then to pay off an alleged debt she said was preventing her from leaving.
The documents and images she sent were also fake. Her passport copy was forged — the photo was photoshopped, the surname had a typo, and the font was inconsistent with a Ukrainian passport, the Kyiv Independent found. The photos, supposedly of her, turned out to be images of another woman — a woman from Russia . Other photos showed signs of AI manipulation.
"I told her, 'I want to see your suitcases. I want to see you holding a piece of paper with my name and the date on it," Karsten told the Kyiv Independent. He received the photo he demanded — but the Kyiv Independent confirmed it was AI-edited.
Even after discovering the fake documents and images, Karsten struggled to let go. At one point, he considered driving to a Ukrainian border crossing when "Viktoria" said she was trapped there trying to leave. Eventually, he became convinced he was talking to scammers.
The Kyiv Independent examined 58 cases referred by Helping to Leave, using available photos and contact details to trace the identities behind the profiles.
The relationships mostly started on dating websites, including UkraineDate, Christian Cupid, and International Cupid. In several instances, the women contacted men directly through Instagram or X. Some cases could not be verified because the available information, such as photos or contact details, was insufficient.
Using facial recognition tools and open-source research, the Kyiv Independent matched 22 profile photos to real women. Two more profiles appeared to rely on AI-generated identities. The remaining cases could not be verified, as they did not include any photos of the women they believed to be communicating with.
Out of the 22 profiles that used real photos, only seven used names that matched the women pictured. In some cases, the women even joined video calls to confirm their identity. But they lied about their whereabouts: the women identified were either living in Ukrainian-controlled territory or had moved abroad. None were in the Russian-occupied territories.
Not all accounts that used real women's photos actually belonged to them. In the remaining 15 cases, the names and surnames did not match the women whose photos appeared on the profiles. Ten of the 15 women were popular Instagram bloggers from Russia, Moldova, Ukraine, Germany , Denmark , and Latvia .
Dozens of women's photos were repeatedly reused across several dating profiles under different identities, often with the accounts presenting themselves as Russian women, the Kyiv Independent found.
This was the case with the images used by "Alona" and "Viktoriia," which were found across multiple profiles. The Kyiv Independent traced the photos used by "Alona" to Natalia Cernisova, a woman from Chisinau, Moldova, and those used by "Viktoriia" to Anna Kolesnyak from Russia. Both women run popular Instagram blogs.
In addition to stolen photos, the accounts used by both "Alona" and "Viktoriia" also sent images and videos that appeared to be AI-manipulated.
The profiles used by "Alona" and "Viktoriia," along with several others reviewed by the Kyiv Independent, are listed in the Ukrainian Dating Scammer Blacklist maintained by Ukrainian Passport, a platform that helps foreigners verify women from Ukraine and Russia.
An investigator with Ukrainian Passport, who asked to not be identified for safety reasons, said some scammers use content from popular Instagram influencers to create fake profiles, and in some cases may even be working with the influencers.
"If necessary, the influencer will even record a video to make the profile seem authentic, while being careful not to reveal too much. Later, she can always say it was for an audition or so. We've seen that happen before," he told the Kyiv Independent.
Anna Bauer, founder of the Kyiv-based Grace Family dating agency, described another way real women's identities can unintentionally enter the online dating ecosystem.
She said scouts sometimes recruit women for professional photo shoots, after which their photographs may be sold between dating agencies. This creates a risk that legitimate images can later be misused by fraudulent operators.
The Kyiv Independent received a response from one Ukrainian Instagram blogger, Anastasiia Mazur-Palamarchuk, whose photos were used in one of the scam profiles. She said her images were used without her consent.
"I'm not registered on any online dating website," she said.
The Kyiv Independent is listing several common lies used by scammers, based on the conversation with Nataliia from Helping to Leave and its own expertise.
Scammers often invent stories about crossing directly from occupied territories into Ukrainian-controlled areas through the front line, sometimes fabricating tales of "special drivers" or secret humanitarian corridors.
Civilians cannot cross active front lines because of ongoing fighting and the constant air attacks in front-line areas.
There is currently only one existing humanitarian corridor, located in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast. The crossing point, which is located on the Ukraine - Belarus border, is used almost exclusively by people fleeing the occupied territories.
People leaving occupied territories have to first go to Russia, then to Belarus, before reaching Ukraine or neighboring EU countries. The journey is usually made by bus or train, while specialized transportation is needed only in specific cases, such as for people with disabilities. Some also leave Russia by air, for example by flying to Georgia, though this route is less common.
While living under Russian occupation is indeed dangerous and harrowing, scammers often exaggerate the severity of their own living conditions to explain why they cannot communicate frequently, and to build sympathy with the men.
Helping to Leave gave an example of a woman who said she lived in Donetsk. She claimed she was living in her basement because of constant shelling, had almost no internet connection, and thus couldn't do a video call.
But the city of Donetsk isn't being shelled. Although Ukraine conducts drone strikes on occupied territories, it says they target military facilities. While this can't be independently verified, the reported death toll from such strikes is typically much lower than that of Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian areas. There is no evidence that Donetsk is under such threat that residents would live in basements.
Scammers use these claims to extort more money from victims, saying the women cannot pass security checks unless bribes are paid to border guards and officials.
While before the full-scale war, bribes might have been an option for some to travel between the occupied parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts and Ukraine-held territories, this practice doesn't exist anymore as there are no checkpoints between these territories.
People who fled occupation with the help from Helping to Leave have not reported being asked to pay bribes along the way, the organization told the Kyiv Independent.
Some scammers claim they can't use phones or messaging apps or make video calls because everything is blocked under occupation.
Many popular messaging apps continue to work in occupied territories, often with the help of VPN services. Limiting communication to email allows scammers to hide their identity and manage multiple victims simultaneously without having to do voice or video calls.
Scammers claim they can't travel through Russia because they only hold Ukrainian documents. They also use this to appeal to the victim's political sympathies.
In reality, taking a Russian passport in the occupied territories is not a political choice but a matter of survival: It is nearly impossible to access healthcare without Russian documents. This is part of Russia’s policy of forced passportization in occupied Ukraine, which means many people living under occupation have likely been forced to obtain Russian documents.
Scammers also request exorbitant travel expenses, far exceeding the actual cost of public or private transportation.
According to Helping to Leave, women in these cases typically ask for around 800 euros or $800 — roughly twice the actual cost of the journey from the Russia-occupied territories to the government-controlled part of Ukraine through Belarus.
A review of emails and messages shared with Helping to Leave and the Kyiv Independent revealed recurring elements in how women claiming to be trapped in Russian-occupied territories describe their situations.
The women presented themselves as trapped and abandoned, with no help available from Ukrainian authorities or humanitarian organizations. In some cases, they suggested that evacuation assistance did not exist, leaving the men to believe they were the only ones who could help.
"Natalia (from Helping to Leave) won't help me get out of here. How can you not understand that?" "Alona" wrote to Stefan.
In reality, when women from the cases reviewed by the Kyiv Independent were referred to the non-profit, they either never contacted it or did not cooperate when coordinators tried to understand what assistance they needed.
When it came to appearing live on a video call with the men, the women similarly said it was impossible, claiming unstable internet in occupied territories, outdated devices, or blocked messaging services.
None of them shared personal social media accounts, either. But in many cases, the Kyiv Independent found that the women whose photos were used in the dating profiles were active on Instagram, where their lives looked nothing like the stories the men were being told. It is unclear whether the real women knew their images were being used.
After matching on dating websites, conversations usually moved to email, Telegram, or WhatsApp. Telegram accounts often hid phone numbers, while WhatsApp accounts were typically registered with Ukrainian numbers.
Some women also sent WhatsApp live locations that appeared to show them in occupied territories. But such data can be manipulated using GPS spoofing tools, making it unreliable as proof of someone's whereabouts. This can be done using specialized apps. The Kyiv Independent was able to share a live location in Paris while physically in Ukraine in just 10 minutes.
When the Kyiv Independent contacted the phone numbers and Telegram accounts provided by the women to the men who believed they were dating, none answered. Most phone numbers were invalid or no longer active, suggesting they may have been temporary numbers used only as burner numbers for the scam and later discarded.
When text messages and excuses failed to persuade men to send money, the people behind the profiles turned to documents to try and back up their claims.
Many women sent what they claimed were Ukrainian passports, but all except one contained signs of digital manipulation, including altered personal details, edited photographs, or invalid passport numbers, the Kyiv Independent found.
Some also sent fake travel tickets or documents that appeared to show fines or penalties allegedly preventing them from crossing the border. They claimed these payments were necessary before they could continue their journey.
Once trust had been established, requests for money followed.
Most of the women suggested cash pickup services such as Western Union, RIA, or MoneyGram. Some also requested PayPal transfers. These methods allowed money to be collected without directly revealing bank account details.
Karsten, who believed he was helping "Viktoriia" escape the city of Donetsk , received a copy of what she said was her ticket for a direct taxi ride from Russian-occupied Donetsk to Kyiv . But the route itself should have been a warning sign: That journey is impossible as it would require crossing an active front line.
He covered the 280-euro "ride." The document he was sent was a crudely photoshopped Ukrainian railway ticket.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion, civilians leaving occupied Donetsk for Ukrainian-controlled territory have generally had to travel through Russia before entering Ukraine through a third country.
Determining who was behind the scheme was one of the most difficult parts of the investigation.
In some cases, the women whose images were used in the profiles took part in the conversations themselves. The Kyiv Independent found four cases in which the women agreed to video calls with the men, confirming that the person in the photos matched the person on the call.
Many profiles never moved beyond text messages. It was much harder to determine who was actually operating the account when the photos had been taken from unrelated women and there was no live contact.
But money transfers provided some clues.
Some women asking for cash pickup through Western Union, RIA, or MoneyGram instructed the men to use the names listed on their dating profiles and to select Ukraine as the recipient's country of residence. Because cash-pickup services require recipients to show identification matching the transfer details, whoever collected the money was likely using the same identity the victim had been shown.
The instructions also contradicted their stories: Despite claiming to live under Russian occupation, the women asked men to list Ukraine as their place of residence when sending money.
While Ukraine and most of the international community recognize the occupied territories as part of Ukraine, in practice they are controlled by Russian authorities and cut off from Ukraine's financial system.
Western Union does not operate in Russian-occupied areas, a customer service representative told the Kyiv Independent. This means any money sent to Ukraine could only have been collected in Ukrainian-controlled territory, not in the occupied areas where the women claimed to live.
The Kyiv Independent also identified at least two cases with apparent links to Russia. In one, the "woman" asked the victim to pay a travel agency she said was helping her leave the country. The bank details she sent named the recipient as Vladislav Gafarov, a Russian national, with an account at a Russian bank.
The phone number the "woman" used to message the victim belongs to Gafarov, according to a leaked 2023 database of clients of Russian microfinance organizations. The same database lists him as an employee of the S.M. Budyonny Military Academy of Communications in St. Petersburg.
Another possibility is that some accounts may be managed by multiple people.
Karsten, who believed he was in a relationship with "Viktoriia," also came to suspect he had not been talking to just one person. Looking back, he noticed that the writing style would sometimes change dramatically — with some messages feeling as though they had been written by a woman, while others seemed to come from a man.
By the time he stopped sending money, Karsten had transferred 2,500 euros. Some victims sent even more: One man who contacted Helping to Leave had transferred around 9,000 euros.
The use of Ukrainian women's identities in online romance scams is nothing new.
Over the years, Ukrainian and international media have documented cases in which foreign men were persuaded to send money or travel to Ukraine to meet women they believed they had formed relationships with, only to discover the relationships were not genuine.
Some traveled across the world only to be stood up, while others realized the dates were part of a business model designed to keep them paying for restaurants, messages, translators, and other services.
Similar scams have also been reported in Russia, Belarus , Kazakhstan , Ghana, and Nigeria, among other countries.
While there are legitimate matchmaking services, past investigations have found cases in which agencies relied on fictitious profiles or paid chat operators to prolong conversations and keep foreign clients spending money.
In 2023, Ukraine's largest job-search platform Work.ua listed matchmaking agencies among common fraud operations that it blocks from its platform.
A video call should be one of the first steps when building a relationship with someone met online, according to Anna Bauer-Zuieva, owner of Grace Family, a long-running Ukrainian dating agency.
"It’s not about sending videos back and forth — it's about a real face-to-face (call)," Bauer-Zuieva told the Kyiv Independent. She said asking a person to show their surroundings during a live call can verify their story.
Scammers often rely on emotional pressure, presenting themselves as vulnerable and in urgent need of help. People looking for a genuine relationship, she said, usually do not begin by presenting themselves as someone who needs to be rescued.
For those who have already fallen victim, recovering money can be much harder. Once money has been collected by a scammer, it is generally not possible to recover it through services such as Western Union and Ria. The companies encourage customers to report suspected fraud, while PayPal advises users to contact customer support if they believe they have been targeted.
Victims can also report suspected fraud to Ukrainian police. According to Ukrainian Passport, people who are outside Ukraine can submit an application, appoint a lawyer in Ukraine to represent their interests, and provide testimony via video call.
For those who want to help people living in occupied territories, Nataliia from Helping to Leave said the safest way is to support verified humanitarian organizations rather than send money directly to someone they have only met online.
Yuliia Taradiuk and Natálie Zehnalová have contributed to this piece.
Linda is a Ukrainian junior reporter investigating Russia’s global influence and disinformation. She has over two years of experience writing news and feature stories for Ukrainian media outlets. She holds an Erasmus Mundus M.A. in Journalism, Media, and Globalisation from Aarhus University and the University of Amsterdam, where she trained in data journalism and communication studies.

title: UK defends US reliance on F-35A and PrSM
body: The government has been asked whether buying the F-35A and the Precision Strike Missile deepens British dependence on the United States, and has answered that collaborating with the closest defence ally will deliver significant capability, according to an answer given in Parliament. Mike Martin, the Liberal Democrat member for Tunbridge Wells, asked whether an assessment had been conducted of the potential impact of the two purchases on Britain’s level of reliance on the United States. Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The Government assesses that collaborating with the UK’s closest defence and security ally on F35A and PrSM will deliver significant capabilities that enhance UK and NATO security. “The Government’s approach is to build on the existing close cooperation with the US while also deepening partnerships with other allies and partners. While US-led, the F35 is a multinational programme, including significant UK equities. PrSM is a trilateral partnership with Australia. The Government’s approach enables the UK to maximise collective security, strengthen deterrence and advance our national interests in an increasingly contested strategic environment. Collaborating with the US on F35A and PrSM will also benefit UK prosperity and increase supply chain resilience.” The answer does not say whether the assessment Mr Martin asked about has been conducted, nor does it address the dependence question directly, offering instead the arguments for the two purchases and the British industrial content in each. British industry holds roughly fifteen per cent by value of every F-35 built according to some figures, others show it as much less though, and the F-35A buy was announced in June last year. The Precision Strike Missile is an American Army programme, and the answer describes British involvement as a trilateral partnership that also takes in Australia. The Precision Strike Missile is a United States Army programme built by Lockheed Martin to replace ATACMS, fired from the same HIMARS and M270 launchers already in British service. The first increment has a stated range of more than 400 kilometres, with later increments intended to reach further and to attack moving targets at sea. Britain set out its intention to acquire the missile in the Strategic Defence Review, and the answer describes the arrangement as trilateral with Australia. The post UK defends US reliance on F-35A and PrSM first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Drop in Gulf student visa applications shows dwindling appetite for UK universities
body: The number of students from the Gulf choosing to study in the UK has plunged in recent years, most drastically from the UAE, figures show. Student visa application numbers have slumped due to a UK migration clampdown that has restricted visas, as well as concerns over social issues, safety and the quality of education in Britain, experts said. While there was an inevitable drop in numbers caused by the Covid pandemic, these had bounced back by 2022, before the UK began issuing its policies to restrict student visas. The number of student visa applications from the UAE then began to drop, falling 59 per cent in the next four years, from 638 in 2022 to 257 students in 2025, Home Office statistics showed. These covered students who have been offered a place at an institution to study for a bachelor, graduate, PhD or other higher education courses. There was a 36 per cent drop in 2025 alone compared with the previous year. There were 13 per cent fewer applications from students in Saudi Arabia between 2023 and 2025, dropping from 5,814 to 5,049. In Bahrain, a 26 per cent decline has been recorded, from 545 applications in 2023 to 403 in 2025. Qatar recorded a drop of about 14 per cent between 2023 and 2025, from 1,056 to 910 applications. The outliers are Kuwait, which saw an 11 per cent rise in applications, from 4,499 in 2023 to 5,034 in 2025, and Oman, which grew from 996 to 1,018. Politicians have found it much easier to control clearly defined legal migration routes, such as coming to the UK to study, than to get a grip on other routes Nick Hillman, Higher Education Policy Institution Figures for spring and summer visa applications will be released by the Home Office next month and are expected to continue the downward trend. The first quarter of this year showed a decline of almost a third (29.2 per cent) of applications from Saudi students. UAE applications for the same period remained steady, moving from 16 in the first three months of 2025 to 15 in the same period of 2026. Professionals in the higher education sector have warned the numbers could keep declining as UK immigration restrictions make studying in the country less appealing. Many students regard a degree in the UK as an investment towards a career in the country. But from next year, students will have only 18 months to find a job in the UK after their graduation, compared to the previous allowance of two years. This follows increases to the Immigration Health Surcharge and student visa fees, and a higher chance of visa refusal. The general salary threshold for skilled workers' visas is also set to rise, with the discount for graduates removed, according the Labour government's White Paper on Immigration. The UK government was criticised this week for removing incentives for overseas students to pursue a degree course at a British university. “Given politicians have found it much easier to control clearly defined legal migration routes, such as coming to the UK to study, than to get a grip on other routes, such as the infamous small boats, the factors pulling international students to come and study in the UK have been trimmed back again,” wrote Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institution in an analysis. Concerned families This is compounded by financial penalties for universities that award spaces to students whose visa applications are later rejected. This has reportedly led to institutions withdrawing their offers to would-be students, mainly from India, China and Nigeria, to avoid paying any penalty should their visa applications be unsuccessful . For Gulf students, other factors such as safety concerns could also be fuelling the decline. A Saudi student was killed last year in a knife attack in Cambridge while studying an English language course, prompting his uncle to say the UK was “rapidly losing its global reputation”. There are also fears of radicalisation on campuses. The UAE – which has urged western governments to ban the Muslim Brotherhood organisation – was reported by the Financial Times this year to have scrapped its state-funded scholarships to some British universities. The UK government introduced new measures to protect students from extremism on campus this year. This includes supporting universities to carry out appropriate risk checks where free speech crosses into unlawful activity or support for terrorism.

title: Serial champions India continue bewildering struggle in bilateral series
body: Can you be critical of a side that has won every major competition it has entered since 2024? Possibly. Especially when you put in performances like the Indian team has done in between those fine results. Since the 2024 T20 World Cup win , India have won the 50-over ICC Champions Trophy, Asia Cup, and successfully defended their T20 world title and the Asian Games gold medal this year. But right alongside, the team were also been whitewashed at home in Tests by New Zealand and South Africa – having been undefeated in their backyard for over a decade, lost the Border Gavaskar Trophy to Australia, embarrassed by Ireland (in T20s) and England (T20s and ODIs) right after their World Cup win this year and are now being taken apart by a spirited West Indies at home. The double T20 world champions were outplayed in the fourth match of the five-game T20 series against the Windies, falling to a 24-run loss in Hyderabad. The series is now tied 2-2. In the preceding ODI series, the West Indies easily chased down a target of 350 and also smashed 400 in the second game. That series was won 2-1 by India but they were stretched well past their limits. It's the same story in the T20s. In fact, India have been hammered for the third straight bilateral T20 series – defeats to Ireland and England away and now an uphill battle against the Caribbean side. If the Windies secure the T20 series win on Saturday, it wouldn’t be a surprise. Shouldn’t that worry Indian cricket management? It should, but what can they do when the team ends up winning every major tournament? India won a world and a continental title in 2026. The same set of players have also been thrashed by Ireland, England and the Windies in the same year. How do you reconcile both facts? Same story or beginning of the end? There are two ways to look at it. One is that India have mastered the art of stumbling their way through low priority bilateral series and somehow finding the perfect formula when the big tournaments come around. The other is India were playing major tournaments in Asian conditions for the last two years and would have been found out if any of the events were held in England or Australia. There is only one way to find out – wait for next two years. The next big assignment for all teams is the ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, followed by the 2028 T20 World Cup Down Under and the Los Angeles Olympics in the same year. Indian fans and cricket administrators might prefer to wait until all three assignments are completed, before taking stock of the situation. Around 10 or so years back, India were the undisputed champions of bilateral series, home and away. But they did not win a single major tournament, much to the pain of the then captain Virat Kohli. The script has flipped completely, where the players endure bewildering losses home and away in all formats, only to go back to their homes with another winners' medal in the cabinet. This can’t last long though. Conditions in South Africa and Australia are going to be daunting even for the most in-form Indian team, let alone a group that can barely stand still. It could open some deep wounds. Time for reinforcements? One thing is clear – India do not have ready replacements for their veterans. The fitness concerns of all-rounder Hardik Pandya and workload management of Jasprit Bumrah have ruined the balance of the white-ball teams, while they still have not found a reliable substitute for Mohammad Shami or even Mohammad Siraj. No wonder the ageing Kohli and Rohit Sharma are guaranteed to play the ODI World Cup next year. Fast bowler Bhuvneshwar Kumar is back in the T20 team for the forthcoming New Zealand tour; he last played for India in 2022. Fellow veteran quick Shami is highly likely to be back before the ODI World Cup, especially since the Indian team’s selection panel is undergoing a change with older yet in-form players being given a look-in once again. Maybe, India will win a couple of more titles and fans will forget about pain of the bilaterals. If not, then there will be a feeding frenzy.

title: Senate Republicans are getting smoked in fundraising
body: Republican Senate candidates are hurting for cash. Nearly every Democratic candidate in battleground Senate races outraised their GOP opponent from July through September. And in some cases, the disparities were stark. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico trounced Republican Ken Paxton $60.2 million to $10.2 million in their main campaign accounts. In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff raised $33.1 million to Rep. Mike Collins’ nearly $2.8 million. In North Carolina, Democrat Roy Cooper raised $12.2 million to Michael Whatley’s $2.1 million. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed hauled in roughly $33 million to former Rep. Mike Rogers’ nearly $10 million. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson raised $20.5 million to GOP Sen. Susan Collins’ $5.2 million. In Ohio, Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown hauled in $23.1 million to GOP Sen. Jon Husted’s $4.8 million. In Iowa, Josh Turek raised $13.9 million to Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s nearly $3.3 million. In Alaska, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola raked in $17 million to GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan’s nearly $2.7 million. In New Hampshire, Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas brought in $8.1 million to Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu’s $1.5 million. And in Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised nearly $9.9 million to GOP Sen. Roger Marshall’s just $866,000. Across those 10 Senate races, the Democratic campaigns raised more than five times as much as the Republican ones. Put another way: Talarico alone raised more than all those Republicans combined. Marshall and Whatley each started October with less than $1 million left in the bank. Mike Collins wasn’t much better-positioned, entering the final weeks of the election with just over $1 million cash on hand. These numbers do not include joint fundraising committees, which allow candidates to raise money and may have some more cash that has not yet been transferred to the campaigns. Democrats have consistently outraised Republicans on the candidate level this cycle. But the yawning gaps heading into the midterm’s home stretch stand as the latest example of the deteriorating environment for the GOP. And while GOP outside groups have significantly more money than Democrats, this candidate cash advantage matters because candidates get TV ads for much cheaper rates, letting their dollars stretch much farther. To underscore how lopsided some of these figures are: At least half a dozen House Democratic challengers raised over $3 million in the third quarter — a sum higher than several GOP Senate incumbents. There are some silver linings for the GOP. In Minnesota, Republican Michele Tafoya raised $4.9 million to Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan’s $4.3 million. Tafoya started the month with $2.1 million to Flanagan’s $1.5 million. Sullivan, Husted, Hinson, Rogers and Susan Collins all entered October with millions more in cash on hand than their Democratic opponents. And Republicans are getting air cover from GOP super PACs bankrolled by billionaire Elon Musk and President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. that have pumped hundreds of millions of dollars into the midterms in recent weeks. Musk was revealed on Thursday as the primary funder of Texas PAC, which has spent $131 million so far boosting Paxton and attacking Talarico. Musk gave $158 million to Senate Republicans’ super PAC arm last quarter, the filings showed, with the group in turn transferring the funds to the pro-Paxton PAC. Republicans are also benefitting from a recent Supreme Court ruling that allows party committees to spend unlimited sums in coordination with candidates, allowing the National Republican Senatorial Committee to offset at least some of the differences. Since the tranche of reports filed Thursday only cover until Sept. 30, the full scope of each candidates’ coffers is unknown. But there are other signs that some are strapped for cash in the final sprint: Whatley has gone dark on television , a clear indication of him running low on funds even as his campaign insists it’s a temporary pause.

title: Zelensky and Belgian PM discuss additional F-16 fighter jet and ammunition deliveries
body:
This was reported by Ukrinform, citing the head of state’s Facebook page.
“I discussed with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever the consequences of round-the-clock Russian attacks on residential buildings, the energy sector, and other critical infrastructure in Ukraine. Just this evening, the Russians struck energy facilities in two regions. Nearly 15,000 people in Volyn were left without power. There are areas in Kyiv and the surrounding region that are partially without power. In some communities, repair crews cannot even begin restoration work due to the threat of repeated Russian strikes,” the post reads.
I provided the Prime Minister with detailed information about Russian terror and our needs, says Volodymyr Zelensky.
According to him, the F-16s are currently proving very helpful in repelling attacks by jet-powered “suicide drones.”
“We are working with Belgium to obtain additional fighter jets as soon as possible. We also discussed the possibility of additional ammunition supplies for them. Every decision on defense support saves people’s lives,” the President emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Volodymyr Zelensky and Emmanuel Macron discussed ways to counter enemy air attacks and accelerate work on a European anti-ballistic missile syste m.

title: The Serbian Chef Championing Greek Cuisine in Singapore
body: In Singapore, Serbian chef Đorđo Ćetković runs a Greek kitchen with an understanding of Mediterranean food that began well beyond Greece. Raised in Loznica, Serbia, and shaped by more than two decades working in European and Asian restaurants, Ćetković sees a close relationship between the cooking of his childhood and the Greek dishes he now prepares. “Coming to Greek cooking was not a sudden conversion,” he tells Greek City Times. “It was noticing that olive oil, lemon, the grill, and the shared table were already a language I understood.” Since May 2026, Ćetković has been Executive Chef at Pano Kato Grill, Pizza & Deli, a Greek and Mediterranean restaurant at Singapore’s Tanglin Mall, where he leads a team of nine. The restaurant, which opened in 2019, belongs to the House of AnLi hospitality and interiors business and has established itself around traditional Mediterranean cooking. For Ćetković, the appointment brought together two culinary traditions he considers closely related, despite their different histories and identities. Born in Tuzla, Bosnia, and raised in the Serbian town of Loznica, with family roots in nearby Zvornik, Ćetković entered professional kitchens in 2003. He describes himself as largely self-taught, having taken on the responsibilities of a sous chef shortly after finishing school. His first formal mentor was Austrian chef Kristian Kohnerr, under whom he trained in Graz between 2004 and 2005. His subsequent career took him through Serbia, Austria, Switzerland, Germany and Portugal before he settled in Singapore. It was an education acquired through work rather than a conventional culinary school, with each kitchen exposing him to different ingredients, techniques and expectations. He remembers the first dish he prepared for a guest: lovačke šnicle, the Serbian hunter’s schnitzel, made with young beef. It remains a telling starting point for a chef whose understanding of food is closely connected to the meals and customs of home. In Singapore, where he has worked in approximately eight restaurants over five years, including Zorba’s, Hanibal at Robertson Quay and establishments within The Black Hole Group, he developed a closer working relationship with Greek and Mediterranean food. “Greek cooking came to me through the work itself,” he explains, “through kitchens in Singapore where Mediterranean and Greek food were already on the menu, and through recognising how close that food sits to the Serbian table I grew up with.” The similarities are particularly apparent in dishes that rely on relatively uncomplicated methods: wrapping, grilling, slow cooking and the preparation of food intended for several people rather than one. Ćetković points to Greek dolmades and Serbian sarma, two traditions of stuffed leaves that share a basic method while differing in their choice of leaves, fillings and seasoning. He also draws a comparison between Greek souvlaki and Serbian ražnjići, both of which depend on the direct heat of the grill. “The names and spices differ; the gesture, meat over heat, meant for company, does not,” he says. His observation extends beyond the Balkans. Encountering satay in Singapore, he recognised something familiar in the skewered meat cooked over an open flame. The seasonings and accompaniments were different, but the method reminded him of ražnjići. Such comparisons are not an argument that these cuisines are interchangeable. Rather, they suggest that certain ways of preparing and sharing food recur across cultures, even where the ingredients and traditions have developed independently. At Pano Kato, Ćetković approaches Greek cooking from that position of familiarity, drawing on his own culinary background without losing sight of the food he has been employed to prepare. His attachment to Serbian cooking remains equally strong. “I keep the roots: Loznica and Zvornik, the sense that food is hospitality, that bread and salt matter, that a dish should feed people who sit together,” he says. The reference to bread and salt is significant. In Serbian hospitality, the traditional offering of bread and salt carries an association with welcome and respect. For Ćetković, those customs have remained part of his understanding of what it means to feed someone, even as his working life has moved considerably further from home. “Serbia is not a costume I put on for guests. It is the ground under the Greek kitchen I run.” That relationship between food, history and identity is also central to Ćetković’s The Grand Heritage Cookbook , a 299-page English-language work bringing together 145 recipes across five distinct culinary chapters. Forty recipes are devoted to Serbian heritage and another forty to Hellenic heritage. A further 25 explore Lenten cooking inspired by the Serbian Orthodox monastery of Hilandar on Mount Athos, while fifteen reconstruct dishes associated with the historical period of Stefan Nemanja. The final 25 recipes reflect Ćetković’s own approach to contemporary fine dining. Some photos from the Hellenic Heritage chapter of Ćetković’s The Grand Heritage Cookbook The inclusion of Hilandar is particularly interesting. Established in the late twelfth century by Stefan Nemanja and his son Saint Sava, the monastery occupies a unique place in the religious and cultural history shared by Serbia and Greece. Situated on Mount Athos, the Orthodox monastic community recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage site, it represents a connection between the two countries that extends well beyond contemporary cuisine. For Ćetković, bringing these traditions together in one cookbook allows him to explore the historical connections between food, faith and everyday life. The chapters move between familiar domestic dishes, monastic traditions and more contemporary interpretations, reflecting the different influences that have shaped his career. His interest in preserving culinary identity extends beyond the restaurant. As Ambassador for Asia of the Culinary Federation of Serbia, Ćetković works to promote Serbian gastronomy and establish connections within the international culinary community. His website also documents his participation in the Worldchefs Congress & Expo in Singapore in 2024. There is another personal dimension to his life in Singapore. He is married to Singaporean Masziana Ćetković, and the country has become both his professional base and his home. His experience now spans several national culinary traditions, though he remains particularly interested in the food of the Balkans and Mediterranean. On his website, he describes tradition as something that can be respected, questioned and expressed through contemporary techniques. It is a philosophy that recognises the importance of inherited knowledge without treating recipes as untouchable. Professional cooking, after all, demands more than an appreciation of cultural heritage. Running a kitchen involves training staff, managing costs and maintaining standards through successive services. Alongside his restaurant work, Ćetković consults on kitchen operations, menu development and restaurant openings, drawing on experience accumulated since 2003. Yet his account of Greek cooking repeatedly returns to something less technical: the experience of eating together. At the Serbian table he remembers from childhood, as at the Greek table he now helps recreate in Singapore, food is rarely understood solely as an individual plate. Its significance is also found in the people gathered around it, the customs that accompany a meal and the dishes passed between generations. “Olive oil, lemon, and the shared table are where the two kitchens meet on the plate,” he says. For a chef whose career has taken him from the Balkans to Western Europe and Southeast Asia, the distance between Serbia and Greece appears considerably smaller when measured through food. What he has carried with him is not simply a collection of recipes, but an understanding of hospitality that remains recognisable in a kitchen thousands of kilometres from where he grew up. For more about Đorđo Ćetković and his cookbook, visit djordjocetkovic.com . Read also Paul Frazis, Australia’s Commercial Broker of the Year: ‘Lending Is About People’ The post The Serbian Chef Championing Greek Cuisine in Singapore appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Premier League predictions: Leeds pile pressure on Michael Carrick and Man United
body: Saturday: Everton v Chelsea (3.30pm kick-off UAE) Everton maintained their unbeaten record after a 2-2 stalemate at Hull City last weekend, with the Merseysiders' fourth draw in six matches leaving them in fifth place on 10 points.
