title: Airbus connects German and Swedish air defence forces into unified NATO shield
body:
Chania, Crete, Oct 14, 2026. Airbus Defence and Space successfully integrated key components of bi-national air defence during NATO exercise SPARTAN ARROW 26 in Crete. For the first time, both the German Air Force IRIS-T SLM air defence system and the Swedish Air Force Patriot air defence system were connected to the German SAMOC (Surface to Air Missile Operations Centre) command post, the central software hub that acts as the "brain" for coordinating air defence weapons. In close cooperation with the armed forces of Germany and Sweden, Airbus demonstrated seamless networking to defend against drones and cruise missiles under realistic conditions and in real time.



Through this successful integration into SAMOC, IRIS-T SLM was coordinated during its first live firing with real missiles by an all-German crew - a key prerequisite for official NATO certification. Simultaneously, the Swedish Air Force completed its first independent PATRIOT live firing via the networked system, marking the certification and validation of the Swedish PATRIOT systems by NATO and demonstrating bi-national interoperability with Germany. In addition, Airbus networked the German Army’s Light Air Defence System (LeFlaSys for short-range drone protection) to deliver a connected, multi-layered defence chain covering long, medium, and short distances.

"Effective air defence today is the result of a seamlessly integrated overall capability, not the performance of individual products" said Andreas Reinecke, Head of Defence Digital & Cyber at Airbus Defence and Space. "From initial target acquisition to a precise hit, our Command & Control solution in Crete showed how smoothly the interaction works. The SAMOC command post connects individual weapon systems into a reliable, digital protective shield for Europe."

The performance data obtained under real operational conditions regarding bandwidth, response time, and jam resistance will feed directly into the further development of NATO's networked command and control capabilities.

title: Skunk Works and the Royal Netherlands Aerospace Centre Expand Strategic Collaboration
body:
WASHINGTON, Oct. 15, 2026. Lockheed Martin Skunk Works® and The Royal Netherlands Aerospace Centre (NLR) today announced a broadening of their strategic partnership at NL-US Defense Industry Days. What began two years ago as an exploratory Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) has matured into a high-impact collaboration, rapidly transitioning advanced technologies from the research lab into operational solutions that directly support the mission readiness of the Royal Netherlands Air Force.



This agreement between the two like-minded organizations highlights the power of combined world-class expertise with global industry leadership to accelerate critical technological breakthroughs. Skunk Works has a more than 80-year history of developing groundbreaking aerospace systems and continues to deliver cutting-edge solutions globally for America and allied nations. Skunk Works' visionary focus on innovation aligns with NLR's mission of making aerospace technology more sustainable, safer, more efficient, and more effective.

Proven results driving future innovation

Since the inception of this MOU, the two organizations have successfully navigated complex operational and security environments inherent to confidential high-tech development. By establishing robust joint frameworks, workshops, and specialized working groups, NLR and Skunk Works have bridged distinct organizational cultures. This operational success has unlocked more opportunities, paving the way for a deeper and more ambitious roadmap.

"We believe that modern aerospace development relies on global integration rather than isolation, making cross-border partnerships essential to deliver systems that no single nation can build alone," said Tineke van der Veen, CEO at Royal NLR. "Referring to the Dutch Defence White Paper 2026, NATO is the cornerstone of our defense, with the United States as our most important ally. Together with Skunk Works, we're committed to cooperate to solve the highest priorities of the air force for the challenges ahead of us."



"Lockheed Martin is excited about continued partnership with NLR through expansion of this MOU," said Ron Fehlen, Vice President and General Manager of Skunk Works. "We have matured specific projects with cutting-edge technologies, such as Thermoplastics, and through our continued collaboration, we will develop new solutions to address pressing aerospace and defense challenges."

In this next phase, we'll focus on four key pillars. These include connectivity to the Dutch industrial base, coordination on military operational analysis, alignment on technology roadmaps, and collaboration on Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS). We'll position the Dutch defense industrial base within the international supply chain, bridge the gap between mission needs and capability requirements, and work together on enabling technologies.

title: Tinubu Meets CDS, Service Chiefs, Musa, NSA, IG, Gaidam over 2027 Polls Security
body: • Matawalle, Famadewa, other heads of agencies in attendance • Tells military he wants free, fair, credible polls next year • Gives marching order for rescue of those kidnapped, abducted nationwide •Musa: we’ll secure nation for all eligible voters to exercise their franchise without fear • Pledges military’s neutrality during elections •Says president will soon launch 10 aircraft and helicopters to boost nation’s aerial surveillance Deji Elumoye in Abuja President Bola Tinubu, yesterday, presided over the National Security Council (NSC) meeting at State House, Abuja, essentially to discuss the security of the 2027 general election. The meeting, which lasted for about five hours at the first floor office of the president, was attended by National Security Adviser, Mallam Nuhu Ribadu; Minister of Defence, General Christopher Musa; and Minister of Police Affairs, Senator Ibrahim Gaidam. Present, also, were Minister of State for Defence, Bello Matawalle, and Special Adviser to the President on Homeland Security, Major-General Adeyinka Famadewa (rtd). Others included Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Olufemi Oluyede and the three service chiefs – Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu; Chief of Naval Staff, Vice Admiral Idi Abbas; Chief of Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Aneke – and Chief of Defence Intelligence, Lieutenant-General Emmanuel Undiandeye. In attendance, too, were Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu; Director-General of National Intelligence Agency (NIA), Ambassador Mohammed Mohammed; and Director-General of Department of State Services (DSS), Adeola Oluwatosin Ajayi. Addressing newsmen after the meeting, Musa said the essence of the meeting was to brief the president on the security situation in the country ahead of the January 2027 polls. He disclosed that they had an intensive deliberation with the president, who told the security chiefs that he was desirous of a free, fair, and credible poll next year. Musa assured all stakeholders, including the political parties, that the military would be neutral during the elections. He stated, “Today’s meeting was to brief Mr. President on the security situation within the country. You know, the elections are coming in January, and it’s important that we keep him abreast on what is ongoing. You can see all heads of security agencies are here. “We had an intensive discussion, and Mr. President made it very clear he wants a free, fair, and credible election. We must do everything possible to ensure that the country is safe and secure for the citizens to go out and vote. “And so, we want to assure Nigerians that we are committed. We are determined to ensure that we provide safety and security for all Nigerians. Everyone should come out and vote. Vote for whoever they want.” Musa added, “The president wants the atmosphere to be free, and it’s important for all other political parties to understand that the security forces are going to be neutral. “We are going to ensure that we give everybody opportunity to go and serve, so they have nothing to worry about, nothing to be afraid of, and that nobody is going to intimidate them for whatever reasons.” The defence minister also defended the military institution against allegations of recruitment of underage soldiers, saying such act might have been carried out by terrorist groups but not Nigerian military. According to him, “We are all professionals. We are fully committed, and it’s also important for us to mention the issue of recent (alleged recruitment of underage soldiers). We have seen some people trying to make a case as if the emphasis is using underage children in our operations. “There is nobody that is underage that is being brought here. I think the discussion that was made was that the accusation was on the terrorists using the underage. “Well, we know that we don’t have control over what they do, and that’s why it’s important for us to understand that we must not allow them remain wherever they are.” Musa further stated that the president gave the military a marching order to ensure the rescue of all those kidnapped and abducted in different parts of the country. He stated, “The directive from the president is: all of us must go all out to fish out and rescue all those that have been abducted, kidnapped wherever they are. There shouldn’t be any camp of any tourists or bandits anywhere in Nigeria. “As we go forward, we are showing Nigerians that we’re fully committed, and that is what we’re going to work towards. So, we thank Mr. President for his support and to assure Nigeria that we’re all working as a team, as Nigerians for Nigeria. We assure you that.” Musa revealed that the president would soon inaugurate 10 additional aircraft and helicopters to boost the country’s aerial security surveillance. He also disclosed that the president planned to extend the new salary structure to police and other paramilitary personnel and pensioners. Musa stated, “I want to assure you, very soon Mr. President is coming to commission a set of new aircraft and helicopters that have been bought. I think about 10 of them, and to show Nigerians that despite the economic issue, the issue of security is in the front burner of Mr President’s view. “And so, for us, we are very happy. The recent increment of salaries for members of the armed forces. I’m sure very soon the police and all others are being addressed, including those of the pensioners. “Nobody is going to be left behind. Mr. President wants every Nigerian and every citizen to be happy with what is ongoing, and he is fully committed in the peaceful efforts on what we are doing today. Musa added, “And we want Nigerians to put their hands together to make sure that Nigeria remains free. Security is everybody’s responsibility. It’s not only for members of security forces. “Everyone has a role to play. And we keep on preaching. Whatever you see that is going wrong, even with our members that are not doing what is right, please, don’t hesitate to report. Action will be taken.”

title: President’s Choice of 12 States for Personal Campaign Signals Battlegrounds for 2027
body: • APC releases nationwide schedule for rally •Tinubu wants another term, but ashamed to face the people, Atiku mocks president •He’s scared to face the electorate, says Makinde/Daura Campaign Organisation Chuks Okocha, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Jonathan Eze in Lagos The decision by President Bola Tinubu to personally lead the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign in 12 strategically selected states ahead of the January 16, 2027 election might have inadvertently revealed where the ruling party expects some of its fiercest electoral contests. Beyond the appearances themselves, the choices offer an interesting insight into the president’s electoral calculations and the states considered critical to Tinubu’s re-election bid. Of the 36 states of the federation, Tinubu has elected to personally campaign in Kaduna, Rivers, Plateau, Oyo, Borno, Enugu, Bauchi, Sokoto, Delta, Kano, Adamawa and Lagos, leaving the remaining 24 states and the Federal Capital Territory to the campaign machinery and other party leaders. Although the president explained at Wednesday’s inauguration of his Presidential Campaign Council that governance must not suffer on account of electioneering, the states selected for his personal appearances appear anything but accidental. Indeed, a closer examination of the results of the 2023 presidential election offers perhaps the clearest explanation for the choice. Of the 12 states, Tinubu won only three — Rivers, Oyo and Borno — in the last presidential election. He lost the remaining nine to his principal opponents, namely Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso. Instructively, Atiku defeated him in Kaduna, Bauchi, Sokoto and Adamawa, while Obi won Plateau, Enugu, Delta and Lagos. Kwankwaso, on his part, carried Kano, delivering nearly one million votes under the platform of the New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP). Put differently, 75 per cent of Tinubu’s proposed personal campaign appearances will take place in states where he suffered electoral defeats in 2023. This is hardly a coincidence that can be dismissed in the circumstances. Take Kaduna, for example. The decision to formally flag off the campaign in the state on October 24 is particularly instructive. Atiku polled 554,360 votes there in 2023 against Tinubu’s 399,293, despite the APC controlling the state government. With Atiku again seeking the presidency, this time on the platform of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Kaduna represents an important electoral contest, particularly given its political significance in the North-west. The inclusion of Kano is perhaps even more revealing. In 2023, Kwankwaso secured 997,279 votes against Tinubu’s 517,341. But the political circumstances have since changed, with Kwankwaso now running alongside Obi on the platform of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC). Thus, Kano is no longer merely about reversing a previous electoral defeat. It is also about confronting the combined political ambitions of two former presidential candidates, one of whom demonstrated considerable electoral strength in the state. Sokoto presents a different calculation. Atiku defeated Tinubu there by just 3,235 votes in 2023, making it one of the closest contests between both candidates. Such a narrow margin naturally makes the state an interesting electoral territory for both parties. Similarly, Adamawa, Atiku’s home state, where the former vice-president secured 417,611 votes against Tinubu’s 182,881, offers the APC another opportunity to test its political strength in an established opposition stronghold. Bauchi also fits into this northern calculation, especially with the changing political alliances ahead of the 2027 contest. In the South-east, the decision to visit Enugu is equally significant. Tinubu recorded a mere 4,772 votes in the state in 2023, compared with Obi’s 428,640. The difference was staggering and underscored the depth of APC’s electoral difficulties in that part of the country. Enugu, therefore, presents not merely an opportunity to seek votes but also a chance for the president to make a direct appeal to an electorate that overwhelmingly rejected his candidacy four years earlier. Plateau and Delta, which Obi also won in 2023, fall within the same broad electoral consideration, although their political circumstances and voting patterns differ considerably. Then comes Lagos, arguably the most symbolic of the 12 states. For a politician whose political influence has been closely associated with Lagos for decades, losing the state to Obi in 2023 was one of the election’s notable developments. Obi polled 582,454 votes against Tinubu’s 572,606, a difference of just 9,848 votes. That Tinubu has chosen Lagos for the grand finale of his campaign on January 9, 2027, could therefore carry significance beyond the customary symbolism of ending a national campaign on familiar political territory. It offers the APC an opportunity to demonstrate the strength of its organisation in a state that remains central to Tinubu’s political history. However, the inclusion of Rivers, Oyo and Borno, which he won in 2023, suggests that the campaign strategy is not entirely about recovering lost ground. Rivers remains politically important because of the influence of the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, and the state’s complicated political alignments. Oyo has assumed additional significance with Governor Seyi Makinde’s presidential ambition, while Borno remains the political base of Vice-President Kashim Shettima. These three states may consequently be seen as territories where the president considers reinforcement of existing support just as important as the pursuit of new votes elsewhere. Taken together, the 12-state itinerary suggests a deliberate attempt to balance electoral recovery with political consolidation. Seven of the states are in the North, while five are in the South, ensuring that the president’s personal appearances cut across all six geopolitical zones. Of course, the 2023 results cannot automatically determine the outcome of the 2027 election. Political alliances have changed, candidates have switched platforms, and the electorate will be judging Tinubu not merely as a candidate but as an incumbent with a record to defend. Nevertheless, the campaign timetable has provided an early glimpse into the geographical priorities of the ruling party. While the APC will campaign nationwide, the president’s decision to personally appear in these 12 states suggests that some electoral contests are receiving particular attention. And if the itinerary is anything to go by, the battle for 2027 may already have its first identified battlegrounds — not necessarily by the opposition’s declaration, but by the president’s own campaign choices. Meanwhile, the APC has released its nationwide campaign rally schedule for the 2027 presidential election covering 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). According to the timetable sighted yesterday, Tinubu is expected to lead the campaign for his re-election in 12 different states, including Kaduna, where the ruling party would officially flag-off the campaign on October 24, 2026. This was as the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, has said Tinubu was too ashamed to ask Nigerians for four more years, the reason he served a notice he would not go round the country to campaign. At the same time, the Makinde/Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO), has also said Tinubu was scared of being jeered and disgraced by Nigerians over his abysmal failures in office, hence his cowardly decision not to go around the country to campaign. In another development, Atiku’s Media Office has said the attempt by Vice President Kashim Shettima to portray him as a beneficiary of Bola Tinubu’s political generosity in 2007 was a distortion of history that should not go unchallenged. APC Releases Nationwide Schedule for Rally, Tinubu Leads Campaign in 12 States The APC has released its nationwide campaign rally schedule for the 2027 presidential election covering 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). According to the timetable sighted yesterday, Tinubu is expected to lead the campaign for his re-election in 12 different states, including Kaduna, where the ruling party would officially flag-off the campaign on October 24, 2026. President Bola Tinubu had Wednesday during the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) held at the Presidential Villa hinted that he won’t be available for all the campaign because he doesn’t want to abandon governance. The campaign is scheduled to run from October 2026 through early January 2027, with Lagos hosting the major closing rally on 9th January 2027. The schedule showed that President Tinubu would also lead the Port Harcourt campaign scheduled to take place on November 7. He would also be on the campaign train to Plateau State on November 14, and would be in action in Ibadan, Oyo State on November 21. Similarly, he would be available to captain the campaign train in Borno State on November 25, and he would also be on ground in Enugu on November 28. The president is also expected to put on his campaign amour in Sokoto State on December 5, and in Asaba, Delta State on December 12. Continuing,Tinubu would lead the campaign train to Kano, the votes hub on December 17, while Bauchi State would play host to the APC campaign train on December 29. The president would lead the campaign to Yola, Adamawa State, the home state of his main challenger, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, on Monday, January 4, 2027, while the grand finale of the campaign would be held in Lagos State on Saturday, January 9, 2027. Other campaign schedules include Owerri, Imo – 30th December; Akure, Ondo state – 11th November; Bauchi – 29th November; Katsina – 2nd December; Uyo, Akwa Ibom – 18th November; Makurdi, Benue State -30th November. Others are Abeokuta, Ogun State, 3rd December; Awka, Anambra state -19th November; Gombe state, 3rd November; Kebbi state -17th November; Edo state – 12th November, Kwara state -10th December. Also, Osun State will host the campaign on December 9, Abia State on December 7; Yobe State on November 16, Zamfara State on December 14; Bayelsa state on December 15, Niger State December 16, and Ekiti State November 5. Ebonyi State is billedd for November 9; Taraba State or December 19, Jigawa State for November 10, Cross River for November 2; Kogi State December 8; Nasarawa State for November 8; and Adamawa State for January 4, 2027. Meanwhile, President Tinubu has issued an order to the Director of Women Mobilisation of the All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council, Dr. Betta Edu, and the party’s women leadership nationwide to galvanise the female electorate, consolidate grassroots support and spearhead an expansive mobilisation drive ahead of the 2027 general election. The president gave the directive on Wednesday afternoon at the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council at the Banquet Hall of the Presidential Villa, Abuja, where he extolled the political significance of women and underscored their indispensable role in the party’s electoral calculations. Recognising women as an influential constituency whose organisational dexterity, numerical strength and penetration of grassroots communities could substantially shape the electoral landscape, Tinubu charged them to convert their longstanding commitment to the APC into a formidable and meticulously coordinated political force. The President pledged his support for legislative efforts to expand women’s representation in elected offices, assuring the gathering that his administration would sponsor the Women Reserve Seat Bill. “You women are the greatest mobilisers, and I assure you a sponsorship of the Women Reserve Seat Bill. Go and work for it, it will come to fruition to increase the number of women representation at both National Assembly and subnational level. I assure you that,” Tinubu declared. Tinubu Wants Another Term, But Ashamed to Face the People, Atiku Mocks President Presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, has said President Bola Tinubu was too ashamed to ask Nigerians for four more years, the reason he served a notice he would not go round the country to campaign. Instead, he claimed that the president chose to send governors, ministers and defectors across the country to defend the hardship of the past three and a half. Also, the Makinde/Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO), has corroborated this when it also said Tinubu was scared of being jeered and disgraced by Nigerians over his abysmal failures in office, hence his cowardly decision not to go around the country to campaign, which is an aberration in a democracy. This, nonetheless, the media office of Atiku has said the attempt by Vice-President Kashim Shettima to portray Atiku as a beneficiary of Tinubu’s political generosity in 2007 was a distortion of history that should not go unchallenged. A statement by the Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, stated that, “Tinubu says he may miss campaign rallies because Nigeria needs his attention. Where was that urgency when Nigerians pleaded for relief? He has had three and a half years to govern. In that time, families have been forced to cut meals, postpone medical care and watch their earnings lose value before they get home. “Now he wants another mandate. Before asking Nigerians for one, he must face them and account for the first term. “Let him look a mother in the eye and explain what his government has done to make food affordable. Let him tell pensioners why they cannot afford their medicines. Let him explain to young Nigerians why years of study and hard work have still not brought them decent jobs. “Tinubu says American creditors cannot wait. Nigerians cannot wait either. They have bills to pay, children to feed and lives to rebuild. They deserve a President who treats their suffering with the same urgency he gives creditors and investors. “Instead, he is assembling a crowd of politicians to speak for him. He can fill every campaign stage in Nigeria. He cannot fill an empty pot with surrogates. He cannot send a politician into a market to persuade prices to fall. “The people on his campaign council did not receive the mandate in 2023. Tinubu did. He made the promises. He took the decisions. He must face the questions. “Nigerians will hear whatever his surrogates have to say. But when they vote, they will remember what they have lived through. No crowd of politicians can stand between Tinubu and his record.” Tinubu Scared to Face Electorate, Says Makinde/Daura Campaign Organisation The Makinde/Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO), has said President Bola Tinubu was scared of being jeered and disgraced by Nigerians over his abysmal failures in office, hence his cowardly decision not to go around the country to campaign. Referring to himself as “Governor Tinubu” at the inauguration of his presidential campaign council, it said indicated a serious state of confabulation, disorientation and disconnection from reality underscoring his unfitness to govern. In a statement by the Director of Strategic Communications of Makinde and Daura Presidential Campaign, Richard Ihediwa, said the campaign considered Tinubu’s decision not to accompany the “Nebuchadnezzar Coalition” to every state of the federation as a desperate attempt to evade public resentment, knowing that his government has renewed the “anger” of Nigerians, rather than their “hope” in the past three and a half years. The Director of strategic communications further said the decision not only constituted a serious affront to the Nigerian electorate, but also made a caricature of democratic ethos. “Mr. President’s decision and his confabulatory statement further confirmed fears by Nigerians that he is not fit to face the rigours of governing a nation like Nigeria. “The decision not to campaign around the country also reinforces public apprehension that the All Progressives Congress (APC) is not ready for a free, fair and credible election but plotting to circumvent and compromise the process against the Will of the people. “A president who believes he has performed well should be confident to defend his record before the people. However, having failed in all of his promises and having no meaningful achievements to boast of, President Tinubu is now fishing for excuses not to face the people.” Attempt by Shettima to Portray Atiku as Beneficiary of Tinubu’s Political Generosity Misrepresents Historical Facts Atiku Abubakar’s Media Office has said the attempt by Vice President Kashim Shettima to portray him as a beneficiary of Bola Tinubu’s political generosity in 2007 was a distortion of history that should not go unchallenged. In a a statement, the media office said, ‘’For Shettima’s education, the Action Congress (AC), on whose platform Atiku contested the 2007 presidential election, was not Tinubu’s personal political property. ‘’The AC emerged in 2006 from a coalition involving Tinubu’s faction of the Alliance for Democracy (AD), the Advanced Congress of Democrats (ACD), the Justice Party and other political interests. ‘’On the AD side were Bola Tinubu, Chief Bisi Akande, Aremo Olusegun Osoba, Otunba Niyi Adebayo and other prominent AD leaders. ‘’On the ACD/PDP breakaway side were Atiku Abubakar, Chief Audu Ogbeh, Chief Tom Ikimi, Alhaji Lawal Kaita, Alhaji Bashir Dalhatu, Alhaji Abubakar Rimi and former Speaker Ghali Na’Abba, among others.’’ The statement claimed that those were political heavyweights who came together to build an alternative political platform in the aftermath of the struggle against President Olusegun Obasanjo’s third-term ambition. The Atiku media office further said it was a coalition of political interests, not a charity established by Tinubu to accommodate Atiku. Accordingly, the Atiku media office said, “Indeed, Chief Bisi Akande, a central figure in the formation of the AC and its former National Chairman, acknowledged in his autobiography: “In 2007, we formed a party, the AC, with Abubakar Atiku.” The Media office of the former vice president said, ‘’Akande also disclosed that the understanding was for Atiku to emerge as the presidential candidate, with Tinubu considered as his running mate. That proposal ultimately failed over objections to a Muslim-Muslim presidential ticket. ‘’Now, if Tinubu merely gave Atiku a political platform out of generosity, why was Tinubu himself being considered for the position of running mate? The answer is simple: they were political partners, not landlord and tenant. ‘’Atiku was already Vice President of Nigeria, with an established national political structure and considerable political influence, long before the AC was formed. Tinubu did not manufacture Atiku’s political relevance. ‘’Shettima should also remember that Atiku fought attempts to exclude him from the 2007 presidential election all the way to the Supreme Court and prevailed. As for Shettima’s attempt to ridicule Atiku by comparing him with Abraham Lincoln and Raila Odinga, what exactly is his point?”

title: Samtel Avionics, Japan’s BULL to explore space debris mitigation solutions
body:
By Aroonim Bhuyan

New Delhi. Indian aerospace and defence electronics company Samtel Avionics Ltd. and Japan’s BULL Co. Ltd. signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on October 15 to explore solutions for mitigating space debris by combining their respective technologies for post-mission satellite disposal and active debris removal.



The agreement establishes a framework for evaluating the integration of BULL’s proprietary passive post-mission disposal (PMD) technologies with Samtel’s satellite platforms, space debris mitigation concepts, debris removal vehicles (DRVs) and associated systems. The collaboration aims to develop practical and sustainable solutions to improve the long-term safety and sustainability of activities in outer space.

Under the MoU, the two companies will examine technical requirements, system interfaces, customisation and integration options, development milestones and potential future implementation. Depending on the outcome of the initial assessment, they may also explore cooperation in product development, manufacturing, licensing, supply and commercialisation.

The companies may additionally pursue selected customer opportunities involving the attachment of BULL’s passive PMD devices to space debris already in orbit, using Samtel’s debris removal vehicles or related systems. Such initiatives will be assessed separately and will require mutual written agreement, while remaining subject to technical, commercial, export-control and regulatory requirements.



Addressing the media here, Puneet Kaura, Managing Director and CEO of Samtel Avionics, described the agreement as a landmark initiative, highlighting the growing challenge posed by space debris to the sustainable development of the global space economy.

Through the partnership, Samtel aims to explore scalable solutions that combine BULL’s passive disposal technologies with its own capabilities in satellite systems and debris removal concepts, while strengthening India-Japan cooperation in space sustainability, Kaura said.



Masakazu Koyanagi, Vice-President of Corporate Development at BULL, welcomed the collaboration, saying it would bring together the Japanese company’s passive post-mission disposal technologies and Samtel’s satellite platforms, debris mitigation concepts and removal systems. He expressed optimism about further collaborative opportunities.

The proposed partnership comes amid growing international attention to the accumulation of debris in Earth’s orbit and the need for effective measures to reduce collision risks and ensure the sustainable use of space. By exploring the integration of passive disposal mechanisms with active debris removal capabilities, the two companies intend to assess potential approaches to addressing the challenge across different stages of a spacecraft’s operational life.

title: W’Bank: $12.4bn Unrepatriated Oil Funds Eroded Nigeria’s External Surplus in H1
body: • Portfolio investments hit $12.2bn, dwarfs $2.2bn direct investment inflows •Lender identifies overlapping budget cycles as key weakness •Calls for better expenditure forecast, credible budget calendar Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja Nigeria’s external accounts lost the benefit of a substantial inflow of foreign exchange in the first half of 2026, as unexplained transactions totalling $12.4 billion wiped out much of the combined gains from the country’s current account surplus and net financial inflows, the World Bank has said. The unexplained outflows, recorded as net errors and omissions in the balance of payments, likely reflected, in part, oil export proceeds that were not repatriated into the country, according to the bank’s latest assessment of the Nigerian economy. The development highlighted a persistent weakness in Nigeria’s foreign exchange market, where limited repatriation of export earnings and low Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) have left the country increasingly dependent on short-term portfolio investments to support foreign exchange supply and build external reserves. However, the global lender did not say the $12.4 billion represented stolen funds or missing oil revenue. The figure only reflected a discrepancy between recorded external transactions and financial flows that could not be fully reconciled. It therefore requires further clarification from the government. According to the World Bank, the gap likely reflected, in part, oil export proceeds that were not repatriated. Such proceeds may be retained in offshore accounts or used to meet existing obligations, including repayments under oil-backed financing arrangements, rather than returned to Nigeria through the domestic foreign exchange market. “In principle, both current account surpluses and net financial inflows should support reserve accumulation, but large net errors and omissions of $12.4 billion in H1 2026 offset much of their combined total, likely reflecting in part oil export proceeds that were not repatriated. “As a result, FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment) has been a major driver of the continued rise in gross international reserves, which increased from $45.5 billion at end-2025 to $53.8 billion at end-August 2026,” the World Bank document titled: “Beyond the Federal Purse: How Higher Revenues Shaped State Priorities”, stated. The World Bank also identified oil pledges as one of the factors limiting the repatriation of export earnings, although it did not establish how much of the $12.4 billion discrepancy was attributable to such arrangements. The discrepancy nevertheless raises questions about the transparency and reconciliation of Nigeria’s export earnings, particularly in the oil sector, where foreign exchange receipts are critical to reserve accumulation and exchange rate stability. Other possible explanations for net errors and omissions include incomplete reporting, differences in the timing of transactions and gaps in the recording of cross-border financial flows. Besides, the World Bank report showed that Nigeria’s current account surplus rose to $12 billion, equivalent to 7 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), in the first half of 2026, compared with $5.5 billion in the second half of 2025 and $8.6 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. However, the country recorded net portfolio investment inflows of $12.2 billion during the period, an 80.8 per cent increase over the second half of 2025, while direct investment liabilities fell by 15 per cent to $2.2 billion. The bank noted that, in principle, the current account surplus and net financial inflows should have supported a stronger accumulation of foreign reserves, but the $12.4 billion net errors and omissions figure offset much of their combined contribution. Nigeria’s gross international reserves nevertheless increased from $45.5 billion at the end of 2025 to $53.8 billion at the end of August 2026, supported largely by portfolio investment inflows. The World Bank, however, cautioned that the absence of a more recent net reserves estimate beyond the $34.8 billion reported at the end of 2025 limited its ability to assess the country’s usable external reserve buffers. The growing reliance on portfolio investments also exposes the economy to sudden capital outflows whenever global financial conditions deteriorate or investors become less willing to hold assets in emerging markets. Between January and August 2026, foreign portfolio investment accounted for 45 per cent of gross inflows through the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, almost entirely in fixed-income instruments, including investments attracted by high domestic yields and relative exchange rate stability. The bank observed that although the functioning of the foreign exchange market had improved markedly since 2024, the supply of foreign exchange continued to depend heavily on short-term foreign portfolio investment. It said foreign direct investment remained low, while the repatriation of export proceeds was still limited, partly because of oil pledges. According to the report, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) had introduced reforms aimed at improving the operation of the foreign exchange market, including integrating bureaux de change into the official market through a centralised platform, standardising due diligence requirements and removing restrictions that previously constrained international oil companies from transferring their export proceeds abroad. Other measures included granting unfettered access to domiciliary account balances, simplifying remittance procedures and raising the advance-payment limit for imports. According to the bank, these reforms could encourage more stable foreign investment by improving the predictability and convertibility of the foreign exchange regime. It also recommended progressively allowing banks to hold net open foreign exchange positions and improving the transparency of the CBN’s intervention framework to deepen the market and reduce exchange rate volatility. The World Bank said sustained macroeconomic stabilisation and structural reforms capable of improving investment returns and reducing risks would be necessary to attract more durable foreign exchange inflows. Beyond the external sector, the report warned that rising expenditure pressures could erode the federal government’s improved fiscal position and widen Nigeria’s consolidated fiscal deficit to about 3.5 per cent of GDP in 2026. The warning comes despite an improvement in federal government revenue in the first half of the year, supported by higher distributable oil revenues, stronger corporate tax collections and increased independent revenues. According to the report, federal revenue rose to N6.2 trillion, equivalent to 2.5 per cent of GDP, in the first half of 2026, from N3.6 trillion, or 1.6 per cent of GDP, in the corresponding period of 2025. The increase, it stressed, helped narrow the federal fiscal deficit to N9.9 trillion, or 4 per cent of GDP, from N11 trillion, equivalent to 5 per cent of GDP, a year earlier. However, the World Bank cautioned that the improvement should be interpreted carefully because reported federal capital spending remained unusually low. Capital expenditure fell to N700 billion, representing 0.3 per cent of GDP, in the first half of 2026, compared with one per cent of GDP in the corresponding period of 2025. At the same time, interest payments rose to N7.7 trillion, or 3.1 per cent of GDP, from N5.6 trillion, equivalent to 2.5 per cent of GDP, reflecting persistently high domestic borrowing costs. Personnel expenditure also increased to N4.2 trillion from N3.7 trillion following wage adjustments. The bank warned that the combination of recurrent expenditure obligations, high debt-service costs and the possible acceleration of capital spending later in the year could put additional pressure on public finances. It also identified overlapping budget cycles, weak alignment between approved allocations and implementation capacity, and delays in expenditure reporting as persistent challenges undermining budget credibility. At the federation level, the report showed that gross Federation Account revenues rose in nominal terms to N18.9 trillion in the first half of 2026 from N17.7 trillion a year earlier, although they declined as a share of GDP to 7.6 per cent from eight per cent. Besides, distributions to the three tiers of government increased to N10.5 trillion from N7.6 trillion, supported partly by lower deductions from Federation Account revenues, the report stated. The World Bank attributed the reduction in deductions partly to a February 2026 executive order that eliminated the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) management fee and Frontier Exploration Fund (FEF) deductions and redirected gas-flaring penalties to the Federation Account. But despite the improvement in revenue distribution and the narrower federal deficit, the bank maintained that higher spending pressures were likely to widen the consolidated fiscal deficit for the full year. It called for better expenditure planning, a more credible budget calendar and timely, comprehensive and consistently classified fiscal reporting to strengthen budget execution and improve public financial management.

title: FACC Disburses N2.428tn September Allocations as Federation Revenue Grosses N3.913tn
body: • Inflation drops to 14.63% amid moderation in food index •Severe in Imo, Enugu, Niger Ndubuisi Francis and James Emejo in Abuja The Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) has disbursed a total of N2.428 trillion to the federal, state, and local governments, as Federation Revenue grossed N3.913 trillion for the month of September 2026. FAAC shared the amount during its October meeting in Abuja, yesterday, Director of Press and Public Relations, Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation (OAGF), Bawa Mokwa, said in a statement. The N2.428 trillion September allocations surpassed the sum of N2.338 trillion shared in the preceding month of August by N90 billion. That was the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures the rate of change in prices of good and commodities, declined to 14.63 per cent in September, from 15.39 per cent in August, National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) said yesterday. The drop was occasioned by falling food prices, which helped to moderate the cost of living, although underlying price pressures showed signs of renewed strength. According to the CPI report for the month under review, headline inflation rate fell by 6.35 percentage points, from 20.98 per cent recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. However, the relief remained uneven, with the core inflation rate, which excludes farm produce and energy, rising on a month-on-month basis, while urban inflation also accelerated during the review period. Citing the communique issued at the meeting, Mokwa said from the N2.428 trillion distributable revenue, the federal government received N832.242 billion, state governments received N799.872 billion, while local government councils got N560.660 billion. The sum of N236.049 billion went to oil mineral producing states as 13 per cent derivation revenue. The N2.428 trillion total distributable revenue for September comprised a distributable statutory revenue of N1.672 trillion and distributable Value Added Tax (VAT) revenue of N756.587 billion. Although gross revenue was N3.913 trillion in the month of September, total deductions for cost of collection stood at N131.758 billion, while total transfers, refunds, and savings accounted for N1.352 trillion. According to the communique, gross statutory revenue of N3.096 trillion was received for the month of September 2026, an amount higher than the sum of N2.850 trillion received in the preceding month by N246.384 billion. Value Added Tax (VAT) also posted a gross revenue of N816.872 billion in September, N17.972 billion, an amount less than the N834.843 billion recorded in the month of August 2026. However, from the N816.872 billion gross VAT revenue, distributable VAT revenue was N756.587 billion from which the federal government received N75.659 billion, state governments got N416.123 billion, and local government councils received N264.805 billion. According to the figures, state and local government councils received larger shares of distributable VAT revenue, while the federal government got a smaller share. The communiqué also showed that gross statutory revenue rose in September, while VAT revenue declined during the period. It equally emerged that gross statutory revenue stood at N3.096 trillion in September, up from N2.850 trillion in August, the N246.384 billion rise reflecting higher revenue available from statutory sources. Overall, FAAC attributed the changes in revenue performance to increases in some tax and petroleum-related revenue sources, alongside declines in others. Petroleum Profit Tax (PPT), Hydrocarbon Tax, petroleum royalties, import duty, Common External Tariff (CET) levies and excise duty recorded significant increases in September. But Companies Income Tax (CIT), Capital Gains Tax (CGT), Stamp Duties Tax (SDT), VAT, mineral royalties, gas-flaring penalties, rental gas-flaring fees and miscellaneous oil revenue declined during the period. Meanwhile, the CPI increased marginally to 146.38 points in September from 146.30 points in August, indicating that the overall price level continued to edge upwards, despite the slower annual inflation rate. Month-on-month, headline inflation declined sharply to 0.06 per cent in September, compared with 0.71 per cent in August, NBS stated. Average prices continued to increase, but at a substantially slower pace than in the preceding month. Food prices provided the strongest relief during the period, as food inflation declined to 19.59 per cent year-on-year in September, from 20.16 per cent in September 2025. Food inflation turned negative on a month-on-month basis, falling to -1.55 per cent from 1.02 per cent in August. NBS attributed the development to changes in the average prices of several food items, including guinea corn flour, white maize flour, local short-grain rice, eggs, fresh onions, palm oil, fresh green beans, Irish potatoes, okra, fresh tomatoes, dried green peas and plantain. The average annual food inflation rate for the 12 months ending September stood at 15.72 per cent, down from 28.37 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025. Despite the moderation, food inflation remained a major concern, with significant differences in price movements across states. Core inflation presented a less encouraging picture, rising to 1.11 per cent month-on-month in September from -0.06 per cent in August. Year-on-year, core inflation stood at 12.95 per cent, down from 22.11 per cent in September 2025. The average annual core inflation rate for the 12 months ending September was 16.54 per cent, compared with 25.68 per cent in the corresponding period of the previous year. The divergence between falling food prices and the acceleration in monthly core inflation suggested that the easing in headline inflation was not broad-based across all components of the consumer basket. Urban inflation also remained elevated, standing at 15.64 per cent year-on-year in September, while its month-on-month rate increased to 0.53 per cent from 0.28 per cent in August. The average annual urban inflation rate for the 12 months ending September was 15.90 per cent, substantially below the 28.48 per cent recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. Rural inflation stood at 12.46 per cent year-on-year, with the monthly rate falling to -0.89 per cent from 1.79 per cent in August. The average annual rural inflation rate declined to 15.32 per cent from 25.67 per cent in September 2025. At the state level, Imo recorded the highest year-on-year headline inflation at 30.04 per cent, followed by Enugu at 22.38 per cent and Niger at 22.05 per cent. Taraba recorded the lowest annual headline inflation at 1.78 per cent, followed by Bauchi at 2.84 per cent and Adamawa at 3.66 per cent. Month-on-month, Imo also recorded the highest headline inflation at 8.64 per cent, followed by Kaduna at 4.46 per cent and Sokoto at 3.01 per cent. In contrast, Adamawa recorded the steepest monthly decline at -6.10 per cent, followed by Bauchi at -5.31 per cent and Kano at -4.49 per cent.

title: Lockheed Martin Expands Advanced Munitions Manufacturing in Texas, Driving Thousands of New American Jobs
body:
DALLA. Lockheed Martin on Oct. 14, 2026 announced plans to create 6,000 jobs across the United States including 2,000 in Texas, as the company expands advanced manufacturing capacity to accelerate production of critical munitions.



At the center of that growth is Lockheed Martin's Grand Prairie operation, where the company is investing $300 million and expanding its manufacturing footprint to more than 735,000 square feet. The expansion includes 100,000 square feet of new space and 85,000 square feet of office space being transformed for advanced manufacturing, creating additional capacity for automation, digital manufacturing and high-precision machining.

The company also announced today that Hadrian will bring an innovative, highly automated machining cell to the Grand Prairie facility, operated by the world-class Lockheed Martin production workforce. Expected to be operational in early 2027, the 24-machine cell will bring commercial-style manufacturing technology directly into Lockheed Martin's production environment and add dedicated capacity for critical defense components.

THE BIG PICTURE

Lockheed Martin is building a manufacturing model designed for speed, scale and sustained production, bringing together the best of defense and commercial manufacturing to build a more resilient, automated and digitally integrated production model designed to deliver critical capabilities faster. The new Hadrian cell is the latest example of that strategy. It follows Lockheed Martin's recently announced collaboration with GM Defense to apply commercial automotive manufacturing expertise to defense production.

EXPERT PERSPECTIVE

"This expansion is more than just a new facility; it is a stronger supply chain and a more resilient industrial base," said Michael P. Duffey, Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment. "Today in Grand Prairie, American industry is answering the call to support our warfighters."

"Lockheed Martin has brought together commercial speed and combat-proven performance because America needs both," said Jim Taiclet, Chairman, President and CEO of Lockheed Martin. "By combining advanced technology with the expertise of our American workforce, we're transforming manufacturing to deliver critical munitions at speed and scale."

"The warfighter can't wait on peacetime timelines. Hadrian is bringing the automation, software and workforce training from our own factories directly inside Lockheed Martin, so we can produce more, faster. Rebuilding the Arsenal of Freedom at the scale America needs will take partnerships that combine expertise and speed, and this is what that looks like," said Chris Power, CEO of Hadrian.



WHY IT MATTERS

 	Delivering critical munitions: Lockheed Martin's Grand Prairie facility supports all Missiles and Fire Control programs, including PAC-3 MSE, THAAD, PrSM and JATM. The expansion and partnership announced today will help Grand Prairie reach record production levels and deliver components to final-assembly sites including Camden, Arkansas, and Troy, Alabama.
 	Investing ahead of demand: The $300 million investment in this expansion is part of the company's broader commitment to invest $8–9 billion through 2030 to scale munitions production and modernize or expand more than 20 facilities across the United States.
 	Building a manufacturing model that can scale: Lockheed Martin is combining a highly skilled workforce with automation, digital manufacturing, precision machining and commercial manufacturing practices to increase capacity and strengthen the defense industrial base.
 	Creating greater predictability: Working with Department of War leadership, Lockheed Martin is applying commercially inspired contracting approaches through landmark agreements for PAC-3 MSE, THAAD, PrSM and JATM. These agreements provide greater predictability to invest in people, equipment and supply chains while accelerating production and delivery.

ADDITIONAL CONTEXT

 	The Grand Prairie facility is already home to hundreds of critical machining and advanced manufacturing assets, and Lockheed Martin is rapidly adding even more capacity. In just a few months, the company has transformed former office space into advanced manufacturing areas and installed more than 30 additional high-precision machines now producing thousands of critical components each week.
 	By the end of 2026, Lockheed Martin expects to have added nearly 100 new advanced machines across the facility.
 	Nearly 800 production employees currently work at the facility which manufactured 250,000 parts in 2025.
 	Today's announcement with Hadrian follows the signing of a seven-year agreement signed by both companies in 2025.

title: IMF-World Bank meetings juggle equal parts relief, dread
body:
On one hand there's more economic resilience than expected but on the other, everyone appears waiting for the other shoe from the war to drop
The annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank are being held in Bangkok this year against a backdrop of equal parts relief and dread.
In her curtain-raising speech, IMF head Kristalina Georgieva said the global economy had navigated through serial shocks with “remarkable agility,” and that the meeting would focus on energy prices, high government debt, and the rise of AI.
The relief comes from the resilience of the global economy in the face of a war in the Middle East that has continued far longer than was expected at the spring meetings held in Washington in April.
The dread comes from worries that the war in the Gulf (and other conflicts) are continuing; that the energy buffers protecting the global economy are being eroded; that AI, which is seemingly offsetting the risks to global growth right now, is a potential source of immense job losses if it works and financial shocks if it does not work; and that rising global bond yields are threatening not just the economy but also fiscal solvency in many countries .
On the positive side, in the most recent edition of the World Economic Outlook (WEO), the IMF noted that its projection for global growth had remained essentially unchanged at 3.1% for 2026 and 3.4% for 2027. The Fund cited the flexibility of oil markets that saw increased production outside the Persian Gulf, the use of alternate transportation routes out of the region, and increased recourse to alternative energy sources as some of the reasons for the resilience.
The other mitigating factor, an extraordinary increase in spending on AI, has also helped cushion the global economy but unevenly and with costs and uncertainties. The technology boom has seen a ramp-up in global investment, but this has been geographically concentrated, with U.S. firms expected to spend close to a trillion dollars this year alone on AI infrastructure. And the corollary to all this investment has been a huge jump in imports of key semiconductor inputs from East Asia, particularly Taiwan and Japan.
The flip side of this boom has been not just an increase in Asian trade surpluses and U.S. trade deficits (often a source of friction), but also a rise in the interest rates of long-dated government debt across many countries as the scale of the buildout forces a competition for savers’ wallets. The AI investment boom has come alongside renewed inflationary pressures that have been exacerbated by the war in the Gulf, and increasing concern about the debt trajectory of G7 members like the U.S. and France.
The rise in interest rates also stems from worries about the independence of the Federal Reserve in the case of the U.S., where President Trump is continuing to pressure the institution via social media and via efforts to remove key personnel.
In France , worries about rising deficits and debt are intersecting with concerns over the 2027 election, as two major contenders, Marine Le Pen on the right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the left seem unwilling to comply with various policy constraints imposed by the European Commission and the European Central Bank.
One outcome of these intersecting factors is that global growth in the WEO is projected to be much more uneven. Growth in emerging markets is expected to be 3.7% in 2026, down just 0.1 percentage points versus the estimates in April, but this includes an India that has proven more resilient seeing a 0.6 percentage point boost to 7.0%, while the Middle East and North Africa see a 1 percentage point drop, led by a dramatic 5.0 percentage point fall in Saudi growth estimates (vs. April) to a 3.3% contraction.
While WEO global projections have barely changed over the last six months, the distribution has. In April, 54 economies were expected to account for 95% of global growth, but now only 32 economies will. Along similar lines, growth prospects have been downgraded for 47% of the economies covered by the Fund. The main factors driving these outcomes are the relative extent (and direction) of exposure to wars in the Middle East and Europe on the one hand and to updraft from the AI investment boom on the other.
For oil-importing countries like South Korea and Taiwan that are also major producers of key equipment required for the AI boom, the impulse from AI-related exports has given their economies a boost that has overpowered the negative impact of higher oil prices. Singapore, Malaysia, and Vietnam have also seen similar effects, but at a smaller scale. In a similar twist, oil exporters in the Global South that are distant from the Persian Gulf have seen growth upgrades versus April expectations, but oil importers with less exposure to the tech boom could face rougher waters. Accordingly, of Africa’s two biggest economies, Nigeria is seen as benefiting, and South Africa as being held back.
These are not the only concerns. 2026-27 is projected to be a Super El Nino year, and one that comes when farmers around the world are already facing stresses from higher diesel and fertilizer prices. The phenomenon is associated with heavier rainfall in some areas (like Northern East Africa and South India) and with drier conditions in others (Southern Africa and North India), raising the specter of higher food prices that hit the poor the hardest.
A more widespread worry is the impact that higher interest rates on U.S. Treasury debt could have on financing conditions for countries of the Global South. However, it should be noted that increasing anxieties about the AI growth trajectory have brought down U.S. Treasury yields as of this writing).
The problem is that many borrowers in the Global South, and particularly those that run trade deficits, are forced to keep interest rates higher than they might otherwise be in order to attract capital when U.S. rates are high, even if their budget deficits and gross debt are much lower than those of developed countries. Current interest rates in Brazil are roughly 9% above the rate of inflation, for example. This, in turn, can slow growth and worsen the debt trajectory.
Finally, there is AI itself – the center of the current boom, and the node of multiple anxieties. One set of medium-term worries is about the extent to which AI will eliminate jobs in services, particularly at the entry-level, a risk highlighted at the IMF meetings by Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam . This is a global issue, but especially prominent in countries with a large youth cohort seeking upward mobility through education, particularly in Africa and South Asia.
One such country is India, where the Gen-Z cockroach movement got its start protesting against leaks and other irregularities in the nationwide competitive exams that govern entry into education and employment.
And if the socio-economic consequences of AI that works “too well” could lead to one set of bad outcomes, the financial consequences if AI does not prove as profitable as hoped could lead to another set of problems. Gartner, a global technology advisory firm (known among other things for having coined the concept of the hype cycle ) expects an additional $6 trillion of AI spending through 2030, but that $3.5 trillion of AI assets could be financially impaired (i.e., not generating sufficient returns) by that date.
The IMF notes that interlocking financing patterns that connect vendors of AI hardware, the builders of data centers that use their chips, and the AI lab enterprises could lead to unanticipated stresses. As if these were not enough, the same IMF publication also highlights the prospect of AI “working well” but at “the wrong things” as the technology enables ever more sophisticated cyberattacks on critical and financial infrastructure.
The world may have dodged a bullet thus far this year, but the shots are still flying.

title: Eisenkot aims to out-hawk Netanyahu ahead of elections
body:
The two leading Israeli candidates are telling voters they will crack down hard on Hamas and fight Iran
Gadi Eisenkot, a leading Israeli politician hoping to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections later this month, pledged Thursday that he would “destroy Hamas’s military wing” within 18 months of taking office.
Eisenkot, a former chief of Israel’s general military staff, said the defeat of Hamas could come through “President [Donald] Trump’s framework” for disarming the group or “through the use of military and operational capabilities.”
Netanyahu’s Likud party struck back by claiming Eisenkot would require help from Arab parties to form a coalition government. “How would you destroy Hamas without getting permission from your partners, Mansour [Abbas] and [Ahmed] Tibi?" the party said, referring to two of Israel’s leading Arab politicians.
As Israelis prepare to go to the polls on October 27, Israel’s top candidates are working hard to out-hawk each other. Eisenkot and Netanyahu each lead parties expected to win just over 20 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. It remains unclear whether either of them will be able to form a majority coalition, particularly given their skepticism of working with Arab parties, which are expected to win 13 seats as of this writing.
Recent comments from both leading candidates provide a reminder that Israeli politics have moved rapidly to the pro-war right in recent years.
Even as American politicians maintain their commitment to a two-state solution, Eisenkot and Netanyahu are attempting to score political points by accusing their opponent of supporting a Palestinian state. “Benjamin is Palestine,” wrote Eisenkot in a recent X post, in which he slammed the prime minister for speaking “in favor of two states dozens of times” and for failing to destroy Hamas and Iran . Netanyahu, for his part, has said Eisenkot will “establish a Palestinian state before GTA 6 comes out,” referring to a popular video game set to launch next month.
The leading candidates also agree on the necessity of continued conflict with Iran. “Israel must do everything, including attacking Iran, to destroy its nuclear capability,” Eisenkot said this week.
Disagreements between Netanyahu and Eisenkot largely come down to domestic issues, including corruption and whether to expand conscription to the ultra-orthodox community, which has long provided a key base of support for Netanyahu’s Likud.
The near-total agreement on foreign policy reflects what Israeli Maj. Gen. (res.) Tamir Hayman recently deemed Israel’s “‘new’ national security concept.” While Israel has not formally declared a change in its strategic perspective, Hayman argued that its actions since October 7 reflect a new approach that, among other things, rejects the idea of permanent peace with Arab states. “War is necessary, and preventive war is preferable because it secures a significant achievement at the outset,” Hayman wrote, paraphrasing the views of many of his colleagues in Israel’s national security sector.
Other notable aspects of this new national security concept include an emphasis on Israel’s Jewish character over its democracy; increased skepticism of the U.S.-Israel relationship; and embracing settlements and civilians as “part of the defense network,” according to Hayman, who is the executive director of Israel’s leading think tank.
These changes would make it particularly difficult for either Eisenkot or Netanyahu to form a government. In 2021, the government of Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid made history by forming a coalition with Mansour Abbas’ Raam party, which became the first ever Arab party to join an Israeli government. But after three years of bitter war, there is little reason to believe such a bloc could form once more, leaving open the possibility that neither side will be able to form a majority coalition.

title: Europeans shouldn't throw out the truck with the diesel deal
body:
The window for Ukraine war peace deal is closing, we need to keep our eye on the ball to ensure it's done right
As the U.S. midterms approach, headlines regarding the Ukraine war are emerging at breakneck pace. But amid the noise and recurring outrage, the fundamental dilemma has not changed: how can the United States build up a self-sustaining European equilibrium that maximizes Washington’s room for maneuver in an increasingly multipolar world?
Achieving a comprehensive settlement to the war in Ukraine is a necessary, albeit insufficient, part of the answer. European leaders perceive Russia’s war of aggression not just as a security threat but as a fundamental breach of the post-Cold War continental compact. It will not soon be forgotten. As long as the fighting continues — and even in the event of a ceasefire that leaves deeper political cleavages unaddressed — Europe and Russia will not arrive at a stable balance of power on their own.
Time is running out to settle the war on terms that would be broadly acceptable to current European sensibilities. We must not lose sight of this bigger picture before it is too late.
Recent days have been chock full of developments, not to mention speculation. Among them is a recently announced deal to lift U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel. The agreement, ostensibly designed to ease pressure on fuel markets ahead of the U.S. midterms, will ultimately have limited impact on American consumption and global prices. More importantly, the deal’s ramifications for war termination negotiations are also unclear.
On the one hand, those arguing that the deal represents an unacceptable lifting of pressure on Russia have little evidence to back up their contention that tightening the screws on Moscow will bear fruit. Nearly five years into a devastating war of attrition that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives, Russia still does not appear on the verge of a full-blown economic collapse. Those who hoped sanctions would eventually compel Moscow to change course must finally realize that hope is not a strategy. Increasing pressure on Russia is not a panacea when it comes to ending the war.
On the other hand, just because pressure has not yielded the desired results does not mean that agreements such as the diesel deal will, on their own, succeed in reinvigorating the diplomatic track. The Trump administration likes to speak the language of economic deals, but these are not a substitute for addressing the longstanding political and security issues that led to war in the first place.
If the administration hoped that the diesel deal would buy enough goodwill for the implementation of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, it appears to have been mistaken. Moscow has clearly interpreted Ukrainian President Zelensky’s declared openness to an energy ceasefire as a sign of weakness — signaling to the Kremlin that Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure are exacting a greater price than Kyiv’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. It is possible that Moscow would agree to an energy ceasefire in exchange for substantially more sanctions relief, but Ukraine would see this as a wrongheaded concession that fills up Russia’s war chest.
Instead, recent reporting suggests that the administration understands the need to enlarge the pie to discuss broader security issues, rather than just trying to de-escalate a conflict where Moscow sees itself as having greater leverage. This is a sound approach. The war itself is rooted in decades of clashing visions over who gets to set the rules of European security and how. And beyond this, enlarging the pie makes it easier for everyone to get a piece.
For now, we should suspend judgment on the proposals allegedly being discussed between American, European and Ukrainian interlocutors. The exact details remain uncertain. Some reported aspects, such as releasing some of Russia’s frozen assets or building new pipeline infrastructure from Russia to Europe, would be very difficult for Europeans to swallow. Others, such as freezing the conflict along the current frontline, clash with Russia’s declared position. Reacting to every piece of news only encourages officials to miss the bigger picture, namely the urgency of reaching a settlement.
While several months remain before the French presidential elections, recent polls show hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon moving into second place. Such an eventuality would virtually guarantee Marine Le Pen’s victory in the second round, throwing Kyiv’s European Union membership bid into disarray and putting the future of European assistance to Ukraine in question. The consequences for Ukraine’s war effort could be devastating.
Many recall former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Mark Milley’s comment in late 2022 that Ukraine should negotiate peace while it remained in a position of strength. His words were not heeded, and Kyiv’s leverage has gradually shrunk ever since. By now, it should be clear that recent months did not see the tide of the war turn in Ukraine’s favor — and that this was merely a narrative designed once again to put off making difficult decisions.
There are good reasons to doubt whether U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have the wherewithal to negotiate the complex issues involved in building a new European security order. And completely apart from Ukraine’s legitimate right to defend itself against aggression, there is also reason to believe that Zelensky has a personal stake in the war continuing, for fear of what may befall him once out of power.
Europeans cannot sacrifice what may be Ukraine’s last chance at a decent outcome. Being a “ geopolitical actor ” means knowing how and when to use both incentive and coercive leverage to shape one’s security environment. This inevitably applies to both belligerents in this conflict, since any settlement will require compromises from both sides, irrespective of who is morally in the right.
It is long past the point where the perfect can be made the enemy of the good. Without determined action, the good may also soon be out of reach.
