title: FG Flags Off N1.83tn Dangote-financed Niger Highway Project
body: • Umahi: Over 5,500km of road projects ongoing across north-central •Bago pledges to mobilise support for Tinubu’s re-election •Dangote puts roads funded by his group at over N5tn Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja The federal government has commenced the reconstruction and dualisation of the 401-kilometre Lambata-Bida-Mokwa-Makera-Kontagora Road in Niger State, in a N1.83 trillion project expected to improve connectivity between communities, agricultural centres and commercial hubs. The project, which is being financed by the Dangote Group through the federal government’s tax-credit scheme, is expected to ease the movement of people and goods across the state and adjoining areas, while opening up new economic opportunities along the corridor. Niger State Governor, Umaru Bago, who performed the flag-off on behalf of President Bola Tinubu in Bida, described the project as a significant milestone in the development of the state and the renewal of hope for residents and motorists who depend on the road. The project will involve the reconstruction and expansion of the highway, which runs from Lambata through Bida, Mokwa and Makera before terminating at Kontagora. According to the federal government, the intervention is expected to improve access to markets, facilitate the transportation of agricultural produce and stimulate commercial activities. Speaking at the ceremony, the Minister of Works, David Umahi, said the Tinubu administration had initiated approximately 5,500 kilometres of road projects across the North-central zone, with Niger State accounting for more than 1,000 kilometres. He attributed the scale of infrastructure development to the fiscal space created by the removal of the petrol subsidy, which he said had enabled the federal government to commit more resources to infrastructure nationwide. Umahi said the Lambata-Bida-Mokwa-Makera-Kontagora project would be constructed using continuously reinforced concrete pavement (CRCP), a technology intended to provide a durable and climate-resilient road surface. He described the choice of pavement as a measure to improve the road’s longevity, adding that the administration’s infrastructure programme required continuity to enable ongoing projects to be completed. The minister also called for Tinubu’s re-election, arguing that another term would enable the president to complete the extensive infrastructure projects already underway across the country. In his remarks, Bago who thanked Tinubu for approving the project, described the highway as a critical economic artery for Niger State and the wider region. He pledged to mobilise support for the president’s re-election, promising to work towards securing victory for Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress (APC) at all levels in the state. Also, the Minister of State for Works, Bello Goronyo, recalled a recent assessment visit to the failed Dikko Junction-Maje Road, a seven-kilometre stretch linked to the major highway project. He said Tinubu had approved immediate palliative works on the corridor, addressing a problem that had affected motorists and host communities for about a decade. Goronyo expressed satisfaction that the intervention had eased the difficulties previously experienced by road users. Besides, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, who spoke on behalf of other Niger State indigenes in the Federal Executive Council (FEC), said the federal government remained committed to accelerating infrastructure development and economic recovery. He said the administration’s economic reforms were designed to strengthen the economy and support a broader transformation of the agricultural sector. Idris also emphasised the importance of transparency in the implementation of government programmes and expressed optimism about continued support for the administration in Niger State. The Chairman of the Senate Committee on Works, Senator Allwell Onyesoh, described the project as part of a deliberate policy to expand infrastructure development across the country. “What is happening today is not novel; it is intentional on the part of Mr President to provide infrastructure across the country,” he said. Chairman of the House of Representatives Committee on Works, Akin Alabi, said the highway was an important transport corridor connecting the northern and southern parts of the country. He said its reconstruction would improve transportation, facilitate economic activities and strengthen the movement of goods and services, pledging adequate legislative oversight to ensure the project’s implementation. Providing details of the project, the Director of Highways, Construction and Rehabilitation, David Yiltong, said the road would improve security, facilitate the movement of people and goods and enhance service delivery in communities along the route. He said the 401-kilometre project would connect several communities and economic centres, strengthening access to agricultural areas and markets. A representative of the Dangote Group, Mansur Ahmed, reaffirmed the company’s commitment to supporting infrastructure development through investments in the road sector. He said the project would open up communities, expand economic opportunities, create jobs and stimulate commercial activities, expressing confidence that it would be completed within the stipulated timeframe. Ahmed put the group’s investment in road infrastructure development across the country at more than N5 trillion. He also cited the ongoing establishment of a rice mill in Wushishi, Niger State, among the group’s other investments and development initiatives in the state. The Senior Special Assistant to the President on Community Engagement for the North-central zone, Abiodun Essiet, called for sustained collaboration among the federal and state governments, private-sector partners and local communities to ensure that infrastructure projects met the needs of residents. Similarly, the Secretary to the Niger State Government, Abubakar Usman, thanked Tinubu for approving the road project and other infrastructure interventions in the state, while acknowledging the Dangote Group’s role in its financing. The Etsu Nupe and Chairman of the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers, Yahaya Abubakar, also expressed appreciation to the president, saying the highway had the potential to improve transportation, expand economic activities and enhance the welfare of communities along the corridor.

title: Order limiting Starlink access for Ukraine's military came from within White House, Reuters reports
body:
An order to implement speed restrictions on Starlink systems for the Ukrainian military came from within the White House, Reuters reported on Oct. 15, citing U.S. and Western officials.
Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning , limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike and interceptor drones.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones. It is restricted from using it inside Russia itself.
Pentagon officials received notice from within the White House that the Starshield service — Starlink's military package — needed to be slowed down, two U.S. officials, and another Western official, told Reuters on the condition of anonymity. Officials did not state who was responsible for issuing the order.
The speed restrictions were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from multiple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that "several" military missions severely disrupting amid the restrictions.
Connectivity for Starlink systems used by the Ukrainian military have "been restored and remains operational," a source in the Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
But a source in Ukraine's drone industry who requested anonymity due to the nature of their work told the Kyiv Independent that "in some cases, it works perfectly, in some places it does not."
While the source of the disruption has yet been publicly confirmed, Ukrainian officials as well as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have pointed towards Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House.
A post on X from Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said .
According to Reuters, a senior U.S. official denied that the request came from U.S. President Donald Trump.
The restrictions came as Ukraine continues to come under significant and sustained pressure from the Trump administration to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries, something Kyiv views as an essential part of its defense against Russia's invasion.
The Ukraine-U.S. relations continue to hit a low point after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries for the rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts — and his team threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halts the attacks.
Washington then unexpectedly unveiled a deal allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A few days later, on Oct. 11, Trump unilaterally announced an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, taking Ukrainian officials by surprise — as Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Personal tensions between Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky appeared to unravel in the days following. When asked whether he felt betrayed by Trump for the diesel export decision, the Ukrainian leader answered: "Really, ‌yes... but it's a ​little bit more complicated than ​just my ​emotions or my feelings."
In response, Trump described the Ukrainian president on Oct. 15 as "not a good guy for (the U.S.) to deal with," adding that he was "not a big fan of Zelensky."

title: EU, UN Push Nigeria to Mobilise More Local Funds as Joint Projects Top $500m
body: Michael Olugbode in Abuja The European Union (EU) and the United Nations (UN) have called on the Nigerian government to mobilise more domestic resources to bridge the country’s development and humanitarian funding gaps. Both organisations warned that international assistance must be matched with stronger national ownership and more effective project delivery. The call came as EU disclosed that its partnership with the UN supported projects worth more than $400 million annually in Nigeria, with a portfolio of about 32 EU-funded projects valued more than $500 million, being implemented in collaboration with 16 UN agencies. EU Ambassador to Nigeria and ECOWAS, Gautier Mignot, speaking after a meeting to review the partnership, said the two institutions were committed to improving the impact of their interventions amid mounting questions about international solidarity, development assistance, and the future of multilateral cooperation. Mignot said the review was aimed not only at renewing the partnership but also identifying implementation gaps, improving coordination, and ensuring that assistance translated into tangible benefits for ordinary Nigerians. He said, “This meeting was a clear indication that we need to work together and have the government of Nigeria increase its engagement and mobilisation of domestic resources to address the development gap and the humanitarian assistance need in the country.” The appeal placed domestic financing and government ownership at the centre of discussions about how Nigeria could sustain development programmes, respond to humanitarian emergencies, and make better use of international support. According to Mignot, EU-UN partnership combines European financial contributions and grants with United Nations’ technical expertise and operational presence on the ground. He said the arrangement also involved Nigerian authorities at both federal and state levels to ensure that projects aligned with the country’s development strategies rather than being operated independent of national priorities. He stated, “Beyond even the financial support, which in Nigeria translates into projects that value more than $400 million a year, we are still having a strong strategic partnership.” Mignot explained that the collaboration had become increasingly important as the international landscape changed and multilateral institutions faced questions about their ability to sustain cooperation, development assistance, and humanitarian support. He said EU and UN remained committed to international solidarity and collective action, adding that periodic reviews are necessary to address challenges and strengthen the delivery of joint programmes. Providing details of the partnership, Mignot said EU and UN had reviewed a portfolio of approximately 32 projects worth more than $500 million, involving 16 UN agencies. The projects brought together EU funding and UN’s technical and political expertise, with Nigerian authorities participating in the broader partnership. He said the objective was to ensure that the resources committed to Nigeria translated into effective interventions and measurable benefits for citizens. The official did not provide a breakdown of the portfolio by sector or clarify the period covered by the more-than-$500 million valuation. The figure, therefore, represents the reported value of the project portfolio, rather than a confirmed annual disbursement. Mignot also did not provide a breakdown of the more than $400 million in annual project value by programme, beneficiary group, or state. Nevertheless, he stressed that the effectiveness of the partnership would ultimately depend on its ability to deliver results on the ground. “We are strong believers in a multilateralism that delivers, that delivers for the people and is efficient on the ground,” he said. The EU official said the bloc’s investment priorities in Nigeria were guided by its Global Gateway Strategy, which seeks to mobilise investments while supporting sectors considered essential to sustainable development. He identified education, governance, democracy, human rights and security as important enablers of investment. Mignot stated that economic opportunities required an environment in which institutions functioned effectively and communities could benefit from development. The emphasis on security also reflects its importance to the implementation of projects and the ability of development partners to reach intended beneficiaries. The official said EU would continue to work with UN and Nigerian authorities to support the priorities, with the partnership serving as a mechanism for combining funding, technical capacity, and coordination. He added that the relationship went beyond financial assistance, providing a strategic framework for responding to development and humanitarian challenges through international cooperation. The call for increased domestic resource mobilisation signals the importance the partners attach to Nigeria’s capacity to complement external assistance with resources generated within the country. While international funding can support projects in education, governance, and humanitarian response, the sustainability of such interventions also depends on national financing, effective institutions, and coordination between governments and development partners. The EU official said the review was intended to determine where the partnership needed improvement, which challenges remained unresolved, and how both institutions could strengthen implementation. He said cooperation with federal and state authorities was central to ensuring that projects reflected Nigeria’s priorities and addressed the needs of citizens. The meeting also reaffirmed EU and UN’s commitment to multilateralism at a time when international cooperation and development assistance faced growing scrutiny. For ordinary Nigerians, the central test of the partnership will be whether its substantial project portfolio translates into better access to essential services, stronger public institutions, improved livelihoods, and more effective humanitarian assistance. Mignot said the partners would continue to work towards more effective delivery. He stressed that the ultimate purpose of international cooperation was to produce tangible results for people rather than merely sustain agreements between institutions.

title: NCC Moves to Strengthen Security in Internet Usage, Inaugurates Working Group
body: Emma Okonji Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), yester-day in Lagos, held its inaugural symposium on “Inter-net Governance”, designed to strengthen security around the use of the internet and build resilience for all internet users in Nigeria. This is to keep internet us-ers safe while browsing the internet in today’s digital era. To drive the process of Internet Governance on a na-tional scale, the commission used the symposium to inaugurate the Internet Governance Working Group (IGWG), drawn from industry experts, with the man-date to enforce consumer protection and online safe-ty, drive digital inclusion and meaningful last-mile connectivity with affordable pricing, and promote global participation in surfing the internet from any convenient location, among others. Speaking at the symposium, Executive Commissioner, Technical Services at NCC, Abraham Oshadami, who represented Executive Vice Chairman of NCC, Dr. Aminu Maida, said the Internet Governance Fo-rums (IGF) at national, regional and global levels had shown the value of bringing different voices to one table to discuss how the internet affected networks, opportunity, trust, security, and the rights of the people who use it. Oshadami stated, “That responsibility is becoming more urgent. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, communicate and access services. It also creates new questions about harmful content, fraud, privacy, accountability and the protection of children and other vulnerable users. These questions cannot be answered by one institution alone. They require informed dialogue and cooperation across the communications sector and beyond.” Oshadami also spoke about the Internet Code of Practice (ICOP) 2026 implementation guideline, issued by the NCC to network operators, which, according to him, provides a framework for promoting a safer and more responsible online environment. He said its success would depend on clear expectations, meaningful engagement with affected stakeholders, and consistent implementation. Oshadami equally spoke on the Cyber Resilience Framework for the Nigeria Communication Sector (CRF-NCS), which mandates network operators to strengthen the security and resilience of the infrastructure on which digital services depend. According to him, these efforts speak to a simple obligation: Nigerians should be able to use the internet with greater confidence. He added that the symposium was an opportunity to hear from one another, identify practical priorities, and strengthen the communications sector’s contribution to internet governance. Presenting the fact sheet on internet governance and why it matters, Assistant Director/Head of Internet Governance Unit at NCC, Ibiso Angela George, said the symposium would link global internet governance discussions to Nigeria’s priorities and turn them into commitments stakeholders could act on. According to her, a central focus of the symposium is strengthening private sector participation in internet governance. George said the discussions will examine what held organisations back, what other regulated sectors could learn, and how participation could become more consistent and meaningful. She said internet governance would help address is-sues around critical internet resources, such as the .ng country domain, help to secure Nigeria’s Domain Name System (DNS), and tackle domain name abuse. George stated, “Nigeria’s communications sector has an important voice in the internet’s future. The symposium brings those voices together and builds lasting participation in the decisions that shape Nigeria’s digital development.”

title: Defense Forces strike Russian Irbis mobile radar station
body:

As noted, aerial reconnaissance detected the position of an enemy radar mounted on a KamAZ chassis.

title: In the new world order, expect fewer alliances and more ‘pop-up partnerships’
body: “America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” The observation, widely attributed to Henry Kissinger but originating with the British statesman Lord Palmerston, has long captured the logic of international relations. Nearly two centuries later, it may offer the clearest explanation of the new world order taking shape. For much of the past century, international relations were organised around relatively permanent alliances, geographical blocs and established institutions. Countries joined international organisations, aligned themselves with major powers and accepted long-term commitments that extended beyond their immediate interests. Today, that architecture is being supplemented by something more fluid: temporary, purpose-driven coalitions that I would call “pop-up alliances”. The emerging geopolitical advantage may no longer be choosing the right side, but retaining the ability to work with several sides. India illustrates this new geopolitical a la carte menu. It participates in the Quad alongside the US, Japan and Australia, maintains defence relationships with Russia, belongs to Brics and deepens economic ties with Europe and the Gulf. The UAE similarly combines Brics membership with extensive western security partnerships and growing commercial relationships through more than 30 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements across Europe, Asia and Africa. These arrangements are not necessarily contradictory. They reflect a world in which countries increasingly choose their partners according to the issue rather than their permanent geopolitical affiliation. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave this thinking a powerful expression at Davos earlier this year, arguing that middle powers must co-operate more deliberately because, as he put it, “if you are not at the table, you are on the menu”. His proposed approach of “variable geometry”, involving different coalitions for different issues, captures an important shift in how international influence is exercised. The next geopolitical map may therefore be drawn less around borders and more around the supply chains, technologies and resources that countries cannot afford to lose Traditionally, great powers built alliances while smaller countries joined them. Increasingly, middle powers are becoming coalition entrepreneurs, bringing together countries around shared capabilities and interests. Influence depends not simply on military strength or economic size, but on the ability to mobilise capital, technology, energy, natural resources and market access. For countries such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Canada, India and Indonesia, this creates opportunities to shape international co-operation rather than merely participate in structures designed elsewhere. The logic also challenges the geographical foundations of traditional alliances. The EU, GCC and the Association of South-East Asian Nations were largely built around regional proximity , whereas emerging partnerships increasingly reflect strategic interdependence. Semiconductor supply chains connect Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands and the US, while critical minerals, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity create overlapping interests across continents. The next geopolitical map may therefore be drawn less around borders and more around the supply chains, technologies and resources that countries cannot afford to lose. Britain’s evolving relationship with Europe offers another revealing example. Brexit represented a decisive departure from institutional integration, yet the subsequent rebuilding of economic and security co-operation demonstrates that geography and mutual dependence cannot simply be legislated away . The debate over closer relations, including possible eventual re-entry, reflects a broader movement towards more selective forms of international co-operation. This is not necessarily the end of globalisation, but rather its rewiring. Countries are reconsidering whom they depend on, for what purposes and under which conditions. Strategic resilience increasingly means maintaining options rather than placing every national interest within a single alliance. In the future of international relations, every country will be permanently looking for new and better friends. This is an emerging model that can be described as “pop-up governance”: flexible partnerships formed around specific challenges, designed to achieve defined outcomes and time-bound and designed to potentially dissolve when their purpose was fulfilled. Traditional institutions such as the UN, EU, GCC and Asean will remain, although some may lose influence as governments seek faster and more targeted arrangements. Alongside them, we are likely to see a growing layer of pop-up alliances, organised around shared interests rather than geography, with clear objectives and sometimes explicit time limits. Some will address defence, geopolitical tensions or economic security . Others will be more forward-looking, bringing together countries to develop water technologies, secure critical raw materials, co-ordinate specialised manufacturing capabilities or accelerate industrial innovation. A coalition formed to develop water desalination technologies, for example, might unite Gulf countries, Singapore, Australia and technology providers without requiring a broader political alliance. Such flexibility carries risks. Temporary coalitions can weaken accountability, exclude smaller economies and undermine established international rules. Their effectiveness will depend on whether they complement permanent institutions rather than simply bypass them. Nevertheless, the direction of change is becoming clearer. The emerging international system may resemble a network of overlapping partnerships, some permanent and others temporary, in which countries co-operate where interests converge while accepting differences elsewhere. Kissinger ’s famous principle remains relevant, but its application is changing. National interests may be enduring, yet the alliances through which countries pursue them need not be. The next measure of diplomatic influence may be less about which alliances a country belongs to, and more about which alliances it has the capacity to create.

title: Prevention becomes predictive: How Abu Dhabi is learning to read health risks before symptoms appear
body: For a family welcoming a newborn, prevention can begin before there is any outward sign of illness. For an adult attending a routine check-up, it could mean understanding a developing health risk early enough to change its course. These are the possibilities behind Abu Dhabi’s move towards predictive health care. Advice on exercise, nutrition and regular screening remains essential. The next step is to make prevention more personal, drawing on an individual’s genetic profile, medical history and measurable changes in their health to determine where earlier action could make a difference. That ambition is reflected in To Sense is to Predict, the theme of the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, taking place from October 20 to 22. For patients and families, its meaning is practical: recognising the signals of disease sooner and turning that information into care. More years in good health Future Health - A Global Initiative by Abu Dhabi’s longevity whitepaper places healthspan, the years a person lives in good health, at the centre of this shift. Its focus is on helping people remain well and independent for longer by connecting scientific advances with prevention and everyday care. For UAE families, that means thinking about health across generations. Earlier recognition of risk could help a parent manage a developing chronic condition, support an older relative’s independence or give a child access to specialist care sooner. Genomics can reveal inherited susceptibility. Biomarkers, measurable indicators such as blood glucose or cholesterol, can help clinicians assess what is happening in the body. Medical records add the history of previous tests, diagnoses and treatment. AI can help analyse these sources of information and identify patterns that warrant clinical attention. The value comes from interpreting those signals together. A genetic finding is one part of a person’s health picture; its significance depends on clinical evidence, family history and other risk factors. Predictive care aims to give clinicians a stronger basis for deciding who needs closer monitoring, which screening is appropriate and when to intervene. Earlier insight must lead to better care. Abu Dhabi’s priority is to translate advances in genomics, data and AI into evidence-based decisions that help people stay well. For patients and families, this means understanding their risks, receiving appropriate screening and having a clear pathway to support or treatment. Connecting information to care Abu Dhabi has established infrastructure that supports this approach. Malaffi, the emirate’s health information exchange, connects records across public and private healthcare providers, giving authorised clinicians access to a patient’s medical history. This helps them assess new findings alongside previous results and coordinate care across different settings. At the population level, the Department of Health’s Population Health Intelligence platform, unveiled with Microsoft in 2025, brings together clinical, lifestyle and environmental data. It is designed to help identify emerging risks and inform targeted prevention, with obesity and cancer among its initial focus areas. The longevity white paper also stresses the importance of helping people act on health information. Understanding a risk is useful when it leads to appropriate follow-up, support with healthier habits or a treatment decision. That requires prevention to become part of routine care, with progress assessed over time. An earlier start for newborns Abu Dhabi’s Newborn Genetic Screening Programme offers a concrete example. Launched by the Department of Health in August 2025, its first phase was implemented at Kanad Hospital in Al Ain and Danat Al Emarat Hospital, in partnership with M42. Using cord blood collected at birth with parental consent, the programme applies whole genome sequencing to screen for more than 815 treatable childhood genetic conditions. These include disorders that may not be apparent at birth but could affect a child’s health if treatment is delayed. The announced expansion aims to reach all maternity hospitals in Abu Dhabi, covering UAE nationals and children of Emirati mothers born in the emirate. For families, the opportunity is earlier knowledge and a clearer route to care. Where screening identifies a concern, clinical assessment and genetic counselling help explain what the finding means and whether treatment or monitoring is needed. From genetic findings to better outcomes Future Health’s genomics and rare diseases whitepaper examines the next scientific challenge: understanding how genetic variants disrupt biology and using that knowledge to develop targeted interventions. It also explores how rare diseases can reveal biological mechanisms relevant to more common conditions. For patients, this reinforces the importance of connecting discovery with clinical care. Identifying a variant is a starting point. Its value depends on accurate interpretation, specialist expertise and access to an appropriate intervention. As the summit brings together healthcare leaders, researchers, policymakers and innovators, the test of predictive prevention will be what changes for families: a condition recognised sooner, a better-informed care plan or more years lived in good health.

title: AISATS Weighs Logistics Park Expansion as Bengaluru Airport Eyes 1 Mn Tonne Cargo Target
body:
AISATS Expands Warehousing Services with Flexible Short-Term Storage
 	AISATS Launches On-Demand Warehousing at BLR Logistics Park to Power Agility for Shippers and Forwarders

Bengaluru, Oct 14, 2026. AISATS is weighing additional warehousing capacity at its Bengaluru airport logistics park as the facility approaches full occupancy, with the airport targeting annual cargo throughput of one million metric tonne by 2030. The company is also expanding its service offering through short-term storage for urgent and specialised shipments, allowing customers to rent space for as little as one day.



The AISATS BLR Logistics Park reached 70 per cent occupancy within its first year of operations and is on track to achieve full occupancy, the company said in a press release. While AISATS has indicated that additional infrastructure may be needed as cargo volumes grow, it has not announced a confirmed expansion plan, investment amount, or timeline. Any capacity addition will depend on cargo growth projections and the airport’s broader hub strategy.

Occupancy Drives Capacity Review

Spread across eight acres, the logistics park brings together Grade A warehousing, a customs-bonded warehouse, a consolidation centre, cold storage and office space, along with services such as packing, labelling and cargo inter-shuttle operations. The facility is located close to the airport and has access to National Highway 44.

The park was developed to bring freight forwarding and cargo preparation activities closer to the airport’s cargo terminals. This allows operators to consolidate shipments from different locations before moving them for air transport, reducing the need for repeated transfers between off-airport warehouses and the airport.

Salim Chaudhary, COO, AI SATS and company executives said the facility was planned around longer-term cargo demand projections, but occupancy has risen faster than anticipated. The company is considering whether a second facility may be required to accommodate future demand, with the timing and scale dependent on the airport operator’s projections.

Bengaluru airport has set a target of handling one million metric tonnes of cargo annually by 2030. AISATS executives said the pace of growth towards that target would help determine the additional logistics infrastructure required. While AISATS has not firmed up its expansion plans or investment outlay, Raj Mahmia, Head Cargo Logistics Services, AISATS, indicated that a facility of this scale would typically entail an investment of Rs 400 to 500 crore.

Short-Term Storage Targets Smaller Shippers

Alongside its review of long-term capacity, AISATS has introduced a Short-term Warehousing Solution (STW) for freight forwarders, shippers and businesses that need storage for urgent, last-minute or temporary cargo requirements. The service covers general and temperature-controlled cargo, with rental periods starting at one day and no requirement for a long-term lease.

The short-term facility currently has a storage capacity of around 25 tonne. AISATS has discussed the possibility of increasing this to 100 tonnes by allocating an additional 10,000 square feet, but the proposal has not been finalised.

The model is intended to help smaller and mid-sized businesses avoid paying monthly rent for dedicated warehouse space that they may use only intermittently. It can also provide additional capacity during seasonal cargo peaks, including Diwali, Christmas and New Year, when some businesses experience a temporary increase in shipments.

AISATS said the service had also been used to store oversized medical equipment requiring special handling, as well as chemicals and pharmaceutical ingredients at its common-user cold storage facility. General cargo storage is priced at 55 paise per kilogram per day, while temperature-sensitive cargo costs 85 paise per kilogram per day, according to information shared during the briefing.

Logistics Park Attracts Global Freight Forwarders

The facility has attracted multinational logistics companies including DHL, DSV, FedEx, Kuehne+Nagel and CEVA Logistics, according to AISATS. The short-term offering extends access to the park’s infrastructure to smaller freight forwarders and shippers that may not require dedicated warehouse space throughout the month.

Customers can also access packing and labelling support, dedicated manpower, forklift services and cargo inter-shuttle operations. The integrated set-up is intended to allow cargo to be prepared and consolidated near the airport before it is transferred to cargo terminals.

AISATS said demand for logistics infrastructure was being driven by sectors including electronics, semiconductors, engineering goods, aerospace and pharmaceuticals. The company did not provide a breakdown of cargo volumes or revenue contributed by these sectors.

“The response from the market has been extremely encouraging, with occupancy already reaching 70 per cent,” Salim Chaudhary said. He added that the short-term warehousing service was designed to provide access to warehousing infrastructure without long-term commitments.

Expansion Depends On Cargo Growth

AISATS said future capacity additions would depend on the commercial viability of the investment and the pace at which the airport’s cargo volumes grow. The company is awaiting greater clarity on the airport’s projections before determining the infrastructure required to support demand.

The logistics park forms part of AISATS’ cargo and logistics operations. The company, a 50:50 joint venture between Air India and Singapore-based SATS, also provides airport ground-handling and cargo services across its network in India.

For now, the immediate focus includes filling the existing park and extending its services to businesses with shorter or specialised storage needs. Any decision on a second facility will depend on the scale and timing of future cargo demand.

title: Czech Deputy PM backs India partnership in aerospace, defence
body:
By R Anil Kumar

Bengaluru, Oct 14. Czech Republic First Deputy Prime Minister Karel Havlicek on Wednesday, October 14, called for stronger industrial cooperation with India in aerospace, defence and advanced manufacturing, saying investments focused on high-value products and new technologies were central to his country's economic strategy.



“It's completely corresponding with also the economic strategy of the Czech Republic, which is based on added value, it's based on new technologies,” Havlicek said at the inauguration of a new production facility of Gopalan Aerospace at Hoskote near Bengaluru.

The inauguration was accompanied by the signing of5 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Gopalan and Czech companies, marking a fresh step towards expanding industrial and business ties between the two countries.

Czech Deputy Foreign Minister Marie Chatardova said more than 30 Czech companies accompanying the delegation to India, were ready to collaborate with Indian partners under the Make in India programme. “All of them are ready to cooperate with Indian partners within the Make in India programme,” Chatardova said, highlighting the potential to translate diplomatic engagement into concrete business partnerships.

The developments underline opportunities for India and the Czech Republic to expand cooperation in aerospace, defence and other advanced technology sectors.

Havlicek, who arrived in India with a business delegation two days earlier, described Bengaluru as “the heart of the new technologies, advanced technologies”, highlighting the city's importance in India's technology and manufacturing ecosystem.

He said Czech entrepreneurs had briefed him in Prague about their activities and investments in Bengaluru, prompting his interest in visiting the city and the facility, linking the sectors to the Czech Republic's focus on innovation and high-value manufacturing.



“I am promoting the Czech Republic as a country for the future, as a country with great entrepreneurs, very good universities, R&D centres, simulators, startups, spin-offs, and a country which is focused on added value,” he said.

He said the Czech Republic was seeking to move beyond its traditional image of historic cities and famous beer and showcase its strengths in innovation, research and development, and advanced industries. Chatardova, who is responsible for Asia and economic diplomacy, said strengthening economic engagement was a priority for the Czech government.

“Economic diplomacy is one of the top priorities of our government, and economic diplomacy for us means not a slogan, but it means something concrete,” she said.

“We are very much result-oriented, and I can observe that same here in India,” she added, expressing hope that cooperation between the two countries would continue to grow. The event was held in the presence of C. Prabhakar, Director of Gopalan Enterprises. The new facility is located in the KIADB Industrial Area at Pillagumpe, Hoskote, on the outskirts of Bengaluru.

The facility inauguration and MoU signing bring together a manufacturing development and a bilateral business initiative.

GOPALAN AEROSPACE BUILDS ON US$40 MILLION INVESTMENT WITH NEW HOSKOTE PRODUCTION LINE

Czech Deputy Prime Minister Karel Havlíček inaugurates the new line as GAIPL advances itsaerospace and defence manufacturing ambitions; five MoUs span UAVs, fire safety, advanced coatings, and unmanned traffic management.

Gopalan Aerospace India Private Limited (GAIPL), partof Gopalan Enterprises, today launched a new production line at its Hoskote facility in Bengaluru, strengthening its capacity to pursue higher-value manufacturing programmes across the aerospace,defence, and space sectors. The launch took place in the presence of H.E. Karel Havlíček, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade of the Czech Republic, and Mr. C. Prabhakar, Director, Gopalan Enterprises.

The occasion also witnessed the signing of five Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) betweenGopalan and Czech partners, covering five areas of potential collaboration: fire-extinguishing solutions; unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), including fixed-wing drones, quadcopters andrelated systems; thermo eflective coating technology; unmanned traffic management systems; and jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles.

The agreements establish a basis forexploring complementary technologies, industrial cooperation and potential manufacturing opportunities across aerospace, defence and advanced engineering.

The production-line launch and the agreements underscore GAIPL’s ambition to build on its existing manufacturing base, expand its technological capabilities and strengthen its participation in increasingly complex programmes and global aerospace supply chains.

An Integrated Aerospace Manufacturing Platform GAIPL has invested approximately US$40 million in its 10.5-acre Hoskote facility, which houses morethan 150,000 sq. ft. of manufacturing infrastructure. Its capabilities span precision CNC machining, sheet metal fabrication, advanced composites, aerostructures, and complex assemblies, supported by Build-to-Print and Build-to-Spec solutions.

Certified to AS9100D and ISO 9001:2015, with Nadcap accreditations for composites and welding, GAIPL serves a customer and programme ecosystem that includes HAL, IAI, L&T, DRDO, TASL,ISRO, NAL, Expleo and ECIL, as well as the Indian Army and Indian Air Force.

The new production line strengthens the company’s ability to support more complex, higher-value aerospace, defence, and space programmes.

Mr. C. Prabhakar, Director, Gopalan Enterprises, said: “India’s aerospace and defence ambitions demand more than manufacturing capacity - they require the ability to engineer and deliver increasingly complex systems to global standards. At Gopalan Aerospace, our strength lies in integrating precision machining, advanced composites, aerostructures, and complex assemblies, with the flexibility to deliver both Build-to-Print and Build-to-Spec solutions. Our investment in Hoskote, strengthens this platform and our ambition to move up the value chain - from manufacturing supplierto strategic capability partner for global aerospace and defence companies. As India expands its role

in global supply chains, we aim to help shape what the country can build and deliver to the world.”

Scaling Growth, Expanding Global ReachGAIPL’s aerospace business generates approximately US$20 million in annual revenue, with at arget of 50% year-on-year growth over the next three to five years. At planned capacity, the Hoskote facility is projected to generate approximately US$50 million in annual revenue.

The company’s growth strategy centres on expanding manufacturing capabilities, taking on higher-value programmes, deepening partnerships with global original equipment manufacturers (OEMs),and pursuing export opportunities.

India–Czech Engagement Opens New Technology Pathways

The five MoUs create a framework for Gopalan to explore collaboration with Czech companies across pecialised technologies, including UAV platforms and associated systems, fire safety, advanced oatings, and unmanned traffic management.

The areas covered reflect complementary capabilitiesthat could support future industrial and technology partnerships.

GAIPL has also been engaging with international technology companies to explore potential collaboration in UAV and drone technologies, technology transfer, joint development, and manufacturing.

The company has been working on indigenous loitering munition UAV systems overthe past three years, reflecting its focus on developing domestic defence technology and manufacturing capabilities.

The specific scope, commitments, and expected outcomes of the MoUs will depend on agreed terms and subsequent discussions between the participating companies. Further details will be shared when approved for public disclosure.

The engagement comes as India seeks to deepen domestic manufacturing, strengthen aerospace, defence supply chains, and expand the role of Indian companies in global programmes.

For GAIPL,the priorities ahead are to build on its integrated manufacturing platform, develop higher-value capabilities and create new opportunities through customer partnerships and international collaboration.

About Gopalan Aerospace India Private Limited

Gopalan Aerospace India Private Limited (GAIPL), part of Gopalan Enterprises, is building advanced manufacturing capabilities for the aerospace, defence, and space sectors. Its integrated capabilities span precision CNC machining, sheet metal fabrication, advanced composites, aerostructures, heavy engineering, UAV systems, and complex assemblies, enabling it to support demanding manufacturing requirements across a range of programmes. Based at Hoskote, Bengaluru, GAIPL combines engineering expertise with precision manufacturing to serve domestic and international customers.

With a focus on quality, capability development and increasingly complex programmes, the company aims to move up the value chain and strengthen its role as a long-term manufacturing and engineering partner to the global aerospace and defence industry.

title: UAE weather: Speed limits reduced after morning fog alerts in Abu Dhabi and Dubai
body: Heavy fog led authorities to reduce speed limits in Abu Dhabi on Friday morning, with a safety warning issued in Dubai . Alerts were sent to motorists in parts of Abu Dhabi, warning them that speed limits had been reduced to 80kph, while drivers were urged to exercise caution on the roads in Dubai due to poor visibility. " Abu Dhabi Police call on motorists to exercise caution due to reduced visibility during the fog," the force wrote on X. "They are urged to follow changing speed limits displayed on electronic information boards." A similar message was issued by police in Dubai, where motorists were told to drive carefully in the heavy fog. #urgent | #fog #AbuDhabi_Police call on motorists to exercise caution due to reduced visibility during the fog. They are urged to follow changing speed limits displayed on electronic information boards. Drive Safely pic.twitter.com/XuwXFivJGd — شرطة أبوظبي (@ADPoliceHQ) October 15, 2026 "With the formation of fog and reduced visibility in some areas of the emirate of Dubai, and in the interest of your safety, we remind you of the importance of reducing speed in accordance with road conditions, and exercising caution and care while driving," Dubai Police said on X. The National Centre of Meteorology predicted the foggy conditions would continue until at least 9am on Friday.

title: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
body:
Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post , we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.
In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model â Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters â right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1 ), well above average human reading speed.
Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.
We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio , using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post . We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.
We evaluate three frontier-class models ( Table 1 ) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts â and thus parameters â active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).
Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark . For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line:
A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.
Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3 , respectively.
Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2 , we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.
Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6Ã faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2 ). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.
Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3 ), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6Ã faster tokens/s.
The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4 ): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra â a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment.
While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.
Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the modelâs inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the modelâs layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5 ) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.
MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation . These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives ( jaccl , pronounced âjackalâ) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch , a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes:
In this command, --backend jaccl specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute).
In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7 ) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged.
It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill â up to ~1.8Ã faster (see Figure 6 ). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192 ) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk k k k , the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk k + 1 k+1 k + 1 , so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.
Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5 ) distributes the LLMâs width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl , is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.
With MLXâs high-level mlx.launch helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with:
Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers.
With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the expertsâ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5.
The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s â the two-cable value reported in Table 2 , the one-cable run being an additional experiment.
Recently, agentic AI on Mac has gained considerable traction, with agentic coding tools seeing widespread adoption among developers. With MLX, powering these tools locally is as simple as launching a server with the mlx_lm.server tool. For example, a server running Muse Spark Open on port 8080 is started with:
As with mlx_lm.benchmark , the mlx_lm.server helper can be prefixed with mlx.launch to parallelize computation across multiple Mac Studios. From there, agentic AI can be enabled with tools like OpenCode , which can be easily configured to use that local LLM server:
Many other local agentic AI experiences can be enabled through a similar approach.
Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon â Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 â that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6Ã the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio.
International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2026
Apple is presenting new research at the annual International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) , which takes place in person in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, from April 23 to 27. We are proud to again sponsor the conference, which brings together the scientific and industrial research communities focused on deep learning. Below is an overview of Appleâs participation at ICLR 2026.
Exploring LLMs with MLX and the Neural Accelerators in the M5 GPU
Mac with Apple silicon is increasingly popular among AI developers and researchers interested in using their Mac to experiment with the latest models and techniques. With MLX, users can explore and run LLMs efficiently on Mac. It allows researchers to experiment with new inference or fine-tuning techniques, or investigate AI techniques in a private environment, on their own hardware. MLX works with all Apple silicon systems, and with the latestâ¦
Our research in machine learning breaks new ground every day.

title: White House Ordered Restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield, Disrupting Drone Defense – Reuters
body:
The order to restrict Ukraine’s military-grade Starshield satellite communications system came directly from inside the White House, according to a Reuters investigation published Thursday, Oct. 15, revealing that Washington moved to limit technology essential to Ukraine’s battlefield operations and defense against Russian drones.
The restrictions disrupted Ukrainian strike missions and slowed interceptor drones used to protect cities from Russian Shahed attacks – at a time when Moscow was launching hundreds of drones and missiles against Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter told Reuters that Pentagon leaders received instructions from within the White House to slow the SpaceX-operated Starshield service used by Ukraine’s military.
The officials did not identify who issued the directive or who implemented it. A senior US official denied that President Donald Trump personally requested the restrictions.
“No such request was ever made by the president,” the official told Reuters.
The White House did not answer questions about whether other administration officials had issued the order.
The revelation comes amid deteriorating relations between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump demanding that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries even as Moscow continues attacking Ukrainian power plants and residential areas.
Ukrainian military officials reported that Starshield terminals stopped functioning when mounted on fast-moving platforms, disrupting drone guidance systems operating over Ukrainian territory.
The restrictions affected attacks on Russian military positions and logistics facilities in occupied Ukraine, while also limiting high-speed interceptor drones designed to destroy incoming Shaheds before they reach Ukrainian cities.
As Kyiv Post first reported Wednesday , Ukrainian forces experienced sudden Starshield restrictions without advance warning, with military units reporting lost connections at speeds ranging from 72 to 161 kilometers per hour (45-100 mph).
The disruptions affected interceptor drones, medium-range strike missions, reconnaissance, frontline logistics and communications relays.
By Thursday morning , Ukrainian Defense Ministry sources confirmed to Kyiv Post that connectivity while moving had been restored, although it remained unclear whether all speed restrictions had been lifted.
Ukraine is seeking to raise the operating speed limit to 450 km/h (280 mph) to allow interceptor drones to pursue faster Russian aerial threats, including jet-powered drones.
Dan Rice, president of American University Kyiv and a former special adviser to Ukraine’s military commander-in-chief, warned that such restrictions could have deadly consequences.
Speaking to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty , Rice described the scale of the threat facing Ukrainian air defenses.
“When you have 500 inbound Shaheeds, jet-powered Shaheeds, and I was hit within 400 meters twice this week,” he said, “you need to have interceptors going out to protect Ukrainian civilians.”
Rice warned that interference with high-speed interceptor operations could allow Russian drones to reach civilian targets, including schools, hospitals and residential buildings.
Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the restrictions also impaired Ukrainian drone missions against Russian military logistics and command facilities approximately 150-250 kilometers (93 to 155 miles) behind Russian lines.
The consequences extend beyond battlefield efficiency.
In an interview with Piers Morgan on Wednesday , President Volodymyr Zelensky said the restrictions had already cost Ukrainian lives.
“People are dying because of his decision,” Zelensky said.
“I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely,” he added.
However, the Ukrainian leader stopped short of identifying who had ordered the restrictions.
“I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to… I don’t know really,” Zelensky said when asked whether he was angry with Elon Musk.
“We are professionals. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he added.
The controversy has also clarified who ultimately controls the military satellite system.
Starshield is a government-focused version of SpaceX’s Starlink network, developed for military and national security operations. Unlike commercial Starlink, the Starshield services at issue operate under US government control.
Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive, confirmed Wednesday that restrictions on the system were a government decision.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X.
The White House directive emerged amid an increasingly bitter confrontation over Ukraine’s campaign against Russian oil infrastructure.
During eight hours of talks in Miami on Oct. 9, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner took a tough position toward Ukrainian officials, Axios reported , citing a person familiar with the discussions.
The US delegation expressed frustration that Kyiv had continued targeting Russian refineries despite repeated American requests to stop.
Washington also defended Trump’s agreement to allow more than 2.25 million barrels of Russian diesel onto US and international markets, arguing that the arrangement could encourage Moscow to soften its position in peace negotiations.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner threatened to cut off US intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued the attacks. A US official denied that such a threat was made.
Zelensky had offered to suspend refinery strikes if Russia stopped attacking Ukraine’s power plants, but Trump wanted Kyiv to halt its attacks unilaterally, according to the US official.
A bipartisan group of 12 US senators urged Trump to reverse the diesel agreement, warning that it would provide Moscow with additional revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
On Thursday, 22 US lawmakers called for full enforcement of Russia sanctions ahead of an Oct. 18 deadline, targeting Moscow’s energy revenues, foreign banks and sanctions evasion networks. They also demanded that Washington revoke the authorization allowing Russian diesel transactions.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian refinery strikes for soaring energy prices, although energy analysts point primarily to the US-Israeli war with Iran and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
In an exclusive interview with Kyiv Post , former US Ambassador to Ukraine Steven Pifer warned that the diesel deal would do little to lower US fuel prices while helping finance Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“American dollars will be going to purchase Russian fuel, and that’s going to help the Russian military machine buy more missiles and bombs to use against Ukraine,” Pifer said.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.
