title: Paul Frazis, Australia’s Commercial Broker of the Year: ‘Lending Is About People’
body: Paul Frazis has built a career reading the story behind the numbers Newly named Australia’s Commercial Broker of the Year, Paul Frazis spent more than two decades inside some of the country’s biggest banks. What he learned after leaving them was that the numbers rarely tell the whole story. Paul Frazis has spent most of his working life around balance sheets, credit committees and lending decisions, yet one of the clearest conclusions he has reached after more than two decades in finance is remarkably simple. “I learned lending is about people. It’s not just about numbers,” he says. “There’s a story behind the numbers, and there’s a person behind the numbers.” Paul Frazis, Australia’s Commercial Broker of the Year, Director, Head of Commercial Lending of George Capital Finance Solutions It is a philosophy that has taken on greater significance since Frazis left institutional banking for debt advisory, and one that has now earned him national recognition. In August, he was named Commercial Broker of the Year at the 2026 Australian Broking Awards, an industry award judged nationally across commercial finance. For Frazis, the recognition appears to sit slightly awkwardly alongside a natural reluctance to make too much of himself. He laughs easily, frequently redirects praise towards his colleagues, and uses the word “humbled” more readily than triumphant. “I learned lending is about people. It’s not just about numbers. There’s a story behind the numbers.” “Being named Australia’s Commercial Broker of the Year was amazing,” he says. “I didn’t think we would get there so soon.” “The hard work, the long hours and the sleepless nights, trying to make sure we get the best results for our clients, it all made it worth it. Coming from Darwin, it was a big achievement. I felt very proud and humbled by the acknowledgement.” The award arrives as the business he helped build approaches its third anniversary. George Capital Finance Solutions was founded by his elder brother George Frazis, one of Australian banking’s more experienced former executives. George previously served as Managing Director and CEO of Bank of Queensland, Chief Executive of Westpac’s Consumer Bank, CEO of St.George Banking Group and Chief Executive of Westpac New Zealand, with earlier senior roles at NAB and Commonwealth Bank. The brothers have assembled a business around an unusual proposition: experienced former bankers using their knowledge of how banks make decisions to advocate from the other side of the table. For Paul, that shift altered the way he looked at a loan. “When I was working in the banks, you were focused on the policy risk, the bank’s plans and their risk frameworks,” he says. “I was working for the bank, not the client, essentially.” At one institution, there was ultimately one institution’s appetite for a deal. Now, he says, “I’ve got 30 options rather than one option”. More importantly, the starting question has changed. Instead of asking simply whether a transaction fits the lender’s requirements today, Frazis wants to know where the business itself is trying to go. “It’s not just about pricing, it’s about structure,” he says. “We don’t just think of it as, what can we do today? It’s more like, where can we get you in five years’ time? Where do you need to be and how can we help you get there?” That distinction matters most, he believes, when a good business does not present neatly on paper. Frazis recalls the example of a profitable but highly seasonal business. Viewed at a particular moment in its cash-flow cycle, the numbers could appear less attractive than the underlying operation actually was. “A bank might not look at the whole picture,” he says. “When you get into the nitty gritty and understand how that business operates, the seasonality, or the cash flow coming in and out, it’s actually a good business.” The advantage of having spent years inside credit systems is knowing what the person on the other side needs to see. “We understand the business before we present it to the bank,” he says. “Then we present it in a way where they think of it differently. You’ve got to remember, we sat on that side of the table as well.” A big Greek family in Darwin To understand why family businesses have become such a natural focus for Frazis, finance only explains part of the story. He is the sixth of seven children born into a Greek migrant family in Darwin, and the second son. George, the eldest boy, is 17 years older. Between them came four sisters, followed by Paul and then the youngest sister. The immediate family was only the beginning. “I’ve got 20 nephews and nieces. I’ve got nine great-nephews and nieces, so it’s a big, big family,” he says. One nephew is only five years younger than him. They effectively grew up together; Frazis later became his best man and godfather to his son. Most of the family remains in Darwin. Once a year they try to reunite for Greek Easter, a gathering that can reach around 50 people once partners, children, nephews and nieces are included. “We’re all very close,” he says. Growing up in a family of that size also provided an early education in competing personalities, hierarchy, negotiation and diplomacy. “Families can be complex,” Frazis says. “Growing up in a big family, you understand some people’s voices might not get heard.” “You understand the family dynamics and the hierarchy. You might have different opinions on certain things, or you might disagree. You come together to find a solution at the end.” Those lessons now surface in meeting rooms rather than around a crowded family table. “People have put their blood, sweat and tears into that business for maybe 20 or 30 years.” Family businesses, Frazis says, are fundamentally different because financial decisions are rarely detached from personal history. “People have put their blood, sweat and tears into that business for maybe 20 or 30 years,” he says. “They want to be successful for their children. There’s succession planning and all that, and it’s more personal and more emotional when it comes to a family business.” He is particularly interested in the delicate transfer of responsibility between generations. Rather than seeing succession as the moment one generation simply exits and another takes control, he believes both have something valuable to contribute. “Each generation has a part to play in a family business,” he says. “Even if someone’s retiring, or the father might retire, it’s always good to still have them in the background because they’re the backbone of the business. They created the business and their insight is invaluable.” “Then you have the next generation coming in. They might have a different point of view, which adds value as well to grow that business to that next level.” It is difficult to miss the parallel with George Capital itself. “George was my hero, essentially, when I was growing up.” For much of Paul’s childhood, George was not simply his older brother but evidence of what might be possible beyond Darwin. “George was my hero, essentially, when I was growing up,” he says. “He achieved so much coming from a small town like Darwin. We came from a hard-working, working-class family. My parents were migrants and they worked hard to give us what they could,. To see what George was able to do coming from a migrant family from Darwin, I always admired that and I always looked up to that.” “We may have different opinions at certain times,” Frazis says. “We challenge each other, but we’re doing it for the team, and we come together and find a solution.” He pauses before settling on how to describe the experience. “Working together with George is probably the most rewarding part of my career so far.” The family involvement has at times extended further. Their niece Katie works in the business, while sisters Anna and Nikki have both been involved. For a period, four Frazis siblings were working within the firm. What the bank cannot see Frazis’s career before George Capital moved through NAB, Westpac, St.George and Judo Bank. The large institutions, he says, taught him “discipline, structure, risk management”. His time at challenger bank Judo showed him something different: greater flexibility and the value of looking beyond standard policy. What he had to unlearn after banking was the idea that the institution’s framework necessarily represented the limits of what could be done. As an adviser, he still needs to understand those policies, only now across multiple lenders. But his allegiance has shifted. “I love helping people and getting them to where they need to be,” he says. “Doing this job now allows me to do that and not be restricted to Big Brother telling me what I can and can’t do.” The language is revealing. Despite a career built around risk, Frazis talks more readily about people than products. A set of accounts might show an unexplained fall in performance. The explanation may be commercial. Or it may be deeply personal. “There might have been a life event,” he says. “There might have been a divorce or there might have been a death, or whatever it might be, that made someone not focus on their business at the time and it’s reflected in the numbers. But you don’t know what that cause was.” His job, as he sees it, is to ask. “Sometimes you have to ask the challenging questions. You might make someone a little bit uncomfortable, but everything we ask and what we do is to assist them.” It also explains his pragmatic view of private credit, an increasingly visible alternative to traditional bank lending. “There’s definitely space for private credit in the market, 100 per cent, and we use it a lot,” he says. Its advantages can include flexibility and speed. But he is equally clear about the trade-offs. “It can be more expensive. It might be a short-term solution where it might only be 12 months. So we make sure our clients understand that.” For a borrower facing a settlement in seven days, for example, private credit may provide breathing room when a traditional bank simply cannot move quickly enough. It can solve the immediate problem while an adviser works on a longer-term structure. “You still need people. You still need that personal touch. You still need judgement-based thinking.” Even artificial intelligence, for all its capacity to accelerate processes, runs into the same philosophical boundary for Frazis. “There’s a story behind every business,” he says. “I don’t think AI is a place where it can be just decision-making.” “You still need people. You still need that personal touch. You still need judgement-based thinking.” It is perhaps fitting, then, that international recognition for George Capital has arrived around the same time as Frazis’s individual award. The firm has won four Gold Stevie Awards and one Silver at the 2026 International Business Awards, including Gold awards in categories covering banking, financial services, venture capital and private equity, and business-service start-ups. It subsequently won the People’s Choice Stevie Award for Venture Capital & Private Equity, taking its 2026 Stevie recognition to six awards. The International Business Awards received more than 3,800 nominations from organisations across 78 nations and territories this year, with winners due to be recognised in Paris on 28 October. For Frazis, the trip carries another significance. Before Paris, he is heading to Kalymnos, the Greek island from which his family comes, to spend time with his parents. Greece remains part of the family rhythm; his parents return regularly, and the brothers retain close links to their heritage. It creates an elegant geographical line through the story: Darwin, Sydney, Kalymnos, Paris. Yet Frazis himself seems less interested in arrival than continuation. George Capital began, he recalls, without an office. Paul was in Australia while George was in Greece, discussing the fledgling business on late-night calls. Meetings happened in cafés. Accreditation had to be secured, clients found, systems built. “It started basically from nothing,” he says. Less than three years later, there are national and international awards attached to the name. Frazis is pleased by them. He is not particularly inclined to stop because of them. “I’m still learning every day,” he says. “We’re meeting new clients, new family businesses. I’m proud of what we’ve achieved so far, but I think we can do more. I want to do more.” “I want to deliver great outcomes for all our clients. I think we have been doing that. I just want to do more of it.” For someone whose career has been spent examining what numbers reveal, the numbers still matter. But for Frazis, the real judgement now comes from understanding the people and the stories behind them. Learn more at georgecapital.com.au Level 3, 219 Castlereagh Street Sydney NSW 2000 Australia (02) 9072 9288 info@georgecfs.com Read also $550 Million in Handshakes: Why Top Gun Banker George Frazis Bet Everything on Relationships The post Paul Frazis, Australia’s Commercial Broker of the Year: ‘Lending Is About People’ appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Russia Strikes Kyiv, Hits Apartment Building in Uman, Injures Five in Overnight Drone Attacks
body:
Russian forces launched another wave of drone attacks across Ukraine in the early hours of Friday, Oct. 16, striking an apartment building in Uman, injuring at least five people and sparking fires at commercial and energy facilities as air defenses battled incoming drones across several regions.
In Uman, in central Ukraine’s Cherkasy region, a drone fell onto a multistory residential building, triggering a fire. A nearby security building was also damaged, trapping a man beneath the rubble before rescuers pulled him to safety.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Five people were reported injured, three of whom required hospitalization, according to regional military administration chief Ihor Taburets. The other two received medical assistance at the scene.
A separate fire broke out at commercial warehouses in the city, but firefighters managed to contain the blaze, Taburets said in an official Telegram update .
Emergency crews continued working at the damaged sites, while authorities established an operational response headquarters.
In western Ukraine, Russian drones struck the Shepetivka district of Khmelnytsky region late Thursday, igniting a fire at an oil storage facility.
Regional military administration chief Serhii Tiurin said Russian forces repeatedly attacked the region with drones, prompting Ukrainian air defenses to respond.
“Today, the enemy repeatedly attacked Khmelnytsky region with drones. Air defenses were operating. There were interceptions,” Tiurin said.
He confirmed that a fire had broken out at the oil depot and that emergency services were responding.
Authorities had not provided a confirmed casualty figure in the initial report.
In the regional capital, Cherkasy, a Russian drone fell on the grounds of a private enterprise, starting another fire.
Taburets said firefighters quickly extinguished the blaze and that there were no immediate reports of casualties.
The incidents in Uman and Cherkasy came amid repeated air raid alerts across the region. Authorities warned residents that the threat had not passed even after emergency crews began responding to the damage.
Russia also attacked the Ukrainian capital late Thursday, damaging critical infrastructure and causing electricity interruptions in parts of Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Falling drone debris ignited a fire at a private residence in the Shevchenkivskyi district. Elsewhere, fires broke out in the Sviatoshynskyi district, including at a nonresidential building.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said firefighters extinguished the blazes in Sviatoshynskyi and received no reports of casualties from those incidents.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko also reported reduced water pressure on the capital’s right bank following damage to energy infrastructure in Kyiv region, illustrating how Russian attacks on the power network continue to disrupt other essential services.
Russian forces also carried out two attacks on Chortkiv, a city in Ternopil region, regional military administration chief Taras Pastukh reported Friday morning.
Emergency crews were dispatched to the strike site, where damage assessments were underway.
There were no immediate reports of casualties, Pastukh said.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued repeated warnings throughout the early hours of Friday as Russian jet-powered drones crossed central and western regions.
The military tracked drones over Cherkasy, Kyiv, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Vinnytsia, Khmelnytsky, Mykolaiv and Dnipropetrovsk regions, with some heading toward Rivne, Lutsk and Khmelnytsky.
The warnings indicated a wide-ranging aerial assault involving fast-moving drones, forcing air defenses to respond across multiple regions.

title: Naseer Shamma returns to UAE National Orchestra with bigger ambitions for the oud
body: When Naseer Shamma joined the UAE National Orchestra for its inaugural concert in January, the performance was a celebration of what the newly formed ensemble could become. Nine months later, the Iraqi oud virtuoso is returning to an orchestra with a full season and more than two dozen concerts across the emirates behind it, and a more ambitious programme ahead. At Friday's Harmony concert at NYU Abu Dhabi's Arts Centre, Shamma will perform four of his compositions in new orchestral arrangements, including a concerto for oud and orchestra. “The first concert was different. It was a celebration. We were saying, here we are, we are together. But now we have a concrete programme. We have something much deeper, with different pieces,” he tells The National . “I think the orchestra is clearly at another level now compared with the first concert. The first show was very good, and if you notice, each concert since then has been about going deeper and finding new forms of creative expression. I am so glad to be part of that journey.” For Shamma, one of the Arab world's most influential oud players and educators, the collaboration continues nearly four decades of experimentation with the instrument's sound, design and repertoire. He has helped to develop a family of ouds covering different musical registers, composed for film and theatre, and founded Bait Al Oud in Cairo in the late 1990s, later expanding the conservatory to Abu Dhabi, Alexandria and Baghdad. His interest in oud-inspired orchestral music is long-standing, having led a 70-member Eastern Orchestra at Abu Dhabi Festival in 2008. Friday's programme includes Concerto for Oud and Orchestra , which Shamma says has been developed through extensive rehearsals and discussions with musicians. Despite previously performing orchestral works, including an adaptation of Vivaldi's Mandolin Concerto for the oud, he describes it as the ideal concerto for the occasion. “I hope it will be a good work because we have taken time with the composition, with rehearsals and with discussing the ideas with different musicians. Now I think it is ready to be presented on stage with the orchestra,” he says. Shamma acknowledges the contributions of earlier Arab composers, including Iraqi oud musician Jamil Bashir, who wrote for the instrument in orchestral settings. He now hopes to expand the repertoire available to future generations of oud players. “For that reason, I think it is time to compose differently. To compose one concerto every year would be great, because this would create a repertoire for other musicians who come after us,” he adds. “Of course, many Arab composers have written concertos for the oud, qanun, nay and other instruments. But when I compose something for the oud as an oud soloist myself, it will be different from what another composer writes. Because that composer may only be a composer, not an oud player.” Writing for a symphony orchestra also means balancing its instrumental range with the oud's distinctive sound and characteristics. “I think the oud has its own special characteristics. Its sound, its power, its chords, its quarter-tones and many other things,” he says. To keep the instrument from getting lost in the orchestra, “we have to preserve the oud's identity ”, Shamma says. “Not in a traditional way but in a contemporary way. It must remain an oud in the middle of the orchestra.” Shamma's collaboration with the orchestra has also developed through his relationship with its musicians. He recalls their curiosity during January's rehearsals about his oud's clarity of sound and his playing style, and how the experience helped to establish a rapport. “It was a beautiful experience. I felt that we had covered a great distance through a single piece of music. “It is a distance that might take two years to cover in ordinary life, just to create a friendship. But we achieved it through one piece lasting eight minutes.” Some of the orchestra's musicians have an earlier connection to Shamma through Abu Dhabi's Bait Al Oud, which he set up with clear expectations. “When I established it in Cairo in 1998, and then the second in Abu Dhabi in 2007, I had a clear idea that one day the UAE would need professional musicians. So I began preparing these musicians.” Several Emirati musicians who trained at the institution have joined the UAE National Orchestra, according to Shamma. “So this is a collaboration. We complement one another. We complete one another's projects,” he says. “We are working to become bridges that lead to the other side, to professional music.” Harmony by the UAE National Orchestra: Friday, October 16 at The Arts Centre, NYU Abu Dhabi. 8pm. Tickets start from Dh100

title: How Abu Dhabi is revealing the roots of the UAE’s global outlook
body: The Gulf has sometimes been portrayed in the West as, until recently, a remote corner of the world, a place defined largely by its desert environment and the relative isolation of its communities. Two new exhibitions in Abu Dhabi museums suggest a different and more compelling account of the history of the region, namely, that far from being a peripheral place, the Gulf was a crossroads of commerce and culture – much like it is today. At Louvre Abu Dhabi , a major exhibition about how the Indian Ocean connected communities from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China and South-East Asia explores a millennium of maritime exchange through more than 200 objects. In December, the Zayed National Museum will explore more than 7,000 years of the camel’s place in the life on the Arabian Peninsula. Together, these exhibitions tell a story of land and sea that helps explain the UAE ’s enduring role in connecting people and places. The Louvre exhibition makes this history tangible. Six detailed ship models evoke the vessels that carried goods across the Indian Ocean. A third-century Buddha sculpture from Gandhara, in present-day Pakistan, offers another reminder that religious and artistic traditions travelled alongside commercial cargoes. The Gulf’s pearl industry was part of this wider network, linking its waters to markets and communities far beyond Arabia. The camel exhibition will turn the focus inland. Bones dating to between 4500 and 4000BC, discovered at Baynunah in Abu Dhabi, provide evidence of an extinct wild camel species. Remains from Dubai ’s Saruq Al Hadid illustrate the later relationship between humans and domesticated camels. Meanwhile, recordings of Taghrooda poetry and Alheda’a, the traditional practice of calling camels, demonstrate how deeply the animal remains embedded in Emirati cultural expression. These exhibitions will present a reminder of how the people of the Gulf participated in networks of exchange and developed traditions suited to their environment. Such connections are still evident today. Ports remain vital to the UAE’s international trade, but are now complemented by aviation and rail links. The camel also endures with the animal featuring in racing, competitions and poetry – its place as part of the Emirates’ national identity is irreplaceable. There is also a wider significance in the way these exhibitions tell their stories. Preserving heritage should mean more than celebrating familiar symbols or indulging in nostalgia. Understanding how the past shaped the present helps us today to recognise the complexity of the societies that preceded our modern times. For anyone seeking to understand the UAE, exhibitions such as these are a good place to start. They represent a vital reminder that the country’s cosmopolitan outlook is not a recent invention, but part of a much longer history of exchange and encounter. In other words, they show how the Gulf embraced globalisation before the term even existed.

title: Why it’s important to deepen our understanding of AI
body: Write to us: Share your feedback on the news of the week Promoting AI awareness I write in reference to the article titled Dubai launches literacy platform to help parents guide children on safe use of AI (October 14): this is a commendable initiative. As AI continues to transform various aspects of our lives, it is essential to ensure that children understand both its benefits and its potential risks. Parents play a crucial role in helping their children navigate this rapidly evolving digital world by encouraging responsible usage, protecting their privacy, identifying misinformation and developing critical thinking skills. The UAE has demonstrated a keen interest in embracing and expanding the use of AI across various sectors. This initiative clearly reflects the country’s long-term vision of promoting AI awareness, digital literacy and technological advancement while prioritising the safety and well-being of younger generations. Equipping parents with the necessary knowledge and guidance is an important step towards building a society that can confidently and responsibly embrace emerging technologies. Such initiatives will not only benefit families but also contribute to preparing future generations for an AI-driven world. A commendable step by Dubai towards ensuring that technological progress goes hand in hand with awareness, responsibility and the safety of children. – K Ragavan, Bengaluru, India A little knowledge ... With regard to the article headlined Abu Dhabi launches major training programme to teach AI skills (October 7): raising awareness about AI is a great thing. What is not so great is when people attend a few workshops and emerge believing they have become AI experts. That is where things can become dangerous and counterproductive. AI projects can be costly and complex, requiring technical expertise, sound judgment and a depth of understanding that simply cannot be acquired in a week-long workshop. There is a significant difference between understanding what AI can do and having the expertise to design, implement and manage AI projects successfully. – Muhammad A, Dubai Taking the longview I refer to the video captioned Speaking at the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Dubai, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence said trust in agentic AI systems would be difficult to rebuild if they caused harm (October 14): precisely and certainly, but the UAE leadership is foresighted. They want their people to be happy and prosperous. – Muhammad Naeem Ul Fateh, Pakistan An unsurprising decision Regarding the news that Sheikha Shamma bint Sultan has been appointed as an executive fellow by the World Economic Forum, raising her growing international profile in sustainability and climate action (October 14), I will say “bravo”, for she is a true embodiment of deep knowledge, unsurpassed intellect and pure talent. And God is a grantor of success. – Dr Aisha Bilkhair Our second home This is regarding the video clip captioned ‘There is no way that somebody will break our back,’ Saudi Arabia’s energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, said following a series of deadly attacks on Riyadh international airport (October 12): we in the Filipino community stand firmly in solidarity with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. We are deeply grateful to this nation, which has become our second home, providing us with opportunities, security and a place to build a better future for our families. In times of challenge, we stand united with the kingdom and its people. We are ready to offer our support in any lawful and appropriate way, contributing to the safety, peace, stability and prosperity of the nation we proudly call our second home. May peace, unity and protection always prevail throughout the kingdom. Long live Saudi Arabia. – James Rey Romero, Jizan, Saudi Arabia Citizens suffer I write in reference to Nada Maucourant Atallah’s article Lebanon’s power failure: Diesel generators, $300-a-month bills - and a corrupt system milking the profits (October 14): thank you for this report on the less visible impact of war. Lebanon is in a stranglehold, and as usual, those paying – literally and figuratively – the highest price are the citizens themselves. – Miguel Quintana, Switzerland Lebanon should be looking at solar and wind power. These diesel generators are making cancer cases rise dramatically. – Kay Francine

title: BoP's Mladenov: Suspension of private sector goods into Gaza is 'unacceptable'
body: Nickolay Mladenov, director-general of the Board of Peace, said on Thursday that he had received a letter from the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) informing him of the suspension of coordination for private-sector goods entering Gaza following reports of threats and coercion by Hamas.In a post on X/Twitter, Mladenov condemned the reported intimidation of merchants and interference with commercial supply chains.I have a received a letter from @cogatonline on the suspension of private-sector goods coordination into Gaza as a result of reports of threats and coercion by Hamas. As I have warned repeatedly, such practices are unacceptable and must end immediately. The intimidation of merchants and interference in the supply chain only deepen the suffering of Gaza's civilians. These developments demonstrate why the rapid deployment of the @NCAG, supported by the International Stabilization Force (ISF), is urgently needed. Civilian supplies, humanitarian assistance and commercial activity must be protected from coercion, exploitation and interference. All parties should work with the @BoardOfPeace and move without delay to implement the Comprehensive Plan endorsed by #UNSC Resolution 2803, including the arrangements required for NCAG and ISF operations in Gaza. This includes the decommissioning of weapons, the transition to legitimate transitional governance and the protection of humanitarian and commercial supply chains.— Nickolay E. MLADENOV (@nmladenov) October 15, 2026“As I have warned repeatedly, such practices are unacceptable and must end immediately. The intimidation of merchants and interference in the supply chain only deepen the suffering of Gaza's civilians,” Mladenov posted.He stressed the urgent need to establish new governance and security arrangements in the Gaza Strip.“These developments demonstrate why the rapid deployment of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) supported by the International Stabilization Force (ISF), is urgently needed,” he wrote.“Civilian supplies, humanitarian assistance and commercial activity must be protected from coercion, exploitation and interference,” Mladenov added.He called on all parties to work with the Board of Peace to implement US President Donald Trump's comprehensive peace plan for Gaza, endorsed by the UN Security Council in Resolution 2803, without delay.Mladenov emphasized the need to move forward with the arrangements required for NCAG and ISF operations in Gaza.“This includes the decommissioning of weapons, the transition to legitimate transitional governance and the protection of humanitarian and commercial supply chains,” he concluded.Commercial goods banned from entering Gaza over tax dispute between local merchants and HamasIsrael said commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza over what it said was a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas, shutting off a vital source of food and other goods in the territory where the population is dependent on aid.COGAT, which oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, made the announcement in a statement on Wednesday, citing what it said was a decision by Gazan merchants to stop coordinating with COGAT on the entry of commercial goods.It said the Gazan merchants had told COGAT that they had made the decision in response to a NIS 10,000 ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza and a demand for 30% of all of their sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash.Hamas later claimed that the NIS 10,000 fee was a voluntary payment by wealthy Gazans to a national fund that seeks to provide for those in need, such as widows and orphans. It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory.Nahed Shhaibar, the head of the private transport union in Gaza, claimed that not a single truck carrying commercial products from Israel entered Gaza on Thursday. However, he said trucks carrying humanitarian aid had entered, as had trucks carrying commercial goods from Egypt via an Israeli-controlled crossing.COGAT said the decision by Gazan merchants would cut the total number of trucks, which carry both humanitarian and commercial goods, entering Gaza each day to around 300, or half.Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Shhaibar claimed the figure was closer to 300, with two-thirds carrying commercial goods.Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day. However, it says it is required to allow only 600 trucks and that commercial goods are needed to supplement aid supplies.

title: 22 US Lawmakers Press Trump to Enforce Russia Sanctions Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline
body:
A bipartisan group of 22 US lawmakers urged President Donald Trump on Thursday, Oct. 15, to fully enforce sweeping sanctions against Russia ahead of an Oct. 18 deadline, warning that continued Russian energy revenues are financing President Vladimir Putin’s war against Ukraine.
In a letter to the White House , Republicans and Democrats called for the full implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, including penalties against Russian officials, financial institutions and foreign companies helping Moscow circumvent Western restrictions.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The appeal comes amid growing bipartisan opposition to Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports, which lawmakers fear could provide the Kremlin with additional revenue while Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
“As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war,” the lawmakers wrote.
They argued that sanctions enforcement was essential to compelling Moscow to engage seriously in negotiations.
“Utilizing the tools for economic pressure in this law will be decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously.”
The letter was led by Democratic Rep. Jim Costa and senior members of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, including Mike Quigley, Marcy Kaptur, Republican Brian Fitzpatrick and Republican Joe Wilson. Republican Michael McCaul , a former House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman, also signed the appeal.
The lawmakers urged the administration to target not only Russian officials and state enterprises but also the international financial and commercial networks sustaining Moscow’s war economy.
Their demands include mandatory sanctions on Russian oligarchs, banks and state-owned companies, alongside penalties targeting foreign financial institutions and intermediaries facilitating Russian transactions.
They also called for secondary tariffs on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, measures against vessels operating in Moscow’s shadow fleet, and restrictions on companies helping Russia evade existing sanctions.
The letter emphasizes that foreign governments and financial institutions facilitating Russian energy trade should not be allowed to shield Moscow from the economic consequences of its invasion.
At the same time, lawmakers urged the White House to protect US allies that are actively reducing their dependence on Russian energy, using exemptions and tariff adjustments permitted under the legislation.
The group requested detailed information on which sanctions and tariffs the administration intends to implement by Oct. 18, whether any provisions will be delayed or waived, and how their effectiveness will be measured.
The letter specifically challenges the Treasury Department’s Oct. 9 decision to issue General License 135, authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel.
Lawmakers warned that relaxing energy restrictions risks restoring revenues to the Kremlin at a time when Washington should be increasing economic pressure on Moscow.
They asked Trump to reverse the authorization and explain how the license complies with existing US restrictions on Russian energy imports.
The controversy follows a separate bipartisan appeal from 12 US senators earlier this week, who criticized the diesel agreement as financially beneficial to Moscow and unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to American consumers.
The senators argued that the volume of Russian diesel expected to enter global markets would have little effect on prices, which have risen sharply amid disruptions linked to the war with Iran.
Trump has defended the agreement as a measure to lower fuel costs, while also blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising energy prices.
The lawmakers outlined five questions requiring clarification ahead of the sanctions law’s first implementation deadline, including which Russian officials, banks and companies would face restrictions and which countries would be subject to secondary tariffs.
They also demanded measurable benchmarks showing whether the measures are reducing Russian energy revenues and discouraging third countries from purchasing Moscow’s oil and gas.
Any presidential waiver, they argued, should be narrowly defined, temporary and linked to verifiable reductions in support for Russia’s war.
The letter further requested congressional briefings and regular updates on enforcement, including reviews of sanctions effectiveness every 180 days.
“Putin has repeatedly shown that he responds to pressure, not goodwill,” the lawmakers wrote.
They concluded that fully enforcing the legislation would demonstrate bipartisan American resolve and increase the economic costs of continuing Russia’s invasion until Moscow agrees to meaningful peace negotiations.
“We remain committed to Ukraine’s defense and to a just and lasting peace,” the letter said.

title: Man injured in Russian attack on enterprise in Derhachi dies in hospital
body:
Viacheslav Zadorenko, head of the Derhachi City Military Administration, reported the death on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
"Unfortunately, a 54-year-old man who was injured in yesterday's Russian FPV drone attack on a transport enterprise in Derhachi died in hospital today," the statement said.

title: Meta Releases Muse Spark Open: 816B Open-Weight MoE With 1M Context
body: Meta Superintelligence Labs has released Muse Spark Open , the open-weight version of its Muse Spark model. Muse Spark Open is an 816B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model that activates 42B parameters per token. It takes text, image, video and audio input, returns text, and holds a 1M-token context window. Meta team claims it to be the most capable US open-weight model to date. For developers, the real news is deployment: the NVFP4 build runs on 2 Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios. TL;DR Size: 816B total / 42B active parameters (256 experts, 8 active per token); 1M-token context. Runs on: 2 Mac Studios (M5 Ultra, 512 GB each) via MLX; 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs or 8 H200s with NVFP4; about 300 GB setups via Unsloth 2-bit GGUF. Performance: Strong on agentic tool use; mid-pack among large open models on coding. Best: MCP-Atlas 89.2, the top score in Meta’s comparison table. Worst: Terminal-Bench 2.1 76.4, behind Kimi K3 (85.0), GLM 5.3 (83.9) and Qwen3.8 (82.0). What is Muse Spark Open? Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal MoE model from Meta, built for coding and long-horizon agentic work. Weights ship in BF16 and NVFP4 on Hugging Face. The open version received extra safety post-training. Meta team states that this makes it more robust without system-level guardrails. How does the architecture work? The model card lists 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each MoE layer holds 256 experts, and top-k routing activates 8 per token. Attention is grouped-query, with 128 query heads and 16 KV heads. A separate 1.8B-parameter Perception Encoder handles visual input. The vocabulary has 202,048 tokens, and training data covers more than 100 languages. Reasoning depth is set with reasoning_effort : low, medium, high or xhigh. The default is xhigh. How does Muse Spark Open perform on benchmarks? Meta compares it with Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B and others at maximum reasoning effort. Its strongest results are on tool use and knowledge reliability: MCP-Atlas: 89.2, ahead of Qwen3.8 (84.5) and GLM 5.3 (84.2). JobBench: 61.8, narrowly ahead of GLM 5.3 (61.4). HLE-Diamond, no tools: 26.1, versus 22.2 for Kimi K3. AA Omniscience: 25, the top score in Meta’s table. ZeroBench with tools: 50.0, versus 41.0 for Kimi K3. Coding is the weak spot. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the Terminus 2 harness, it scores 76.4. Kimi K3 reaches 85.0, GLM 5.3 scores 83.9 and Qwen3.8 scores 82.0. Its Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is 39. That sits behind GLM 5.3 (45), Kimi K3 (44) and Qwen3.8 (40). So “most capable US” holds, but Chinese open models still lead overall. Some rival scores are self-reported; the evaluation methodology lists each source. Per Meta’s developer guide , BF16 weights are about 1.6 TB. NVFP4 quantizes only the experts and lands near 530 GB. The model card recommends at least 700 GB of VRAM for NVFP4 and 2 TB for BF16. Data center: NVFP4 on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs or 8 H200s. Desktop: 2 M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 512 GB each, linked over Thunderbolt 5 with RDMA. MLX tensor parallelism splits every layer across both machines. Workstation: Unsloth Dynamic GGUFs down to 2-bit fit in about 300 GB of combined memory. Where can developers run it? Day-one engines include SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth. Hosted APIs are live on Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. OpenRouter lists $1.25 per 1M input tokens and $4.25 per 1M output tokens. Two draft models speed up decoding: DFlash V2 for SGLang and DSpark for vLLM. Meta reports 3.7x single-request throughput with DFlash V2 on AMD MI355X. Fine-tuning works with TorchTitan, Hugging Face TRL and NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel. What does the Muse Model License allow? The Muse Model License permits use, fine-tuning, distillation and redistribution. 2 conditions matter most: Products must display “Built with Muse Spark Open.” Model-as-a-Service providers above $20M in 12-month revenue need a separate agreement with Meta. Internal use, research and powering your own product features are exempt from the revenue clause. title: Soaring diesel prices taking a toll on Oklahoma rancher
body:
"It's probably the most stressful time in my life," Scott Belden told ABC News.
In Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, third-generation rancher Scott Belden is in the middle of harvest. And anxious.
"It's probably the most stressful time in my life," Belden, 55, said.
It's not just the demanding time of year that has the lifelong rancher uneasy -- the record-breaking cost of diesel is also putting additional pressure on him and his business.
"The inputs are out of control. The diesel prices are out of control, along with everything else. So we're just in a very trying time. Very uncertain," he said.
Oil prices have spiked since the start of the Iran war. The average price for a gallon of diesel was $6.32 on Thursday, according to AAA, and prices have increased by more than 65% since the war began back in February.
Belden says he wakes up at 3 a.m., worrying about how to make it all work with the crushing fuel costs hitting his bottom line. All his vehicles and equipment run on diesel, and during harvest, he burns 90 to 100 gallons of the fuel a day.
Belden's ranch includes cattle and custom harvesting for hay -- the latter he says is "absolutely unprofitable" with the costs of fuel.
"If I want to continue to operate, I'm going to buy diesel. No matter what the price is, I'm going to buy diesel," he said.
"It don't take no [mathematician] to figure out that it's costing me $1,000 to $1,400 more a week," he said.
"It's a very trying time when you know, you don't know when that's going to end. You don't know, and you can't -- you can't always pass that on to your customers because you set the prices, and they're all -- they're all struggling, too. You know everybody's in this together," he added.
With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, polling shows the economy and cost of living are a top concern for many voters.
A three-time Donald Trump voter, Belden believes Republicans will pay the price for the ongoing pain at the pump.
"Middle of America is hurting," Belden warned. "The lifeblood of America is diesel fuel. Everything you eat, consume, wear is delivered with a diesel-powered vehicle. So, I do believe it's going to hurt them tremendously."
While Belden stands by his vote for the president, he is glad Trump is term-limited.
"The president has a lot to do with these fuel prices," he said. "He's made some decisions that didn't go the way he thought they'd go, and now we're weeping the consequences of some of them decisions. And so I wouldn't say regret, but I'm glad we'll get someone new next time."
Trump has said higher fuel prices are worth the cost of preventing Iran from building nuclear weapons and that they will come down quickly after the war is over, although he has over the last few weeks shifted the blame to Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in their ongoing war.
The president last week made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import 300,000 tons of its diesel fuel and promised that millions more are coming, though experts say that won't do a lot to bring costs down.
Belden says he's expecting prices to stay high, despite Trump's promises.
"I believe everything goes up and comes down, but I've learned they go up real fast and come down real slow," he said.
While he has absorbed the increased operating costs so far, he warned that it won't be possible much longer.
"I think we're all in trouble. If we don't get control of this diesel fuel and get it -- like right now -- people, people are probably consuming the loss, like as myself, but that cannot continue. So if they don't get control of the diesel fuel soon, we're really going to see a spike."
"We're just going to have to pray that we make the right decisions and that our customers stick with us."

title: Trump Calls Ukraine’s Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries a ‘Disgrace,’ Says Zelensky Harder to Deal With Than Putin
body:
US President Donald Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace” and accused Kyiv of driving up global energy prices, even as Moscow continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
“Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump told Newsmax in an interview published Thursday, Oct. 15, when asked about Ukraine’s decision to resume attacks on Russian refineries.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
However, energy analysts say Trump’s deal to resume Russian diesel exports is unlikely to significantly lower fuel prices, as the main driver of the global price surge has been the US-Israel war with Iran, which has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump also renewed his criticism of President Volodymyr Zelensky, portraying him as a greater obstacle to ending Russia’s war against Ukraine than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“It should end soon. I think they actually both would like to see it end,” Trump said.
“But I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
His remarks came after Zelensky announced that Ukraine would no longer observe a pause in strikes against Russian refineries, citing Moscow’s continued attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities despite a ceasefire announced by Trump.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the Financial Times in an interview published Thursday.
Kyiv had temporarily suspended refinery attacks following Washington’s request, but Russian forces continued launching missiles and drones against Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, leaving hundreds of thousands without electricity.
On Thursday, Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Russia’s Ryazan Oblast, triggering a fire at the facility approximately 300 kilometers (186 miles) southeast of Moscow.
The dispute has deepened tensions between Kyiv and Washington following Trump’s agreement with Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel, a move Zelensky has criticized for providing economic relief to Moscow while it continues its invasion.
Zelensky met NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels on Thursday and held talks with European leaders ahead of Friday’s EU summit, seeking continued military and political support for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president has argued that stopping attacks on Russian refineries must be matched by an end to Moscow’s strikes on Ukraine’s electricity grid, rather than a one-sided restriction on Kyiv’s ability to fight back.
“Don’t attack us. Don’t kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel,” Zelensky said in an Oct. 11 interview with ABC News, outlining Ukraine’s position on a reciprocal energy ceasefire.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Gazans prepare to return home from Abu Dhabi's Emirates Humanitarian City
body: Dozens of Gazans who have been receiving medical treatment at Emirates Humanitarian City in Abu Dhabi are to return to their home country. The humanitarian centre has been a refuge from the Israel- Gaza conflict for thousands of Palestinians since 2023, but many long to be reunited with their families back home. Among them is 59-year-old Ibtisam Salout. She is preparing to return to Gaza in the coming days, after three years in the UAE. Ms Salout is a mother of nine and has 45 grandchildren. “The first thing I’ll do is gather them all and hold them tight. Yes, all of them," she says. She checks her suitcases before checking them again: the dresses for her daughters, the chocolates for her grandchildren. “The sneakers are for the boys. They sent me a photo and asked for these brands specifically," she says. Ms Salout is from Deir Al Balah. She arrived in the UAE in 2023 for treatment. She had breast cancer and her treatment had been interrupted after October 7. The UAE has provided medical treatment and comprehensive health care for 1,000 cancer patients and 1,000 injured children from the Gaza Strip. “When I arrived, they began treatment immediately and discovered the cancer was also in my lymph nodes. They saved my life,” Ms Salout says. Every patient is allowed an escort, but she does not have one. “I didn’t bring anyone with me. My husband said, ‘You are in the safest country in the world, with the kindest people taking care of you. I would be more worried about you in Gaza. Get better and come back to us. I’ll stay with the children and wait for you.' ” Today, she is cancer-free and ready to go back home to Gaza. “I’ll kiss its ground before running to my family," says Ms Salout. Her house has been partially destroyed, but her husband and children continue to live there. “We fixed it up like we will fix Gaza,” she says. Bittersweet farewell Ms Salout is one of dozens of Palestinians who have completed their treatment and are heading back home. There remain close to 3,000 Gazans at the UAE’s Humanitarian City under treatment. “The plan was always that they would return home once they completed their treatment, but it is hard to part with them after so many years. They have become our family," says Falah Al Qahtani, spokesperson for EHC. A few Gazans have married at EHC, and others have had children. Younger children are enrolled in schools and nurseries, while adult Gazans are enrolled in online universities. Almost every week, there is a celebration at the complex: a birth, a birthday or a graduation. “This is a bittersweet farewell. We are happy that they are heading back home. We are happy that they are happy and can go back, but they have also formed deep connections with us and the country.” For Ms Salout, this is not goodbye. “You have to come to Gaza. I’ll make you fatteh, and I make the best maftool. You can ask anyone,” she says with pride. There are 30 people living with her but, she says; “I’ve told them to keep a clean room always ready for 'the Emirati'. Without them, I wouldn’t have been alive today.” Shelter from horrors of war The EHC has served as a sanctuary for many of those affected by the violence of the war. The centre is part of the UAE's continuing humanitarian operations in solidarity with the Palestinians. About medical 150 appointments are carried out each day within the vast complex, not including admissions to hospitals in Abu Dhabi for complex surgery. A building at EHC has a pharmacy, clinics, a ward with hospital beds staffed by doctors, paediatricians, an internal medicine doctor, psychiatrists, dentists and a rehabilitation specialist. The complex has a medical team of more than 50 doctors, nurses, therapists and administrators. There is also a school serving more than 400 children.

title: What are Saudi Arabia's options as Houthi attacks escalate?
body: From Riyadh to Taiz, it has been a week of tragedy. While Saudi Arabia faces a wave of deadly attacks by the Houthis , hundreds of thousands of people in the southern Yemeni city are largely cut off from food and fuel. The fighting continues to intensify between the rebel group and Yemeni government forces, but the most recent attacks on Saudi targets, both inside and outside the country, have tested the kingdom’s patience. At least 13 people were killed and hundreds injured in a missile strike on Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend. Since then, the Houthis have continued to target airports and oil facilities across the kingdom, as well as the headquarters of Saudi Aramco . In this episode of Beyond the Headlines , host Nada AlTaher examines the security options Saudi Arabia could consider in the wake of the most recent escalation, and asks how the country can find a way out without being drawn into a wider war. She speaks to Nawaf Obaid, senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, and to Mahdi Ghuloom, geopolitics researcher at the Observer Research Foundation Middle East.

title: Comparing Chromium Development at Google and Igalia
body:
We can admit it, marketing is not our strong suit. Our strength is writing the kind of articles that developers, administrators, and free-software supporters depend on to know what is going on in the Linux world. Please subscribe today to help us keep doing that, and so we don’t have to get good at marketing.
Sharon Yang is a Chromium developer who worked at Google on the browser and now works on it at Igalia. On the final day of FOSSY 2026, she gave a presentation on her experiences with both of those companies, comparing and contrasting the ways each one operates and how that affects work on the code base. She enjoyed working at Google and feels the same about Igalia, so the talk was not aimed at complaints—instead it was meant to give a feel for two companies that are rather different.
The talk was entitled "From Corporate to Co-op" highlighting one of the main differences between the enormous company, Google, and the employee-owned cooperative at Igalia. She is from Vancouver and went to the University of British Columbia, where FOSSY was held. While she was a student, she did an internship at Google, working on the Chrome browser, which is the Google product based on Chromium. In her slides , she showed a photo of herself—complete with propeller hat—in front of a Google sign.
When she was a student, her life was measured in semesters, but some of the people she worked with at Google had been working on Chrome for four years, which was amazing to her at the time. She ended up working at Google full-time for six years, all of it on Chrome. Most of her work was on the content layer of the browser, which is part of the open-source Chromium browser. So she works in the same repository ( GitHub mirror ), and with many of the same people, at Igalia as she did at Google. She briefly reflected on her time at Google: " I had a good time working on Chrome, the people were nice, I enjoyed it, it was cool, there was lunch, it was good stuff ", she said to laughter.
Eventually, she thought it might be time to move on, and perhaps out of the Seattle area where she was living, so she started looking around at the end of 2024. She had seen Igalia email addresses in the code base and met some of the people from the company at the BlinkOn conferences . Igalia is an open-source consulting company that is hired to work on various things, including Chromium; it is the largest contributor to Chromium that is not a browser maker, in fact. She joined Igalia and moved back to Canada a little less than a year before the talk in August.
She contrasted the two companies, starting with the number of employees: Google has around 180,000, while Igalia has around 180. In terms of revenue, last year Google had more than $400 billion, " Igalia, much smaller, we'll just say under a billion dollars ", which was greeted with laughter. Google is owned by institutional investors, while Igalia is owned by employees, which the audience applauded. Google has a wide range of compensation, from the CEO's $600 million salary package to her pay (somewhere in the range of $100,000-$300,000) when she worked there; at Igalia, all employees are paid the same, top to bottom and across the globe.
While they are " massively different entities ", both companies have teams working on things in common; she works on Chromium, but there are also teams from each working on accessibility and on web standards.
Chrome and Chromium are " kind of the same, they're kind of not ". Chrome is a Google product, with Google branding and colors, while Chromium is an open-source project that anyone can use to build a browser. Chromium is missing proprietary pieces like digital rights management (DRM), " AI integration ", and certain codecs; " and it's blue ". There are various other browsers based on Chromium, including Microsoft Edge and Brave , as well.
Most of the Google Chrome team members do most or all of their work in the Chromium repository. Obviously, the proprietary pieces are handled elsewhere, but she and other Google Chrome developers rarely have to interact with that code. Near the end of her time at Google, she had to get help to do a simple task that required access to the " totally different universe " where the proprietary parts live.
She then compared the experience of working for the two companies. The first week is pretty much the same at any new job, she said. The initial steps are getting to know your coworkers, reading internal documentation, learning how to communicate internally, and so on. Igalia has a whole set of open-source tools that it uses, which is nice.
There are some differences, as well. For example, there is a system for doing faster builds of Chromium, " otherwise you'll just spend all your time building Chromium ". That system is immediately available to Google employees, but external users have to request access to it. A bigger area of friction is access to bug reports, which are meant to be open to everyone unless they are security bugs. Due to a bug-tracker migration a few years ago, though, there are bugs that should be visible to outsiders, but are only visible to Google employees. " It is not a malicious thing ", and it is easy enough to get the access fixed, but it is something extra she has to do once a week or so.
There is other information that could be more readily available to the public, but is not because it is stored in Google Docs without being shared. Ensuring that the public has access " is a best-effort thing and people forget ", which is unfortunate. In addition, all of the tools for tasks like bug tracking are maintained by Google and, essentially, for Google, so outsiders have no way to provide feedback or request features and changes. They are " relatively minor points of friction " but they are enough to feel that " I am now separate from this ".
After a month in her new job, she started to see even more similarities with her previous one. The team members are all still available via the same communication channels (e.g. Slack), and she is likewise available to them. Some of the work that Igalia does comes directly or indirectly from Google; she is working a Chromium project that comes through the Linux Foundation, which Google is a member of. " I'm working on the same repository, I'm using the same tools, I'm getting money from Google, what's changed here? "
The answer it seems is " kind of everything and kind of nothing ". The types of projects are different at Igalia, though. At Google, she worked on the projects that were important to the people in her management chain; those are often new features or " a flashy metric that they want to improve ". They are often aimed at getting promotions for the engineers and those in the reporting chain.
The projects handed to Igalia to work on come directly from the technical staff, so they tend to be " code-health or tech-debt kind of projects ". For example, Igalia worked on componentizing the Chromium code base and its current project is " improving web-platform-test interoperability between browsers ". It is important work that is good to do, but " it is just so hard to imagine anyone at Google doing it for their day job "; it is " not the kind of work that gets prioritized or rewarded ". Many of the people that she worked with on Chromium at Google would love to be able to do that work. " These are people who care about the code base, they want it to be good, but there's just no room in their day job to do that, which is too bad. "
She was initially attracted to the Chrome team because all of the people on it seemed to be welcoming. That remained true throughout her tenure at Google and has continued into her work at Igalia. " People who work on Chromium have just generally been friendly and inclusive in all domains, which is good, and is not to be taken for granted. " She has been able to maintain relationships with her former coworkers, review their patches, leave comments on work that they have in common, and so on. " It's a nicer experience than sending a code review to some stranger. "
She put up a slide of an organization chart from a typical company, with her picture in a leaf node as the only filled-in box. In a chart like that, the engineer is at the bottom of the hierarchy; they have a manager, who has a more senior manager, and so on. An engineer is concerned with technical decisions, such as which language to use or how to test the code being written, while at the top, they are deciding things like company direction and vision. The people in the middle are doing some technical work, but it is often not entirely clear what it is that they do; " who knows? ", she said to laughter. " The people at the top are paid a lot more than the people at the bottom. "
At Igalia, things are quite different. The " org chart is intentionally flat " and there are no managers. There are various teams, such as the Chromium team that she is on, a Linux kernel team, and more. The flat hierarchy means that " all of the employees do a lot of work that you typically wouldn't do as a leaf-node employee at a big company ", which includes making company decisions, such as which projects to take on, whether to increase headcount, and how much vacation time there is.
Igalia is a cooperative, so votes are taken on those kinds of questions. " These are not decisions you have any influence at all over at a big company. " One of the nice things about that arrangement is that the people who are making the decision are the ones who are affected by it, which is " just not the case at a standard company ". The most obvious example for that is layoffs, Yang said.
There is a cost to doing things that way, of course. The meetings for those decisions are lengthy and run for two days—in a European time zone. When she was at Google, she was in the dominant time zone (US Pacific), and her teammates elsewhere had to have meetings at weird times, so this feels a bit like karma for her, she said. But that is a " minor price to pay " for a structure that is " so fundamentally different and feels good ".
It took her a while to fully recognize just how different Igalia's structure is; the impacts of it did not sink in right away. The biggest impact for her was promotions, which do not exist in a flat organization where everyone is paid the same amount. When she was a new graduate, promotion was her focus because it is expected of new hires; " Meta literally fires you if you don't reach a certain level in a certain time ".
Trying to ensure that she was working on the right projects and " demonstrating the right skills " in order to be promoted was stressful and took a lot of effort. Much of it is out of the engineer's hands and is up to their manager. She was lucky and had a great manager at Google, but even if they are good, they have multiple people reporting to them. " For you, it's like your whole professional life, but for them it's one of the million things that they have to do. "
The flat pay structure is also a welcome change—there are no pay discrepancies. As a woman and someone who was formerly working on a visa, " these are very real concerns you have, and now that's just all gone ". Everyone is on the same level playing field, which leads to more trust and collaboration. " If that sounds fun, go join or start a coop ", she said to applause. That was the end of her prepared talk, but she had plenty of time for questions, which were numerous, perhaps unsurprisingly.
The first was about where direction came from in a flat structure; how are decisions made about what she should work on? That depends on the project, Yang said, some are closely aligned with the engineers at the client company, while other projects are less hands-on. When working with the client's engineers, the direction likely comes from the client side as in a more typical organization. Sometimes projects are more open-ended, where the client agrees to pay for work on a specific task for, say, a year to see where things end up; in that case, the Igalia team decides on what to tackle.
Another attendee wondered what it was that Igalia's clients needed done with Chromium. Once again, it varies, she said. Her project is cleaning up the testing, which is something that Google wants and it does not fit anywhere in its team. Other clients want customized browsers for internal use, so parts of the Igalia Chromium team are also working on downstream projects.
The hiring process was up next. One attendee wondered how Igalia decided that it needed to hire for a position and how the person to hire was chosen. " Which teams get headcount is decided at a company level ", she said, so if the Chromium team wants to hire, it makes a pitch to the assembly, which is the voting body. If that is approved, the team will interview candidates and choose who it thinks should be hired, which goes back to the assembly. Normally, that choice will be approved unless there is some red flag that someone elsewhere in the company is aware of. Yang reminded attendees that she was still fairly new at Igalia, but that there were other employees sitting in on the talk who might chime in to help clarify things; in this case she just got a thumbs up from them, she said.
Having 180 employees in a flat structure already sounds a bit unwieldy, an attendee noted, is there a size where Igalia will essentially be forced into a hierarchical structure just because of its size? Yang said that she asked the same thing when she was interviewing, " everyone agreed that this is definitely an issue but there's not a clear solution yet ". Her partner suggested that honeybees might provide a reasonable model of how a split could be done; when a hive gets too big, part of the hive leaves as a swarm to found a new hive.
An employee at another employee-owned coop suggested that there were synergies between open source and cooperatives, which might help when the time comes to split up. He wondered if there were plans for Igalia to release its internal tools and coop-operating documents as open source, which could facilitate a new, separate company if that was needed. Yang noted that her coworker Danielle Mayabb had a session in the next slot about running the company using FOSS tools.
A researcher who studied companies with flat structures asked whether some of the organizational structure came back into the picture within the different teams. The teams are responsible for decisions like whether to take a project or not, Yang said, and there are product managers that coordinate between teams. The product managers work closely with clients, but they have no inherent extra power, like a manager at a typical job.
Along the way, she had said that she was not yet part of the assembly, so an attendee asked how that worked, how long it took, whether a vote was needed, and so on. Yang recommended the video of a talk by Valerie Young at the first FOSSY in 2023, which goes into more detail. Yang said that somewhere around the one-year mark it would be decided whether an employee would join the assembly, though she did not specify exactly how that was done. " If you've done an exceptionally bad job, you won't be permitted in. "
That was a good segue to the next question, which was about what would prevent an employee in the coop from just ceasing to work. In a flat hierarchy, who is monitoring what employees are doing? Can someone just stop working without detection? She joked that she would give it a try and come back next year with a talk on that. More seriously, there are people who are providing feedback on the performance of their coworkers; each person has a mentor in the company who fills some of the roles of a manager at other companies, including gathering assessments of the work that is being done. " People are monitoring your performance and it is a collection of all of the people that you work with. "
An attendee noted that there is a saying in the coop movement: " If you've seen one coop, you've seen one coop. " That is why it is so helpful for coops to share their internal structure; as with open-source software, other coops can learn from the trial and error that went into forming the coop. Yang noted that there used to be a coop track at FOSSY and that there was talk of bringing it back for next year.

I've looked around at the Igalia web site a few times in the past from the viewpoint of "oh cool, a company of contractors who value upstreaming". But as a system engineer/integrator and not a software engineer, I fear I will only get to peek in from the outside. Definitely an interesting concept. Thanks for the article and thanks to Sharon for the talk! Intruiging... Posted Oct 1, 2026 19:39 UTC (Thu) by timchevalier (guest, #186877) [ Link ] I'm an Igalian and we do have an internal systems and tools team that sometimes has openings for more systems-focused and less software-development-focused work. You can watch https://www.igalia.com/jobs/ to see if they're hiring! Otherwise, I encourage you to consider starting your own cooperative. Another Igalian, Valerie Young, gave a talk on Igalia's structure that some people have found interesting: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=du7fC8VCbXg . Mondragon Posted Sep 30, 2026 23:46 UTC (Wed) by NightMonkey (subscriber, #23051) [ Link ] (1 responses) The folks at Igalia most likely already know and have studied one of the largest and most successful Worker's Cooperative in the world: Mondragon: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mondragon_Corporation While it is *still* capitalism, the Worker's Cooperative model at least gives workers the ability to steer the corporate ship. Whether the ship sails or sinks or grounds itself is then up to the workers who produce the products it offers... Nonprofits in Capitalism Posted Oct 2, 2026 19:45 UTC (Fri) by linuxrocks123 (subscriber, #34648) [ Link ] I have done some research and have some thoughts on the efficiency of nonprofit entities relative to businesses. This is a controversial topic, so I am posting those thoughts elsewhere: https://soylentnews.org/~linuxrocks123/journal/20699 I would encourage discussing this topic over there rather than over here. Hierarchies aren't magic Posted Oct 1, 2026 2:13 UTC (Thu) by kleptog (subscriber, #1183) [ Link ] (3 responses) > In a flat hierarchy, who is monitoring what employees are doing? A hierarchy doesn't save you here. IME managers are not very good at noticing when people aren't actually doing their work. And even if they do notice, they're not actually empowered to do anything about it. So you get a focus on metrics that don't actually measure what's important, and people get good at manipulating the metrics to make themselves look good. 180 seems like the kind of size where you can basically know everyone there and have a good feeling who is doing their job and not, without having to rely on stupid metrics. Coops are definitely an interesting model for open source. Hierarchies aren't magic Posted Oct 1, 2026 6:21 UTC (Thu) by ssmith32 (subscriber, #72404) [ Link ] (1 responses) Indeed. I once worked at a company where a QE went a year just marking everything as "pass". The manager didn't clue in - another QE did. Hierarchies aren't magic Posted Oct 5, 2026 23:53 UTC (Mon) by noahm (subscriber, #40155) [ Link ] I had a corporate job once where a new manager was hired for my team. He basically ghosted us shortly after getting hired. He showed up once bringing some small gifts for his new reports, and promptly vanished. It was a remote role, so we didn't expect to see much of him, but he seemed really slow to respond to email. It took a while for the company to catch on and finally fire him. A bit of research into his employment history revealed that this was basically his MO.
