title: Millions spent on Patriarch’s funeral: scandal involving Georgia’s former culture minister Tinatin Rukhadze
body: Scandal involving former officials in Georgia On 14 October 2026, Davit Okitashvili, a supporter of the Georgian Dream party, publicly accused former Culture Minister Tinatin Rukhadze of misusing funds allocated for the funeral of the Patriarch of Georgia and called on the prosecutor’s office to launch an investigation. Okitashvili also criticised former State Security Service chief Mamuka Mdinaradze, whom he described as Rukhadze’s political patron. Other Georgian Dream supporters also responded to Okitashvili’s allegations. Opposition figures believe such attacks on former senior officials may be intended to pave the way for their arrests. How much did the Patriarch’s funeral cost? Patriarch Ilia II was buried on 22 March 2026. The government allocated a total of 5.59 million lari to organise the funeral, distributing the funds among six government agencies. The largest share — 3 million lari — went to the Ministry of Culture, which Tinatin Rukhadze headed at the time. It later emerged that the authorities had not spent more than half of the allocated funds. On 8 May, the government revised the funding to reflect actual expenditure, reducing the total to 2.56 million lari. Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations From ‘crown prince’ to prisoner: Irakli Garibashvili’s break with Georgia’s ruling party Patriarch’s funeral: farewell ceremony of unprecedented scale in Tbilisi. Photos/videos The Ministry of Culture spent just 722,600 lari of the 3 million lari originally allocated to it. The remaining 2.28 million lari went unspent. However, it remains unclear exactly how the ministry spent the 722,600 lari: who received the money, what services they provided and how transparently the ministry selected contractors. September: first questions and the prime minister’s response Questions about spending on the Patriarch’s funeral emerged in September, following an investigative report by the Pirveli television channel. Acting Culture Minister Mikheil Kiknadze initially said that the audit documents reflected the shortcomings investigators had identified. However, he later added: “I did not say that there had been any violations.” Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also commented on the issue on 14 September. He said the Ministry of Culture had spent only 722,000 lari of the 3 million lari allocated to it. “If anyone had wanted to steal the money, they could easily have taken all three million,” Kobakhidze said. He also made the following promise: “This is preliminary information. I will examine the matter in greater detail and provide the public with a detailed account.” The Patriarchate defends Rukhadze On 16 September, Archpriest Andria Jaghmaidze, head of the Patriarchate’s public relations service, issued a statement. He said the Patriarchate had known from the outset that a significant portion of the money allocated for the funeral would remain unspent. “During that period, we were in frequent contact with Ms Tika Rukhadze, and we knew from her that most organisations and individuals who provided various services had declined any remuneration or payment,” Jaghmaidze wrote. He expressed hope that people would stop using the Patriarch’s name as a pretext for unfounded accusations and slander. What links Tika Rukhadze to Tikhart? According to Transparency International Georgia , Tinatin Rukhadze earned 410,000 lari as a consultant for Tikhart, an event management company, in the two years before she became culture minister. The organisation also reports that Tikhart secured government contracts worth a total of 3.8 million lari through direct procurement, bypassing competitive tenders. These circumstances raise questions about whether the company also received payment for organising the Patriarch’s funeral. However, no publicly available information confirms that it did. Transparency International Georgia has called on the Ministry of Culture to disclose who received the 722,600 lari spent on the funeral and specify which services they provided. Another problem is that the government does not have to disclose procurement information for purchases financed through the government’s reserve fund. This makes it harder for the public to scrutinise how the authorities spend public money. The minister’s resignation and a new political climate Tinatin Rukhadze became culture minister in October 2024. On 28 July 2026, she left the post, citing health reasons. No evidence has established a link between her resignation and the allegations concerning funeral expenditure. On 15 September, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Maia Bitadze, a Georgian Dream MP, as culture minister, specifically praising her integrity. Around the same time, Mamuka Mdinaradze also left his political post as head of the State Security Service. Rukhadze and Mdinaradze subsequently became targets of coordinated public attacks. October: accusations from a Georgian Dream supporter On 14 October, Davit Okitashvili, president of the Georgian Chamber of Culture and an active Georgian Dream supporter, publicly accused Tinatin Rukhadze of obstructing his projects and damaging his reputation. He also described Mamuka Mdinaradze as the former minister’s patron. Okitashvili raised questions about the cost of the Patriarch’s funeral and called on the prosecutor’s office and the State Audit Office to investigate the spending. In a post, he asked Rukhadze: “Ms Tika, where did the millions go?!” Other Georgian Dream representatives supported Okitashvili’s post, including party activist and MP Dimitri Samkharadze. What does Mamuka Mdinaradze have to do with it? Okitashvili did not limit his attacks to the former culture minister. He claimed that Mamuka Mdinaradze had acted as Rukhadze’s political patron. According to Okitashvili, Mdinaradze helped secure her appointment as minister, and she subsequently acted under his influence. In an interview with Palitranews on 15 October, Okitashvili repeated these allegations. He also claimed that both Rukhadze and Mdinaradze had betrayed Georgian Dream. However, he noted that the prosecutor’s office had not contacted him. Georgian Dream representatives also responded to Okitashvili’s accusations. MP Tengiz Sharmanashvili said the prosecutor’s office should ask Okitashvili what evidence he had. If his claims proved credible, investigators should question those involved, including Rukhadze and Mdinaradze. Opposition warns of possible arrests The opposition also reacted to the October developments. Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Okitashvili’s statements might be intended to prepare the public for the possible arrests of Tinatin Rukhadze and Mamuka Mdinaradze. Gvaramia suggested that Bidzina Ivanishvili could be behind the process. Ana Tsitlidze, a representative of the United National Movement, accused Rukhadze and Bakur Bakuradze, the former director general of Rustavi 2, of embezzling funds allocated for the Patriarch’s funeral. She also suggested that authorities might arrest Mamuka Mdinaradze. Former MP Eka Beselia suspected that Okitashvili’s statement might form part of a pre-planned process. She said that if an investigation began immediately after his statement, it would confirm her suspicions. Scandal involving former officials in Georgia

title: Ben-Gvir plans to change IDF ethics code, emphasize 'Jewish values,' if named defense minister
body: National Security Minister and chairman of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, Itamar Ben-Gvir, unveiled a plan to change the IDF's Code of Ethics if he is named the new defense minister. The proposed changes, presented as part of Ben-Gvir's plan for the Defense Ministry in a Thursday statement, would significantly revise the IDF's ethical framework, known as "The Spirit of the IDF," with the stated goal of strengthening the military's Jewish identity and emphasizing victory in battle.This would include replacing the principle of "Purity of Arms" with "Righteousness of Arms" and placing greater emphasis on Jewish values, military victory, and the defeat of Israel's enemies.Under the proposal, the IDF's main objective would be defined as achieving victory and decisively defeating the enemies of the State of Israel and the Jewish people, alongside maintaining national security. The proposal would also expand the sources from which the IDF derives its values, placing greater emphasis on Jewish moral values ​​rooted in the Bible, Jewish ethics, Jewish law, and the traditions of the Jewish people.It would further define Israel as the Jewish people's national home and the IDF as a "Jewish, state-run army."'Purity of Arms' to be replaced with 'Righteousness of Arms'One of the proposed changes concerns the principle of "Purity of Arms," which Ben-Gvir seeks to remove from the IDF Code of Ethics and replace with "Righteousness of Arms."The revised code would explicitly establish the principle "If someone comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first" as a fundamental moral guideline for soldiers carrying out their missions.At the same time, the proposal removes language in the existing code requiring soldiers to use force "only to the extent necessary."It also removes explicit provisions prohibiting harm to "non-combatants" and prisoners of war.In addition, all references to "universal moral values" which appeared in the existing version would be removed from the new code.Revised framework of core IDF valuesThe proposal sets out a revised framework of core IDF values, beginning with the military's purpose and continuing with its commitment to the Jewish people, human dignity, and its role as a state institution."The purpose of the IDF is to achieve victory and decisively defeat the enemies of the State of Israel and the Jewish people, while safeguarding the security of the state, its citizens, and its residents," the proposal states as the IDF's mission. It continued, stating that "service in the IDF is founded on love for the Jewish people and the homeland, as well as commitment and dedication to the State of Israel, a Jewish state that serves as the democratic national home of the Jewish people, and to its citizens and residents."The revised ethics code included that "the IDF and its soldiers are committed to preserving human dignity. Every person possesses inherent worth, regardless of origin, religion, nationality, gender, status, or position."Lastly, the proposal emphasized that the IDF is "the people's army, a Jewish and state-oriented military subject to the authority of the law and the government."Under this principle, IDF soldiers are expected to place their mission, the military's values, and the security of the state above all other considerations while carrying out their duties with integrity, professionalism, and conduct appropriate to their role as representatives of the IDF.

title: Viral Muslim Tourist ‘Attacks’ Greece Over No Halal and Mosque Options
body: A Muslim tourist has sparked an online debate after posting a viral video in which he advises other Muslims against visiting Greece, claiming he didn’t find a mosque or halal food during a holiday on a Greek island. The solo traveller , who said he had recently returned from Morocco, complained that he could find only one restaurant offering halal food during his stay. He also questioned whether he could trust the establishment because it operated as a bar as well as a restaurant. “Don’t make this mistake. If you’re Muslim, don’t go to Greece,” he said in the video, which has attracted international attention . The video also reached the United States, where a Newsforce presenter criticised the tourist’s complaint. “There are 55 Muslim countries where you can eat halal. In Greece, they make delicious pork gyros, not halal,” the presenter said, before making an insulting remark about the tourist. The video prompted a wave of comments from Greek and international social media users, many of whom supported Greece’s culinary traditions and challenged the traveller’s criticism. “Thank you very much for your post. You saved us the trouble of banning you from anywhere in our country, by asking your Muslim colleagues to ban themselves from entering! You’re doing us a great favour!” one commenter wrote. Another user, identifying as Greek, simply commented: “As a Greek, I agree. Don’t come.” A third compared the complaint to seeking pork in Saudi Arabia, writing: “It’s like looking for pork in Saudi Arabia. Don’t go; you have nothing to do in Greece.” Another international user welcomed the video, writing: “I’m sure the people of Greece would hope for more videos like this.” Full Transcript: “Never go to Greece as a Muslim. So I had just come back from Morocco and I was like, let me go on a solo trip, one man up to Greece. And I went to an island in Greece and basically the whole time I just stayed up. “The reason why is because in this island, number one, there’s no masjids (mosques) in the whole island. Number two, there’s no halal food in the whole island. Literally the only “halal” food that I found was some restaurant that was a bar at the same time. “So how can I trust that? I was literally eating Margherita pizza the whole time. Number three, I was thinking this is going to be a good detox location. It’s an island, there’s the beach, I can just chill, go swimming. How can it be more busy and more loud than anywhere in London? Turns out I just landed in an island full of English people. “I’ll be honest, never again in my life. You know, I genuinely don’t understand how people enjoy this life. If you’re going to travel, go do things. How can you go on holiday to go to the exact same place that you left, but just as a party area? Never again. If you’re Muslim, never go to these islands.” The post Viral Muslim Tourist ‘Attacks’ Greece Over No Halal and Mosque Options appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Thank You, Deno
body:
Deno is joining Cloudflare & winding down its investment in the runtime. We're all better off because of its existence.
Ryan Dahl announced last week that the Deno team is joining Cloudflare. The Deno runtime winds down over the next year, JSR keeps running on Cloudflare's infrastructure, & the team's new job, per Cloudflare's post , is merging Deno's celld into workerd .
The announcement came two years to the day after Deno 2 shipped. Bun joined Anthropic ten months ago. The tempting conclusion is that the alternative-runtime experiment is over & Node has won by default. In reality, the ecosystem has gotten the benefits Deno was pushing, just not from Deno itself.
Unfortunately, Deno never really hit critical mass in production; Node is as dominant in 2026 as it was in 2018. What Deno did achieve was to reinvigorate & put pressure on the incumbent, & that pressure didn't only run one way.
Deno started as a clean break. Ryan stood up at JSConf EU in 2018 & listed what he'd do differently from Node: deny-by-default permissions, TypeScript as a first-class input, web-standard APIs on the server, ES modules only, a single executable. And, pointedly, no npm , no package.json & no node_modules . Dependencies were URLs. The slides put it plainly: "There is no need to list dependencies."
A lot of us who'd spent years on npm & Node were skeptical of that last part (not the permissions or the TypeScript, which were obviously good) & said so at the time. We'd been there before, in the hotlinking era, when every page pulled jquery.min.js off somebody else's server & broke when it moved or got compromised. A URL tells you where something was, not what it is. Once you care that the bytes you tested are the bytes you ship, you need an integrity hash & somewhere to record it, & you've reinvented the lockfile. Matteo Collina of the Node TSC said in 2020 that "another left-pad incident is waiting to happen, but this time there is no 'central entity' that can fix it." Some of this skepticism was defensive but happened to be right in the end.
Deno 1.0 shipped in 2020 on the original terms, & then spent the next four years walking them back one piece at a time. First the deps.ts convention, one file that re-exported every URL: a manifest in all but name. Then lock.json , an integrity hash per URL: a lockfile. Then import maps, so you could write bare specifiers again. Deno's own documentation today recommends registries over HTTPS imports because they "can drift to different versions across files" & "trust the serving host." Those were the objections from 2018, restated as guidance.
Then Bun showed up. Bun 0.1 was released in July 2022 with the opposite bet: rebuild the toolchain from scratch for speed, but run existing npm packages, read package.json & act as a drop-in replacement for node . About six weeks later, Deno published "Big Changes Ahead for Deno" , announcing npm: specifiers, a commitment to make 80–90% of npm packages work within three months & a new goal of being "the fastest JavaScript runtime." Deno credited user feedback for the shift; the timing suggests Bun was a large part of it. Deno 2 , in October 2024, finished the job with full Node & npm compatibility. Four years after launching as the alternative to Node's ecosystem, Deno had become another way to run it.
That was the right call, & it was also an admission that the ecosystem wasn't going to abandon over a decade's worth of dependencies overnight. Cloudflare's workerd , which it open-sourced in 2022 , grew its own Node compatibility layer for the same reason: that's where the packages are.
Node ended up needing to respond. Since 2018 it has shipped a global fetch , WebSocket , Web Streams & Web Crypto; a stable test runner & --watch ; --env-file & single-executable builds; a stable permission model ; type stripping on by default; node:sqlite ; & require(esm) . Node's contributors (many volunteers) did the hard work to listen & make big changes, & they deserve a ton of credit for it, but I don't think it happens on that timeline without three other runtimes shipping many of these ideas first. A mature open source project rarely lacks good ideas. It lacks urgency, & competitors supply that urgency.
The standards work came out of the same pressure: WinterCG formed in 2022 because several serious runtimes made "what's the minimum common API?" a practical question, & now, as Ecma TC55 , it should outlast whichever runtimes consolidate next.
For most of its history the JavaScript package ecosystem was a monoculture: one client, one registry, & an API contract informal enough that it stayed effectively undocumented for a decade & a half. Nearly every improvement since came from someone refusing to accept the status quo.
Yarn (2016) insisted installs be deterministic & gave us the lockfile, workspaces & an offline cache; npm 5 shipped package-lock.json the next year. pnpm showed that node_modules didn't have to be hundreds of megabytes of duplicated files. Bun made install fast enough that the incumbents had to revisit their performance. Deno argued you should be able to read a dependency's source before you take it, & while URL imports didn't last, that idea did.
The clearest recent example is install scripts. pnpm & Bun stopped running them by default; vlt never did . The argument had been made inside npm for the entire time I worked there without ever becoming the default. In June of this year, after a run of supply-chain worms, GitHub announced that npm 12 would stop running them by default too. Nothing about the idea changed in those years; enough other package managers shipped it that npm could no longer treat it as radical. The pressure runs in both directions too: we borrowed catalogs from pnpm, & pnpm's namedRegistries borrowed our named-registry aliases.
On the registry side, JSR deserves credit. It made a different set of bets than we did: publish TypeScript source, require ESM, generate docs from code. We disagreed with parts of it & added jsr: support to vlt anyway because our users asked for it. It survives the wind-down because, as far as I can tell, it's cheap to run, its API is documented, & Cloudflare had a reason to keep it alive.
The two most popular independent, venture-backed JavaScript runtimes now live inside companies whose business is something else. Jarred Sumner said the Bun team's relationship with the Claude Code team "probably will look similar to the relationship between Google Chrome <> V8," with more independence, & Cloudflare's post makes clear that workerd's roadmap is Cloudflare's. That's how JavaScriptCore & V8 have always been funded, & it's still a change.
Whether a community fork of the Deno runtime emerges will tell us whether the ecosystem values a secure-by-default, standards-first runtime enough to pay for one that isn't attached to a cloud. And celld-into-workerd is new optionality at a layer that has had very little: a self-hostable, open implementation of Workers & Durable Objects, led by Ryan & Bert Belder.
JavaScript has insurance at almost every layer: three production engines, several runtimes, several package managers. When one layer consolidates, as the runtime layer is doing now, the others hold. The churn that makes this possible is also what people complain about most. "JavaScript fatigue" has been a running joke for a decade: a new framework every week, a new bundler every month, & yet another package manager, which, yes, I'm aware I've contributed to. But nobody had to leave Node to get fetch , a permission model or TypeScript without a build step, & nobody has to switch package managers to get install scripts turned off by default anymore. Those things showed up in the tools people were already using because someone else shipped them first & the incumbent had to answer. The projects didn't always win, but the ideas usually did, & end-users collected them either way.
To Ryan, Bert, Bartek & the rest of the Deno team (past & present): your collective efforts have enriched our shared ecosystem. Thank you!

title: RPKI now protects 70% of internet routes
body:
Start using accurate IP data for cybersecurity, compliance, and personalization—no limits, no cost.
(Update, October 29, 2026: a country-by-country view of the address figures in this post is now in our RPKI report .)
The Internet relies on networks telling each other which IP addresses they can deliver traffic to, using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol). These routing announcements have historically depended heavily on trust. When a network announces addresses it shouldn’t, accidentally or deliberately, traffic can be sent to the wrong place and services can become unreachable.
On February 24, 2008, Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) tried to block YouTube inside Pakistan by announcing a more specific route for YouTube's addresses. Its upstream provider, PCCW Global (AS3491), accepted the announcement and passed it to the rest of the Internet, redirecting YouTube traffic to Pakistan globally for roughly two hours ( RIPE NCC's case study ). Work on RPKI, which lets networks reject announcements like that one, had started at the IETF two years earlier, and the regional Internet registries began issuing RPKI certificates in 2011.
RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) lets the holder of a block of IP addresses publish a signed record, a Route Origin Authorization (ROA), naming the networks (Autonomous Systems, or ASes) allowed to announce it. Network operators that check RPKI compare announcements against those records and can reject the ones that fail.
We looked at a year of IPinfo’s daily RPKI data to see how much of the Internet it now protects, and where it falls short. What we found (TL;DR):
In August, the Internet Society Pulse found RPKI-related activity accounts for under 1% of daily BGP update volume, a share that is rising but still small, so RPKI is not itself destabilizing routing. We wanted to know whether RPKI was actually protecting Internet routing.
Routes with an RPKI record and routes with none travel equally far: a typical one is seen by 596 and 595 vantage points. Routes that fail the check are seen by just two. Now that enough networks check, they are dropping these invalid routes. Nearly half of all invalid routes reach only a single vantage point. When the wrong network announces the addresses, the clearest kind of hijack or mistake, 71% reach only one.
This changes how country-level RPKI statistics should be read. A country can look bad because of announcements almost nobody sees.
Simply counting invalid routes can badly exaggerate how much of a country is affected. Spain has the highest share of invalid IPv4 prefixes at 28.2%. Count the addresses in those routes instead, weighted by how many vantage points see each one, and it falls to 0.057%. Slovakia falls from 17.4% to almost zero. Italy has the highest figure of any country with at least a million IPv4 addresses, 0.121%, up from 0.075% a year ago, and 90% of it is one network.
WIND TRE (AS1267) announces 34 routes in its own address space that its own ROAs don't allow: 19 are more specific than the ROAs permit, and 15 come from AS1267 while the ROA names WIND TRE's other network, AS24608. None reaches more than 77 vantage points, against about 617 for the signed blocks around them.
Counted by IPv4 addresses on September 28 each year, the share in RPKI-valid routes rose from 42.7% in 2023 to 47.9% in 2024, 53.1% in 2025 and 65.0% in 2026. The last jump was 11.9 points, against about five in each previous year.
Removing China shows how much of that was one country. Outside China, the share rose from 58.0% to 63.2%, a 5.2-point gain, a little less than the year before.
China’s change was also sudden: 3.7% of its IPv4 addresses were in valid routes in September 2025, and 83.0% a year later. Most of that happened this year: at the end of December 2025, just 2.9% of China's routed prefixes were valid. It also changed which way it moves the world figure. In 2025 China pulled the global average down: 53.1% worldwide against 58.0% without China. In 2026 it pushed it up: 65.0% against 63.2%. Others moved a long way too: Egypt from 23% to 99%, Kazakhstan from 16% to 84%, Mexico from 37% to 78%, and South Africa from 38% to 60%.
Where the unprotected addresses are is just as concentrated. Of all routed IPv4 space not in RPKI-valid routes on September 28, nearly 60% is in the United States, and about one in four addresses belongs to the US Department of Defense (more on who holds IPv4 in an upcoming post). Most of that is space the Department began announcing in 2021 to watch for misuse, not to run services.
In early 2025 there were concerns that IPv6 adoption of RPKI was slowing. Instead, it accelerated and has now overtaken IPv4. In RPKI's 2024 year in review for RIPE Labs, Job Snijders noted IPv6 ROA growth "seems to be stalling." Over our window, IPv6 routed prefixes marked valid rose from 56% to 79% while IPv4 prefixes rose from 54% to 68%, putting IPv6 roughly ten points ahead. The Hurricane Electric RPKI report shows the same ordering.
Two other metrics he flagged also changed: the average number of address blocks per ROA climbed back from 2.31 at the end of December to 2.62, and publication points, which he counted falling from 63 to 53 and read as consolidation, rose from 73 to 91 as more organizations began hosting their own repositories instead of relying on their registry.
RPKI validates who may originate a prefix. It does not validate the path, and it cannot catch an attacker who stays inside the permission you published, so it's not bulletproof.
On August 28, 2026, a route for 162.55.80.0/24 (a block of 256 addresses) appeared with Hetzner's AS24940 forged as the origin. Hetzner's ROA covered the surrounding /16, a block 256 times larger, and allowed announcements as small as a /24, so the forged route satisfied it. The route was RPKI-valid, no legitimate /24 existed to compete with it, and longest-prefix-match meant everyone preferred it. That was enough to obtain a genuine TLS certificate and serve a malicious Virtualizor update to hypervisors, as documented by Kentik .
We measured how common that posture is. Of 855,217 RPKI-covered IPv4 routes, 138,698, or 16.2%, have a ROA looser than the route announced and no more-specific route of their own filling the gap. For IPv6 it is 20.9%. That leaves roughly 18 million more-specific prefixes an attacker could announce today, forge the origin, and come out RPKI-valid and uncontested.
Operators in the same business make very different choices here. Among hosting providers, Contabo has an open window on 540 of 553 covered routes and DigitalOcean on 780 of 863, while OVH sits at 11.5%. Access providers are worse still: Cablevision at 98.1%, Shaw at 96.5%, Bharti Airtel at 85.0%.
RFC 9319 already says the best practice is to leave maxLength unset. maxLength is the setting that lets a ROA also cover smaller blocks inside it, so leaving it unset means a ROA matches only the block actually announced. Hetzner tightened three prefixes after the incident, including the one that was hijacked, though 49 of its 63 covered routes remain open.
RPKI coverage can also disappear without causing an outage. A missing ROA simply removes the protection, and nobody notices unless they look. We found several cases where that happened over the past year.
Unlike China, Mauritius saw its RPKI coverage fall. The share of its IPv4 addresses in valid routes fell from 94.0% to 69.0% between September 2025 and September 2026. SEACOM (AS37100) lost four of its six ROAs on January 1. One covered 105.16.0.0/12, a block of about a million addresses, 46% of which are in Mauritius. That block alone explains Mauritius's drop, and it still had no ROA on September 28.
Two other operators show the same thing happening and then being fixed. Saudi Telecom (AS25019) lost RPKI protection on 19 routes, including six large blocks totaling about 1.6 million addresses, when the ROAs for those six blocks disappeared between March 30 and April 13. Saudi Arabia's coverage recovered when the ROAs came back on September 21 and 22.
In Morocco, Orange Maroc (AS36925) is the only large operator that publishes ROAs, and most of them went missing twice: from July 2025 to July 2026, and again from July 25 to September 3. Morocco went from 20% covered to almost none, and back.
Depending on how you check, an RPKI record can look broken while it is still protecting its routes. We ran into this while counting.
Every signed record carries a link to the certificate above it. When an operator moves its repository, that link can go stale, and a check that inspects records one by one will report a hard failure. But the validation that actually produces the list routers use never follows that link, it walks down from the trust anchors instead.
We found thousands of records flagged as failed that were present in every independently validated set we checked, with their routes still RPKI-valid. So if you are reading anyone's RPKI numbers, including ours, it is worth knowing which of the two they counted. A count of failing records is not a measure of lost protection.
ROAs secure the origin of a route. They say nothing about whether the path used to reach that origin makes sense.
ASPA, or Autonomous System Provider Authorization, addresses that. A network publishes a signed record naming its authorized upstream providers, which lets others check observed AS paths against them and catch route leaks that origin validation misses.
Deployment is early but fast. On September 28, 2025, 131 networks had published ASPA records. By September 28, 2026 there were 3,272, 25 times as many.
The growth comes in steps rather than a curve. RIPE NCC sat at about 85 networks from September to late November, then climbed to 470 by the end of December. ARIN stepped up from January 21, APNIC at the end of June and again in September, when its count nearly doubled. Each jump follows a registry making ASPA signing available, so tooling has been the main driver. One detail worth highlighting: APNIC announced its support on July 9 , and its curve started climbing on June 26.
That coverage is now enough to ask the better question: how much of observed routing is ASPA-valid?
On September 28, 2026, 9.7% of observed routing passed ASPA checks, up from 6.2% a year earlier. Most of that is automatic: under the draft rules, a path through only one or two networks always passes, and those short paths were about 6% of routing in both years.
Take them out and the records networks have published verify about 3.5% of routing, up from roughly 0.1%.
Almost all the rest is not failing. It is unknown, because too few networks along those paths have published records to tell. In practice, ASPA can check only a small slice of routing today, and that slice grows with every network that publishes a record.
Of the paths that can be judged, those breaking ASPA’s rules mid-path, the signal a collector can read with most confidence, rose from effectively zero to 0.048% of observations. That is not necessarily routing getting worse: a path can only be called invalid once enough of it has declared providers, so as publication grew, paths that were previously unjudgeable became testable and some failed.
Attributing those failures needs care, because the gap sits mid-path: one provider with a stale record makes every one of its customers' routes look invalid, so ranking by origin blames the wrong party.
Attribute to the hop instead and the networks at the top are the ones doing it right. Cogent, Arelion, and GTT each declare AS0, which says they buy transit from nobody. That is true, and it is exactly what stops a stale record further down the path from hiding as "no attestation." The real gaps are smaller: of 3,272 networks publishing ASPA records, 479 have upstream providers visible in our routing data that they never declared, across 658 missing relationships.
The largest single cause is one operator. Syrian Telecom (AS29386) publishes a record naming four carriers. Three of them carry just 16% of the transit we observe through it, and the fourth carries none. The four carriers that handle the other 84% are missing from the record, so about 40% of paths arriving through them fail the check, and the rest come out unknown.
Through Syrian Telecom's own routes and those of two Syrian networks that reach the Internet through it, that record accounts for 21% of all mid-path ASPA failures on the Internet. Another 3 points come from AS201550, a second Syrian Telecom network whose record copies the same four carriers instead of naming the Syrian Telecom networks it connects through. So the global ASPA failure rate is not yet a measure of the Internet’s health: about a quarter of it comes from one operator’s incomplete records.
Eighteen years after PCCW Global passed on Pakistan Telecom's announcement for YouTube's addresses, PCCW is a gap in the newer system. ASPA would not have stopped the 2008 incident; RPKI's origin check is what covers that. But ASPA lets others check PCCW's place in a path, and AS3491 has not published a record. That breaks nothing on its own. Still, nearly 6,000 paths crossing PCCW read ASPA-invalid today, because networks below it publish records that leave PCCW out.
RPKI now protects most Internet routes, and invalid routes barely travel. The gaps that remain are mostly in the hands of the networks that own the addresses:
IPinfo tracks the RPKI status of every routed prefix daily: ipinfo.io/data/rpki .
Methodology : All figures come from IPinfo’s daily routing and RPKI data, comparing September 28 of each year unless stated. Routing data comes from the public RIPE RIS and RouteViews collectors. A route’s reach is the number of their BGP peers (vantage points) that carry it, and reach figures are medians. “RPKI-valid” means a route matches the validated set of ROAs that routers use, not the status of individual records. Country figures use IPv4 only and count addresses: each route is split across countries using IPinfo geolocation (the current mapping for every year), each address is counted once, and it counts as covered if any valid route includes it. In Chart 3, the prefix share uses each prefix’s first address, and the weighted share multiplies each route’s addresses by its reach. The maxLength figures cover routes seen by at least two vantage points. ASPA figures are weighted by how often each route is observed, and the 0.048% counts failures in the middle of a path only.
João Tomé is an Internet Data Research Editor at IPinfo, finding trends and stories about how the Internet works and changes. He has a background in journalism, data storytelling, and podcasting, including five years at Cloudflare. joaotome.com

title: Israel Returns Stolen Greek Artefacts as Athens Intensifies Parthenon Sculptures Campaign
body: Israel has returned 22 ancient Greek artefacts that were illegally removed from the country, marking the first such repatriation between the two nations. The handover took place on 13 October at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. Culture Minister Lina Mendoni received the objects from Israeli Ambassador Pninat Yanay. The collection includes 15 Attic vessels, six Corinthian vases and a small bronze female statuette dating mainly from the Archaic and Classical periods. Israeli authorities seized the items in 2020 during an investigation into illegal antiquities trafficking. Mendoni called the return a landmark that strengthens cooperation against cultural trafficking and carries symbolic weight. “Every return of a cultural object to its place of origin has a broader symbolic and moral dimension,” she said. The repatriation coincides with Athens intensifying its campaign for the permanent return of the Parthenon sculptures from the British Museum. Greece continues to reject loan or rotation proposals and presents successful returns such as this one as evidence that cultural heritage belongs in its country of origin. title: EU Climate Policy to 2040: Initial Steps towards More Flexibility and Effort Sharing
body: By setting a 90 per cent emissions reduction target for 2040, the European Union (EU) has taken a key step forward. This decision marks the start of a substantial realignment of its core climate policy instruments. The Commission’s implementation package is expected to comprise more than a dozen legislative proposals, the final form of which is to be negotiated by the Council and the European Parliament. The proposals include, among other items, the crediting of emission reductions from international mitigation projects within the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), the further development of rules governing land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF) and the integration of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) into EU climate policy. Moreover, a political decision is needed on the future role of national targets within the EU’s climate policy architecture. Although the EU can still be regarded as a frontrunner at the global level, given its 90 per cent emissions reduction target, the inclusion of flexibilities in achieving this target creates uncertainties that significantly undermine the credibility and effectiveness of EU climate policy. It is therefore crucial that the Commission promptly presents its detailed proposals on international carbon credits and on updating the overall regulatory framework.

title: When it came to Cal AI’s viral success, a small army of influencers paid off
body:
Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.
Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.
Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.
“From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.”
The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”
Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.
Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much.
“I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter.
Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million .
Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app.

title: Lavrov Rules Out Ukraine War Ceasefire
body:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov ruled out a ceasefire in Ukraine and accused President Volodymyr Zelensky of directly challenging US President Donald Trump over Washington’s controversial diesel deal with Moscow during a press conference in Baku on Thursday, Oct. 15.
Speaking after the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), Lavrov said Russia would not agree to a pause in fighting that could allow Ukraine to replenish its military capabilities.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“There will be no ceasefire” that would allow Zelensky to be rearmed, Lavrov said, according to Interfax .
He was responding to a question about whether Moscow would consider concessions in future peace negotiations if Ukraine held presidential elections.
Lavrov claimed Zelensky had imposed deliberately unacceptable conditions for holding elections, portraying the Ukrainian leader as unwilling to pursue a political settlement.
The Russian minister also attacked Zelensky’s opposition to a recent US-Russia agreement easing sanctions on Russian diesel, describing the Ukrainian president’s position as a direct confrontation with Trump.
“This is a direct challenge to President Trump, who actively supported this deal and has spoken about it publicly on more than one occasion,” Lavrov said.
The remarks came as Kyiv defended its campaign against Russian oil refineries, which Ukraine considers legitimate military-economic targets because of their role in sustaining Moscow’s war effort.
Lavrov’s statements also underscored Moscow’s continued rejection of an unconditional halt to fighting.
Lavrov also dismissed prospects for a negotiated settlement under current conditions, saying Western proposals had moved away from understandings reached during the August 2025 summit between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Anchorage, Alaska.
“After Anchorage, there has been a constant retreat of Western initiatives and ideas toward positions that only move us further away from a sustainable peace, or at least from a negotiated solution,” Lavrov said.
He dismissed the ideas circulating in Western media as insufficient for a lasting settlement and insisted that Russia’s war objectives remained unchanged.
Beyond Ukraine, Lavrov used his visit to Azerbaijan to signal Moscow’s interest in participating in the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a proposed transport corridor linking mainland Azerbaijan with its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenia.
“We have not yet received any requests regarding participation in this project,” he said, adding that the interested parties were aware of Russia’s capabilities and willingness to join.
He pointed to Russian Railways’ existing involvement in Armenia’s railway network as evidence of Moscow’s experience with the region’s infrastructure.

title: Greek TV Presenter Claims Kimberly Guilfoyle Is Leaving Athens With Unpaid Bills
body: Greek television presenter Anthi Voulgari has claimed that former US ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle may be leaving Athens with unpaid bills for hair and beauty services, adding another controversy to the American diplomat’s abrupt departure from Greece. Speaking on MEGA television’s morning programme Koinonia Ora MEGA on Thursday, 15 October, Voulgari suggested that Guilfoyle’s lavish lifestyle in Athens may have left some expenses unsettled. The presenter was careful to acknowledge that the information had not been independently verified. The comments came just days after the White House requested Guilfoyle’s resignation following allegations of misconduct during her diplomatic posting, bringing an unexpected end to her high-profile tenure in the Greek capital. Discussing reports that Guilfoyle was preparing to leave, Voulgari initially made light of the former ambassador’s extensive wardrobe. “Guilfoyle is packing up. She’s packing because she had so many clothes,” she told co-host Iordanis Hasapopoulos. “Well, the days of grandeur are over now, my dear Iordanis. Now she’s just Kim. Kimberly.” Voulgari then hinted that she had received information about Guilfoyle’s personal spending while living in Athens. “I’m hearing something behind the scenes. I want to verify it first. Should I share it as a little gossip, or shouldn’t I?” she said. Continuing in a conversational tone, the presenter added: “Come on, just between us. I’m hearing she’s leaving without settling her bills. Hair appointments, beauty treatments… various places, apparently. That’s what I’m hearing at the moment. But perhaps she had made other arrangements.” The remarks quickly attracted attention in the Greek media, particularly given Guilfoyle’s reputation for glamorous appearances and her prominent presence at social and political events throughout her time in Athens. There has been no independent confirmation of Voulgari’s claims, and no evidence has been presented publicly to establish that Guilfoyle owes money to local businesses. The presenter herself emphasised that she had yet to substantiate the information. The television exchange comes amid considerably more serious questions surrounding Guilfoyle’s diplomatic conduct. On 13 October, the White House confirmed that President Donald Trump’s administration had requested her resignation following reports alleging that she sought money, gifts and favours in connection with access to senior administration figures. Among the allegations reported by The Wall Street Journal was a claim that Guilfoyle had sought $100,000 from a Trump supporter to cover a personal credit card bill. Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing and maintained her support for Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Her departure has attracted considerable attention in Greece, where her appointment had initially been regarded as an indication of the country’s close relationship with the Trump administration. A former Fox News personality and prominent Trump supporter, Guilfoyle brought an unusually public profile to the ambassadorial role. Her appearances alongside Greek political figures, business leaders and celebrities regularly generated headlines, extending her visibility well beyond conventional diplomatic circles. For now, Voulgari’s allegations about unpaid personal expenses remain unsubstantiated. Nevertheless, the comments illustrate how rapidly the public discussion surrounding Guilfoyle has shifted from her influential connections and glamorous lifestyle to questions about her conduct during her time in Greece. title: First Footage Shows Firing of China’s Bomber-Launched YJ-21 Anti-Ship Ballistic Missile
body: Footage released by Chinese state media has for the first time shown the launch of a YJ-21 anti-ship ballistic missile by a Chinese People’s liberation Army H-6K bomber, eight years after the missile was unveiled. First seen at the 2018 Zhuhai Airshow, the missile is estimated to have an engagement range of approximately 2000 kilometres and Mach 8-10 speed. With a significantly lighter weight than the larger CH-AS-X-13 strategic ballistic missile deployed by H-6N bombers, up to four YJ-21 missiles can reportedly be carried by a single H-6K, allowing squadrons of bombers to overwhelm adversaries’ defences. The fast expanding capabilities of the Chinese Y-20 tanker fleet is increasingly extending the ranges of bomber operations to allow for strikes against hostile warships further out to sea. Cruising at speeds of over Mach 6, and with a Mach 10 terminal speed, the YJ-21’s ability to evade enemy air defences and cause tremendous damage with the sheer kinetic energy of its impact makes it a particularly significant threat to U.S. Navy carrier groups. The missile type has gained less attention than its ship-based counterpart, the YJ-20 hypersonic ballistic missile , which has in many respects had the greatest impact for the People’s Liberation Army’s overall anti-shipping capabilities of all its new missile types. The YJ-20’s highly compact design able to be accommodated in the vertical launch cells of both Type 052D and Type 055 class destroyers , and in the cells of both nuclear and diesel-electric powered attack submarines. The H-6 is the most widely fielded type of bomber in the world, with approximately 270 of the aircraft estimated to currently be in service. The YJ-21 has in many respects provided a successor to the YJ-12 as its primary anti-ship armament . The YJ-12 was developed in the 2010s for high-speed penetration of naval air defence systems, and combines a 400 kilometre engagement range with a 200 kilogram warhead and a speed exceeding Mach 3. According to a United States Naval War College Review report, it not only has a superior range than equivalent Western missile types, but can also be launched from beyond the engagement range of shipborne air defence systems. The significant strengthening of Chines anti-ship missile capabilities was recently highlighted in a Pentagon war game showing how the People’s Liberation Army could utilise its missile, anti-space and cyber assets to engage and destroy the most advanced U.S. Navy carrier groups, during which combinations of supersonic missiles like the YJ-12, hypersonic missiles like the YJ-21, and various subsonic missiles, could all play complementary roles.

title: A tool to compare LLM benchmarks
body:
The model I would choose for coding may differ from the one I would choose for writing. I built Model Atlas with Codex to compare published LLM benchmarks using weights for the work I have in mind. It started as a Codex artifact. I couldn’t find another tool that let me make this comparison.
Weights run from 0 to 10. Profiles have equal weight within each capability. Scores compare a fixed group of observed models. A score of 100 does not mean perfect capability.
The full Model Atlas index includes the benchmark catalog, published scores, inference settings and coverage controls. The figures below come from the same compiled dataset as the interactive tool and update with each build.
In the 23 October 2026 Model Atlas snapshot, Artificial Analysis’s HLE profile contains 53 configurations. Its IFBench profile contains 16 configurations in the same snapshot. A model can have a published result for one test and none for another.
The October refresh adds Kimi K3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 and NVIDIA’s Bolt E4B configurations. It also adds AA’s CritPt v2 evaluation , which lets models run Python while solving physics problems. HealthBench and HealthBench Professional each have their own comparison because their question sets and judges differ.
I set the capability weights to match the work I have in mind. The scored profiles draw on Artificial Analysis , Arena Creative Writing , MathArena , JobBench and MCP-Atlas . For example, JobBench tests professional work. MCP-Atlas tests agents using tools through the Model Context Protocol. In the benchmark catalog, Compare selects one evaluation profile and requires complete coverage. This shows the models tested together under that profile. Use in index adds the profile to a combined score. New profiles start unselected. The default comparison uses six established profiles, with model coverage refreshed as new results become available.
By default, each profile converts published scores to percentile ranks within its fixed group of tested configurations. Tied results share the middle rank. Percentiles retain the order of results but discard the size of the gaps between them. Filtering to open weights does not recalculate those ranks against a smaller group.
The index averages the available profile scores within each capability, with equal weight for each profile. My capability weights then determine the combined score. Missing results reduce coverage, which accounts for the selected profiles and their capability weights. At a lower coverage threshold, a model can rank using only part of the selected evidence. That can favour models whose reported results cover their strengths.
The catalog reviews benchmarks from release pages and model cards from Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, NVIDIA and other publishers. It records test methods and limits, including benchmarks that cannot yet support a comparison. A benchmark’s inclusion in a release table alone does not establish that its scores can be combined with another source’s results. For example, Meta’s 2026 Muse Spark Open release reports 61.8% on JobBench and 89.2% on MCP-Atlas. Neither benchmark-owner leaderboard in the October snapshot lists Spark Open. Its JobBench result therefore remains a separate release record. Its MCP-Atlas result enters a separate profile for Meta’s six-model comparison, where Spark Open ranks first. That result does not fill a gap in its Artificial Analysis configuration or determine its rank across other capabilities.
Topics: LLM benchmark comparison, AI model comparison tool, LLM leaderboard, open-weight LLM benchmarks, custom LLM ranking

title: Ukraine Resumes Strikes on Russian Refineries After Ending Trump Energy Truce
body: Ukraine has restarted attacks on Russian oil refineries after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was “done” complying with the energy ceasefire proposed by U.S. President Donald Trump. Ukrainian drones struck Russia’s Ryazan region overnight on 14–15 October, causing a fire at an oil refinery. Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov reported damage to the refinery, a warehouse and vehicles, with no casualties. Ukraine had held off on targeting Russian refineries after Trump announced an energy ceasefire on 11 October, which he linked to rising diesel prices. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that Russia continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, so the restriction was lifted. “The block is out. We’re done,” he said. Zelenskyy also criticised the Trump administration’s business approach toward Moscow and its respect for long-serving leaders such as Vladimir Putin. Asked about easing strikes to improve relations with Washington, he said Ukraine’s minimum demand would be additional Patriot interceptors. The same night, a Russian drone hit a Naftogaz gas production facility in Ukraine’s Poltava region, starting a fire and halting operations. The Kremlin denied that any Ukrainian pause had taken place. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said strikes on Russian energy sites had continued and accused Kyiv of undermining U.S. peace efforts. title: Macron Says Ukraine Must Have ‘All Means’ to Defend Itself, Pledges New Aviation Aid
body:
French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday, Oct. 15, that Ukraine must receive the military capabilities necessary to defend itself against Russian attacks, as he met President Volodymyr Zelensky in Brussels and pledged continued support for Kyiv.
“It is crucial” that Ukraine receive “all the means necessary to protect itself,” Macron said following their talks on the sidelines of an EU leaders’ summit.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I also reiterated our determination to continue supporting Ukraine in the search for a robust and lasting peace,” the French president added.
The meeting came as Russia continued its attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure, including a fresh drone strike on the western city of Lutsk during the presidents’ discussions.
Zelensky described the talks as “very substantive,” praising France for helping Ukraine respond to Russia’s escalating attacks.
“Literally during our meeting, Russia launched another vile drone strike against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in Lutsk. There are power outages in the city,” Zelensky said in a statement published by the Ukrainian Presidential Office .
The Ukrainian leader noted that Russian attacks had continued almost without interruption in recent days.
The meeting took place amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Zelensky arrived at the EU summit seeking stronger European backing after stating that Ukraine would no longer observe a pause in strikes on Russian oil refineries, citing Moscow’s continued bombardment of Ukrainian energy facilities.
Relations have deteriorated following a recent US-Russia deal easing restrictions on Russian diesel exports, alongside reported disruptions to US intelligence sharing and military satellite communications that Ukraine relies on for its defense.
Zelensky announced that France would provide additional assistance to strengthen Ukraine’s combat aviation before the end of October.
The two leaders also agreed to accelerate work on Freyja, a European anti-ballistic missile defense initiative aimed at developing an alternative to expensive, US-made missile interceptors.
Ukraine is developing its own interceptor missile and launcher as part of the project, with European partners expected to contribute radar systems, sensors and other critical technologies.
According to Zelensky, the partners are seeking concrete results by the end of 2026, although the system remains under development.
The initiative comes as Ukraine faces shortages of interceptors for US-made Patriot systems, leaving energy facilities, residential neighborhoods and other civilian infrastructure vulnerable to Russian missile attacks.

title: Killer balloons an option as US Army seeks to ‘exploit the stratosphere’
body: On the heels of an experimentation ramp-up that has seen the U.S. Army’s high-altitude balloons deployed to Europe, the Pacific and the Middle East, a missile defense official said Wednesday that all options were on the table as the service seeks to make the most of the capability. Col. Joseph Mroszczyk , director of U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command’s Transformation Integration Directorate – Space Superiority (TID-SS), said in a briefing with reporters Wednesday at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting that he was pushing for “a family of stratospheric systems” that included high-altitude balloons of all sizes. “What that enables us to do is provide space-like capabilities, really exploiting a transition point between what is normally considered the aerial layer and the space domain,” Mroszczyk said. “That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from the stratosphere … being able to go and take advantage of winds that are pushing you where you want to go already, to be able to get either launched effects or other types of payloads for sensing and communication and extension of your launched effects portfolio.” While using balloons as shooters, as Ukraine has reportedly done , likely presents a bigger set of challenges than using them for sensing, Mroszczyk said nothing was off the table. “I wouldn’t say that we’re going to hold back from opportunities and options that would include something that could be kinetic in nature,” he said. “But right now, we’re doing experiments across the board with all types of different payloads.” The stratosphere is the layer of Earth’s atmosphere above the lowest layer, the troposphere. The Army uses the term to refer to the stretch from about 60,000 to 100,000 feet, or 11 to 19 miles above Earth. On Wednesday, Mroszczyk invoked the term “ space littorals ” to describe the band, referencing the Navy’s language for the shallow waters nearest the coast. High-altitude balloons are not a new military concept. Famously, a Chinese balloon drifted into U.S. airspace in 2023, raising national security alarms and leading to the discovery of several previous incursions that had gone undetected. A 2019 Army University Press article extolled the potential of military balloons as space operations came to the forefront. “Intuitively, balloons at such heights could perform missions such as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, communications, missile warning, and precision navigation and timing,” Lt. Col. Anthony Tingle wrote . “As the space domain becomes increasingly precarious, balloons offer resilience and redundancy against overhead capability shortfalls.” The Army’s current interest in the balloons and their potential is unprecedented, though. In the briefing on Wednesday, the commander of U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, said the systems had been deployed for testing and demonstration to Europe, the Pacific and Morocco. Breaking Defense reported further about the balloons’ presence in the Middle East this week, citing officials who said small swarms of a few dozen drones were deployed in the region for testing after a plan to do a much larger demonstration in the Pacific was scrapped. The commander of the Army’s 3rd Multi-Domain Task Force, Col. Wade Germann, told Military Times earlier this week that his unit was actively developing new operating concepts for the balloons. “We work them in a format called constellation approach, where we’ll put a couple of the high, high-end, really exclusive ones up there with different payloads and systems on them,” Germann said. “And then we’ll work in a different venue where we’ll look at cheap, very expendable, rapidly employable, in that you can put up hundreds at a time and create multiple dilemmas for the enemy on.” Germann said the Army was working with industry to develop the most useful capabilities and determine not only the right payloads, but the right lifting gas and launch methodology. “That’s the way that we’re working with our partners out in the field to gain that real-time feedback and make these things happen,” he said. Over the course of the coming year, Mroszczyk said, the Army planned to conduct multiple balloon experiments aimed at determining the best ways to “exploit the stratosphere.” Rafferty said seeing the balloons in action had turned him into a “huge believer” in their potential. “Every time they are demonstrated in the Pacific or in Europe, there are more and more; they gain more and more support,” he said. “So we’re, I think, really excited about this next year, about what we’re going to do to further the program.”

title: MQ-72C Cargo Helicopter Drone Capabilities Demonstrated For U.S. Army
body: Airbus recently put the demonstrator for its MQ-72C drone helicopter through the paces for the U.S. Army. The MQ-72C has been in development for several years now for a U.S. Marine Corps competition seeking a new uncrewed cargo-carrying Aerial Logistics Connector (ALC). The Marines see uncrewed logistics ‘connectors’ as key to future expeditionary and distributed operations , and a similar Army requirement could be on the horizon, especially to support long-range air assaults . Jaysen Yochim, Senior Director for the ALC program at Airbus, talked about the demonstration for the Army with our Howard Altman at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention on Monday. Airbus is currently teamed with L3Harris Technologies, Shield AI, and Parry Labs on development of this drone helicopter for the Marines, as you can learn more about here . The current iteration of the MQ-72C is based on the crewed UH-72B Lakota, which is in turn a variant of Airbus’ H145 twin-engine light helicopter. The Army operates crewed UH-72s today , but only in non-combat roles, including counter-drug and border patrol missions, and almost exclusively within the borders of the United States. US Army crewed UH-72 Lakota helicopters. US Army US Army UH-72A Lakotas. US Army The MQ-72C demonstration for the Army, which Airbus self-funded, took place last week at Huntsville Executive Airport just outside of Huntsville, Alabama. The service has a major presence in the Huntsville area, which is focused heavily on supporting aviation and missile developments. As of April of this year, Airbus and its partners had already conducted four rounds of autonomous flight testing of the initial demonstrator version of this design, which is not in a fully uncrewed configuration. “We did a demonstration for the Army down in Huntsville, really to show all the capabilities that we’ve been able to develop so far on the Marine Corps-funded program,” Yochim said. “We had a total of five demonstration flights that we did down there, showing everything from the autonomous capability of the aircraft in a hover.” This included “complex hovering patterns, both step turns and fly-through turns, similar to what you’d see on an airfield, to just show how it can be integrated onto an airfield inside of the existing routing structure and everything that exists on an airfield,” he continued. “We did multiple traffic patterns to demonstrate just a normal traffic pattern, like a normal day would be, but also traffic patterns or a flight with a no-fly zone popping up in the middle of the flight.” The video below shows previous flight testing of the MQ-72C demonstrator. In that latter instance, the MQ-72C had to “autonomously make decisions” about how it was “going to route itself around the no-fly zones” once they popped up, he added. The human operator did provide the initial flight plan. There was also a pilot on board during the autonomous flight demonstrations, but only as an added safety margin, and they “never had to take control of the aircraft once,” according to Yochim. Though the demonstrator now has provisions for a pilot, the intention is for the MQ-72C to eventually operate in a completely uncrewed mode. The current version of the design has two LIDAR sensors, facing front and back, as well as an electro-optical camera at the nose end, to help with navigation and otherwise provide situational awareness while operating in the uncrewed mode. Those sensors feed “imagery into the flight computer with HiveMind that’s interpreting that through its perception systems to make decisions on the go,” Yochim explained. HiveMind is an autonomy software package from Shield AI, which is in use on a growing number of other uncrewed platforms, as you can read more about here . Yochim also talked about work that has already been done to start laying the groundwork for controlling the MQ-72C in the fully uncrewed mode. Parry Labs has been leading ground control station work. “Over the summer is really where now the aircraft, rather than having a pilot inside the aircraft, or sorry, an autonomous operator inside the aircraft, using a gaming computer to tell the aircraft what to do, now the aircraft is receiving commands from a ground control station,” he told us. “That is that human in the loop, sending commands to the aircraft over Starlink, so that it has beyond line-of-sight. We’ve had flights that have been autonomously commanded from up to 70 miles away. All of that is stuff that’s happened in the last year. We also have where the aircraft can be commanded from both a ground control station like this and also with the Samsung tablet.” SpaceX’s Starlink space-based network and its more secure, government-focused cousin, Starshield, are in increasingly widespread use across the U.S. military for communications and other purposes . At present, Starlink also dominates the commercial market for these services globally. Starlink and Starshield offer highly persistent and robust connectivity that is ideal for uncrewed aircraft command and control operations. The current MQ-72C demonstrator also lacks certain features that are expected to be found on the final configuration. Plans for a set of clamshell doors at the nose notably still have yet to be realized. The UH-72 design already features clamshell doors at the rear of the fuselage, as seen below. The end goal is for the uncrewed version to have an open pass-through main cabin, offering major advantages for loading and unloading cargo, and doing so rapidly. US Army National Guard A look in through the rear of a UH-72A in a medical evacuation configuration. US Army National Guard The nose door arrangement has been “designed. It’s been 3D rendered. It’s gone through some testing on that end, but not flight testing,” Airbus’ Yochim told us. “The flight testing, wind tunnel testing, things like that, take time, and it’s just not been the priority to get there with getting the aircraft ready.” Yochim said that Airbus is now looking toward the 2029-2030 timeframe for integrating the nose doors. This is tied, in part, to the Marine Corps’ ALC program, where delayed funding has shifted the schedule to the right. On that front, the Marine Corps is aiming for demonstration of this capability in an operationally relevant context next year. The Airbus-led team is also not the only one under contract for that program, with Near Earth Autonomy and Honeywell also working on a design based on the Leonardo AW139 helicopter. The expectation is that the Marines will eventually pick a single ALC design to actually acquire. In the meantime, Airbus is clearly eyeing other opportunities, including with the U.S. Army. The company’s main arm in Europe is also now pitching a functionally identical U145 drone helicopter based on the current generation H145 design. At @ILA_Berlin , we introduce the Airbus U145: an uncrewed, fully autonomous variant of the H145. Optimised for cargo with no cockpit, an integrated nose door, and full autonomy, its first flight is set for late 2026. https://t.co/MbodUxYxyI pic.twitter.com/2EnMXzog6c — Airbus Helicopters (@AirbusHeli) June 8, 2026 Airbus did the “demonstration to just show the Army the capabilities that we’ve been developing with the Marine Corps,” Yochim told us. “So the Marine Corps has been funding the program up to now, and so the message we are giving the Army is this is how far your sister unit [sic; service] has been able to get us with the funding that we’ve had. It’s already product that’s out there. It’s already product that’s working.” As mentioned, the Marines see ALC as part of a larger family of uncrewed logistics ‘connectors,’ in the air and on the surface, which will be critical to supporting expeditionary and distributed operations involving units spread across far-flung forward locations. The service sees this as particularly central to an island-hopping campaign scenario in the context of a larger potential high-end fight with China in the Pacific, where traditional logistics chains will be top targets. The conflict with Iran has only underscored how disruptive those threats can be. The Army is facing many of the same kinds of future operational scenarios, especially when it comes to supporting future airmobile operations. The service is already expecting air assaults to take place over far greater distances in the future thanks to the introduction of the MV-75A tiltrotor . Those units will need to be supported once they arrive at their objectives, which could be heavily contested. A rendering of a pair of MV-75A tiltrotors. Bell “We did several [air assaults] over the last few years directly from Fort Campbell to the Joint Readiness Training Center, which is 500 miles, give or take. The [Marine Corps’ MV-22] Osprey can do that very fast and in one leap,” Army Maj. Gen. David Gardner, head of the 101st Airborne Division, told our sister site Task & Purpose at AUSA . “Our current helicopters, you’ve got to make some fuel and re-arming stops along the way, and the distance isn’t there. But now that helped us think through as a division how we were going to command and control something that moved, expanded our battlefield, so to speak, twice as far, three times, four times as far, and twice as fast.” The 101st is the Army’s premier air assault formation and is set to be the first to fly MV-75As operationally. “We can put some things inside the helicopter, and we can put some things under a helicopter with a sling load . We’re not going to sling load something moving 250-ish knots for 500 miles. We’re not going to hang Humvees under that,” Gardner also told Task & Purpose . “We learned some things about how we need to get our equipment to the battlefield, how we need to get our sustainment to the battlefield at those distances, how we might need to rely on autonomous logistics delivery systems.” A US Army CH-47 Chinook helicopter seen carrying a Humvee and an M119 105mm towed howitzer slung underneath. US Army It should be stressed that the market for semi-autonomous aerial logistics support is heating up, and that the MQ-72C is not the only option to meet such a requirement. As noted, there is another competitor in the running just for the Marines’ ALC effort, the AW139-based offering from Near Earth Autonomy and Honeywell. Last year, Sikorsky, now a subsidiary of Lockheed Martin, revealed that it was working on a fully uncrewed version of the Black Hawk helicopter that also features a clamshell nose . Sikorsky has also been working with Robinson Unmanned on a pilotless version of the smaller R66 helicopter that again features clamshell doors at the front of the fuselage. Bell, together with Near Earth Autonomy, is developing an uncrewed cargo-carrying version of its Model 505 Jet Ranger X, as well. The drone versions of the R66 and Jet Ranger X are aimed primarily at another Marine Corps ‘connector’ program called the Medium Aerial Resupply Vehicle-Expeditionary Logistics (MARV-EL). A rendering of the uncrewed Bell 505. Near Earth Autonomy As mentioned, the Army does already operate crewed UH-72s, but it also flies Black Hawks. The service is also expanding its use of contractor-operated R66s for pilot training . The Army does not appear to have formalized any requirement for a cargo-carrying drone helicopter yet. At the same time, the comments from Maj. Gen. Gardner certainly suggest one may be emerging now. There was at least enough interest within the Army already to accept Airbus’ offer of a demonstration of its MQ-72C last week. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post MQ-72C Cargo Helicopter Drone Capabilities Demonstrated For U.S. Army appeared first on TWZ .
