title: Army Building Up New Space Operations Branch
body: The Army has long been dependent on space capabilities to navigate terrain, communicate in hard-to-reach areas, and identify and strike targets. Now, the service wants to deepen its space operations expertise and is making plans to expand its own cadre of operators in the coming years. In June, the service established its a Space Operations Branch , consolidating space-related career paths and created to train Soldiers to operate and deploy space systems. This week, during the annual Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting in Washington, after transverring 600 enlisted Soldiers into the branch Oct. 1, Army officials predicted the Space Operations Branch will eventually include thousands of officers and troops. The 600 transfers were reclassified as 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialists, the Army’s Military Occupational Specialty code for space troops—uniting them with 40A Space Operations Officers. The enlisted Soldiers had previously been temporarily reassigned to space-related units from Air Defense Artillery, Signal, and Military Intelligence fields. Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 during the conference, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, director of the Army’s Transformation Integration Directorate for Space Superiority and High Altitude, said the service’s space operations cadre has almost doubled since 2012, and he expects that to continue within the new Space Operations Branch. “When we talk about the branch and the targets, having a couple thousand dedicated folks within the branch, between the enlisted and the officer side, is a significant contribution across the service,” Mroszczyk said when asked if the Army has a target level of growth for the branch. He didn’t offer more specifics on how long it might take the service to get there. After the Space Force was created in 2019, space operators and units transferred from the Air Force, Navy, and Army, with the bulk of Space Force operators coming from the Air Force. Army officials have continued to make the case that they need to have their own space-focused Soldiers. While critics charge that this risks duplicating effort and blurring roles and missions, the Army says the difference is that while the Space Force is focused on maintaining space superiority in orbit, its role is integrating space capability and effects into tactical multidomain operations from the ground. Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an Oct. 13 interview that as demand for these capabilities grows, the Army needs to provide the same professional pathways and training for space operators that it does for other specializations, like artillery, infantry, and aviation. “Training, education, experience, and talent management is how you create great leaders, and that’s how you build great units with great leaders,” Rafferty said. “It became apparent to the Army that in order to capitalize on the momentum, the gains that we’ve made in Army space-delivered capabilities, we need to professionalize the branch and do it fast.” Rafferty highlighted a few areas where the Army expects to need more space personnel and effects in the coming years. The service on Oct. 8 activated its a new Multi-Domain Task Force at Fort Carson, Colo., one of four elements stationed around the world and designed to integrate air, land, sea, space, and cyber operations in theater. A fifth is slated for activation in 2028. Each task force incorporates space effects, and Rafferty said that as the service adds more MDTFs, it will naturally need more space personnel and systems. He also pointed to the creation of a new Theater Strike Effects Group at U.S. Army Pacific, which will require space support. The service also wants to expand the focus of its 1st Space Brigade—headquartered at Fort Carson, but distributed across six countries—beyond GPS, theater missile warning, and satellite communications into new capability areas. He did not provide details. As for space systems, the Army hasn’t revealed plans to field its own satellites, but Rafferty and others said the service has an interest in building out an architecture of stratospheric platforms in the “near-space” region—between 60,000 and 100,000 feet in altitude. “That’s a—no pun intended—space that is just ripe with potential, and the opportunities for various payloads to be on those is remarkable right now,” Rafferty said. “It’s affordable and scalable, and we’ve just got to really pursue that as part of the space branch growth.” Mroszczyk described the region as a sort of transition point between the air and space domains where platforms could host a variety of payloads supporting missions like sensing and communications, and even serve as platforms for “launched effects”—the Army’s term for small, air- or ground-launched autonomous systems. As an example, Mroszczyk said high-altitude platforms could form a “complementary” layer for some of the Space Force’s data transport efforts, like the Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture or the Space Data Network . Systems in that layer could help distribute data during a conflict and provide resiliency should space systems be targeted. He told reporters the Army is looking at a range of systems—from smaller platforms to larger balloons—and is planning multiple experiments in the coming year. “That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from a stratospheric balloon,” he said. The post Army Building Up New Space Operations Branch appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

Sega is removing Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition from storefronts following a disastrous launch where users complained about issues like bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI.
Complete Edition , a remaster of the 2011 strategy game, launched on Tuesday, and it bundled the main game and all of its DLC with promised upgrades including “improved visuals,” “1440p and 4K UI scaling,” and modernized controls. It has an “Overwhelmingly Negative” rating on Steam , where it has already been pulled, and posts on Reddit showcase artwork that users believe AI messed up.
“We’re aware that Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards,” Sega and developer Creative Assembly wrote in a post . “We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.” The two companies say they will “reinstate the original game,” and existing owners will “still be able to access ” Complete Edition .
Sega and Creative Assembly say that they are “working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 - Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War.” A studio called Mataboo is also listed as a developer for the game on Steam, and Mataboo highlights its work on the game on its website .

title: 16 October Orthodox Gospel Teaches Us to Look Beyond Appearances
body: 16 October Orthodox Gospel Tells of the Centurion Who Recognised Christ On 16 October, the Greek Orthodox Church commemorates Saint Longinus the Centurion, a Roman soldier who, according to Christian tradition, was present at the Crucifixion and came to recognise Christ as the Son of God. The Gospel appointed for the day, Matthew 27:33-54, recounts the final hours of Christ’s life, culminating in an extraordinary declaration from one of the men assigned to guard him. The centurion is not among Christ’s disciples. He is a Roman officer, part of the military force overseeing an execution. Yet it is he, together with the soldiers watching alongside him, who responds to the events surrounding Christ’s death with the words: “Truly this was the Son of God!” The reading begins at Golgotha, where Jesus is brought to be crucified. The soldiers offer him wine mixed with gall, which he refuses to drink. After fastening him to the Cross, they divide his garments by casting lots and sit down to keep watch. Above his head is placed the charge against him: “This is Jesus the King of the Jews.” Two criminals are crucified beside him, while those passing by mock him. The chief priests, scribes and elders join in, challenging Jesus to save himself if he is truly the Son of God. Their words reveal something important about the expectations surrounding Christ. They demand a demonstration of power that would make his identity impossible to dispute. If he can save others, they reason, surely he should be able to save himself. Yet the Gospel does not describe Jesus coming down from the Cross. Instead, Matthew records darkness falling over the land, followed by Christ’s final cry and death. The curtain of the temple is torn in two, the earth shakes and rocks split apart. The soldiers who have been keeping watch are overcome by what they witness. It is at this moment that the centurion and those with him acknowledge Jesus as the Son of God. The contrast is striking. Religious authorities who have heard Christ’s teaching and witnessed his ministry reject his claims, while a Roman officer assigned to oversee his execution recognises something extraordinary in the events surrounding his death. Matthew does not name the centurion. The identification with Saint Longinus comes from Christian tradition, which remembers him as a soldier serving under Pontius Pilate who subsequently became a follower of Christ. According to the account preserved by the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America, Longinus left military service after the Resurrection and travelled to Cappadocia, where he preached Christianity. He was eventually arrested and executed for his faith. His commemoration on 16 October therefore brings together two moments in his life: his recognition of Christ at the Crucifixion and the consequences of the faith he later professed. There is something particularly significant about the circumstances of that recognition. The centurion has not arrived at Golgotha seeking spiritual guidance. He is there to perform a military duty. He witnesses suffering, humiliation and death, none of which would ordinarily suggest the presence of divine authority. Yet the Gospel presents his response as one of recognition rather than dismissal. The people mocking Jesus have demanded that he prove himself by escaping the Cross. The centurion, by contrast, makes his declaration after Christ has died. For Orthodox Christians, this distinction is central to the meaning of the Crucifixion. Christ’s suffering is not understood as evidence that his mission has failed. The Cross, inseparable from the Resurrection, stands at the centre of the Church’s understanding of salvation. The Epistle appointed for 16 October, Philippians 3:8-19, approaches that same reversal of expectations from the perspective of Saint Paul. Writing to the Christians at Philippi, Paul reflects on the things he once regarded as important and explains how profoundly his understanding of them has changed. He speaks of having suffered the loss of all things for the sake of knowing Christ. The righteousness he seeks is no longer something he considers his own achievement, but something received through faith. Paul’s language is uncompromising. His relationship with Christ has altered what he considers valuable, including the religious standing and accomplishments that had previously shaped his identity. He also makes clear that this transformation is unfinished. He does not claim to have attained perfection or completed the work of Christian discipleship. Instead, he describes himself as continuing towards the goal before him, leaving behind what has passed and directing his attention towards what lies ahead. That admission is important. Paul is writing as an apostle and an established leader of the early Church, yet he does not present himself as someone who has reached a state beyond further change. Faith, in his account, requires continuing effort. Read alongside the Gospel, the Epistle offers another perspective on the difference between outward appearances and spiritual understanding. At Golgotha, the centurion witnesses an execution and recognises the Son of God. In Philippians, Paul considers the achievements and distinctions that once defined his life and finds that they no longer hold the same importance. Both passages concern a change in how a person understands what is taking place before them. For Longinus, according to Church tradition, that recognition eventually requires him to abandon his position within the Roman military and accept the dangers of openly professing Christianity. For Paul, it means accepting hardship, loss and persecution while continuing a ministry that has already cost him considerably. Neither account presents faith as something that guarantees an easier life. In both, recognising Christ changes the direction of a person’s life and brings responsibilities that may be difficult to fulfil. The commemoration of Saint Longinus is also a reminder that the people who encounter Christ in the Gospels do not all arrive with the same understanding or expectations. Some are disciples who have followed him for years. Others are strangers, outsiders or even people involved in his arrest and execution. Their proximity to religious teaching does not necessarily determine their response. That is especially evident in Matthew’s account of the Crucifixion. Those who challenge Jesus to demonstrate his power believe they know what proof should look like. The centurion reaches a different conclusion from the events they are all witnessing. The Gospel does not tell us everything about his thoughts or what he understood at that moment. It records his declaration, while the Church’s tradition preserves the account of the life that followed. What makes his story enduring is the unexpected setting in which that declaration is made. Christ is on the Cross, apparently powerless before those who have condemned him. The soldiers are carrying out their orders, and the crowd has largely responded with ridicule. Yet among those assigned to watch his death is a man who comes to recognise him. For the Orthodox Church, Saint Longinus is remembered not simply because he was present at the Crucifixion, but because what he witnessed changed his life. His story gives particular force to the words of Saint Paul, who understood that recognising Christ was only the beginning of a much longer commitment. Read also 2 October Orthodox Gospel Challenges What It Means to Be Blessed The post 16 October Orthodox Gospel Teaches Us to Look Beyond Appearances appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Russia is losing the Black Sea grain war it started. Its answer is to sink civilian ships off Romania and Bulgaria
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian drones have hit two more ships in the western Black Sea Rival Russian and Ukrainian countershipping campaigns have throttled grain exports since this summer Diplomatic efforts to restore a grain shipping ceasefire haven't yet moved Moscow On or just before Wednesday, 14 October, Russian Geran-4 one-way attack drones struck two more cargo ships —one in the Buh River Estuary near Mykolaiv and another in Chornomorsk, 20 km south of Odesa. They're the latest strikes in competing Russian and Ukrainian countershipping campaigns that have, since this summer, throttled Black Sea grain exports. The jet-propelled Geran-4s are Russia's weapons of choice for these ship strikes. The drones haul warheads of up to 90 kg at up to 500 km/h and can fly more than 700 km. They already had AI-assisted targeting , and the Russians recently added terrain-matching navigation to make them less reliant on satellites and harder to jam with signal-scrambling electronic warfare. For months, the Geran-4s and other Russian munitions have pummeled Ukrainian ports and the ships hauling grain from them. But Ukrainian forces were actually the first to escalate the shipping fight in an effort to squeeze Russian logistics. Russian Geran-4 jet-drones struck two more cargo ships, in the Buh River Estuary and at Chornomorsk Port in Odesa Oblast. pic.twitter.com/wOXcJFAj5O — AMK Mapping (@AMK_Mapping_) October 14, 2026 As recently as early this summer, hundreds of Russian tankers and dry cargo ships plied the Black Sea and adjacent Sea of Azov, hauling fuel and bulk supplies between ports in Russia and Russian-occupied ports in southern Ukraine. Most of the Russian vessels were unregistered and sailed without transponders, making them a kind of regional adjunct of Moscow’s “shadow fleet” that ships Russian oil and other goods to the global market in defiance of international sanctions. Map: Euromaidan Press Ukrainian drones had already hit ships hauling stolen Ukrainian grain out of occupied ports in June. On 6 July, Ukraine’s deep strike drone force finally started hunting the rest of the Russian ships. By day eight of the countershipping effort, the Ukrainians had hit 105 vessels . By day 12, drones including AI-assisted Fire Point FP-1/2s had struck 159, even a few tugboats sent to assist the damaged tankers. Just a few days after Ukraine launched its countershipping campaign, Russia launched a retaliatory campaign targeting Ukraine’s Black Sea grain ports as well as the ships, many of them foreign-flagged, that haul grain through Türkiye’s Bosporus Strait out to the Mediterranean Sea and onward to foreign ports. Soon, the Russian shadow fleet’s hundreds of ships were either drifting, disabled, or sheltering in Russian ports. On the other side of the Black Sea, Ukraine’s lucrative grain trade was in a state of collapse. Ports were under constant attack. International shippers were increasingly reluctant to send their vessels into the Black Sea. Ukrainian grain. Photo: Ukrainian World Congress Trade freefall Grain shipment figures on both sides tell a stark tale . According to the Russian Grain Union, in September approximately 1.36 million tons of wheat shipped from Russian ports, including ports on the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, compared to 5.4 million tons in September 2025—a 75% reduction. Meanwhile, Ukraine exported 1.094 million tons of wheat in September, down from 2.051 million tons in September 2025—a 47% reduction. The only thing preventing further throttling of Ukrainian grain exports was Izmail, Renia, and Kilia—the country’s three small ports on the Danube River, which forms Ukraine’s southern border with Romania and flows into the western Black Sea a relatively short 435 km from the Bosporus Strait. But the Russians were beginning to target the Danube ports and the grain ships heading to and from them, too. In October, Russian drones sank the Saint Kitts-flagged M/V Royad Mammadov , bound from Izmail to Ravenna, Italy, with Ukrainian grain, and the Togo-flagged M/V Alfa Watan , and damaged the Palau-flagged M/V Able , killing at least two seafarers. “The Black Sea grain standoff, in which both Russia and Ukraine continue to suffer losses, persists,” Polish open-source intelligence analyst Thorkill wrote . With global food prices rising partially as a result of the bottleneck in grain exports through the Bosporus, the United Nations and Türkiye have been trying to arrange talks between Russia and Ukraine regarding a possible Black Sea ceasefire. A previous grain deal, brokered by Türkiye and the UN in 2022, collapsed a year later. Ukraine kept ships moving through its own corridor until Russian strikes shut it down this summer. Update, 16 October: Drones hit at least four more merchant ships off Bulgaria and Romania between 13 and 15 October, sinking the HS Dignity off Krapets. At least 17 seafarers are missing. Romanian President Nicușor Dan called the attacks “attempts by Russia” to destabilize Romania and Bulgaria and said NATO’s North Atlantic Council would discuss them. Explore further “Supplying Crimea is turning into a nightmare”: Ukrainian drones hit Russian trucks 770 times in September, and winter will make it worse, analyst says

title: New Montana “Super Range” Complex Could Add Critical Weapons Testing Capacity
body: A plan for a new military weapons “super range” test center in Montana announced by President Donald Trump Wednesday night seeks to address a growing concern about the need for more such facilities. As the U.S. races to develop autonomous capabilities , hypersonic munitions , laser and directed energy weapons and improved electronic warfare systems , a limiting factor has been the lack of suitable locations for testing. While the U.S. military has a wide array of installations where it can test these systems, it’s still not enough. In addition to the massive increase in weapons development and the need for more realistic training, the changing nature of war is outstripping the capacity of existing facilities as future kill webs will extend thousands of miles, not hundreds . There are only so many places with enough space to try out these systems even to a limited degree without butting up against statutes and regulations while also avoiding interference with civilian air traffic and communications, all in an environment remote enough to avoid prying eyes. The need for more and bigger testing grounds is an issue TWZ has long raised . In addition to the backdrop of the increase in a wide range of weapons testing, much of it aimed at China, Trump’s super range announcement was delivered as the Pentagon and services are specifically creating commands dedicated to autonomous weapons . On Tuesday, during the annual Association of the U.S. Army (AUSA) conference in Washington, D.C., attended by TWZ , the acting Army Secretary unveiled one such new command , which we will discuss in greater detail later in this story. “I’m pleased to inform ​you and announce that right here in Montana, the Department of War is ⁠going ⁠to establish a new ⁠”super range” ​for testing advanced weapons and technologies, technologies including potential autonomous weapons, space, and electronic ​warfare technology, supersonics and ⁠hypersonics,” Trump said during a campaign rally in Kalispell. “Montana will help ensure the American military always reigns supreme.” . @POTUS : "I'm pleased to inform you and announce that right here in Montana, the @DeptofWar is going to establish a new Super Range for testing advanced weapons and technologies, including potential autonomous weapons, space and electronic warfare technology, supersonics, and… pic.twitter.com/W4YqKfq8X4 — Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 15, 2026 Trump provided no additional details about where this new “super range” will be located, when it will come online, exactly which systems will be tested or how much it will cost. Thursday morning, the office of U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy noted that he has been “a strong advocate for building an advanced training range in Montana, securing $10 million for a feasibility study in the FY27 National Defense Authorization Act that passed the Senate Armed Services Committee earlier this year.” “The 21st-century battlefield is being redefined by new weapons and evolving technical frontiers that require a novel approach to how America will resource its warfighting capabilities,” the senator said in a statement. “Contested spectrum, electronic warfare, hypersonics, space capabilities and enhanced targeting require a new class of testing and evaluation facilities for our military. The U.S. faces a clear choice: adapt and expand our development infrastructure to the realities of modern warfare, or risk falling behind adversaries who iterate faster.” The Montana Republican highlighted the value of his state’s huge swaths of undeveloped land for this effort. “By combining our state’s vast landscapes, innovative spirit, and proud tradition of military service, we are the Last Best Place to ensure America’s fighting men and women have the technological edge they need to dominate the battlefield and win the wars of tomorrow,” he explained. Montana (Google Earth) Like Trump, Sheehy offered no specifics about exactly where in Montana the “super range” will be located, when it will come online or how much it will cost. We have reached out to the White House, Sheehy and the Pentagon for more details. The Pentagon deferred us to the White House, which referred us back to the Pentagon. We also contacted the office of U.S. Sen. Steve Daines and Gov. Greg Gianforte. There are already a number of facilities in Montana conducting the kind of military weapons testing described by Trump. One that closely matches what would be needed from such a location is the Montana Spaceport & Test Range and the affiliated Limestone Hills Innovation & Test Campus. A public-private aerospace and defense initiative, it already conducts testing for next-generation space vehicles, hypersonic, supersonic and ballistic weapons, drones and counter-drone systems and electronic warfare equipment. Another potential site could be an expansion of the Big Sky Autonomous Systems Range (BSASR). Located near Bozeman, it is “the Lobo Institute’s primary training and testing facility for U.S. and allied military, federal, and partner organizations.” Operated under the Lobo Tactical division, BSASR is “a 6,000-acre, fully fenced complex purpose-built for advanced unmanned aerial systems operations, full-spectrum live fire, mounted and dismounted mobility, and full mission profile exercises grounded in the latest tactics, techniques, and procedures from active conflict zones,” according to the Lobo Institute. “The range pairs realistic terrain with the regulatory, infrastructure, and instructor depth required to train against the operational realities of today’s and tomorrow’s battlefields — and it does so in a remote, controlled environment where units can push hard while keeping risk to acceptable levels.” Training at the Big Sky Autonomous Systems Range in Montana. (BSASR) We have reached out to both facilities for more details. The new super range could also leverage existing range space on the ground and in the air. There is also the large Hays Military Operations Area (MOA) which could be expanded for this new test range effort. MOAs are blocks of airspace designated for military training. Malmstrom Air Force Base and its ICBM fields could also potentially be utilized. Overall, it’s possible a number of existing range areas could be interconnected, both digitally and via airspace corridors, to create a larger complex, as well. The Pentagon has long realized the need to increase the areas where it can test out these systems, especially to evaluate them under combat-like conditions. “The current open-air range space should be increased and better integrated to support system-of-systems assessments of air, land, and sea combat systems with capability for emerging long-range fires, hypersonic missiles, EMS warfare, unmanned systems, nuclear effects, and directed energy (DE) weapons,” the Pentagon’s Director of Operational Test & Evaluation (DOT&E) stated in a report last year . “The DoW needs to invest in and coordinate expanding and connecting the airspace available to the open-air ranges enabling testing and training of advanced capabilities.” DOT&E The current facilities are inadequate, DOT&E further explained. “Threat systems and our own capabilities far exceed the current available air space on the open-air ranges,” according to the report. “The ranges need support and assistance to coordinate additional airspace and corridors with the FAA and industry. Expanding and connecting range air space is necessary to facilitate testing and training critical long-range capabilities that our warfighters need and to replicate the threats they will face.” In addition, the report states that “to test missiles with longer ranges and gather data to support simulation validation, including for hypersonic missiles, the DoW should invest in long-range, overland missile flight test corridors with land-based impact areas and mobile hypersonic-specific range instrumentation to produce the required lethality data against threat-representative targets for terminal area assessments.” Rendering of an X-51A Waverider hypersonic weapon. Powered by a Pratt & Whitney Rocketdyne SJY61 scramjet engine, it is designed to ride on its own shockwaves and accelerate to about Mach 6. (U.S. Air Force) The Defense Department had largely been conducting the testing of hypersonic weapons — those that can reach speeds of Mach 5 and above — at sea given the need for the long ranges for evaluation. Still, even that was limited. The Pentagon restricted the number and location of hypersonic tests it carried out each year because of the aging fleet of ships it used as its primary data collection assets to track the capabilities while in flight. Retired Block 20 and Block 30 RQ-4 Global Hawks belonging to the U.S. Air Force, reconfigured as RangeHawks under the SkyRange hypersonic weapon testing infrastructure program, would help address some of those restrictions. You can read more about that in our story here . However, if testing moves to an overland phase, the need for expanded air corridors could grow increasingly critical. Last year, the Pentagon’s Test Resource Management Center (TRMC) identified three candidate locations to perform those tests, one over Alaska, another at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico and a third in Australia, Defense News reported at the time . An interceptor launches from an Indirect Fire Protection Capability (IFPC) system operated by soldiers assigned to the 1st Battalion, 51st Air Defense Artillery Regiment, 7th Infantry Division (Multi-Domain Command Pacific), during a test at White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico, on July 28, 2026. (U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Michael Majors and White Sands Missile Range Public Affairs) Sgt. Michael Majors Hypersonic testing in Australia is already underway. Earlier this month, we broke the news that the U.S. Air Force’s scramjet-powered Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) had finally reached the flight test phase, with at least one “release” having been carried out so far over a range in Australia. The U.S. Air Force’s scramjet-powered Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM) has finally reached the flight test phase, with at least one “release” having been carried out so far over a range in Australia. (Raytheon) Raytheon The military is also looking to expand where it can test electronic warfare systems to help ease the bottleneck at White Sands and a few other locations. Such testing is limited due to U.S. restrictions on jamming, which can interfere with civilian systems. Before he resigned after tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll in June said the service had plans to set up at least two domestic ranges that mimic realistic conditions on Ukraine’s battlefields, where the electromagnetic spectrum is a highly contested domain . This spectrum would be even more heavily disputed in a fight with China. “You can have a kind of electronic warfare and all of the contested environment created, and you can have drone manufacturers and counter-drone tool-builders engaging together,” Driscoll told reporters . “Then, we also want soldiers to be able to go there, so that they can strengthen their skills and work hand-in-hand with developers.” A drone swarm returns from a mission during the XVIII Airborne Corps’ Scarlet Dragon 26-3 at Fort Bragg, N.C., Sept. 15, 2026. (U.S. Army photo by Pfc. Iliana Lopez) Pfc. Iliana Lopez Driscoll said there are already places in the U.S. where the Army can test safely, and separately, the service is looking at a global range outside the U.S. to do “much more aggressive testing,” including with hypersonics. When asked, Driscoll declined to say where these ranges would be until planning is farther along. “At least some of the current counter-drone training for soldiers, like one CBS News saw in April , does not include electronic jamming — in part because the U.S. restricts jamming domestically,” CBS reported . In August, the Army opened premier test ranges for the use of private industry to conduct internal research and development. Additionally, the service co-hosted a Denied, Disrupted, Intermittent and Limited testing environment, at Camp Grayling in September , and there are three more scheduled for Fiscal Year 2027, an Army spokesperson told us. (U.S. Army) Trump’s news about the “super range” was delivered as the Pentagon and the services are working to ramp up the development and production of a range of autonomous systems. Last month, as we noted earlier in this story, the Pentagon announced plans for a new functional combatant command, very broadly akin to U.S. Special Operations Command (SOCOM) or U.S. Space Command (SPACECOM), but for operational activities involving autonomous and robotic capabilities. In addition, Hegseth also announced new initiatives to help further accelerate the fielding of uncrewed systems in the air, at sea, and on land, as well as to explore future warfighting challenges. All of this builds on previous and long-overdue efforts to prioritize the fielding of various tiers of drones, as well as artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies, across domains, but there are questions about how these new efforts will translate into tangible developments. . @SECWAR “Today, at my direction—we are announcing the creation of Autonomous Warfare Command, or AutoWarCom: A new 4-star combatant command—with service-like authorities—built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the Joint Force in the fastest peacetime shift in… pic.twitter.com/kYWBxy6Dij — DOW Rapid Response (@DOWResponse) September 30, 2026 On Tuesday, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced the creation of the service’s Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM). “This is our way to make sure that we take all of the great work that’s been happening with the resources that we have today, and we centralize it,” Telle said. “We’re pushing autonomy down into our units, but when it comes to having and making sure that the left hand in the Army knows what the right hand of the Army is doing, this happens at FASCOM; then FASCOM feeds up into AutoWarCom.” Telle added that FASCOM “will work with the other services to create scale for purchasing power and share best practices on autonomy.” “It is too soon to speculate about anything related to FASCOM,” the Army told us. “Specifics on structure, command, mission, etc. will be announced at a future dates [and] will require the kind of additional testing facilities that a new Montana super range could provide.” The use of highly cooperative autonomous weapons platforms that can swarm and operate collectively over large areas will also tax existing ranges beyond their capacity. Details about the new range proposed by Trump are scant, and it remains to be seen whether it will live up to the hype or even be built. As we noted earlier in this piece, a feasibility study, which hasn’t even been funded yet, is still needed before major work can begin. However, if and when it does come online, a new Montana test range will be welcomed by a military in need of additional places to test out its latest capabilities. Contact the author: howard@twz.com The post New Montana “Super Range” Complex Could Add Critical Weapons Testing Capacity appeared first on TWZ .

title: Pentagon averts cyber pay cuts — for now — with one-year C-MIP ‘transition plan’
body: The Pentagon implemented a one-year “transition plan” for its Cyber Mastery Incentive Pay (C-MIP) initiative, DefenseScoop has learned, for now staving off pay cuts that troops and service leaders were bracing for just days before the new program was set to launch and giving them more time to upskill. In June, the Pentagon billed C-MIP as a way to financially reward troops for achieving progressively advanced cyber skills as part of a sweeping change to the department’s cyber force generation process. But C-MIP was also set to end older cyber incentive pay models offered by the services, meaning certain troops would lose between $100 and $1,000 a month once the new program took effect Oct. 1, DefenseScoop previously reported . After the services scrambled to prepare for the new program and leaders warned subordinates about looming pay cuts, the Pentagon authorized the military branches to preserve their legacy incentive pay programs for a year, according to officials and a memo reviewed by DefenseScoop. The plan averts immediate financial blows to the cyber force that experts said could sink morale at a time when the field needs to focus on an increasingly tumultuous domain. Now, cyber troops who were expecting to see pay cuts under C-MIP can receive pay through the new program or legacy service models — whichever is higher — until Sept. 30, 2027, according to the memo, which acknowledged that the transition was in part meant to avoid financial impacts to the force. The memo was dated the same day C-MIP went into effect. “To ensure a smoother transition, we’ve formalized a one-year plan to facilitate the transition for service members,” Katie Sutton, the Pentagon’s top cyber advisor, told DefenseScoop in an emailed statement, adding that the department received “invaluable” feedback from the services. “We are asking our personnel to continuously improve their technical acumen in the cyber domain to maintain our competitive advantage and counter our adversaries.” While the transition is meant to give troops time to gain skills under the C-MIP model, it’s unclear whether a year will be enough to do so. “The Department intends to reevaluate the transition period prior to the one-year expiration to ensure all service members have had adequate opportunities to upskill,” a Pentagon official told DefenseScoop last week. “At the conclusion of the transition period, service members will be compensated strictly in accordance with their mastery level and the special duties they are executing under the C-MIP framework.” The official said in a previous response that the transition plan “mitigates financial impacts” and that “many service members will see an increase in pay,” while those slated for cuts will have time to upskill, “ensuring service members currently receiving incentive pays do not experience an immediate reduction.” The Pentagon said more than 21% of the Cyber Mission Force has earned higher qualifications since the June announcement and will see pay increases under C-MIP, but declined to offer a detailed breakdown over operational security concerns. During the transition period, troops who are qualified in one of five designated work roles and assigned to Cyber Operational Forces 1 and 2 — which include the Cyber Mission Force’s teams and supporting headquarters elements, according to a Foundation for Defense of Democracies report — can receive the higher of C-MIP or legacy service pay. Those who fall outside of that scope, including COF 1 and COF 2 troops who are qualified in work roles other than the five C-MIP identifies, will continue to receive legacy service pay, according to the memo. The Pentagon may expand C-MIP to additional COFs and other roles, contingent on an evaluation of the transition plan and further approval from department leadership. Service secretaries need to submit updated incentive pay plans by Jan. 1, 2027 through the cyber policy office for approval by the Pentagon’s personnel arm. When announcing C-MIP, Pentagon officials said the new program falls under the department’s Cybercom 2.0 initiative and was intended to “shed legacy incentive models” offered by the services — primarily the Army and Air Force — for a standard framework. The Navy previously had a limited-scope incentive pay model. The C-MIP framework has two tiers: Skill Incentive Pay (SIP), which is intended to reward progression across five work roles at basic, senior and master levels, and Special Duty Assignment Pay (SDAP), which requires cyber troops to take on additional duties to earn. Those five work roles are cyberspace operator, exploitation analyst, capabilities developer, host analyst and network analyst. Basic and senior level troops in nearly all of them were set to take immediate pay cuts before the transition plan, according to a Sept. 14 pay chart comparing C-MIP with the Army’s Cyber Assignment Incentive Pay (CAIP), DefenseScoop previously reported on. At the annual AUSA conference in Washington this week, senior Army cyber officials acknowledged troops were previously at risk of losing pay under C-MIP, but said they no longer would under the transition plan. “I’ll start with: Nobody’s losing pay,” said Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank, the head of Army Cyber Command, who had sent an email days before C-MIP’s launch to prepare subordinate leaders for discussions with concerned troops over pay cuts. “When we rolled out Cyber Mastery Incentive pay, we were in a place where potentially we were going to lose pay,” he added. Referencing the yearlong legacy pay extension, he said the service worked with the Pentagon’s cyber policy office “to ensure nobody’s losing pay.” Before the transition memo, the Army had planned to pay soldiers the higher of the C-MIP rate or half of their legacy CAIP rate for a year, DefenseScoop previously reported. Brandon Pugh, the Army’s principal cyber advisor, said “there’s going to be a lot of lessons learned over the next year” during the C-MIP transition. “Part of my job is making sure this is rolled out, that Army soldiers are being benefited and supported,” he said at the AUSA panel. “If not, that’s going to be our job, to advocate to [the Office of the Secretary of War] so they can see where there’s been perhaps some challenges that we can try to course correct over the next year.” The post Pentagon averts cyber pay cuts — for now — with one-year C-MIP ‘transition plan’ appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: Trump lashes out at Republicans as Ken Paxton struggles in Texas
body: President Donald Trump is blaming fellow Republicans as his endorsed candidate, Ken Paxton, appears to be in a fierce struggle for a Senate seat in Texas with Democratic challenger James Talarico in a state the GOP has long taken for granted. Trump, in a lengthy post to Truth Social Thursday, singled out longtime Republican strategist Karl Rove and Sen. John Cornyn, the incumbent who failed to secure the president's endorsement in a heated primary. Rove and Cornyn, Trump said, are doing “everything possible” to make it harder for Paxton to defeat Talarico, a state lawmaker and Presbyterian seminarian who is making a suprisingly strong run for Senate in deep red Texas. “They are hurting Texas and, more importantly, hurting the United States of America!” Trump wrote. “If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career.” Cornyn, a longtime fixture in Texas politics, lost his bid for reelection in a contentious Republican primary in which he and his supporters portrayed Paxton as a deeply flawed candidate. As Election Day approaches, public polling over the past two months has shown Talarico with a narrow edge against Paxton, the state's attorney general. Trump urged his supporters to back Paxton. “Your favorite President (ME!) is asking all of those who supported Senator John Cornyn to UNITE, and immediately switch your support to Ken Paxton,” Trump said. “He will be a Great Senator, just like he is a Great Attorney General. " The race has also become one of the most expensive non-presidential battles. Talarico raised $64 million this summer — the largest third-quarter haul of any Senate candidate in history. He has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year. Paxton raised $18 million in the third quarter of 2026 and last month announced a new $20 million ad buy . Earlier this month, though, a Trump operative told POLITICO that MAGA Inc. and its affiliates are could spend nearly $45 million on direct mail, TV and digital advertising in Texas through Oct. 12. Already, $235 million has been spent by outside conservative groups and party committees against Talarico as national Republicans scramble to boost Paxton. Some Republicans have grown concerned that the cost of the Texas race is diverting money needed in other states and have expressed frustrations with Paxton after leaked audio showed him blaming Trump for his woes. Trump easily won Texas in 2024 , winning just over 56% of the vote. But concerns about Republicans’ chances this November have surged as the president’s approval rating plummets.

title: Former CIA Base Turning Into Key Chinese Air Force Facility in Laos
body: China’s first dedicated overseas military aviation facility has opened at a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) airfield in Laos. The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy began operating at Ban Keun Airport on September 29, 2026, marking a significant expansion of China’s military cooperation with its landlocked neighbour. The site, approximately 50 kilometres north of the Laotian capital Vientiane, was previously used by Air America, a covertly CIA-owned airline that supported U.S.-backed forces during the Cold War era conflict in Indochina. The new facility is officially intended to train Laotian military pilots, but its location, infrastructure and reported deployment of Chinese-origin aircraft have drawn attention to its potential wider strategic significance. U.S. forces conducted extensive covert operations in Laos alongside their military campaign in neighbouring Vietnam. Although Laos was formally neutral, it became a major theatre of the wider conflict, with the CIA having organised and supported local forces, including Hmong fighters, while Air America provided transportation, resupply, and other services essential to sustaining operations in difficult terrain. The agency’s own historical account describes its air operations in Laos between 1955 and 1974 as among the largest paramilitary operations it had undertaken. Air America was central to the CIA’s ability to sustain its operations in the country, and although having presented itself as a civilian airline, it was secretly owned by the agency and played the key role in efforts to build paramilitary forces abroad. Ban Keun was known as Lima Site 44 and served as one of the airfields used by Air America during the conflict. The site was used to support American-backed operations, with Air America helicopters transporting Hmong troops and supplies to other locations. The facility was a key departure point for helicopter operations from as early as 1968, and formed part of a broader network of airstrips that allowed American personnel and their local partners to move troops and supplies across Laos’s mountainous landscape, often beyond the reach of conventional road infrastructure. The possibility of basing in Laos has been raised at a time when China has continued to expand the leads of its air force in both the ranges of its fighters, and in the availability of modern tanker support for aerial refuelling. The J-20 is currently assessed to the world’s longest ranged fighter type, with over double the combat radii of its U.S. rivals. Its successor being developed under the J-XX program is estimated to have a range approaching twice as long as the J-20’s.

title: USAFA Board Calls for Opening Part of Long-Closed Chapel
body: The U.S. Air Force Academy’s Board of Visitors wants the service academy to partially reopen its iconic chapel ahead of schedule next year when it sheds the “big white box” that has enclosed it through years of renovations. The idea is one of more than a dozen recommendations the board made in its semiannual report released Oct. 15, ahead of a planned Oct. 16 meeting. The Cadet Chapel, designed by architect Walter Netsch Jr. and opened in 1962, is a National Historic Landmark, renowned for its use of tetrahedrons and its 17 spires. But it has been closed since 2019 for repairs due to leaks and water damage. Originally expected to cost $158 million and to be completed by 2023, renovation costs more than doubled to $335 million due to asbestos removal, among other problems, and the job won’t be finished until 2028. The chapel has been enclosed in the “the box,” as cadets call it, for seven years. Locals and alums describe the scene as an “ eyesore ” and President Donald Trump has decried the troubled project, saying last October, “this mess should be investigated.” A formation of U.S. Air Force Academy cadets stand at attention with the enclosed Cadet Chapel in the background in 2023. U.S. Air Force photo by Craig Z. Rodarte At one point, officials feared the renovations wouldn’t be complete until spring 2029. But this summer, the Air Force Civil Engineer Center announced the box would start coming down in August 2027 and be fully deconstructed by January 2028. Chaplains will be allowed back in around April 2028, and the building will fully reopen to the public in August 2028. The news was hailed by local media. USAFA’s Board of Visitors—a congressionally mandated oversight committee—called the new timeline “highly commendable,” but the board argues more can be done. The board is “deeply concerned that the spiritual and character development of an entire generation of future officers is being compromised by the extended renovation timeline of the Cadet Chapel,” the report states. Members want to reopen the lower level of the chapel by December 2027, even as work continues on the upper level. A white paper attached to the report makes the case that removing “the box”is a “strategic opportunity” to give cadets at least some access to the building, reorienting the eyesore to its spiritual purpose. To make that happen, the paper argues for: Accelerating the removal of the box by one month Prioritizing repairs and renovations for the lower level Creating “safe and isolated” access points for cadets to enter and exit the lower level Updating any legal and administrative frameworks to support the effort The lower level of the building hosts Catholic and Jewish chapels, while the upper level has a Protestant chapel. The white paper argues that the lower chapels “can be dynamically time-shared” while the upper chapel is finished to “provide an immediate, centralized home for worship for all faith groups across the cadet wing.” Assignments and Accreditation Other Board of Visitors’ recommendations touch on USAFA’s role as an academic institution. One recommendation calls for the Air Force to “elevate the value” of an officer assignment to USAFA as a “career-enhancing duty” for Air Force and Space Force officers. “While the Board fundamentally considers instructing and working at USAFA to be a premier developmental assignment, Career Field Managers are often reluctant to promote this duty,” the board report states. “Most positions at USAFA are not career-field-specific and therefore CFMs must ‘release’ officers to perform these duties. Career field management teams frequently view these releases as a ‘tax’ and perceive them negatively, as the individual is temporarily leaving their primary specialty.” The issue is common to special duties such as recruiting, which also takes Airmen and Guardians out of their career field. To overcome the problem, the board wants the academy and Air Force Personnel Center to incentivize Academy duty by rewarding personnel who take USAFA assignments. They also recommend the Air Force examine promotion rates for officers who served as instructors to see whether the assignments improve or hurt career advancement. More than 2,000 Airmen and Guardians work at USAFA , in jobs ranging from faculty to administration and support roles. In recent times, the number of uniformed faculty has grown as more military instructors have arrived in the wake of a rash of departures by civilian staff spurred by cuts to the federal workforce. The exodus of civilian staff last year led one alumnus to file a complaint with the Higher Learning Commission, the academy’s accrediting institution. The complaint was settled without affecting the school’s accreditation. Meanwhile, the board report is calling for USAFA to sever its relationship with the HLC and instead join the other service academies and the Air Force’s other degree-granting institutions—including the Air Force Institute of Technology and Air University—to band together under a single accreditor. A board working group favor joining the new Commission for Public Higher Education, founded by six states’ public university systems whose political leaders argue the new commission is needed to combat liberal bias and burdensome bureaucracy among current accreditors. The working group says CPHE “guarantees an apolitical baseline and alignment with requirements specific to the military education system.” Previous Recommendations The Board of Visitors is chaired Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), a former by former F-22 pilot and academy alumnus. The boarfd’s previous report, released in February , called for the academy to grow its cadet wing by 10 percent and build a new “tri-complex” of buildings to house a new “Air, Space, and Cyber Education Center,” including a new “home” base for the U.S. Space Force. The bulk of the recommendations in that February report remain open, awaiting action from Congress. Decisions could come in the 2027 National Defense Authorization bill, but the measure remains stalled and will not be resolved until after the midterm elections. The post USAFA Board Calls for Opening Part of Long-Closed Chapel appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Ukrainian officials blame Pentagon for withholding life-saving intel from Kyiv
body: KYIV, Ukraine — The U.S. appears to have stopped sharing some forms of key intelligence with Kyiv, Ukrainian officials said Wednesday, dealing a blow to the country’s capacity to defend its skies and to continue its highly effective mid- and long-range strike campaign. U.S. President Donald Trump has so far denied that there had been any interruption in Starlink connectivity or incoming missile warnings — the two forms of American intelligence that Ukrainian officials say are no longer flowing freely to Kyiv. The crisis comes just days after Trump told allies that the U.S. would ease sanctions on Russian diesel last week during peace talks in Miami. He then reportedly threatened to cut off intelligence and weapons sales to Kyiv if it kept striking Russia’s oil infrastructure, according to CNN . “Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refining and the energy sector in general for two days after the American President announced a ceasefire in the energy sector. But Russia did not listen,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. “Unfortunately, there was a ballistic missile strike on Kyiv yesterday, and there was no warning from our partners regarding this attack. Usually, such a warning is provided, and it is a crucial factor that aids our defense.” Partner intelligence is an indispensable asset for Kyiv, which relies on NATO and especially U.S. information for both offensive and defensive operations. Curtailing that relationship could cost civilian lives along with the virtual stalemate Ukraine has managed to establish along the frontline, according to Ukrainian officials. “Intelligence data on the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save people’s lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is what helps prevent people being killed when there is a warning about ballistics,” Zelenskyy said on Telegram. On Sunday, Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow — without the confirmation of either party, officials from both countries said. Ukraine initially resisted Trump’s push to spare Russia’s oil network, repeating that it would stop hitting refineries only if Moscow stopped striking Ukrainian power plants. After Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” that Moscow never accepted, Kyiv held its fire for three days. Russia, however, did not. Kyiv residents heard at least five powerful explosions Sunday night before air-raid sirens sounded. Rumors immediately circulated that the missing alert stemmed from a disruption in partner intelligence, but officials initially urged people not to jump to conclusions. “You can call me an optimist, but I don’t believe (I don’t want to believe) that the United States will leave us without this information,” presidential adviser and communications expert Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov wrote Monday on Telegram , noting that Ukraine still relies on partners for reports of ballistic missile launches. “Because it’s about the survival of civilians,” he wrote. But when more missiles and drones struck Kyiv the following day, mainly targeting energy infrastructure and the power grid, reports began surfacing across the country that strike drones, interceptors and frontline vehicles were losing connection above roughly 100 mph (160 km/h), units across the country reported. By Wednesday, multiple officials confirmed that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted Starshield, the military version of its Starlink service, without notice, just as Kyiv struggles against faster Russian jet drones , larger ballistic and cruise missile barrages and a global shortage of missile interceptors . “This complicates UAV missions, particularly those involving interceptors and mid-range strike drones, and hampers capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relay,” the Ministry of Defense said in a statement on Wednesday. Zelenskyy ended the pause on hitting Russian energy facilities on Wednesday after Kremlin forces kept striking Ukraine’s grid days after Trump declared a ceasefire. “We’re done,” he told the Financial Times after making the decision.

title: Zelensky Urges Belgium to Deliver More F-16s as Russia Pounds Ukraine’s Energy Grid
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky urged Belgium to accelerate deliveries of F-16 fighter jets and provide additional ammunition during talks with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever on Thursday, Oct. 15, as Russia intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The discussions came as fresh Russian strikes targeted energy facilities in two Ukrainian regions, leaving nearly 15,000 people without electricity in Volyn and causing partial blackouts in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
In some communities, repair crews could not even begin restoring power because of the threat of further Russian strikes, Zelensky said in a Facebook statement following the meeting.
Zelensky briefed De Wever on the consequences of Russia’s round-the-clock attacks on residential buildings, energy facilities and other critical infrastructure, emphasizing Ukraine’s urgent need for stronger air defenses.
According to the Ukrainian leader, F-16 fighter jets were proving particularly effective against Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones.
“F-16s are now helping significantly in repelling attacks by jet-powered Shaheds,” Zelensky said.
“We are working with Belgium to receive additional fighter jets as soon as possible. We also discussed the possibility of additional ammunition deliveries for them. Every decision on defense support saves lives,” he added.
Belgium has committed to supplying F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine, with the first aircraft scheduled for delivery in 2026.
During an earlier meeting in Brussels on June 18, Zelensky and De Wever discussed the delivery schedule, with the Ukrainian president emphasizing the importance of avoiding delays in subsequent shipments.
The Belgian prime minister also outlined preparations for a new defense assistance package and further contributions to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which helps finance urgently needed American weapons for Ukraine.
Ukraine and Belgium had reportedly reached an agreement to transfer three F-16 fighter jets by the end of 2026, alongside urgent ammunition deliveries.
During separate talks with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels on Thursday, Zelensky said Russia had launched almost 1,000 drones since the beginning of Wednesday, Oct. 14.
He stressed the need for continued deliveries of ballistic missile interceptors and F-16 ammunition, particularly as Ukraine faced restrictions on Starlink operations.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: The tech backlash is now in theaters
body:

Between The Social Reckoning , You Can See Everything , Musk , and Artificial , filmmakers are taking Big Tech to task.
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
Though movies about disruptive tech founders are nothing new, 2026 has been unusually stacked with features that take a much more critical look at how Silicon Valley is reshaping our reality. Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning frames Mark Zuckerberg as a robotic villain whose ambitions are destabilizing society . Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything paints a damning picture of Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes as she prepares for her ongoing stint in prison . After years of being widely celebrated as a visionary, you can see how the larger narrative around Elon Musk has shifted in projects like Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary . And while Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial is a dark comedy, it is also a character study that makes Sam Altman look like a manipulative sociopath .
Even though some of these movies are fictionalized dramas, each of them draws from the wealth of critical reporting that has revealed their subjects to be less-than-savory characters. You get the sense that these filmmakers are trying to tell stories that are meant to resonate with audiences whose views of Big Tech have long since begun to dim. But it also feels like some of Hollywood’s biggest studios are finally embracing the idea that the tech backlash isn’t letting up anytime soon.
Especially when you compare them to classics like The Social Network , the latest wave of cinematic dramas based on Silicon Valley power struggles has been far less sympathetic to their central figures. David Fincher’s 2010 film starring Jesse Eisenberg presented Zuckerberg as a complicated and misunderstood savant, but The Social Reckoning builds its story around the idea that the Facebook / Meta head is a man whose obsession with growth poses an existential threat to democracy. By focusing on the allegations leveled by whistleblower Frances Haugen , the movie is able to highlight Zuckerberg’s public transformation into a powerful executive who wields autocratic control over a multibillion-dollar social media empire.
What The Social Reckoning lacks in timeliness ( The Wall Street Journal began reporting Haugen’s warnings in 2021) and stylistic flair, it makes up for in the way it connects Facebook / Meta’s past internal decisions to events that are still playing out in real time. The movie’s scenes that dig into Instagram’s negative impacts on teens’ mental health and the relationship between Facebook’s algorithm and the spread of misinformation feel as if they’re speaking directly to present-day concerns about how much influence Meta has over people’s lives. Similarly, Gibney’s Musk documentary acts as both a chronicle of the xAI / SpaceX head’s past and an inquiry into why the public was ever willing to let Musk accrue so much power within governments across the world.
Musk’s response to Gibney’s film has been telling. X has blocked the feature from being advertised on the platform, and Musk — a self-proclaimed “free speech absolutist” — has threatened to take legal action against Gibney for producing a “hit piece.” It wasn’t entirely surprising to see Musk personally badmouthing a project that casts him in a negative light, but it was curious to see the Musk ads initially missing from other social media platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok .
Though the Meta subsidiaries and YouTube ultimately reversed their decisions, TikTok has stuck to its guns — which feels notable given the company’s indirect connections to the Trump administration by way of Skydance Corporation CEO David Ellison. David’s father — Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison — is a longtime Donald Trump supporter and one of the American billionaires who led the consortium of investors that purchased TikTok’s US business late last year . Ellison has reportedly promised Gibney that Musk will air on HBO (now a part of Skydance) sometime next January. The film is currently screening in select theaters, but it is hard to argue that it hasn’t had to deal with an unusual amount of outside interference in the weeks leading up to its release.
Guadagnino’s Artificial — which was originally going to be released by Amazon — also faced unexpected marketing challenges this year. The streaming giant backed out of its deal to distribute the film this past June , just months after announcing that it was investing $50 billion in OpenAI. All of that made it seem very much like Amazon and other studios financially involved with AI companies might be cooling on the idea of releasing projects critical of the technology’s creators. Now that Artificial has begun screening and people have a sense of how it takes Altman to task, it’s easy to see why Amazon didn’t want to have its name attached . More than anything else, that decision may be what convinces people to see Artificial in theaters when it releases widely on December 25th, and OpenAI’s impending IPO could make the movie’s messages about Altman feel that much more relevant.
What sets Fielder’s You Can See Everything apart from each of these other recent tech films is how direct a view it gives you into the actual life of its subject. The documentary’s production began well after Holmes had already been sentenced to more than 11 years in prison , and Fielder uses his access to grill her about why she doesn’t believe that she defrauded Theranos investors . Invited to live with Holmes and her partner William Evans in a rental home during the month before she was set to begin her sentence, Fielder allows himself to become a character who can’t entirely tell whether his hosts’ supposed wish for radical transparency is genuine.
That central tension turns You Can See Everything into a surprisingly fascinating watch that challenges you to consider who’s actually in control of the documentary. Throughout the movie, Fielder repeatedly wonders if Holmes is using him as part of her recent PR campaign , and he leaves the audience to draw their own conclusions.
It often feels like Fielder is asking viewers to really listen to how Holmes presents herself on camera and then reconcile that person with what you might have read about Holmes in the news or seen in Hulu’s The Dropout . Whether or not Holmes is really just a committed performer who’s trying to manipulate the public shapes every beat of the film, and it makes You Can See Everything feel like a truly in-depth and honest examination of one of Silicon Valley’s most infamous figures — one who’s already captured so much of the public’s attention.
Even though some of these films have been box office flops , their existence reflects a larger cultural shift in how people are thinking about modern technology and the powers behind it. Hollywood has spent years poking fun at and mythologizing founders , and portions of the industry are finally beginning to take a more critical view . As we continue to deal with the fallout of things like Elon Musk’s tenure at DOGE and OpenAI’s quest to bake generative AI into every aspect of our lives , audiences’ appetites for movies like these could grow. And with all of these founders racing to monopolize the next tech frontier , the entertainment industry will probably have plenty of source material to draw from.
