title: How to Save Firefox Tabs for Later (All Methods, From Built-In to Extensions)
body: How to Save Firefox Tabs for Later (All Methods, From Built-In to Extensions) You have a set of tabs open you need to come back to. How do you save them without losing your place? Here are all the methods available in Firefox, from built-in to extension-based. Method 1: Bookmark All Tabs The fastest built-in option: Right-click any tab → "Bookmark All Tabs" (or Ctrl+Shift+D ) Choose a folder name All tabs are saved as bookmarks Problem : To reopen them, you'd have to open each bookmark manually. No one-click restore. Best for : Permanent archiving of a set of research links you'll reference later. Method 2: Pinned Tabs Right-click a tab → "Pin Tab." Pinned tabs persist between Firefox restarts and occupy minimal tab bar space. Problem : Pinned tabs stay open — they're not a "save and close" solution. Still consuming memory. Best for : Sites you want always available (email, calendar, project manager). Method 3: Firefox Sync + Session Restore If Firefox crashes or you close it normally, Firefox offers to restore your session on next launch. With Firefox Sync (requires a Mozilla account), your open tabs sync across devices so you can continue on another machine. Problem : Session restore only works if Firefox crashed or you explicitly closed the window with multiple tabs Sync requires a Mozilla account and sends your tab URLs to Mozilla's servers Not a named, organized "workspace" system Best for : Continuity across devices, or basic crash recovery. Method 4: Firefox View (Built-in) Firefox 106+ has a "Firefox View" tab (the Firefox icon at the far left of your tab strip, or Ctrl+Shift+Tab ). It shows: Recently closed tabs Tabs open on other synced devices Problem : Limited to recently closed, not saved workspaces. Requires Firefox Sync for cross-device. Method 5: Named Session Save (Extension) For intentional "save this set of tabs as a named workspace and close them," the built-in options fall short. This is where a session manager extension fills the gap. Tab Manager & Session Saver workflow: Click the extension icon → give your current session a name ("Project X research," "Weekend reading," "Client A tabs") Click save → all current tabs are captured Close the tabs (they're saved) Later: open the extension, find your named session, click restore → all tabs reopen in order Sessions are stored in browser.storage.local — no cloud, no account, data stays on your device. Best for : Context switching between distinct work projects Temporarily closing a research set without losing your place Recovering after a crash with a named restore point Anyone managing multiple distinct tab contexts (work vs personal vs research) Method 6: Tab Groups (Firefox 131+) Firefox 131 added built-in tab groups — you can name and color-code groups of tabs and collapse them. Important distinction : Tab groups keep tabs open and organized but don't save across sessions. If you restart Firefox, your groups don't restore (as of this writing). This is visual organization, not session saving. Quick Comparison Method Saves for later One-click restore Requires account Multiple named workspaces Bookmark All Tabs ✅ ❌ ❌ ✅ (manual folders) Pinned tabs ❌ (stays open) — ❌ ❌ Firefox Sync Partial ❌ ✅ (Mozilla) ❌ Firefox View Recent only ✅ (partial) Optional ❌ Tab Manager extension ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ Tab Groups ❌ — ❌ ✅ (in-session) The Right Tool for the Job Want to save permanently? Bookmark All Tabs Want to access on another device? Firefox Sync Want to save a specific named workspace and close it? Tab Manager extension Want in-session visual organization? Tab Groups The built-in tools cover basic needs. For power users who regularly maintain multiple distinct tab contexts and want to save/restore them as named workspaces, the extension approach is the most flexible.

title: The Resume Awakens: How One Line Changed My Job Hunt
body: The Quest Begins (The "Why") Honestly, I used to think my resume was fine. I listed my jobs, threw in a bunch of technologies, and called it a day. I’d send it out, wait… and hear nothing. It felt like I was shouting into a void while recruiters scrolled past my PDF like it was just another loot drop in a endless dungeon. After a dozen applications with zero callbacks, I started wondering if my resume was actually a cursed item—more hindrance than help. The turning point came when a friend who works at a big tech company glanced at my PDF and said, “Dude, you’re telling me what you did, not why it mattered.” That hit me like a plot twist in a good sci‑fi novel. I realized I was describing tasks, not impact. If I wanted to stand out, I needed to show the result of my work, not just the checklist. The Revelation (The Insight) The secret sauce? Turn every bullet into a mini‑story that answers: What did I do, how did I do it, and what measurable outcome did it create? In other words, use the simple formula: [Action verb] + [What you built/improved] + [Quantifiable result] It sounds basic, but most resumes skip the last part. When you add a number—whether it’s a percentage, a time saved, a revenue figure, or a user count—you give recruiters concrete proof that you can move the needle. I started re‑writing each line using that pattern, and the difference was night and day. Suddenly, my experience didn’t read like a job description; it read like a case study of value delivered. Wielding the Power (Code & Examples) Before – The Struggle - Worked on the payment processing module. - Wrote unit tests for new features. - Collaborated with the frontend team to improve UI. These bullets are vague. They tell the recruiter what I touched, but not how well I did it or why it mattered. After – The Victory - **Optimized** the payment processing module, reducing transaction latency by **35%** and cutting failed checkout rates from **12%** to **4%** . - **Authored** over **150** unit tests, increasing test coverage from **68%** to **92%** and preventing **≈20** production bugs per release. - **Partnered** with the frontend team to redesign the checkout flow, boosting conversion rates by **18%** (≈$250K additional quarterly revenue). Notice the shift: each line now starts with a strong action verb, specifies the concrete change, and ends with a hard number. The recruiter can instantly see the impact. Traps to Avoid Vanilla metrics – “Improved performance” is meaningless without context. Always attach a unit (%, ms, $, users). Inflated numbers – If you didn’t measure it, don’t fabricate it. Recruiters sniff out exaggeration faster than a debugger spots an infinite loop. Missing the verb – “Responsible for…” is a snooze‑fest. Swap it for built , designed , automated , slashed , boosted , etc. Real Example from My Own Resume Before: Developed a REST API for internal tooling. After: Designed a REST API that consolidated three legacy services, decreasing average request time from 220ms to 85ms and saving the team ≈10 hours of manual work per week. That single line got me three interview invites in a week where I’d previously gotten none. Why This New Power Matters When you quantify your impact, you stop being just another name in a stack of PDFs and become a problem‑solver with proof . Recruiters spend seconds scanning a resume; a clear metric makes them pause, think, “This person can deliver results,” and move you to the “yes” pile. It also boosts your confidence in interviews. You can walk in ready to talk about the how and the why behind each number, turning the conversation from a vague recount of duties into a compelling narrative of value. Give it a try: take one bullet from your current resume, rewrite it using the [Action] + [What] + [Result] pattern, and watch the difference. Your Quest Starts Now Here’s a quick challenge: open your resume, find the blandest bullet, and rewrite it with a real number—if you don’t have one, estimate conservatively based on what you know (e.g., “reduced build time by roughly 15%”). Post the before/after in the comments if you feel brave, or just keep it for your next application. Ready to let your resume awaken the force inside you? Go crush it! 🚀

title: Incomplete and Corrupted ZIP Prevention: Tenant-Safe Multipart Export Upload Retry Gates
body: A large B2B SaaS export should use multipart upload only when its size justifies the extra state. The decision rule is stricter than "all parts returned success": keep the export private, complete the multipart upload, verify the final object with HEAD, and only then expose a tenant-scoped download link. If archive generation fails, abort that upload before retrying. TL;DR: A ZIP that downloads but will not open often points to an upload that never reached a valid completed state, or to stale multipart state being reused. Treat completion as a commit. Record the upload ID and part results, abort failed jobs, and make HEAD verification the gate between uploading and ready . The byte path should bypass the application. A worker creates the private multipart session, the browser or worker sends parts to presigned destinations, and object storage assembles them. Your app carries control data, not a multi-gigabyte archive. Tenant isolation stays in that control plane: derive the bucket and key from authenticated tenant context, never accept either as free-form client authority, and issue short-lived signed access only after verification. How can an incomplete multipart export upload corrupt a ZIP download? Yes. Individual part success does not prove that the final object exists in completed form. Completion can be missing, a retry can refer to an earlier upload ID, or the application can publish a link while the job is between its last part and the complete call. A ZIP exposes the mistake because its central directory is near the end; a truncated object may download normally and fail only when opened. Use explicit states: generating , uploading , completing , verifying , ready , and failed . Only ready may trigger a customer notification. The database row should bind tenant_id , export ID, bucket, object key, and multipart upload ID. A retry gets a new attempt record or resumes the exact recorded attempt. It must never guess from a prefix. One boundary matters. If generation or any part upload fails, move the job to failed and explicitly abort its multipart session. No automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments is assumed here, and the one-day lifecycle floor is not a substitute for immediate cleanup. This prevents abandoned parts from confusing the next attempt. Stop there. Put verification in front of notification This Python program is a publication gate for an Infrai-backed export. The base URL comes from deployment configuration so an unlinked comparison doesn't embed a vendor destination. It verifies the completed private object with HEAD and surfaces rate limits for queue-level retry. import argparse import json import os from urllib.parse import quote import requests def verify_completed_object ( bucket : str , key : str ) -> dict : base_url = os . environ [ " INFRAI_BASE_URL " ]. rstrip ( " / " ) api_key = os . environ [ " INFRAI_API_KEY " ] path = " /storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key} " . format ( bucket = quote ( bucket , safe = "" ), key = quote ( key , safe = "" ), ) response = requests . request ( method = " GET " , url = f " { base_url }{ path } " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { api_key } " }, timeout = 30 , ) if response . status_code == 429 : delay = response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " , " unknown " ) raise RuntimeError ( f " rate limited; retry after { delay } seconds " ) if not response . ok : raise RuntimeError ( f " HEAD failed ( { response . status_code } ): { response . text } " ) return response . json () parser = argparse . ArgumentParser () parser . add_argument ( " --bucket " , required = True ) parser . add_argument ( " --key " , required = True ) args = parser . parse_args () print ( json . dumps ( verify_completed_object ( args . bucket , args . key ), indent = 2 )) Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented v1 API base in deployment configuration. Run this after multipart completion, against the exact tenant-scoped key. A production worker should retry a 429 with exponential backoff and honor Retry-After ; the queue should reschedule instead of spinning. The write side should carry an idempotency key so a retry cannot apply completion twice. HEAD proves that the final object is addressable. It doesn't prove ZIP semantics. Before upload, close the archive, run Python's ZipFile.testzip() , and record its byte length and SHA-256 digest with the job. Compare returned size or checksum metadata only when the provider documents equivalent semantics. In particular, don't assume a multipart object's ETag is an MD5 digest. Verify first. That gives an eval harness three crisp failure assertions: no notification before verifying succeeds, every failed generation attempts abort, and a retry cannot switch tenants or reuse an unrelated upload ID. Those checks are more useful than a notebook test that downloads one happy-path file. Tenant isolation changes the design A presigned upload moves bytes away from the app, but it doesn't move authorization away from the app. The server must map the signed-in principal to one tenant, choose a private namespace such as tenant_id/exports/export_id.zip , and constrain create, complete, verify, and download actions to that record. Never let a browser nominate another tenant's bucket or prefix. Signed-only access fits the capability boundary here: there is no public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null. This works for private customer exports, not static-site hosting, an image host, or permanent public links. There is no object versioning or object lock, so accidental overwrite recovery and WORM retention need an external design. Strict concurrent writes also need queue or database coordination because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable. The clean ownership rule is one active writer per export ID. Queue serialization or a transactional database lease keeps two workers from completing different sessions onto the same key. Keep keys immutable after a job becomes ready ; a regenerated export gets a new ID and key. Short-lived URLs help, but cache behavior matters. If a download response can pass through a shared cache, set a private cache policy at the serving layer and keep reusable signed URLs out of analytics events and logs. Percent-encode key path segments consistently. Spaces, percent signs, and slashes are mundane ways to create a link that works in one client and fails in another. Choosing the storage control plane Providers differ less on the multipart concept than on the operational contract around it. The trade-off is worth stating plainly. Option Useful fit Boundary to design around Amazon S3 Teams already operating AWS can use its documented multipart lifecycle and presigned requests. IAM, bucket policy, lifecycle configuration, and application tenancy remain separate concerns. Cloudflare R2 Practical for S3 API-oriented applications in R2's storage environment. Validate each S3 API feature the workflow uses; compatibility isn't universal equivalence. Google Cloud Storage Natural for systems standardized on Google's resumable uploads and signed URLs. Its resumable-upload flow isn't the same contract as S3 multipart APIs. Azure Blob Storage Fits Azure estates using block blobs, staged blocks, and SAS access. Block IDs, commit behavior, and SAS policy require an Azure-specific adapter. Infrai Fits an app that values one contract while switching among supported R2, S3, OSS, or COS vendors. It doesn't cover GCS or B2 here; fragments need explicit abort, and private signed access is the intended pattern. Infrai's first relevant advantage is contract stability: application code can retain one capability interface while the configured storage vendor changes. Its plain REST API requires no SDK, so a Python worker, browser control plane, or any other language and runtime can issue ordinary HTTP requests against the same contract instead of maintaining provider-specific clients. That removes a concrete source of drift in this export workflow: create, completion, verification, and abort logic can share authentication and response conventions even when the storage provider behind them changes. A separate advantage is that Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. It covers 295 routes across 20 modules and returns request and response schemas. Every documented Infrai capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. An eval harness can validate request shapes during a build, while a notebook prototype and production worker derive from the same machine-readable contract. This reduces hand-copied integration code at the exact boundary where a missing completion or mismatched retry state creates a corrupt export. There is a real cost to that breadth. A stable common interface gives up some provider-specific controls, and this option is a poor fit for teams requiring cross-region replication, automated cross-cloud bulk migration, hour-level fragment expiry, or server-side metadata search. No adapter makes provider semantics identical. Keep a conformance suite that uploads several parts, completes once, verifies the object, rejects a duplicate job transition, aborts an injected failure, and proves tenant B can't read tenant A's export. Run it against every vendor configuration before routing production jobs there. The prompt cost is zero. The operational signal is excellent. The operational finish line An export is finished when the application can defend the full transition, not when a progress bar reaches 100%. Persist each part result before scheduling the next step. On worker restart, reconcile the database attempt rather than creating a silent second session. Complete once with an idempotent write, then HEAD the exact private key. Only after that succeeds should the service mint a short-lived link and send the ready notification. Watch the negative path with equal care. A failed generator must close local files, abort its known multipart upload, and leave the job retryable without stale state. Alert on jobs stuck in completing or verifying , and measure orphan-abort failures separately from download failures. Test a deliberately truncated ZIP, a missing final part, a 429 during verification, duplicate queue delivery, and a cross-tenant key substitution. Keep this invariant visible in code review: no completed object, no link . It is compact enough for an eval, strict enough for incident response, and independent of whichever storage vendor sits behind the capability next quarter. References Amazon S3 multipart upload overview Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility Google Cloud Storage resumable uploads Azure Blob Storage: Put Block List MDN: Cache-Control RFC 3986: URI Generic Syntax

title: What I self-host
body:
I’ve always had a foot in the self-hosting world, long before it was called that. My freshman year of university, I ran a website from a Linux box underneath my bed. There was some downtime when my roommate got tired of the fan noise and turned it off. For several years I ran MythTV , then XBMC (later known as Kodi).
Recently, I lived for a few years in India, where streaming services are extremely inexpensive by western standards. We had Netflix, Disney Plus (Hotstar in India), and Spotify. After leaving India, I was unwilling to pay western prices for these services. But I had also become fed up with the engagement treadmill, particularly for my son. We wanted to limit his viewing choices to certain programming, but the constant “recommended for you” and “up next” caused conflict. While there are ways to limit content to specific titles, or disable auto-play, doing this for each service and keeping track of when client applications change and need to be reconfigured is too much work.
So, I “cut the cord” in a different sense, ditching streaming services for self-hosted Jellyfin . Over the course of the next year and a half, Jellyfin opened the door to self-hosting many other services, reducing my dependence on cloud service providers, and providing a welcome stability. No longer am I constantly confronted with unnecessary site redesigns, new features of questionable value, and a barrage of e-mails about terms-of-service updates, binding arbitration, data breaches, etc. I read the release notes of new versions of the software I host and decide if and when I want to upgrade.
With the exception of VPN servers that run on my router, I do not expose any services directly to the public internet. I don’t care how convenient it would be, or how secure an application is. Especially with AI-assisted hacking, I simply don’t think it’s wise. My ISP also uses CGNAT for its IPv4 addresses, so my home network is not directly reachable from the public internet via IPv4. My VPN servers are only publicly routable on IPv6, a limitation that has some downsides but is workable for my use cases, and likely helps limit unfriendly attempted connections. The biggest downside is that my VPN will almost never function on a public Wifi network, since these rarely offer IPv6. When using my phone, I can disable Wi-Fi and connect over mobile data… if there is service.
I prefer running services natively when possible, but will containerize complex services or those with many dependencies. Love: a service that’s a single Go binary. A service that only comes as a Docker compose file and wants to run MySQL, Redis, and three other containers? I’m already looking for an alternative. If the dependencies aren’t overwhelming, native is better, faster, and more efficient. I can use the same management tools and commands across multiple services. There’s no mental overhead of having to get into this container to run some command, finding out this container is missing curl, that one runs busybox so all the arguments are different, or dealing with a virtual network and host port mapping.
Related, I don’t do Docker anymore. It’s not really a principled position, but I grew tired of having to manage a completely separate service control system on my server. I’m already using systemd, and at this point Podman’s integration with systemd is excellent.
Last year I bought a Beelink Mini PC, specifically an S12 Pro with an Intel N100 processor, 16 GB RAM, and a 512 GB internal SSD. It was before the rampocalypse, so I paid EUR 180. The same listing on Amazon is currently EUR 359. Ouch! Attached to the server is a 6 TB hard drive for media storage.
My comment on Hacker News about what I self-host prompted some questions about how all of this could run on 16 GB RAM. As I describe below, there are some choices I’ve made that reduce resource demand on my server, but ultimately it turns out you don’t need much hardware to run a lot of stuff. Obviously I’m not running any local inference on this hardware, but for everything non-AI, it has just worked out of the box, or with some simple configuration tweaks.
Budgeting software with desktop clients and a web application, custom reports, and rules-based categorization. I only use this for budgeting and checking/savings/credit accounts. For tracking investment accounts, I use a cloud service. Some day I’ll try to move away from the latter…
While Actual Budget supports automatic transaction import from various banks, I don’t use this feature. Instead, after each month end, I download the prior month’s transactions (OFX format preferred, CSV if no other option) and import them manually. This works for me because I primarily use Actual Budget for expense tracking, not… actual… budgeting.
Add, download and store audiobooks and podcasts on your server, listen to them on your phone. I haven’t used the audiobook feature much, I set it up more for my kids, but it has very nice chapter handling. In the past for podcasts I used PlayerFM, then Pocket Casts, but now unless I’m out of the house without VPN connectivity, I use Audiobookshelf .
ARM automates ripping and transcoding DVDs (and Blu-rays, but I don’t do those). Yes, it’s 2026 and I still rip DVDs. Remember, we cut the cord, so not only is this a conduit for new-to-us content, but it’s also a way for us to get bilingual content (English and French).
Web UI for Restic backup software. Backups are important! Especially for Immich (photos). Restic does a good job deduplicating and compressing backed up data, and Backrest makes it easy to manage the storage retention policies. Notifications in case of failure go to Gotify.
Beszel is a simple monitoring dashboard that collects basic stats from agents (in the old-fashioned sense of a small background service) to display CPU load, memory and disk usage, temperature, battery, etc. Helps me keep an eye on various other hosts I have around the house (several Rapsberry Pis and a Proxmox cluster that may be the subject of a future post).
Caddy is a web server and reverse proxy. Early on I didn’t understand the value of a reverse proxy, and I thought I would be fine accessing my services with a local DNS name, or even IP address, and port number. But then I started adding more and more services, and some required HTTPS. So I got a domain name (not this one) and set up Caddy to automatically obtain LetsEncrypt SSL certificates, and now nearly all of my services are accessible on my LAN (or over VPN) with HTTPS and friendly subdomain names. Adding a new service is a quick edit to the Caddyfile.
Cockpit is a web-based admin console for the server. It uses normal system authentication methods. For me, it’s mainly useful for spotting failed services when no notifications are set up for them.
Forgejo is a fork of Gitea, and deploys as a single binary. Github’s uptime is the butt of a lot of jokes these days, but I also appreciate the speed of having my own git remote. Eventually I’ll set up CI/CD and runners, if only to deploy this blog.
Web-based RSS reader . These days I basically visit two websites, though, so I’ve not been using it much. I do subscribe to the Github releases of some of the services I self-host so I can check out the features and bugfixes in new versions.
Network video recorder (NVR). I first started with Zoneminder because I’m of a certain age. But it became clear that Zoneminder is past its prime. Frigate has been fantastic. I run it with 8 IP cameras. It provides alerts for people and cars entering the driveway, integrates with Home Assistant to power various automations (e.g., when a person is detected in the backyard, turn on the camera floodlight). I may write a future post with some details about my IP camera adventures.
I run all of my cameras at lower resolutions than they support, primarily to avoid Wi-Fi network congestion. Most cameras also support an even lower-resolution RTSP substream, which is what Frigate uses for motion and object detection. Keeping the camera resolutions low avoids excessive CPU and memory from video processing, and excessive disk usage from recordings. They are good enough to identify faces, and privacy laws in my country prohibit filming public rights of way, so my cameras are not aimed at distant points.
Subsonic-compatible server written in Go. I purchased a perpetual Subsonic license a long time ago, but the original project is ancient and the modern alternatives are better. I run two separate instances of Gonic , one serves kid music, the other serves adult music.
Simple notification service written in Go. Many self-hosted services directly support Gotify notifications, or can send them via a custom HTTP POST. In conjunction with Uptime Kuma, I use Gotify to get notifications about any services or devices that are down, what my kids are watching on Jellyfin, when a new podcast episode is available in Audiobookshelf, etc.
Home Assistant probably deserves its own post. It’s fantastic, and I cannot imagine trying to accomplish the same things within a proprietary ecosystem like Google Home, Amazon Alexa, or Apple Home. Things are better now that device manufacturers are standardizing on protocols like Matter, but the control and flexibility you get with Home Assistant is hard to beat. It has a steep learning curve, though, and I need to think about realistic ways to handle potential server failure without compromising the functionality of my home.
At some point I realized I was running so many services, I needed another service just to keep track of them all. Homepage was a good solution. It has widgets for almost all the services I run, so I can get a quick overview of what’s going on, or just a quick link to the subdomain of a service.
Google Photos alternative. I was tired of Google constantly promoting paid storage plans in their apps. I was able to manage my storage space, but my wife was always about to run out of room. We moved to Immich last year, just after version 2 was released. It’s much faster to load pages full of photos when all the network activity is within your house. I’ve come up with a solution for sharing albums with family, as well. Still a lot of work to do with Immich - I have many duplicates, and now that storage isn’t a concern, I’ve been less disciplined about culling photos and videos.
As I mentioned in the introduction, I’ve self-hosted media for a long time, going all the way back to MythTV twenty-some years ago. Jellyfin is opinionated about its media organization, but it generally works well. I only use it for movies, TV, and home videos, so I can’t speak to its other features (e-books, music, photos, etc.). While my son still remembers Netflix, he is satisfied with Jellyfin. I appreciate the lack of auto-play, never seeing recommendations, and not having to scroll past a bunch of garbage to find what I want to watch.
One of my ways of managing resource demand is by generally preferring 720p media over 1080p or higher. And obviously when ripping DVDs, it’s either 576p or 480p. I do have a 4k TV, but it’s not extremely large, and while I can tell the difference in resolution between SD and HD, for almost everything, 720p seems to be good enough for me.
Sometimes there are solutions that just work, and don’t really need to change. I think MPD is one of these. It’s been around for 23 years. While Gonic is great for listening to music on my phone, even streaming music from home to my phone while I’m away via VPN, MPD is how I play music through Snapcast to the whole house audio system. I run two instances of MPD, one for music, and one for podcasts.
I used to keep track of transactions and receipts for special accounts (HSA, 529, etc.) in a SQLite file I accessed directly with SQL Workbench/J. But things became more complicated as I moved between countries, currencies, and different insurance systems, and also wanted to offer my wife the ability to enter transactions. I migrated to PocketBase , which is ultimately still just a SQLite file, but with a nice web-based management frontend that I abuse as a generic CRUD frontend. It’s simple enough for my wife to use as well, and I can still run arbitrary queries against the underlying database file.
Readeck lets me tag and archive copies of stuff I read. I was a heavy Zotero user in graduate school, but I’ve not needed to write a bibliography in years. However, I still read things that I want to ensure I can access later. I tried Wallabag first, but it had trouble archiving things that were paywalled, even when I was logged in on my phone. In contrast, Readeck will archive what my phone is seeing and store it on my server.
Samba provides shared network storage, making it easy to copy files to and from the server, or share important documents with my wife. It’s funny how a file sharing protocol first developed in the 1980s and most associated with Windows remains the best option for cross-platform file sharing on a LAN.
Snapcast provides whole-house synchronized audio. Think Sonos, but without the expensive vendor lock-in and planned obsolescence. This also deserves its own post. It’s complicated to set up, but it works really well. I eventually plan to purchase some additional devices primarily for use as Snapcast receivers.
Syncthing is part of a backup strategy for my photos in Immich. I’ve set up a one-way sync (receive only) on my Macbook, so that a copy of all the photos in Immich eventually make their way to my Macbook’s external drive.
After a few instances of my wife saying “X isn’t working” and needing to restart a service manually, I realized I needed a way to keep track of what services were running, or not. Uptime Kuma is simple but has a useful set of features. I can ping devices to ensure they’re online, check the status of Podman containers, look for HTTP 2XX response codes from various services, or even parse a JSON payload and extract some details for the health check. If something goes down, I can send a Gotify notification (after a few retries, of course).
Self-hosted version of Bitwarden. For years, I used KeePass , but never had a good syncing solution, so just avoided logging into things on my phone. Meanwhile, my wife used LastPass, which had various breaches and incidents, besides autofill just not working very well. Migrating her to KeePass was not practical, and I settled on VaultWarden , which is an open-source API-compatible reimplementation of BitWarden that works with the official BitWarden clients. I’m not a huge fan of the BitWarden browser extension, but it’s mostly fine. The Android application is good enough, and syncs seamlessly and automatically when I’m connected to my LAN; otherwise, I can connect via VPN and manually trigger a sync if needed.
I am a little concerned that Bitwarden may eventually become hostile to VaultWarden and break the client compatibility. At this point, the only other major Bitwarden compatible client I’m aware of is Keyguard , which does not have an open source license and uses a freemium model.
I’ve been a Trello user for about a decade. But after Trello’s disastrous multi-day outage earlier this year, I decided to find a self-hosted alternative. I ruled out anything that involved spinning up a PostgreSQL or MySQL database for a service that will serve two users. Vikunja uses SQLite by default, though it can be configured to use other database backends. It’s not perfect, and the Android application has some missing features, but it’s good enough for me. Single binary deployment? Yes, please.
Simple web application to download YouTube Music playlists. I normally use yt-dlp for downloading YouTube videos, or NewPipe for watching on my phone, but Yubal will properly name, organize, and tag music downloaded from YouTube Music.
Here are a few things I don’t self-host, tried but decided against, or am unlikely to try.
Sonarr, Lidarr, Radarr , etc. Every time I read about setting it up, it just sounds like a resource-intensive mess that’s fundamentally prone to frequent breakage. That’s the opposite of what I’m looking for when choosing self-hosted services.
While it would be nice to completely part ways with Google, it’s hard to beat Google Docs as a highly convenient and easily accessible way to store and share information. Still, I choose LibreOffice Writer and Calc unless I have a specific reason why the document needs to be in the cloud. Since I already have a shared network drive, it seems pointless to run a service like Collabora Online (a web-based office suite) instead of just using LibreOffice locally.
I tried Firefly III before Actual Budget, thinking I needed built-in support for multiple currencies. It was a complex setup, involving multiple containers, including a container just for importing data. Actual Budget was much simpler to set up and use. For my foreign currency accounts, I have my own simple script to handle exchange rate conversion, so everything in Actual Budget stays in USD.
I like Google Maps Timeline, but after Google limited the location data to the individual device, I hoped to find a self-hosted version. But I could never get the OwnTracks Android application to consistently report my position, no matter how many battery or location settings I tried. Dawarich is another option in this space, but it wants to run “at least” four containers (PostgreSQL, Redis, Sidekiq, web application). For me, that’s not a compelling trade of resources required versus value I’m likely to obtain.
Music Assistant might work better for you if you don’t already have a music setup you like. In my case, I already had Gonic, Snapcast, and MPD working well. Music Assistant felt like it wanted to “own” everything; for example, it seemed to continually rearrange my Snapcast device groups.
Self-hosting e-mail seems like a lot of work for very little benefit. I cannot risk not being able to send or receive e-mails. Eventually I would like to transition away from Gmail to a paid provider.
That’s 17 native services and 11 Podman services, all managed by systemd. htop currently shows about 7.5 GB of memory in use, and CPUs fluctuating between 30% and 40%. It turns out this Mini PC can run a lot! Given how expensive computer hardware has become due to the AI crunch, I hope we’ll continue to see self-hostable projects that prioritize simplicity and efficiency.

title: Why are we even doing all this?
body:
[This is a guest post by Rikab Gambhir . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]
First, they came for the artists, and I did not speak out, because I was not an artist. Then, they came for the mathematicians, and I did not speak out, because I was not a mathematician. Then, they came for the physicists, and it was actually really cool and they gave me free tokens and promised to solve my entire field for me and now I can finally devote myself to the important work of publishing papers instead of doing physics
In early October, OpenAI fulfilled every mathematician’s childhood dream.
I am not a mathematician myself (merely a theoretical particle physicist, which some argue barely counts as a scientist either), so I can’t 100% say for certain what inspires someone to pursue mathematics. But, I imagine this dream is common to all academics:
Looking up at the stars in wonderment, or enjoying a complex puzzle game, or being inspired by an encouraging teacher, and dreaming that one day an unfeeling corporate robot[1] will burn a rainforest to compile a list of 700 highly obscure barely-readable facts that *might* be true that nobody can understand as part of a marketing gimmick to raise hype for an IPO[2] .
This is probably why most of you reading this got into academia. At least, that’s why I did.
In 1941, Jorge Luis Borges imagined a library containing every possible book that could ever be written. Somewhere in this Library of Babel is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the complete all-orders theory of quantum gravity, and all the papers I will ever write. Of course, there are also incorrect proofs, theories, and misleading Lean certificates , but that is besides the point.
By the research standards of 2026, Borges’s Library of Babel would be the most successful research institution in human history, containing an inconceivably large number of potentially correct mathematical and physical results, blowing OpenAI’s mere 722 write-ups and even the physics community’s recent 2500 write-ups out of the water.
Of course, most recognize that Borges was a visionless fool who failed to recognize the commercial potential of his library, as he never actually built it. He did not have the entrepreneurial STEM-spirit to raise venture capital, launch an IPO, and announce that he had the potential to solve all of mathematics. He was too concerned about the futility of sorting through randomized slop trying to understand what is correct and what isn’t and how to understand it all. But what did Borges know? He was only a writer, and we have already established that artists are obsolete.
Fortunately, OpenAI has brought us one step closer to realizing Borges’s vision. Rather than generating every possible mathematical paper, they’ve found a way to probabilistically generate things that look correct. An important aspect of this increase in efficiency is outsourcing the tedious, unprestigious, and unprofitable work of determining the actual correctness and understanding to the mathematics community (in the past, this was reserved typically for the group writing the paper), while also not wasting any time making the papers human-comprehensible. This is, of course, a tremendous breakthrough. In centuries past, scientists and mathematicians were limited in their ability to solve problems by their ability to understand the solutions. This bottleneck has been removed, and now there is no theoretical limit to the amount of scientific and mathematical factoids we can fail to understand.
From what I know about the academic community (mostly from Twitter and LinkedIn, which I assume are representative), there seems to be near-unanimous agreement that the purpose of math and science research is to gather a large quantity of potentially true factoids in a repository that nobody will actually ever read, in a ritual called “advancing humanity’s[3] knowledge”. That these results are well-written, understandable, pleasant to read or look at, or even completely correct is a secondary concern — in fact, in the pursuit of advancing humanity’s knowledge as quickly as possible, many academics will recoil in anger at the suggestion that it is worth spending any time making results understandable to humans. It is inefficient to explain or check a result when those resources can be spent generating another.
This aligns with my own lived experiences — I didn’t become a theoretical physicist to learn about the universe or better appreciate the beauty of nature myself (that’s philosophy, which I would never be a doctor of). Nor did I spend years learning to write code, make pleasing plots, or craft well-written papers for the simple satisfaction of creating something (that’s art, and we’ve already established that art is obsolete). Rather, I became a physicist to stare at large databases of histograms produced by a Lovecraftian-autocomplete of dubious correctness and say “yeah that’s probably ok I guess” to add to humanity’s knowledge frontier.
I live to serve the knowledge frontier and nothing else .
Math and science are about cold, hard answers, just as art is about producing images, music is about producing sound waves, and literature is about producing strings of text. These things exist to be consumed as content. No rational person, least of all us masters of rationality in STEM, pursues these for the joy of creation, learning, or beauty — all of these are inefficiencies, and we mustn’t be inefficient lest we stifle humanity’s progress. LLMs are not burdened with these inefficiencies, and they will be merely the pursuits of those left behind with nothing more productive to do all day.
Personally, I look forward to the day when ChatGPT can enjoy a sunset or a nice meal on my behalf and free up my time, in the same way I save time on scenic hikes using Uber. And now that AI has solved all our problems, we can devote ourselves to more important work: going into quantitative finance, vibecoding sports-betting apps, consuming AI-generated TikTok shorts, and arguing with political bots on Twitter.
Ultimately, this isn’t just about mathematics or physics — it’s about fundamentally reimagining what it means to be human. By outsourcing the burdens of curiosity, creativity, and understanding, we can finally focus on what matters most: generating value, maximizing productivity, and accelerating progress towards the ultimate goal of science: a complete repo of potentially true facts in a Library of Babel that nobody will bother reading.
By Rikab Gambhir (The @ finitephysicist )
Thank you to Terry Tao and Rachel Ward for the opportunity to write a guest blog post! And thank you to Radha Mastandrea, Benoit Assi, Manuel Szewc, Jure Zupan, and Jesse Thaler for their feedback on this essay.
Remember why you chose to go into science and math in the first place!
[1] To be clear, in your childhood dream, you don’t get to make the robot yourself. It’s a giant corporation’s robot that they made in part by stealing things from you and your friends. It’s also not a particularly cool or robot, it can only talk in HR-speak.
[2] To be clear, in your childhood dream, it’s somebody else’s IPO and they get all the money, not you.
[3] Here, “humanity” is metaphorical, and does not refer to any actual real person understanding anything.

title: Trump claims executive privilege to keep Kennedy Center conversations secret
body:
The privilege could cover Trump's conversations with non-government advisers.
President Donald Trump is making a broad assertion of executive privilege to keep secret the conversations he has had about plans to renovate the Kennedy Center, the Justice Department said in a court filing this week.
A White House lawyer says in court documents released on Wednesday that Trump's executive privilege --which is the right of a president to keep confidential the communications he has with advisers -- would also cover his conversations with advisers who don't serve in government.
The move comes as Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex officio trustee of the Kennedy Center, seeks to obtain information in her ongoing lawsuit challenging the planned closure and renovation of the performing arts center, and whether Trump has plans to demolish it.
In a sworn declaration, Deputy White House Counsel Josh Hoyt said Trump’s executive privilege claim would cover any conversations the president has had with "his advisors (government and non-government)," including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Kennedy Center Executive Director Matt Floca, as well as anyone on his or the center's staff who may have advised Trump or his aides about "the President's duties and the effective functioning of the Kennedy Center."
Beyond the president's role as Kennedy Center board chairman, a position to which he was elected last year by his handpicked trustees, administration lawyers say, "in his capacity as President," Trump has "an official role in the Center’s operations."
The Justice Department argues that since the law gives Trump the power to select who serves on the board, he must be positioned to assess whether current and future board members are "managing the Center ably and in accordance with their duties and statutory obligations."
In a deposition taken earlier this month, an attorney who sat beside Floca repeatedly invoked executive privilege, rejecting questions from Beatty’s lawyer about the director's conversations with Trump, and even suggesting that queries about Floca’s talks with Lutnick could also violate Trump's privilege.
Pushing back on the claims, Beatty’s lawyers have argued in court that "these blanket assertions of executive privilege are both procedurally and substantively improper."
The Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board voted last month to close it for renovations after a federal judge's ruling blocked Trump's name from appearing on the outside of the building, a lawsuit Beatty initially brought last year.
In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued an order blocking the planned two-year closure of the center for renovations, saying the board had not properly weighed the impact of the closure on the center’s finances and programming when it voted on the plan in March.
The Justice Department later asked the judge to dissolve that order so planned renovations could proceed. Cooper has yet to rule on that motion.

title: Binance.US seeks $1B valuation in potential $100M funding round: Report
body:
The crypto exchange was reportedly looking to use the additional funding to regain market share following Binance’s 2023 settlement with US authorities.
Binance.US is reportedly seeking to raise up to $100 million in a funding round that could value the cryptocurrency exchange at $1 billion.
According to a Thursday Bloomberg report , the US-based crypto exchange is pursuing private investment as it looks to expand its business. The potential $1 billion valuation would be well below the $4.5 billion pre-money valuation it secured in 2022, when it raised $200 million in seed funding.
Binance.US reportedly informed World Liberty Financial, the crypto platform co-founded by US President Donald Trump and his sons, about the funding round, but the company will not be participating. Last year, Binance was embroiled in a controversial $2 billion investment between an entity tied to the United Arab Emirates royalty and World Liberty using the platform’s USD1 stablecoin.
The proposed funding round is reportedly part of Binance.US’ efforts to regain market share against larger rivals following a 2023 settlement between Binance Holdings Ltd. and US authorities. As part of the agreement, Binance Holdings agreed to pay $4.3 billion in penalties and accept additional monitoring and oversight, while its then-CEO, Changpeng Zhao, pleaded guilty to a felony charge. Zhao completed a four-month sentence in prison before receiving a pardon from Trump in 2025.
Related: Binance says employees questioned in UAE cleared and released

title: Posting strike videos online may help Russia tune its drones’ optical targeting. Moscow now pays people to film hits, Ukrainian adviser warns
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Filming a drone strike and posting it online may be quietly teaching Russia’s drones to aim better. Russia is collecting footage of its Geran attack drones striking Ukraine, probably to check how its optical target-recognition and guidance algorithms perform in combat, presidential defense-technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov says . Russia has fitted its jet-powered Geran drones with machine vision that lets them recognize and track targets on their own in the final seconds of flight, a capability Ukraine’s electronic warfare cannot easily defeat. Now, Moscow is paying people inside Ukraine to film where those drones land, which Flash says is no coincidence after four years of not asking. “Across many Telegram channels, the enemy is asking traitors to film videos of ‘Geran’ impacts and transmit information for a reward. For four years they didn’t ask, and suddenly it has become so crucial,” Beskrestnov notes. The reason, he believes, lies in those optical guidance systems. Russian forces need impact footage to see how its algorithms are performing in real combat conditions, according to the expert. The warning Flash is pressing on civilians His takeaway for them is blunt: stop posting the videos of Russian assaults. He stresses the serious danger of publishing footage of impact sites and urges people not to film or share it. “This serves as a signal to everyone: do not film and do not publish videos of ‘Shahed’ hits. You see how vital and necessary this is to Russia,” Beskrestnov adds. Earlier, Ukrenergo board chairman Vitaly Zaichenko said that a Russian drone severed a unique power transmission tower at the Dnipro River crossing in Kyiv, and it cannot be restored. He added that the company was developing new technical solutions "on the fly, and very fast." It would start the procedures for those solutions from 15 October. Russia’s use of drones able to sever metal towers is a new and serious challenge for Ukraine’s power engineers. title: Mitch Daniels rebukes JD Vance over free-market retreat
body: Former Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels said he thinks Vice President JD Vance and other Republicans are wrong to move away from the party’s traditional embrace of free-market economics — and that their shift could create an opening for a “pro-freedom” movement. “I think they are in error,” Daniels said in an interview when asked about Vance’s criticism of economist Milton Friedman , who championed free-market capitalism. “I think what Vance is saying is that there are aspects to the free market which can be disruptive of culture and tradition. I mean, that's what the free market does. It's dynamic,” he told POLITICO. “It's the only mechanism, in my view, for preserving the American dream, and that's the most important element of our culture.” The vice president’s intra-party critics have argued that Vance has been moving away from free-market economics and toward a larger role for the government in shaping the economy in his defense of the Trump administration’s economic policies, especially its wide-ranging tariffs. “What the president is doing is changing 40 years of a failed bipartisan consensus in Washington, D.C., that has sold out American workers and destroyed the underlying economic strength of the United States of America,” Vance said in a Fox News interview last year. The move is seen by some as Vance testing a more populist and protectionist message as he eyes the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. But the two men were at one point closer politically. In Vance's bestseller "Hillbilly Elegy," Vance described Daniels as his “political hero.” Daniels has said that Vance sought his counsel on running for office in 2018 and Daniels advised against it because it was likely to be a bad year for Republicans. The vice president’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Daniels’ remarks. Daniels recently released his new book, “Impatience Is a Virtue.” In it, the veteran of Indiana politics — who also led the Office of Management and Budget under President George W. Bush — detailed his career championing the free market. Daniels told POLITICO that President Donald Trump was both a “symptom” and “a propellant” of voters’ discontent, pointing to their “feeling of being patronized, condescended, looked down on, ignored, disrespected.” And Trump’s political success came from his ability to unite and represent these discontented voters. Still, Daniels argued the evolution of the Republican Party under Trump has created room for a “pro-freedom party” that champions economic freedom and individual autonomy. “Whether that is the next iteration of this Republican Party or you find some other vehicle, I don't know,” he said. “But I think that there's a need, and as I say, there's certainly, I think, a market for that viewpoint waiting to be expressed by somebody.” The former governor, now back at Purdue University as the interim president after leading the school for a decade until 2022, sidestepped a question about his party identification and another one on whether he sees Vance emerging as the “pro-freedom” candidate. “It’s all TBD; I don’t know,” he said of Vance. Daniels also defended his view on another 2028 hopeful, Democrat Pete Buttigieg, who was the mayor of South Bend, Indiana, during the tail end of Daniels' governorship. In his book, Daniels said Buttigieg is smart, but his principal asset that excites Democratic activists is his sexual identity. Buttigieg became the first openly gay person confirmed to be a Cabinet secretary when he was tapped to lead then-President Joe Biden’s Transportation Department. A spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “This differentiates him in a way that would be appealing to large portions of the core Democratic electorate,” he said. “Absent that, he would be a less likely national figure.”

title: CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt
body:
CoreWeave 's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.
CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.
Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive .
Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.
Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.
While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.
Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.
The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.
A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.
"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.
CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."
The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft , Meta , IBM and Caterpillar , Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.
"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.
Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle 's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.
"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

title: AV and Thunder Tiger Sign MOU to Explore Uncrewed Systems Integration and Co-Production in Taiwan
body: AeroVironment, Inc., a global defense technology leader, and Thunder Tiger Corp., a Taiwan-based developer and manufacturer of unmanned systems, today announced a memorandum of understanding to explore collaboration on uncrewed systems integration, potential unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) localization and co-production and future capability co-development in Taiwan. AeroVironment press release The agreement establishes a framework for evaluating multiple areas of cooperation, including the potential integration of select AV Switchblade Family of Systems configurations with Thunder Tiger’s unmanned surface and ground platforms. The companies will also explore opportunities to leverage Taiwan’s industrial capacity to support future unmanned aircraft co-production and co-development. The companies formally signed the memorandum of understanding during the Association of the United States Army Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, D.C. “Modern defense demands the ability to rapidly integrate proven capabilities and produce them at scale,” said Church Hutton, senior vice president and chief growth officer at AV. “Our focus is on bringing proven technology and industrial capabilities together to create more options for how unmanned systems are developed, integrated and produced.” Under the agreement, AV and Thunder Tiger intend to evaluate the technical feasibility of integrating a launcher designed to carry multiple Switchblade all-up rounds with Thunder Tiger’s unmanned surface vessel, including opportunities to advance interoperability and support future demonstrations. The collaboration reflects AV’s broader approach to create and expand international industrial partnerships and explore opportunities to accelerate the development, integration and production of uncrewed systems. – End – The post AV and Thunder Tiger Sign MOU to Explore Uncrewed Systems Integration and Co-Production in Taiwan appeared first on Naval News .

title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
body:
KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.
Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.
"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."
For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House , its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas.
Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.
KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.
Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.
For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.
It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway , the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.
