title: Same LLM, same input tokens, different answers on a MacBook and a Jetson
body:
A model file is not a behaviour. The earlier posts on ONNX and GGUF followed a model’s file to the chip; this one asks what the chip then computes. The same weights, run on two different processors and their software stacks, compute slightly different numbers, and sometimes those numbers lead to a different answer. The cause is that floating-point addition is not associative: each processor’s kernels accumulate the model’s dot products in a different order, so the rounding errors, and the results, differ in the last bits.
One model, two devices, and as little else as possible allowed to vary.
Panel A counts answers. With fp16 on both devices, the scores agree to within half a percentage point. Most evaluations stop at this number, and it hides what happened underneath:
We have not isolated the cause of the 11-point drop. The int8 answers stay fluent but make arithmetic slips, and break the expected answer format about twice as often as fp16, on 60 of the 250 problems against 31. Whatever the cause, it is what this toolchain produced on this board, which is the argument for measuring there.
Panel B shows why answers move at all: every number the model computes shifts slightly between the devices. On these measurements the int8 path increases the mean gaps by roughly 30 to 50 times, depending on the metric.
Panel C shows the same thing for every MMLU answer choice. With fp16 the 4,560 log-likelihoods sit on the diagonal, the largest gap 0.06. With int8 they spread, by up to 7.5, and the choices of the questions whose answer changed, in red, sit near the top, among the model’s leading options.
Floating-point addition is not associative: (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can round to different results. Every layer of a model sums thousands of products, and each processor’s kernels order those sums differently, fuse different operations and accumulate at different precisions.
The result is a tiny, deterministic difference. None of the 200 output vectors we compared, the logits of the first 200 MMLU prompts, was bit-identical across the devices: the average entry differed by 0.006 and the largest by 0.07, on logits whose largest values are in the tens.
Such small differences change the output only when the model’s top two candidates are nearly tied. With greedy decoding, each step emits the token with the highest logit, the model’s raw score for a candidate token. When the top two logits are equal, or one fp16 step apart, a rounding difference on the other device can reverse their order.
fp16 cannot represent every number: between 16 and 32, neighbouring values are 1/64 apart. The leading logits fall in that range, so the gaps we observed come in whole steps of 1/64, with 17 exceptions in 30,388. The smallest non-zero gap we saw is exactly 1/64, one step. Two candidates one step apart are as close as fp16 can place them without a tie.
The histogram shows how rarely this happens. For almost every word, the best candidate is well ahead of the second, and both devices write the same word. Only 111 of the 30,388 words, 0.4%, were near-ties, an exact tie or one step apart. Yet in all 38 problems where the two texts differ, the first different word came at one of those near-ties: 23 exact ties and 15 one step apart.
Aggregate scores hide these flips, because close calls fall mostly on questions the model already gets wrong: 17 of the 18 GSM8K answers that changed in fp16 were wrong on both devices. A benchmark run on a laptop, or on a cloud GPU, therefore says little about what the same file answers on the board.
So far the differences are an accident. Two recent papers show they can be engineered. Three levels of evidence need keeping apart: ordinary divergence between platforms, which our study measures; attacks that exploit it, which the papers demonstrate on their own models and platforms; and the risk to a particular edge deployment, which neither establishes.
The authors call the weakness a time-of-check, time-of-use gap: a model is checked on one platform and served on another. FloatDoor was shown on datacentre hardware, not on edge boards, but an edge deployment has the same two platforms, the machine where the model is evaluated and the board where it runs. The defences the authors test, 32-bit inference or pruning, cost memory an 8 GB board rarely has, and until such defences are standard they see a trusted model supply chain as the only safeguard.
The model you evaluated and the model your device runs may compute different answers, even when they share the same weights. Three checks close the gaps.
Each check covers a failure the others miss. FloatDoor passes any identity check by design, since the audited and the served model share one hash. What it defeats is testing on the wrong platform, and testing on the right one catches it only if your test set covers the behaviour the attacker chose. Proof of identity catches the opposite failure: a model, runtime or board swapped after the test. Neither says whether the weights were trustworthy to begin with, which is the authors’ point about supply chains.
This is a small study: one model, one pair of devices, and fixed benchmark subsets rather than random samples, so the rates above describe these items and should not be read as estimates for the full benchmarks.
The 7.2% uses the flexible answer extraction of lm-eval, the evaluation harness we used; the strict one gives 5.6%. The int8 condition quantizes weights only. A deployment that also quantizes activations could behave differently; we have not measured that configuration. TensorRT’s own fp16 kernels could not be tested separately, because that engine did not fit in the Jetson’s 8 GB.
The tie histogram uses the MacBook’s logits; the Jetson’s were not logged. Versions: macOS 26.6 and PyTorch 2.11 on the MacBook; JetPack 6.2 in MAXN_SUPER power mode, PyTorch 2.11 and CUDA 12.6 on the Jetson, and TensorRT-LLM 0.12 on TensorRT 10.4 in NVIDIA’s container for the int8 runs.
The attack numbers are the papers’ own, on their models and platforms, as of October 2026. The prompts and token IDs, per-item outputs and disagreement labels, and the scripts behind every figure are in our study repository, and we share them on request.
Kernwerk runs these checks for you and binds the results in one signed report.
What we take on, and what you get from each:
We do not sell silicon, so nothing stops the report from saying the board changed your model’s answers, and by how much.
Shipping a model to a device you do not control? We test it on the board it will run on, and make the board prove it runs that model. Talk to us.

title: Sudan: SLA-MM commander joins RSF-aligned Tasis with 220 fighters
body: Major General Dosa Issa al-Tayeb al-Tijani, a commander and co-founder of the Sudan Liberation Army faction led by Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi (SLA-MM), has announced his defection from the Joint Force and his decision to join the Sudan Founding Alliance, known as Tasis, with 220 personnel and 22 combat vehicles. Dosa said on Tuesday that his decision to join the alliance and work alongside commander Suleiman Sandal Haggar followed 25 years of struggle alongside prominent leaders who, he said, had made significant contributions to Sudan’s survival as members of the Sudan Liberation Movement. He pledged to work with his new allies to advance a unified political project under the Tasis banner. He said his move, together with the fighters accompanying him, marks a new chapter in Sudan’s liberation struggle and efforts to build a country founded on equality and justice. Tasis is a coalition that includes the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North faction led by Abdelaziz al-Hilu, and allied political and armed groups. In 2025, the alliance established a parallel administration, known as the Government of Peace, to govern territories under its control. The administration is not internationally recognised as Sudan’s national government. Sandal, who leads a faction of the Justice and Equality Movement, welcomed Dosa’s defection in a separate statement seen by Radio Tamazuj. He said he was pleased with the development and his meeting with Dosa, whom he described as someone he had known from the battlefield rather than through urban political circles. Sandal said the move would strengthen their ability to work as a united team towards the alliance’s objectives, particularly by harnessing the potential of young people, whom he described as the hope and architects of the future. The defection comes amid shifting alliances among Sudanese armed movements, including factions that signed the 2020 Juba Peace Agreement. The Joint Force, which comprises armed movements allied with Sudan’s army, has fought against the RSF during the war that began in April 2023. The Joint Force could not immediately be reached for comment. The post Sudan: SLA-MM commander joins RSF-aligned Tasis with 220 fighters appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
body:
Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.
The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.
Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget . The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.
Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”
The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.
Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.
Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms.

title: Flipkart Group FY26: Revenue Nears ₹1.5 Lakh Cr, Loss Narrows To ₹8,468 Cr
body: Flipkart Group reported an 18.2% jump in consolidated revenue from operations to ₹1.45 Lakh Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), up from ₹1.23 Lakh Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, its consolidated net loss narrowed marginally by 2.1% to ₹8,468 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹8,646 Cr in FY25. The numbers reflect the performance of the Flipkart Group as a whole, rather than the standalone financials of the Flipkart ecommerce marketplace. The financial results come after the Walmart-backed ecommerce giant completed its reverse flip from Singapore to India in March 2026. The restructuring brought the group’s holding structure back to India, ahead of a potential domestic public listing. The consolidated entity includes businesses such as Myntra and Cleartrip, alongside logistics, platform services and other specialised operations. “As part of its re-domiciliation to India, (the) Flipkart Group is publishing consolidated financial results under Flipkart Internet Private Limited. The results reflect the group’s performance over the reporting period for the year ended March 2026 and provide a historical view of the business rather than a current trading update,” said the ecommerce giant in a blog post . On the operational front, the company said that its gross margins rose 23% YoY in FY26, while adjusted EBITDA improved by around ₹1,500 Cr during the fiscal. “Adjusted operating margin improved by 230 basis points, from -7.7% to -5.4%, supported by higher gross margins and lower overheads,” added the ecommerce major. Flipkart also noted its adjusted operating business losses, before finance costs, tax, other income and exceptional items, narrowed by 17%, or around ₹1,600 Cr, during the fiscal under review. However, this improvement in operating losses translated into only a marginal reduction in net losses. Flipkart attributed the higher net losses to higher finance costs, the derecognition of deferred tax assets recognised in earlier periods and certain exceptional items. How Did Flipkart’s B2C Arm Perform? Meanwhile, the ecommerce major’s B2C arm, Flipkart Internet Private Limited, reported a 19.3% YoY decline in revenue from operations to ₹16,295 Cr in FY26 compared with ₹20,202 Cr in the year-ago fiscal . Including other income of ₹744 Cr (down from ₹947 Cr in FY25), the B2C vertical’s total income stood at ₹17,039 Cr in FY26, 19.4% lower than ₹21,149 Cr in the previous fiscal. On the expenses front, Flipkart Internet Pvt Ltd’s total expenses fell 3.6% to ₹22,522 Cr from ₹23,361 Cr in FY25. Overall, the B2C business’ net loss rose to ₹5,498 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,694 Cr a year earlier. Notably, the FY25 figures were restated to account for the business combination. Where Did Flipkart Group Spend In FY26? Despite the growing top line and narrowing losses, Flipkart Group’s total expenses rose 16% to ₹1.54 Lakh Cr in FY26 as against ₹1.33 Lakh Cr in the year-ago period. Purchase Of Traded Goods: This was the biggest cost-centre for the company. Expenses under this head climbed 17.4% YoY to ₹1.17 Lakh Cr in the fiscal under review. Employee Benefit Expenses: The group’s employee benefit costs remained relatively flat at ₹8,376 Cr compared with ₹8,268 Cr in FY25. Finance Costs: Expenditure under this bucket nearly doubled to ₹1,209 Cr from ₹649 Cr in FY25. Logistics & Storage Service Charges: Expenses under this header stood at ₹15,154 Cr in FY26, up 28.9% from ₹11,759 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. The expense accounted for nearly 54% of the group’s total other expenses of ₹28,277 Cr in FY26, highlighting the cost of running its logistics, warehousing and delivery operations. The post Flipkart Group FY26: Revenue Nears ₹1.5 Lakh Cr, Loss Narrows To ₹8,468 Cr appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: US Army eyes developing soldier-worn drone detection gear
body: WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Army is in the early stages of developing and testing a wearable or lightweight device that could alert soldiers to the presence of hostile drones without substantially adding to their combat load, officials said in a briefing with reporters on Wednesday. Speaking at the Association of the United Army’s annual meeting here, U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) C5ISR Center Director Beth Perry said this kind of sensing tech had been the subject of recent “innovation sprints” within the center. “As we categorize the threat in the [counter-unmanned aerial systems] space, in the drone space, and we understand all of the different platforms, they all have different acoustic signatures,” Petty said. “And so being able to do some [work] on the soldier-based, very lightweight sensing technology that will pick up, hey, you know, there’s a drone following you … that’s a very early innovation project.” Perry said such a sensor might integrate with software to provide identification, which would then allow the soldier or unit to take action. The work comes after a fear soldiers are expressing over developing a level of comfort in a battlespace where they might be unknowingly observed or targeted at any time, said Jami Davis, assistant director for Soldier and Platform Mission Equipment. “I think one of the overarching things we’ve heard from our user community this year is very basic things,” Davis said. “Their priority is the soldier knowing he’s being observed by a UAS, right? Like it’s very basic things that we can provide to help kind of even give our soldiers situational awareness.” Being able to provide that awareness without giving the soldier another thing to carry has been a priority," Davis added. “Our technology is always pushing for … lighter, smaller, more integrated to reduce the soldier load and improve the capability,” she said. “So definitely, you know there are industry solutions out there. Our objective really is just to try and make those better, smaller, lighter, more integrated, so that a tactical soldier doesn’t have to carry more unique, threat-unique equipment.” Multiple defense contractors have offered variants of drone-sensing solutions that integrate with other gear, like radios, or stand alone as a wearable device that detects through RF or acoustic detection. Earlier this year, Stars and Stripes reported that an Army sergeant in Germany had also improvised his own RF-based personal drone-sensing device that could fit in a pocket or a pouch and be assembled in an hour for about $120. Perry said she couldn’t yet talk about the form factor of the device the C5ISR center started developing or the way forward for the effort. “It’s still things that we’re doing in the lab that we see as a way for us to provide a low [size, weight and power] solution for a known threat, but not something that we’ve tested yet,” she said. “You know, we work on the large technology spectrum, things that are very early to things that are closer to the field, and that one in particular is very early.”

title: US Army eyes developing soldier-worn drone detection gear
body: WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Army is in the early stages of developing and testing a wearable or lightweight device that could alert soldiers to the presence of hostile drones without substantially adding to their combat load, officials said in a briefing with reporters on Wednesday. Speaking at the Association of the United Army’s annual meeting here, U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) C5ISR Center Director Beth Perry said this kind of sensing tech had been the subject of recent “innovation sprints” within the center. “As we categorize the threat in the [counter-unmanned aerial systems] space, in the drone space, and we understand all of the different platforms, they all have different acoustic signatures,” Petty said. “And so being able to do some [work] on the soldier-based, very lightweight sensing technology that will pick up, hey, you know, there’s a drone following you … that’s a very early innovation project.” Perry said such a sensor might integrate with software to provide identification, which would then allow the soldier or unit to take action. Six states participating in an initiative to improve a Eurasia-to-Europe trade corridor have agreed on measures to reduce transit times at intermodal nodes along the route.
Meeting in Tashkent on October 11, railway officials from Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan signed a protocol to enhance the cost competitiveness of the CASCA+ corridor. The six states pledged to work on achieving efficiencies in transferring cargo from one mode of transport to another at Caspian and Black Sea ports.
The protocol also calls on the participating states to simplify tariff regimes and improve customs clearance procedures.
“This approach can attract new volumes of cargo and strengthen CASCA+’s status as one of the most reliable and fastest land bridges in Eurasia,” according to a commentary published by the Turkmen government-aligned news outlet Orient.tm.
The concept for the six-state CASCA+ route dates back to 2019, but efforts to develop the route got underway in earnest in June 2025. Meanwhile, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, and Georgia have engaged Romania is discussions to create a supplemental route to CASCA+ that stretches across the Black Sea.

title: Ukraine’s shell factories outpace state orders, arms company chief says: Kyiv spent five months buying from them this year, leaving six to produce

Yet its main problem is not production but the absence of a predictable state order, Ukrainian Armor chief executive Vladyslav Belbas said on Radio NV. Private firms built those plants with their own money under constant Russian fire, but they still do not know how much the state will buy next year, or when it will sign the contracts that keep the lines running. The paradox is stark: Ukraine went from depending on Western shell deliveries at the start of the invasion to making more than its budget can buy, with room to export as much again. “Now we supply ourselves with more than the budget can buy, and we can supply the same amount again for export. The building of an artillery-ammunition industry has happened. For certain types of ammunition, we can even speak of a closed cycle, ” Belbas says. He calls the shift a clear gain of recent years, with similar progress across many types of weapons. Factories built on private money, waiting on the state The producers are flying blind on demand. Private makers receive no state investment and are paid only for finished products, having built their plants themselves, yet they do not know in advance how much the state will buy or when it will sign contracts, he explains. “All producers have been saying for years that we need a stable, clear order so that plants and workshops run without stopping. Private producers have not received a single coin of investment from the state. It is very hard to live and develop without forecasting,” Belbas says. A procurement clock that runs out before the shells do The calendar works against the factories. Contracting for next year has not begun because the budget is not yet set, and the procedures drag on: this year buying artillery ammunition took five months, leaving six for production, he notes. For now, long-range ammunition is being actively contracted, and foreign deliveries are arriving, and he expects no supply problems by year’s end except for special munitions, including cluster rounds. Bluesky’s Attie AI tool, which initially launched earlier this year as a way to use AI to build your own feeds, now lets you make “small” social apps like games, polls, and dashboards that you can then share with others as their own websites. The apps I’ve messed around with are pretty lightweight novelties, though I liked the drum machine.

title: Amazon devices chief sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps
body:
Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI.
Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed.
“A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.”
By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do.
“As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said.
Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone.
These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them.
Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work.
“You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. And that’s what we do. That’s critical.”
The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI.
“Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said.
That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you.
“I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. I don’t think that’s the case,” he clarified. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful.”

title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B Open Multimodal Agent Model
body:
NVIDIA just released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL , an open vision-language model built for always-on enterprise agents. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts model from NVIDIA that activates 12B parameters per token. It reads text, images, documents and video, then reasons, calls tools and writes code in one model. For developers, 1 open checkpoint replaces a separate text model along with a separate vision model. NVIDIA also shipped 2 edge models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B and Bolt E4B. TL;DR Size: 120B total parameters, 12B active (MoE). Context up to 1M tokens. Runs on: 1x DGX Spark, 1x H200, 2x H100 or 1x GB200 with the NVFP4 checkpoint. A BF16 checkpoint is also published. Performance: Strong reasoning, agentic coding and document vision. NVIDIA claims up to 5x higher single-GPU throughput than open peers. Best: 89.90 on GPQA-Diamond (NVFP4). Worst: 17.78 on tau3-bench banking (NVFP4). What is Nemotron 3.5 Super VL? It is an open multimodal agent model. Weights ship under the OpenMDW-1.1 license . NVIDIA also released open datasets , training recipes and RL environments in NeMo Gym. The model card lists text, image and video inputs with text output. Video is limited to MP4 clips up to 2 minutes. Reasoning can be toggled on or off through the chat template. How does the architecture work? The backbone interleaves Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts and attention layers. Each MoE layer holds 512 routed experts. A C-RADIO vision encoder and a connector feed images, document pages and video frames into the language backbone. Speed comes from four techniques: Multi-token prediction: a native drafter proposes several tokens, verified in 1 forward pass. LiLiCorr: a speculative drafter for DGX Spark, up to 2.3x faster token generation. NVFP4 with quantization-aware distillation: 4-bit weights and activations on Blackwell, 4-bit weights with 16-bit activations elsewhere. Context reuse: prefix caching keeps both attention caches and Mamba states across agent turns. The model was distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA team states that it trained on about 26 trillion tokens. Post-training used roughly 3.8 million samples plus RL across dozens of environments. Continued pretraining added 10B Indic tokens. How does it perform on benchmarks? All scores below are NVIDIA-reported, from the NVFP4 checkpoint on the model card. Area Benchmark Score Reasoning GPQA-Diamond 89.90 Coding SWE-bench Verified 71.07 Coding Terminal-Bench 2.1 60.80 Web agent BrowseComp 77.5 Instruction following IFBench 71.50 Charts CharXiv reasoning 79.88 Documents MMLongBench-Doc 62.82 Computer use OSWorld-Verified 52.3 Long-horizon agent tau3-bench banking 17.78 On agent harness evals, Super VL beats Nemotron 3 Ultra. It scores 63.44% on Hermes Bench versus 56.33%. On LangChain evals it scores 87.05% versus 84.3%. Ultra carries about 4.6x more total parameters. NVIDIA team reports over 600 output tokens per second on Artificial Analysis agentic tasks via a Baseten endpoint. Its chart marks a 5x speed gap over Inkling Small.

Harnesses and benchmark versions differ, so treat gaps of a few points with caution. How can developers deploy it? Super VL is available on Hugging Face , OpenRouter , ModelScope and as an NVIDIA NIM . Supported runtimes are vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM on Blackwell and Hopper. Local paths include llama.cpp and Unsloth . For production, Dynamo recipes add KV-aware routing. On 16 B200 GPUs at 50 tokens per second per user, NVIDIA reports 8x more users served. First-token latency drops 85%. Customization runs through NeMo AutoModel for SFT and LoRA, and NeMo RL for reinforcement learning. NVIDIA cites early results: Scale AI for Skydance vendor credit processing: 40x lower inference cost and 5x lower latency. Ramp receipt-to-JSON extraction: up to 50% higher throughput and 10x lower latency expected. AI21 for Alice threat intelligence: 40% higher accuracy. What are the Nemotron 3.5 Bolt models? Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B targets local agents. NVIDIA’s launch notes describe it as distilled from Super VL. Native 2-bit quantization fits it into 24GB of memory on RTX and DGX Spark systems. NVIDIA says it ranks #1 among open models in its class on PinchBench . It ranks #2 on BrowseComp among open models. It is available now on Hugging Face with llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth and vLLM support. Bolt E4B 4GB arrives October 23. It targets voice assistants and embedded agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson and RTX or DGX Spark. Key Takeaways 120B MoE, 12B active, 1M context, open weights under OpenMDW-1.1. 1 model handles text, images, documents, video, tools and code. NVFP4 checkpoint runs on a single DGX Spark, H200 or GB200. 89.90 GPQA-Diamond, but only 17.78 on tau3-bench banking. Bolt 74B-A9B brings a 24GB local agent model to RTX PCs. title: Harvard’s endowment jumps 27% in fiscal 2026, lifted by SpaceX as top holding
body:
Harvard University's endowment grew 27.1% in fiscal year 2026, its strongest return in five years, the school said in its annual financial report released on Thursday.
The endowment, which beat the S&P 500's 22.3% total return in the same period by 4.8 percentage points, now totals nearly $68 billion. The outperformance came amid actions by the Trump administration to penalize the school and withhold funding from the university.
"While markets can easily take back what they give, that return will strengthen the endowment's capacity to support the University over time," Harvard's chief financial officer Ritu Kalra and treasurer Timothy Barakett wrote in the 49-page annual report. "The University deliberately smooths distributions so that operating support does not rise and fall with the markets. Strong investment returns therefore support Harvard's work gradually, through future distributions."
The returns marked the best year for the endowment, managed by the Harvard Management Company, since 2021. Harvard's fiscal year ends on June 30.
In its second-quarter 13F filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission , Harvard unveiled a $2.2 billion stake in Elon Musk's SpaceX rocket and satellite company. It marked the endowment's largest single holding by value, trailed by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company at just under $350 million.
Harvard's financial picture, though, is undermined by moves by the federal government. Federally-sponsored research revenue declined 19.5% to $509 million in fiscal 2026.
And starting in the current fiscal year, "endowment resources will face an additional constraint, with the federal excise tax on Harvard's net investment income rising nearly six-fold, from 1.4% to 8%," Kalra and Barakett wrote. "We estimate the higher rate will cost roughly $300 million a year."
"[I]n a year of returns like this one," the federal excise tax "would be several times larger," they noted.
President Alan Garber acknowledged such headwinds, but said in the report that Harvard can still succeed.
"Together, we have the opportunity to set the University on a path to excellence that none of us can imagine today," he said. "Notwithstanding the challenges and uncertainty, this is a thrilling time to be part of a great American institution devoted to Veritas."

title: Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now
body:
GET THIS IN YOUR INBOX FIRST: Subscribe to CNBC's "Power Insider" newsletter.
Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.
That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.
Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out. If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.
As I've reported , prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.
Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.
I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.
You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.
On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.
The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.
Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.
The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL) . Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.
Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.
Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."
Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.
Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.
In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.
The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM) , Valero (VLO) , Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF) .
Fun Fact → While nearly every other company calls Texas home, refiner PBF is headquartered in a suburban office park just off a highway in New Jersey.
Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.
First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR) . The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

title: Show HN: Where waves come from – an interactive explainer of ocean swell
body:
The waves you'll surf this weekend are already out there. A storm you'll never see made them days ago, maybe on the other side of an ocean. This page follows them from the storm to your beach.
Wind dragging over water makes ripples. The ripples give the wind something to push on, so they grow. Blow harder, or for longer, and you get bigger waves that are longer from crest to crest. They also need room. The stretch of sea the wind blows over is called the fetch, and once the waves reach the end of it they stop growing. That's why a gale on a lake makes nasty chop but never a long swell, however long it blows.
Those heights are the sea out where the wind blows, not surf. Forecasters size up a sea by the average of its biggest third of waves, and in a big storm that can be as tall as a three-storey building. The wind here also blows perfectly steadily, which real winds never quite do, so real seas tend to come out a little smaller.
Only part of that sea reaches your beach as swell. On the way it shrinks in three ways. It spreads out over a wider and wider stretch of ocean. Its periods string out, so only a slice of the storm's waves goes past at any one time. And the short waves die off. The swell that's left keeps roughly the storm's period, but after crossing an ocean it's usually a third to half the storm's height, and less from a small storm. You can try it in the ocean scene below.
A real storm blows like this for a day or two over a patch of ocean the size of France. What it leaves is a mess: waves of every size, running every which way, piling into each other.
Long waves travel faster than short ones. So once the waves leave the storm, they spread out: the longest race ahead, the short ones fall behind, and the shortest just die. A few days out, the mess has turned into neat lines of waves that are all about the same size. That's a swell.
Surfers who watch buoys know this pattern. A new swell shows up as a few long, slow waves, 18 or 20 seconds apart, often hardly any height at all. Over the next day the period drops and the waves fill in. The farther away the storm, the longer that takes.
Swell goes a very long way. Out in deep water it loses surprisingly little, and a 15-second swell covers about 1,000 km a day. In 1963 the oceanographer Walter Munk and his team followed swells from storms in the Southern Ocean all the way up the Pacific to Alaska, more than 10,000 km .
A storm doesn't send swell equally all round, though. Most of it goes the way the wind blows, in a fan, so a beach off to one side gets a smaller swell, or none.
This is why a beach only gets swell from some directions: it needs open water between it and the storm. It's also why some spots wake up only in winter, when the storms are in the right place, and why a south swell in California can come from a storm south of New Zealand a week and a half earlier: storms down there mostly blow towards the east and north-east, aiming their swell up the Pacific.
Sit on the beach and you'll see the waves don't come evenly: a few big ones, then a lull. That's because a swell is never one clean period. It's a bundle of close ones, say 12, 12.5 and 13 seconds, that drift in and out of step. When they line up, their waves add up into a set. When they fall out of step, they cancel out and you get the lull. Two swells are the simplest version of that, so here are two.
So "every seventh wave" isn't a rule. How many waves come in a set depends on how close the periods are, and it changes from one swell to the next.
Every swell at your beach left a storm somewhere. Here are the ones there right now, each with the line it came in on. Pick a spot, use where you are, or tap the globe.
Ripple shows every swell coming to your spot for the next 16 days, from every wave model side by side.
Want to go further? Swell period, explained shows why a smaller swell with a longer period is often the bigger day.

title: The next developer interface is ambient intelligence
body: For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine. AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls. We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different. AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. The development workflow now is about understanding the structure of codebases, the customer, and what a good solution should feel like. This makes developers’ jobs even more important, and their time more valuable. It makes judgment more valuable. It makes taste more valuable. An agent can generate three implementations before you finish your tea, but someone still has to decide whether the abstraction belongs, the migration is safe, the tests prove anything useful, and the result solves the problem. That is the most important change in the craft: the developer remains accountable for the outcome, even as more mechanics are delegated. So what does this mean for the emerging developer workflow? The goal is to embed AI into the workflow, not beside it. It’s more of an ambient intelligence. That requires portable context. MCP connects agents to tools and services; repository instructions and skills encode conventions; hooks enforce policy and validate output. Simpler interfaces need explicit context underneath. I see three layers: modality captures intent; the harness plans and acts; the control plane lets developers inspect, redirect, and approve. The best products connect all three without surrendering control. Together, they let developers move across text, voice, and physical controls without losing context. Why physical controls are interesting again I, and many others in the maker community, have been experimenting with ambient control devices, from inexpensive hackable picture frames to ESP32 devices with screens attached. Agentic coding is past just a keyboard and a terminal into alternative interfaces. Getting this kind of technology into everyone’s hands is something that I’m very passionate about and so over the past 18 months we’ve been working with Logitech on their MX Keypad and how it can help this new way of working. The Logitech MX Keypad turns familiar developer actions into programmable inputs to accelerate workflows that are ambient and contextual to the work devs are doing. In GitHub Copilot app, a key can submit a parameterized prompt, open or resume a Copilot session, invoke an IDE command, or trigger a multi-step sequence. The hardware earns its place only when that shortcut removes enough friction to keep you in the code, but still gives you control. Physical controls work when an action repeats often enough that removing a few steps preserves concentration. Not every developer needs another device on the desk, and not every interruption deserves a key. However, with this experience the developer decides which actions earn that shortcut and when the keyboard, command palette, or voice is better. Maintaining flow is the key, and a good interface gives some of that attention back. GUIs made software visual. Mouse made navigation easier. The web made it connected. Mobile made touch natural. Agents add intent and action. The interface now includes ambient control. The interface moves into the background That is why GitHub worked with Logitech to integrate the GitHub Copilot app directly into the experience. Developers can run agentic workflows in control, map a repeated prompt, start or resume a session, and decide through real use whether a physical control helps you stay in flow. This is still early, so the important questions are engineering questions. How much repository and organizational context should an agent retain? Which tool calls can run automatically? How should credentials, network access, and secrets be scoped? What evidence should accompany a change? How do multiple agents coordinate without duplicating work or creating conflicting pull requests? Products such as MX Keypad let us explore one practical part of that system: how developers invoke, steer, and resume agentic work without losing focus. For decades, developers learned to speak computer: syntax, commands, APIs, shortcuts, and the occasional incantation copied from a seven-year-old issue comment. Now computers are getting better at meeting us halfway. The best interface will not have the most panels or AI buttons. It will understand enough context, preserve meaningful control, and get out of the way so we can build software that matters. The goal is not to remove developers from the work. It is to remove friction around the work. Pairing MX Keypad with GitHub Copilot Pro+ gives developers a concrete experiment: choose one repeated interruption, map it to a control, and see whether it preserves focus. If you want to try it, you can do so here and get three months of GitHub Copilot Pro+. The post The next developer interface is ambient intelligence appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

title: Romania Holds Russia Responsible as Attacks on 4 Black Sea Merchant Ships Kill 8
body:
Romania holds Russia fully responsible for the latest wave of strikes on civilian vessels in the Black Sea that has left eight people dead over the last 24 hours.
In a statement on Thursday, Oct. 15, acting Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu said the commercial shipping vessels were struck in Romania’s territorial waters and exclusive economic zone, accusing Moscow of turning the sea into a danger zone for civilian ships as part of its war against Ukraine.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“These are callous and murderous attacks against civilians,” Țoiu said. “Russia bears full responsibility for these developments.”
The latest attack struck a civilian ship in Romania’s exclusive economic zone on Thursday morning.
The vessel, named the Wine Trader, reported a fire at around 7:00 am (0400 GMT), approximately 13 nautical miles southeast of the Romanian city of Sulina, the Romanian Naval Authority said in a press release.
Air and naval units from the Romanian Coast Guard and the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations, both under the Interior Ministry, are still searching for crew members who remain missing.
Five sailors were airlifted by helicopter and taken to a hospital in Constanța, all in stable condition. Some are being for burn injuries and smoke inhalation, according to Țoiu.
At least 163 civilian and commercial vessels were hit in the Black Sea during the first eight months of this year, according to Turkey’s IMEAK chamber of shipping.
Țoiu said the maritime attacks coincide with a growing number of Russian Shahed and other aerial and maritime drones entering Romanian territory, with three such incursions recorded on Thursday alone.
The Romanian military fighter jets were scrambled for preventive air policing.
While the investigations are still underway, Bucharest confirmed that NATO allies and European partners have been informed of the attacks.
Romania would continue work to strengthen the alliance’s collective ability to respond to such incidents and bolster its deterrence and defense posture.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte will convene the North Atlantic Council within days, following a meeting with Romanian President Nicușor Dan and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, Țoiu said.
She also renewed Romania’s call for a ceasefire in the Black Sea to restore safe navigation along a key route for global food trade.
On Wednesday, Oct. 14, Dan announced that he held a telephone discussion with Bulgaria’s President Iliana Iotova regarding the recent drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea off the Bulgarian coast, as well as other incidents that affected infrastructure and shipping in Romanian waters.
“These drone attacks are direct consequences of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and endanger not only shipping in our region but also vital agricultural supplies to other continents,” he said, echoing President Volodymyr Zelensky’s repeated warnings that the strikes could cause a serious global food problem, particularly in the Middle East and Africa.
The latest strikes come as Russia escalates its hostile rhetoric toward the West and steps up hybrid warfare across Europe, from frequent cyberattacks to drone sightings that have disrupted airports and commercial flights, prompting several EU member states to warn that Moscow is already waging a direct war against the continent.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned the strikes and urged European allies for stronger protection of the freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.
He reaffirmed support for Romania and warned that Russia was essentially turning the Black Sea into a zone of danger for civilian shipping, with its reckless actions threatening international trade and global food security.
“Freedom of navigation is not negotiable,” Sybiha warned. “Russia must not be allowed to dictate the rules through deception and force. Together, we must ensure that the Black Sea remains open, safe and free.”
During the night of May 28-29, a Russian drone struck an apartment building in Galați , a southeastern Romanian city near the Ukrainian border, triggering a fire and injuring two people.
Romania responded to what Dan called the most serious security incident on Romanian territory since the start of Russia’s war against Ukraine by expelling Russia’s consul general in Constanța and closing its consulate.
On June 26, Russia announced the closure of Romania’s mission in St. Petersburg and expelled its consul general in retaliation for Bucharest’s decision.
Almost exactly a month later, Romania ordered a Russian embassy employee to be expelled in what its foreign ministry called a “firm response” to drones repeatedly breaching its airspace.
The move came after Romanian forces shot down three drones over the weekend, the last of which was intercepted by a Romanian F-16 fighter jet over the country’s territorial waters near the Sulina-Chilia area on Sunday morning, July 26.
The interception marked the third such incident over the course of three consecutive days.
On Aug. 20, a Romanian F-16 fighter destroyed an explosives-laden marine drone near the strategic Neptun Deep gas project. Bucharest again held Russia responsible for the incident.
A Russian drone violated NATO airspace on September 13, prompting Romania to scramble F-16 fighter jets.
Zelensky claimed the drone penetrated “about 10 kilometers into Romanian territory and operated in NATO airspace for around 50 minutes,” adding that the drone’s route was “always calculated” and not a “coincidence, a mistake, or the initiative of some lower-level commanders.”
Moldovan President Maia Sandu had said the same about the repeated drone incursion over Moldova’s airspace, claiming that some drones entering the country’s airspace are not accidental strays, but rather deliberately sent there by Russia .
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Defense Business Brief: Wrapping up AUSA
body: WASHINGTON— Six anti-war protestors disrupted an autonomous warfare discussion featuring Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and the military service secretaries Wednesday at the Army’s annual conference. By the time the third protester shouted denouncements of the U.S.-Iran war, some members of the audience had begun chanting “USA, USA.” The politically charged atmosphere isn’t typical at the show. But this year, it served as a contrast for what appeared to be a more prominent international presence than previous years—from the number of international companies represented to the size of the displays. Ukrainian companies made their debut with a massive tent just two blocks from the convention center. Overall, there were 165 international companies and nine international pavilions on the showroom floor, representing Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Greece, Israel, Korea, and Norway, the Association of the U.S. Army, or AUSA, told Defense One . The roughly 2,000-member international delegation was about average, representing 92 countries—including 27 army chiefs, 14 sergeants major of the Army, 17 ambassadors, and two ministers of defense, according to AUSA. But the ambassador count this year was also higher, AUSA said. That could be an indication that while political tensions rise , there’s still an appetite for diplomacy—and foreign military sales . Welcome You’ve reached the Defense Business Brief, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com . Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here , and tell your friends to subscribe ! 1:1 with Mike Wior, CEO + co-founder of Allen Control Systems. ACS was one of 10 companies to land a counterdrone IDIQ contract with the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force-401 last month, and things haven’t slowed down since. The company makes a robotic turret , called Bullfrog, that can turn machine guns into a counterdrone weapon using AI and autonomy. “We just got our $500 million IDIQ. We are, obviously, working on getting funds into that as quickly as we can…getting to that point where we can prove on the battlefield, yes this works, and we should be replicating this across all the different services that need this type of capability,” Wior told Defense One during a break from the bustling AUSA conference showfloor. But the lack of a budget could stymie progress the Pentagon is trying to make in cultivating a tech-forward industrial base, he said. “Is the military going to be able to sustain this new ecosystem of defense tech companies? Can companies survive in this environment? What do they need to survive in this environment…when the military ultimately doesn't have full control over their own budgets?” he said. “It's a challenging environment as a startup.” But ACS is still pushing forward with a new facility. “We just opened a 200,000 square foot facility in North Austin” with the goal of increasing production capacity beyond 50 turrets a month once the orders come in, Wior said. “Whenever the orders come in, we start to fill out that IDIQ, and we can expand pretty quickly…by leveraging commercial off-the-shelf components, we have a lot of flexibility there, and then it's just a matter of expanding the workforce.” And they’re eyeing international deals. “We want to see more of an international economy for defense products…and we want to make our technologies available to other countries. Because that's needed, I think, in this environment where if it's just the United States government and they have a two-year appropriations problem, you might lose some really, really great technologies to attrition—just the ability to stay around long enough and participate.” Up, up, and away. The Army Space and Missile Defense Agency wants “a family of stratospheric systems,” such as high-altitude balloons, in a range of platform sizes that can provide “space-like capabilities” closer to Earth, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, who leads the agency’s transformation integration directorate for space superiority, told reporters Wednesday. “From about 60,000 feet to 100,000 feet is what we focus on in the stratosphere. That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads” while also being able to “take advantage of winds that are pushing you where you want to go already…to get either launched effects or other types of payloads for sensing and communications.” The agency hopes to start multiple experiments in the coming year. Bonus: The agency is also “working on a virtual space training environment,” Mroszczyk said. “We're building the virtual space layer to be able to visualize and understand how space effects can play in modern operations.” Biodefense prep. The Army wants biothreats to be a routine feature in major military exercises, as outlined in its updated biodefense strategy released last month. Turning that doctrine into actual readiness requires incorporating biothreats into “big” military exercises where it's “an operational constraint, and the whole of staff has to come to bear against it,” Alison Tamasi, the Army Nuclear and CWMD Agency’s chief of survivability and effects analysis division, told reporters Monday. “Our next target on the wall is looking toward some of those routine things like [Army warfighter exercises] where we can start to put bio defense in as one of the injects.” Context: These can be tabletop exercises, typically at the corps level or lower, where commanders and subject-matter experts map out responses to proposed scenarios, such as a viral outbreak at a port. Making moves + other news Anduril will let employees sell shares through a tender offer, bringing the company’s value to about $90 billion. BAE Systems now has two new counterdrone systems: a multi-domain artillery cannon system and high-power microwave. Leonardo DRS landed a $500 million IDIQ contract with the Pentagon’s counterdrone task force, JIATF-401, for tactical expeditionary sensing tech. Merlin Aerospace completed the first flight test of its new autonomous pilot, which is being designed to aid in missions like “maritime search and patrol,” the company announced on social media. The Pentagon signed an agreement with the Small Business Administration to increase access to strategic capital to help “defense-critical manufacturers, suppliers, and innovators.” In the deal, the Pentagon will identify companies that need financing through its Business Operators for National Defense (BOND) initiative and refer potential candidates to SBA. ]]>

title: Some 'classic' money advice is actually pretty new—and not all of it is worthwhile, says historian
body:
In the world of personal finance, many of the lessons we're taught are touted as historical . Since the dawn of time, the experts tell us, those who got ahead financially lived within their means, saved diligently and spent and invested carefully.
It made Joseph Moore — a historian and author of " How to Get Rich in American History ," published in April — wonder if Americans had been receiving, following and prospering from the same advice for the past few centuries. What he found surprised him.
"Is there timeless wisdom of money that we should all be following, from Ben Franklin to now? The answer is no," Moore says. "It turns out, what 'always' worked is always changing."
Some common financial principles that seem old are recent phenomena, Moore says, and some situations that seem new are, in fact, quite common throughout history.
In both such cases, knowing your history can be helpful. After all, if previous generations flourished without more recent advice, maybe the current wisdom isn't as valuable as we think. Conversely, maybe you don't need to find a creative solution to a problem that isn't actually that novel.
Here are three misconceptions Moore points out from the history of American personal finance — and what you can learn from them.
Americans are struggling with housing affordability amid high mortgage rates and rising home prices. But it's not a historically unique problem, Moore says.
"We absolutely are in a housing crisis caused by a housing shortage," he says. "It's neither the first nor the worst."
Moore points to 1948, when the ratio of people who wanted to buy a house to available inventory was about double what it is now, as the worst culprit. The year 1981, when the median new mortgage consumed more than half of the median household income, was no picnic either , he says.
That doesn't mean that the current shortage isn't real or that you should suck it up because other people had it worse, Moore says.
But it is worth looking at how people have historically solved it — personally, not politically. And in the case of a housing shortage, Moore's answers aren't glamorous.
One historical solution was moving more often. Currently, the housing market is worse in some places than others. Folks used to be more likely to pick up and go to places where opportunities were better, Moore says. For most of the country's history, between 1 in 3 and 1 in 5 Americans moved every year, he says, pointing to research by historian and journalist Yoni Appelbaum. Now, it's more like 1 in 13 , Moore notes.
Another common solution for unaffordable homes: sharing housing. In 19 th -century America, it wasn't at all uncommon for homeowners to rent out rooms in their house to help with the mortgage, Moore says. The same logic applies to modern-day renters who split spaces with roommates to keep costs down, he says.
"It's a shortage of space, so you have to monetize space," says Moore.
Investors are often told that the path to long-term wealth is simple: Invest consistently in a low-cost, broadly diversified stock portfolio. Need proof ? Consider the S&P 500's upward trajectory since before the stock market crash in 1929, and think of all the compounding returns you could have earned over that period had you invested.
"Something really new that we act like is really old is that compound interest is what builds wealth," Moore says. "Nobody got rich by compound interest for most of U.S. history, and if they did, they were generally already wealthy."
Think about it: Index funds weren't around, nor were fractional shares. If you wanted to own every stock in an index, you'd need to have the money to buy shares of each, plus a fee for your broker, of course.
"For most of American history, less than 10% of Americans owned stocks at all. That's not how people got wealthy," Moore says. "They got wealthy by concentrating most of their efforts in small businesses and careers, real estate and job tools. [Few people] compounded their way to wealth until the greatest generation and baby boomers, when the technology came online to allow you to use compounding."
Investors should still take advantage of the innovations that made diversified, low-cost portfolios widely accessible, Moore says. Just remember that there's more than one way to build wealth.
One piece of financial advice that feels tried and true is to create a budget and stick to it. How else can you make sure you don't overspend and keep yourself on track toward your financial goals?
But Moore says that the household spending spreadsheet is a relatively new phenomenon.
"Nobody in the 1800s budgeted the way we talk about budgeting," he says. "These forward-facing spending categories would be completely foreign to anyone's thinking."
For most of American history, what folks did instead was look at their money in big buckets. A couple might divide things between the husband's and wife's income, for instance, he says. Or, to keep things even simpler, they divided income between what they needed to survive, and whatever was leftover.
More complex budgeting schemes came into fashion in the early 20 th century, Moore says, with financial guides at the time touting how much you could save by slashing the likes of alcohol and tobacco — the lattes and avocado toast of their day.
There's no one right way to manage money. But if you find budgeting tedious, Moore argues that attitude puts you in line with generations of Americans who kept things simple by practicing what we'd now call reverse budgeting : paying their bills, putting money away for goals and then spending the rest as they saw fit.

title: Ukraine Strikes Major Russian Oil Refinery
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
It took Ukraine just hours to turn President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s “we’re done” into a refinery fire.
Ukrainian drones struck Russia’s Ryazan refinery on Thursday, ending Kyiv’s brief pause in attacks on Russian energy infrastructure after Zelenskyy said Moscow had ignored the ceasefire promoted by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The Rosneft-owned refinery sits about 300 kilometers southeast of Moscow and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia’s refinery throughput. Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov confirmed a fire at the facility following what he described as a major Ukrainian drone attack. The extent of the damage is still being assessed.
Ukraine had suspended refinery attacks for three days following Trump’s Sunday announcement that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop hitting energy infrastructure.
But more than 500 Russian drones were launched overnight into Thursday, according to Ukrainian authorities. State-owned Naftogaz said a gas production facility in the Poltava region was damaged and operations there were suspended.
Zelenskyy told the Financial Times Thursday that the restriction on refinery attacks was finished.
“The block is out. We’re done,” he said.
For the diesel market, the end to the ceasefire is painful.
Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries as global diesel supplies tighten and U.S. diesel prices remain above $6 per gallon. Russian refining has already been repeatedly disrupted by Ukrainian drone attacks, reducing fuel production and exports.
Ryazan has been hit before, making Thursday’s strike another potential setback for a refining system that has spent much of 2026 repairing damaged units while trying to maintain fuel supply.
The attack turns an announcement made early Thursday into an actual change on the ground. Hours after Zelenskyy said refinery strikes would resume, one of Russia’s largest refining centers was burning again.

title: Tesla plans next-generation Roadster reveal after almost a decade of delays
body:
Tesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car.
The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering.
"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company."
Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012.
The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology to enable it to hover. While Musk fanatics expressed their excitement on social media, the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company.
At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then clung to it upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground.
The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience.
Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced, and the company didn't disclose specifications about other performance-level variants of the new Roadster. It was unclear whether the vehicle would be street-legal, with Musk saying on stage that, "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car."
The Roadster unveiling has added to speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX.
For years, Musk's companies have worked with and paid each other, even sharing some personnel. The collaboration has increased in 2026, with speculation about a possible SpaceX-Tesla tie-up swirling since the aerospace and defense company went public in June. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC ahead of the IPO that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier."
Barclays analyst Dan Levy predicted in a note out this week that such a transaction could happen before the end of 2026.
SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, while Tesla has a market cap of $1.4 trillion, making them two of just 12 U.S. companies worth at least $1 trillion.
Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China.
Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017 , and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly."
The prototype Tesla showed on Thursday is built to be as lightweight as possible with a steer-by-wire system, steering yoke, and an array of technologies developed by SpaceX, including thrusters, carbon overlay pressure vessels and diffusers, and powerful fans that enable the car to do some gymnastics.
One feature Tesla left out of its forthcoming Roadster is the company's "FSD" or automated driving system. Musk said the new Roadster will be the last vehicle the company produces that's intended to be controlled by a human driver.
Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either.
Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his reservation and refund requests.
"I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait."
Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure.
Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC ahead of the event that he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000.
O'Connor wrote in a message that he would be attending the show and was "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." After the event, O'Connor said what he saw was "off the charts."
Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.
