title: Bluesky wants to make it easier to buy, sell, and fundraise on the network
body:
Bluesky plans to introduce payments in the coming months, a first step in its strategy to make money without relying on advertising. CEO Toni Schneider and COO Rose Wang outlined the plans Thursday at TechCrunch Disrupt , explaining how the company hopes to build on the commerce and fundraising activity already happening on its decentralized social network.
“People are actually selling things, fundraising very successfully, supporting each other on the network,” Schneider said. “We want to make that easier, and the way we’re going to do this is if you see something on the network that you like and support, you can support that monetarily, and we want to do it in a way that works for Bluesky and for all the other apps out there as well, so that it works across the entire network.”
Schneider, the former CEO of Automattic, took the reins of the company in March after longtime CEO Jay Graber stepped down. He said, while onstage, that he was surprised by the reaction to his appointment, with some users joking that it marked the beginning of the end for the platform. Those comments reflected fears that a leadership change would bring unwanted changes to Bluesky.
Schneider said he understands that users can leave Bluesky for another platform if the company introduces features or changes they dislike, a reality that he said keeps the leadership team accountable as it prepares to introduce monetization in the coming months.
The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only viable business model for a social network.
“I think there’s a story around monetization that feels like advertising is the inevitable thing we have to do that will ruin the network,” Wang said. “What was really promising about having Toni join us is he built at WordPress Automatic a $10 billion business where a billion of it goes back to the parent company and the rest of it goes to the ecosystem.”
Wang also pointed to Bluesky’s status as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which she said puts the company’s mission at the center of its business strategy.
“Yes, we need to make money, but because of our infrastructure, we cannot lock people in,” Wang said. “And so the thing that really matters for us is the people who are creating value on the networks these days are the ones who are getting the value that is coming in or the money that’s coming in. And I kind of think of it as like feudal society where we’re working for a few landlords and they dictate everything, and then we have to pay up our dues as tariffs.”
Bluesky aims to give users ownership of their digital identities and control over their networks while creating a more open internet where value and revenue can flow directly to the people who generate them.
“First, we’ll start with payments, but I think it’s about disrupting the actual infrastructure layer, which is what we’re doing, and not just building another app,” Wang said.

title: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
body:
The federal government sued the state of California on Thursday in an escalating battle over how to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting by mail in federal elections.
The lawsuit is the latest action by the Department of Justice targeting state administration of elections, which President Donald Trump has often criticized as susceptible to fraud and voting by noncitizens.
The civil complaint, which the DOJ had threatened to file, asks a judge to prevent California officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined."
The Department of Justice asks that a judge order the state to set aside mail ballots from voters "identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens," and to verify their citizenship status before their ballot is counted.
Non-citizens are barred from voting in federal elections.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a post on X on Wednesday, said, in anticipation of the suit, "More dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality."
"Trump is now demanding that California election officials VIOLATE federal law," Newsom wrote. "Apparently, the rule of law only matters when it's convenient for MAGA's dear leader. California's elections are NOT Donald Trump's to control. We will ensure EVERY California voter can participate in a free and fair election.
The suit in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles came two days after acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, in a letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, gave the state 48 hours to determine whether any U.S. citizens were on a list of people the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots for the Nov. 3 election.
The DOJ previously gave officials in Los Angeles County a thumb drive containing the questioned names to officials in Los Angeles County.
McCotter told Weber the state needed to tell local election officials to segregate mail ballots until the citizenship status of their voters could be determined, and not send a ballot to anyone who had not yet received one.
"If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," McCotter said in his letter.
Weber's office, in a statement on Thursday, said, "In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullen made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls."
"Given the many high-profile examples of states purging US citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims," Weber's office said. "They refused and provided California with nothing."
"Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request."
Weber, in a statement Thursday, said the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."
She also said that California "has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls."
"My office and California election officials remain committed – as always – to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election," Weber said.
Weber's office declined to comment on the lawsuit Thursday, but pointed to a letter she had sent McCotter in response to his letter.
Weber, in her letter, said, "California's election administration will continue to be governed by applicable federal and state law, not by unsubstantiated claims and outrageous demands."
She said that "despite failing to send the list of alleged non-citizens to my office, you demand that we request transmittal of the list, review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours."
"This is an emergency of the DOJ's creation," Weber said.

title: Boom or Bust, Bitcoin Wins the AI Trade, Bitwise CIO Says
body:
No matter how the AI story ends, Bitwise’s chief investment officer argues, the trade leads to the same place: Bitcoin higher.
In a note to investors published Wednesday, Matt Hougan laid out his case using the “Choose Your Own Adventure” books of his childhood, where wildly different choices often funneled readers to the same ending.
He said the range of macro outcomes facing investors today is the widest he’s seen in his career, with pundits split between AI doubling GDP and AI causing human extinction. His answer was to walk down each path and see where it leads.
If AI delivers “superabundance,” Hougan wrote, productivity explodes and intelligence-based work gets cheap, but that abundance becomes a tailwind for genuinely scarce assets, as value migrates to things that can’t be reproduced, like waterfront land, gold, and Bitcoin.
If the AI bubble bursts instead, triggering a 2008-style recession, Bitcoin initially sells off with other risk assets, but Hougan argued a government bailout would follow, and given that the AI buildout is “the biggest infrastructure investment in the history of America,” the resulting money-printing would be enormous.
“This is exactly the environment bitcoin was built for,” he wrote, putting the odds of a bailout at “nearly 100%.”
The third path, a muddle-through of roughly 3% growth and 4% rates, simply lets Bitcoin keep doing what it’s been doing: drawing ETF flows, advisor adoption and corporate and sovereign balance-sheet allocations as government debt mounts. “Bitcoin wins by showing up,” he wrote.
The memo lands amid exactly the kind of macro anxiety Hougan is addressing. BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned this week that a halt to data center construction could tip the U.S. into recession, underscoring how tightly AI infrastructure and the broader economy have become intertwined.
Hougan was careful to hedge. He stressed Bitcoin won’t rise in a straight line, noting it fell 50% in days during the 2020 COVID panic before rebounding roughly 20-fold, and acknowledged the thesis could break for non-macro reasons. Among them: a global government crackdown or the quantum-computing threat to older wallets, a rising risk even as researchers debate whether AI could break crypto’s encryption before quantum computers arrive.
Still, his conclusion was unequivocal: for long-term investors, the big macro questions “matter less than most people think,” because nearly every path still ends with Bitcoin.

title: Origin Bags $20 Mn To Build Autonomous Construction Robots
body: Emerging out of stealth mode, robotics startup Origin has raised $20 Mn (around ₹189 Cr) in a funding round co-led by Accel and Zacua Ventures. The round also saw participation from Unilazer Ventures, Schema Ventures and Z21. Angel investors from Anduril, Skild AI, 1X and Tesla also participated in the fundraise. As part of the investment, Zacua Ventures’ founding partner Vivin Hegde has also joined the startup’s board as a director. The startup said that the fresh capital will primarily be utilised to deploy its flagship OG-1 robot and build a fleet of construction robots. A chunk of the capital will also be used to support “large-scale” pilots with customers in the US and Europe and explore new use cases for bots. “We think of Origin as a time machine for construction, helping crews complete work faster while moving the industry toward autonomous job sites. Wall finishing and painting are only our starting trades; our ambition is to automate the full range of interior trades so contractors can build faster with consistent quality,” said Origin cofounder and CEO Yogesh Ghaturle. Founded in 2025 by Ghaturle, Ashish Daga and Tushar Makkar, the US-headquartered startup develops autonomous robotics for construction work. It aims to address widespread labour shortages in the construction sector and claims that its robots can work 3X faster than a human. Its flagship robot, OG-1, is currently capable of automatically completing wall-finishing tasks such as applying compound, sanding, and priming. The startup claims to have already deployed its robots at construction sites in New York, adding that its bots are also being deployed across commercial spaces, apartments, data centers, hotels and warehouses. Under the hood, OG-1 is powered by a proprietary foundation model that the startup calls a construction action model. The model integrates a reasoning system to plan complex sub-tasks, an action policy to help it navigate autonomously and a controller for feedback-driven movement. Going forward, the startup plans to deploy 150 robots by the end of 2027. It is also exploring additional pilots for its offerings in countries like Germany, Sweden, France and Saudi Arabia. Origin also noted that incoming investor Zacua will support its expansion plans through its network of contractors, developers and manufacturers. With the latest fundraise, Origin is eyeing a piece of the global construction robotics sector, which is projected to become a $12 Bn opportunity by 2036 . Back home in India, startups like Pace Robotics and Flo Mobility are also raising big bucks to take a lead in the burgeoning space. title: Anthropic is letting METR researchers look under the hood with employee-level access
body:
Anthropic is giving employee-level access to six researchers from METR , a nonprofit that tests frontier AI models, to independently assess Anthropic’s models, safety practices, and risk management, the company said in a blog post on Thursday.
The arrangement comes at a time where incidents of AI agents acting outside their instructions have been disclosed every week or two since late August. The incidents have sharpened calls for independent checks on AI companies.
“We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making,” Anthropic said in the blog post. “We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.”
Under the new arrangement, the METR team has Anthropic-issued company laptops, office space, and access to internal tools roughly on par with what Anthropic’s own risk assessment teams use. “Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk” the company said.
Anthropic compared the arrangement to banking, similar to how regulators place resident examiners inside the largest banks.
METR will publish its own assessments of Anthropic’s risks, incidents, and practices, and the company has given up the right to block them.
“Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into narrow, pre-defined categories,” the company said, such as customer data, anything attorney-client privileged, or relating to information about its model architectures. “METR is free to characterize our redactions publicly, and say whether it believes the redactions were justified, as long as it does so without revealing the redacted information” Anthropic added.
METR is the only evaluator so far at the top of a three-tier system Anthropic is building. Evaluators in the bottom tier, like biosecurity nonprofit SecureBio, run narrow reviews and require Anthropic’s approval to publish. The middle tier gets more information and can publish without approval, while the top tier adds METR’s employee-level access.
Thursday’s announcement makes good on a promise Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei made in a September essay , where he proposed embedding outside evaluators inside AI labs as a first step toward slowing the technology’s development. OpenAI quickly pledged the same , and both companies, along with Google, Meta, Nvidia, and xAI, have since signed a White House accord committing to independent review.

title: 2 women accuse Matt Gaetz of sex trafficking in new lawsuit
body: TALLAHASSEE, Florida — Two women this week sued former GOP Florida Rep. Matt Gaetz and two others — including a former state legislator — in federal court and accused the men of engaging in an alleged sex trafficking scheme during a time when Gaetz was still in Congress. The lawsuit, which seeks damages from Gaetz and other defendants, was filed in Orlando by two women who were in their early 20s when they first met Gaetz. The women are not named in the lawsuit. The details mirror allegations that were at the center of a House Ethics Committee probe that found Gaetz had sex with a minor, solicited prostitutes and used illegal drugs. “The defendants collectively used their public office, power, and wealth to prey on the economic vulnerability of the plaintiffs to commit the acts outlined below,” states the 38-page lawsuit. That House probe helped derail Gaetz’s bid to become attorney general under President Donald Trump. He resigned from his Northwest Florida congressional seat to seek the post but decided to withdraw his name ahead of a potentially messy confirmation battle in the Senate. Gaetz, who has repeatedly denied he ever had sex with a minor, said he would vigorously contest the allegations in the lawsuit. “I look forward to taking the plaintiffs’ depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false,” Gaetz said in a text message. “The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional committee report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance.” The civil suit is the latest development in the long-running scandal involving Gaetz, a former ally of Trump who has continuously denied any involvement in underage sex or trafficking of women after news broke in 2021 that the Justice Department was investigating him. The lawsuit this week by Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 was first reported by the Miami Herald . It alleges that Gaetz and former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg “coordinated the recruitment, payments, drugs and travel to obtain commercial sex acts from young women.” The lawsuit includes former Florida legislator and lobbyist Chris Dorworth because his Central Florida home was the site of a party where he allegedly “participated in the activities alleged there.” Greenberg is serving an 11-year federal sentence after he pleaded guilty to multiple federal offenses including underage sex trafficking of a minor and wire fraud. Greenberg cooperated with federal investigators who were probing Gaetz but the U.S. Department of Justice closed the investigation without filing charges. The lawsuit says it “arises from the recruitment and sexual exploitation” that occurred from 2017 through January 2019 and included trips to various locations such as Las Vegas, New York City and the Bahamas. It accuses Gaetz and Greenberg of making promises to help the two women financially or with college bills. “They led her to believe they would resolve her financial needs as long as she continued to perform sexual acts for them and their associates,” the lawsuit states about Jane Doe 1. “They used the age, wealth and political power gap between themselves and Jane Doe 1 to keep her compliant and silent.” Jane Doe 2, the lawsuit states, was “paid less” than promised and “through this pattern defendants caused Jane Doe 2 to believe she would lose her education and serious financial harm if she stopped performing sexual acts.” Stencer Kuvin, a West Palm Beach attorney representing the two women, said in an email that federal law designed to protect sex trafficking victims has a 10-year statute of limitations “which potentially could run [out] next year based upon the allegations in the complaint.” Gaetz, a firebrand and ally of Trump, was once seen as a potential candidate for Florida governor or attorney general. Since he left Congress, he has hosted his own show on the One America News Network and he was appointed to the board of a nonprofit charged with distributing proceeds from a settlement Florida received after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill along the Gulf Coast.

title: Banks with Jeffrey Epstein ties eyed by Democrats Warren and Garcia
body:
Financial institutions and bank executives that may have aided the late financier Jeffrey Epstein' s sex trafficking operation are in the sights of a bipartisan group of lawmakers .
Legislation introduced Thursday — and led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., and Rep. Robert Garcia , D-Calif. — would require financial regulators to produce records related to Epstein, compel those regulators to investigate banks and executives with ties to the deceased convicted sex offender, and require industry bans and civil penalties for those found to have aided him.
"I have spent the last year calling on Donald Trump 's financial regulators to launch investigations into the big banks and executives who may have enabled Jeffrey Epstein's horrific crimes," Warren, who leads the Senate banking committee's Democrats, said in a statement. "Since they have failed to act, Congress must. The bipartisan Epstein Wall Street Records Act will ensure overdue accountability for the wealthy and well-connected on Wall Street who put profits over people."
The legislation is co-led in the House by Reps. Ro Khanna , D-Calif., Thomas Massie , R-Ky., and Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill. Sens. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., Ron Wyden , D-Ore., and Ben Ray Lujan , D-N.M., signed on to the Senate version. The House version has 17 Democratic co-sponsors.
The proposal would apply to the Federal Reserve , Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation , Treasury's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Securities and Exchange Commission. Spokespeople for the Federal Reserve and the OCC declined to comment. Spokespeople for the other regulators did not respond to requests for comment.
Since the start of Trump's second term, Democrats and a small group of Republicans have pressed the president to release records related to Epstein and to investigate the individuals and businesses associated with him.
Warren has sought answers from Barclays , Goldman Sachs , and JP Morgan Chase on their connections to Epstein. And Wyden, in his capacity as the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, released an investigation in August that found "significant evidence that JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, and Bank of America violated federal anti-money laundering laws by failing to screen and report Epstein's suspicious financial transactions in a timely manner."
Barclays, Goldman Sachs and JP Morgan Chase all declined to comment on Thursday.
The fallout from the Epstein files has been politically perilous for Republicans , who largely opposed an effort, led by Massie and Khanna, to force a vote to release the documents. After Trump belatedly signaled his support for the legislation, the Epstein Files Transparency Act passed both chambers of Congress with near unanimity and was signed into law in November 2025. The legislation was meant to force the Department of Justice to release its records related to Epstein.
But ahead of November's midterm election , Democrats in recent weeks have ramped up campaign ads hitting their GOP opponents for past opposition to releasing the Epstein files. And those who advocated for public disclosure of the files have continued to push for accountability in Washington and on Wall Street.
"The Epstein Files Transparency Act forced the Attorney General to release DOJ, FBI, and U.S. Attorney's Offices' files. This bill does the same for bank regulators. Justice for the survivors means following the money," Massie, who had a falling out with Trump over his effort to release the Epstein files, said in a statement.

title: Show HN: HireReady, interview prep with spaced repetition and AI voice mocks
body:
HireReady is an online technical interview preparation tool for software engineers. It combines AI-powered voice mock interviews, FSRS-5 spaced repetition scheduling, and 1,300+ practice questions covering coding (data structures and algorithms), system design, and behavioral interviews. HireReady helps candidates prepare for technical interviews at companies including Google, Amazon, Meta, Apple, Microsoft, Netflix, Stripe, Uber, Airbnb, and other top tech companies.
Key features include: AI voice interviews available 24/7 using OpenAI Realtime API, spaced repetition that schedules reviews at optimal intervals for long-term retention, a built-in code editor, STAR method behavioral coaching, company-specific question sets, progress tracking, and gamification with XP and streaks. HireReady is a progressive web app that works on desktop and mobile.
HireReady offers a free tier with 20 questions per day. The $39 Job Hunt Pass adds 90 days of unlimited practice, with a $199 lifetime option. It is an alternative to LeetCode, HackerRank, Pramp, Interviewing.io, and CodeSignal for software engineers who want all interview types in one platform with built-in spaced repetition for long-term retention.

body:

Chinese labs have become a go-to source for AI models businesses can download, customize and run on their own infrastructure. Alibaba’s Qwen, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI’s Kimi help set the competitive standard for open-weight systems, giving developers alternatives to proprietary models accessed through commercial APIs.
That shift shows up in adoption as well as benchmarks. Hugging Face’s March 2026 assessment says Chinese models accounted for 41% of downloads over the preceding year, surpassing U.S. models. In September, OpenRouter reported that open-weight models handled 60% of token volume from U.S.-originating requests on its platform, with Chinese labs supplying most of its open-model traffic.
Now Meta is releasing Muse Spark Open , an 816-billion-parameter model it calls “the most capable US open-weight model to date.” Announced October 15, the release gives enterprises another U.S.-developed option for running and adapting a large model themselves — and on relatively affordable consumer hardware, no less.
The geographic qualifier matters to the competition between AI labs and to buyers with specific procurement requirements. For enterprise teams choosing on practical grounds, the tests are task completion, reliability, licensing and operating cost. Where a model is developed does not by itself determine where business data is processed: OpenRouter already offers U.S. hosting for Chinese models , including DeepSeek V4 Pro and Kimi K3.
Meta’s published results make Spark Open a contender with specific strengths, rather than an overall open-weight leader. Its model card reports an Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of 39 , below MiMo-V2.6-Pro’s independently published 46 .
Meta’s table puts Spark Open ahead of its listed rivals on the JobBench and MCP-Atlas tool-use tests, but behind Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3 on terminal coding, extended software-engineering tasks and the GDPVal-AA professional-work evaluation. A separate public Artificial Analysis assessment of Spark Open could not be verified at publication.
The announcement does not establish a cost lead: it omits hosted token rates, while Meta’s desktop configuration uses a pair of M5 Ultra Mac Studios with a memory configuration that hasn't publicly shipped yet.
Spark Open’s case rests on what enterprises gain from its particular combination of capabilities, hardware support and commercial terms. U.S. leadership alone does not settle that buying decision.
According to the Spark Open model card , the model uses a mixture-of-experts design, activating 42 billion of its 816 billion parameters for each token. It supports a context of up to 1 million tokens and accepts text, images, video and audio. Its output is text.
That distinction matters for prospective applications. A developer can use the model to interpret recordings, inspect screenshots or analyze documents alongside written instructions. The release does not make Spark Open an image, audio or video generator.
Meta’s desktop configuration combines two M5 Ultra Mac Studios, each offering up to 512GB of unified memory. In its launch announcement , Meta describes the pair as providing a terabyte of memory and says MLX enables local operation.
The desktop pitch comes with a catch: Apple’s 512GB-memory configuration doesn’t arrive until late October , and its price remains unannounced . Current pricing points to an investment of tens of thousands of dollars. Apple lists a 256GB M5 Ultra workstation with a 1TB SSD at $10,799 ; four would provide the same combined terabyte of memory for $43,196 before tax and accessories. That provides a reference for the cost of assembling comparable memory capacity today, rather than a confirmed price for Meta’s two-computer setup.
The model card lists at least 700GB of accelerator memory for the NVFP4 version and 2TB for BF16. Activating a smaller share of the model during generation does not reduce those stated memory requirements to those of a standalone 42-billion-parameter model.
Meta describes local demonstrations in which Muse Code, powered by Spark Open, modifies the Ice Cubes Mastodon application and operates DaVinci Resolve to review footage and prepare vertical crops. These are company demonstrations; the announcement supplies no measured token-generation rate or complete hardware cost for the two-computer setup.
Developers can also use familiar serving software. Meta lists SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Transformers, MLX, llama.cpp and Unsloth, with support spanning AMD, Apple, Intel and Nvidia hardware. It points to PyTorch’s TorchTitan for further tuning.
Meta’s benchmark table places Spark Open ahead of the listed competitors on JobBench and MCP-Atlas. The same table shows GLM 5.3, Kimi K3 and Qwen3.8 ahead on several other measures.
These figures come from Meta’s materials, using the reasoning settings shown above. DeepSWE figures use each model’s preferred or best-available harness, so the surrounding agent software is part of the comparison.
Meta reports the Intelligence Index score of 39 in its model card. At publication, VentureBeat could not verify a separate public assessment of Spark Open from Artificial Analysis; the score should therefore remain attributed to Meta’s table. Artificial Analysis’s evaluations of the hosted Spark and Wonder models concern separate releases.
Spark Open also leads the listed models on HLE-Diamond without tools, scoring 26.1 against Kimi K3’s 22.2 and Qwen3.8’s 17.3. On visual evaluations with tools, it records 50 on ZeroBench against Kimi K3’s 41, and 73.6 on SimpleVQA against 71.9.
The U.S. qualification in Meta’s headline claim matters. Its table lists Intelligence Index scores of 26 for Inkling and 23 for Nemotron 3 Ultra, below Spark Open’s 39. Several other open-weight competitors nevertheless score higher. These results support a competitive U.S. release, with task-specific advantages; they do not establish a universal performance lead.
That U.S. distinction helps explain the enthusiasm of Interconnects author Nathan Lambert. “I waited so long for US open weight models to be relevant again,” he wrote on X . “Still more work to do!”
Independent listings from Artificial Analysis put that geographic distinction in sharper focus. The evaluator lists Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 46 , GLM-5.3 at 45 and Kimi K3 at 44 . It also lists GLM-5.3-Flash at 42 , while Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next each score 40. All six published scores exceed the 39 Meta reports for Spark Open.
Those comparisons remain provisional for Meta’s released checkpoint until its result can be independently confirmed. They nevertheless show why leadership among U.S.-developed open-weight models is a narrower claim than leadership across downloadable models worldwide. Spark Open adds another U.S. option for enterprise teams, while the higher published scores of several Chinese releases remain part of the competitive picture.
The Muse Model License grants rights to run, modify, fine-tune, distill and redistribute the software, subject to its conditions and usage policy.
Its revenue provision targets businesses providing models as a service. When the licensee and its affiliates generate more than $20 million in aggregate gross revenue during any consecutive 12 months, the license requires notification to Meta and a separate written agreement before offering Spark Open or its derivatives within that model-serving business.
The revenue measure covers the licensee and its affiliates, rather than only revenue attributable to Spark Open. But the provision explicitly exempts internal deployment, research, commercial activities outside model serving, and use inside a company’s own product when that product is not itself a model-as-a-service offering.
For an enterprise developing an internal assistant or incorporating AI features into an application, that exemption is material. The $20 million figure is not a general ceiling on free commercial deployment.
Other obligations still apply. Products must carry the attribution “Built with Muse Spark Open” in a permitted location, which can include documentation, a website or settings. The license also defines derivatives broadly enough to encompass models improved using Spark Open’s outputs. Meta states that it claims no ownership of generated outputs.
The appropriate description is therefore an open-weight release under a custom license. Downloadable access does not remove the license’s commercial conditions or usage restrictions.
Spark Open’s Hugging Face access notice asks applicants for their “full legal name,” “date of birth,” and “full organization name with all corporate identifiers.”
It instructs them to avoid acronyms and special characters, says the submitted form cannot be edited, and warns that failing to follow the instructions could affect access to this and other models on Hugging Face. The notice says the information falls under Meta’s privacy policy.
That is an unusually detailed request compared with Hugging Face’s default access gate. The platform’s documentation describes a default process in which users share their username and email address with a model’s authors. Publishers can add fields and customize the notice; the birth-date request is not a universal requirement for downloading models from Hugging Face.
The wording nevertheless has clear precedents. The Hugging Face pages for Meta’s Llama 4 Scout , Meta-SecAlign-8B and OMol25 display the same instructions.
A release outside Meta, Trillion Labs’ Tri-21B , also displays the same notice, referring to Trillion Labs’ privacy policy.
Those examples establish precedent for the published request, although they do not establish how each publisher verifies the submitted information. For enterprise evaluators, the immediate distinction is between being allowed to operate downloaded weights and the personal information requested to obtain them from a particular repository.
Meta’s announcement names Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI as API access routes. It lists Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face and Microsoft Foundry Models for obtaining weights.
Enterprises should distinguish those listings from identical support across every service. Meta’s deployment documentation says Groq access requires approval for an organization and describes a 131,072-token context limit on GroqCloud. It lists a 1,048,576-token context for Fireworks. The host can therefore constrain the model’s advertised capacity.
Together AI lists Spark Open API pricing at $1.25 per million input tokens, $0.15 per million cached input tokens and $4.25 per million output tokens. That means, over API, it is
Gemini 3.8 Flash — through Dec. 31, 2026
Muse Spark Open — Together AI serverless
Gemini 3.8 Flash — starting Jan. 1, 2027
Grok 4.7 Fast (Cursor) — >256K input, up to 500K
Gemini 4 Argon — post-introductory pricing
Its launch post confirms those rates for serverless access with a 1-million-token context window. Those are Together’s published rates; they do not establish uniform pricing across Meta’s launch partners.
For self-hosted deployments, the license fee is only one component of cost. Hardware, serving capacity and operational support remain part of the buying decision.
Spark Open arrives amid a broader expansion of Meta’s developer offerings.
On October 12, Meta introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full for software engineering and professional tasks involving subjects such as legal documents, finance and health. Meta’s research blog describes stronger underlying models and capabilities intended to retain useful context and sustain work through obstacles.
Independent testing provides evidence of progress. Artificial Analysis reports Intelligence Index v4.3 scores of 52 for Wonder and 56 for Full at maximum reasoning effort, compared with 48 for Spark 1.3 at maximum effort.
On its coding-agent index, Full running in Muse Code scores 68, alongside Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 at 68 and above the listed Opus 5.5 configuration at 66; Wonder scores 63. These are results for model-and-agent combinations.
The evaluator also reports a GDPval-AA v2.1 score of 1,857 Elo for Full, within the confidence intervals of Opus 5.5 at 1,866 and Sonnet 5.5 at 1,838. That places the systems close together on this professional-work evaluation.
Access and cost qualify those results. Meta’s pricing documentation sets Wonder at $4 per million input tokens, $0.20 for cached input and $20 for output. Meta’s Wonder product page lists a 1-million-token context for both versions, but Full has no published token price: it is available through Muse Code’s $50 monthly Power Usage or $200 Maximum Usage subscriptions.
According to Meta’s subscription rules , those subscriptions apply to Muse Code rather than arbitrary API keys. Usage limits remain, and separate keys incur pay-as-you-go charges.
Subscriptions also default to Contributor mode, allowing Meta to use submitted content for model training in exchange for greater usage. Users can disable that setting, and both Wonder models remain available on eligible plans in either mode. That setting deserves attention before a team submits proprietary code or documents.
Performance gains also carry a higher measured operating cost. Artificial Analysis estimates $4.52 per Intelligence Index task for Wonder, compared with $1.60 for Spark 1.3, $1.99 for Gemini 4 Argon and $0.72 for GPT-6.1 Sol in the tested configurations. Those benchmark costs do not predict every production workload, but they show why token prices alone cannot settle a model comparison.
Meta introduced the original Muse Spark on April 8 , describing it as the first model from its rebuilt Superintelligence Labs organization. Initial access came through Meta AI’s website and application, with an API preview restricted to selected users.
The launch emphasized multimodal reasoning and tool use. Meta also acknowledged remaining gaps in coding and tasks requiring sustained execution—areas that feature prominently in its subsequent releases.
The later hosted Spark models remain less expensive than Wonder. Meta’s current rates list Spark 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 at $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 for output in Standard mode. Contributor variants of 1.2 and 1.3 cost $0.10 and $0.20 respectively, with permission to use customer content for training. Those rates describe the hosted Spark versions, not Spark Open.
Muse Glimmer, released August 10 , serves a different deployment need. It is a 30-billion-parameter model under Apache 2.0, designed for local agents that use tools, interpret images and recover from failed steps.
Meta says its compressed language-model weights occupy less than 20GB, allowing the broader setup to operate within 24GB or 32GB memory configurations. That is a substantially smaller hardware requirement than Spark Open’s. For hosted use, Together AI lists Glimmer at $0.35 per million input tokens and $1.50 for output.
Meta’s downloadable-model history predates Muse. The company released the original LLaMA in February 2023 in sizes reaching 65 billion parameters, initially using a research-focused, noncommercial license.
Llama 2 followed in July 2023 , expanding availability to commercial applications. In July 2024, Meta released Llama 3.1’s 405-billion-parameter model alongside smaller versions.
The April 2025 Llama 4 release introduced the downloadable Scout and Maverick models, combining native multimodal processing with mixture-of-experts designs. Those architectural ideas also appear in Spark Open.
Taken together, Meta’s 2026 releases suggest a more segmented commercial strategy. Glimmer offers a comparatively compact download under Apache 2.0. Spark Open offers a much larger download with custom commercial conditions. Hosted Spark provides lower token prices, while Wonder and Full target more demanding work through APIs and subscriptions.
For enterprise buyers, the practical choice now spans capability, deployment control, licensing, data use and operating cost. Spark Open adds a substantial new option for teams prepared to run or customize their own infrastructure. Whether that option pays off depends on its performance on their actual tasks—and on what it costs to complete them.

title: Central Asian Leaders Link Trade and Security at Baku Summit
body: Central Asian leaders called for better transport links and joint action on water shortages at the Baku summit in Azerbaijan on October 15, arguing that practical cooperation could prevent political disputes from turning into conflict. The seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) adopted the Baku Declaration, admitted Laos as a new member , and approved Azerbaijan’s continued chairmanship through 2028. Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev called for an “infrastructure of trust” based on transparent government actions and the fulfillment of commitments. His proposed concept would connect conflict prevention with joint transport and energy projects, trade, and digital links. He pointed to the damage that conflicts in Asia were causing to economies and security far from the fighting. Mirziyoyev warned, “When dialogue weakens, the risk of misguided decisions increases.” He urged governments to prevent political disagreements from becoming armed confrontations. Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed a preventive diplomacy mechanism within CICA, enabling members to contribute before a crisis develops. He told the summit, “Peace is best built before crises emerge.” According to the Azerbaijani state news agency AZERTAC’s account, the Baku Declaration includes provisions on economic ties, transport and digital connections, and energy security. It addresses the opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence. Trade Routes Across the Caspian Sea The meeting came one week after the Avaza summit , where Central Asian presidents and Azerbaijan’s Ilham Aliyev discussed east-west and north-south trade routes. In Baku, those regional priorities entered a wider Asian forum, alongside calls to make commercial relationships more dependable. Tokayev proposed a CICA Transport Connectivity Strategy covering major routes, including the Middle Corridor across the Caspian Sea. He linked Azerbaijan’s rapprochement with Armenia to new opportunities for east-west transport. Tajikistan’s President Emomali Rahmon called in his summit address for simpler customs and logistics procedures and better connections between different forms of transport. He presented economic cooperation as a foundation for lasting peace, alongside continued action against terrorism and its financing. On the summit’s sidelines, the foreign ministers of Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan discussed transport and transit cooperation . Their talks covered improvements to logistics infrastructure and international routes connecting Central Asia with the Caucasus, according to Turkmenistan’s government account. During a separate bilateral meeting, Tokayev and Aliyev inaugurated the Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Cable Line remotely, opening an approximately 380-kilometer connection between Aktau in Kazakhstan and Sumgayit in Azerbaijan. The project forms part of the Digital Silk Way initiative , with onward connections intended to carry data between China, Central Asia, and Europe. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development gives the cable a design capacity exceeding 400 terabits per second . The ministry says the additional route will provide backup for existing international connections and allow operators to distribute traffic across more channels. It expects the connection to attract investment in data centers and cloud services as Kazakhstan seeks a larger role in carrying international data. Kyrgyzstan’s President Sadyr Japarov similarly called for fiber-optic routes linking Asia and Europe. He invited technology companies to build data centers and computing facilities in Kyrgyzstan, citing its hydropower resources and climate. He said Kyrgyzstan’s trade with CICA members had more than doubled over four years to exceed $14 billion in 2025. Calls for AI Safeguards and Water Conservation The push for more digital infrastructure was accompanied by proposals to manage its risks. Mirziyoyev suggested an expert platform within CICA to develop shared recommendations on responsible artificial intelligence, under an Asian initiative on technological trust. Tokayev called for artificial intelligence to become a sixth dimension of CICA’s work, citing risks to interstate stability. Kazakhstan advocated a CICA Water Partnership for joint research, technology exchange, and water-saving solutions. Uzbekistan suggested a Partnership for Climate Resilience that would combine water-saving technologies with green energy and continuous environmental monitoring. Japarov proposed a joint trust fund under United Nations auspices to protect Issyk-Kul and offered an initial contribution of $10 million, according to a presidential statement carried by Kyrgyzstan’s state news agency Kabar. He presented the fund as a means of attracting technology, scientific expertise, and international financing to protect vulnerable mountain ecosystems. Tokayev and Mirziyoyev called for continued work on CICA’s charter. Members agreed in Astana in 2022 to turn the conference into a full international organization, and both presidents presented the charter as a next step in that process. The gap between proposals and implementation had already been raised at Avaza. In his October 8 address , Tokayev said more than 200 initiatives had been put forward in the regional consultative format since 2018, but only a small proportion had been implemented. He called on foreign ministries to review those initiatives and assess which remained relevant and achievable.

title: The most important alliances will lead to critical minerals
body: The raison d’être of the “ Concert of Europe ,” the preeminent compact between the great powers of the 19th century, was to maintain the balance of power and suppress revolutionary movements. The post-World War II alliance systems sought collective security and deterrence. And the most relevant alliances of the 21st century will be the ones that secure the materials needed for key armaments and new technologies. In the first decades after the Cold War, the global economy seemed to settle on a dispensation that was heavily digital, light on assets, and tilted toward “just-in-time” manufacturing. It also leaned on heavily financialized business models that privileged services, software, and ever smaller and faster microprocessors. Then came what American mining entrepreneur Robert Friedland dubbed the “ revenge of the miners .” Emerging technologies—starting with electric vehicles and running through data centers and artificial intelligence—required prodigious quantities of material inputs from bulk metals to rare earth elements. And so did modern conflicts, from Russia’s war on Ukraine to the American-Israeli conflict with Iran. The physical economy is back, and with a vengeance. Years of underinvestment and long lead-up times mean that surging global demand will exceed supplies of most critical minerals for the foreseeable future. Further exacerbating the challenge for many countries, especially the United States and its traditional allies, is the dominant position that a single country, China , has painstakingly consolidated in the global production and processing of many critical minerals. It produces up to 98 percent of the world’s processed gallium and germanium, 95 percent of its refined magnesium, more than 90 percent of its rare earths and battery-grade graphite, 80 percent of its cobalt and tungsten, and 70 percent of its titanium. China is even the top producer of several metals that are mostly mined elsewhere. The military effects of this commercial advantage are highlighted by this year’s conflict in the Middle East. One study by researchers at the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines looked at the first 96 hours of combat after the war was launched on Feb. 28. In that period, the scholars estimated, U.S. and Israeli forces deployed 5,197 offensive and defensive munitions, consuming some 2,197 kg of cobalt and 11,444 kg of tungsten—materials of which China controls roughly 80 percent of the supply. (Remember that, unlike metals used in buildings or other manufactured good, metals used in armaments get only one use and cannot be readily recovered or recycled.) The much-discussed challenge of replacing the Pentagon’s depleted arsenal is not only about production facilities but about the materials they need. The need to reduce this dependence on a geopolitical competitor was the impetus behind President Trump’s Executive Order 14415 . It restricts defense contractors’ use of waivers to source critical minerals and other material inputs from foreign adversaries, expanding oversight over supply chains of subcontractors. It also instructs the Secretary of War to fast-track efforts to identify alternatives and other remedies to supply-chain gaps. Nor is defense materiel the only driver of demand for critical minerals. The AI revolution has turbocharged competition for some two dozen minerals for everything from power infrastructure (prices for copper , for example, hit near-record highs in early September) to transformer cores where grain-oriented electrical steel has been identified as an especially constrained enabling material, while shortages of gallium, germanium, graphite, lithium, cobalt, and rare earths threaten both chip manufacturing and the buildout of data centers. The U.S. administration’s concerns about supply-chain vulnerabilities are shared with some of America’s closest allies, with the leaders of the G7 striking an urgent tone in the joint declaration on securing supply chains for critical minerals coming out of their June summit in Évian-les-Bains: “In light of the high degree of market concentration, the need to reduce vulnerabilities regarding those resources and the growing use of arbitrary trade restrictions, we recall the urgency of diversifying our supply chains and building our collective resilience.” Moreover, in a marked departure from the past G7 communiqués on the subject which tended to be long on platitudes and short on substance, the group committed to specific quantifiable targets for reducing its members’ dependence on the unnamed “single supplier outside the G7 and partner countries” whose “use of non-market policies and practices and economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions and retaliatory measures on critical minerals and their related dual-use items” threaten the security of G7 to less than 60 percent by 2030 for REEs and permanent magnets and thereafter to half “as soon as possible.” This undertaking will not be easy and is only possible as a collective effort to develop resources where they can be found among friends (or, at least, non-adversaries), supporting processing value chains, and incentivizing production through the judicious use of guaranteed offtake agreements. Success for any alliance will be predicated on its expanding the political geography. While Australia, Brazil, and South Korea were included in the G7 discussions this year, noticeably absent was anyone from Africa, the continent being home to one-third of the earth’s mineral resources, including a majority of some key minerals like cobalt, manganese, and the platinum group metals. Success will depend as well on embracing new technologies to increase production. Infrastructure, too, is the key to unlocking bottlenecks in global critical minerals supply chains, while cultivating numbers of qualified personnel is essential to optimizing the transformation of raw ores into high-purity materials as is the availability of reliable, cost-effective energy at massive industrial scale for all the steps from crushing and grinding to chemical separation and thermal refining—all requirements which in turn will shape the composition of alliances for strategic materiel. At the start of the Cold War, American journalist Walter Lippmann famously described alliances as resembling chains. Prevailing in the 21st century’s struggle for geopolitical and economic advantage will require forging new links to build a chain that is strong, seamless, and resilient. Ambassador J. Peter Pham, former U.S. Special Envoy for the Great Lakes and Sahel Regions of Africa and a distinguished fellow at the Atlantic Council, is Executive Chairman of Ivanhoe Atlantic. This commentary is published in coordination with the 2026 Global Security Forum , of which Defense One is a media partner ]]>

title: ‘Revolutionary’: Bell touts MV-75 Cheyenne II as combat game changer
body: The U.S. Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II is expected to bring increased capability to the service, not just through its boosted speed and range but also with its “digital backbone.” Although the Cheyenne being equipped with over double the speed and range of current weapons systems will be transformative, Bell, the defense manufacturer for the aircraft, anticipates the real “revolutionary” part to be its software, Frank Lazzara, Bell’s director of MV-75 Sales & Strategy, told Military Times in an interview. The Cheyenne program is the service’s inaugural “digital-first” weapons system with a modular open systems approach , or MOSA, that allows the Army to virtually refine its architecture and helps acquire intellectual property and data rights needed to control future upgrades and avoid vendor lock-in. “The Army is trying to set the standard for the government to have control over their maintenance, their upgradeability, like they’ve never had before,” Lazzara said at the 2026 Association of the United States Army conference in Washington, D.C. Bell’s open system approach differs from others, he said, because it is guided and directed by the Army, giving them more control and changing the way business is conducted throughout the lifecycle of the aircraft. “This is the model for what the government should get when they acquire a weapon system of this level and an acquisition at this level,” Lazzara said. “That’s what gets lost out there.” “You can hang another system on an old aircraft, and you might have a little bit more capability, but you’re never going to have the capability you have in this aircraft, plus the ability to much more easily upgrade and maintain your aircraft through its life cycle,” he continued. “That’s where the payoff really happens.” The Cheyenne , which is designed to be a multi-mission aircraft, is the Army’s next-generation tiltrotor assault and utility aircraft, slated to replace part of the force’s UH-60 Black Hawk fleet. Its missions include long-range assault, utility, medical evacuations and humanitarian assistance. The aircraft is designed to fly at speeds over 300 miles per hour, can carry up to 14 soldiers and support an external load of up to 10,000 pounds. The aircraft was crafted for operations in the Indo-Pacific given its ability to cover vast distances quickly, but it can also be used in a close-in fight, special operations or as a deterrent in other theaters, Lazzara said. While looking at a model of the aircraft on display at AUSA, Lazzara said that it is intended to make a pilot’s job easier. Someday, pilots may even be able to control Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCA, as it is plugged into MOSA. There’s a heavy emphasis on controlly cost since it is a “delicate balance” because increasing capabilities and maintaining a low cost as contracted. Nothing on the aircraft was designed to be over a certain weight, allowing current equipment to be used in its construction, keeping the cost low. The project office for the Future Long Range Assault Aircraft, or FLARRA , conducted a design evaluation of the aircraft, gathering together operators, trainers and engineers in the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade to give feedback on the design. The 101st, based at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, was selected as the first unit to field the helicopter, with an expected arrival in 2027. The aircraft was previously set for a 2031 or 2032 delivery date, but the service announced the accelerated production timeline in January. The evaluations, which are meant to include soldiers in the process, led to some design decisions, including seating configuration and no cockpit doors, Lazzara said. But now, Bell is at a point in the development process where it’s time to “snap the line” and only progress with what’s already been decided. Bell is under a contract to deliver six training test aircraft and two limited-use test aircraft, but the development timing is “tough.” “We’re in a little bit of what I would call re-evaluating what that looks like based on leadership changes in the Army, and there’s really just kind of a different feeling in the Army right now with leadership changes both at the secretary level and the chief level,” Lazzara said. He said that there’s a series of meetings happening soon between Bell’s program team and the government to discuss the way forward, including what a feasible baseline schedule would look like without compromising capability and making sure both are aligned on funding. The Army’s fiscal 2027 funding request allotted $2.1 billion for the Cheyenne program in the Research, Development, Test and Evaluation framework, according to budget documents , a significant boost from $350 million in fiscal 2026. By the end of fiscal 2040, the Army anticipated up to 334 aircraft, according to a 2025 Congressional Research Service report . “We’re obviously concerned about a [continuing resolution] because that becomes a challenge if we are under continuing resolution for a long period of time,” Lazzara said. “So a lot of what the government and our team will be talking about … is that as well. What are the contingency plans?” “It’s a very well-supported program,” he continued. “Funding requests went through almost as exactly as we asked for it. So clearly supported on the Hill through funding. That funding for next year or ‘27, this year now fiscal, is significantly more than ‘26. So if we’re limited to ‘26 funding, you have to find ways to work through those challenges, and that’s what they’re working on now.” The government is currently under a short-term continuing resolution, or CR, with temporary funding measures in place through Dec. 11. Another CR or the fiscal 2027 appropriations bill would have to be passed before that deadline to avoid a government shutdown.

The project office for the Future Long Range Assault Aircraft, or FLARRA , conducted a design evaluation of the aircraft, gathering together operators, trainers and engineers in the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade to give feedback on the design. The 101st, based at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, was selected as the first unit to field the helicopter, with an expected arrival in 2027. The aircraft was previously set for a 2031 or 2032 delivery date, but the service announced the accelerated production timeline in January. The evaluations, which are meant to include soldiers in the process, led to some design decisions, including seating configuration and no cockpit doors, Lazzara said. But now, Bell is at a point in the development process where it’s time to “snap the line” and only progress with what’s already been decided. Bell is under a contract to deliver six training test aircraft and two limited-use test aircraft, but the development timing is “tough.” “We’re in a little bit of what I would call re-evaluating what that looks like based on leadership changes in the Army, and there’s really just kind of a different feeling in the Army right now with leadership changes both at the secretary level and the chief level,” Lazzara said. He said that there’s a series of meetings happening soon between Bell’s program team and the government to discuss the way forward, including what a feasible baseline schedule would look like without compromising capability and making sure both are aligned on funding. The Army’s fiscal 2027 funding request allotted $2.1 billion for the Cheyenne program in the Research, Development, Test and Evaluation framework, according to budget documents , a significant boost from $350 million in fiscal 2026. By the end of fiscal 2040, the Army anticipated up to 334 aircraft, according to a 2025 Congressional Research Service report . “We’re obviously concerned about a [continuing resolution] because that becomes a challenge if we are under continuing resolution for a long period of time,” Lazzara said. “So a lot of what the government and our team will be talking about … is that as well. What are the contingency plans?” “It’s a very well-supported program,” he continued. “Funding requests went through almost as exactly as we asked for it. So clearly supported on the Hill through funding. That funding for next year or ‘27, this year now fiscal, is significantly more than ‘26. So if we’re limited to ‘26 funding, you have to find ways to work through those challenges, and that’s what they’re working on now.” The government is currently under a short-term continuing resolution, or CR, with temporary funding measures in place through Dec. 11. Another CR or the fiscal 2027 appropriations bill would have to be passed before that deadline to avoid a government shutdown.

title: ‘Revolutionary’: Bell touts MV-75 Cheyenne II as combat game changer

The International Energy Agency will release more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible and accelerate the rest of its emergency oil draw,
Total releases are now set to exceed the 400 million barrels pledged in March.
About 330 million barrels have already been released since the Strait of Hormuz crisis triggered the record coordinated stock draw. IEA members still have roughly 100 million barrels left to deliver under the March action, with some countries having released more than their original commitments and others still holding barrels back.
The diesel portion disappointed the market.
IEA members had discussed releasing as much as 50 million barrels of diesel as part of a broader 100-million-barrel package of crude and refined products. European gasoil prices moved higher following Thursday’s announcement, with traders apparently hoping for a bigger immediate injection.
The United States wanted more, too. U.S. officials have pressed other IEA members to make additional emergency barrels available as diesel prices remain near record levels ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Spain will release another 4.4 million barrels from strategic reserves in October. It has so far delivered 3.7 million barrels of the 11.5 million barrels it pledged in March.
Diesel remains the weak spot in the global fuel system.
Refinery disruptions in the Middle East and reduced Russian fuel production have trimmed diesel exports, even as Persian Gulf crude shipments have begun to recover.
Governments have already put roughly 330 million emergency barrels into the market, with another 100 million or so still scheduled.
And while more than 20 million barrels of diesel are now being moved up in the timeline, the market was clearly hoping for more.

title: U.S. Targets Central Asia's Energy and Critical Minerals in Major Trade Push
body: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will meet the foreign ministers of the Central Asian republics - Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan - in Samarkand, Uzbekistan on 19 October 2026. Rubio will be accompanied by a delegation of more than 100 U.S. companies. Washington has framed the agenda around economic connectivity, energy security, and shared regional priorities. The meeting should convert earlier political commitments into financed projects, while managing the region's balancing act between the U.S., Russia, and China. The choice of Samarkand is symbolic as it hosted the first C51 ministerial in 2015.  The C51 was launched in 2015 and organizes U.S. engagement with the five republics around three pillars economics, energy, and security; the Critical Minerals Dialogue operates in parallel. The Central Asian foreign ministers visited Washington in November last year, where Rubio said he intended to visit the region in 2026. The size of the business delegation signals that Washington wants commercial results rather than another declaration and may be seeking to lock down its influence in the region which escalates the conflict with neighboring Iran.  The key issues  Critical minerals and processing. Central Asia holds significant deposits of tungsten, uranium, rare earths, copper, and other strategic minerals. The practical questions are which projects are bankable, who provides geological data and financing, and how much processing happens in the region rather than abroad. The republics want value-added production, not raw-ore exports, and Uzbekistan has said this explicitly, though the region's water deficit may limit processing opportunity. Ministers should identify a short list of flagship projects with named partners and timelines and agree on transparent licensing and investor protections.  Connectivity and trade corridors. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route "Middle Corridor" across the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, and Georgia, and onward to Europe via Turkey, offers an alternative to routes via Russia, but it is constrained by port capacity, rail interoperability, customs delays, and tariff stacking. Issues to address include harmonized customs procedures, digital trade documentation, financing for rolling stock and port upgrades, and coordination with Caucasus transit partners. Ministers need a concrete corridor roadmap, not general language on improving connectivity.  Related Europe's Gas Prices Close to 2022 High as Hormuz LNG Flows Remain Limited  Energy security. Central Asia needs reliable power for its own growth and has export potential in hydropower, solar, wind, and natural gas. Priorities include grid integration and regional power trade, U.S. technology and investment in generation and storage, and nuclear and natural gas-related cooperation where relevant. Winter supply reliability and aging Soviet-era infrastructure remain acute vulnerabilities.  Water and climate resilience. Water is tied directly to energy upstream states Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan want hydropower, while downstream states Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan need irrigation flows. Glacier melt and drought are intensifying the pressure. The U.S. should offer data, monitoring, and technical assistance, and can support regional frameworks without taking sides on specific dams or allocation disputes.  The region is in the midst of a water crisis and faces a "water debt" - a financing gap of over US$12billion by 2030 to modernize water and sanitation infrastructure. A lack of water will endanger the region's ambitious development plans and may become a source of political instability.  Investment climate and business follow-through. The American delegation will want clarity on regulatory predictability, contract enforcement, dispute resolution, currency convertibility, and favorable tax treatment. For Washington, financing tools such as the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and the Export-Import Bank of the United Statesare Washington key tools to secure deals. For Uzbekistan, World Trade Organization accession and improved trade access are priorities. Ministers should set up a mechanism, ideally a standing business council or working group, to track which announced deals actually close.  Security, Iran, Afghanistan, and counterterrorism. Security cooperation covers border management, counterterrorism, counter-narcotics, and information sharing. Afghanistan is the hardest question the republics view the Taliban relationship pragmatically and are deepening trade, transit, and energy links with Kabul, while the U.S. wants to avoid steps that legitimize the Taliban. The republics actively trade with Iran and Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic is causing anxiety in the region. A frank exchange on red lines, trade, projects such as transit and electricity lines, and shared threat assessments is a must.  Strategic balance and sanctions. The republics value the C51 as a way to diversify partnerships, not to choose sides as the region is newly independent and not part of someone else's empire for the first time since the 18th Century. Russian and Chinese influence is deeply embedded through trade, labor migration, energy infrastructure, cultural, and security ties. Sanctions compliance, particularly re-export of restricted goods to Russia, is a sensitive issue that should be raised privately rather than publicly. Washington should present itself as offering options, not demanding alignment with its grievances with its superpower competitors.  Governance and civil society. The rule of law, judicial independence, media freedom, and civil society underpin long-term investor confidence. The Trump administration prioritizes commercial and security interests, but language on institutional reform tied to investment protection can address governance without public confrontation or the appearance of American meddling.  The path to success  The republics expect investment and market access; U.S. companies expect predictability. Both sides risk disappointment if announcements outpace deal closings. The five capitals work to present a united front, but they do not always agree. Turkmenistan is "permanently neutral" and is more cautious about regional frameworks.  Moscow and Beijing will watch the meeting closely. Tweeting about it as anti-Russian or anti-Chinese would complicate the republics' positions. Washington should seek commitments on human rights improvements. Omitting governance entirely could draw criticism from the U.S. Congress and civil society, while pressing too hard and publicly could reduce regional goodwill.  Washington must be clear that it is a reliable, long-term, commercial and security partner that respects the sovereignty of each state and offers real alternatives, not conditions, and won't press-gang the republics into its conflicts with China, Russia, Afghanistan, and Iran. The republics should stress that regional cooperation, especially on water, transit, and customs, multiplies the value of external investment and strengthens bargaining power with all partners.  By James Durso for Oilprice.com
