title: Navantia signs a contract to modernize two patrol vessels for Angolan Navy
body: On October 15, 2026, Spanish shipbuilder Navantia announced a contract with the Angolan Navy for the modernization of two Mandume-class patrol boats. Navantia press release Navantia has signed in Angola a contract to repair and modernize two Mandume-class patrol vessels for the Angolan Navy. The work will take place at the San Fernando (Cádiz) shipyard. The contract, signed with Simportex, the Angolan state-owned company responsible for procurement for the Ministry of Defence, involves the modernization of the patrol vessels Golfinho and Atlântico , built at the Spanish state-owned Empresa Nacional Bazán – now Navantia – in the early 1990s. Signing: Alvaro Lobo (Navantia Commercial director for Africa) and General Luis Manuel da Fonseca Sotto Maior Pizarro (President of Simportex) (Credit: Navantia) This order from the Angolan government marks another step forward in Navantia’s international defence market for its Repairs and Services business area, particularly in Africa, where commercial efforts are being made to support navies in modernizing their existing ships. In addition, the contract includes training for a number of officers of the Angolan Navy in Spain, as well as two years of life-cycle support and knowledge transfer to the Navy to enable the maintenance of the vessels in Angola. – End – The post Navantia signs a contract to modernize two patrol vessels for Angolan Navy appeared first on Naval News .

title: Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more
body:
Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences.
The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform , which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build.
These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere.
Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.”
The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era.
Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this.
“Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.”
When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles.
To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang.
“Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.”
That network today has 47 million registered users , though it’s seen a decline in engagement , as some users who tested it out later returned to X.
Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said.
“There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.”

title: Yemen’s government needs weapons, but they can’t come from the US or Israel, expert tells 'Post'
body: The most effective way to defeat the Houthis and reverse their territorial gains would be to empower government forces to fight the group, though such support cannot come from the United States or Israel, an expert at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), the world's oldest and the UK's leading defense and security think tank, told The Jerusalem Post.Speaking anonymously to protect his connections in Yemen, “A” said international forces need to view the war in Yemen differently from the fight against al-Qaeda, which struggled to hold territory and maintain control. He also advised against viewing the conflict through an international lens, framing it as purely a proxy war between Saudi and Iranian-backed groups rather than a local conflict between a legitimate but ill-equipped government and an armed group over domestic grievances.“Locals who deal with local dynamics are there to stay, so they have a better understanding of how to navigate the complexities,” he reasoned, noting that international framing could also allow the Houthis to profit from the narrative that they are defending the Yemeni people against foreign aggression.Empowering local forces also means more than supplying weapons, he stressed, noting that the Houthis have been able to exploit deprivation in Yemen. The civil war, drought and other natural disasters have contributed to one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises.Even before the latest escalation in the conflict, more than 17.1 million Yemenis were experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million on the brink of famine, according to the UNHRC.Houthi support can be undermined by quality governmentSupport for the Houthis can be threatened if local populations can be offered a good quality of life in areas governed by the legitimate authorities, he said.Pointing to the heavily populated city of Taiz, the war's new front line, he noted that the siege 10 years prior was designed to systematically deprive civilians, spreading suffering as a means to apply pressure, and it was using the same strategy now.The Houthis first attempted to take control of Taiz in 2015, seizing control of military bases, the local airport, and key government infrastructure. By August, the streets were overrun by members of the pro-government resistance and, unable to capture the city in full, it encircled the territory, blocking the entry of fuel, water, medicine, and commercial goods.Though international truces occasionally diluted the impact of the siege, it wasn't until 2024 that a main road opened, allowing the transport of goods and people.Since early October, the Houthis have begun encircling the city.Without arms, government can't counter Houthi threatA warned that without arms, local authorities will be able to do little to break the blockade.“The Houthis are being armed by the Iranians, and they're not hiding that. They're not denying it. The other side is still trying to convince the international community to give them access to what's necessary,” he said.He stressed that despite sharing a common enemy with the internationally recognized government of Yemen's forces, Israel and the United States should not directly arm or fund them.Instead, their role should be limited to disrupting Iranian weapons shipments to the Houthis. Any more direct involvement, A warned, could play into the Houthis' hands.Having built much of their support around portraying themselves as defenders of Gaza, the Houthis could exploit any perceived association between Yemen's government and Israel to undermine its legitimacy and strengthen their own position.

title: Meet the agency using AI to screen grant applicants for links to potential adversaries
body: The Department of Transportation has been using artificial intelligence to determine whether grant recipients have ties to adversarial nations, an agency official said on Wednesday. The federal government has taken a variety of steps in recent years to limit hostile foreign governments’ access to American research, including restricting access to individuals or entities connected with countries like Iran or Russia. As the U.S. seeks to maintain its dominance over China in the global tech race, the Trump administration and Congress in particular have also been tightening the rules on collaborating with organizations or scientists who could conceivably share sensitive technologies or information with Beijing. It’s not easy, however, for officials or research institutions to unravel these threads, particularly when bad actors are surreptitiously working on behalf of nation states. But new capabilities could help to better chart these connections. Neil Chaudhry, senior advisor for AI at Transportation, said his agency has worked with partners to create “some really robust AI tools” to analyze the recipients of its research grants. “When we get to a down-select from grants that are some really promising research projects, we sort of do a deep dive on the [principal investigators] in the grant that says … do they have direct links to the [Chinese Communist Party] leadership, or do they have links to Russian oligarchs?” Chaudhry said during a panel at the SAP Public Sector Summit in Washington, D.C. “What we don't want to do is go on a fishing expedition,” he said, adding that identifying these kinds of relationships is “not based on the color of their skin and their nationality or something,” but on factors such as whether an individual or entity may be receiving funding from questionable sources. “If it's a company that's funded by a [venture capital firm] in Silicon Valley, that VC is probably funded by another VC in the Middle East or in Malaysia, and that VC is then wholly funded by the Chinese industrial bank,” Chaudhry said. “And then when that startup goes out of business, we don't know what just happened to that IP that the U.S. government spent money developing.” Transportation did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication. Transportation’s latest AI use-case inventory , which was published earlier this year, does not include the research grant-focused capability. Although other agencies have been using automation or more in-depth analysis tools to identify potential connections to foreign adversaries, Transportation’s use of AI seems to be relatively unique. A November 2024 report from the Government Accountability Office found that reviewed agencies had taken a variety of steps to comply with federal requirements mandating that they better identify foreign risks in the Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer programs. GAO noted that the programs, which were created to allow U.S. small businesses to engage in federally funded R&D, “face risks of foreign actors seeking to illicitly acquire federally funded research and technologies.” The watchdog noted at the time that some agencies — like the Air Force, National Science Foundation and NASA — were taking some steps “either to automate the processing of due diligence disclosure forms or support the vetting of applicants and identify associated risks.” ]]>

title: Vercel adds always-on workers to run more of your backend
body: Vercel is giving developers more options for running their backends on its platform. At its Ship conference in San Francisco on Thursday, the company introduced Daemons, a new service for continuously running background workers, and made its Python support generally available. It also made Drives, its persistent storage for AI agents, generally available. Always-on workers, pull-based jobs Daemons, which is now in public beta, lets developers deploy a container and specify how many instances should run in each region. Vercel makes sure those processes keep running and restarts them if they exit or crash. At launch, it supports pull-based workloads that allow workers to fetch jobs from a queue or database and then process them as they arrive. Vercel CTO Malte Ubl tells The New Stack that the company’s current push in terms of going further down the stack. “Let’s look at what people are doing, and let’s make sure that a larger chunk of them could just only use Vercel as their infrastructure provider,” he says. The company already offers queues and durable workflows , while its Services feature lets developers deploy frontends and backends together. These features cover request-driven work, Ubl says, but not everything a sophisticated backend does. “What really doesn’t fit well into that bucket is what you do find in sophisticated backend workloads,” he says, “where you want to do essentially processing on some kind of queue,” he says. He uses Vercel’s own deployment pipeline as an example for that kind of workload. Credit: Vercel. “When you call our API to make a deployment, we don’t do that deployment in that process that handles your request, because we can’t actually do an infinite number of concurrent deployments,” Ubl says. GitHub rate limits are one reason to back off, and Vercel’s existing compute primitives didn’t give developers “good control over the amount of concurrency” for that kind of worker. With Daemons, “they come up, they start saying, here I am, give me work, and then they just process as it goes,” he says. The company’s example for using Daemons combines a Next.js frontend with a Python API, as well as a containerized video processor. The container packages Python dependencies and the FFmpeg media framework, and then pulls jobs from Vercel Queues to generate playback files and thumbnails. Transcoding is a typical case, Ubl says, with “extremely CPU-bound workloads” where “I just need computers that I want to always be 100% CPU.” That also puts Daemons at the opposite end of the spectrum from Vercel’s sandboxes. “They’re almost the opposite of temporary,” he says of Daemons. “For temporary, you have sandboxes,” he says. Daemons stay on but aren’t invoked by requests from the internet. They reach out for work instead. Developers can deploy through Git or the Vercel CLI. Vercel builds the container image and stores it in its Container Registry . The company itself runs a good chunk of its control plane API on Vercel. That accounts for about a billion requests a month, Ubl says, and Vercel is now starting to move many of its asynchronous workloads onto Daemons. Vercel didn’t invent the model, he acknowledges, “we ship it because people very much want this.” Managed runtime or container If you’re deep in the Vercel ecosystem, you may wonder how all of this relates to Vercel Functions . Vercel says 5,000 teams have made 150,000 container deployments since container support entered public beta. Containers let developers package applications with their own runtimes and system libraries, expanding the range of software they can deploy. The trade-off here is who keeps the image current, Uble argues. With a managed runtime for Node, Bun, or Python, Vercel applies a security release without the customer redeploying, Ubl says. With a container, “you do have to redeploy. It’s ultimately your responsibility,” he says. “From our point of view, it’s just bytes.” Python support, meanwhile, is now generally available for frameworks including FastAPI, Flask, and Django. Applications run on standard CPython with PyPI dependencies, while Vercel handles framework detection, builds, and scaling. The company says 150,000 teams already run Python backends on its platform, including engineers at OpenAI, Polymarket, and Exa. Files that survive a change of environment Vercel Drives is a great example of how agents are changing the requirements for backend services like storage. Vercel’s Drives service separates an agent’s files from the sandbox executing its code. An agent can mount the drive in a new sandbox, change runtimes, and continue working with the files it already created. “I wouldn’t claim it’s an industry first, but it’s certainly an instance of a new type of storage product,” Ubl says. He describes it as a hybrid of an EBS-style networked drive and object storage, something he doesn’t think AWS offers. Writes always land on local NVMe disk and stream asynchronously to object storage, he says, and reads come from the local disk when the data is already there — or stream in block by block. “You have a very large number of independent disks, which, because they’re just files in S3, are arbitrarily cheap to operate,” he says. Drives versus snapshots Many sandbox providers, Vercel included, offer snapshots, Ubl says, but he argues drives are the better model. “The problem with snapshots is they get really big, because you ultimately snapshot all kinds of stuff that is the same every time,” he says. “In practice, what agents really do is there’s some directory, I don’t know, /home/agent. That’s where everything is. Everything else they don’t really care about.” Mounting that one directory means every agent can boot from the same cached base image, he says. “It’s cheaper for them, it’s faster. There’s essentially no downside.” Vercel isn’t removing snapshots, Ubl adds, but it is encouraging customers to switch. Drives lets those agents reuse each other’s work. One can prepare a dataset while others mount read-only copies to analyze it or generate reports, saving their results separately. Agents can also fork a drive to test different approaches in independent writable workspaces. Those forks don’t merge back into the original. In practice, Ubl says, that means telling the agent where to write. “When you use a sandbox, you always tell your agent where it should write things,” he says, typically a root directory such as /workspace. “Essentially every prompt will start with that sentence, and then that’s just what you mount into your durable drive, and that’s it.” Drives and forking are generally available. The service is available on all Vercel plans, with default capacities of 1 TiB, or 1 GiB on Hobby, and configurations up to 16 TiB. For a team already deploying its frontend on Vercel, running a worker or Python API there becomes an easier decision. Each additional backend service it can keep on the platform is one fewer deployment system its developers have to maintain. The post Vercel adds always-on workers to run more of your backend appeared first on The New Stack .

title: E Ink Kaleido 4
body:
BILLERICA, Mass., October 15 - E Ink (8069.TW), a pioneer and leading global developer of ePaper technology, announced the release E Ink Kaleido™ 4. The latest generation delivers improvements in color performance, brightness and contrast to support a more detailed and fluid ePaper experience. The M10C II smart ePaper notebook from Hanvon Technology, a leader in China's eReader market, marks the world's first end-product to feature E Ink Kaleido 4.
As ePaper applications continue to expand from eBooks to classroom and workplace environments, the content on the device is also becoming increasingly diverse, ranging from color PDFs, PowerPoint presentations and data charts to educational illustrations, science and technology reference materials and engineering drawings. Therefore, color ePaper must achieve a better balance of color, brightness, contrast and clarity to fully convey information accurately.
With its new design, E Ink Kaleido 4 supports a broader range of digital content. Compared to the previous generation, E Ink Kaleido 4 doubles its color gamut volume to more than 40K, increases white reflectance by 15%, and improves contrast by 50%. Additionally, with the introduction of new algorithms, E Ink Kaleido 4 is capable of video playback at up to 18 frames per second (FPS). These enhancements enable color ePaper to present not only text, but also images, charts, presentations and video content with greater clarity, while reducing the perception of screen graininess.
"Color ePaper needs to deliver more than simply 'color,'" said Johnson Lee, Chairman and CEO of E Ink. "We are pleased to work with Hanvon Technology to launch the world's first product featuring E Ink Kaleido 4, jointly expanding the applications of next-generation color ePaper across professional reading, learning and mobile office scenarios."
Bringing E Ink Kaleido 4 to Life in the M10C II
E Ink Kaleido 4 incorporates a new oxide TFT backplane that supports higher driving voltages and faster screen refresh. Combined with Hanvon Technology's proprietary "Enhanced Pressure Floating" technology and T2000 timing controller, it enables 27% faster page turning and scrolling on the M10C II. A redesigned front-light system also delivers clearer, more natural color reproduction.
The M10C II pairs E Ink Kaleido 4 with Hanvon Technology's OCR, voice and AI-powered office applications, along with features such as cloud library synchronization, ripple-reduction technology, responsive third-party app scaling and optimized font rendering. For handwriting, its wireless, battery-free digital pen offers 8,192 levels of pressure sensitivity, while a micro-etched tempered-glass surface reduces glare and parallax and further provides a paper-like writing resistance. Together, these capabilities create a smoother experience for reading, writing, note-taking and on-the-go productivity.
"The global debut of the M10C II featuring E Ink Kaleido 4 is not simply a screen upgrade," said Wang Jie, Vice President of Hanvon Technology. "Built around next-generation color ePaper, we have systematically optimized the display, fast refresh, handwriting, recording and AI capabilities. With the M10C II, we hope to take color ePaper beyond reading devices and into productivity scenarios such as R&D tools, professional document review, meeting records and mobile office applications."
To learn more about E Ink Kaleido 4, visit the E Ink website .
E Ink Holdings Inc. (8069.TWO), based on technology from MIT's Media Lab, provides an ideal display medium for applications spanning eReaders and eNotes, ESLs and retail media, digital signage, IoT devices and more, enabling customers to put displays in locations previously impossible. E Ink's electrophoretic display products make it a worldwide leader for ePaper. Its low-power displays enable customers to reach their sustainability goals, and E Ink has pledged using 100% renewable energy in 2030 and reaching net zero carbon emissions by 2040. E Ink has been recognized for its efforts by receiving validation from Science-Based Targets (SBTi) and is listed in both the DJSI World and DJSI Emerging Indexes and is listed in Taiwan's Taipei Exchange (TPEx) and the Luxembourg market. For more information, please visit www.eink.com. E Ink. We Make Surfaces Smart and Green.

title: Democrat Talarico says he raised record $64 million over summer in Texas Senate race
body:
Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter, his campaign announced Thursday, setting what the campaign said is a Senate fundraising record as Republicans pour outside money into the race to bolster GOP nominee Ken Paxton in the 2026 midterm election .
The haul was the largest ever reported by a Senate candidate in the July-through-September quarter, according to the campaign, surpassing the previous record of $57 million set by South Carolina Democrat Jaime Harrison, who unsuccessfully ran against Republican Lindsey Graham in 2020.
Talarico has raised more than $134 million since launching his campaign last year, according to his campaign ahead of the quarterly filing deadline with the Federal Election Commission.
“Grassroots contributors from across Texas are coming together to end billionaire control over our politics and bring down costs for working families,” Talarico said in a statement.
The campaign said more than 1.3 million people have donated and that 97% of contributions were $100 or less. Paxton, by comparison, announced earlier this month that his campaign and two affiliated fundraising committees raised a combined $18 million during the quarter.
The candidates' full financial picture will become clearer after their quarterly reports are filed with the FEC . The filings will show how much each campaign spent and how much cash they had left entering the final stretch.
But the gap in direct fundraising tells only part of the financial story. Republican outside groups have spent more than $175 million since Sept. 1 supporting Paxton or attacking Talarico, according to AdImpact, helping offset Paxton's weaker campaign fundraising. Overall political advertising in the race has surpassed $500 million.
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk has emerged as a major force in the race, giving $10 million to a pro-Paxton super PAC, according to figures confirmed Monday by a spokesman for Musk's America PAC, while his America PAC has spent about $9.4 million attacking Talarico and another $1.8 million supporting Paxton, according to FEC filings.
The source of that money matters as federal law guarantees candidates lower broadcast rates for television advertising than super PACs, allowing Talarico's campaign dollars to go further in buying TV exposure than outside Republican groups.
No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and the party has not won a U.S. Senate race there since 1988. But Talarico leads Paxton 48.5% to 45.2% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average , a 3.3-percentage point advantage, forcing Republicans to devote significant resources to what has traditionally been safe territory.
Talarico's fundraising also eclipses previous high-water marks for Texas Democrats. Beto O'Rourke raised $38.1 million in the third quarter of 2018 during his challenge to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

title: Muse Spark Open is Meta's answer to Qwen, GLM, and Kimi in the open-weight race
body:
After its Llama series, Meta is returning to open-weight territory with Muse Spark Open. Meta calls it the most capable US open-weight model, built for coding and agentic tasks, with 816 billion parameters (42 billion active), up to one million tokens of context, and support for text, image, video, and audio. On benchmarks like JobBench, MCP-Atlas, HLE-Diamond, and ZeroBench, Meta says it scores well ahead of Qwen 3.8, GLM 5.3, and Kimi K3 in several categories but still falls well short of Meta's paid Muse Wonder Full models .
The model is optimized for Apple's M5 Ultra and runs locally on two Mac Studios with 512 GB of unified memory each, according to Meta. Weights are on Hugging Face . The license is free to use but requires the label "Built with Muse Spark Open." Providers pulling in more than $20 million a year who want to offer the model as an API service need a separate agreement with Meta. More details are in the research blog .

title: U.S. Claims Control of Hormuz as Ship Attacks Hit New High
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
An image purportedly shows the Singapore-flagged container ship GFS PRIDE listing heavily and emitting thick black smoke following an attack in the Strait of Hormuz on October 13, 2026. The vessel subsequently sank, with all 21 crew members safely evacuated. The image has not been independently verified.
U.S. Central Command says the United States and its regional partners control the Strait of Hormuz, citing more than 40 commercial ships moving through the waterway in the past 24 hours, even as maritime security officials warn that attacks on merchant vessels are increasing and the threat to shipping remains severe.
The statement Thursday came as the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) released a new assessment documenting a series of attacks on commercial shipping, including the sinking of a containership, and warning that further strikes remain highly likely.
“The United States and regional partners control the strait as commercial vessels continue to transit despite unwarranted IRGC aggression,” CENTCOM said in a statement rejecting three Iranian claims .
But the military’s assertion of control comes against a markedly different picture of commercial shipping conditions. Traffic remains far below prewar levels, vessels continue to face attacks along established transit routes, and Iran is still attempting to influence how ships move through the strait.
According to JMIC’s October 15 advisory , U.S.-facilitated traffic totaled 121 vessel transits between October 11 and 14, an average of approximately 30 ships per day. That compares with a historical average of roughly 138 daily transits in 2025, before the war.
CENTCOM’s latest figure of more than 40 ships covers a different 24-hour period and may indicate an increase in traffic. Still, the four-day JMIC average represents only about 22% of the prewar benchmark.
Independent commercial tracking continues to show substantially fewer transits than U.S. military-assisted figures. JMIC reported single-digit daily movements in its separate tracking data, although the two sources use different methodologies and do not measure the same categories of traffic.
The distinction matters because while ships are continuing to pass through Hormuz, the volume of traffic remains a fraction of normal levels.
JMIC maintained its threat assessment for the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE , warning that deliberate hostile action against commercial vessels remains highly likely.
The latest advisory documented eight projectile attacks in the strait on October 11 and 13, involving four tankers and four containerships. A separate attack on the products tanker PETRO DOLPHIN near Sohar, Oman, left two crew members missing.
The most serious recent incident involved the Singapore-flagged GFS PRIDE , which was struck by a projectile on October 13 , caught fire and subsequently sank on October 14. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated.
CENTCOM rejected an Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claim that the vessel had struck a naval mine while traveling along an unauthorized route.
“The civilian container ship M/V GFS Pride was hit by an IRGC projectile,” CENTCOM said, adding that the vessel sank while being towed to shore.
The military also maintained that the strait’s primary shipping routes remain clear of mines.
JMIC separately said there was no evidence supporting Iran’s claim that a mine caused the sinking. However, the advisory continued to warn mariners about potential mining activity within and around the established traffic separation scheme.
It also warned of a continuing threat from IRGC surveillance, drone overflights, radio hailing and attempts to direct merchant ships toward the northern Iranian-controlled route.
Vessels using the southern Omani corridor remain exposed to attacks, while those broadcasting their positions through the Automatic Identification System (AIS) face an elevated targeting risk, according to JMIC.
The organization also cautioned mariners about floating containers and debris near the wreck of GFS PRIDE .
The latest attacks are part of a broader escalation that began before October. JMIC now counts 149 confirmed vessel incidents across the region since March 1, including nine newly documented incidents in its latest reporting period.
The International Maritime Organization separately lists 113 highlighted confirmed incidents and 24 seafarer fatalities as of October 14. The two organizations maintain different incident datasets and their totals are not directly comparable.
Meanwhile, large numbers of commercial vessels remain at anchor throughout the region. JMIC reported approximately 180 vessels near Fujairah and Khor Fakkan, another 178 between Dubai, Jebel Ali and Ras Al Khaimah, and 74 around Musandam and Sohar as of October 15.
The security situation is further complicated by the continuing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports.
According to the latest figures cited by JMIC, U.S. forces had redirected 135 commercial vessels and disabled four during blockade enforcement operations as of October 10-11. Neutral shipping remains permitted to transit, although vessels can expect military hailing, monitoring and possible inspections.
The latest JMIC advisory also warned that ships using either the northern Iranian-controlled route or the southern Omani corridor should expect continued security risks and reduced traffic.
That leaves a significant gap between the military’s claim of control and the conditions facing commercial operators.
U.S. forces are facilitating vessel movements through the strait, and commercial ships continue to transit. But attacks have continued despite the military presence, and shipping volumes remain well below their prewar levels.
For shipowners, charterers and crews, the remaining question is whether the United States can provide enough security for normal commercial operations to resume, rather than simply keeping the waterway open to traffic willing to accept the risks.

title: Palestinians challenge Abbas's decision to postpone election in new court filing
body: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas's decision to postpone the long-delayed Palestinian Legislative Council elections has faced a legal challenge, with Samer Sinijlawi, leader of Masar Jadid (New Path), filing an appeal in court on Thursday seeking to overturn the decision.In Case No. 450/20, Sinijlawi asked the administrative court to overturn Abbas's decision to postpone the November 28 election until September 11 next year, arguing that Palestinians have been denied the rights guaranteed under the Palestinian Basic Law for too long.“Our court challenge is about defending the right of Palestinians to choose their representatives and hold their leaders accountable. After 20 years without legislative elections, another postponement has profound consequences for public trust and the possibility of peaceful democratic change,” he told The Jerusalem Post. “For our candidates in Gaza, this election offered a chance to bring their communities' experiences and priorities into national decision-making. People who have lost their homes, livelihoods, and loved ones deserve a voice in the decisions that will shape their lives and Gaza's recovery.”Abbas justified the postponement by citing alleged “obstacles posed by Israeli measures” and the need to establish suitable political, security, and on-the-ground conditions for “free, fair, and inclusive elections.”Officials from the Palestinian Central Elections Commission have alleged that Israel blocked access to east Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip. However, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar denied the allegations, describing them as “yet another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability.”Abbas advised to delay the voteThere have long been reports that senior officials around Abbas pressured him to postpone the elections out of fear that Hamas would win. Yoni Ben-Menachem, a senior researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, reported that Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh specifically advised Abbas to use the issue of east Jerusalem as a pretext for delaying the vote, citing the same reason used to postpone the elections in 2021.In the court filing seen by the Post, Sinijlawi argued that the postponement violated the Palestinian Basic Law, which guarantees a democratic system of government. He also cited the principle of legality and submission to the law, which requires authorities to act within their legally prescribed jurisdiction and comply with applicable procedures, formalities, and safeguards, as well as political rights and his legitimate electoral interest.Sinijlawi further argued that there were no sound legal or factual grounds to justify the postponement and that the decision may have prejudiced his legal interests following the commencement of nomination procedures.'Palestinians deserve a clear explanation'“We recognize the enormous difficulties facing elections in Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem. But Palestinians deserve a clear explanation of why those difficulties require this postponement, what alternatives were considered, and what guarantees exist that the new date will be honoured. Those are questions of accountability and legality,” Sinijlawi said. “We have turned to the Palestinian Administrative Court because we believe in pursuing change through peaceful, lawful, and institutional means. We are asking for the original election date to be restored, or for elections to take place at the earliest possible opportunity.”The same week Abbas again postponed the elections, European Commission Vice President and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas renewed Europe's commitment to deploying an election observation mission. It remains unclear why Abbas did not accept the offer, although European countries have pressed him to allow the elections to proceed.When asked about the potential impact of the postponement on the international standing of a future Palestinian state, Sinijlawi said, “A Palestinian political system that allows new voices to compete and citizens to hold leaders accountable is essential to building a credible partner for peace. Every time we encourage young Palestinians to believe in the ballot box, we must be able to show them that this path is open. We will continue working to keep it open.”

title: US Hoovers up Bitcoin While the World Runs on Its Digital Dollars: Report
body: Bitcoin Magazine US Hoovers up Bitcoin While the World Runs on Its Digital Dollars: Report America is accumulating bitcoin while exporting dollar-pegged stablecoins to everyone else, according to a new Chainalysis report. The blockchain data said in its Wednesday report, “North America: Inside the Growth of Agentic Commerce,” that the U.S. became a net importer of Bitcoin in 2026 — for the first time since 2022. According to the data, institutions this year have been buying bitcoin while retail largely sells. “A dollar stablecoin is a way to hold dollars without an American bank account, and Americans already have one,” the report read. “The rest of the world is pivoting to a digital dollar because it meets a need that American users don’t share. Meanwhile, Americans are leaning harder on bitcoin as an infinitely scarce store of value.” It added that U.S. dominance keeps climbing: Since the 2024 launch of spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds, America’s share of global Bitcoin activity has risen every single reporting period — even as the overall U.S. crypto economy ($2.78 trillion) contracted 2.2% in a brutal bear market, retaining most of 2025’s near-doubling. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission approved bitcoin ETFs in January 2024 after a decade of denying the products. Managed by Wall Street titans like BlackRock, Fidelity, and most recently, Morgan Stanley , the funds had the most successful debut in the history of ETFs. Institutions and Wall Street can now buy shares of the funds which track the price of bitcoin and take care of buying and selling the digital coin. The approval of the ETFs has helped the industry mature, the report noted, and helped the U.S. become an overall bigger bitcoin investor. Stablecoins, meanwhile, have turned U.S. debt into a “currency-of-choice for peer-to-peer economies as well as businesses working across borders,” the report continued. “In the 2026 period we continued to see stablecoins enter new use cases most especially abroad, benefitting the U.S. companies, and the U.S. government, with billions of dollars in economic activity,” it added. Since Donald Trump became president, he has signed a number of pro-crypto laws and executive orders. The GENIUS Act , signed in 2025, allows banks and other entities to issue stablecoins if they back the tokens with assets like U.S. Treasuries and provide monthly disclosures of their reserves. This post US Hoovers up Bitcoin While the World Runs on Its Digital Dollars: Report first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Mathew Di Salvo .

title: Ukraine Exhausts Patriot Interceptor Stocks, Leaving It Exposed to Russian Ballistic Missiles
body:
Ukraine has depleted its stocks of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles, stripping it of one of the very few tools capable of deterring Russian ballistic missiles, a source familiar with the situation said on Thursday, Oct. 15.
According to CNN’s exclusive , the shortfall was particularly felt during Russia’s latest large-scale attack overnight into Wednesday, Oct. 14, when most incoming ballistic missiles reached their targets. The strike hit three power plants in Kyiv and energy facilities in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring at least 25 in the capital.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the [interceptor] missiles,” the source, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported shooting down four Russian ballistic missiles during that attack, which CNN said suggests Ukraine fired its last remaining Patriots.
Patriot interceptors are currently in short supply worldwide. Many of the countries have already depleted their stocks or are seeking to rebuild them amid the war in Iran and Russia’s escalating rhetoric towards Europe.
On July 20, Lockheed Martin introduced the PAC-3 ACE , a Patriot interceptor designed to deter air and missile threats at less than half the cost of the PAC-3 MSE variant. Initial production was expected to start within 36 months.
Current PAC-3 interceptors cost roughly $4 million per missile, and their high cost is compounded by the rate at which they are expended during sustained operations.
The launch came as Ukraine already faced a critical shortage of ballistic missile defense.
For the country, the PAC-3 is currently among the very few weapons capable of intercepting Russia’s Iskander-M, a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
Ukraine’s reliance on the weapons deliveries became clear by July, when the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reportedly exhausted its stocks during two Russian barrages; on July 1-2 Russia launched 24 ballistic missiles, four of which were intercepted, and on July 5-6, Russia launched 23 ballistic missiles, none of which were intercepted.
Around the same time, Russia launched four Zircons on July 1-2 and six on July 5-6, none of which were intercepted either.
As of Oct. 1, Lockheed Martin is in advanced talks over PAC-3 production outside the US as demand triples.
Dan Tenney, the company’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, told Kyiv Post that the company is investing up to $9 billion through 2030 to expand missile production, strengthen supply chains and bring new factories online.
For much of this year, Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its Western allies for faster deliveries of Patriot interceptors.
The weapons systems were on the agenda again on Thursday, Oct. 15, during President Volodymyr Zelensky’s meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels , where the Ukrainian president urged its allies for steady arms deliveries as Russia continues its terror on civilian infrastructure nationwide.
On Sept. 8, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Germany would deliver PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from it’s own Bundeswehr stocks, while Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said contracts are being signed with partners for about 1,000 Patriot missiles.
During his meeting with Zelensky on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York late September, US President Donald Trump had made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to produce Patriot missiles domestically.
Trump initially announced the license transfer during the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey early July, but later backtracked on the promises, saying Washington must exercise caution when sharing sensitive military technology.
On Sept. 5-6, senior US envoys from Trump’s administration – Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff – traveled to Moscow in an effort to broker an end to the war, where they held three hours of discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin followed by an informal dinner. A day later, they headed to Kyiv for the first time during their tenure.
Although all three sides described the meeting as substantive and positive, no breakthrough was reached.
The diplomatic efforts appeared to be gaining momentum, until last week, when Kyiv-Washington ties took a sour turn.
While the Ukrainian delegation was in Miami hoping to negotiate an end to Russia’s aggression, Trump abruptly announced that he signed a diesel deal with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
Trump then declared an immediate energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv on Oct. 11 on Truth Social media, claiming both sides had agreed.
Although neither strikes formally agreed and Ukrainian authorities appeared to find out about the truce by the news circulating online, Kyiv had refrained from striking Russia’s power infrastructure.
Meanwhile, Russia increased its strikes significantly, with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying on Oct. 14 that the truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it .
Zelensky has since lifted Ukraine’s self-imposed pause on those strikes. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told The Financial Times .
Around the same time, overnight on Oct. 13-14 the US aerospace giant Starlink and its owner Elon Musk tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour), disrupting Kyiv’s drone operations.
The move crippled Ukraine’s key mid-range strike drones, used in strikes on Russian logistics, and interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
“It is clear that the Russians are trying to exploit problems with Starlink’s operation in Ukraine, as interceptor drones rely significantly on this connection,” Zelensky said after meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London.
Musk’s response was that the US military – including Trump himself – decides speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals, not SpaceX.
Around the same time on Oct. 14, US intelligence officials told Ukraine’s embassy in Washington that information sharing would stop immediately if Kyiv kept striking Russian energy targets.
Zelensky confirmed the warning reached the military rather than him directly. “They said this to my generals, not to me.”
Trump, for his part, insisted cooperation continues and denied that the US cut off intelligence , although Ukrainian forces received no partner warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches toward Kyiv on two consecutive nights at the beginning of the week.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: BlackRock’s Larry Fink Warns AI Data Center Halt Could Tip US Into Recession
body:
BlackRock CEO Larry Fink has a blunt warning about what could derail the U.S. economy: slamming the brakes on the data centers powering the AI boom.
Speaking to CNBC on Wednesday after BlackRock posted better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, Fink said the surge in AI infrastructure spending has become so central to economic growth that choking it off would be dangerous.
“If we have a moratorium of some sort in this country, we will be in a recession,” he said, adding that “so much of our economy is based on the build-out of this capex.”
The comments come as data centers have become a flashpoint ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with local opposition mounting over their electricity demands, water use and strain on power grids.
According to Brookings, at least 100 localities had approved moratoriums by July, and New York has paused certain permits for up to a year. Fink pushed back on the backlash, calling much of it “misinformation” and insisting that “data centers are not the problem,” pointing instead to the construction jobs and energy-infrastructure demand the buildout is generating.
The scale of the spending underscores his argument. Wall Street analysts estimate AI capital expenditures could top $1 trillion in 2027 and exceed $5 trillion cumulatively through 2030, making the sector a meaningful driver of the roughly 3% annualized GDP growth Fink wants to sustain. He has argued more private capital is needed to keep it going, and said BlackRock has spoken with chipmakers including AMD and Broadcom about the effort.
But Fink is swimming against a sharply rising tide of public opposition . An Annenberg Public Policy Center survey this summer found 61% of Americans oppose new data centers in their area, up from 49% in the spring, with majorities of Democrats, Republicans and independents all against them.
The concerns center on soaring electricity demand, water use and strain on local grids. That backlash has already produced real restrictions : New York has a moratorium on hyperscale data centers, Texas has paused approvals, and cities from Austin to Jersey City have imposed limits , with Data Center Watch counting roughly $130 billion in projects blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026 alone.
It has also become a live electoral issue. The fight is central to Ohio’s Senate race, where Democrat Sherrod Brown has campaigned against the buildout, and a super PAC backed by AI billionaires including Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman has poured millions into ads defending data centers across battleground states. President Donald Trump has weighed in too, warning that communities resisting the facilities risk ending up “backwards and poor.”
Against that backdrop, Fink pushed back directly, suggesting the AI buildout in the United States is propping up the U.S. economy and any shift would result in a significant downturn.
The warning carries weight for crypto, given how closely Bitcoin now tracks broader risk sentiment and macro conditions.
Fink, who runs the world’s largest asset manager and oversees its dominant spot Bitcoin ETF, has become one of Wall Street’s most prominent crypto converts . He has called Bitcoin an asset for a “ frightened world ” and framed it as a legitimate alternative investment, while BlackRock has flagged AI agents as a potential next wave of crypto demand .

title: Army Wants High-Energy Laser Weapons It Can Put On “Any Vehicle In The Motorpool”
body: The U.S. Army is pursuing a family of modular and scalable laser directed energy weapons that can be fitted to any vehicle in its inventory. The service sees this as key to expanding the operational use of lasers, particularly to provide an extra layer of defense against drone threats, and outside of dedicated units. The Army is already fielding high-energy lasers operationally on a limited basis, including along the border wth Mexico , but the technology has faced continued hurdles to more widespread use in recent years. Army officials and industry representatives discussed what is currently called the Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program during a panel discussion this week at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention , at which TWZ was in attendance. In September, AeroVironment received the first production contract under E-HEL to supply examples of its 30-kilowatt-class LOCUST X3 laser directed energy weapon system. The Army has already acquired earlier LOCUST variants, including vehicle-mounted and palletized types , through more experimental programs, and these are the systems now deployed along the southern border. The U.S. Navy has also at least tested a containerized version of LOCUST for shipboard use as part of its own larger laser ambitions . “We’re focused on any vehicle in the motorpool. I want to try to integrate future capability of high-energy lasers into it,” Army Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, the Capability Program Executive for Defensive Fires with the Portfolio Acquisition Executive Office for Fires, said during the panel on Monday. “And, so, our E-HEL is on a sled. With that, I can look at integrating it onto multiple different vehicles.” “And then, as I think about vehicle agnosticness, if I open up my aperture to MOS [military occupation speciality] agnostic, and ensure that it’s easy to train, easy to operate, I can not just focus on air and missile defense organizations,” he continued. “I can now look at any formation type to be able to put a high-energy laser capability into it for the counter-UAS [uncrewed aerial systems] fight.” “That gives me even more opportunities to share this capability across all Army formations, and give our senior leaders [the] maximum amount of thought process and input into where the system goes, who the soldier is that’s operating it, and I’ve given them quite a solution,” he added. “It’s a great dilemma to have of where do I put all this capability.” In 2022, the Army reactivated the 4th Battalion, 60th Air Defense Artillery Regiment (4-60th ADA) at Fort Sill, Oklahoma, as part of plans to field new laser-armed Directed Energy Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense (DE M-SHORAD) systems based on the 8×8 Stryker light armored vehicle. Reliability and other issues with DE M-SHORAD vehicles led the Army to shift focus , and 4-60th ADA has since assumed a more traditional air defense role. The problems with the DE M-SHORAD system are indicative of struggles that have dogged laser-directed energy weapon developments across the U.S. military , and that have led to several other programs being severely truncated or outright cancelled in recent years. One of the Stryker-based DE M-SHORAD system prototypes. US Army One of the Army’s initial prototype DE M-SHORAD vehicles. US Army The Army does now have the aforementioned LOCUST systems, including versions mounted on 4×4 Joint Light Tactical Vehicles (JLTV) and Infantry Squad Vehicles (ISV), as well as the palletized types. Those systems appear to be currently fielded on a more ad hoc level to units at forward locations. A LOCUST system seen integrated onto a JLTV. AeroVironment LOCUST is well suited to the Army’s current vision for fielding E-HEL without being tied to specific vehicles or unit types. At the core of the system is a turret with the laser beam projector, as well as built-in electro-optical and infrared video cameras for target acquisition and tracking. Other sensors, such as small-form-factor high-frequency radars and passive radio frequency signal detection systems on host vehicles, as well as off-board radars and other capabilities positioned elsewhere, can be used to cue the turret. A close-up look at the turret on an earlier palletized version of LOCUST acquired by the Army. US Army With the 30-kilowatt power rating, the new X3 versions of LOCUST the Army is acquiring now are still at the lower end of the power spectrum for laser directed energy weapons. All versions of LOCUST to date are geared explicitly toward countering small drones. It is possible that the Army could field other types of laser directed energy weapon systems through E-HEL in the future. The service, in cooperation with other branches of the U.S. military, is also pursuing designs with far higher power ratings through separate programs. Just being able to field LOCUST X3 more broadly would still offer valuable additional layers of defense against drones across different types of Army units. More broadly speaking, the central benefit that laser directed energy weapons offer is the promise of functionally unlimited magazine depth, though this is dependent on there being sufficient power and cooling capacity. This, in turn, translates to a substantial reduction in the cost-per-intercept equation compared to traditional anti-air interceptors. All of this is especially advantageous for tackling drone threats, which do not have to be large or expensive to present real dangers. By miniaturizing and ruggedizing lower-power systems like LOCUST, the Army could distribute these capabilities across a broad area, or deploy them in a more concentrated fashion, depending on the fight. Even a convoy with a number of the vehicles sprinkled in with them could help defend it from pop-up attacks In this context, mobility and flexibility are also important boons. LOCUST systems mounted on light vehicles can be readily positioned and repositioned to respond to changes on the battlefield, as well as be brought to forward locations slung under helicopters. Palletized and containerized versions offer additional kinds of flexibility for providing point defense at sites on land, as well as installation on ships. Army personnel assigned to Joint Task Force-Southern Border (JTF-SB) prepare to sling load a LOCUST-equipped Infantry Squad Vehicle (ISV) under a CH-47 Chinook helicopter during training as part of an Air Assault Sustainment Course at Fort Bliss, Texas, on July 16, 2025. US Army At the panel on Monday, Brig. Gen. Yelverton stressed that when it comes to laser weapons systems, in general, the technology is no longer a matter of “science fiction” but has become “science reality.” The U.S. military says laser systems positioned along the border with Mexico have downed real targets , though many questions remain about those deployments . Regardless, challenges do clearly remain. “Lasers are real. We can do it. We can go out. We can shoot things,” Kirk Williams, Chief Engineer at the Army’s Directed Energy Project Office, another one of the panelists, said. “But what we got to do now is make these systems reliable enough so that the soldiers have the faith in them when they need them, and that’s really the main point that we’re trying to go after right now.” “We’re getting to the point where the systems are reliable enough, but we still have to make them maintainable and repairable because this is an Army system,” he continued. “It’s going to be on a battlefield. Things are going to break. We can break things in very creative ways, right? So if it’s not reliable, or if it’s not maintainable, if it’s not repairable, that’s a problem.” “We’re also looking to reduce size, weight, and power,” he added. “JLTV has a lot better payload capacity than ISV. So we really need to be able to get something smaller if we want to have the same effectiveness on an ISV. So that same modular architecture will allow us to go in, take some of those components, make trade-offs.” A JLTV-based LOCUST system seen deployed near the US-Mexico border. US Army The focus on modular and open systems architectures will also help when it comes to integrating new and improved functionality down the line. It will also feed into the larger goal of having E-HEL options not tied to a particular vehicle or other platform. “By going after the modular architecture, that gives us the flexibility to not only go after increases in reliability, but also increases in performance,” Williams further explained. “It gives us the way to inject new technology into existing systems, and then hopefully it also gives us a way of getting better prices out of some of our vendors.” In addition, “one of the things we learned is you can have a really cool integrated system, and then when that truck needs an oil change, well, then your laser weapon system is down for the count,” he added. “So, trying to make it so that you can just pull it off of any vehicle, put it on any other vehicle is really one of the things that we’re trying to go after.” The Army is also very cognizant of the basic fact that a single laser can only engage one target at once. The beam from any laser weapon system also drops in power as it gets further from the source, just because of the need to propagate through the atmosphere. Weather and other environmental conditions like smoke and dust then also become a factor. This has driven demand for more power (and cooling capacity) to improve effectiveness, especially at range. Developments in adaptive optics can also help overcome these issues to a degree, but lasers currently remain very short-range weapons overall. A picture the US Army says shows an engagement of a drone using a laser directed energy weapon near the border with Mexico on August 25, 2026. US Army “That’s why it’s important to us to get enough energy on the target to kill it as quickly as possible and move on to the next threat. Speaking about the magazine, you know I have battery power on there, so depending upon which system, around 80 seconds, 120 seconds, whatever that is, you know that’s the magazine depth I have,” Brig. Gen. Yelverton said on Monday. “The quicker I get on the target, kill it, and off the target, I start rebuilding, regenerating that magazine depth.” “It’s the targeting system. It’s the optics system that lets you focus on the target,” Williams also chimed in at this point on the panel discussion. “I mentioned trying to make the trackers better and take some of the onus off of the operator. If we can do better aim point control and keep the laser in the same spot, it gives you a better and a quicker kill.” Earlier on, Williams had highlighted how artificial intelligence-assisted targeting capabilities could be a particularly important addition to laser directed energy weapons. Networking multiple systems together could help with sorting and assigning targets as efficiently as possible. When it comes to the actual operational employment of laser directed energy weapons, “as these systems get smaller, as they get more powerful, the quicker we could get them into our soldiers’ hands,” Army Col. Charles Kean, Deputy Commanding Officer for Support at the 7th Infantry Division at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state, another one of the panelists, said. A promotional image showing JLTV-based and self-contained configurations of the LOCUST X3. AeroVironment This, in turn, will open up important new opportunities to “operate with them forward, test them in the mud, the dirt, the humidity of the Pacific, test them down in the southern border where they’re different conditions, whether it’s in the Middle East and Europe, it’s applicable across the board,” Kean continued. “We have to understand it, get it in our hands as quickly as possible, so we could iterate it, iterate on it, and make it better and continue to iterate, because the adversaries continue to iterate in reverse against us.” This last point is worth highlighting. The U.S. military’s chief global competitor, China, has been particularly active in the development and fielding of ground-based laser and other directed energy weapons , as well as designs for shipboard use . Chinese firms are selling laser weapon systems to foreign armed forces , as well. Other countries, including American allies and partners, are also very actively pursuing these capabilities . Touted as the "world’s most powerful," China’s LY-1 ship-based laser air defense system was displayed on an eight-wheeled truck, with no specs released. pic.twitter.com/WalkQffaA9 — Polymarket Intel (@PolymarketIntel) September 3, 2025 Col. Kean also stressed that laser directed energy weapons would still only be one part of a larger layered air and missile defense ecosystem for the Army. As it stands now, the Army hopes to have the first LOCUST X3 systems acquired through E-HEL in operational service by early 2028 . A similar timeframe has been put forward for the separate Joint Laser Weapon System (JLWS) program, which the Army is also involved in. JLWS is aiming to produce a viable containerized 150-kilowatt-class laser directed energy weapon, with plans to work toward 300- and 500-kilowatt-class designs. At the panel on Monday, Scott Keeney, CEO of laser systems developer nLIGHT, which has been working together with AeroVironment on LOCUST, among other projects, said he saw further scaling up of capabilities to the one-megawatt-class as being on the horizon. This is a power rating the U.S. Navy has also talked about as a future goal . The Army clearly sees E-HEL already as a path to truly operationalizing laser directed energy capabilities across the system, but the service itself acknowledges that there is still significant work to be done to make this goal a reality. Contact the author: joe@twz.com The post Army Wants High-Energy Laser Weapons It Can Put On “Any Vehicle In The Motorpool” appeared first on TWZ .

title: As airstrikes in Gaza continue, support for 'armed resistance' grows, Hamas popularity drops - poll
body: More than half of Palestinians support a two-state agreement with east Jerusalem serving as the capital of a Palestinian state, according to a new poll published on Wednesday by the Ramallah-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research think tank.Though 53% overall support two states, with 56% endorsing consultative talks with Israeli figures they deemed “anti-occupation,” only 48% of Gazan respondents said they would agree with the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside a Jewish one.The survey collected data from 909 Palestinians in the West Bank and 488 in the Gaza Strip, living outside Israel-controlled territory, and had a margin of error of 3.5%.Asked what the current obstacle to Palestinian statehood was, 41% said it was the expansion of Israeli settlements while only 23% said it was internal Palestinian divisions.The Palestinian think tank attributed the increase in support for armed resistance among Gaza residents to ongoing Israeli strikes in the Gaza Strip. Compared with the August poll, support for armed resistance rose from 21% to 37%, slightly above the overall average of 33% recorded across both Palestinian territories. Diplomacy remained the most popular option, however, with 42% of Palestinians supporting it and a further 18% supporting popular nonviolent resistance as the most effective path toward establishing a Palestinian state.Neither Hamas nor Israel won the war, say 62% of PalestiniansDespite the increase in support for armed “resistance,” 62% of Palestinians polled said neither Israel nor Hamas had won the war. While 17% said Israel had emerged victorious, only 16% viewed Hamas as the winner. Still, around three-quarters of Palestinians overall, 69% in the Gaza Strip and 78% in the West Bank, felt Israel should withdraw from the Gaza Strip before Hamas disarms.Most Palestinians were also pessimistic about the ceasefire's prospects, with 61% expecting insecurity to continue. Only 42% said they trusted the technocratic committee to govern Gaza. Trust in the committee was significantly higher among Palestinians in Gaza than among those in the West Bank, at 60% and 29%, respectively.In terms of party affiliation, only 19% of Palestinians identified with Hamas, down from 24% in August and 35% ten months earlier. Less than a quarter (22%) said they supported Fatah, but a commanding 33% identified with none of the listed parties.Additionally, while the August poll found a three-way race for leadership between Marwan Barghouti, Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya, and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, the latest poll suggests growing support for independent figures. Only 34% said they would support Barghouti's leadership, while 13% backed Palestinian businessman Bashar Masri nationwide, rising to 21% among respondents in Gaza. Mustafa Barghouti received 12% support.PA elections pushed back to next SeptemberThere is also still a strong desire for the Palestinian Authority to move ahead with the elections in November, which Abbas has pushed back to September next year. More than half, 53%, support holding elections on schedule on November 28 without delay, and an additional 21% favor a short operational postponement of under six months to ensure administrative inclusivity, while 20% oppose holding elections altogether.Overall voter turnout intention was found to be around 55% among eligible voters, though only 31% of young citizens aged 18–22 report being registered on the voter rolls, and their overall voting intention lags at just 46%.There is also significant willingness to vote for a newly formed candidate list, around 56%, and when testing nine candidate lists among likely voters who have finalized their choices, the National Independent List led by Bashar Masri tied for first place with the list backed by imprisoned leader Marwan Barghouti, each securing 22% of the vote.Both the independent figure and imprisoned Fatah leader hold more support than the jointHamas-Dahlan List, which only received 20% support, and the official Fatah list led by Palestinian Vice-President Hussein al-Sheikh and backed by President Abbas (13%), and the National Initiative led by Mustafa Barghouti (13%).According to the survey, Masri's appeal was closely linked to confidence in his ability to manage Gaza's economic recovery and improve the cost of living, with 30% saying they trusted him to do so. Mustafa Barghouti received a similar level of trust, at 29%. Confidence in senior Palestinian Authority figures was considerably lower, with only 6% trusting Hussein al-Sheikh and 8% trusting Jibril Rajoub to manage these challenges.

title: Army playing ‘ACEs’ to meet commanders’ capability needs
body: The Army is getting ready to expand its Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) initiative that’s intended to deliver new operational technologies to commanders on shortened timelines, according to the director of the Global-Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate. The G-TEAD, as the organization is known, oversees the process. “We call them ACEs, which allow us to identify, test, and provide contracting mechanisms to prototype solutions at operational speed. What this means in practice is a total shift from traditional years-long acquisition timelines to a responsive operational capability delivered in months and sometimes weeks, depending on the capability. By pairing embedded expertise directly with the commanders, G-TEAD bridges the gap between the speed of dual-use innovation and the tactical needs of our warfighters,” Col. Christopher Hill Sr., director of G-TEAD, told reporters Wednesday during a media roundtable on the sidelines of AUSA’s annual convention. “Through our ACEs, we’re not just modernizing on paper; we’re putting field-tested, combat-ready capabilities into hands of soldiers at the dynamic edges of multi-domain operations worldwide, while at the same time working alongside the [portfolio acquisition executives] and the newly formed [Futures and Autonomous Systems Command] to scale and transition these capabilities into the portfolios of program managers,” he added. The G-TEAD has embedded teams within Army service component commands that provide forces for geographic combatant commands. Those teams operate in theater, working directly with the commanding generals to translate operational priorities into “actionable technology requirements” that drive the Accelerated Capability Events. The ACE process starts with a “problem set” from the commanding general that lays out their priorities. After verifying that portfolio acquisition executives and other elements of the acquisition enterprise don’t already have a capability that would fit the bill, the G-TEAD reaches out to vendors. “We go out to industry and say, ‘OK, this is the problem set that still remains,’” Hill explained. “We normally get somewhere between 150 to 250 responses. We will downselect those to 15. Fifteen vendors are then invited to come out to a soldier-led demonstration. … At the end of the demonstration, five of those 15 will be awarded contracts. Those same five will be given the feedback from the soldiers from that demonstration. They also will be given the technical feedback from [Army Test and Evaluation Command]. They will then be told 45 days from now there’s going to be an operational assessment [and] where we’re going to do that. … Why 45 days? Because like on the battlefield, things change, and these companies need to prove to us that they can change based upon feedback. So, the feedback that they received at the demo, you got 45 days to incorporate it. So, when you show up at the operational assessment, if your system looks the same, you’ve proven to us that you’re not an agile company.” The systems that are assessed typically include a combination of hardware and software, Hill told DefenseScoop. Once the operational assessment is completed, the G-TEAD will present the interested commander with the data. “It is his decision [about which vendor capabilities to select], not the acquisition enterprise. Our mantra is: warfighting command gets 51% of the vote. He will make the final decision. … That’s when I come in with dollars and put it towards those companies. So, that’s the first time we actually buy kit,” Hill told reporters. The G-TEAD also works on the “transition piece” of the puzzle, Hill noted, working with the office of the Army’s acquisition, technology and logistics chief and Army Transformation and Training Command to make a final decision about whether the tech should also be transitioned to a portfolio acquisition executive. “If the answer is yes, that’s when the scaling comes in,” Hill said. The G-TEAD aims to hold ACEs quarterly. The organization holds enterprise synchronization forums with Army service component commands to facilitate planning. “What that allows us to do is we look six months out and we say, ‘OK, six months from now what are the ACEs that are happening across the world?” Hill told reporters. “We have the senior leaders that will come in … to talk about why is this [capability] important? Why do I need this as a commander?” The G-TEAD also reaches out to vendors. “We bring industry in to say, ‘alright, six months from now, this is what we’re going to be doing in these theaters. Oh, by the way, we’ve done a few of these, so let us tell you what you need to do to win. These are the things that we’re looking for. If you don’t do these things, your chance of winning are less. So let us help you help us.’ The ACEs that are going to happen six months from now, the RFIs for these events — they’re going to drop . … Prepare yourself. You got time to get out and talk to other companies, because you may need the team with another company. Maybe you don’t provide the entire capability” that’s needed, Hill said. The G-TEAD plans to do additional Accelerated Capability Events for organizations like U.S. Army Europe and Africa (USAREUR-AF), U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC) and Southern European Task Force, Africa (SETAF-AF). The directorate is currently “at the forming stage” with U.S. Army Central (ARCENT) “to determine what that cadence is going to be,” Hill said. An ACE with USAREUR-AF is slated for November, and another is scheduled for February with SETAF-AF, according to Hill. The post Army playing ‘ACEs’ to meet commanders’ capability needs appeared first on DefenseScoop .
