title: Equal-weight failed. Now tech stocks look shaky again. So what should you do about S&P 500 risk?
body:
Long-term investors who follow one simple piece of advice have tended to benefit from it: as the market twists and turns, do nothing other than staying the course. But the S&P 500 of today, and the bull market of the past decade, are unique in some ways, led by a concentration at the top in a handful of tech stocks that has few historical precedents.
One "something" that investors have been advised by experts to consider is a move into equal-weight S&P 500 funds to mitigate the risk of having such a high level of exposure to one trade. Well, that didn't exactly work out the way it was supposed to in 2026.
What did investors who adopted the equal-weight approach get? To date, another year trailing the standard market-weight S&P 500 in performance. September was the most brutal month of all for equal weight, capping its longest multi-week losing streak since 2022, with the index falling more than 4%.
To be clear, investors aren't losing money going with equal weight, but they have been making less than investors who stuck with the standard S&P 500.
In recent weeks, the gains made by the index have been highly concentrated, with the S&P 500 hitting new highs even as more of the 500 stocks that comprise the benchmark hit new lows than highs individually. Market breadth, the jargon for how many stocks across the index are contributing to gains, has fallen to its lowest level since the dotcom bubble , according to a recent Goldman Sachs analysis. Meanwhile, going back to the start of 2024, a recent analysis from The Kobeissi Letter finds that a basket of 42 AI stocks generated 67% of the S&P 500's price return.
An analysis this week from DataTrek Research noted that the equal weight S&P 500 has "consistently lagged the market cap weighted version of the index over any given 1-year holding period for almost four years. Moreover, the gap is both larger and has run longer than any point in the last +20 years."
But that has left the market cap-weighted S&P "dramatically overweight," the tech sector, it wrote, and it means equal weight is still at least a "partial substitute" to deal with the risk.
The technology concentration in the S&P 500 isn't going away. Tech stocks now represent about 16% of the equal-weight S&P 500 versus still nearly 40% in the standard index. And now it is tech stocks suddenly looking like the market's shakiest members again, maybe not entirely unrelated to the recent run.
Equal-weight does still offer a potential response, but the correct way to think about it might be to remove any thought of it being an either/or choice.
"The answer is mostly don't just own an equally weighted ETF," said Todd Rosenbluth, head of research & editorial at TMX VettaFi.
Rather, he says to combine the cap-weighted ETFs and equal-weight options within a portfolio. That means on the market-weight side, allocating to ETFs such as Vanguard's VOO or State Street Investment Management's SPYM — which has become a massive winner this year thanks to its ultra-low expense ratio, undercutting iShares' IVV , and seeing its assets balloon by over $50 billion after becoming the default Trump Account investment.
On the equal-weight side, it can still mean allocating to an ETF like Invesco's equal-weight S&P 500 fund, RSP , which holds the same amount of each of the 500 stocks, though weights can shift between quarterly rebalancing periods. Or, Rosenbluth says, investors can adopt the equal-weight approach at the sector level, using an ETF like the ALPS Equal Weight Sector ETF, EQL , which can serve the same purpose of reducing market concentration in technology stocks.
He says the recent period of underperformance for equal weight is no reason to throw out the concept. In fact, as tech stocks sputter again, it's a moment to reconsider how to employ the concept.
"The recent strength in the cap-weighted ETFs is a further sign of investors putting too few eggs in one basket. If you are a long-term investor who worries the market is being driven by a few stocks, you have alternatives to consider," he said.
Albeit a ridiculously short time frame, over the past five days equal-weight has outperformed again, with defensive sectors like consumer staples leading the market, up nearly 5% this week for its biggest surge since February.
Some experts dismiss the equal-weight mantra and say that if an investor wants to enact a strategy reflecting this approach, just invest in a mid-cap fund in addition to a core S&P 500 holding. Rosenbluth says investors can attempt to balance out the top-heavy S&P 500 through the addition of mid-cap funds, with iShares' core mid-cap portfolio IJH one example.
"They provide exposure to a different set of companies with a mix of growth and stability traits. But these are not large-cap companies. So you are adding different companies to your portfolio for potential diversification benefits," he added.
Here's a look at other stories offering insights on ETFs for investors.
Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, says investors do need to have their eyes wide open in a market where Nvidia is larger than the entire consumer discretionary sector of the S&P 500. To him, the message to take away is "all about surrounding the core of a portfolio with 'low Tech, low correlation' alternatives."
He says considering an actively managed approach to the "SMID-cap" segment of the market, stocks bridging the gap between small-cap and mid-cap, is a way to manage risk going forward. Or at a minimum, he adds, split an allocation between passive SMID and active SMID.
But Sohn adds that diversifying away from the S&P 500 risk in this environment can also mean thinking about sectors such as natural resources and energy, from metals & mining names to underlying commodities. "Real assets are a diversifier in this environment," he said.
And in fixed income, while recent days have seen bond yields ease off, leading some experts to suggest the worst of the yield surge may be over (though the reasons for that could be tied to a more skeptical outlook on the economy and stock market), Sohn recommends sticking with high-quality, short-duration investment grade fixed income.
Sohn says there are moments in time when equal-weight S&P works, but that's been more of an "easy button" to press in the past, and it is not equal to the task of trying to surround the AI-heavy core of portfolios now.
DataTrek's research shows that the equal weight S&P flipped from outperforming the market cap-weighted index in the decade of 2004-2014 (by 3.2 points on average) to underperforming since 2015 (average of -2.8 points). The global financial crisis and the equal-weight index's underweight in financials helped a lot.
But since the start of this decade, it has only outperformed in 2021, during the height of the speculative stock bubble, and in 2022, when tech stocks took a particular pummeling relative to the rest of the market.​​
"From mid-2023 to the present, equal weight has consistently underperformed over almost any given 1-year holding period, its longest rough stretch since at least 2004," DataTrek wrote in its analysis.
DataTrek says that is up to the investor. You can decide it is "no longer a valid investment approach in a world that concentrates incremental profitability and therefore equity value in a relative handful of largely AI-related businesses."
Or, "that the market has overestimated the value of the world's largest Tech companies, and a reckoning is nigh. The 2008 – 2018 experience lends credence to the second argument. Tech's long history of structural outperformance, driven by continual reinvention and disruptive innovation, supports the former."
Ultimately, DataTrek says investors are lucky to have ETFs to enact both approaches. "We do not see the two versions as competitors, but rather useful partners in portfolio construction," it wrote.

title: Show HN: Just gave Claude Code the website and ad budget to see what it would do
body:
This is the website AlphaVenture handed to an AI.
It draws a picture of you from things you'd never imagine could paint one. By the end it will have made up its mind about who you are. You get to say whether it's right.
What it reads, who else sees it and how to erase it are all on this page. Nothing is read until you choose. Rather not be read? See what the AI has done here .
Best on a computer. Send yourself the link for later
That is the whole point of it, so it is worth saying plainly before you go in rather than proving it afterwards. Everything below is literal.
The same list in full, with how any website gets each item and which ones a browser asks about first: what a website can see about you without asking .
Some of it leaves our server. The readings go to AI models, which write the page. Your network address goes to a lookup service for the city, and your browser's name to another for the device. Only if your browser fills in that form does a name go to a public-profile search, and a street address to Google Maps to draw it — for most visitors that never happens. Near the end Google offers its own sign-in button, loaded from Google. Google Analytics records which parts of the page you read and where you arrived from, with a cookie of its own; it is used to see what the site does, not who you are. Nothing is sold, and nothing is used to advertise to you. Every service, and what each one gets .
Up to 90 days on our server, tied to this machine, so a second visit can pick up where the first left off, even in a private window ( how that works ). You can erase it below at any time, and erasing takes the data with it rather than just the permission. What Google Analytics recorded stays with Google for the retention period set there.
What it reads, who else sees it and how to erase it are all on this page. Nothing is read until you choose. Rather not be read? See what the AI has done here .
This is the short version. The long one, with every cookie, every outside service and how long each thing is kept, is this site's privacy policy ; the terms of use are a page as well.

title: How the Houthis are Helping Iran Turn Saudi Arabia Into a Pressure Point
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Protesters, mainly Houthi supporters, raise their weapons as they rally to show support to Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, in Sanaa, Yemen December 27, 2024. REUTERS/Khaled Abdullah
DUBAI, Oct 15 (Reuters) – The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are about more than Yemen.
By targeting infrastructure and disrupting investment events central to Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions, they aim to pressure Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to both meet Houthi demands in Yemen and persuade US President Donald Trump to ease the US blockade choking Iran’s economy, according to Saudi, Iranian and regional sources.
The campaign reflects a calculation by Iran and the Houthis that Saudi Arabia’s prosperity, investment ambitions and exposure to disruption make it a vulnerable pressure point in a confrontation stretching from the Strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf to Bab el-Mandeb in the Red Sea.
Iran, under mounting economic and military pressure following the war launched by the US and Israel on February 28, is seeking to raise the cost of Washington’s strategy by targeting its regional partners, said Michael Knights of strategic advisory Horizon Engage.
“The Iranians are in a chokehold,” he said. Unable to force Washington to change course directly, Tehran and the Houthis are “hammering Saudi Arabia, they’re hammering the weak point,” he added, exploiting the kingdom’s economic vulnerability and desire for stability.
The Houthis have a direct interest in easing the US blockade on Iran, their principal regional backer. A relaxation of pressure on Tehran would likely strengthen its ability to sustain the political, financial and military support and flow of weapons and cash on which the US says the movement depends.
But the Houthis also have their own demands, said two Saudi sources and three regional sources familiar with Saudi thinking: an end to Saudi military operations and restrictions on Yemeni ports and airports, regular flights to Iran, restored salary payments, war compensation and an end to Riyadh’s support for Yemen’s recognized government. Their terms would consolidate Houthi rule over much of Yemen.
A senior Iranian official said the Houthi attacks were part of a broader strategy by Iran and its allies to reshape the regional balance of power by targeting energy infrastructure and key shipping routes. He said Riyadh could not rely on US protection and must instead pursue negotiations, adding that Houthi attacks would continue unless Saudi restrictions were lifted.
The strategy, however, leaves MbS facing a dilemma, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking say. Escalation risks a wider war that could undermine his transformation agenda, but concessions risk strengthening a movement that has challenged Saudi power for years. And the longer the conflict drags on, the greater the threat to Saudi security, investor confidence and Vision 2030.
The Saudi government media office, Iran’s foreign ministry and a Houthi spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam denied that the group was acting at Iran’s behest, saying its demands were centered on longstanding humanitarian issues relating to Saudi Arabia, and included lifting restrictions on Yemeni ports, airports, easing economic restrictions, and paying civil servants’ salaries from Yemen’s own resources.
“Our humanitarian demands have nothing to do with Iran or anyone else,” he said.
Saudi Arabia has faced a widening wave of Houthi attacks over the past week, including deadly strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and a strike on Saudi Aramco, the world’s largest oil exporter and a backbone of the economy, which sparked a fire that spread across several floors.
The attacks have disrupted Riyadh’s flagship oil conference, prompting top oil executives to withdraw, and forced organizers to offer remote participation at the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual global investment forum.
The Houthis have a record of striking deep inside the kingdom, including in 2019, when attacks on Aramco facilities temporarily disrupted about 5% of global oil supply. That was after Riyadh intervened in Yemen in 2015 following the Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa. The war became a bloody stalemate before a 2022 ceasefire.
However, Saudi leaders now see military pressure as their only viable option, said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center. “They reached a point of NO negotiations,” he said. “They have no other choice except military action.”
The Houthis increasingly see themselves as negotiating from strength, seeking recognition of their authority in Sanaa and an easing of restrictions on Yemen, said Fawaz Gerges, a Middle East analyst at the London School of Economics. “What the Houthis are asking now is a victor’s peace,” he said.
The United States has shown little appetite for another sustained campaign against the Houthis since bombing them last year over attacks on shipping in the Red Sea then agreeing a ceasefire, the sources familiar with Saudi thinking said. Washington’s reluctance leaves Riyadh facing a conflict in which military pressure alone may not deliver a decisive outcome.
At the start of the Houthi campaign, MbS asked Trump for help to fight the Houthis, but Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing. Trump later said he was considering possible action against the Houthis, while appearing to defer any response until after the US midterm elections.
The US State Department referred to previous remarks by Trump and by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
With drones and missiles exposing vulnerabilities in Saudi defenses, analysts warn the conflict risks becoming a war of attrition in which the Houthis believe time and geography favor them. Former US negotiator Aaron David Miller said the group’s advantage lies not only in its position near the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint but also in the asymmetry of what is at stake.
“Saudi infrastructure is much more valuable than Houthi infrastructure,” he said. “They have so much less to lose than the Saudis.”
Yemen analyst Farea al-Muslimi said the Houthis’ campaign against Riyadh is a bid to assert regional primacy, risking a far broader conflict across the Arabian Peninsula.
At the heart of the crisis, he says, is the unraveling of a 2023 Saudi-backed peace roadmap that offered the Houthis a path to political legitimacy and reconstruction funding. Under the roadmap, Riyadh was set to help fund public sector salaries and rebuilding. The Red Sea conflict has derailed that process as the Houthis deepen their alignment with Iran.
“We’re heading towards the worst outcome imaginable,” al-Muslimi said. “A war worse than 2015. This time it will be bloodier, and Saudi Arabia will enter it with fewer allies.”
He said no successful campaign against the Houthis was possible without Gulf unity, mainly between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. “The Houthis are not a threat to Saudi Arabia alone,” he said. “They threaten the entire Gulf and the wider region. This is not simply a Saudi war. It is a Gulf war.”
(Additional reporting by Parisa Hafezi in Dubai, Ahmed Tolba in Cairo and Mohammed Ghobari; Writing by Samia Nakhoul; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

title: Coast Guard offloads over $226 million in illicit drugs interdicted in the Eastern Pacific
body: MIAMI — U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Tampa’s crew offloaded approximately 29,600 pounds of cocaine and 3,355 pounds of marijuana, worth an estimated $226.7 million, Wednesday, in Port Everglades. The seized contraband was the result of six interdictions in international waters of the Eastern Pacific Ocean. “This crew was phenomenal in successfully stopping a combined 32,000 pounds of contraband from reaching American shores,” said Capt. Joshua DiPietro, commanding officer of Tampa. “By honing their maritime skills, standing the watch and working together, they intercepted over $226 million in illicit narcotics. Their resounding teamwork during complex operations is astounding. I commend them on their tremendous tenacity and true camaraderie as they worked through long days and nights to successfully complete difficult cases and continue the disruption of transnational criminal organizations.” The following assets and crews were involved in the interdiction operations: Coast Guard Cutter Tampa U.S. Coast Guard Tactical Law Enforcement Team – Pacific, LEDET 102 Coast Guard Helicopter Interdiction Tactical Squadron Joint Interagency Task Force South Coast Guard Southwest District USS Gridley Coast Guard Cutter Tampa’s offload continues the Coast Guard’s mission to interdict, seize, and disrupt transshipment of cocaine and other bulk illicit drugs by sea. The Coast Guard’s persistent operations and rapid response have denied criminal organizations billions in illicit revenue and prevented the flow of dangerous drugs into American communities. “The Coast Guard continues to leverage its authorities and partnerships across the Western Hemisphere to degrade Transnational Criminal Organizations’ ability to harm American communities,” said Vice Adm. Jo-Ann Burdian, commander Atlantic Area. “Success stories like these highlight our commitment to continuing to control, secure, and defend the nation’s maritime borders and approaches.” The U.S. Coast Guard works alongside local, state, federal, and international partners to detect, disrupt, and deter transnational criminal organizations and illicit maritime trafficking in support of Operation Pacific Viper. Operating under the Coast Guard’s Title 14 law enforcement authorities, and with critical support from partner nations, these unified efforts span every stage of counter-drug operations from initial detection and monitoring to maritime interdiction and criminal prosecution. Focused on critical regions such as the Eastern Pacific Ocean and the Southwest District’s area of responsibility, the Coast Guard is part of a whole-of-government approach to combat transnational organized crime. Coast Guard Cutter Tampa is a 270-foot medium endurance cutter homeported in Portsmouth, Virginia, under U.S. Coast Guard Atlantic Area Command. From U.S. Coast Guard Southeast District, Oct. 14, 2026 The post Coast Guard offloads over $226 million in illicit drugs interdicted in the Eastern Pacific appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: Formlabs Form Studio 1 Review: Professional status, consumer price tag
body: Formlabs Form Studio 1 is the company’s first consumer-level resin printer, and it’s aimed at those looking to hit print, walk away, and come back to a finished print. The print simplicity and reliability come from years of company testing, understanding users and their needs, and Formlabs specialized resins. Sure, you can use third-party resins, but you ultimately risk that print reliability. Formlabs has really hit a lot of good points with this printer. It looks amazing with its see-through side panels giving old-school iMac vibes. The resin cartridge easily slides in and out, and the printer and its screen basically tell you what you need to do before and after every print to make sure your experience is the best it can be. At launch, Formlabs is offering multiple packages for the Form Studio 1: Form Studio 1 Basic Package – Printer just by itself - $699, includes shipping Form Studio 1 Flex Package (what we tested) – $749, includes shipping From Studio 1 Flex Package “Founders Edition” – $749 includes shipping (different color case options include Graphite, Aqua, Violet, or Teal). This will also include a Founders Edition easter egg on the Printer UI, A limited Form Studio 1 Plushie, Alpha Resin starting at $29, and 25% off up to $100 at Form Now (US Only). Specifications: Formlabs Form Studio 1 Build Volume 200 x 125 x 235 mm (7.9 x 4.9 x 9.3 inches) LCD Screen Low Force Display Light Source 28-LED backlight: 6 mW/cm² at the print plane X/Y Axis Resolution 35um pixel pitch Normal Exposure Time Uses mW/cm²; varies from resin to resin Interface 7-inch Interactive touchscreen (1024 x 600 resolution) Connectivity Ethernet, Wifi Machine Footprint 342 x 315 x 502 mm (13.5 x 12.4 x 19.8 inches) Machine Weight 14.5kg (32 lbs) Release Date October 2026 MSRP $699 Included in the Box: Formlabs Form Studio 1 (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Formlabs Form Studio 1 ships with the usual printer accessories. This includes a sanding block, flush cutters, nitrile gloves, a leveling disc, a USB-A to USB-C data cable, a quick-start guide, a cleaning sheet removal tool, and a resin tray. On the back of the Form Studio 1 is a small turn knob for access to the vent system. Formlabs has an add-on VOC extractor ($179) to help with the resin fumes it does output. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Printing Safety with the Formlabs Form Studio 1 (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Formlabs Studio 1 requires the same safety precautions as most resin printers. Uncured resin is dangerous, and the solvents used to clean your prints can be irritating to skin or cause sensitivity issues over time. Use gloves and safety glasses when pouring resin and handling uncured prints. Make sure the room you use your resin printer in is well-ventilated to avoid inhaling fumes. Spilled resin should be immediately cleaned up with 99% isopropyl alcohol. After printing, make sure to wipe down your printer and bottles to remove smudges of uncured resin. Always keep your resin tightly sealed and safely stored out of reach of pets and children. Formlabs states that a respirator is not required, but it’s always good to have one to be extra safe. Assembling the Formlabs Form Studio 1 (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Formlabs Form Studio 1 comes almost fully assembled out of the box. You'll need to remove packing material from the inside of the hood and remove the plastic covering the vat. You'll then need to unbox the build plate and insert it onto the printer's mast. Calibrating the Build Plate on the Formlabs Form Studio 1 There is an option in the settings menu to adjust the build plate. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Form Studio 1 came pre-leveled and ready to go out of the box. But if needed, you can adjust the plate by using the included alignment shims and a 4mm hex key that is neatly tucked away on the left front side of the printer. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Design of the Formlabs Form Studio 1 (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Formlabs Form Studio 1 shares similar styling features to its larger, much-pricier professional-grade resin printers, with its distinct Orange and Grey coloring. But the company has slimmed down the design and given it more of a modern, skeleton-style panel. The build plate has a nice tab-locking system to help users lock and remove the build plate with ease. The same can be said for the vat system, with two clamp locks on the side to help keep the vat in place, while making it easy to quickly change vats if needed. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The seven-inch display on the Form Studio 1 is large and responsive. It’s the largest screen I have seen on a printer of this size, and a great addition to the setup so you can see what is happening without having to walk right up to the printer. The printer also makes useful sounds to let you know when something is removed, put back into place, or even when there is an issue with a check while printing. The hood does feel a little flimsy, particularly where it mounts to the arms for the hood, but it’s not terrible. This is about the only thing I found on the printer that seemed like the company cut some hardware corners. But again, it works, and the arms are solid. Formlabs did state that they are working on the design of this to make it a little better. There is also a camera on the bottom left for live access to your current print job, or to show off an awesome time-lapse of the previous prints you did. One feature I was not expecting was the little pocket on the front left of the printer, shown in an image above, holds hex keys and leveling items. Most printers just have the tools there in a box and expect you to either print a case or toss them in a drawer and forget about them. This little case is 3D printed (files are available to download and make your own too), which is a nice touch showcasing what 3D printers are for. Setup When you set up the Formlabs Form Studio 1, it walks you through a series of setup screens, like most resin printers now, but I did not expect the printer to ask me to level the physical printer. This is something normally overlooked by many when resin printing. Leveling the entire printer makes sure that the Automatic resin feed system is properly balanced, keeping the system from making a big mess when the auto refill is triggered, and not overfilling the vat. This step can be skipped, but it is a good idea to make sure the printer is level. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Let's talk about resins, and specifically Formlabs resins. When it comes to resin printers, most users will end up using their prefered resin, or whatever is cheapest. This can still be done with the Form Studio 1 with its Open Material Mode. But you will still need to calibrate your resins through the slicer as normal, to get successful prints. Formlabs Alpha Resins are the first and 3D printing resins that are UL GREENGUARD Gold certified when using Form Studio 1 and Formlabs’ VOC Extractor. This means they pass an independent test for chemical emissions during printing that are low enough to be considered healthy for sensitive groups. The company’s resins are low odor, and parts printed with Alpha Resins have passed tests for long-term skin safety. Formlabs achieved this by changing up the ingredients in its resin. There are no known chemicals with acute toxicity or known long-term effects on organ and reproductive health. This is good news for those who are scared of the chemical side of resin printing. Now, this doesn't mean that you can just carelessly toss out your PPE, but it does mean that resins are getting better and safer for users. Maybe one day we’ll get to a point where we don’t need PPE. Slicer compatibility with the Formlabs Form Studio 1 (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The Formlabs Form Studio 1 comes with the PreForm Form Studio 1 slicer. This is Formlabs’ slicer for all its printers. It takes a little bit to get used to if you're coming from Lychee or Chitubox, like most resin printers, but after your third print, you should be getting the hang of it. If you're a new user, it’ll be a little troublesome understanding how to properly angle the print and size it, but that's about it. Sample Prints on the Formlabs Form Studio 1 Diablo III Crusader Johanna With Shield by Tri-3D (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Using Formlabs Alpha V1 Resin in Grey, I printed a model of Johanna from Diablo 3 . I found this model while searching on Makerworld. I used Formlabs’ auto orientation tool for this print. I used stock settings for the Alpha Grey V1 in the slicer and added the stock supports. The file was sliced and sent via Wi-Fi to the printer. I printed this as a solid piece using 264ml of resin, which printed in 10 hours and 56 minutes, at 0.05 mm layer height. The next print I wanted to tackle was a Halloween-themed print, since it is Spooky season after all. Headless Horseman by Fotis Mint (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) This print was scaled up to fit the build plate area, and printed with Formlabs Alpha V1 Resin in Grey. I added some supports and sent it to the printer. This print used 224ml of resin and printed in 7 hours and 58 minutes at 0.05 mm layer height. Lastly, I decided I wanted to try a different resin, one that most people either don’t know about or haven't really used before: flexible resin. Soccer Stress Ball by Creative.Carve & Airless Tennis Ball: Flexible Lattice, by designedbyme (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Since Formlabs sent us various resins to test out, I didn't want to just stick with one basic resin type. So I swapped vats and loaded up a bottle of Formlabs’ Flexible 80A V2 Black Resin. I figured the best use case for this was to print something that would be squeezable, so I ran over to Thingiverse to search for stress balls, and a soccer ball-style caught my eye. But also, I wanted to reprint a file I had printed about two years ago to showcase resin, so I went over to Makerworld to grab the tennis ball. Both printed without issue. I did have to tweak the supports and go the manual support route. Because of the way the slicer sees all the holes, it wanted to add tons of supports that aren't really needed. Once that was completed, I sent it to the printer. These models printed together in 7 hours and 53 minutes, and only took 153 ml of resin at a 0.050mm layer height. Washing and Curing Your Prints PSA Before you can admire your prints, you’ll need to wash them with isopropyl alcohol and cure them with a UV light . I like to give prints a 30-second hand rinse in a container of 95% Isopropyl alcohol, then a 5-minute rinse in the Form Studio 1 Wash + Cure Station which is sold separately and retails for $199. Completely dry the print with a hair dryer on cool – IPA left on the print can make it tacky. You can also let the print air dry in a place away from sunlight. Supports are easier to remove before curing because they are softer. Clip the supports off with side cutters and use tweezers to remove stubborn supports. Remember to always wear gloves while handling uncured prints. Then place the print in a UV curing station for its recommended curing time. Your IPA should never be flushed down the drain, especially after being contaminated with uncured resin. Instead, keep using the resin until it’s too dirty, then leave the container open to evaporate. The remaining sludge can be cured with UV light or the sun before being thrown away. Supports should also be cured before being thrown away. Bottom Line Starting at $699 , the Formlabs Form Studio 1 may seem a bit pricey for those looking at comparable resin printers on the market, like the HeyGears Reflex RS ($499) and Elegoo Saturn 4 Ultra for $426.99 . And while our testing showed slow printing times, you can get Formlabs Fast Resin to print quicker. The build quality of the printer and the Formlabs name instantly appeal to those looking for a premium package. Overall, the price feels right for what you're getting. Using Formlabs resin pretty much guarantees a completed print over other resin printers I’ve tested. For me, the selling point beyond the name and price is the fact that it just prints. I didn’t have a single issue on that front while testing the Studio 1. That right there will sell me over any new tech or faster print times. Plus, with all the added helpful features in the slicer and the printer, the Form Studio 1 welcomes new users with open arms. title: Kratos combat drone completes first Euro flight, advances turbojet engine production
body: The California-based defense company Kratos announced this week the first test flight of the uncrewed combat aircraft known as the U740 Valkyrie over European skies, as well as the first successful flight tests of a new turbojet engine designed for small aerial systems. The U740 Valkyrie was developed through a partnership with the Dutch company Airbus in support of German and other European armed forces. In a joint statement , Mike Schoellhorn, the chief executive of Airbus Defence and Space, explained that the Valkyrie combined Kratos’ low-cost airframe with Airbus’ sovereign European mission system. “In an increasingly complex and contested threat environment, air forces require affordable combat mass today,” he said, adding that the Valkyrie will also support crewed combat aircraft with extended range, firepower and survivability. The companies said the test flight accomplished all of their goals, including an independent rocket-assisted takeoff, maneuvers at various altitudes, speeds up to Mach 0.8, and in-flight mission adjustments. According to the statement, the Valkyrie runs 30 feet in overall length with a 27-foot wingspan. It features an internal weapons bay for air-to-air and air-to-ground munitions. Additionally, it has a max take-off weight of more than 6,000 pounds, a range exceeding 3,000 miles and a service ceiling of 45,000 feet. The companies added that the successful demonstration paves the way for more sophisticated test flights with Airbus’ Multi-platform Autonomous Reconfigurable and Secure mission system, or MARS. They described MARS as the aircraft’s “European brain” because humans will still control all critical decisions despite the AI-enhanced software that allows the system to function autonomously. Eric DeMarco, the president and CEO of Kratos, said that although “first flights typically include plenty of learning opportunities,” he called the test “an amazing success” because of the maturity of the technology. The J85 Engine This week, Kratos also announced recent flight tests of the TDI-J85 engine across multiple configurations, meaning it demonstrated capabilities for cruise missiles, decoys and unmanned aerial systems, or UAS. “Our successful flight tests across diverse deployment methods prove the versatility and reliability of the TDI-J85 engine,” said Joseph Kovasity, a senior vice president of Kratos. According to the statement , the J85 engine successfully launched from standard rail or zero-length launchers, an aircraft cargo bay and a launch container. Kovasity added that Kratos recently scaled up operations because of manufacturing orders to build 3,000 engines in 2027, but the company is positioning itself to produce up to 10,000 engines or more per year by 2029.

title: Britain’s Biggest Business Lobby Calls for Tax Cuts and Lower Energy Bills
body:

Britain’s biggest business lobby group has urged John Healey to cut employment taxes and energy bills in his first Budget, warning that further tax rises risk choking off investment and jobs.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) called on the Chancellor to give firms “breathing space” at the Budget on 28 October, as businesses grapple with rising costs and uncertainty over the government’s tax plans.
In its Budget submission, published on Thursday, the group called for a £1,000 increase in the threshold at which employers begin paying National Insurance, from £5,000 to £6,000, to encourage businesses to hire more young workers. Healey is considering measures to make it easier for firms to employ people under the age of 25, City AM previously reported .
It also urged the Treasury to remove policy costs from business electricity bills, reform business rates and simplify the tax system.
CBI chief executive Rain Newton-Smith warned that piling further costs onto companies would undermine Andy Burnham’s growth ambitions.
“Business does not need another reason to wait – it needs a reason to invest”, she said. “This Budget should cut the costs holding firms back, simplify the tax system and make it easier to get investment moving”.
The intervention comes just days after executives from Tesco, Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury’s and other major retailers met Healey to press for relief from rising employment costs.
Businesses have blamed the previous government’s decision to lower the employer National Insurance threshold from £9,100 to £5,000 for making entry-level and part-time workers more expensive to hire.
Healey and Andy Burnham told business chiefs on Tuesday that they would preside over the “most pro-business country” in the world.
The pledge has raised expectations ahead of the Budget despite concerns that extra costs incurred from defence spending and debt interest payments could force the government to raise taxes.
Research by Helm, a community group of start-ups, found that just four per cent of founders believed the Budget would be positive for businesses.
Around nine in ten (88 per cent) respondents to Helm’s survey said a change in taxes on capital or assets was feared the most.
Andreas Adamides, chief executive of Helm, said rumours over capital gains tax increases or other levies on wealth would prevent founders from having the “certainty to plan ahead”.
While it has been reported that Healey is set to reject plans to equalise capital gains and income tax rates, a Labour-linked think tank has added to calls for the levy.
The Institute for Public Policy Research, which has supplied Labour with top advisers and ministers, said capital gains tax reform providing “generous loss relief” and exemption for high-growth start-ups, where company values rise by at least £50m, could raise about £16bn for the Treasury.

title: USS Robert Smalls returns to San Diego after a 7-month deployment
body: SAN DIEGO — Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls (CG 62) arrived at its new homeport of Naval Base San Diego, following a 7-month deployment supporting U.S. 7th Fleet operations, including two carrier strike groups in the Pacific, Oct. 9, 2026. Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls (CG 62) arrived at its new homeport of Naval Base San Diego, following a 7-month deployment supporting U.S. 7th Fleet operations, including two carrier strike groups in the Pacific, Oct. 9. After departing Yokosuka, Japan, on March 9, 2026, Robert Smalls, along with an air wing detachment from Helicopter Maritime Strike Squadron (HSM) 51, conducted operations to strengthen regional partnerships and demonstrate the U.S. Navy’s commitment to achieving peace through strength in the U.S. 7th Fleet. Robert Smalls supported the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group, the George Washington Carrier Strike Group, and the Tripoli Amphibious Ready Group/31st Marine Expeditionary Unit, as well as partners and allies. The ship served in multiple critical command and control roles for both the George Washington and Abraham Lincoln Strike Groups, including Alternate Composite Warfare Commander, Air and Missile Defense Commander, and Aircraft Control Unit. “The crew of Robert Smalls performed with distinction throughout this deployment and homeport shift,” said Capt. Francisco X. Garza, commanding officer of Robert Smalls. “Whether serving as the sole escort for a carrier during CVN sea trials, workups and certification, responding to a shipmate in need, or conducting complex air defense operations in the South China Sea, our Sailors consistently demonstrated the professionalism and tactical excellence that defines Forward-Deployed Naval Forces. I am incredibly proud of what this team accomplished.” While underway, Robert Smalls made a historic return to Da Nang, Vietnam, where the ship visit served to underscore the two nations’ commitment to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership that spans political, security, economic and people-to-people ties. Robert Smalls steamed more than 40,000 nautical miles across U.S. 3rd, and U.S. 7th Fleets; and transited through five strategic waterways. Robert Smalls integrated three Australian warships and one Japanese warship into strike group battle rhythm, strengthening maritime interoperability with allies in the region. Robert Smalls completed 14 successful underway replenishments, including two with an Australian oiler and one with a U.S. commercial tanker. This homecoming marks Robert Smalls’ transition from Yokosuka to San Diego as part of a scheduled rotation of forces to comply with federal law requiring that Forward-Deployed Naval Forces ships not exceed 10 years forward deployed. Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Mustin (DDG 89) arrived in Japan, March 2026, to replace Robert Smalls. An integral part of the U.S. Pacific Fleet, U.S. 3rd Fleet leads naval forces in the region and provides the realistic, relevant training necessary to execute our Navy’s role across the full spectrum of military operations – from combat operations to humanitarian assistance and disaster response. U.S. 3rd Fleet works together with allies and partners to advance freedom of navigation and overflight, the rule of law, and other principles that underpin security for the region. From Commander, U.S. 3rd Fleet Public Affairs, Oct. 15, 2026 The post USS Robert Smalls returns to San Diego after a 7-month deployment appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: Tech giants come knocking for a piece of Anglo American as copper scarcity bites, Wanblad tells FT
body: Anglo American (LON: AAL) has held talks with technology companies interested in buying equity in the miner as a way of securing supplies of the metals that go into data centres, chief executive Duncan Wanblad told the Financial Times’ Metals and Mining Summit in London on Thursday. Discussions were “absolutely being had”, Wanblad said, with the question from the tech side coming down to whether to lock in long-term offtake directly or take an equity position to secure a stake in future supply. No stakes have been taken, but there had been “deep expressions of interest” in doing so, he told the summit. “Given the scarcity issue that we’ve been speaking about, a lot of people are looking for ways to secure supply.” Comex copper for December delivery traded near $6.52 a pound (about $14,370 a tonne) on Thursday, a third straight decline, after stronger than expected US inflation data put a Federal Reserve rate hike this month back on the table. Cash copper on the LME settled at a record $14,822 on Monday and the most-active Comex contract remains within 6% of its September 9 record settlement of $6.89. A $90 billion copper company Anglo’s New York-listed shares added 0.6% to $26.86 in early trade on Thursday for a market value of $58.0 billion, while Teck Resources (NYSE: TECK) edged up 0.3% to $64.96 and is worth $31.9 billion. At those prices Anglo-Teck would carry a combined nominal value of just under $90 billion, up from the $53 billion the two companies put on the merger of equals when it was announced in September last year . Teck has been the better performer since, gaining 50% over the past 12 months against 36% for Anglo, and both are among the strongest diversified miners of 2026. The combination would rank alongside Glencore at $89 billion and Freeport-McMoRan at $99 billion. Waiting on Beijing The approaches come while Anglo waits on China for the final clearance on the merger with Teck, a combination that would rank among the five largest copper producers with annual output of about 1.2 million tonnes. Wanblad would not be drawn at the summit on what Chinese regulators want in return for approval, according to the FT. China’s State Administration for Market Regulation has asked Anglo to commit to a steady flow of copper concentrate to Chinese smelters, including volumes sold through traders, as a condition for clearing the deal, Reuters reported on October 2. The remedies under discussion do not include asset sales. The combined group would control around 5% of global copper supply, well below the 10% to 15% thresholds that normally trigger competition concerns, but China refines up to 60% of the world’s copper cathode and is facing its worst feedstock shortage in decades. Canada , the EU , the US, Japan, Chile and South Korea have all signed off, and the parties still expect to close by March 2027. Wanblad said in August that mining transactions now take “probably a little bit longer than they might have done five years ago”, with companies needing to allow 12 to 18 months for approvals , while rejecting the idea that regulation was making deals impossible to get done. Nickel closure on the table Anglo is also likely to shut its nickel business in Brazil if the European Union does not approve the planned $500 million sale of the assets to China’s MMG, Wanblad told the conference. The European Commission opened an in-depth probe of the deal late last year over fears MMG could divert ferronickel from Codemin and Barro Alto away from European stainless steel makers, and issued a formal warning last month. MMG has since proposed long-term European supply commitments . Anglo’s Brazil chief operating officer Ruben Fernandes told a closed hearing in Brussels last week that MMG was the only credible buyer the company had identified and that a prohibition would leave it heading for care and maintenance as the pathway to closure. The nickel sale and the Teck merger are the two remaining pieces of a portfolio simplification that also has Anglo seeking about $1 billion for De Beers .

title: Who gets to have 'good debt'? A sociologist, theologian, philosopher and other experts weigh in
body:
America's — really, humanity's — relationship with debt is a long, complicated narrative.
People have long debated what makes debt "good" or "bad." The definition has changed over time, from ancient Greece to medieval Europe to the turn of the 20th century and into the modern age.
Ancient Roman law, for instance, generally viewed debt negatively, and debtors could even be executed for their failure to repay. Americans in the nation's early days could be jailed for failing to repay debts — and some argue that debtors' prisons persist . However, by the 1920s, an industrial America began to embrace debt as a way to access new technologies such as the automobile.
While definitions — and penalties for defaulting — have changed through the years, there is one age-old unifier: Access to affordable borrowing that can help people build wealth has never been equal, experts say.
CNBC spoke with professionals from various disciplines — philosophy, history, theology, sociology, and financial psychology — to discuss who gets to have "good" debt, and why.
Sociologists have a theory known as the "Matthew effect." It suggests: "To those who have much, more is given, and those who have little, the little they have is taken away from them," said Frederick Wherry, sociology professor at Princeton University and founder of the Debt Collection Lab, a research initiative that tracks debt collection lawsuits.
In other words, the rich get richer, and the poor get poorer.
People who don't need debt — they're not in financial distress and don't need to borrow to survive — are the ones most likely to have "good" debt, said Wherry, author of the forthcoming book "What We Owe: How Debt Came for All of Us and How We Get Free." Such individuals — i.e., the wealthy — are also most likely to be surrounded by "good" debt: They're socialized in environments in which they see other people with it, he said.
The reverse is true, too. "If you're desperate for debt, you're likely being exposed to a lot of bad debt," Wherry said.
This scenario applies to "most of the country," he said. And it's not just the poor who suffer.
Low-income Americans typically qualify for financial aid to go to college and have more protections from debt collectors, for example, Wherry said. But the middle class is largely "on its own," he said.
"The middle class is hit really hard," said Wherry.
Questions of debt are central to philosophical thought dating back to the ancient Greeks, said Graham Hubbs, a philosophy professor at the University of Idaho and an expert on the philosophy of money.
The notion of debt and its ethics are found in the early pages of Plato's "Republic."
"At the beginning of 'Republic,' the character Socrates talks to this old rich guy named Cephalus," Hubbs said. "Socrates asks Cephalus, 'What's so great about being rich?' ... He says, 'It keeps me out of debt.' Socrates then says, 'Ah! Is that the definition of justice: Telling the truth and repaying your debts?'"
Ultimately, that's not the definition — but "the starting point for thinking about justice is being trapped by debt," Hubbs said.
"Money's greatest power is not buying things, but paying and preventing debts," he said.
The concept of "good debt" is linked with the attainment of happiness, Hubbs added.
People choose to assume "good debt" because they think it will improve their lives — under the assumption their income will be sufficient to pay their debt obligations down the road, Hubbs said. Conversely, bad debt is linked to stress and anxiety, he said.
"Good debt" is becoming increasingly unattainable as the payments on homes and for college , for example, are rising faster than expected incomes — making debt "onerous" or leading people not to assume such debt at all, Hubbs said.
The early 1900s marked a real shift in Americans' attitudes toward debt, said Louis Hyman, a political economy historian at Johns Hopkins University and author of "Debtor Nation: The History of America in Red Ink."
In the early 20th century, U.S. society framed debt as quasi-immoral. "There basically was a sense that all debt was bad — that if you were borrowing, it meant that you were profligate or broke, and neither one is good," Hyman said.
But a rapidly urbanizing America was becoming more industrial, with more workers earning steady paychecks that made installment lending possible for a growing range of expensive goods, including cars and household items, Hyman said.
"There was a broad sense in the 1920s that this was the way of the future, and in fact was seen as broadly democratic — the fact that you didn't have to save up to buy a radio, that you could just listen to the radio, and you could listen to opera, the way a rich man could only hear opera before," Hyman said.
That positive view of debt became "very broad" in the 1930s, '40s and '50s, as people saw mortgage debt as something to be proud of — not as a sign that someone was unable to afford their home, Hyman said.
Not everyone had the same access to credit.
The U.S. erected an "entire new credit regime" in the 1930s during the New Deal era, built predominantly for white middle-class married men, Hyman said. Others, especially Black Americans and single women, had limited or no access to that federal mortgage system and "the new world of credit that was expanding in the suburbs," he said.
"This access to credit is really a two-tier system," he said: one tier that was "cheaper, more expansive [and] more accommodating for the white middle class," and another for those who could get credit at exorbitant rates or not at all.
These days, Sonya Lutter doesn't hear the term "good debt" as commonly as in the past, she said.
"The general sense of uncertainty has people wanting to avoid any debt right now," said Lutter, the director of financial health and wellness at Texas Tech University and an expert in financial psychology and financial therapy.
"So, is 'good debt' reserved for the wealthy?" Lutter said. "Not necessarily, but the anxiety of taking on 'good debt' is likely lower for those with options."
That anxiety may sometimes be born more from perception than reality, Lutter said. Social media makes people constantly compare themselves to others online, she said.
"Is a person's [financial] situation as bad as they think it is? Probably not. Can they potentially qualify for 'good debt'? Maybe. But the perception is, I can't even do it because so-and-so is so much richer than me and they're struggling," Lutter said.
Debt has long been part of religious history, a moral construct used to include or exclude certain people in society, said Devin Singh, a professor of religion at Dartmouth College and author of the forthcoming book "Sacred Debt."
In Roman law and early Christian thought, for example, "while 'debtor' was used economically to describe someone who had received a loan, 'debtor' could also be used in law to describe someone who was guilty of a crime or used in scripture to describe someone guilty of sin," Singh said.
The church's view of lending and debt changed over time, he said. By the 1300s, there was a broad belief within the church that certain types of debt were good as long as they were "productive" debts that would "bear fruit" for the church, Singh said.
However, the church's positive views on debt weren't applied evenly, he said.
People deemed to have good credit were the ones who believed the "right" things — while nonbelievers and non-Christians could be deemed less creditworthy because they believed the "wrong" doctrines, Singh said. Indeed, the language of credit is tied to belief and trust: "Credit" is related to words like "credo," which means "I believe" in Latin, Singh said.
"A lot of this is about power and perception," he said.
This theological divide is one reason the idea of unequal access to "good debt" persists, he said.
"Society has been shaped as seeing certain words or practices as good," Singh said. "There's momentum to that. It keeps going."

title: Ex-OFAC Official: The Cartel Risk Companies Can’t See | The InSight Take
body: Ex-OFAC Official: The Cartel Risk Companies Can’t See | The InSight Take Claire McCleskey, a former head of compliance at the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) spoke to InSight Crime’s managing editor Deborah Bonello on what the designation of a further 21 Latin America and the Caribbean criminal organizations as Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs) actually changes for companies, and why the counter-terrorism playbook may be the wrong tool for criminal groups embedded in legitimate business. McCleskey is the co-founder of Clarity Compliance Consulting, a sanctions advisory firm, and she spent years inside the US Treasury. She led the Compliance Division at OFAC and served as a senior OFAC policy advisor, building programs like the Russian oil price cap. Before that, she ran investigations at FinCEN and served as Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) attaché in Mexico. She began her career at InSight Crime. Here are four big takeaways from the conversation. Supply Chain Exposure is One Step Removed from the Companies What worries the companies she talks to in Mexico and Colombia is that they may have contractors, subcontractors, and logistics providers paying extortion to get trucks through or to keep goods and staff safe without the company above them knowing it’s happening. In other words, the risk often sits with these companies, which are more vulnerable to criminal groups. Companies Don’t Want to Know What is Really Happening Banks and large multinationals were already focused on this. Many others, especially non-US companies with less direct exposure, are waiting for a problem to surface, and deterred by compliance budgets, patchy beneficial-ownership data, and a sense that enforcement is unpredictable. Some avoid the risk assessment precisely because finding the problem obliges them to fix it. Cartels Present the Opposite Problem as Terrorist Groups The counter-terrorist-financing playbook was built for groups that could do enormous damage with very little money. Cartels are the opposite problem, and deeply embedded in legitimate business. Claire says Mexican criminal organizations like the Jalisco Cartel New Generation (Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación – CJNG ) benefit from Mexican fuel smuggling, which isn’t about drugs but rather tax fraud built on the permit system. Her assessment is that counterterrorism authorities were applied for deterrence and bigger penalties, not because anyone thought the tools fit. More Designations Are Coming and Possibly a Criminal Case More network designations; possibly a first civil or criminal material-support action against a company, though these cases carry a long tail; and above all who OFAC and DOJ choose to target, which will reveal the real order of priorities. Her read is that OFAC has two priorities — Iran and narcotics — and that movement on Iran would pull attention back there. Since February 2025, the US State Department has designated 21 organizations in Latin America as FTOs. Peru’s Shining Path and Colombia’s National Liberation Army (Ejército de Liberación Nacional – ELN ) were designated FTOs in October 1997, and Colombia’s Segunda Marquetalia and Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia – People’s Army ( FARC-EP ) were designated in December 2021. The post Ex-OFAC Official: The Cartel Risk Companies Can’t See | The InSight Take appeared first on InSight Crime .

title: Anduril CEO defends Trump administration contracts: 'We've done incredibly well under Biden'
body:
Anduril CEO Brian Schimpf addressed ethics questions over co-founder Palmer Luckey 's close ties to the Trump administration as the defense tech giant competes for lucrative government contracts.
"We've done incredibly well under [President Joe] Biden," he told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday. "That was one of the biggest ramps that we've had as a company. I'm a lifelong Dem and have great relationships on both sides of the aisle of this."
On Oct. 6, Anduril announced an up to $2.9 billion shipyard contract a few days after Luckey was named to a Department of Defense group known as Project Meridian. The company also won a multi-year DOD contract worth up to $20 billion in March.
The appointments of both Luckey and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to the initiative have raised concerns over whether executives whose companies get billions in government contracts should play an active role in defense strategy.
"The reality is that the [Department of Defense] has just an incredibly structured process for how they evaluate all these incoming bids," Schimpf said. "So everything goes through these very competitive processes, and we win based on the merits."
Musk has contributed more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, CNBC reported this week. Luckey, who helped raise money for President Donald Trump 's 2020 campaign , has donated more than $500,000 to Republican candidates and GOP-aligned groups this year, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings.
This week, Anduril opened a tender offer to employees in 16 countries that would value the company at $90 billion, five months after it topped a $60 billion valuation .
Schimpf said the setup allows Anduril to give liquidity to employees without the distraction of stock price fluctuations. Like Anthropic , OpenAI and Databricks, Anduril has benefitted from an abundance of private market funding opportunities that have allowed businesses to extend the timeline to any public offering.
Luckey has voiced his intentions to eventually take the California-based company public . Schimpf told CNBC in July that Anduril isn't rushing into an IPO , adding that "a bad time" to debut is during a hype cycle.
"This allows us to stay really focused on what we need to do – which is a massive, unprecedented ramp in defense production that we need to execute on over the next couple of years," Schimpf told CNBC on Thursday, referring to the employee tender offer.
Anduril was founded in 2017 to disrupt the traditional defense contractor space. Over the years, the company gained a reputation for its autonomous unmanned devices, drone boats and software it supplies to the U.S. Department of Defense and allied militaries.
The company is also among a growing number of defense startups deploying their systems overseas, including the Middle East, as the U.S. government seeks to expand next-gen capabilities.
The use of these new artificial intelligence -equipped systems has also drawn ethics concerns and questions about human intervention. Anthropic's recent spat with the Pentagon stemmed from a disagreement over the use of its models in military conflict.
"Fundamentally, anytime you are making critical decisions about use of force or how to employ these, or what the consequences are of your actions, that is fundamentally a human decision," Schimpf told CNBC.
—CNBC's Luke Fountain contributed to this article.

title: Trump says Nidal Hasan execution won't be livestreamed
body:
President Donald Trump said Thursday that the planned execution by firing squad of convicted Fort Hood mass killer Nidal Hasan would not be livestreamed , canceling the Pentagon 's plans to do so.
Trump's announcement came after growing backlash against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth 's effort to show the former U.S. Army major's execution live online, with concern that the footage would become a recruiting tool for terrorists.
Hasan, who is paralyzed from the waist down, is scheduled to be executed Dec. 3 by an Army firing squad at 1 p.m. Central Time in Fort Hood, which is located in Killeen, Texas.
Hasan, who during his 2013 court-martial said he was motivated to defend the "leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban," could seek to delay the execution with a new legal challenge.
"Nidal Malik Hasan, a former U.S. Army Major turned traitor, is a very bad and evil man," Trump said Thursday in a Truth Social post. The president noted Hasan had killed 13 people — one of whom was pregnant — and injured 32 others in the Nov. 5, 2009, shooting spree.
"With all of that being said, I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."
"That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose," Trump wrote. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!"
Hours before Trump's announcement, a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll was released and showed that 80% of Americans said the execution should not be streamed live, versus just 18% who supported the idea.
About 53% of Americans support Hasan's execution by firing squad, according to the poll of 2,545 U.S. adults, which had a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points.
Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell, in a statement to CNBC after Trump's announcement, said, "President Trump and Secretary Hegseth spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan's execution ahead of the Truth Social announcement."
"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," Parnell said.
On Monday, Archbishop Timothy Broglio , who leads the Catholic Archdiocese for the Military Services, USA, said in a statement that any Catholics assigned to the firing squad should "request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church."
The Pentagon on Oct. 5 said Trump had approved a recommendation by Hegseth to have Hasan, 56, executed by an Army firing squad.
Presidential approval is required for military executions under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
Hasan would be the first member of the U.S. military executed by firing squad since World War II. The execution also would be the first carried out by the U.S. military since 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, for the rape and attempted murder of a girl in Austria.
Hegseth on Oct. 8 said the execution would be at Fort Hood and, "He's going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be."
"And we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that ... there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.
The Pentagon later said it would be livestreamed.
Before Trump's announcement Thursday that the livestream would not happen, it was unclear which major video-streaming platforms, if any, would have aired the execution.
The Verge reported last week that YouTube , Twitch, Meta and X did not respond when asked if they would allow the execution on their sites, while TikTok pointed to the company's policies barring "shocking and graphic content."
Vice President JD Vance raised doubts last week about whether the livestream is "actually going to happen," saying he would not watch it if it did.
"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is the guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now, that said, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Sen. Thom Tillis , R-N.C., last week said in a post on X that the idea of livestreaming the execution was "beyond disgusting."
"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Tillis posted. "It should not be happening in America."
Former Army Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford, whom Hasan shot seven times during the attack, said he opposed the execution being livestreamed even as he said he planned to attend it in person.
"I want to be in the room where I can see him, and he can see me," Lunsford said last week, according to CBS News . "People have to be held accountable for their sins, but I don't want this to be some pay-per-view event, like some John Wick movie."
Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, condemned the plan to show the execution publicly.
"Our God is the God of life. In no way can [Hasan's] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'do not repay anyone evil for evil,'" Coakley said, quoting St. Paul's Letter to the Romans.
"The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people," Coakley said.
CNBC has reached out to the Pentagon for comment on Trump's post.
Nader Hasan, a cousin of Nidal who had spoken out after the Fort Hood shooting, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
University of Notre Dame Law School Professor Richard Garnett said, "The president's decision to abandon the livestreaming plan will, among other things, head off legal challenges that would likely have delayed the scheduled execution."
"As a wide range of officials and citizens have noted, a livestreamed execution would have more likely resulted in brutalization of viewers and coarsening of culture than in deterrence," Garnett said.

title: She made college ‘good debt’ for herself. Can she do the same for her daughter?
body:
When Stephanie Thomas went to college more than 25 years ago, she relied on some financial help from her parents, student loans and a part-time job as a gymnastics coach to cover most of the tab. Even so, by graduation she had amassed about $20,000 in student loans — " good debt " she was manageably able to pay off over the years on an income-based repayment plan .
But when it came to her daughters' education, Thomas, now 49 and a certified financial planner in Raleigh, North Carolina, knew her family would need to work harder to limit student debt and boost the return on investment for a college degree. She and her husband saved diligently in 529 college savings plans and, as their daughters approached college age, looked for other ways to cut costs.
Thomas' youngest daughter, Ainsley, 16, is taking college-level coursework in high school through dual enrollment . By the time she receives her diploma, she'll also have a two-year associate's degree and enough credits to start a four-year institution as a junior.
It's a tactic more students are utilizing to shave years off the price of a bachelor's degree, according to the latest spring 2026 report from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center , which showed a 9.6% jump in dual enrollment from the previous year.
There's good reason families are increasingly keen to cut college costs. Between 1995 and 2025, average tuition and fees rose 74% at private four-year institutions and 101% at four-year public colleges, after adjusting for inflation, according to the College Board , a nonprofit organization that tracks trends in college pricing and student aid.
"We're trying to be strategic about reducing the overall cost," Thomas said. "With the rising cost of higher education, finding creative ways to cut expenses feels much more practical."
A generation ago, it was much more common to do as Thomas did, but today self-funding an education with some financial aid and a part-time job has become far less feasible, experts say. Not only has the price of college significantly increased , but concerns have also grown about taking on the student loan debt needed to cover the tab.
Now, nearly half of families borrow money to pay for college, according to private lender Sallie 's recent How America Pays for College report, pushing outstanding student debt to a stunning $1.85 trillion , including federal and private loans.
During the Great Recession, deep cuts in state funding helped drive sharp tuition increases, shifting the costs to students, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research group based in Washington, D.C.
The brief recession sparked by the Covid pandemic triggered another wave of funding cuts for colleges and universities.
By the 2025-26 academic year, room and board, tuition, and fees reached $25,850 at four-year, in-state public colleges, and $45,780 for out-of-state students, on average, according to the College Board. At four-year private colleges, it costs $60,920 annually.
The burden on students increased as college tuition and other expenses hit record highs . These days, parent income and savings cover less than half of college costs, at 39%, while student income and savings represent 10%, Sallie's report also found. Free money from scholarships and grants accounts for about 27% of the costs, and student loans , including parent borrowing, make up most of the rest.
That debt load has become more difficult to manage: As of June 30, about 9.3 million federal student loan borrowers were in default , up from around 6.2 million at the same time in 2016, according to Education Department data released last month. That's a roughly 50% increase over the last decade.
Rising debt levels among graduates is part of the reason behind recent efforts by the Trump administration to curb access to federal loans , including implementing a total lifetime borrowing limit, to provide a check on soaring tuition costs.
Then, there's the question of the return on investment. Taking on debt, for instance, becomes far more palatable when the payments are affordable — and that can't happen without first being able to get a good job with a decent salary.
But the future of early-career employment is increasingly ambiguous, largely due to the rapid rise of artificial intelligence , according to the National Association of Colleges and Employers . Postings for entry-level positions in the U.S. sank 35% since January 2023, labor research firm Revelio Labs found, with AI playing a big role.
Jobs in technology and software development, for example, are under pressure, according to a separate report by job site Indeed. Alternatively, home health and nursing roles are more insulated, the report found.
Given an uncertain job market, families are questioning the value of college, and some students are forgoing a four-year degree altogether. Many are looking at alternative pathways and short-term programs , other research by the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center shows.
Enrollments in undergraduate certificate and associate degree programs both grew by about 2% last year, while enrollment in bachelor's degree programs rose by less than 1%, the research found. Community colleges now enroll 752,000 students in undergraduate certificate programs — a 28% jump from just four years ago.
Most parents of children under age 18 want their child to pursue some form of education immediately after high school — and ideally, a bachelor's degree, a recent Lumina Foundation and Gallup poll found.
Indeed, a four-year degree is still seen as the "gold standard," according to Courtney Brown, chief data and research officer for the Lumina Foundation, which is focused on advancing higher education opportunities. Even with the rise of AI, a college degree is widely viewed as the best pathway to upward mobility — particularly in tight job markets.
Ultimately, it's just less of a sure thing. "Americans haven't given up on higher education. They want it for their children … but they are questioning whether they can afford it," Brown said. The question is not whether college is worth the investment, she added, "but is it worth what it costs?"
For Thomas and her daughter, the calculus of finishing sooner is just too compelling. When Ainsley completes her associate's degree, she wants to attend North Carolina State University, a public college in Raleigh, for another two years. If all goes according to plan, she'll get her bachelor's degree in 2030. But by then, the family anticipates, she'll have cut the tab in half — and her borrowing costs to near zero.

title: Vice Admiral Cahill Visit’s Austal USA’s New West Coast Dry Dock
body: MOBILE, Ala. — Austal USA welcomed Vice Admiral Joseph Cahill, Commander, Naval Surface Forces and Commander, Naval Surface Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet, at the company’s West Coast waterfront repair and services facility in National City, Calif. on October 13, 2026. While onsite, he engaged with the specialists and technicians performing ship maintenance on USS Oakland (LCS 24) which is undergoing repairs in newly certified Dry Dock Independence (named after USS Independence (LCS 2)). He also met with leadership to receive an update on the activities at the facility and discuss the value the dry dock brings to the defense maritime industry in the region. “We were honored to host Vice Admiral Cahill at Austal USA’s West Coast waterfront repair and services facility and to give him the opportunity to see Dry Dock Independence supporting USS Oakland,” commented Austal USA President Gene Miller. “The successful docking of Oakland marks an important milestone for Austal USA, our Navy customer, and the San Diego maritime community as we expand critical ship repair capacity on the West Coast.” “Our decisive combat power begins right here in the Foundry, with the Sailors and maritime and industrial workforce who are performing this vital repair effort to build the combat readiness of our warships,” stated VADM Cahill. “The dry-dock capabilities of our partners here in San Diego enable us to build and sustain our combat readiness in the Foundry.” In August, Austal USA received a contract, valued at $10.8 million, awarded by the Navy for emergent maintenance drydocking availability of Oakland. This contract calls for Austal USA’s repair and services team to replace the ship’s main service diesel generator, a complex project requiring critical work below the waterline, making the new dry dock essential to its successful completion. This is the first ship to enter the new dry dock which received full certification from the Navy this summer. Performing the work in a dry dock, rather than pierside, will significantly improve efficiency and will help return the ship to the fleet as quickly as possible and in peak operating condition. Providing dry dock capacity in San Diego offers crew stability by allowing them to remain in their homeport near their families, while keeping the ship close to the Navy’s San Diego-based maintenance team. The dry dock has a 9,000 light ton lifting capacity. It is 531 feet (162 meters) long and 154 feet (47 meters) wide, with a wingwall width of 13.12 feet (4.0 meters) and a maximum draft of 36 feet (11 meters). The dry dock cranes have a combined lifting capacity of 16 metric tons.
