title: Five killed as Houthis target Yemen's presidential palace in Aden with missiles
body: Yemen's Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing five people, the government said, as the Saudi-led coalition listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in recent weeks.Yemen's prime minister and cabinet members who were at the Maashiq presidential palace complex were unharmed, Information Minister Moammar Al-Eryani said, adding that the Houthis had fired five missiles at the complex.The Houthi-run Saba news agency, citing a military official, said the group had targeted a military operations headquarters run by Saudi officers at the complex, as well as weapons depots. Reuters could not independently verify the claims.The Iran-aligned group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the strike on what he described as a Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden was part of the group's declared policy of "targeting Saudi military build-ups wherever they are."Three witnesses had earlier told Reuters they heard loud booms in the vicinity of the palace.The Iran-backed group also recently warned airlines that Saudi airspace and airports remain unsafe.Strikes on Saudi installations intensifyThe Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said that the country's Houthis had attempted to attack dozens of Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, as fighting between the Iran-aligned group and Saudi Arabia intensified.The Houthis have been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites for a week, in response to the kingdom's backing of government forces in Yemen's renewed civil war. The coalition's latest statement highlighted the risk to Saudi civilian infrastructure as the conflict escalated.Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said at a press conference that the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and wounding 333 others. The airport, one of Saudi Arabia's main international aviation hubs, was among the civilian infrastructure targeted in what the coalition described as a series of attacks.The coalition also said Houthi attacks on Abha airport, in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border, had killed three people and wounded 28.Maliki said the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats.The spokesperson also said the coalition had destroyed 127 weapons storage facilities and launch platforms in Yemen's mountainous areas.He called on the Houthis to immediately halt operations targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, and said the group should read the coalition's statement carefully and "between the lines."Shortly after the coalition's statement, the Houthi military spokesperson said Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe, renewing a warning to airlines while excluding airspace over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. The UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major fighting, and a de facto truce held even after it expired six months later. But efforts to turn it into a lasting political settlement have stalled as regional tensions have intensified.

title: Five Arrested in NATO Warship Services Fraud Probe
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
NATO warships alongside a pier in Kiel, Germany, during the BALTOPS 2023 exercise. European authorities are investigating suspected fraud involving port services provided to NATO military vessels. The ships pictured are not known to be connected to the investigation. (U.S. Navy photo)
Five people have been arrested in Norway as part of an international investigation into suspected fraud and bribery involving a company providing port services to NATO warships.
The arrests were carried out Wednesday, October 14, alongside coordinated searches in Romania and Germany, according to Eurojust , the European Union’s agency for criminal justice cooperation.
Investigators suspect the company and its subcontractors submitted fraudulent invoices to the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) for husbandry services provided to military vessels during port calls in northwestern Europe.
Husbandry services cover essential shoreside support for ships and their crews during port visits.
Authorities estimate the alleged scheme has cost NATO member countries more than €1 million, although the full extent of the suspected fraud remains under investigation.
The investigation also includes allegations that the company used an intermediary to bribe foreign public officials in exchange for favorable treatment in its contractual dealings with the NSPA.
The NSPA, NATO’s primary logistics and procurement agency, identified the suspicious invoices and subsequently worked with investigators to provide evidence and information.
Wednesday’s coordinated operation resulted in five arrests in Norway, where authorities also searched residential and business properties. In Romania, investigators searched company premises and several homes, while German authorities searched two businesses and a residence.
The cross-border investigation began receiving support from Eurojust in April 2025. A joint investigation team was established three months later, bringing together authorities from Norway, Romania and the United Kingdom to share evidence and coordinate their work.
German authorities also participated in the latest operation, with searches conducted in Hamburg under a European Investigation Order.
Authorities involved include Norway’s economic crime agency Økokrim, Romania’s National Anticorruption Directorate, the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service and Ministry of Defence Police, and prosecutors and police in Hamburg.
Eurojust did not identify the company or the individuals arrested and said it could not provide further details while the investigation continues.

title: Apple and Meta team up to make Muse AI model run on Mac computers
body:
Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg have clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins at Apple , the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.
Meta and Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily run Meta's new open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.
The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-called mixture-of-experts architecture . As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.
Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.
Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Meta estimated in early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.
Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Open collaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.
Zuckerberg posted a picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."
Ternus responded , "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"
Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerful open-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.
The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.
" We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips and published technical documentation about its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.
Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.
Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.
Plus, users will need to buy multiple machines.
The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which has become a point of contention in Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its older open-weight Llama family of models , it has since focused on creating proprietary models under the leadership of Wang , who joined Meta when the company invested more than $14 billion into his former startup Scale AI last year.
While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.
"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman , was a major Zuckerberg hire last year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.
Their leaders have also traded harsh words.
Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.
Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.
Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.
And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.
Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.
In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration " dramatically underperformed " and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute with Elon Musk 's xAI. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.
Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal with Google , to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.
Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.
Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Muse personal agent app and its latest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder, released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.
Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbed Muse Glimmer , with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.
Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.
"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

title: OpenAI promised developers six months’ notice. GPT-4o users got three.
body: OpenAI is retiring four GPT-4 models from its API on January 14, 2027. The deprecation notice the company sent developers Wednesday covers GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1, and GPT-4.1 mini, along with their dated snapshots and every fine-tuned model built on top of them. With just three months to migrate production traffic, OpenAI’s recommended replacement, GPT-6 Luna, handles reasoning and tool calls differently enough that swapping the model ID may be the easiest part of the migration. With just three months to migrate production traffic, OpenAI’s recommended replacement, GPT-6 Luna, handles reasoning and tool calls differently enough that swapping the model ID may be the easiest part of the migration. GPT-4o’s long goodbye GPT-4o arrived on May 13, 2024, as OpenAI’s flagship and built a following loyal enough to change the company’s plans. When GPT-5 replaced it in August 2025, Reddit filled with complaints, and OpenAI brought it back for paying ChatGPT subscribers the very next day. That reprieve lasted until February 13, 2026, when GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 disappeared from ChatGPT. Both remained available through the API, but that access now is sunsetting. By then, OpenAI said just 0.1% of daily ChatGPT users were still choosing GPT-4o, although the model continued serving API requests for applications built around it. GPT-4.1 was a different kind of release, arriving on April 14, 2025, as an API-only family that skipped ChatGPT entirely and went straight after developers with stronger coding, better instruction following, room for up to a million tokens of context, and more reliable diff formats for anyone letting a model loose on large files. Kevin Weil , OpenAI’s chief product officer, called them models “trained just for developers” during the launch livestream, and Sam Altman went on X to say developers “seem very happy” with them. Luna pricing has fine print Luna is the fastest and cheapest tier of GPT-6, and on paper it covers the basics GPT-4.1 offered, with a 1.05 million-token context window , structured outputs and function calling. At $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, it’s cheaper than GPT-5.6 Luna , which charged twice as much for input and $1.20 per million output tokens. Once a prompt passes 272,000 input tokens, the input rate doubles the output rate raises by 50% for the entire request. That could eat into the savings for RAG pipelines and coding agents working with large codebases. OpenAI’s migration guide says GPT-6 Luna defaults to medium reasoning effort but supports function calling through Chat Completions only with reasoning_effort=none. Combining reasoning and tool calls requires the Responses API. Enabling reasoning also rules out temperature, top_p, top_logprobs, and logprobs, all supported by GPT-4.1. The company recommends using its Docs skill in Codex to update API calls across a project, but those changes won’t account for differences in model behavior. Anthropic ran into a similar problem last month when Opus 5.5 introduced four breaking changes , causing 400 errors in existing agent integrations. Other changes altered how agents behaved without triggering errors, making those regressions harder to catch. No fine-tuning on Luna New self-serve fine-tuning jobs end on January 6, 2027, eight days before the GPT-4 models retire. Existing fine-tuned models will continue serving inference requests until January 14, leaving a short window to run replacements alongside them. New self-serve fine-tuning jobs end on January 6, 2027, eight days before the GPT-4 models retire. Six months’ notice, three delivered Other deadlines are on OpenAI’s deprecation schedule , which includes GPT-4.1 nano, the first GPT-4o snapshot, and older GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and o-series models retiring October 23. GPT-5 and o3 snapshots follow December 11, with selected legacy audio, real-time, and transcription models scheduled for January 20, 2027. GPT-5.1, GPT-5.3-Codex and GPT-5.4-Nano are set to retire April 1. The List models API now includes a shutdown_date field, making it possible to check upcoming retirements automatically. Customers who need more time may be able to keep older models running through dedicated capacity, although they’ll have to arrange that with OpenAI’s sales team. The three-month warning also falls short of OpenAI’s own deprecation policy, which promises at least six months’ notice for generally available models. The policy allows exceptions for safety or compliance reasons, but there’s no explanation for why GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 are getting only half that time. The three-month warning also falls short of OpenAI’s own deprecation policy, which promises at least six months’ notice for generally available models. Sony has announced a trio of new Walkman portable media players that start at an already absurd $1,899.99 for the NW-ZX900 and climb all the way up to $5,899 for the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3. Sandwiched in between is the $2,999.99 Walkman NW-WM1AM3, which is nearly identical to the WM1ZM3, just minus the gaudy gold shell.
All three devices are aimed squarely at the audiophile market, if the price tag didn’t make that clear. All three feature Sony’s DSD ( Direct Stream Digital ) Remastering Engine, which upsamples standard PCM audio to an 11.2MHz DSD stream, which it claims delivers a more analog-like sound. They also all feature gold-plating on the rear chassis that’s meant to reduce interference and lower noise.
The higher-end Walkman NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3 add hand-soldered oxygen-free copper (OFC) wiring and upgraded power circuitry to lower noise even further. A milled OFC block isolates the digital circuits from the analog ones to limit potential interference.
What sets the WM1ZM3 apart is that the entire chassis is made of OFC and then gold-plated.
This is not the first time Sony has gone all out on a gold media player. In fact, you can pick up the previous model — the NW-WM1ZM2 — on sale now for just $2,599.99. A veritable steal. Though, an old iPod bought off eBay is still probably the better bargain.

title: Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
body:
Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart , the machine learning (ML) hub of Amazon SageMaker AI . The model was trained on real developer workflows, such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions, and it supports a context window of 1 million tokens. You can deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account in a few steps, without managing the serving infrastructure yourself. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: BF16 ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B ) and NVFP4 quantized ( Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 ). In this post, we introduce Muse Spark Open and show you how to deploy the model with Amazon SageMaker Studio and the SageMaker Python SDK , send it a first inference request, and clean up. Overview of Muse Spark Open Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained for agentic coding workflows, with a focus on first-attempt accuracy, tool calling, and understanding of large codebases. It’s a reasoning model, and it accepts text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video as input and returns text. Muse Spark Open uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active for each token. The model holds the capacity of a very large network, while the compute it spends on each token is closer to that of a much smaller dense model. Meta releases the weights under the Muse Model License, which includes the Muse Spark Usage Policy. The following table summarizes the model. Attribute Muse Spark Open Provider Meta Architecture Mixture of experts (MoE), reasoning model Parameters 816B total, 42B active Context length 1M tokens Input modalities Text, image, document, audio, audio-video Output modalities Text Variants in SageMaker JumpStart BF16 and NVFP4 License Muse Model License, including the Muse Spark Usage Policy Built for long-running coding agents Meta trained Muse Spark Open on the way developers work in real repositories: code generation, debugging, multi-file refactors, and tasks that run for a long time. With the 1 million-token context window, the model can take in a whole project, including its dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files. You don’t need to split a task into smaller pieces to fit the context. Meta also designed Muse Spark Open as an agentic model from the start. Meta says the model plans, acts, observes the result, and corrects itself over long horizons, rather than making single tool calls. As a reasoning model, it works through a task before it acts, and the SageMaker AI endpoint returns that reasoning alongside the answer, so you can follow what an agent is doing and why. Meta trained the model to browse the web, coordinate subagents for work that can be split up, and operate computers across desktop, mobile, and browser environments. These are capabilities of the model. On SageMaker AI, your application or agent framework provides the tools, browser, and computer-use environment that the model calls. Beyond code, Meta reports that Muse Spark Open reasons across images, documents, audio, and video. Two properties of the model shape how you serve it. First, sparse activation keeps per-token compute low, but serving still requires enough GPU memory to hold all 816 billion parameters, so the instance choice comes down to memory capacity. Second, the NVFP4 variant stores weights in NVIDIA’s 4-bit floating point format, which needs roughly a quarter of the memory of the BF16 weights. On SageMaker AI, that difference decides the instance: the NVFP4 variant runs on ml.p5e.48xlarge , and the BF16 variant runs on ml.p6-b300.48xlarge . That makes NVFP4 the variant to try first when you size for cost. Evaluate it on your own workloads to confirm the quality fits your use case. With open weights on SageMaker AI, you also control the deployment. The endpoint runs in your AWS account, so your source code and prompts are processed on infrastructure that you configure and control. You can attach the endpoint to your own Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) , encrypt its storage volume with a key from AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , and turn on network isolation for the container. You also choose the instance type and scaling limits, and you pin the model version, so the model only changes when you redeploy. Use cases You can use Muse Spark Open for a wide range of applications. Meta’s focus on coding and agentic workflows suits it to the following use cases: Coding assistants over private repositories : Answer questions about large codebases, refactor them, and debug them with the full project in context, while the code is processed on an endpoint in your account. Long-running coding agents : Run agents that plan a change, edit across multiple files, run tests in your own sandbox, and correct course based on the results. Multimodal engineering workflows : Turn screenshots, design documents, or a recorded bug report with audio and video into a reproduction plan or a draft fix. Getting started with SageMaker JumpStart You can deploy Muse Spark Open from SageMaker Studio or with the SageMaker Python SDK. Each path creates a real-time SageMaker AI endpoint in your account. Prerequisites Before you start, make sure that you have the following: An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI models and endpoints. An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role for SageMaker AI. For this walkthrough, the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy is sufficient. For production, scope the role to the actions and resources that your deployment needs. For details, refer to How to use SageMaker AI execution roles . A SageMaker AI domain with access to SageMaker Studio, for the Studio path. For setup instructions, refer to Use quick setup for Amazon SageMaker AI . Service quota for the endpoint instance type: ml.p5e.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the NVFP4 variant, or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the BF16 variant. To raise a quota, refer to Requesting a quota increase . For the SDK path: Python 3.10 or later and SageMaker Python SDK v3 ( pip install --upgrade sagemaker ). An AWS Region where Muse Spark Open is available in SageMaker JumpStart. At launch, Muse Spark Open is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). To check availability in other Regions, open SageMaker JumpStart in your Region. The instances that host Muse Spark Open are multi-GPU instances, and you pay for an endpoint for as long as it runs, whether or not it serves requests. Delete the endpoint when you finish, as described in the clean-up section of this post. For rates, refer to Amazon SageMaker AI pricing . Deploy using SageMaker Studio The SageMaker Studio path suits a first evaluation: you find the model, review its license, and deploy it from one model detail card. To find Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart Open SageMaker Studio. In the navigation pane, choose JumpStart . In the search box, enter Muse Spark Open. Choose Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B for the BF16 variant or Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 for the NVFP4 variant to open its model detail card. Figure 1 shows the model detail card, which lists the model description, license, and the Deploy option. Figure 1: The Muse Spark Open model detail card in SageMaker JumpStart To deploy the model On the model detail card, choose Deploy . Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so SageMaker Studio shows its end-user license agreement (EULA). Review the agreement and accept it to continue. For Endpoint name , keep the generated name or enter your own. For Instance type , select ml.p5e.48xlarge for NVFP4 or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for BF16. SageMaker Studio lists only the instance types that the model supports. For Initial instance count , enter 1. (Optional) Under Advanced options , select a VPC and an AWS KMS key, or turn on network isolation. Choose Deploy . Figure 2 shows the deployment settings for the NVFP4 variant. Figure 2: Deployment settings for Muse Spark Open Deployment typically takes 15–20 minutes while SageMaker AI provisions the instance and loads the weights. When the endpoint status changes to InService , the endpoint is ready for requests, as shown in Figure 3. Figure 3: The Muse Spark Open endpoint in service Deploy using the SageMaker Python SDK SageMaker JumpStart identifies each variant by a model ID: BF16: meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b . NVFP4: meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b-nvfp4 . The following code deploys the NVFP4 variant with SageMaker Python SDK v3. You can run it in a SageMaker Studio notebook, which uses your domain’s execution role. In any other Python environment with AWS credentials, pass your SageMaker AI execution role with the role_arn parameter. Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so you must set accept_eula=True to deploy it. To pin a specific model version, add model_version to JumpStartConfig . from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig from sagemaker.serve import ModelBuilder from sagemaker.train.configs import Compute # NVFP4 variant; for BF16, use "meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b" with ml.p6-b300.48xlarge model_id = "meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b-nvfp4" jumpstart_config = JumpStartConfig( model_id=model_id, accept_eula=True, # Confirms that you accept Meta's license terms ) model_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config( jumpstart_config=jumpstart_config, compute=Compute(instance_type="ml.p5e.48xlarge"), # role_arn="
", # Required outside SageMaker Studio ) model = model_builder.build(model_name="muse-spark-open-nvfp4") endpoint = model_builder.deploy(endpoint_name="muse-spark-open-nvfp4") Run inference When the endpoint is in service, send it a request with the invoke method. The endpoint accepts an OpenAI-compatible chat payload with a messages list and returns a chat completion. The final answer is in message.content , the model’s reasoning is in message.reasoning_content , and usage.reasoning_tokens reports how many tokens the reasoning used. Because Muse Spark Open is a reasoning model, leave enough room in max_tokens for its reasoning and the final answer. import json payload = { "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Write a Python function that validates ISO 8601 dates, and add pytest unit tests for it.", } ], "max_tokens": 4096, } response = endpoint.invoke( body=json.dumps(payload), content_type="application/json", ) result = json.loads(response.body.read().decode("utf-8")) message = result["choices"][0]["message"] print("Reasoning:", message.get("reasoning_content")) print("Answer:", message["content"]) The endpoint also supports streaming. To receive tokens as they’re generated, add "stream": true to the request body and call endpoint.invoke_with_response_stream instead of invoke . Clean up To stop incurring charges, delete the endpoint when you no longer need it. If you deployed with the SDK, delete the model, the endpoint, and the endpoint configuration: from sagemaker.core.resources import EndpointConfig endpoint_config = EndpointConfig.get(endpoint_config_name=endpoint.endpoint_name) model.delete() endpoint.delete() endpoint_config.delete() If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, delete the endpoint in the SageMaker AI console: choose Inference , then Endpoints , select the endpoint, and choose Actions , Delete . Conclusion In this post, we showed how to deploy Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint in your own AWS account. You used SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK and sent the model a first inference request. Benchmark both variants on your own repositories before you choose an instance for production. To get started, search for Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio. For more deployment options, such as inference components and optimized deployment configurations, refer to JumpStart foundation model usage in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Before you deploy, review the Muse Model License, which SageMaker JumpStart shows when you deploy the model. For help planning a production deployment, contact AWS . About the authors Aris Tsakpinis Aris is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect for Generative AI focusing on open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock and the broader generative AI open-source ecosystem. Alongside his professional role, he is pursuing a PhD in Machine Learning Engineering at the University of Regensburg, where his research focuses on applied natural language processing in scientific domains. Liam Neal Reilly Liam is a Software Engineer on the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart team at AWS, where he focuses on deploying and optimizing open-weight AI models. He received his undergraduate degree from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he researched human-robot interaction, and he continues to follow developments in robotics and world models. Outside of work, he enjoys cooking and rock climbing.

title: Machines Can Crunch Numbers, but Humans Still Need to Understand Them
body: Summary: Recent AI breakthroughs invite the question of whether human minds are still the “ultimate resource,” as Julian Simon claimed. AI can generate answers far faster than humans can check them, but Joel Mokyr’s distinction between knowing that something works and knowing why shows that both kinds of knowledge must advance together. Candidate proofs are not theorems, and predictions are not findings. That is why the age of AI calls for more educated minds, not fewer. Last week, OpenAI published more than 370 mathematical results spanning algebra, theoretical computer science, and mathematical logic. Most came from a single prompt and about three hours of computing time. “If a human did this, it would be an instant Fields Medal, no questions asked,” wrote Alex Kontorovich, a professor of mathematics at Rutgers University. In his 1981 book, economist Julian Simon called people “the ultimate resource” because nothing else can create new ideas. Simon argued that new human ideas lead to innovation, and innovation drives economic growth and underpins modern prosperity. Forty-five years on, and with announcements of AI breakthroughs dominating headlines almost every week, it’s easy to be skeptical of Simon’s claim. OpenAI announced last month that after 88 hours of work, its AI had cracked the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness puzzle, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems that has baffled mathematicians for almost a century. On the same day, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome Atlas, which maps the predicted molecular effects of all nine billion possible single-letter changes to human DNA. If the nature of innovation is changing, are we still “the ultimate resource”? Ideas, as the science writer Matt Ridley wrote in 2010, “have sex.” In The Rational Optimist, Ridley argued that innovation is not the work of solitary geniuses but happens when human minds come together. As societies become increasingly open and specialized, more people with different expertise meet, discuss, and recombine ideas. The result is what Ridley called the “collective brain”: the knowledge spread across society that no individual holds. For recent AI breakthroughs, every system runs on humanity’s collective brain. OpenAI’s agents worked from a cached copy of the internet, and AlphaGenome was trained on thousands of experiments on human and mouse DNA, all of it somebody’s lab work. For years it was implied – simply because no alternative existed – that for ideas to have sex, both partners had to be human. If ideas no longer need two human minds to have sex, as Ridley put it, one might conclude the collective brain has found a replacement for humans altogether. That assessment is overly pessimistic, however. Since these breakthroughs recombine ideas humans had already written down (albeit at inhuman speeds), the machines look less like second parents and more like a very fast medium through which human ideas meet and get down to business. One-nil, humans. Beyond depending on existing human knowledge, OpenAI’s breakthrough also relied on human methods. To tackle Navier-Stokes, OpenAI ran about 10,000 agents at once, divided into groups that explored different areas and talked among themselves. As groups made progress, the most useful insights were consolidated and fed back to the other agents. Roughly 2.7 million messages were exchanged before an answer emerged. Many rival agents working in parallel, immense specialization, most of them failing while the rest built on what was most valuable. Free market galore! Humanity is surely better off with the additional knowledge AIs produce. Yet whether it is agents creating mathematical proofs that could solve centuries-old problems, or my own AI delivering thousands of words of research reports I haven’t found time to read, the bottleneck to innovation still lies with us. In DeepMind’s case, AlphaGenome Atlas can predict what genetic variants can do, but it doesn’t comprehend the biology beneath them. A list of predictions settles nothing on its own. A human mind must decide which subset to study, and Atlas’s predictions are not findings until somebody in a laboratory confirms them. Knowing that a DNA variant matters isn’t the same as knowing why. In OpenAI’s case, mathematicians worldwide are still assessing the proof’s validity. Three days after the announcement, without naming any company, 25 Fields Medal winners published an open letter about AI and the discipline of mathematics, noting that “solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.” The signatories note that AI can accelerate mathematical work, but human understanding produces the next question worth asking. The gap between output and understanding predates AI. The economic historian Joel Mokyr, who won the 2025 Nobel, distinguishes two types of knowledge. “Prescriptive knowledge” is knowing that something works. Think Edward Jenner knowing that exposure to cowpox provides immunity against smallpox, long before anyone knew why. “Propositional knowledge” is understanding why something works, such as comprehending the underlying science or natural laws. Mokyr’s answer to why the Industrial Revolution did not stall like earlier golden ages is that Europe got both types of knowledge moving together. The latest wave of AI discoveries could make one pessimistic about humanity’s role in the future of innovation. But Mokyr’s point is that the two types of knowledge should move together, and understanding why something works matters just as much as knowing that it does. Candidate proofs are not theorems, and predictions are not findings. AIs can crunch statistical correlations, draw on what humans already know, and generate prescriptive knowledge far faster than any human mind can convert the output into something verified, trusted, and useful. That is why we need more educated minds, not fewer. The scarce resource, indeed the ultimate resource, is still us. A version of this article was first published in the Washington Examiner on 10/13/2026. The post Machines Can Crunch Numbers, but Humans Still Need to Understand Them appeared first on Human Progress .

title: SK hynix reportedly playing hardball with Trump admin over 3D NAND fab
body: Reports that Solidigm was considering building a 3D NAND fab in the U.S. came as a surprise last month, as no company has manufactured NAND flash memory in America for years. However, the potential investment now appears to be part of a calculated move by Solidigm's parent SK hynix, which is reportedly asking the U.S. government to authorize additional semiconductor manufacturing equipment shipments to its Dalian facility in China in exchange for a commitment to build a new NAND fab in the U.S., according to Reuters . Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The Dalian fab is the world's only facility to produce 192-layer floating gate 3D NAND for Solidigm's data center-grade SSDs for AI, enterprise, and hyperscale data centers. Its manufacturing operations rely on equipment from major American suppliers, including Applied Materials, KLA, and Lam Research, whose exports to China require a license from the U.S. government. Although the U.S. authorities tend to authorize shipments of some tools to semiconductor facilities in the People's Republic that are operated by multinational companies like Samsung or SK hynix, they only want to keep the fabs running, as they are against expansions of capacity of fabs in China or introducing new manufacturing technologies to these facilities. Solidigm has requested U.S. export licenses for additional tools, but the U.S. government has yet to authorize the shipments. Last December, the U.S. Commerce Department granted SK hynix a limited authorization for equipment deliveries to Dalian for 2026, but it has not issued a similar equipment export authorization for 2027, according to Reuters . In a bid to persuade the U.S. government to authorize shipments of necessary tools to its Dalian facility, SK hynix proposes to build a 3D NAND facility in America. This would fill an important gap in the Trump administration’s efforts to bring semiconductor manufacturing back to the U.S. SK hynix's Solidigm subsidiary wants to install additional manufacturing equipment in the unused portions of its Dalian Mod B facility, which was completed in 2023. The company never fully equipped the building because of the memory market downturn at the time, so while some production tools are installed, substantial space remains unused and is available for additional tools. Given that Solidigm sells every single SSD it produces, unused capacity means lost revenue. Meanwhile, because the building was completed in 2023, installation of tools into that facility does not constitute a capacity expansion. Additional NAND production in China could generate profits that Solidigm could use to finance its proposed American fab and support its operations until domestic manufacturing capacity becomes available. The company is also considering an initial public offering as early as 2027 to raise additional capital. Solidigm has previously confirmed its commitment to further development of floating-gate 3D NAND technology. In an interview with Tom's Hardware at Computex 2026 , Avi Shetty, who leads Solidigm's AI solutions and ecosystem business, said that the company intended to develop 5 th and 6 th Generation floating-gate NAND beyond its existing 192-layer technology. He also emphasized the importance of maximizing factory utilization and profitability. However, he did not disclose plans to expand manufacturing output at the company's Dalian facility, not to mention a new fab in the U.S. Nonetheless, the new reports about SK hynix's intentions clearly indicate that the company not only intends to keep developing new generations of Solidigm's floating-gate NAND, but also to expand its production in China and the U.S.

title: French Rafale fighters operate from civilian airport in training for attacks on air bases
body:
The French Air and Space Force deployed three Dassault Rafale fighter jets to a civilian airport in southwestern France during an exercise designed to test its ability to continue flying missions if military air bases become unavailable.
The aircraft operated from Pau-Pyrénées Airport in late September as part of BASEX, a nationwide exercise conducted between September 23 and October 2. The deployment was disclosed by the French military on October 13.
The three Rafales belonged to the 30th Fighter Wing, based at Mont-de-Marsan Air Base, approximately 80 kilometers north of Pau.
A detachment of about 25 personnel accompanied the fighters, including pilots, maintenance technicians and security personnel. The relatively small team was intended to demonstrate that combat aircraft could operate away from their permanent bases with limited logistical support.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The Rafales conducted training sorties from Pau, supported by a deployable mobile facility known as SAMD, which provided the infrastructure required for mission briefings and flight preparation.
The exercise tested how quickly fighters could relocate from their home base and resume operations from an alternative airfield.
The French military conducted a second deployment at Dinard Airport, in northwestern France, using two CASA CN235 military transport aircraft from the 64th Transport Wing at Évreux Air Base.
Approximately 30 personnel supported the operation, including aircrews, mechanics and security teams.
The CN235s conducted training flights from Dinard and participated in exercises involving explosive ordnance disposal teams and airport emergency services.
Unlike operations from established military bases, the deployment relied partly on civilian airport infrastructure, including local refueling facilities.
According to the French Air and Space Force, both deployments were coordinated with airport authorities to avoid disrupting commercial aviation activities.
The operations followed the French adaptation of the Agile Combat Employment concept, known as FRA-ACE, which seeks to reduce the vulnerability of military aviation by dispersing aircraft across multiple locations.
The approach is particularly relevant to the threat posed by long-range missiles and drones, which can damage runways, hangars, fuel storage facilities and other infrastructure needed to sustain combat operations.
Instead of concentrating aircraft and support personnel at a small number of permanent installations, air forces can temporarily relocate fighters to secondary airfields and continue conducting missions.
France has conducted similar exercises before. In September 2025, three Mirage 2000D fighters operated from Metz-Nancy-Lorraine Airport. Between March 31 and April 2, 2026, two Airbus A400M military transports deployed to Châteauroux Airport, while two Mirage 2000-5 fighters operated from Dole-Jura Airport.
French Rafales have also participated in dispersal training abroad, including a deployment to Uppsala, Sweden, in January 2026.
The latest BASEX exercise also tested the ability of French military installations to respond to simultaneous threats, including drone attacks, sabotage and cyber incidents, without interrupting essential air operations.

title: Google Says AI Isn't Building Itself Yet—Even Though It Writes 75% of the Code
body:
Google DeepMind went looking for proof that AI is speeding up the development of AI itself. It didn’t find any.
In the safety report for Gemini 4 Argon, its most powerful model, the lab concluded AI research isn’t moving any faster, even though AI now writes most of the code DeepMind’s engineers ship.
The finding cuts against the scenario that has spooked AI executives into calling for a slowdown. It’s called recursive self-improvement: an AI builds a smarter version of itself, which builds an even smarter one, until progress outruns anyone’s ability to test, regulate, or switch it off—what the report calls “a situation where existing guardrails are severely inadequate.”
“There is currently no significant end-to-end acceleration of ML R&D, AI-driven or otherwise,” Haydn Belfield, a Google DeepMind researcher who worked on the assessment, wrote in a thread on X . “We therefore conclude that the risk from AI-driven ML R&D is currently low.”
ML R&D is shorthand for machine learning research and development, the work of building new AI models.
1/9 In the Gemini 4 Argon Safety & Security Report, we published our first holistic empirical assessment of ML R&D automation and acceleration inside Google DeepMind — combining capability benchmarks, a macro capability index, data on AI-written code and trajectory outcomes, and… pic.twitter.com/Vr8Q5Obbsp
— Haydn Belfield (@HaydnBelfield) October 14, 2026
DeepMind tracks the issue because “AI could speed up frontier capability gains faster than safety, governance, and societal adaptation can keep pace,” Belfield wrote. More automation also means giving AI agents broader access to company systems, more room for a misaligned model (one pursuing goals its makers never intended) to cause trouble.
To measure progress, the team built GCI v1, an internal index that blends the scores of 123 AI models across 92 benchmarks into a single number per model—think of it as an IQ score for AI. “Frontier Gemini capabilities have improved at a remarkably steady pace of ~0.1 GCI points/month,” Belfield wrote.
In the report’s chart of that index, Gemini 1.5 Pro sits near 0.5 points in late 2024 and Gemini 3.8 Flash just above 2.9 in September 2026, with nearly every release hugging a straight line. Argon is the one dot poking above it, at roughly 3.3, though its error bar (the range its true score could plausibly fall in) stretches low enough to touch the trend.
“While Gemini 4 Argon sits above [the] trend, we trace this to increased compute and organizational investment rather than reflecting AI-driven acceleration,” Belfield wrote. Google unveiled Gemini 4 Argon on September 30.
Most production code at DeepMind is now more than 75% AI-written, and the share of fully delegated pull requests (bundles of code changes submitted for review before they go live) rose from 7.5% to 11.9% between April and September. But “~88% of pull requests still require multi-turn human steering or human code authorship—and code changes remain subject to human review before submission,” Belfield wrote.
A survey of 12 senior DeepMind leaders and researchers found automation is highest in “well-specified, verifiable execution tasks and lowest in open-ended scientific ideation, novel experimental design, diagnosing subtle training instabilities, and long-horizon research taste.” In plain terms, AI is great at executing instructions and bad at deciding which ideas are worth chasing.
DeepMind also reviewed 1,389 logs of Argon working as an agent inside the company. The bigger the task, the less likely the model finished it alone and the more often a human stepped in.
The report landed a month after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued that recursive self-improvement is already accelerating, a warning Sam Altman and Elon Musk endorsed and one that sent chip stocks down almost 6% . Days earlier, former Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon had quit the industry , warning AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade.”
DeepMind’s numbers cover only its own lab, and the same report says it can’t rule out that an unrestricted Argon crosses its danger thresholds for cyberattacks and bioweapons information.

title: Volvo makes a bigger bet on Nvidia for hands-free automated driving
body:
Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. The companies announced on Thursday that Volvo will use three pieces of Nvidia hardware and software in its future vehicles to provide an automated driving system that can navigate urban streets and highways.
Under the expanded partnership, Volvo will combine its vehicle safety systems and engineering with Nvidia’s Hyperion sensor and compute architecture, Alpamayo driving software stack, and Halos safety evaluation layer.
The Alpamayo stack is redundant and diverse, according to Ali Kani, who heads up Nvidia’s automotive division. It combines Alpamayo, a family of AI models, datasets, and simulation and development tools used to build autonomous-driving software, with classical software that uses machine learning and camera and radar perception, he said.
“The point is we run these two stacks at the same time, and we have multimodal sensors in our philosophy because it’s a safer product that way,” Kani said, adding that the open source Alpamayo software has now been downloaded by more than 650,000 developers.
Volvo didn’t reveal the value of the partnership or which vehicle model would be the first to use this new Nvidia tech stack. But Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo’s head of software development, hinted at the scale of the deal and how it represents the automaker’s evolution toward developing a full-tech stack designed for its electric vehicles as well as its plug-in hybrids and gas-powered vehicles.
“Automakers used to be very much like car-line-based development and working with various suppliers, etc. and we have completely changed and migrated into being a full-tech stack company,” Bakkenes said, adding that Volvo will start this partnership with a brand new vehicle that “will come in the not-too-near future.”
He said the first vehicle with this new Nvidia tech stack will debut within the decade, and “then of course the technology can go beyond that.”
While Volvo’s relationship with Nvidia isn’t new, the expanded partnership represents the automaker’s effort to bring the latest automated driving software to all of its vehicles — not just its EVs.
All of Volvo’s battery-electric vehicles use Nvidia’s Orin computer chip, which processes information from cameras, radar, and other sensors to help a vehicle understand its surroundings and make driving decisions.
“What we’re going to do in the future is actually standardize more on Hyperion — also from a sensor set perspective — to really open up the stack for the wider partnership with Nvidia,” Bakkenes said.

title: How Adam Hamilton plans on winning Kansas' Senate race
body:
Can a Dem flip the Kansas Senate seat for the first time in nearly a century?
The most surprising battleground race is shaping up in ruby red Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932.
But Rev. Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, could buck that trend.
He's challenging incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall – and the two candidates are neck-and-neck in recent polling .
"I think Kansas has a chance to send a message to America to say, look, we got to come together, we got to work together," Hamilton said in an interview with ABC News' Jon Karl that aired Sunday. "I'll only get elected with Republicans voting for me."
President Donald Trump handily won the Sunflower State by 16 points in 2024, but a recent New York Times/Siena poll found 55% of likely voters disapprove of his job as president.
Hamilton, who brands himself an "independent-minded" Democrat, said he's both a liberal and a conservative.
"I'm proud to be a Democrat, but what matters to me more than the letter behind your name is who you are, what you stand for, your character, and I think there's a lot of people like that in our state," Hamilton told Karl.
After the ABC News interview aired, Marshall responded on social media, calling Hamilton "the ultimate snake oil salesman" and claiming the pastor, despite his messaging as being a moderate, has been "a proud donor to Obama, Biden, and Kamala Harris."
The megachurch pastor has been affiliated with both parties in the past and was a registered Democrat during the Obama administration. He was appointed by President Obama to serve on the President's Advisory Council on Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships.
Throughout the Senate campaign, Marshall has called Hamilton "too woke."
But on issues like transgender rights, Hamilton said he believes there are two genders and that men should not be competing in women's sports, even though "people might identify in different ways."
"The president has taken a group of people that represent a very tiny minority of people who are bullied and picked on and harassed, and he's tried to make them a campaign issue," Hamilton said. "He's trying to use them in order to somehow make the case that people should be afraid of trans people as well as Democrats, and I think that again is pathetic."
While Marshall links him to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , Hamilton has expressed a willingness to push back against top Democratic leadership if elected.
"I get asked, 'If Chuck Schumer tells you to do something, what are you going to do?' And my answer is, 'If it's good for Kansas, I'm all in. But if it's bad for Kansas, I'm a hard no,'" Hamilton said.
Bob Beatty, the political science chair and professor at the University of Washburn, attributed the pastor's strong communication and fundraising skills to his experience leading the Church of the Resurrection in Leawood. He said Hamilton "is like a gift from the political gods to the Democrats."
But as the polls tighten, outside spending is now pouring in. The top Senate Republican and Democrat-aligned super PACS are spending millions to boost their preferred candidates.
"I can't remember a race here in Kansas that's become so ... dirty ... so ugly," said Philip Perry, a 66-year-old rancher and three-time Trump voter based in the northeastern city of Oskaloosa.
Perry, a former president of the Kansas Livestock Association, said he's been "disappointed" by the current administration. The group withheld an endorsement in the Senate race this year.
"To hear from Washington that they're going to do something to lower the price of our product, that really kind of hits home, especially when we supported this administration so much," he said.
Perry said he has shaken hands with Hamilton in church and praised him for doing "a tremendous job of bringing people together in that Kansas City metro area."
But he said that Marshall has done "a good enough job" and will vote for the incumbent.
In the home stretch, the biggest challenge for Republicans is winning the battle for the narrative, according to Rob Fillion, the executive director for the state's GOP party.
"One of the biggest problems we're seeing is somewhat confusion," Fillion said. "Almost every ad is a negative ad, and so I think both the Republican Party and the Democrat Party are guilty of this. They have voters not knowing what and who they're voting for."
He told ABC News he expects the race will be tighter than in the past given it's a midterm year. Marshall will likely prevail, he added.
The senator has held few public events since a town hall meeting in March 2025, when he walked away from voters angry about federal job cuts. Marshall appeared at stops as part of the Kansas GOP's statewide bus tour this week.
In September, Vice President JD Vance held a rally in Kansas, what Hamilton considered "a great compliment that the second most powerful man in America came here to try to save Roger Marshall."
The Iran war has driven up the price of gas, diesel fuel and fertilizer, hurting farmers already grappling with uncertainty over the president's tariff policies .
It's affecting voters like Steve Bowlin, a 70-year-old third-generation farmer based in Olathe who sits on the board of the Johnson County Farm Bureau.
Bowlin, who grows produce, said he worries whether his decades-old family farm will survive. "People don't understand what it takes to put food on the table," Bowlin said.
He told ABC News he does not believe that Washington is hearing his concerns. And the president's endorsement of Sen. Roger Marshall is not a factor when it comes to his vote this fall.
"I don't care who he endorses," Bowlin said. "I want somebody that is talking for the American farmer."
Marshall says Republicans are 'coming home'
In a state that has voted for both Republicans and Democrats to the governorship, Hamilton is seeking to build a large coalition.
Two former Republican governors -- Bill Graves and Mike Hayden -- are backing Hamilton. So is Marshall's former GOP primary opponent, Arch Naramore.
Former GOP Gov. Sam Brownback has endorsed Marshall.
On Friday, Marshall toured a radar manufacturing plant with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. He brushed off concerns about Republican support for his opponent.
"I think it’s a very finite amount of people," Marshall told ABC News. "What I see across the state is Republicans coming home."
That could be the case, but some Republicans like Bruce Bratman, who voted for Trump three times, told ABC News he is knocking doors for Hamilton.
At a packed theater in Hutchinson, in a county Trump carried by about 34 percentage points in the last presidential election, some Republican and independents turned out for Hamilton.
"I think it'd be crazy not to elect him," said Laura Shea, an unaffiliated voter. "I think we'd be crazy if we elected the representative we have now, who I don't feel, and a lot of people don't feel, is representing us. We don't see him from the things he does or doesn't do."
Ed Berger, a former Republican state senator who represented Hutchinson, also pledged support for Hamilton.
"Our current senator is not representing Kansas. He's not standing up to policies that hurt Kansans everyday," Berger told ABC News. "The senator should represent his constituency and have the courage to stand up to the executive branch."
Joshua Farr, a self-described constitutional conservative, went to the Hutchinson event to learn more about the candidate.
"I might vote for Hamilton this time. It's just, I don't really like Democrats. Democrats tend to be more liberal and I'm not that liberal," Farr said.
At a campaign event held at a college chapel in Lindsborg, Hamilton led the crowd in a hymn and did not mention his opponent by name.
"Most of us around here are not actually enemies. If we're liberals or conservatives, we just see the world differently," Hamilton said.

title: Show HN: Keyword clustering that runs in the browser
body:
Paste a list or drop an export from Ahrefs, Semrush or Keyword Planner. Get topic clusters you can build pages around, with intent labels and a CSV out. The model runs in this tab. Nothing is uploaded.
0 keywords Â· Volumes rank the clusters and pick their names. Up to 25,000 keywords per run.
Intent labels are a rule-based guess from the words in each keyword, not from search results.
A small sentence-embedding model, the kind behind semantic search, turns every keyword into 384 numbers. Keywords that mean the same thing point the same way, even when they share no words.
The list is walked from highest volume down. Each keyword joins the nearest existing cluster if it is similar enough, otherwise it starts one. Then every keyword is rechecked against every cluster until nothing moves.
The same pass runs again on the clusters themselves at a looser setting. The result is a two-level map: topics for hubs, clusters for pages, keywords for headings.
The tightness slider is the similarity a keyword needs to join a cluster. Around 0.55 you get broad topics, around 0.75 near-duplicates. Most lists look right between 0.58 and 0.68. Move it after a run and the page re-clusters instantly, because the vectors are kept.
Honest version. The paid tools cluster by overlap in Google's results, which is the industry's definition of "same page". This tool clusters by meaning, which is free and fast and catches most of the same groupings, but not all.
No. There is no server behind this page. The model and the page are static files, and your keywords never leave the browser. The only third-party request is the open-source runtime library from a CDN. Open your browser's network tab and watch.
all-MiniLM-L6-v2, an open sentence-embedding model, quantized to 8-bit so it is 22 MB. It runs through transformers.js on WebAssembly, using several CPU threads when the browser allows it.
SERP clustering says two keywords belong together when Google shows mostly the same pages for both. That needs a search-results feed for every keyword, which costs money. This tool says two keywords belong together when they mean the same thing. On most lists the two methods agree. They disagree on keywords Google treats as one query despite different wording, and on phrases that read alike but get different results.
Up to 25,000 keywords per run. Around 10,000 takes about a minute on a recent laptop, longer on a phone. The slider re-clusters instantly after the first run.
Yes. There is no license to worry about and nothing is stored. Download the CSV or copy for Sheets, and keep your own copy.
It costs nothing to run, so it can cost nothing to use. If enough people want more, a paid version with saved projects, bigger runs and SERP overlap using your own API key is the plan. Leave an email below if that is you.
Leave an email and tell us what you would need. One message when something ships. No list, no drip.

Volvo plans to launch hands-free, point-to-point driving by 2030, powered by Nvidia’s latest AI technology. The Chinese-owned, Swedish-designed automaker said Thursday it would use Nvidia’s autonomous driving stack to power a new partially automated driving system similar to Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised).
Volvo says the new point-to-point system will be Level 2++, meaning it can handle complex urban environments, including traffic lights, stop signs, and unprotected left turns without explicit driver control. In addition to Tesla’s FSD, it will also resemble the Nvidia-powered system that Mercedes-Benz recently rolled out for the all-new CLA sedan , said Ali Kani, VP and general manager of the automotive team at Nvidia, in an interview with The Verge .
Volvo will use Nvidia’s Hyperion platform, which includes the chipmaker’s high-powered silicon, as well as additional sensors mounted around the vehicle so the car can see and perceive its surroundings. The automaker will also utilize Nvidia’s Alpamayo software, which uses “reasoning” models to make sense of complex road conditions and plan where to steer, brake, or accelerate. The setup will not include lidar, though it could include the laser sensor if Volvo decides to add it in the future.
By expanding its preexisting partnership with Volvo, the automaker is trying to correct some of its failed automated driving projects of the past. The automaker had to effectively sideline its Ride Pilot Level 3 unsupervised autonomous driving system in the US after failing to obtain regulatory approval. Volvo also planned to add lidar sensors to some of its models, but that plan fell away after its supplier Luminar went bankrupt .
Volvo is also bringing its own reputation for safety to the table. The automaker wants to combine its safety expertise with Nvidia’s technology to improve the overall system, including contributing its proprietary driver-understanding systems, which analyze driver behavior in considerably greater detail than a basic driver monitoring system, said Alwin Bakkenes, head of global software engineering at Volvo Cars.
“Our brand Volvo is synonymous with safety, and safety is synonymous with trust,” Bakkenes said in an interview. “People get into our cars not expecting anything bad to happen, but they feel intrinsically that if they’re ever in a situation … we will do our utmost to keep people safe, to protect them from harm.”
Another important component is Volvo’s connected safety technology that allows its vehicles to exchange information about hazards and conditions ahead , including roadworks. Sharing this information can effectively extend the system’s awareness beyond what an individual vehicle’s sensors can detect, potentially improving the operating capabilities of the self-driving functionality.
Volvo plans to make the new point-to-point driving system available across its vehicle lineup, from entry-level to high-end versions — though the company didn’t reveal which models will come first. The timeline was also a little vague, with Bakkenes only confirming that it will launch “before the end of the decade.”
Kani also pointed to the commercial implications, noting that point-to-point driving may prove to be more valuable than a system limited to highway assistance. Nvidia sees the partnership as an opportunity not only to advance the technology but also to help Volvo develop its business model around ongoing software-based offerings, he said.

title: U.S. Air Force Tests Mk21A Reentry Vehicle for Sentinel ICBM
body: The Mk21A reentry vehicle, designed to be carried atop the LGM-35A Sentinel, continues to be tested as the Air Force steadily pushes the new ICBM’s development ahead of a Critical Design Review and first test flight in 2027. A Mk21A reentry vehicle (RV) was tested aboard a Minotaur I rocket on Oct. 9, 2026, from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center (AFNWC) announced , further advancing the development of components of the Sentinel Inter-Continental Ballistic Missile (ICBM). The trial was described as an “in-flight environmental test.” These tests are usually meant to generate general data on the surrounding physical conditions like heat, vibration, aerodynamic load, friction and the impact on internal physical components the RV might experience.The data is then used to refine computer simulation models and better predict the system’s performance – in this case the Mk21A RV – which is in the Engineering Manufacturing Development (EMD). Regarding the rocket, the Minotaur I is an expendable launch system derived from the Minuteman II missile, and is often used to launch small U.S. government satellites. Additionally, it is also used for testing activities which do not require the use of a complete ICBM. In fact, this is not the first time the Mk21A RV has been tested aboard the Minotaur I, with one trial taking place from Vandenberg SFB on June 17, 2024 . The press release did not provide an image of the latest test, but rather shared a picture of the 2024 trial. The U.S. Air Force recently flight tested its new Mk21A reentry vehicle, which is being developed for the future LGM-35A Sentinel ICBM. The unarmed vehicle was launched aboard a Northrop Grumman-provided Minotaur I rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, in an in-flight environmental test overseen by the U.S. Space Force’s Rocket Systems Launch Program. Minotaur rockets are used to test new payload technologies in operationally realistic environments. Lockheed Martin is building the Mk21A under a contract for the engineering and manufacturing development (EMD) phase. Once it reaches full operational capability, it will be integrated onto the Sentinel. Sentinel, formerly the Ground Based Strategic Deterrent (GBSD), is being developed by Northrop Grumman and will replace the Air Force’s LGM-30G Minuteman III missiles. — Comandante (@commandante_) October 14, 2026 The service said that, “after attaining full operational capability, the Mk21A RV will be integrated on a future intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM).” The term “future” avoids explicit mention of the LGM-35A Sentinel ICBM, although the service already confirmed the relation between the two systems. The Mk21A is being developed to accommodate the W87-1 nuclear warhead for the Sentinel program. In a multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle (MIRV) configuration, an ICBM can deploy multiple reentry vehicles, each carrying a warhead. The test of the RV follows the announcement of the Sentinel ICBM being vertically stacked at Vandenberg SFB last month, in anticipation of its first test launch next year. This will be preceded by a Critical Design Review (CDR) for the entire Sentinel system by March 2027. A Minotaur I rocket carrying an unarmed Mk21A reentry vehicle is prepared for launch at Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., June 16, 2024. | Source: U.S. Air Force/Senior Airman Joshua LeRoi The test launch According to the AFNWC, the unarmed Mk21A reentry vehicle tested from Vandenberg SFB on the morning of Oct. 9 aboard a Northrop Grumman Minotaur I was part of “an in-flight environmental test supporting the development of the Air Force’s new Mk21A RV.” The test was overseen by the U.S. Space Force’s Rocket System’s Launch Program. The release explained that “Minotaur launch vehicles support testing and demonstration of new payload technologies in operationally realistic environments.” AFNWC also confirmed that “The Mk21A RV is currently under contract with Lockheed Martin for its engineering and manufacturing development phase.” Maj. Gen. William Rogers, U.S. Air Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for ICBMs and AFNWC director of ICBM systems, described the Mk21A as “crucial to modernizing our ICBMs in response to the rapidly changing global threat picture posed by our adversaries.” He further said “The reentry vehicle’s development will ensure a safe, secure and effective deterrent for generations to come.” An April 18, 2024 image released by Sandia National Laboratories showing preparations for a test of a Mark 21 fuze, designed for deployment on both the Minuteman III and the upcoming Sentinel ICBM. | Source: Sandia National Laboratories Brig. Gen. Amanda Okeson, program manager at the AFNWC’s ICBM Systems Directorate, said “investment in modernization of the ICBM mission remains a top priority for the Air Force.” The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center is the lead for the Air Force’s Mk21A reentry vehicle’s acquisition effort. The center is responsible for synchronizing all aspects of nuclear materiel management on behalf of Air Force Materiel Command (AFMC), while supporting the Air Force Global Strike Command (AFGSC). A Mark 21 Fuze in the laboratory. | Source: Sandia National Laboratories Mk21A contracts and Sentinel ICBM For the Mk21A Reentry Vehicle, the AFNWC had awarded Lockheed a $996 million contract in October 2023, followed by an additional $453 million contract modification in November 2025 . An April acquisition report released by the Pentagon in September said that the last contract modification was part of a new baseline, intended to “decouple [the Mk21A’s] schedule from external programs and continue development with an updated, more resilient plan.” The aforementioned Pentagon acquisition report describe the Mk21A RV’s components as the “shape stable nose tip; high impulse transducer; arming and fuzing subsystem (AFS); aeroshell forward section, body section, and rear cover; radio frequency subsystem with antennas; RV spin subsystem; in-flight disconnect cable; and other electrical cables.” We’re moving with speed and scale to deliver Sentinel to the @USAirForce – accelerating the path to flight test with a fully integrated Sentinel missile assembly and successful Critical Design Review. Learn more: https://t.co/neDmHIVoHF https://t.co/67b1HMqLVW — Northrop Grumman (@NGCNews) September 14, 2026 As The Aviationist has reported previously , the Sentinel program has experienced its share of cost overruns, compounded by the relatively recent decision not to re-use existing Minuteman silos . The price escalation had also triggered a Congressional review under the Nunn-McCurdy Act, which qualifies a project to be cancelled if the cost overshoots 25% of the original baseline, until the Department of War certifies to lawmakers that the program meets criteria to continue.

title: Oil Shipping Costs Spike, Lifting Prices from Pump to Grocery
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
FILE PHOTO: Tankers sail in the Gulf, near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from northern Ras al-Khaimah, near the border with Oman’s Musandam governance, amid the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, in United Arab Emirates, March 11, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo
HOUSTON/LOS ANGELES, Oct 15 (Reuters) – When the oil supertanker Esteem Explorer sails from the United States to Japan in late November, loaded with about 2 million barrels of crude, the journey will cost $81 million. The same journey would have cost $9.1 million last year, on average.
The shipping cost translates into $40.50 per barrel, about nine times last year’s rate. While oil’s soaring selling price worries consumers, the Esteem Explorer’s expensive voyage illustrates how transport costs are further inflating the price. Refiners process oil into fuel to move food, retail goods and construction materials, and rising costs are stoking inflation in countries that depend on imports.
Every $10-per-barrel increase in shipping costs adds about 23 cents per gallon to gasoline, said Kenneth Medlock, a fellow in energy and resource economics at the Houston-based Baker Institute for Public Policy. On that basis, the Esteem Explorer’s shipping cost works out to at least 80 cents more per gallon of gasoline than last year, according to Reuters calculations.
“It’s sort of like a slow-moving train. It doesn’t all happen instantly … but the longer this drags on, the more sticky it becomes, which means you get more of a sustained impact at the grocery store, in the convenience store, at the mall,” Medlock said. “Everything gets more expensive because that’s how we move stuff around.”
Freight rates account for more than 40% of the price of US oil, based on Wednesday’s price around $95 per barrel, compared with 7% on average in 2025, according to LSEG shipping and oil price data.
Countries reliant on imports — including India, the Philippines and Indonesia — bear the brunt of the soaring costs, Medlock said.
Record oil tanker rates are already squeezing Asian refiners’ profits, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday.
Refiners process oil into gasoline for cars, diesel for semi-trucks and farm equipment, and jet fuel for airplanes.
Attacks on ships related to the US-Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war have boosted freight and insurance rates.
Rates to move oil from the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea in the Middle East to Asia surged to a record high around $34 per barrel this week, as shippers price in a risk premium for attacks on vessels. Fearing attack, ships are also sailing longer routes than before, tying up tankers longer.
Shippers moving Saudi oil are using more vessels than before — transferring oil ship to ship — to reduce the risks for individual ships after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s main pipeline increased exports via the Strait of Hormuz. That strategy has reduced ship availability, raising costs and increasing the time cargoes are on the water.
The resulting shortage of very large crude carriers such as the Esteem Explorer has lifted prices for smaller vessels. Freight rates have quadrupled since the Iran war began in February for Suezmax ships, which can carry up to 1 million barrels of oil, for a route between the US Gulf Coast and Asia, and for Aframaxes, which carry up to 750,000 barrels, on the US Gulf Coast to Europe route, according to Signal Ocean.
While some shippers contract vessels for three to five years, many of them charter ships on the spot market about a month prior to loading. The long-term contracts, in which shippers and vessel owners lock in prices, could prove to be bargains for the shippers if prices rise further.
Oil market upheaval has provided a windfall for tanker owners. They have recently earned as much as $1.3 million per ship per day for a round trip from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz to Asia, said Georgios Sakellariou, a Signal Ocean freight analyst. That compared with earnings of $55,000 per ship per day on average in 2025.
“If you’d have told me six weeks ago that we were seeing a million dollars per day, I wouldn’t have believed you,” said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, senior analyst at maritime intelligence firm Windward.
This year may be the most profitable ever, said a person at a company that owns and operates tankers primarily in the Americas.
“Our expectation is that as long as there is more crude oil demand than supply, tanker rates will remain strong. However, as soon as the crude oil market loosens, tanker rates will come off the boil quickly,” said Erik Broekhuizen, head of tanker research and consulting at ship broker Poten & Partners.
(Reporting by Arathy Somasekhar in Houston and Lisa Baertlein in Los Angeles; Editing by Rod Nickel)
