title: Brussels Drops ‘Urgency’ Language on Ukraine’s Next Accession Steps
body:
The EU officials have removed the phrase “as soon as possible” from their draft conclusion for the Oct. 15-16 European Council summit regarding the opening of the remaining accession clusters for Ukraine and Moldova.
The change was reported Thursday by European Pravda , whose correspondent compared versions of the draft dated Oct. 13 and Oct. 14. in Brussels.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Accession negotiations cover 33 chapters grouped into six clusters that organize the legal and institutional reforms Ukraine must adopt and implement in order to formally join the EU.
So far, Ukraine and Moldova opened Cluster 1 – Fundamentals on June 15, and Cluster 6 – External Relations on July 14. Clusters 2 and 3 were opened on Tuesday, Oct. 13. after Hungary lifted its long-standing veto on Ukraine’s accession bid.
The two countries’ paths remain closely linked, and any decision regarding their accession requires unanimous support from all 27 states.
The softer wording comes as Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, said it aims to open Ukraine’s two remaining clusters – Cluster 4, on the green agenda and sustainable connectivity, and Cluster 5, on resources, agriculture and cohesion – before the end of 2026.
In the Oct. 13 version, the section on Ukraine said EU leaders looked forward to opening all other clusters as soon as possible, in line with the bloc’s merit-based approach.
The updated draft keeps the expectation that the clusters will be opened under the merit-based approach but no longer includes any reference to timing.
The same edit was made to a separate paragraph on Moldova, which also previously called for the remaining clusters to be opened as soon as possible.
According to European Pravda, both paragraphs still welcome the intergovernmental conferences held on Tuesday, Oct. 13, at which Clusters 2 and 3 were opened for Ukraine and Moldova , following months of stagnation due to Hungary’s veto.
The breakthrough finally came through after Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, passed amendments expanding education rights for national minorities and introduced a special status for general secondary schools serving national minorities.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar welcomed the move in a statement , saying that the amendments would make it fundamentally easier for Hungarian children in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region to use their native language.
Hours after Ukraine adopted the law, Hungary dropped its long-standing veto and made it possible for the country to continue its path towards the EU.
“I can confirm that all EU member states have agreed to: open clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine and Moldova,” Irish Minister of State for European Affairs and Defence Thomas Byrne said on Monday, Oct. 12, calling Oct. 13 another “Super Tuesday” for the candidate countries.
The European Commission previously proposed limiting Ukraine’s access to EU farm subsidies and markets for sensitive products even after accession , which Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi rejected on Tuesday, Oct. 5. by saying that Kyiv cannot accept permanent restrictions.
Ukraine’s application had been largely stalled for years due to vetoes from Hungary ’s former-leader Viktor Orbán. His defeat by Magyar in April removed the blockage, allowing talks to resume.
However, Magyar’s diplomatic stance on Ukraine continues to repeatedly shift, and Ukrainian authorities have linked it to that of Orbán for several times.
In June, President Volodymyr Zelensky and Magyar sealed what the Hungarian PM described as a “ historic agreement ,” formally securing the political, educational, cultural and linguistic rights of ethnic Hungarian communities in Transcarpathia.
Budapest later tied the opening of further clusters to Ukraine turning those commitments into law.
Around the same time in June, Magyar said he secured the removal of language accelerating Ukraine’s EU accession from the European Council summit declaration after four hours of negotiations.
The conclusion welcomed Ukraine’s accession process but omitted its speeding up.
By blocking the joint letter to the European Council and Commission outlining the EU’s common position on opening five remaining clusters, Hungary became the sole objector among all member states.
During a Council of the EU working group meeting on July 17, Hungary blocked the procedure . Although Budapest agreed to advance Cluster 3 for Moldova, other member states rejected the request decoupling the two candidate countries.
Hungary then blocked Clusters 2 and 3 again on July 22.
“There are six clusters in total, and we don’t think opening them all at once is a good idea – partly because the ink on the first one isn’t even dry yet, and partly because it would send the wrong message to the countries of the Western Balkans,” Magyar told reporters at the Council meeting in Brussels.
On Sept. 8, Ukraine faced its fourth refusal from Hungary , as Kyiv said Budapest had yet to specify its demands in exchange for lifting its objection.
“For 17 months, the government of Viktor Orbán blocked the opening of clusters, although Ukraine has fulfilled all the conditions for this,” Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told European Pravda .
“But even having lost power, Orbán’s team continues to disrupt the normalization of Hungary’s relations with Ukraine,” he continued.
During his tenure, Orbán repeatedly cited concerns over the rights of the Hungarian minority as a reason Hungary had delayed opening the first negotiation cluster.
Hungary previously also blocked technical work on clusters 2 through 6 for Ukraine, later lifting its objection to Cluster 6, covering foreign and security policy, trade policy, and relations with third countries.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: New Tool Recommendation system cuts your firm's input token costs by 37%, according to Arcade.dev
body:
Credit: VentureBeat made with OpenAI ChatGPT-Images-2.5
Arcade.dev , a startup that helps AI agents work inside business software while controlling what they are allowed to do, is introducing Tool Recommendation , a feature that helps agents find the right actions to take without repeatedly loading a lengthy list of software functions into their conversations.
The release targets a practical problem for enterprise AI: Connecting an agent to more business systems also makes its instructions larger and more expensive.
Arcade.dev, also known as "Arcade," says its approach reduces the tokens devoted to tool discovery by as much as 91% , with modeled input-cost savings reaching 37%.
In a separate test of complete workflows, the company reports a smaller but more directly applicable result: a 7.6% reduction in the combined input/output token bill.
The feature becomes available to customers of the firm's Arcade Cloud fully managed software-as-a-service platform on October 15 without a separate feature charge, an Arcade spokesperson told VentureBeat.
The company's normal platform and usage fees still apply to paid plans, while enterprise deployments, including on-premises installations, are priced individually.
Arcade enters a market where Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI already offer ways to discover tools on demand. Its pitch combines that capability with a runtime that checks permissions, applies company policies and records agent activity across different models.
The first thing to understand is that Arcade is not a chatbot or a new large language model.
It supplies the behind-the-scenes software that allows AI agents powered by models such as Claude or ChatGPT to take actions in workplace systems.
For example, when an agent needs to update a Salesforce record or send an email through Gmail, Arcade can connect it to the application, check whether the employee and agent are authorized to take that action, handle the necessary credentials and record what happened.
The company's existing platform brings together three core capabilities:
Security and permission checks for AI agents
A catalog of ready-made software actions and tools for developers to build their own
Central controls for administrators to manage and audit the actions agents take.
Its MCP Gateway can gather tools from Arcade and other providers behind a single connection. MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is an emerging common way of connecting AI assistants with outside applications. Arcade also launched a Private Registry on October 7 , giving employees a place to see which tools their agents can use and request ones that are missing.
Arcade lists LangChain, Relevance AI, Snyk and Sybill among the organizations using its technology and publishes testimonials from representatives of those companies.
Its site also features Duracell and YUR, along with unnamed customers it describes as a Fortune 100 financial institution and a Nasdaq-100 consumer internet company. Those references do not demonstrate that any named customer has achieved the token savings reported for the new feature.
Co-founder and chief technology officer Sam Partee presented Arcade's security and oversight technology at the VentureBeat Transform 2026 Innovation Showcase in July.
At that event, he described how the platform lets agents act with the appropriate user permissions while keeping their activity visible to security teams.
The new Tool Recommendation system builds on that existing infrastructure: beyond determining whether an agent may act, Arcade now wants to make it easier and cheaper for the agent to identify what action to take.
A tool is a callable function: search an inbox, retrieve a customer record, update a ticket or create a document. An agent needs descriptions of those functions and their required inputs before it can choose and use them.
According to Arcade's announcement, its catalog exceeds 8,000 tools. Describing the whole inventory would consume roughly 1.75 million tokens before a user submits a request. Even a much smaller catalog creates recurring overhead as an interaction continues.
Tool Recommendation replaces that inventory with a few entry points for discovering applications, requesting relevant functions and executing a selected action. The agent describes its immediate need; Arcade searches and ranks the catalog, returns a shortlist, and runs the chosen function.
Arcade uses smaller, specialized models to match and rank relevant tools instead of making a larger AI model repeatedly read the entire catalog. It does not replace the agent's underlying intelligence: The agent's own model still decides which suggested action to execute.
Partee told VentureBeat in an exclusive interview that Arcade builds on smaller models from the open-source ecosystem and data about actions taken by agents.
"We are able to take that data and train small language models to predict basically what you're going to want to do," he told VentureBeat in an interview.
Unlike a social media feed tailored to an individual, he said, many agent tasks fall into broader categories, such as sending an email, editing a draft or updating a Salesforce record.
Partee traced the work to an earlier site reliability engineering agent, when language models frequently struggled to select a tool and format its inputs.
"If you gave a model back then five tools, it wouldn't produce the right JSON," he recalled.
As models improved, the same recommendation approach could be applied more broadly to selecting actions and supplying the inputs needed to carry them out.
That could matter for work spanning several systems: A renewal process might require customer data, support history, financial information and a drafted response. Tool discovery allows different functions to enter the interaction when needed. Whether that improves a particular workflow depends on the quality of the shortlist and the cost of the extra searches.
Arcade says Tool Recommendation works through MCP and can be switched on at its gateway, the connection point between an agent and its available tools, without rebuilding existing integrations. The company says it can work across multiple models, agent-building frameworks and applications that support MCP. This matters because customers do not have to replace Claude, ChatGPT or their own agents to use the recommendation system.
Arcade's methodology makes several distinctions that enterprise buyers should preserve.
The maximum 37% reduction comes from modeling input costs against an assistant supplied with 100 fixed tools. For a typical interaction containing three requests and approximately eight tool calls per request, Arcade estimates savings around 20%, depending on the model.
Partee offered a similar estimate in the interview: "You can just be your average user in a 10 turn session and be saving 18 to 20% of your tokens."
That figure describes an expected token reduction for a representative session, not independently verified savings in an enterprise customer's total bill.
The calculation excludes output tokens and assumes the client keeps large tool results outside the conversation. When those results remain in the interaction, the company estimates savings of only 5% to 7%. Short interactions produce the largest modeled percentage improvement.
Its projection of approximately $119,000 saved annually for 1,000 Claude Opus 5 users assumes 20 conversations per person per month. That is a scenario estimate, rather than reported savings from a named customer's deployment.
The 91% claim has a narrower denominator. It concerns input tokens associated with function descriptions and recommendation responses over a modeled 10-turn interaction, excluding the conversation itself and returned business data.
In that calculation, GPT-5.6's count falls from 256,650 to 22,164; Claude Opus 5's falls from 411,729 to 38,170.
"These are definition-token savings, not whole-session savings," Arcade writes in the methodology accompanying its announcement.
The more comprehensive test pairs workflows with and without discovery across 408 sessions covering 64 workflows, using Codex and Claude Code. Arcade reports a 7.6% reduction in total token charges, including input and output, with a 95% interval of 2.5% to 12.6% and unchanged task completion.
The reported reduction is 9.7% for Claude Code and 5.5% for Codex; the Codex interval includes zero. VentureBeat has not independently reproduced these tests.
Partee acknowledged that repeatedly calling the recommendation system could consume enough resources to erase the savings or even make an interaction more expensive. He maintained that this would be unusual but did not provide independently verifiable figures for how often it happens.
Arcade also evaluates tool retrieval using ToolRet , a public benchmark. Recall@10 measures how many of the required tools appear among the first ten returned results. It does not measure completion of an entire business task.
Arcade supplied the following data to show how its Tool Recommendation system compares to an existing rival, Microsoft Foundry:
Sources: Arcade's announcement graphic and Microsoft's published evaluation . The runs use different settings.
Arcade's production setup includes an additional ranking stage and benchmark instructions. Microsoft's test omits the instruction string to avoid the expense and delay of generating it with another model call. Microsoft also describes a retrieval approach that avoids a resource-intensive ranking model during serving.
Arcade acknowledges that the comparison indicates a potential advantage rather than establishing a controlled head-to-head result. The scores warrant testing, but do not establish that Arcade delivers better task completion or lower total costs than Foundry.
Microsoft's Foundry Toolboxes approach exposes search and execution entry points, then supplies the matching definitions. Microsoft describes it as independent of a particular model family and able to span different tool sources. Model flexibility therefore is not unique to Arcade.
Anthropic's Tool Search Tool similarly postpones loading definitions until Claude needs them. Its implementation supports built-in text-search methods as well as custom retrieval. Anthropic reports an 85% token reduction in its own example, but that uses a different baseline from Arcade's measurements.
OpenAI's Responses API supports deferred functions and MCP tools, with hosted or application-executed search. Its documentation says newly discovered definitions enter at the end of the context to preserve caching; support begins with GPT-5.4.
The distinction Arcade emphasizes is packaging discovery with execution controls in a layer customers can use across their chosen AI systems.
According to the company, that layer checks both a user's rights and the agent's permitted actions, keeps credentials outside the model's context, applies policy hooks before and after calls, and supplies audit records through OpenTelemetry. Those hooks can also support checks for sensitive data.
Partee said this approach also lets Arcade accommodate newer frontier models without rebuilding its recommendation system for each vendor.
After roughly three or four major model releases, he said, the technology's behavior had remained substantially consistent. "We should be able every time a new model is released to be able to guarantee something of the same level within a week," he said.
That is a forward-looking expectation, not an independently tested service guarantee; he also cautioned that the technology is changing quickly. He said the feature can work in Claude, ChatGPT and other agent environments.
Arcade already charges for its underlying platform, with public prices based on usage rather than the number of employees. Its advertised options are:
2,000 authorization events and 2,000 tool calls per month on Arcade Cloud, with community support.
$0.10 per authorization event and $0.01 per tool call; hosted on Arcade Cloud, with next-business-day email support.
Annual bundles of authorization events and tool calls, volume discounts, cloud/private-cloud/isolated deployment options, 24/7 support and additional governance controls.
Authorization events relate to connecting agents to user accounts; tool calls are the requests agents make to carry out specific actions. These published fees cover Arcade's platform, not the separate charges customers may incur for the large language models powering their agents.
Arcade says Tool Recommendation itself adds no separate feature charge for Arcade Cloud users. That should not be confused with unlimited free usage: Customers on the Team plan still face normal charges for authorization events and tool calls. Arcade also offers its underlying platform in customer-controlled clouds, on premises and in isolated environments. A separate enterprise rollout of the new recommendation feature is planned, but the company has not published a price or specific rollout schedule for those deployments.
Partee described larger organizations as the commercial focus, particularly those paying Arcade for security and management of agents across their workforces. For those customers, he said, "yes, I'm going to ask people to pay for that." His remarks concerned enterprise deployments, rather than the standard Arcade Cloud feature included at no extra charge.
That means a reduction in AI-model tokens does not automatically translate into the same percentage reduction in an enterprise's total AI spending. Buyers also have to account for Arcade's platform and per-action fees, any enterprise licensing costs and the cost of operating their own infrastructure. Arcade has not supplied a named customer's all-in cost comparison for the new feature.
The feature also is not automatically economical for every agent. Arcade's own modeling favors a fixed tool list below roughly 25 to 28 tools. For larger inventories, buyers need to measure search overhead, completion rates and the final bill on their own workloads.
For companies using several business applications and AI models, the practical proposition is broader than token savings: Arcade aims to provide one place to decide what an agent can do, connect it to the systems where work happens, record its actions and now suggest the relevant tool without cluttering the AI's conversation. The strongest evidence in its materials is the measured reduction in complete-workflow costs; the larger percentages explain where additional savings might arise under specific assumptions.

title: Nvidia squeezed a 74B agent model into 24GB so it can run on your laptop
body: Nvidia on Thursday announced a few new additions to its Nemotron family : Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B vision-language model for enterprise agents and two small Bolt models ( Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB) for running coding, research, and conversational workloads locally. The Bolt models, Nvidia says , are meant to run “everyday agentic tasks on laptops, balancing speed and intelligence needed to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing.” And while they come in very different sizes and are meant for different use cases, the focus for all three is on speed and efficiency. The two larger models are available today, while the smaller Bolt E4B 4G model will launch in the near future. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL The marquee release here is Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120-billion-parameter model that combines reasoning and tool use with image and document understanding. In the announcement, Kari Briski, Nvidia’s VP for open models and software, notes that the large model is meant to deliver “leading accuracy on multimodal agentic tasks — instruction following, tool use, multistep business workflows, and visual understanding — comparable with NVIDIA’s largest reasoning model at roughly one-fifth the parameter count.” Super VL builds on Nemotron 3 Super , which launched in March. Both have 120 billion total parameters, with 12 billion active during inference, and context windows of up to 1 million tokens. But while the earlier model only accepted text, Super VL now adds support for image and video input (though not output). Mixed results against Qwen But when it comes to the benchmarks , though, especially when compared to other open models of comparable size, the results are mixed. In Nvidia’s own evaluations, Super VL outperforms Alibaba’s Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on scientific reasoning and terminal tasks, while scoring slightly lower on SWE-bench Verified and document understanding. The five tests are GPQA-Diamond, Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Verified, IFBench, and MMLongBench-Doc. Super VL scores 66.7 on Terminal-Bench, compared with Qwen3.5’s 48.7, but trails it on SWE-bench Verified, 71.1 to 71.9. Qwen has 122 billion total parameters and 10 billion active, compared with Super VL’s 120 billion and 12 billion. The newer Qwen3.8-Flash-Next scores higher on all five tests, though its additional embedding and prediction components bring its total parameter count to about 180 billion. Thinking Machines’ Inkling-Small has 276 billion total parameters and 12 billion active. It also trails Super VL on terminal tasks but scores higher on instruction following. Nvidia also reports Super VL ahead of Ultra on Hermes Bench and LangChain behavioral evaluations , scoring 63.44% versus 56.33% and 87.05% versus 84.3%, respectively. Overall, though, the focus here was clearly on speed. Nvidia reports fourfold faster completion of 10,000 SWE-bench Pro tasks on four B200 GPUs, though its chart shows lower accuracy than Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DeepSeek V4 Flash. Hybrid Mamba architecture, faster decoding As for how Nvidia built the model, it’s worth noting that the Nemotron coalition is sticking to the 3.5 family’s hybrid architecture, which combines Mamba-2, attention, and mixture-of-experts layers — but with the addition of a vision encoder. Nvidia also continued training the language model using distillation from Nemotron 3 Ultra before further training for software engineering, vision, and agent tasks, according to its model card . To speed up text generation, Nvidia also uses LiLiCorr , a technique for speculative decoding. With this, a smaller helper model drafts several tokens ahead, which Super VL checks together instead of generating each token individually. Nvidia says this speeds up token generation on DGX Spark by up to 2.3 times compared with decoding without speculation. For document workflows, Nvidia says Super VL focuses on optical character recognition, tables, charts, and structured information. On CharXiv , a chart-reasoning benchmark, Nvidia reports 80.8% accuracy, compared with Nano Omni’s 63%. Python code interpretation raises Super VL’s result to 84%. Bolt runs 74B in 24GB If you’re interested in running local models, the new Bolt models may be the most interesting release here — and their benchmarks tend to outperform most comparable models. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is derived from Super VL. Its hybrid mixture-of-experts architecture activates 9 billion of its 74 billion parameters at a time. In Nvidia’s tests , Bolt scores 51.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, versus 44.4 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 37.2 for Gemma4 26B-A4B, both tested in BF16. Bolt uses mixed precision, including two-bit experts. To get to this size, Nvidia used two-bit quantization to reduce the 74B model’s memory footprint to 24GB. The company says it is optimizing the model for RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, with support for llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, and vLLM. Nemotron Bolt 3.5 24GB benchmarks. Credit: Nvidia. A second, even smaller version of this model, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, is scheduled for later this month. With this one, Nvidia is targeting conversational and physical agents on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and Spark hardware, including device assistants and interactive characters that need multiturn tool use and awareness of application state. Availability The new models are now available for download on Hugging Face under the OpenMDW 1.1 license , which permits commercial use and modification. The post Nvidia squeezed a 74B agent model into 24GB so it can run on your laptop appeared first on The New Stack .

E Ink announced the next generation of its Kaleido color e-paper screen technology today, delivering several welcome improvements. The company’s existing Kaleido 3 displays can be found in e-readers and tablets from companies like Kobo , PocketBook , and Boox , while Amazon’s Kindle Colorsoft uses a customized version to improve performance. The new Kaleido 4 technology addresses some of Kaleido 3’s shortcomings with improved color reproduction, better contrast, and faster screen refreshes.
Other E Ink technologies, like its Gallery 3 display found in the Remarkable Paper Pro , use colored pigments that move around to form full-color images, but Kaleido 3 employs a color filter over an e-paper panel with just black and white pigments. That approach results in color e-paper screens with fast refresh rates, but it generates color images at a lower resolution with a limited palette that tends to make them look desaturated. The extra color filter also leaves plain text looking darker than it does on e-readers with only a black-and-white E Ink screen.
E Ink claims its new Kaleido 4 display tech doubles the “color gamut volume” of its predecessor, which should improve how color images look. However, the technology is still limited to producing just 4,096 colors (modern LCD and OLED displays can produce millions) and, as with Kaleido 3, at a lower resolution than black-and-white text is displayed. But Kaleido 4 does increase white reflectance by 15 percent and boosts contrast by 50 percent, so plain text will potentially look less muddy than it often does with Kaleido 3.
The reason that E Ink’s seemingly superior Gallery 3 technology hasn’t been used in more devices is because those displays have a slow refresh rate that can often feel frustrating to use. Kaleido 3 refreshes much faster, and thanks to a new oxide TFT backplane (that sounds similar to what the Kindle Colorsoft uses), Kaleido 4’s performance is even faster with refresh rates up to 18fps, making the screens capable of playing back video.
Companies like Amazon and Kobo haven’t yet announced any new devices that will feature Kaleido 4 screens, but Hanvon Technology will be the first to adopt the new technology in its upcoming M10C II tablet. It will only be available in China, but the M10C II will feature a Kaleido 4 display with a micro-etched tempered-glass surface designed to reduce glare while providing a more authentic paper-like feel when taking notes using its battery-free pen.

title: Routine testosterone screening of US troops may require extensive follow-on care, study finds
body: A quarter of troops measured below testosterone thresholds, a study of Army personnel found, with similar results compared to the general U.S. population. According to the research, published Thursday in JAMA , 20% of male soldiers younger than 30 years had testosterone levels less than the threshold established by the American Urological Association of 300 nanograms per deciliter, or ng/dL. Roughly a third of service members — 32.8% — aged 30 and older fell below the threshold. According to the analysis, one-time testosterone testing of troops determined that 100,691 active-duty soldiers had morning testosterone levels of less than 300 ng/dL. The results are an example of what the Department of Defense may encounter under a new program that requires all male service members 30 years and older to be screened for low testosterone, said the researchers from the Pennington Biomedical Research Center in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine in Natick, Massachusetts. The results, the researchers said, “suggest that routine testosterone screening will result in confirmatory testing and clinical evaluation for many male service members. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced in July that the Pentagon would begin screening testosterone levels of all service members over age 30 and would be voluntary for those below 30 request it and are experiencing symptoms such as fatigue, low libido, depressed mood, impaired concentration or diminished physical performance. In a video posted to social media, Hegseth said maintaining proper testosterone levels was a way to ensure that troops stay on the “leading edge of lethality.” “This initiative is not about artificial enhancement. It’s about restoring and optimizing your natural capabilities, protecting your longevity and ensuring you have the biological foundation required to sustain and fight,” Hegseth said. Environmental exposures, including lead exposure, combat, physical injuries, sleep deprivation and mental health conditions can contribute to low testosterone in service members. Treatment for severe cases — medically known as hypogonadism — can have serious side effects, such as mood swings, irritability and aggression, blood clots and low sperm count that can cause infertility. Under the new Defense Health Agency clinical practice guidelines , service members will be screened in the morning on two separate days and assessed for further evaluation if they fall below the 300 ng/dL standard. They may choose to undergo treatment, which involves once- or twice-weekly injections depending on the medication, or a daily oral medication or gel. Treatment will not be mandatory. The interest in testosterone replacement therapy in the DoD follows a growing $4.5 billion industry centered around testosterone, with the hormone touted as a supplement that contributes to increased physical performance, sex drive, concentration and youthful energy. Studies in 2018 by the NIH on 800 older men demonstrated that testosterone therapy improved erectile dysfunction, libido and mood, but had little or no improvement on measures such as fatigue, memory or overall well-being. The research, published Thursday, was based on an analysis of data from the Military Health and Nutrition Examination study, a survey conducted at five Army bases from August 2024 through January 2026. The authors noted that the low testosterone levels in service members do not indicate that they all had hypogonadism. A study conducted last year of active-duty men found that .43%, or 12,112 of more than 2.8 million service members, were diagnosed with hypogonadism, and those with the highest rates were the most senior, largely general officers and warrant officers. The authors of the JAMA research letter cautioned that testing could result in excess medical visits, costs and treatment. “Positive screening result requires clinical interpretation and typically prompts repeat testing, further evaluation, counseling regarding modifiable factors, and consideration of treatment if indicated. Because testosterone replacement therapy is long term and has potential adverse effects, distinguishing an isolated low screening value from clinically significant hypogonadism is essential,” the researchers wrote.

title: Trump Denies Cutting Ukraine Intelligence Amid Satellite Restrictions
body: US President Donald Trump said Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had received no advance warning from its international partners before a new wave of Russian attacks on the capital and battlefield reports of a throttling of Starlink satellite access.  Trump told reporters on October 14, "No, we haven't," when asked whether the United States had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.  "We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end," he said, adding Washington was working with both Kyiv and Moscow to end the war, now in its fifth year.  Zelenskyy said Russian forces launched 39 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Kharkiv on October 13, including targeting a thermal power plant. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike that impacted a high-rise apartment building killed at least three people.  "Once again, no advance warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on social media, adding Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing further ballistic missile launches.  The absence of an early warning does not establish that Washington withheld intelligence. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Ukraine was still receiving US military intelligence and suggested the delay may have been related to the type of Russian weapon used.  Some analysts noted Zelenskyy's claims came after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to lift bans on the export of Russian diesel fuel. The timing of the reported intelligence lapse, they said, could indicate Trump is trying to ratchet up pressure on Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries.  Kurt Volker, a former US ambassador to NATO and special representative for Ukraine during Trump's first administration, however, told RFE/RL he had been informed that cloud cover had prevented American satellites from detecting the missile launch. He cautioned that he could not independently verify the explanation.  Such an explanation, experts said, would point to a limitation in intelligence collection rather than a deliberate suspension of intelligence sharing.  Ukraine relies heavily on American intelligence to defend against incoming missiles, drones and aircraft, and early warnings can help save civilian lives and protect critical infrastructure.  Although the exact number is not known, several analysts said the United States likely operates somewhere between 300 to 500 military intelligence satellites that orbit the Earth, providing multiple passes over any given location every hour. That compares with an estimated 15 to 20 military reconnaissance satellites operated by European countries.  Ukraine has developed independent intelligence capabilities and can identify many Russian military sites it wants to strike, but detecting incoming attacks is a different challenge, one for which Kyiv remains heavily reliant on American capabilities.  "For defense, I think it's very important," Volker said, describing US satellite-based intelligence as the best available source of early warning.  New AI Tool, Starlink Uncertainty  NATO also provides intelligence support to Ukraine through a combination of institutional alliance programs, artificial intelligence systems, and bilateral intelligence sharing from individual member states.  While the military alliance as an official body restricts its institutional role to nonlethal assistance to prevent direct conflict with Russia, individual allies, mainly the United States, provide highly granular, real-time tactical intelligence.  As part of its drive to boost its own defense, Ukraine said on October 13 that its forces will soon start using an artificial intelligence model -- jointly developed with NATO -- to predict where and when Russia's drone strikes will land.  Dubbed "Model No. 13," the tool analyzes past combat data, weather conditions, and battlefield conditions to determine with "high probability" how Russian troops will use drones on the front lines, the ministry said in a statement.  The model can forecast the strike's time, location, intensity, and type of drone used, it said.  "The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems," the ministry's statement read.  Ukraine also relies heavily on SpaceX's Starlink satellite service to guide longer-range drone strikes in occupied southern and eastern Ukraine on Russian logistics and refineries inside Russia proper.  Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said on Telegram on October 14 that some Starlink services appear to have been limited, namely a halting in the operation of its military-grade version, Starshield, above 100 miles per hour 160 km/h.  Starshield terminals are provided to Ukraine under a contract from the US Defense Department, which did not respond to queries seeking comment about the reports of the limited service.  Denys Sienik, Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the United States, confirmed to RFE/RL on October 14 that armed forces are experiencing "speed restrictions" for Starlink terminals "operating while in motion."  "Starshield is a life-saving technology that helps us save civilian lives and prevent further destruction in Ukraine caused by Russia," he said.  Zelenskyy said it was a pity that his country had experienced difficulties with Starlink services and intelligence-sharing, adding there had been "a lot of different surprises" from the United States in its bilateral relations with Kyiv.  "We just want to be very honest, very clear, and be strong partners," he said in London on October 14 alongside British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.  While two Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, who later spoke with RFE/RL on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the subject, said that Kyiv was currently seeing improved connection quality at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour, the limit appears to remain in place for now.  They said this complicates the interception of Russia's jet-powered drones, which have been launched at Ukraine with increasing frequency in recent months.  Ukraine would need the speed to be restored to at least 280 miles per hour, another source who also spoke with RFE/RL said.  "Nothing is more important in war than critical battlefield intelligence," Sean Wiswesser, a former senior CIA operations officer, told RFE/RL.  "We should not underestimate the critical role US intelligence sharing has played for Ukraine in this war," Wiswesser added, noting Washington had continued providing intelligence despite political disagreements and difficulties in the past.  Following the latest incidents, the bipartisan US Congressional Ukraine Caucus said it was alarmed by the developments, adding that "restrictions that put civilians in harm's way are unconscionable and will not be accepted by Congress."  The throttling of service has not been independently verified. SpaceX is controlled by Elon Musk, an ally of Trump. The slowdown does not appear to affect commercial users of Starlink but rather mainly military operators of the specialized Starshield terminals.  "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote of Starshield provision to Ukraine on X on October 14, whereas "usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities."  He added that Starlink "cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."  The company had already once refused a request from Kyiv for access to the system for operations in the Black Sea near Russian-occupied Crimea, as well as other parts of the front line including Kherson and Donetsk.  Musk said at the time the request was refused because "SpaceX would be explicitly complicit in a major act of war and conflict escalation."  Energy Cease-Fire  The intelligence concerns also come amid a dispute over Trump's announcement of an energy cease-fire between Russia and Ukraine and his decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.  Trump announced the proposed truce on October 11, but neither side has clearly confirmed such an agreement, while Trump said on October 12 that "they agreed [to the cease-fire]. You know why Because I said, 'You agree' -- that's why. They agreed because I said they agreed, and that thing has to get settled."  Volker said he had no reason to believe an energy cease-fire was in effect because neither government had formally agreed to one.  "What would convince me is if I heard from the Russians that they would agree to an energy cease-fire if Ukraine reciprocated," he said, noting Kyiv had already indicated its willingness to accept such an arrangement if Moscow did the same.  "We've not heard that, and Russia's actions demonstrate that they do not agree with that," Volker said.  Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure for contributing to higher US fuel prices, a political concern for Republicans ahead of congressional midterm elections.  Many analysts have pointed instead to the US war in Iran as a much larger factor in the price increases, a view Zelenskyy has also expressed.  By RFE/RL
